Exp 16 2 Abstract The present study compared usability among three date entry designs: Picklist, keyed-entry, and hybrid. The findings show that the hybrid design has the lowest date entry accuracy rate, though accuracy is generally high across all three designs. Date entry completion time is longer for the picklist design compared to both keyed entry and hybrid. Date entry is generally easy with any of the three designs though the keyed-entry design appears least easy; and the picklist and keyed- entry designs are almost equally preferred by most participants, with very few preferring the hybrid design. Keywords: Mobile Survey, Date entry, Picklist, Keyed-entry, Hybrid Suggested Citation: Brian Falcone, Shelley Feuer, Lin Wang (2023). Mobile Survey Design Research - Experiment 16: Date Entry Method. Exp 16 3 Introduction 1. Purpose To investigate the optimal date entry method among those commonly used in mobile Web surveys. Specifically, three designs of date entry were compared: picklist, keyed-entry, or hybrid of picklist and keyed-entry. The picklist design refers to a design in which a date component is “picked” from a list of options, for example, a month entry was picked from a list of 12 months. The keyed-entry design refers to a design in which a date component is typed into a text field as usual text typing. The hybrid design refers to a combination of picklist and keyed-entry in which a date component is “picked” from a list of options while another date component was typed in a text field, for example, a month entry was picked from a list of 12 months while a year entry was typed in. 2. Specific Research Question Do respondents enter dates more accurately, faster, and with better satisfaction, using a picklist, a keyed-entry, or a hybrid format? Methods 1. Participants Thirty participants participated in the study and their demographics are summarized in Table 1. Seventy-three percent of participants reported using a smartphone for more than two years, 10% between one and two years, 17% between 6 months and one year. Seventy percent of participants reported using a smartphone every day, while the other 30% used their smartphone less than daily. The participants reported their familiarity with smartphone being an average of 3.6 (SD = 0.8) on a scale of 1 to 5, where higher scores represented more familiarity. The participants had habitual near vision of 20/50 or better (sufficient for reading newspaper) and had no color vision impairment. All participants received a Privacy Act Statement that states the purpose of the study, information to be collected, and the authority under which the information is collected. A written consent to data collection was obtained from all participants. The data collection was approved by the U.S. Office of Management and Budget. Each participant received a monetary incentive for participating in the study. All participants were from the metropolitan area of Washington DC and were recruited at community centers. Table 1. Screen Design Three versions of the mobile survey were designed using different date-entry formats: (1) picklist only (Figure 1, A), (2) keyed-entry only (Figure 1, B), and (3) a hybrid of picklist and keyed-entry (Figure 1, C). Figure 1. Panel A: an example of picklist design. The month entry is to be entered by picking a month from the picklist. Panel B: an example of keyed-entry design. The month entry is to be entered by typing text in the text fields. Panel C: an example of hybrid design. The month entry is to be entered by picking a month from the picklist, while the day and year entry is typed in the text field. 3. Performance Measures a. Completion Time: Length of time it takes the participant to enter data, from the time any text field or picklist is activated until the time the “next” button is selected. b. Accuracy: A binary variable indicating whether final date entered was correct or not. (A) (B) (C)

Exp 16 5 c. Difficulty rating: Self-report of task difficulty on a 5-point scale with 1 being very easy and 5 being very difficult. d. Preference: Preferred date entry format among the six designs. 4. Experimental Factors a. Date-Entry Type Level 1: Picklist Level 2: Keyed-entry Level 3: Hybrid – The combination of Picklist and Keyed-entry (month: picklist, day: keyed entry, year: keyed-entry). 5. Experimental Design This was a within-subjects design with one experimental factor, Date-Entry Type (Picklist, Keyed-entry, Hybrid). Under each design, the participant was given dates in a congruent format (Figure 2, A) with date entry design in half of trials and incongruent in the other half of trials (Figure 2, B). The order of presentation of the 3 designs and congruency was counterbalanced across participants. (A) (B) Figure 2. A: an example of congruent design for hybrid condition. The month is presented as a word and is to be entered by picking a month from the picklist. B: an example of incongruent design for hybrid condition. The month is presented numerically and is to be entered by picking a month from the picklist. 6. Experimental Procedure a. The participant was presented with a date on the screen and read it aloud to ensure accurate perception. b. The participant entered the date directly beneath the one presented on the screen using picklist, keyed-entry, or hybrid. c. The participant tapped the ‘next’ button which brought up a new screen with another date. d. After the survey was complete, the participant rated the ease of completing the task on a 5-point Likert scale where ‘1’ was very easy and ‘5’ was very difficult. e. The participants were shown all six date-entry designs and asked to select a preferred design.

Exp 16 6 7. Data Analysis Completion Time: We conducted a repeated measures ANOVA with Date-Entry Type (Picklist, Keyed-entry, Hybrid) as the within-subjects factor and Completion Time as the outcome. Accuracy: We used generalized estimating equations (GEE) to fit a repeated measures logistic regression, predicting accuracy from date-entry type. Difficulty rating: We used generalized estimating equations (GEE) to fit a repeated measures logistic regression, predicting difficulty from date-entry type. Preference: We analyzed the frequencies of participants’ choice to determine which design was most preferred. Results Completion time: The results of the repeated measures ANOVA showed an effect of Date-Entry Type on completion time (F(2, 27) = 8.24, p < .002).The results indicated longer time on task in the picklist format (M = 28.25 sec, SD = 13.97) compared to both the keyed- entry format (M = 22.82 sec, SD = 10.97, p = .024) and hybrid format (M = 20.55 sec, SD = 7.63, p = .0004). The difference in time on task between the keyed entry and hybrid conditions was not statistically significant (p = .15). Accuracy: Date entry correct rate by condition is shown in Table 2. While there was a high rate of correct date entry across conditions (> 92%), we used generalized estimating equations (GEE) to fit a repeated measures logistic regression, predicting accuracy from date-entry type. Compared to the hybrid design, the odds ratio of an accurate response was significantly higher when the date entry format was picklist or keyed-entry, b = 1.00 (.39), 95% CI [.23, 1.77], p = .01 and b = 1.57 (.46), 95% CI [.67, 2.47], p = .0007, respectively. Summary of the outcomes Picklist Keyed-entry Hybrid Date entry accuracy (%) 97.1 98.3 92.5 Date entry time (sec) 28.25 22.82 20.55 Easiness (% saying 1 or 2) 70 63.4 76.6 Preference 43 40 7 Recommendation The present study compared usability among three date entry designs: Picklist, keyed- entry, and hybrid. The findings show that the hybrid design has the lowest date entry accuracy rate, though accuracy is generally high across all three designs. Date entry completion time is longer for the picklist design compared to both keyed entry and hybrid. Date entry is generally easy with any of the three designs though the keyed-entry design appears least easy; and the picklist and keyed-entry designs are almost equally preferred by most participants, with a few preferring the hybrid design. We recommend keyed-entry format as the first choice for date entry given its effectiveness and general efficiency over picklist. Hybrid is still a viable option especially when efficiency is of import.

Abstract RTI International staff conducted cognitive testing with 40 participants to further assess a draft survey instrument intended to measure public opinion about the use of administrative records by the Census Bureau and about the creation of a demographic frame. Census Bureau staff provided the instrument for testing. The cognitive testing evaluated the survey questions for possible issues that may hinder a respondent’s answering process. Findings from the research resulted in revisions to the question prior to fielding the web survey. This report explains the cognitive testing methods, including the description of the target population and participant eligibility criteria, the strategies of participant recruitment and screening, and the survey questions tested during cognitive interviewing. Additionally, this report includes the qualitative analysis of the cognitive interviews, the recommendations for question revisions and the feedback and the revision decisions for the final questionnaire provided by the Census Bureau. 1-1 1. Overview RTI International staff conducted cognitive testing with 40 participants to further assess a draft survey instrument intended to measure public opinion about the use of administrative records by the Census Bureau and about the creation of a demographic frame. Census Bureau staff provided the instrument for testing. The cognitive testing evaluated the survey questions for possible issues that may hinder a respondent’s answering process. Findings from the research resulted in revisions to the question prior to fielding the web survey. This report explains the cognitive testing methods, including the description of the target population and participant eligibility criteria, the strategies of participant recruitment and screening, and the survey questions tested during cognitive interviewing. Additionally, this report includes the qualitative analysis of the cognitive interviews, the recommendations for question revisions and the feedback and the revision decisions for the final questionnaire provided by the Census Bureau.

2-1 2. Research Methods 2.1 Cognitive Testing Overview Cognitive testing consists of one-on-one in-person interviews (via either face-to-face or virtual communication mode) to assess a questionnaire in terms of general comprehension, clarity of question and response wording, effectiveness of skip logic, and visual aids. The goal is to gain an understanding of how well the questions work when administered to a sample of the survey’s target population. The interviews follow a protocol with pre-scripted probes. Cognitive interviewers also use spontaneous probes to gain a better understanding of questions. Cognitive interviewing works best for the following: • Learning about the respondents’ thought processes while answering the questions; • Measuring the response process, including comprehension, retrieval, judgement, and response; • Observing non-verbal, human reactions; • Testing navigation in self-administered modes, particularly mail surveys; • Assessing the potential for measurement error in survey items; • Examining potentially big or complex issues; and • Gauging opinions on the survey as a whole. The cognitive interviews for the Research on Public Opinion on Administrative Records (RoPOAR) were conducted virtually using Microsoft Teams, providing the flexibility to achieve geographic diversity with the participant recruitment. 2.2 Target Population and Participation Eligibility Criteria The cognitive testing target population for the Research on Public Opinion on Administrative Records project was non-institutionalized English-speaking adults and monolingual Spanish- speaking adults (18+) who live in the United States. RTI assessed prospective recruits’ characteristics through a project screener and invited those with desired traits to participate in cognitive interviews. RTI worked with the Census Bureau to operationalize these desired traits and set quotas or minimums for recruitment. Table 2.1 lists the characteristics used to recruit participants for the cognitive interviews. Table 2-1. Desired Participant Characteristics Age Gender Number of children in a household Race Urban/rural living Education attainment Language spoken at home

RoPOAR: Cognitive Testing Report 2-2 2.3 Methods of Participant Recruitment and Screening To ensure efficient and successful recruitment of the target populations, the RTI team used a combination of online recruitment strategies and community-based methods. Specifically, we used online advertising and targeted community-based advertising to solicit participation based on the desired participant characteristics. Online Advertisements. RTI placed advertisements on Craigslist in a variety of markets. The advertisements described the research and included a link to the web-based screener. Potential participants navigated to the online screener and answered questions to determine eligibility for the study. We conducted interviews remotely, through Microsoft Teams, and were thus able to recruit nationally. Online advertising was primarily used for recruiting English-speaking interview participants. Community-Based Strategies. Recruitment also took place using community-based strategies. RTI’s partner, Research Support Services, reached out to community-based organizations that work with monolingual Spanish speakers for assistance getting the word out about the study to their clients to recruit Spanish speakers. Screening for these individuals often took place in person or over the phone. 2.3.1 Web Screening RTI and the Census Bureau collaborated to develop the eligibility screener. The screener included questions to ascertain eligibility and to measure variables of interest that allow us to recruit a diverse sample of cognitive interview participants. The screener was hosted on Qualtrics, a survey data collection platform hosted within Census Bureau’s virtual desktop interface (VDI) under the Census Bureau’s institutional license. The web link of the screening instrument was included in online advertisements and physical flyers for recruitment. Participants clicked on the link in the advertisements and answered the questions in the screening survey. The data from the web screener was downloaded to a recruitment tracking sheet (also located within the Census Bureau’s VDI) to aid in scheduling and interviewing. For the recruitment of English participants, 140 individuals were screened via the web screener, and 42 were recruited for interviews. We completed 25 interviews from these recruits. At the same time, 10 of the recruits did not respond to our outreach effort (i.e., two email attempts). Three did not attend their scheduled interview, two withdrew their participation during the interview, and two participants were excluded from the study because of technological challengers or language barriers that resulted in termination of the interview. For the recruitment of Spanish participants, 22 individuals were screened and recruited to participate in the interviews. We completed 15 interviews with these recruits. Similarly, four recruits were considered ineligible for participation, one recruit declined to be screened further, and two did not attend their scheduled interviews.

Section 2 — Research Methods 2-3 2.3.2 Phone Screening and In-Person Screening For certain characteristics where eligible individuals are less likely to complete an online screener (e.g., monolingual Spanish speakers), advertisements included a phone number instead of a web link. Calls were received by Spanish-speaking recruiters who administered the screener over the phone and entered respondents’ answers into the web screener. Recruiters were able to determine eligibility based on responses and assigned cases to interviewers. English advertisements did not include a phone number, and interested parties were routed to the online screener. 2.4 Instrumentation and Data Collection The cognitive interviews were conducted via Microsoft Teams using section-by-section probing; the protocol featured concurrent probes administered throughout the interview. Audio and Video Recording. Cognitive interviewers audio recorded all interviews where participants consented to such recording. If the participant did not agree, the interviewer took detailed notes during the cognitive interview. All participants consented to either audio or video recording for their interviews. Interview recordings were delivered to the Census Bureau after each round of interviews. Informed Consent. Cognitive interviewers obtained informed consent from English participants using the electronic consent forms provided by the Census Bureau and programmed in Qualtrics. Participants’ data from the consent form were submitted to the Census Bureau at the end of data collection. For Spanish participants, cognitive interviewers obtained verbal consent before proceeding with the interview. Payment. Participants received a $40 incentive for the virtual interviews. The incentives were furnished via Amazon gift card. The project team obtained a payment voucher or payment record at the time of payment to participants. All incentive vouchers were submitted to the Census Bureau. Case Summaries. RTI prepared case summaries for each completed interview. The summaries captured the interview narrative, including highlights of reactions to the probes and notable observations from interviewers. For Spanish interviews, summaries were written in English, but key concepts or thoughts were provided in Spanish with back- translations in English to aid understanding and maintain context. Interviewer Training. A project-specific training prepared interviewers to conduct interviews. All cognitive interviewers attended a 4-hour virtual training that (1) discussed study background and research objectives; (2) reviewed the testing questions and what they are intended to measure; (3) reviewed the scripted probes and research questions they are intended to address; (4) discussed informed consent, confidentiality, and Title 13 requirements; (5) discussed logistics; and (6) reviewed writing effective case summaries.

RoPOAR: Cognitive Testing Report 2-4 Project staff provided copies of interviewer training materials to the Census Bureau. Bilingual interviewers received an additional training that focused on unique issues related to conducting interviews in Spanish. Development of Interview Protocols. The Census Bureau and RTI reviewed and discussed the testing goals as part of project start-up activities. These discussions established the necessary context to develop the interview protocols and item-level probes. RTI developed the interview protocol with the Census Bureau’s input and review. The interview protocols were developed in English and then translated into Spanish. The protocols documented the administration details, consent forms, and materials required for cognitive interviewing, including a list of scripted cognitive interview probes to focus on how respondents settled on a response and on their understanding of specific terms and phrases. The first protocols developed included 45 questions, with probes on nearly all questions. However, it was clear once interviewing began that all 45 questions could not be reviewed with respondents without increasing the length of the interviews. To keep the estimated burden at 1 hour, 14 questions were removed. The decision to remove these questions was based on successful implementation on previous Census Bureau surveys and little feedback from the interviews conducted so far. This decision also allowed for more in-depth questioning about the remaining 31 questions. Ten interviews were completed with the original 45-question protocol. Based on the feedback from the first 18 interviews (10 with the original protocol and 8 with the reduced protocol), several adjustments were made to the questions to test proposed revisions. Three questions (Q4, Q8, and Q11) were moved to directly after Q22 to attempt to provide participants with further context. We hypothesized that this move may give participants additional context by answering Q17–Q22 first, before answering more general questions. We believed this could help increase confidence in participants’ responses. We also made several adjustments to the wording of items in Q44 to improve clarity. Because a second round of interviewing was not feasible, implementing these changes during data collection allowed us to gather some limited feedback to inform final question wording and order. Seven participants completed this final version of the protocol. 2.5 Qualitative Data Analysis Strategy The RTI and RSS team used a systematic process to analyze the cognitive interview data and address the research questions. The process began with the analysts reading all case summaries to familiarize themselves with the data. The case summaries were imported into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet allowing the analysts to easily sort and filter the data to compare responses with questions and probes across all participants. Next, analysts

Section 2 — Research Methods 2-5 synthesized and reduced the data to meaningful categories and themes (e.g., misinterpreted term X or concept Y was not understood consistently). Some of these themes were identified in advance based on the testing goals. Other themes emerged during analysis. Overall conclusions were drawn based on individual findings. For questions that performed poorly, analysts provided recommendations for improving the questions. Those revised questions were adapted for use in the Ipsos panel survey. In Chapter 3, we present the overarching and common themes observed from the cognitive interview findings. Chapter 4 describes detailed findings, revision recommendations and feedback from the Census Bureau (if applicable) for each cognitive testing instrument question.

3-1 3. Overall Themes This chapter explores common question issues in further detail. Most of the cognitive testing findings focused on the issues identified in the common themes discussed below—especially how respondents understand the question and specific terms in the question. A complete write-up of the recommendations is included in Chapter 4, which discusses proposed updates for each question. 3.1 Different Reactions to Community and Individual Benefits of Government Data Collection In the instrument, there are several questions that asked respondents about their opinions of the risk and benefits of government data collection. A common issue identified during the cognitive interview was that participants found community benefits to be more concrete than individual benefits when considering their answers to these questions. While probing for examples of community risks and benefits, the most commonly mentioned benefit was the allocation of funding or resources for social services and improvements to the community such as funding for building or fixing sidewalks, parks, and schools. Risks of government data collection included misuse of the data to limit access to resources or funding and the government exerting more control over the community, such as gerrymandering or police overreach. When answering these questions, participants struggled to think about personal benefits from the data that the government collects about them. Some of these participants could only think about community-level benefits as opposed to how they benefit directly. When participants could think of individual benefits, they thought about things like government assistance programs, the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) or driver’s licenses, student loans or financial aid for college, and funding for schools. For example, one participant provided an explanation as to why the individual benefit may not be obvious, suggesting that “[I can think of] benefits in aggregate maybe, like the Census Bureau knowing there are people in this neighborhood who have this median income or x amount of people who don’t have health insurance in this area and maybe we can help that. Every benefit I think of comes down to the community level; I probably benefit, but in a very diffuse, hard to quantify way” (P52). In other words, although participants may be able to think of examples around government assistance and allocation of funding, the connection between government data collection and individual benefits can be unclear for those who have not needed government assistance or used other services like public schools. The questionnaire tested how different stated benefits impacted participants’ views on the formation of the Census demographic frame. None of the benefits specifically mention a community impact. However, participants were most likely to think about community impact when discussing the benefit of the database.

RoPOAR: Cognitive Testing Report 3-2 Some Spanish-speaking participants had additional and specific concerns regarding whether the government is collecting information about them—that it could potentially be used by immigration enforcement to target them. These participants expressed that the safest thing for them to do would be to not share any information. English-speaking and Spanish-speaking participants in our study defined community in slightly different ways. Across both groups, participants thought of geographic location as a defining feature of their community. English-speaking participants also included people who receive similar services, such as schools, libraries, or fire departments, many of which are geographically defined. However, Spanish-speaking respondents included their ethnic group as a main feature of their community. 3.2 Varying Perception of Risks and Benefits Throughout the questionnaire, multiple questions asked participants to weigh the risks and benefits of data collection conducted by companies and the government. They found it easier to consider the risks and benefits of company data collection than government data collection. Overall, participants had a stronger negative reaction to data collection from private companies. They could see and report clear risks of data breaches that might lead to identity theft. Company data breaches are also highly publicized or newsworthy events, and participants were more aware of company data breaches than government data breaches. Similarly, the positives of company data collection were not always clear, which means that participants saw the risks as more substantial because there were no balancing benefits. When participants could think of benefits of company data collection, they thought primarily about targeted ads. Participants found Question Q4 about the risks versus benefits of company data collection easier to answer than Q8 about government data collection. Similar to the earlier discussion about community benefits and risks being more concrete for participants, participants seemed to have a better understanding and more well-formed opinions about company data collection than government data collection regarding the risks and benefits of both. When weighing the risks and benefits of government data collection, perception of control seems to mediate feelings. For participants who think they have no control over the data the government collects, the risks and benefits are a moot point, as demonstrated by the comment from P07: “[There are] both benefits and risks and no way to avoid the government getting this information.” As a result, some participants prefer a neutral answer option to be able to report that they view the benefits and risks as equal. Another finding about risks and benefits is that participants who clearly understood the benefits felt more positively about combining and sharing data. For example, Q18 provided an introduction and then asked: “To what extent are you in favor of or against linking information about individuals?” Participants who were in favor of linking were more often

Section 3 — Overall Themes 3-3 able to think of clear benefits to linking the data, such as greater efficiency or more accurate statistics. Those who were against data linking failed to see or report any clear benefits. During the interviews, participants shared a similar reaction to the frame experiment, Q20, as they did to Q18. This question was set up as an experiment to test different statements and how they impact the extent to which respondents are in favor or against the Census Bureau building a database. Different benefits of the database were displayed on this screen, providing different frames around the topic. The frames included filling out surveys less often, helping government agencies make better use of taxpayer money, delivering services and benefits more efficiently, increasing the accuracy of statistics, and completing missing survey responses. The response options asked whether participants were strongly in favor of it, somewhat in favor of it, neither in favor nor against it, somewhat against it, or strongly against it. Participants were first asked about one frame and then about a second frame. They compared the two frames and reported whether their answers would change. Originally, these statements were expected to be perceived as benefits, and the goal of testing was to investigate how the different benefit framings impact perceptions of the database. However, participants did not always perceive the frame statements as benefits. The first frame (filling out [Census] surveys less often) failed to effectively communicate a benefit to all participants because they are unfamiliar with the other surveys the Census Bureau completes. Because many people only receive the decennial Census survey once every 10 years, filling out surveys less often is not a clear benefit. For example, while comparing the statements between Frame 1 and Frame 2 (making better use of taxpayer money), the comment from P52 states “[Frame 2] gives a clear understanding of the benefit I’d get out of this arrangement as a taxpayer. Makes the advantage much clearer [than Frame 1].” Although the frame statements were not universally interpreted as benefits as originally intended during the cognitive interview, findings still indicated that the question would meet the research goals of evaluating which statements improve the favorability of the database because the question is able to uncover and compare the varying opinions about these statements. To further improve Frame 1, a slight wording change was made to make the statement more concrete and expand it from only the Census Bureau to other government surveys. Additionally, the Census Bureau also decided to move forward with an experiment where half of the participants will be presented with a neutral answer option for these risk/benefits questions, which allows the instrument to explore the idea that some participants see the risks and benefits as equal.

RoPOAR: Cognitive Testing Report 3-4 3.3 Different Opinions about Data Sharing Another common theme that emerged from the cognitive interviews is how willing participants are to share different types of data with different entities. Specifically, the testing instrument presented a set of questions (Q12−Q14) asking participants about their willingness to share data with different entities. These included the federal government and participants’ state and local governments. The findings suggest that most participants did not have trouble defining “federal government,” but many participants had trouble differentiating clearly between “state” and “local” government. Participants may have different reference points to establish their local government depending on the size of the city (or town) they live in. For example, “local” government could include an entire county for some rural residents but only the township for other rural respondents. Similarly, local government could mean something more localized like a borough or a neighborhood district for some urban residents, while it can mean the city or the general metropolitan area that may overlap multiple counties for other urban respondents. Although participants might not consistently understand local government when answering the question, they indicated that they were more willing to share data with their local government compared with the federal government, because they believed they could receive more direct benefits. Interestingly, participants also felt positively about filling out the decennial Census for the Census Bureau, reflecting a higher level of trust specifically for the Census Bureau. Taken together, we recommend that these items remain unchanged because the varying definitions of local governments do not seem to prevent participants from forming their opinions about data sharing with different government entities. Additionally, participants were asked about specific information that the Census Bureau could gather from other agencies, including contact information, occupancy of an address, demographic information, home ownership, income, and number of people in a household (Q23−Q28). When participants were probed further, they indicated that they were also willing to share certain kinds of data but were more hesitant about other data. Participants were willing to share publicly available data, such as voter registration or home ownership; demographic information such as age, gender, or race; and number of people in their household. They are less willing to share income, social security number, and specific employment information such as employer name with the Census Bureau. Spanish-speaking participants were particularly worried about sharing any personal identifying information like names, addresses, and dates of birth. One Spanish speaker worried about sharing her ethnicity, nationality, and race as well. Given that the study only conducted 15 Spanish interviews, the concerns about sharing ethnicity and nationality may be more prevalent in the wider population.

Section 3 — Overall Themes 3-5 It is also worth noting that the Spanish interviews have identified one translation issue for further improvement. Ten of 15 Spanish speakers were thinking of identifying information when asked about sharing their data when they read “sus datos” (your data), which is sometimes used colloquially to mean contact information. To reduce the potential confusion, the Census Bureau approved a change to the translation to ask about “datos sobre usted” (data about you). Finally, another interesting data sharing–related theme that came up across questions is that participants want to explicitly consent to further data sharing. During instrument testing, participants were asked about the extent to which they were in favor of or against combining these data sources (Q17) and the extent to which they were in favor of or against the information they provided for one purpose being used by the government in additional ways (Q21). Across these questions, participants indicated that their opinion about being in favor or against the item relied on whether they would be able to provide explicit consent at the point of data collection. They wanted to be able to consent for their data to be shared in additional ways and with additional parties beyond when they initially provide it. This sentiment is true both for information provided to the government and to companies, illustrated clearly by the following quotes from the participants. For example, P79 stated “It should be someone's active choice to give that data.” This participant wanted to consent actively to providing data for future uses. Another participant (P18) said “When you’re filling out passport applications for example, is it going to be made clear that that information will be shared with other agencies, or will it just be shared?” This participant wondered whether the people would know that the data shared in one instance would be used elsewhere. 3.4 Unfamiliarity Regarding the Census Bureau’s Function Consistent with the findings from prior research by the Census Bureau whereby the public may be unfamiliar with what the Census Bureau does outside of the decennial Census, our cognitive interviews also identified the same reaction from participants. For instance, when participants think about data sharing, they were confused about the Census Bureau accessing data that they believed it already has access to through the decennial Census. Some participants believed that the Census Bureau should already have age, contact information, and the number of people in a household. They were confused when questions asked about the Census Bureau retrieving this information from other agencies. One participant said: “Doesn’t the Census already ask [about the number of people in your household]? Am I missing something? I’m for [the Census getting this information] but confused because they already ask this” (P121). Similarly, P52 made the following comment while assessing the Frame 1 (answering government surveys less often): “I’ll have to answer less questions because the Census knows more about me already. Although they only ask questions once a decade so I’m not sure how much less questions they could ask.”

RoPOAR: Cognitive Testing Report 3-6 This finding suggests that the public is not acutely aware of other surveys the Census Bureau runs and has not faced the burden of too many surveys. 3.5 Desire for Additional Contextual Information about Survey The final thematic finding is that participants want more information to inform their response selection. Participants wanted to know more context to better understand the questions to form their opinions given the considerations revolving around privacy and confidentiality. This is also related to the finding that participants are unclear on the Census Bureau’s functions. For example, participants wanted to know more about the purpose and benefits of sharing data between private companies and the Census Bureau. They were unsure why the Census Bureau would need data from private companies and how this could benefit the public in general. Participants reacted negatively to the mention of “private companies.” As a result, some participants selected “neither” to reflect their lack of knowledge about the data sharing or the Census Bureau’s function when they answered the corresponding questions during the interviews. Participants also wanted more information about the “additional ways” their data would be shared as mentioned in Q21. The term “additional ways” was described as too vague and hard for participants to understand. Some struggled to make selections because they wanted more information about what additional ways their data would be used by the governments with the information they already provided. For example, P123 said “I would want to know what the new purposes are, more transparency. I would be more in favor if I knew more about how it's being used.” This participant expressed that their approval of the database would increase even further if they knew more information. Alternatively, P10 said “I don’t know what ‘new purposes’ means. That’s vague. When things are vague, it makes me uncomfortable. Could mean more taxes. Could mean better healthcare. So, not knowing what that is, is terrifying because I don’t trust the government at all.” This reflects that some people are wary or suspicious of the government, and without additional information, they rely on their overall suspicions to form their opinions. Still, not all participants who wanted more information answered neither. Those who wanted more information but did not answer “neither” seemed to default to their overall feelings about the topic when they did not have enough information in the question to provide a nuanced answer. In addition, the findings also show that when participants struggled to understand some of the complicated questions in the questionnaire, they sometimes selected the midpoint, “neither in favor nor against it” indicating that it served as a “don’t know” option or an indicator for wanting for more information. For example, P18 stated “I don’t really know a huge amount about it and what the consequences would be, or even

Spanish text ¿Cuánto siente usted que se beneficia personalmente --si es que se beneficia-- de los datos que las compañías obtienen sobre usted? Table 4-2. Responses to Q02 Response English n=25 Spanish n=15 Benefit a great deal Me beneficio mucho 2 0 Benefit some Me beneficio algo 12 2 Benefit very little Me beneficio muy poco 8 2 Do not benefit No me beneficio 3 11 Findings (n=40) Most participants did not have trouble understanding the term “personally benefit” as intended. However, there were some differences in interpretation across English- and Spanish-speaking participants. When asked for examples of benefits, English-speaking participants mentioned examples such as targeted advertisements or improving the consumer experience (n=10), online search optimization (n=4), saving money (n=6) and time (n=3), algorithms predicting what users like (n=2), and autofill forms (n=2). For example, one participant commented, “My search optimization is better or lots of sneaky little things happening behind the scenes that help me use the internet more efficiently and sell me more things.” Many Spanish-speaking participants, however, seemed to think of “beneficios” more narrowly and only included material benefits, rather than including some of the less tangible benefits provided as examples by English-speaking participants. For example, participants mentioned supplies provided to those in need by a non-profit, such as food. In addition, two Spanish-speaking participants seemed to associate the term “beneficia” specifically with financial and material assistance or welfare, as opposed to the more general understanding demonstrated by most English-speaking participants. Last, when providing examples of companies that collect data, some Spanish-speaking participants did not differentiate between private companies and government entities while answering this question.

RoPOAR: Cognitive Testing Report 4-4 Notably, 10 participants across both languages were not sure how they could personally benefit or did not think they personally benefitted at all. Participants were asked about the use of the word “feel” in this question and whether they thought “feel” and “think” were asking about a different concept. More specifically, 16 participants said there was no difference between “think” and “feel” while 16 participants said there was a difference between “think” and “feel”, but some of these participants struggled to verbalize the difference or noted that the difference was small or negligible. Participants were also asked if their answer would change if this question used the word “think” instead of “feel” and three participants said they would change their answer in this case. One of these participants answered, “Benefit some” with the original question wording of “feel,” but said they would answer “Benefit very little” if the question said “think” because they said that “think” indicated to them more rational thought and “feel” was more about emotions. Another one of these participants answered, “Do not benefit” with the original question wording of “feel,” but said they would answer “Benefit very little” if the question said “think” because they thought more about rewards. The third participant said when she reads “cuánto creo” she would like to see a pamphlet with an explanation of the benefits; she said when she is asked “how she feels” she answers based on her emotions and the answers were biased by her feelings. In addition, three Spanish-speaking participants had a hard time understanding the probe about thinking versus feeling and were unable to answer. In summary, although participants were split on whether they thought “think” and “feel” mean different things or not, most participants (n=24) said they would not change their answer if the question asked “think” instead of “feel.” Overall, findings indicate that changing the question wording to “think” instead of “feel” would result in no change in the cognitive process that respondents are using to provide a response. Other findings from cognitive testing include the following: one participant noted that they would prefer that the first response option said, “Benefit a good amount” instead of “Benefit a great deal,” and two participants mentioned that they were not sure what happens with the data that are collected about them. Recommendations Overall: Some Issues In English, participants understand “think” and “feel” as interchangeable and findings indicate that this wording does not impact their response choice. However, there are some significant issues in Spanish, with several Spanish speakers limiting their consideration of benefits to financial or material benefits. Changing the Spanish translation might help address this, but it cannot be confirmed whether alternative translations used will resolve this issue without further testing. However, we believe that “obtener ventajas” as opposed to “beneficiarse” could reduce the association with benefits in the sense of financial

Section 4 — Final Question Recommendations 4-31 Participants provided the following examples of specific federal government agencies or institutions: Census Bureau (n=4); IRS (n=3); Social Security (n=2); NIH (n=1); FBI, CIA, and ATF (n=1); the U.S. Postal Service (n=1); the Supreme Court (n=1); the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Commerce, and the Department of Defense (n=1); and the Department of Education (n=1). In general, participants saw some overlap between state and local government and sometimes could not articulate the difference. In defining “state government,” several participants could not define this further beyond “my state” (n=15). A few participants mentioned specific politicians or roles, such as judges (n=1), senators (n=1), governors (n=4), or state House of Representatives (n=1). In defining “local government,” participants often mentioned city/city council/city hall (n=6), the mayor (n=8), the county or town (n=8), or the police/sheriff department (n=1). However, another 10 participants were not sure what “local government” meant and had difficulty defining this. Two Spanish speaking participants were not clear on the difference between the federal and state governments. Participants could easily list examples of data they were thinking about while answering these questions but could not easily place these data at the different levels of federal, state, and local government. Some common examples of data included income taxes/income/financial data (n=13); information collected by the DMV, like vehicle registration and driver’s license (n=6); household composition (n=6); voter registration (n=4); employment history (n=5); and personally identifiable information like name, contact information, DOB, address, or SSN (n=14). Several participants were more willing to share some types of data than others, especially general information (such as demographic data) (n=8). However, one participant said that she was less willing to share her ethnicity, nationality, or race. Overall, participants are more willing to share data with their local government than federal government, because they believe they can receive more direct benefits (n=8). However, five participants noted that they are more willing to share data with the Census Bureau/fill out the Census. English and Spanish participants had different reactions to sharing data with the federal government. Some English participants assumed that some federal data was already being collected and shared—that some of this was out of their control (n=6). Two Spanish participants were more willing to share some information with federal government compared to state/local. One participant was more willing to share information with the federal government because they saw the state and local governments as more corrupt and less reliable. Another participant was also more willing to share sensitive information, like SSN, with the federal government than with state or local governments. She explained this was because she had worked as a Census enumerator and saw the seriousness with which

RoPOAR: Cognitive Testing Report 4-32 data are protected and how data are handled. One participant said she would be willing to share any data if needed to receive any benefits from social programs. Three participants changed their answers during the think aloud process or during probing, wanting to better reflect their comparative willingness to share data across the three levels of government. Two participants decided to change their answers after they thought through what the constructs of “federal” and “state” meant to them, specifically when comparing these two. One participant changed their answer to “moderately” instead of “slightly” for local, wanting to show that they are more willing to share at the local level compared to the federal and state level because to them “local” is associated with their community. Recommendations Overall: Some Issues Most participants did not have trouble defining “federal government,” but many participants had trouble differentiating between “state” and “local” government. In addition, most participants could not place examples of data being collected about them at the federal, state, or local level. One reason for this may be that participants have different reference points to establish their local government depending on the size of the city (or town) they live in. For example, “local” government could include an entire county for some rural residents but only the township for other rural respondents. Similarly, local government could mean something more localized like a borough or a neighborhood district for some urban residents, while for other urban respondents it can mean the city or the general metropolitan area that may overlap multiple counties. Because of the issues distinguishing between local and state governments and the different types of data available to both, we recommend collapsing these government types (i.e., Q13 and Q14) into one single question, presented below. We also recommend no changes to Q12 about federal government. Because 10 of the 15 Spanish speakers thought of identifying information when asked about what data they were considering (when only four English speakers did the same), we believe there may be a translation issue at work. "Sus datos" is sometimes used colloquially to mean personal info or contact info. We believe a small change to the translation of asking about “datos sobre usted” (data about you) could minimize this, but it is of course not possible to know for sure without testing. There is also a possibility that because of the generally lower education levels of the Spanish speakers in the sample, they may simply be less familiar with as many types of data as the English speakers. Either way, we do not believe the change will impair understanding.

Section 4 — Final Question Recommendations 4-35 Findings (n=13) When asked what a “single central database” means to them, eight participants could clearly provide a description. These participants described a “single central database” as a bank of information that all government agencies have access to (n=5) or a giant electronic database (n=3). However, three participants struggled to clearly communicate what a “a single central database” means, failing to demonstrate that they are knowledgeable about this topic. Furthermore, two participants were very unsure about their answer to Q15 and thought a “Don’t know” option would be helpful. In general, responses to the two questions were consistent (i.e., either “Yes” to both or “No” to both), indicating that when people think a single central database exists, they also think it should exist, or vice versa. One participant said “Yes” to Q15 and “No” to Q16 because they thought the database already exists but should not exist because of data security concerns, while two participants said “No” to Q15 and “Yes” to Q16 because they thought the data base does not currently exist but would be more efficient, more secure, and should exist. Similar to Q17 (Government agencies already collect data separately about people's jobs, earnings, and participation in government programs but do not always share the data across agencies…) discussed below, it may be unclear to participants whether the examples are an exhaustive list. Two participants were okay with the three pieces of information listed in the question but were not okay with other types of information, like SSN and income. These participants may have been primed by previous discussions to consider other types of data. Another three participants mentioned risks of a single central database in terms of data security. Recommendations Overall: Some Issues Because of the largely consistent answers across both questions, these items may be measuring similar constructs that are not disparate for respondents. We had a small sample size for testing this question due to previous testing that has already been completed. Further input about the results of previous testing should be helpful as we consider how to proceed with these two items. We may want to consider Q16 for deletion because it is an opinion question asking about a central database, which overlaps with other questions in the survey. If the Census Bureau is interested in respondents’ responses to combining only name, address, and date of birth, then this question does have a distinct construct. However, it is not clear that participants understand this list as exhaustive.

RoPOAR: Cognitive Testing Report 4-36 There are no other factual questions in the survey, so we do think it is important to move forward with Q15, but we may want to clarify whether the data items listed are examples or an exhaustive list. We may want to consider and adding a “Don’t know” option for Q15 because it is a factual question and “don’t know” represents a valid response. There were two participants in this sample (n=9) who struggled to choose a response and preferred to have a “Don’t know” option. We may also consider including a mention of “only” in the question stem. Revising the framing of the question with the additional word of “only” may improve the consistency of respondent comprehension. Section 4 — Final Question Recommendations 4-41 Findings (n=39) Most participants understand the phrase “linking information,” but eight struggled with the phrase. Three participants were concerned about personally identifiable data being available publicly. One participant specifically struggled to understand what “statistics” meant. One participant focused more on the Census Bureau using information to produce statistics, and it was unclear if they understood the concept of linking. One participant thought this meant data from cognitive interviews would be linked. One participant understood “link this information together” to mean that their individual information would be combined with the information of others in the same community, rather than with another government entity. One Spanish-speaking participant also had a hard time understanding “conectar” (to link) and thought perhaps they meant “colectar” (to collect) and was unclear on what the question was asking. Another participant provided an incoherent response that illustrated they did not understand the question very well. Two participants thought Q18 was very similar to the previous question Q17 (To what extent are you in favor of or against combining these data sources?). Participants who were in favor of linking can more often think of clear benefits to linking the data, such as greater efficiency or more accurate statistics (n=5). Four participants wanted more information to form a confident opinion. Three of these participants answered “neither,” indicating that this category serves as a “don’t know” response for some participants. Two participants were unclear on the purpose of the Census Bureau linking all the information. One participant commented, “If Census wants to know how many people are in your house, that’s fine but why do they need all that other information?” This participant felt especially unclear on the benefits of linking the data together. Three participants changed their responses after discussion the question further, all in a positive direction (i.e., from “neither” to “somewhat in favor”). These participants reread the question at least once. Further discussion helped them think through the pros and cons of linking information and influenced them to respond more positively than their initial reaction. Recommendations Overall: Some Issues This question contains a lot of information for participants to absorb, and it is difficult for some of them to understand. The comprehension issue is reflected when three participants changed their answers during probing, the number of people selecting “neither” as a substitute for “don’t know,” and the confusion over what “linking information” means.

For example, one participant said in reaction to Frame 5 that “People may be skipping for a reason, and you’re taking that right away from them to not answer.” This sentiment was echoed by at least one other participant. Two other participants made a similar comment about Frame 1, with one participant confused about the statement, questioning the reason of conducting surveys if the Census Bureau wants to let people answer surveys less often with this database. Even as another participant understood the meaning of Frame 1, he still expressed a mild concern of lacking the direct personal connection to the benefit: “I’ll have to answer less questions because the Census knows more about me already. If you’re not someone who relies on government services, then it’s not going to mean anything.” Similarly, another participant felt that Frame 2 was too broad without examples and was more leading than Frame 1. When participants discussed the two different frames they reviewed, they preferred the frame that had clearer benefits and was more concrete and relatable. For example, a participant indicated that “[Frame 2] is better - the other [Frame 1] refers to surveys and this one is more pointed and focused on fiscal responsibility.” Additionally, “[Frame 2] gives a clear understanding of the benefit I’d get out of this arrangement as a taxpayer. Makes the advantage much clearer [than Frame 1].” Another two participants considered Frame 3 a better statement than Frame 2 and Frame 4, respectively. For example, one participant explained, “I prefer the first one [Frame 3]. Efficiency is the larger word that encompasses accuracy. If one is efficient, then it is because you have access to accurate data. [You] could be accurate but not very efficient.” Another participant also found Frame 3 easier to understand than Frame 2. The other eight participants expressed their discontent regarding the Census Bureau collecting information from private companies for the database. For example, one participant commented, “I think it’s better that the government shares information among themselves, but I’m a little uncomfortable with private companies being a part of it.” One participant was confused by the mention of “compañías privadas” (private companies) in the question and asked, “Like companies hired by the government to do direct surveys or what?” Two participants who saw frames that referenced missing information commented they thought that missing information was often left off for a reason, and the government should go back to people and ask for it rather than ask private companies for it. Recommendations Overall: Some Issues Although most participants understood and interpreted all five frames in the context of the question consistently and report their opinion with little difficulty, the findings indicated some concerns about the vagueness of all five frames. These concerns are consistent with the expert review report, as our experts suspected that the frames may not clearly resonate with respondents as benefits. Although Frame 1 seems to be a concrete and direct benefit for individuals in the expert review, some participants either did not see the statement as a concrete and relatable benefit or considered the benefits of other frames (such as Frame 2) as more concrete or relatable. It is possible that “filling out surveys less often” is not as relatable as expected, when the average person only has to fill out the Census every 10 years. The mention of information availability may also invoke unrelated skepticism about privacy and distract survey respondents further from discerning their opinion about the benefits of the database. Similarly, Frame 5 elicits the same concerns as Frame 1 but to a lesser extent. In addition, some participants expressed their discontent of losing the discretion of providing a nonresponse for privacy reasons. Frames 2, 3 and 4 are seen as more relatable, concrete benefits of the database by some participants compared with Frames 1 and 5. Although these frames worked as intended during the cognitive interview, a few participants still expressed their desire of examples because they were not very confident about their understanding of these frames. If the goal of the frame experiment is to understand whether the general population may express a different opinion about the database based on the different benefits, then Frame 1 may be a potential candidate for removal from the experiment, given that it did not work

RoPOAR: Cognitive Testing Report 4-52 as well as expected with the issues revealed during the cognitive interview. Additionally, Frame 5 might be considered for removal for the same concerns. If it is important to keep Frame 1, then we may want to consider removing the phrase “because your information is already available” because it may trigger privacy concerns rather than being understood as a benefit. Census feedback Q20 will move forward with the existing design for the national data collection with a minor tweak for Frame 1. The wording for Frame 1 will be updated to “This database will mean that you are asked to fill out government surveys less often because your information is already available from other agencies.”

Participants also struggled to think of additional ways their information would be used outside of the examples and benefits listed in the question, relying instead only on the information provided in the question text.

Further clarification was not gathered. Overall, most participants felt the items were clear and confidently provided responses. However, participants struggled with a few phrases. First, several participants were unsure what “froze your credit” meant but were all confident they had never done it (n=14). Two participants interpreted this phrase as canceling credit cards, perhaps because they were lost or stolen. One participant was confused about how to answer this question because they had requested a notification for a credit check but had not frozen their credit. They pointed out that this item is double-barreled. They correctly answered “yes” to this item in the end. One participant thought a freeze was when a person calls their bank and asks them to release their information. One participant thought it meant to set an alarm for when there are unrecognized charges so unauthorized people cannot use their credit. Another participant guessed that it might be when someone stops paying bills so that people cannot track their credit. Another item that some participants struggled with was “Used more secure methods of communications, such as encrypted emails.” Two participants were unclear what “encrypted emails” were; however, both were able to answer “no” without difficulty. One participant was thinking about two-factor authentication instead of encrypted messaging. One participant said they did not understand what was meant by “encriptados” (encrypted) in the context of encrypted emails but that they assumed it was a feature they used from Google. Another Spanish speaker also commented that they did not know that their emails could be encrypted. Seven participants were not sure about the definition of “cookies.” One of these participants answered “yes” to this item. One participant incorrectly understood cookies as the security filters that websites have. Another guessed that it was an additional charge you could be charged for downloading something from the internet. One participant chose to leave the item asking about if they “Avoided or stopped using a social media service to protect privacy” blank, commenting that they had not stopped using it but had provided incomplete and fake information to protect their privacy. In addition to the issues with clarity reported by English speakers, some Spanish speakers commented on not being familiar with some specific terms. Two participants commented that they did not understand what was meant by “configuraciones por defecto” (default settings). Another participant also asked about the term but did understand it as intended when asked to elaborate on their understanding. Six Spanish-speaking participants had never heard of “El Registro No Llame” (The Do Not Call Registry). Two Spanish-speaking participants also commented on the two items that reference asking “a government department, public service, or private company” to either share what information they have

RoPOAR: Cognitive Testing Report 4-84 about you or delete your information. They said that they would have no idea how to ask the government to do these things if they wanted to. A few participants faced some challenges with the item “Blocked a smartphone app or stopped an app from accessing other details on your phone, such as your location, contacts, or tracking other activity.” One participant, who saw the original question, answered “yes” but revealed during probing that she stopped an app from accessing other details on her phone because she was concerned about battery life, not privacy. One participant initially thought about deleting apps, then during probing thought about changing app settings. Another participant who saw the original question changed their answer from “no” to “yes” during probing, but it was unclear why. One Spanish-speaking participant commented that they imagined it was like when you block someone on Facebook. Another Spanish-speaking participant was thinking about how they often block the phone numbers from which they get text message ads on their phone, rather than blocking apps from accessing information from their phone. One participant brought up the word “regularly” when responding to the item “Regularly cleared browser history or deleted cookies.” This participant reflected that they did not regularly clear browser history or delete cookies, saying “no, not regularly” as they selected the response “no.” This indicates that “regularly” may be influencing responses for some people. Most participants thought the list was exhaustive, but a few mentioned additional measures they have taken to protect their privacy: using two-factor identification or VPN (n=1); blocking phone calls; choosing iPhone over Android due to additional privacy measures (n=1); not providing personal information over the phone or asking questions to confirm legitimacy when receiving calls about personal information (n=2); and deleting one’s credit card information from websites (n=1). Recommendations Overall: Some Issues Evidence from testing indicates that including “to protect your privacy” is necessary in the items to cement the context for participants, contradictory to recommendations from the expert report. This idea was illustrated clearly with the addition of this phrase to the item about encrypted emails. The many items in the table and the fact that the question stem did not stay on screen likely contributed to the improved performance of items with the phrase “to protect your privacy.” In addition to the changes already implemented during testing, it would also be useful to program the question stem to stay on screen while participants evaluate all items in the grid.

Section 4 — Final Question Recommendations 4-85 Keeping the question stem on screen should help keep the privacy context in mind for participants, but all items should be examined with the key findings in mind as we consider whether to add “to protect your privacy” to additional items, such as “cleared browser history.” Due to the issues some participants had around understanding and responding to the item about blocking or stopping an app on their smartphone, we recommend shortening the text to reduce cognitive burden. The suggested change is as follows: “Stopped a smartphone app from tracking your location, contacts, or other activity to protect your privacy.” Although participants struggled with “froze your credit,” it does not impact the response process because it is clear to them whether they have taken this action or not. We also have less concern about participants who are unable to verbalize the definition of “cookies.” Given the regular interactions people have with accepting cookies on websites, they should be able to answer accurately even with misunderstandings of the term “cookies.” We may want to consider the analytic goals of the item “regularly cleared browser history or deleted cookies” and whether it is important to measure frequency of this privacy behavior. “Regularly” may lead to a varied interpretation, and we may consider something more concrete such as “weekly” or “monthly.” Alternatively, if the analytic goal is focused on ever performing this behavior, then “regularly” could be dropped from the statement. Although a few participants mentioned other measures they have taken to protect their privacy, the most common measures seem well-represented. We do not recommend adding additional items. Though there were some comprehension issues that appear to have been worse among Spanish speakers than English speakers, specifically related to freezing credit, encrypted emails, default settings, and the Do-Not-Call registry, we do not believe these are translation related, but rather stem from a generally lower level of familiarity with the concepts and technologies among the Spanish-speaking participants. For this reason, we do not recommend any changes to the translations. Census feedback For the web instrument for the national data collection, the question stem of Q44 will be programmed to stay on screen while respondents evaluate all items in the grid. We agree to include the clause “to protect your privacy” for the corresponding items as recommended and revise the second item’s wording to “Blocked a smartphone app from tracking your location, contacts, or accessing other details to protect your privacy.”

Abstract The U.S. Census Bureau’s Frames Program seeks to assess public opinion regarding a national demographic frame that would include person-level demographic, social, and economic characteristics for the U.S. population. Working jointly with the Center for Behavioral Science Methods, staff from the Frames Program and RTI International designed a 2-year, multi-mode research study. The research comprises three tasks: (1) develop and test an instrument to assess public perceptions of the use of administrative records, (2) conduct a nationally representative web survey using an address-based probability panel, and (3) conduct focus groups with hard-to- count populations and individuals who participated in the Ipsos web survey. This report explains the focus group methodology, including a description of the target populations and participant eligibility criteria and the strategies for participant recruitment and screening. Additionally, this report includes the qualitative analysis of the focus group data collected and discusses findings, with potential next step considerations provided to the Census Bureau. 2-1 2. Focus Group Methodology For the Research on Public Opinion of Administrative Records (RoPOAR) Subproject 3 Study, RTI International (RTI) conducted 12 focus groups to assess public opinion regarding a national demographic frame that would include person-level demographic, social, and economic characteristics for the U.S. population. These focus groups were conducted with hard-to-count populations and individuals who participated in the Ipsos web survey fielded in Subproject 2. In preparation for the focus groups, RTI drafted the focus groups’ virtual and in-person moderator guides (Appendices A and B), with input from the Census Bureau team. Other materials developed included an in-person participant screener (Appendix C), virtual and in-person consent forms (Appendices D and E), in-person recruitment advertisements (Appendix F), a potential frame benefits handout (Appendix G), and various email templates to remind participants of the focus groups (Appendix H). All materials were developed in English and Spanish. Moderators and notetakers took part in a training session and were taught the subject matter to have a clear understanding of the focus groups’ purpose and process. The training session included the following topics: • Background and goals of the study • Sites, dates, and staffing • Preparation for and activities during and after the groups • Informed consent, confidentiality, and quality assurance • Moderation training • Notetaking training • Review and practice with moderator’s guides Following the training, staff were given additional time to practice to better understand the moderator guide. The focus groups were moderated by skilled experienced moderators (with more than 5 years of focus group moderating experience). Moderators maintained a non-judgmental attitude and guided the discussion so that it stayed on course and covered all the topics in the time allotted. Moderators occasionally probed participants to clarify responses and gather additional information as they facilitated the discussion. Notetakers provided on-site logistical support and took notes throughout the focus group sessions. In total, RTI conducted three virtual focus groups (participants were respondents to the Ipsos survey conducted in Sub Project 2) and nine in-person focus groups, two of which

2-2 were completed in Spanish. The distribution and composition of focus group participants are covered in Table 2.1. Table 2.1. 3-1 3. Participant Recruitment and Characteristics RTI developed several recruitment strategies for the in-person focus groups to ensure a sufficient number of participants would take part in the focus groups. These strategies included the following: • Posting social media advertisements on Craigslist, which is an online community forum. These ads were posted in both English and Spanish. • Contacting organizations or community groups to introduce the study and partner with them to find participants with the characteristics needed for the group discussion. • Posting physical flyers (e.g., at community centers, public libraries, bus stops/stations, grocery stores, college student unions, laundromats, etc.) • Word of mouth advertising / Snowball sampling techniques. A web-based focus group screening instrument was developed and programmed to determine study eligibility. Interested individuals responding to advertisements were provided a website link to the self-administered screening instrument. Some individuals preferred to be screened by calling the recruitment phone number listed on the advertisement, and the recruiter entered the information directly into the database. This was mostly the preferred mode for Spanish-speaking individuals who called the recruiter directly. Some cohorts were difficult to recruit, like young white and young African American participants, while there were few challenges recruiting other groups. The recruiters continued to recruit participants until there were more people recruited than needed (over recruitment) as a strategy in case we experienced a higher-than-expected no-show rate. Following screening, eligible participants were selected and invited to participate in the focus groups. After the selected participants agreed to participate, they were sent a confirmation email listing the date, time, and location/invite link of the focus group session. This research used a convenience, opt-in sample of U.S. adults. We recruited participants who aligned with the geographic, demographic, and language targets for a given group. For the nine in person focus groups, discussions were held in the following four locations: • Washington, DC (1 group) • Berkeley, CA (2 groups) • Chicago, IL (3 groups) • Research Triangle Park, NC (3 groups) Three focus groups were conducted virtually, with those who took part in the Ipsos panel online survey. Of the three groups, two were conducted with participants that were determined to have a low trust in government institutions. This was determined by

3-2 analyzing the responses to several of the questions answered in the Ipsos survey, as discussed in Section 2. The third group was comprised of participants that were determined to have a high trust in government institutions. Table 3.1 displays the participant characteristics for the 3 virtual focus groups.
