4-1 4. Focus Group Results Each of the following sections, 4.1 through 4.4 align with the in-person moderator’s guide. The virtual guide did not cover the potential frame benefits as participants had seen these previously when they responded to the Ipsos survey. The moderator’s guides were developed to first ask participants broadly what they thought was meant by “data” and then about government data collection more specifically. In Section 4.2, we began providing participants with some details about the frame, beginning with a broad description and then a more detailed description. Participants were asked how they felt about the database and what questions remained. In Section 4.3 we asked participants about perceived benefits of the frame (in-person groups only) and in Section 4.4, we asked about remaining concerns that participants had. During analysis it was determined that there were no noticeable differences between the virtual and in-person groups, so they are discussed together in the following sections. The discussion includes focus group identifiers that map to Table 2.1, for reference. 4.1 General Government Data Collection At the beginning of each focus group, participants were asked what they thought of when they heard the term “data.” The participants explained that they generally thought of data collected by both government agencies and private companies. Several participants from different focus groups mentioned data as being numbers [FG7 – Higher Education, FG2 – Low Trust], statistics or trends [FG7 – Higher Education, FG12 – Older AA], and social media data [FG5 – Low Trust, FG7 – Higher Education, FG9 – Low Education, FG10 – Hispanic]. Several other participants [FG2 – Low Trust] referred to “information.” Some participants [FG4 – Young White] provided examples such as, “Tech companies using data for marketing and to drive sales” and “Numerically measured data.” Some participants generally thought of government data such as demographics, providing examples such as age, race, and population density and health care, such as vaccine status. Other participants [FG5 – Low Trust] thought of “statistics” and “video data.” One participant thought of “surveillance.” The participants explained that some companies collect and use data on customers, such as Google and Meta. Participants from one Spanish-speaking group [FG6 – Hispanic] understood “data” as personal information, such as names, date of birth, or addresses. The participants mentioned that these data are collected when they perform commercial transactions and when they complete government forms, such as the decennial census and migration registries (when entering the country). One participant explained, “If you enter as a tourist, (the government) will have all the information. I entered around 22 years ago, and the government doesn’t miss anything, all my information is there, the information that you provide and the one you don’t provide, they also know it.”

4-2 Some participants [FG8 – Older White] focused on their feelings toward the collection of data, either negatively or positively. One participant explained, “I’m not comfortable at all, it’s overwhelming, too much of it. I don’t have a cell phone. There is so much out there with identity theft. I try to disengage from it.” Another participant commented, “I’m on the other side of the coin. I think there’s a wealth of information out there; part of that is for business. When asked how people can benefit from the data government has about people and their communities, most participants provided examples of how the community benefits. Other participants thought of allocation of resources and funding to schools and congressional allocation of representatives [FG3 – High Trust, FG7 – Higher Education], city planning and public transportation [FG4 – Young White, FG7 – Higher Education, FG9 – Low Education, FG12 – Older AA]. Table 4.1 General Description of the Frame The Census Bureau plans to build a new database about people that combines information from other government agencies, government surveys you may have answered in the past, and private companies. The database would only be used to produce statistics. Participants were then asked for their overall reactions, types of data they thought might be included in the frame, any questions participants had after hearing the description, potential benefits of the frame development, the purpose of the frame, and how easy it was to understand the concept. After this initial discussion, participants in the focus groups were provided a more detailed description of the frame (Table 4.2). Table 4.2 Detailed Description of the Frame I’m going to give you some more information about this database. This database would link together information about individuals. Some examples are age, sex, race, ethnicity, education, income. The data would come from sources such as the Social Security Administration, IRS, and government programs such as SNAP and WIC. This detailed description included additional information about the types of data that would be included and the sources of these data. Participants were again asked their overall reactions, whether they felt more comfortable after hearing more about the frame, and their feelings about linking data from private companies. Most of the group participants had negative reactions to the idea of the Census Bureau building a new database combining information from several sources. The most positive reaction came from one of the Spanish-speaking focus groups [FG5 – Low Trust]. The main

4-6 positive benefit from this Spanish-speaking group was that the database could provide better population counts, which could include people who may not complete the decennial census, such as undocumented Latinx people. These Spanish-speaking participants [FG6 – Hispanic] expressed positive reactions when hearing the more detailed description of the frame. The participants explained that the information included in these examples was already being provided voluntarily, so they did not see a problem with it being linked together. Participants from the Low Trust [FG1 – Low Trust, FG2 – Low Trust, FG5 – Low Trust] and Low Education [FG9 – Low Education] groups had the most negative reactions to the new frame. For example, one participant [FG2 – Low Trust] explained, “In no way, shape, or form am I going to give the government every single piece of information about me, and then have a database on every single person.” Participants from the Low Trust groups had many questions about how the database would work, what the benefits would be, and how their data would be kept secure. Concerns raised by these groups will be further discussed in Section 4.4. Participants mostly thought that the concept of the database was easy to understand, but some participants wanted more information. One group [FG11 – Young AA] emphasized that although the concept was easy to understand, they did not understand the purpose of the database. One participant [FG7 – Higher Education] thought it would be a good idea to have a phone number available for people to call to ask questions. Other participants [FG9 – Low Education; FG12 – Older AA] thought that only people with specialized knowledge about databases or statistics would be able to fully understand this complicated idea. Four participants from one focus group [FG2 – Low Trust] agreed that people would not really care enough to try to understand because they have more pressing priorities, such as “living paycheck to paycheck.” There was some confusion over whether the Census Bureau had already established the database described in the frame. Some participants believed that the Census Bureau or the government at large already has a central database. These participants questioned how the description provided in the frame is different from what they already believe is happening or should be happening. A couple of participants from one focus group [FG7 – Higher Education] felt the government should have already been creating a single, central database by working together with other agencies to obtain the information they need. One participant from another focus group [FG3 – High Trust] expressed amusement that the government has yet to create this database. Three participants from one focus group [FG11 – Young AA] questioned how this database would be different from what is already happening. One of them [FG11 – Young AA] speculated, “If they aren’t acquiring the information themselves, I guess they are outsourcing it versus doing it themselves like they were doing previously? They had people

Section 4 4-7 coming to your door asking you questions but now they will get the information from other sources?” Another participant [FG11 – Young AA] wondered, “Maybe they feel they aren’t getting enough information from the people, so they are having to go to the companies? They could be getting a lack of data, so they have to go this route.” Two participants from another focus group [FG12 – Older AA] also thought that Census Bureau was already collecting data in the way the frame described. One participant [FG12 – Older AA] explained, “when they take our information, they have the different age brackets, different income. I feel like they’re doing that now.” Another participant [FG12 – Older AA] reiterated that they had previously “assumed this is already happening in one form or another.” Relatedly, one participant from a Low Trust focus group [FG1 – Low Trust] felt this database was not needed because the Census Bureau already has all the data they need. Participants were asked their thoughts about having the Census Bureau lead the frame development effort rather than other government agencies. Most participants had a favorable view of the Census Bureau and believe that it is a non-threatening, trusted government agency. Many thought that the Census Bureau was the best agency to lead this initiative and that it was aligned with the mission of the Census Bureau to monitor the population of the United States. Participants saw the Census Bureau as a respected institution known for helping people. Almost all participants thought that the Census Bureau would be the better agency compared to the IRS to lead this effort. For example, one participant [FG8 – Older White] stated “[the] Census Bureau is a fairly innocuous group, better than the IRS.” Another participant [FG4 – Young White] stated “The Census bureau is slightly less nefarious [than other government agencies].” Even one of the Low Trust groups [FG5 – Low Trust] had a positive impression of the Census Bureau leading this effort. One participant [FG5- Low Trust] stated, “The Census is supposed to be about collecting data about people and communities. Better than a negative agency such as the IRS.” This theme of a positive reaction to and high trust for the Census Bureau was also observed during the cognitive interviews completed as part of Subproject 1. However, a few participants in one focus group [FG11 -Young AA] thought that the IRS would be better because people may be more willing to share their information. Furthermore, they thought that people were scared of the IRS and they would therefore be more likely to share their information with the Census Bureau than the IRS. Some participants [FG11- Young AA; F12- Older AA] did not think that the agency leading the effort mattered since multiple agencies would be working together to share information. According to one participant [FG11- Young AA], “I don’t think it matters to me who leads it – the Census or a different agency. They are going to be working together to get the information anyway.” Some Spanish-speaking participants [FG6 – Hispanic, FG10 – Hispanic] had concerns about how the Census Bureau may use the database to monitor or track undocumented persons, echoing concerns that the same Spanish-speaking group had about participating in the

4-8 decennial census earlier in the discussion. For low-trust groups [FG1 – Low Trust, FG2 – Low Trust, FG5 – Low Trust], the government agency is a moot point; they object to the database entirely and it does not matter which agency leads the effort. As one participant [FG2 – Low Trust] explained, “From the consensus in this group, specifically, it just sounds like we don’t trust the government here. Doesn’t matter what question you ask; we are going to say no.” When asked why the Census Bureau would want to create this type of database, participants had somewhat vague ideas about what the reason might be. Some participants across various focus groups [FG4 – Young White; FG8 – Older White; FG12 – Older AA] mentioned ideas such as saving money or increasing efficiency without providing any concrete examples. For example, one participant [FG8 – Older White] stated, “It sounds like they want to centralize, and it could be time saving.” Several participants mentioned increased data accuracy with a few different ideas about how that may happen. One participant [FG12 – Older AA] thought that the Census Bureau may currently have inaccurate or incomplete data and combining sources from various agencies would help improve the data Census Bureau already has. Another participant [FG6 – Hispanic] thought that combining data would provide the Census Bureau with access to data for people who may not complete the decennial census, such as undocumented persons. One participant [FG11 – Young AA] thought that pulling the same data from multiple sources could help the Census Bureau confirm that they had the most accurate and correct data. Two participants thought that the COVID-19 pandemic may be one reason why the Census Bureau was interested in creating the frame. One participant [FG11 – Young AA] thought that the Census Bureau was limited with data collection during the COVID-19 pandemic and needed to bolster the data they missed over the past few years. Another participant [FG12 – Older AA] echoed this idea, stating, “During COVID, the Census wasn’t getting the information they needed.” A few participants provided additional examples of reasons they thought the Census Bureau would create this database. One participant [FG9 – Low Education] hoped that the information in the database would be used for “good” stating, “My hope is that the information is being used for good. Not being used to enforce, look for illegal immigrants, harboring more people. Not big brother spying for me. It’s my duty to provide information to help people. My hope is that it is used to reduce water bills, reduce traffic, create public transit.” Another [FG11 – Young AA] thought that the information might be used for safety reasons, such as to find or stop criminals who pose a threat to communities. Another [FG11 – Young AA] thought that the information could be used by someone interested in tracing their own heritage or genealogy. Some Spanish-speaking participants [FG10 – Hispanic;

Section 4 4-9 FG6 – Hispanic] were unable to think of any reason why the Census Bureau would want to create the frame. After being shown the general description of the frame, participants were asked to list the agencies they thought the Census Bureau might get data from. The IRS was the agency most groups thought the Census Bureau would get data from (mentioned in 9 out of 12 groups), followed by the Social Security Administration (mentioned in 5 out of 12 groups). Other agencies mentioned in multiple groups were the DMV, the FBI, Department of Health and Human Services, and welfare agencies (including WIC, SNAP, HUD, and Medicaid/Medicare). Other state and federal agencies mentioned only one time included the Department of Transportation, Department of Treasury, Department of Justice, Federal Bureau of Prisons, Veteran’s Affairs, Department on Aging, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the military in general, and Department of Death Certificates. It was unclear whether some of these agencies actually exist, but they were provided as examples. Some participants [FG11 – Young AA; FG12 – Older AA; FG9 – Low Education] thought that medical records from private doctor’s offices or mental health records may be included in the database. However, one participant [FG11 – Young AA] explained that primary care provider offices cannot give information about people to the Census because of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). One participant [FG9 – Low Education] believed that nothing would be off limits in terms of data accessible within the proposed database, explaining that this included their “health, dental, age, race, and income.” The participants had questions and concerns when asked how they felt about linking data from private companies. Reactions to the idea of linking private company data was more negative across all groups than linking government information alone. One participant [FG8 – Older White] stated, “I have no problem centralizing data from government agencies only, but the problem would be private companies.” Some participants had concerns around privacy and government overreach. For example, one participant [FG7 – Higher Education] commented, “It means government buying data from private companies, it’s just another privacy sink where we’re losing more of our privacy to government, and they’ve figured out a way to do it legally.” Another participant [FG10 – Hispanic] stated, “[The government does] not have to know if I have good or bad credit score, of if I’ve paid my car. There is information that is strictly mine […], they need to limit it to what they need. They don’t have to have access, that is my privacy.” Another participant concerned about private companies [FG1 - Low Trust] added, “[Private companies] need to step out of the government; they need to be away from this conversation.” Some other participants were suspicious of the motives of private companies and worried that they do not have public interest as the main goal [FG9 – Low Education; FG11 – Young AA; FG2 – Low Trust]. Some worried that the information from private

4-10 companies may not be very accurate [FG9 – Low Education]. Many participants want a clear separation between government activities and private companies. The focus group participants questioned whether private companies would have access to the database and were concerned that private companies could profit from the database [FG6 – Hispanic; FG10 – Hispanic]. Some participants had questions about their privacy, which private companies would be involved, what data would be purchased (such as credit scores or debt), and who would make the decisions to link additional data. Some participants [FG9 – Low Education] were unsure what it meant for the database to link to their address using data from private companies. A few participants expressed neutral or positive reactions to the idea of data provided by private companies. One participant [FG9 – Low Education] did not offer strong opinions but thought the government having their data combined with private companies’ data would not necessarily be bad because these would only be statistics so it would just be another source of information. This participant [FG9 – Low Education] also shared that getting another source of information could be a good thing, and they hoped that the government would have their best interests at heart. Some of the participants in the Low Education focus group agreed that Google has up-to-date, accurate data so it would make sense for the Census Bureau to partner with Google. Another participant from a different focus group [FG7 – Higher Education] stated, “More people are using more information from Amazon than from Census, and it could potentially be more accurate. It could be broader categories that the government could use, like ethnicity. Statistically it could help out the outcome.” These positive reactions were very limited and even groups that had a positive impression of the frame [FG6 – Hispanic] disliked the idea of data from private companies being involved. We did not identify any patterns across the focus groups for the types of questions that came up because of the focus group characteristics, such as low trust or higher education. As one participant [FG7 – Higher Education] stated, “For what purpose is this? How will they utilize it? Who will have access to it? I have a lot of questions.” Another participant [FG5 – Low Trust] asked, “Why do you feel the need to do it? What do you expect to accomplish? How will it benefit the population?” One participant [FG1 – Low Trust] said they wanted to know “What data is being collected? Why is it needed? What problem is it actually solving?”

Many participants could easily see community benefits related to the creation of the database. Participants could see the benefit of creating the database to better understand individual communities and allocate resources more efficiently [FG4 – Young White; FG6 – Hispanic; FG7 – Higher Education; FG10 – Hispanic; FG11 – Young AA; FG12 – Older AA; FG3 – High Trust]. Other community benefits included funding for schools, parks, medical centers or hospitals, and public street maintenance. Four focus groups [FG10 – Hispanic; FG11 – Young AA; FG12 – Older AA; FG6 – Hispanic] discussed the possibility that the frame could help individuals receive government services or unemployment. Participants had a harder time thinking about personal benefits and many could think of no personal benefits when explicitly asked, even when the community benefits were clear [FG10 – Hispanic; FG11 – Young AA; FG12 – Older AA]. This theme of more concrete community benefits was also observed during the cognitive interviews completed in Subproject 1. Other benefits participants mentioned once are presented in the table below (Table 4.4).

Table 4.5 Five Potential Frame Benefits 1 Developing this database could mean that you are asked to fill out surveys less often because your information is already available. 2 Developing this database could help government agencies make better use of taxpayer money. 3 Developing this database could help your local government deliver services and benefits more efficiently. 4 Developing this database would mean that information and statistics about the country are more accurate. 5 Developing this database would help complete survey responses when information is missing. Benefit 1: Fewer Surveys Benefit 1 was not a compelling benefit for most participants, with many seeing it is as negative. Participants across four focus [FG4 – Young White; FG7 – Higher Education; FG9 – Low Education; FG12 – Older AA] groups saw the first benefit as negative because they believed it was important to fill out surveys to ensure that the information the government has access to is as up-to-date and accurate as possible. Three participants in the Low

4-14 Education focus group [FG9 – Low Education] were thinking about the decennial census and worried that data within the database would be outdated and inaccurate when surveys are collected less often. Three participants had similar sentiments in the Older African American focus group [FG12 – Older AA]. These three participants pointed out that filling out surveys less often could hurt you in that the information on file may be outdated. In the words of one participant [FG12 – Older AA], “It’s good to be able to re-up information with the government on where you are at in life…your current status.” This sentiment was echoed by another participant [FG12 – Older AA] who said, “I like the idea, but I would still want to update my information.” The other two focus groups [FG4 – Young White; FG7 – Higher Education] echoed similar worries about the accuracy of information being diminished if surveys were filled out less often. One participant from a Low Trust group [FG2 – Low Trust] mentioned that limiting the number of surveys someone takes would remove their right or opportunity to provide an opinion. Another participant from a Spanish-speaking group [FG6 – Hispanic] thought that it was beneficial for people to fill out surveys so that they can share their ideas and opinions, especially when there may be issues that need to be resolved. In addition to seeing fewer surveys as a negative, other participants were simply unclear as to how the completion of fewer surveys would be a concrete benefit. A few participants across a few focus groups said they did not mind filling out surveys [FG4 – Young White; FG9 – Low Education], while others mentioned that even when they receive surveys, they do not typically fill them out [FG6 – Hispanic]. Two participants [FG4 – Young White] did not feel like Benefit 1 was much of a benefit because they do not mind providing survey data. Another participant [FG6 – Hispanic] mentioned that she gets surveys but never completes them, so it was unclear to her whether Benefit 1 was truly a benefit. One participant [FG8 – Older White] also mentioned that surveys are normally optional anyway and that few people fill out surveys even if they receive them. Participants from two focus groups also discussed that there were not very many surveys anyway and they struggled to see Benefit 1 as a benefit. Participants in one focus groups [FG11 – Young AA] commented that they do not feel like they fill out a lot of government surveys currently and therefore they did not see this as a positive feature or benefit of the database. One participant from another focus group [FG8 – Older White] thought that it is not inconvenient to fill out surveys and that there are not so many of them. This idea that Benefit 1 was not a compelling benefit was also discovered during the cognitive interviews. The cognitive interview data illustrated that many people were aware only of the decennial census that they complete once every 10 years. They were unaware of other surveys run by the Census Bureau and did not see a clear benefit of completing fewer surveys. This finding was replicated in some of the focus groups, with some participants thinking the surveys mentioned in Benefit 1 referred only to the decennial census [FG9 – Low Education; FG12 – Older AA].

How will it affect privacy?” Participants from another Low Trust group [FG2 – Low Trust] had similar concerns about law enforcement accessing the database and using the database to identify people who had not paid their taxes. Participants in this group [FG2 – Low Trust] were concerned that the database would be used to find people who do not follow government rules. Participants in a Low Trust group [FG1 – Low Trust] had concerns about whether the database would be used to discriminate against people, with one participant elaborating “If you have all the power, we can use the power for good or for evil. 5-1 5. Summary and Conclusions In reviewing the focus group findings, several “themes” became evident. The following are overall findings from review of the focus group discussions: 1. Consistently, the low trust groups demonstrated the strongest opposition to the frame. They were suspicious of anything that the government was involved with and advocated for smaller government. Providing additional information about the frame or the potential benefits were met with cynicism and, at times, anger. The high trust groups were more open to the idea but had many questions that were left unanswered. 2. Participants were first provided with a general description of the frame, later followed by a more detailed description. In general, participants had a lot of questions after hearing both descriptions. Several of them felt like the Census Bureau is “holding back” and should provide a more detailed and transparent description of what the frame would include, where the data are coming from, why the frame is needed, how the data will be used, and how the frame will be protected. 3. Many of the participants thought the Census Bureau already has an established central database. The participants questioned why there would be a need to build a database when government agencies already work together and share information. Some participants thought it was possible that the Census Bureau did not have all the information they needed so that is why they are looking to gather information and involve private companies. However, this raised questions among some participants as to what types of data private companies could provide. 4. Some participants thought that medical or mental health records might be included in this database, although one participant explained that this wouldn’t be possible due to HIPAA. In general, participants conflated the topics of health information and government data. They did not recognize that health data are excepted from data sharing arrangements. 5. Some participants questioned whether personally identifiable information would be included in the database. In several cases, participants were unfamiliar with the term “statistics” and did not seem to have a good understanding of the type of data that would be included in the database, such as demographic information. Rather, some participants thought of all types of data as potentially being gathered. For example, government tax records, DMV records, health records, cell phone data, social media activity, etc.

5-2 6. When thinking about the Census Bureau’s motivation for creating the frame, several participants raised the topic of profits or monetization of the frame. They believed that the Census would seek to sell the data or make money from this product. 7. Participants tended to overestimate rates of data sharing between private companies and the government. Their discussions of data privacy assumed that the government had access to people’s social media data or purchase history from companies such as Google, Meta, and Amazon. 8. Overall, participants generally did not like the idea of gathering data from private companies to be included in the frame. Some felt it was "government overreach" and others questioned the quality of data from private companies. However, a few participants felt companies like Google and Amazon maintained up-to-date accurate data. 9. The participants only thought of a few individual benefits to building the frame but did recognize several potential community benefits. Those five perceived benefits are as follows: a. Benefit 1 (fewer surveys) was not found to be a compelling benefit for most participants, with many seeing it is as negative. Participants explained that they were fine with completing surveys and felt this would be the best way to maintain the most accurate information. b. Benefit 2 (better use of taxpayer money) was seen by some participants as a perceived benefit, with participants explaining that the database could positively impact community services such as parks, schools, day care centers, health services, and general infrastructure. c. Benefit 3 (deliver services more efficiently) was perceived as one of the most concrete benefits for participants. d. Benefit 4 (more accurate statistics) was not as clear of a benefit for many participants. Participants had trouble understanding the benefit of accurate statistics and information alone. They wanted more information about how these accurate statistics would be used to improve peoples’ lives. e. Benefit 5 (complete survey responses) was viewed as a benefit, and participants thought it would be worthwhile to have more complete information. 10. Several participants were generally concerned about a “loss of information” through hacking or other malicious intent. Privacy protections and potential data breaches were brought up within several of the focus groups.

Section 5 5-3 11. Some participants raised concerns about data quality. If information was compiled from other agencies, participants were not sure how accurate or up-to-date the information would be. 12. Several of the participants were not aware that the Census Bureau conducts research outside of the decennial census. This added to the confusion of some participants as they thought of the data collected during the decennial census and could not envision what data would be included in the frame. However, some participants in the Spanish-speaking group saw this as a benefit as they acknowledge that Latinx participation in the decennial census is low. The data compiled in this new database could help to “complete” the information. 13. Participants expressed preferences about being asked to provide consent for their data being included in the frame. The concept of whether they can opt out of the database was raised frequently. They also preferred to receive mail or communications campaigns announcing the project and would like to be able to review / correct their frame data. 14. Overall, participants were open to the Census Bureau heading up this effort when considering alternative agencies, such as the IRS. Participants generally felt that this would naturally fall on the Census Bureau as they are the agency that collects information about the U.S. population. These overall findings should be considered when planning for the next stage in the development of communications about the demographic frame. Addressing these concerns and questions will help to reduce the public’s concerns and add more transparency to the effort.

ii Abstract This report presents findings from the cognitive pretesting of redesigned mail materials that are mailed to respondents of the American Community Survey (ACS). The mail materials were redesigned as part of the ACS Strategic Framework Evaluation. The Strategic Framework was developed by the Census Bureau as a framework for evaluating ACS mail materials and developing new materials based on findings from relevant research literature (Oliver et al., 2017). The analytic framework was used to evaluate the various messages presented in the English-language mail materials in use by the ACS at that time (Schreiner et al., 2020). A cross- directorate team was formed to develop new mail materials based on the literature and informed by the analysis of production ACS materials. Part of this strategy involved selecting unique thematic messages to communicate in each of the five ACS mailings. The Census Bureau’s ACS Strategic Framework Mail Materials Design Team developed three new sets of materials, or treatments, to include in the 2021 Strategic Framework Mail Materials Test (2021 SFMMT). A fourth treatment, referred to as Outside Researcher (OR), was developed by researchers outside of the Census Bureau. All four treatments focused on using plain language principles, including the standard language required by the Census Bureau, and incorporating the intended thematic message of each mail piece recommended by the Strategic Framework. In addition to the changes to content, the Design Team incorporated design features such as the use of color, icons, pictures, and novel structure in their three treatments. Each of the three treatments focused on using these novel features in a particular way consistently across mailings to highlight key information and thematic messages in each mail piece. Overall, the iterative rounds of testing confirmed that all four treatments worked well to convey the messages outlined in the Strategic Framework. While the use of color, images, and novel structure in three of the treatments diverged from the typical approach to mail materials taken by the Census Bureau for the ACS, our findings showed that participants still viewed the materials as legitimate and motivating. Post-round revisions ensured that all materials were in good shape for an eventual experimental field test. 6 1 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY This report presents findings from the cognitive pretesting of redesigned mail materials that are mailed to respondents of the American Community Survey (ACS). The mail materials were redesigned as part of the ACS Strategic Framework Evaluation. The Strategic Framework was developed by the Census Bureau as a framework for evaluating ACS mail materials and developing new materials based on findings from relevant research literature (Oliver et al., 2017). The analytic framework was used to evaluate the various messages presented in the English-language mail materials in use by the ACS at that time (Schreiner et al., 2020). A cross- directorate team was formed to develop new mail materials based on the literature and informed by the analysis of production ACS materials. Part of this strategy involved selecting unique thematic messages to communicate in each of the five ACS mailings. The Census Bureau’s ACS Strategic Framework Mail Materials Design Team developed three new sets of materials, or treatments, to include in the 2021 Strategic Framework Mail Materials Test (2021 SFMMT). Each new treatment took a different holistic approach to conveying the suggested messages from the Strategic Framework evaluation recommendations. The Design Team had many ideas for changes that may be effective but no a priori reason to think one approach may be more effective than the others. These treatments were referred to as Classic with a Twist (CWT), Fresh Look (FL), and To the Point (TTP).1 All three treatments focused on using plain language principles, including the standard language required by the Census Bureau, and incorporating the intended thematic message of each mail piece recommended by the Strategic Framework. In addition to the changes to content, the Design Team incorporated design features such as the use of color, icons, pictures, and novel structure. Each of the three treatments focused on using these novel features in a particular way consistently across mailings to highlight key information and thematic messages in each mail piece. A fourth treatment, referred to as Outside Researcher (OR)2, was developed by researchers outside of the Census Bureau3. They started with some of the earlier Census Bureau designs and stripped away some of the wording to create materials with minimal text in a traditional letter format. While these materials did not follow the messaging suggested by the Strategic Framework reports, they adhered to the principle that reducing text makes the materials easier to read, which was one of the guiding principles for the Design Team. The newly designed materials were cognitively tested by Census Bureau researchers in the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM). The Design Team was interested in how participants perceived each of the four treatments. Specifically, the team was interested in how appealing they found each treatment, whether the use of plain language and novel design features increased readability and effectively highlighted the thematic messages, and whether each treatment increased the likelihood of responding to the ACS. Although the Design Team was interested in the performance of each treatment, the goal of cognitive testing was not to 1 Treatments were renamed for a later field test. Classic with a Twist was renamed the Icon Treatment. Fresh Look was renamed the Sidebar Treatment. To the Point was renamed the Column and Header Treatment. 2 The Outside Researcher treatment was renamed the Minimalist Treatment for the field test. 3 Judd Kessler from the University of Pennsylvania and Christine Exley from Harvard Business School.

7 identify which treatment performed best. All four treatments were intended to be used in a follow-up field test to assess their performance. Results of the field test can be found in Oliver, Contard, and Barth (2023). CBSM’s research team conducted three iterative rounds of cognitive testing with 63 participants. After each round, findings and recommended changes were presented to the project sponsors. The iterative approach allowed for changes made to the materials to be tested in subsequent rounds to evaluate whether they performed as intended. The goal of the cognitive interviews was to answer the following research questions: Questions about global design features: Q1. Does the use of color, images, and novel structure enhance the appeal of the letters? Does color affect readability or believability (perception of ‘official’ government mail)? (These features were only used in the CTW, FL, and TTP treatments.) Overall, participants reacted positively to the newly designed mail materials. Participants responded positively to the use of color, images, and novel structure in the letters. Any mention of the features affecting readability indicated that they improved readability. When explicitly probed, some participants did say that the use of these features made the mailing seem less official. However, many of these participants also indicated that other aspects of the mailing like the Census Bureau logo made the mailing seem official, so the novel features did not have a noticeable impact on believability. Q2. Do the strategies of reducing the amount of text and using plain language in the bodies of the letters improve readability and clarity of letter content? Efforts to improve the readability and clarity of the mail materials were successful. While there were no specific probes on the topic, interviewers were instructed to monitor for any indications that participants were having trouble reading or comprehending the letters. Aside from a couple of comments about one confusing sentence (discussed in section 6.7.2), participants did not indicate (explicitly or nonverbally) that the letters were difficult to read or comprehend. In every round, at least one participant from each treatment made spontaneous statements about the mailings being clear, easy to read, straight to the point, or understandable. Q3. Does Spanish messaging evoke any reaction? The use of Spanish messaging on the English-language letters did not evoke any particularly strong reactions during the cognitive interviews. Those participants that did comment on the messaging either made neutral statements noting that it was there, or positive comments acknowledging that the language would be useful for those who need it. Q4. Does including “OFFICIAL U.S. GOVERNMENT MAIL” on the envelope increase “believability” (M1 and M3 only)?

8 The wording “OFFICIAL U.S. GOVERNMENT MAIL” on the envelopes of Mailing 1 and Mailing 3 did increase legitimacy. However, the wording was not always noticed by participants. Other features like the Census Bureau logo and a box on the envelope which included the words, “YOUR RESPONSE IS REQUIRED BY LAW,” seemed to draw most of the attention, increasing believability. Since the wording did not draw much attention in Round 1, the font was made larger and bolder before Round 2. This change succeeded in drawing more attention to the wording, but other features on the envelope continued to make more of an impact on legitimacy. Q5. Do participants think that the treatment is a cohesive package? Do icons or the column and header/bullet format improve readability (CWT/TTP)? How do readers react to the sidebar design (FL)? Since participants saw each mail piece back-to-back and only saw one treatment prior to the side-by-side comparison, it was hard to gauge the extent to which they thought the treatment was a cohesive package. Some participants did make comments, while looking at later mail pieces, noting that there are certain distinct features that would clue them in to the fact that they had received previous mailings if they received them spaced out in the mail. These comments were usually about the Census Bureau logo and the use of the color green. Participants in the Classic with a Twist treatment generally seemed to like the icons and found them easy to read and understand. Participants in the Fresh Look treatment seemed to have a positive reaction to the sidebar. Participants in the To the Point treatment generally liked the column and header/bullet format of mailings and found the layout of this information easy to read and to understand. While there were a few comments about some of these features being unnecessary or not personally appealing, no one expressed strong negative reactions or indicated that the features would make them less likely to respond to the survey. Questions specific to mailings: Mailing 1 Q6. Do changes to mailings intended to increase trust and legitimacy actually convey that to the reader? Participants tended to perceive Mailing 1 as legitimate. Multiple aspects of the mailing contributed to this; the most frequently noted ones were the Census Bureau logo, the director’s signature, the content in the FAQs, and the messaging on the outside of the envelope. There were no changes made to the Mailing as a result of findings from this research question. Mailing 2 Q7. Does highlighting community benefits resonate with the reader? Are they turned off by some benefits or conversely are they inspired by some benefits (enough so to feel that

9 their response is important)? Does highlighting the use of ACS data by non-profit organizations resonate with the reader? Highlighting the ways in which responding to the ACS can benefit the community resonated with a majority of participants across all rounds. Participants often commented positively on the community benefits while looking at Mailing 2. For many participants, this was the aspect of the mail materials that they said would actually motivate them to respond to the survey. None of the benefits listed evoked negative reactions. However, the use of ACS data by non-profits did not resonate with participants. Mailing 3 Q8. Does using messages about civic duty resonate with the reader? Or does reading about “jury duty” and “paying taxes” irritate the reader? The sentences about civic duty helped participants understand the importance of completing the ACS and why it is required by law. Participants generally liked the inclusion of the sentences. However, in Round 1, the phrasing used in the Classic with a Twist and the To the Point treatments was seen as a bit harsh. As a result, we recommended revising those sentences using phrasing similar to the sentences in the Fresh Look treatment. The revised phrasing performed well in Rounds 2 and 3. Q9. Does using normative messaging resonate with the reader? Participants’ opinions on the messages that reference members of the community responding to the ACS were mixed. While a few participants felt like the message would encourage them to respond, most reactions were neutral, and the messaging did not evoke strong reactions in any participants. Mailing 5 Q10. How does implementing a commitment device affect self-response? Does the commitment device make participants think they should circle or check an option and mail this piece back to the Census Bureau? The inclusion of a due date as a commitment device in Mailing 5 was a strong motivating factor to respond to the ACS. Participants felt that the due date created a sense of urgency and would prompt them to take action quickly. Participants also liked that the commitment device mentions three ways to respond, noting that the new option to respond by phone will be a positive to some people. While a couple of participants said the “select one” or “choose one way” to respond feature made it seem like they should mail it back, they said it was also clear that they were not supposed to do so. Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four treatments. During the interview, participants were shown all five mailings in their assigned treatment one at a time and instructed to think aloud as they viewed the materials. Next, participants probed about reactions each mail piece (see Appendix A for interview protocol). After answering probes

10 about each mail piece, participants were shown all four treatments for selected mailings side by side. The side-by-side comparisons included think aloud technique and scripted probes. In addition to the research questions used to guide the overall approach to the cognitive interviews, interviewers were trained to note and probe on any confusion or issues participants may have during the interviews. At times, the cognitive interviewing team noticed recurring issues that suggested a need to revise the mail materials. These included confusion about the purpose of the instruction card in Mailing 1 and messaging about how it was not necessary to contact the Census Bureau to request a paper questionnaire. Changes made throughout the rounds of testing lessened participants’ confusion about these issues. We also tested changes to the cover of the questionnaire in Mailing 3 and language in Mailing 5 in response to recommendations from a National Academy of Sciences panel, convened before the third round of testing. The changes made to the questionnaire did not have a big impact. Participants were equally likely to prefer the original and revised versions. The changes made to the language in Mailing 5 successfully created a sense of urgency, which participants said would motivate them to respond. Overall, the iterative rounds of testing confirmed that the treatments worked well to convey the messages outlined in the Strategic Framework. While the use of color, images, and novel structure diverged from the typical approach to mail materials taken by the Census Bureau for the ACS, our findings showed that participants still viewed the materials as legitimate and motivating. Post-round revisions ensured that all materials were in good shape for an eventual experimental field test.

11 2 INTRODUCTION In an effort to increase self-response rates, reduce respondent burden, and reduce program costs for the American Community Survey (ACS), Census Bureau staff from the Decennial Statistical Studies Division (DSSD) and the American Community Survey Office (ACSO) developed the Strategic Framework project. The Strategic Framework project was a long-term multi-phase project that used a holistic approach to redesign the ACS Mail Materials. At the request of DSSD and ACSO, the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) conducted cognitive testing of four treatments of newly designed mail materials as part of the project. Researchers conducted three iterative rounds of cognitive testing on the mail materials to ensure all treatments were easy to understand and communicated intended messages. In each subsequent round, revisions were made to improve materials based on observations made in testing. Results of these cognitive interviews were used to produce the final versions of the Strategic Framework mail materials, which were experimentally field tested in September of 2021. This report presents the findings from the 63 cognitive interviews that CBSM conducted between November 2019 and March 2020. 3 STRATEGIC FRAMEWORK 3.1 Overview The Strategic Framework is a framework for survey messaging that was developed by researchers in DSSD and ACSO to evaluate the then current ACS mail materials (in 2017) and to develop new materials (Oliver et al., 2017). The Framework is based on best practices in survey communication and draws on findings related to theories of communication and behavior from various disciplines. The researchers used this analytic framework to evaluate all the messages presented in all the English-language mail materials in use by the ACS at that time (Schreiner et al., 2020). The mail materials included all letters, brochures, postcards, and envelopes used across five sequential mailings. The first and third mailings were envelopes with multiple materials, the second and fifth mailings were pressure-sealed reminders with three sealed perforated edges, and the fourth was a postcard (see Table 1). Analysts reviewed the materials and coded all the messages in the mail pieces, including symbolic messages such as the Census Bureau logo. The analysts organized the coded messages into four major categories: trust, benefits, burden reduction, and other. The Strategic Framework analysts concluded that the ACS materials presented too many messages to respondents; that some messages were repeated too often; that for some of the messages there was no evidence that they could motivate response to a survey; and there were messages that were proven to motivate a survey response that were not employed in the materials. The Strategic Framework team next created a strategy for developing alternative mail materials based on insights gained from their review of relevant research literature and informed by the findings of their analysis of production ACS materials. This strategy emphasized a holistic approach by which the entire sequence of mailings is considered a continuous communication with respondents over time. Each mail contact would strategically present new messages to

12 appeal to different types of respondents and avoid unnecessarily repetitious messages. The new sets of ACS mail materials that would convey legitimacy and promote trust in the Census Bureau and use plain language principles to facilitate readability, comprehension, and retention of messages. A cross-directorate team was convened to develop mail pieces based on the Strategic Framework that could be tested in a planned field experiment using the ACS Methods Panel, called the 2021 Strategic Framework Mail Materials Test. 3.2 Intended Messages The Strategic Framework prescribed a series of thematic messages that would be presented in sequence across five mailings (Oliver et al., 2017). The first mailing would focus on presenting the Census Bureau as a credible agency with a beneficial mission in order to build trust and confidence in the Bureau and establish the legitimacy of the survey request. The second request would highlight the benefits that the ACS provides to American communities, specifically in terms of providing useful data about communities to their leaders and decision- makers and linking those benefits to the recipient’s participation in the survey. The messages in the third mailing were intended to reduce the perceived burden associated with the survey request by using normative messages and emphasizing the different response mode options and the availability of telephone assistance. The fourth mailing would reiterate earlier messages in order to promote retention and consideration of those messages and, since it is a postcard sent within days of the third mailing, served as a quick reminder of the survey request. The fifth and final mailing was framed as a last chance to respond to the ACS using a self- response mode or possibly be visited by a Census Bureau interviewer in person. The thematic message in the fifth mailing was a sense of urgency to respond via a due date. 4 MATERIALS 4.1 ACS Mail Materials in the Strategic Framework Field Test The ACS Strategic Framework Mail Materials Design Team developed three new treatments to include in the 2021 Strategic Framework Mail Materials Test. A fourth treatment was developed by researchers outside of the Census Bureau using early drafts of the new materials developed by the Design Team4. Across all four treatments, there was a consistent focus on using plain language principles, including the standard language required by the Census Bureau. The three treatments developed by the Census Bureau’s Design Team focused on incorporating the thematic message of each mail piece recommended in the Strategic Framework. Short messages in Spanish were included on the backs of Mailing 3 and the bottom of Mailing 5 to increase self-response from recipients whose primary language is Spanish. Unlike the original mailings (see Figure 1 below), the three treatments designed by the Design Team incorporated green in various ways. The color was chosen to match the shade of green on the ACS questionnaire and to maintain consistency across mail pieces and create a branded feel. Each treatment uses a distinctive visual design and messaging. 4 Judd Kessler from the University of Pennsylvania and Christine Exley from Harvard Business School.

In the initial SF mail package, the Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) brochure and the multi-lingual brochure were removed (FAQs were added to the back of the invitation letter, and multi-lingual text was added to the instruction card). In the third SF mailing, the instruction card and FAQ brochure were removed, and the back of the letter contained instructions in Spanish. Figure 1. See Appendix B for all mail materials used in cognitive testing, including all revised materials across the three rounds. 4.1.1 Classic with A Twist The “Classic with a Twist” (CWT) treatment was designed to be a clean-cut take on the original mailings. Mail pieces in this treatment had a more traditional look and feel, using the standard structure for letters. The “twist” in this treatment is the incorporation of clean design elements

15 and content structure intended to highlight information and simplify language. Whenever possible, plain language was used to convey the intended message(s) of each mailing using as few words as possible. Visually, this treatment differed from the original mailings with the use of icons and the way that green was used. Each icon was designed to visually represent the adjacent text, quickly indicating the point of key pieces of information. Except for pressure-sealed mailings, which were limited to black and white, icons in all other mailings were green. In addition to green icons, this treatment also included boxes with a shaded green background to call out key information. Overall, the treatment intended to keep each mailing as short and clean as possible to ensure recipients read the mailing in its entirety. Knowing that some individuals choose to skim mailings regardless of length, the visual elements were intended to increase the likelihood that individuals skimming the letter would be drawn to the information most likely to motivate them to self-respond to the ACS. 4.1.2 Fresh Look The “Fresh Look” (FL) design was created to give a traditional letter a new graphical look and appeal. The distinguishing feature of this set of mailings is the use of a colorful sidebar placed to the left or right of the body of the letter. This design was inspired by the initial invitation letter used for the 1997 Economic Census in which a quote from Alan Greenspan, then-chairman of the Federal Reserve Bank, about the importance of the Economic Census to the American economy was presented in a sidebar. The sidebars in the Fresh Look mailings were used to highlight targeted messages, which allowed for reduced and more-focused text in the body of the mailing. The addition of the sidebar also reduced the margins for the body of the text, which was hypothesized to have the added benefit of making the body text easier to read. The sidebars were shaded green, except for the black-and-white Figure 2. Example from the Classic with a Twist treatment Figure 3. Example from the Fresh Look treatment

16 mailings, and contained colorful images such as a representation of the 50 States and Puerto Rico, silhouettes of small-town and city skylines, etc. 4.1.3 To the Point The “To the Point” design (TTP) was based on a minimalist approach, allowing the reader to get “to the point” of the mail piece quickly. The distinctive visual element of the TTP mailings is the use of two-column sections within the bodies of the letters to draw attention to concise, easily readable targeted messages. Two of the mailings presented headers in green. The headings have bold-printed text containing questions or topics hypothesized to be salient to participants, which are arrayed next to text addressing those points. This design was intended to approximate the effect of a Frequently Asked Questions document whereby salient topics are introduced and then addressed. The third mailing used a similar two-column section to present a short, bulleted list of ways that local leaders can use ACS data to address community needs. As with the CWT treatment, the instructions and the survey website URL were presented in a green-shaded box. The visual theme of headers in green text was repeated in the full FAQs on the back of the letter. 4.1.4 Outside Researcher The “Outside Researcher” design (OR) focused on simplicity and repetition of main concepts to communicate clearly the most critical information to potential participants and did not incorporate novel visual elements. Compared to the other experimental letters, the content and structure of the OR letters was more typical of production ACS letters, though with significantly fewer words. The OR letters used brief, focused paragraphs that emphasized the mandatory nature of the survey, response mode options, the availability of telephone assistance, etc., with key text highlighted in bold print. Decisions on whether and how to incorporate recommended revisions to the OR treatment were left to the discretion of the outside researchers who designed the materials. Figure 4. 17 5 STUDY METHODOLOGY After the draft mail materials were created, we conducted 63 cognitive interviews in the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area from November 2019 to March 2020. Cognitive interviews were conducted by four experienced interviewers from the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) who were trained on the cognitive interview protocol prior to testing. The goal of the cognitive interviews was to determine whether the newly developed materials were successful in communicating the messaging in the Strategic Framework, designed to increase response. We were also specifically interested in whether the design features in each treatment helped convey those messages and how those design features impacted readability and believability. Some research questions were about the design features across all mailings, while others were specific to individual mail pieces. There were no research questions specific to the Mailing 4 postcard. Questions about global design features: Q1. Does the use of color, images, and novel structure enhance the appeal of the letters? Does color affect readability or believability (perception of ‘official’ government mail)? Q2. Do the strategies of reducing the amount of text and using plain language in the bodies of the letters improve readability and clarity of letter content? Q3. Does Spanish messaging evoke any reaction? Q4. Does including “OFFICIAL U.S. GOVERNMENT MAIL” on the envelope increase “believability” (M1 and M3 only)? Q5. Do participants think that the treatment is a cohesive package? Do icons or the column and header/bullet format improve readability (CWT/TTP)? How do readers react to the sidebar design (FL)? Questions specific to mailings: Mailing 1 Q6. Do changes to mailings intended to increase trust and legitimacy actually convey that to the reader? Mailing 2 Q7. Does highlighting community benefits resonate with the reader? Are they turned off by some benefits or conversely are they inspired by some benefits (enough so to feel that their response is important)? Does highlighting the use of ACS data by non-profit organizations resonate with the reader? Mailing 3 Q8. Does using messages about civic duty resonate with the reader? Or does reading about “jury duty” and “paying taxes” irritate the reader? Q9. Does using normative messaging resonate with the reader?

18 Mailing 5 Q10. How does implementing a commitment device affect self-response? Does the commitment device make participants think they should circle or check an option and mail this piece back to the Census Bureau? 5.1 Recruitment We targeted participants who represented a variety of demographic characteristics (i.e., sex, race, ethnicity, household income, educational attainment, and age). Recruitment methods included the following: (1) advertisements through Craigslist.com and (2) a broadcast message distributed to all Census Bureau employees who work in the headquarters building in Suitland, MD and may have family or friends interested in participating. Potential participants who contacted CBSM regarding interest in the study were administered a screener by telephone. The screener asked questions about a participant’s demographic characteristics and the handling of the mail in the participant’s household. We only recruited participants who handled the mail for their household or shared that responsibility with other household members in order to target the population of people who would interact with these mailings in real life. The cognitive interviews lasted approximately one hour and took place either at the Census Bureau headquarters in Suitland, MD or at a convenient location in the D.C. metropolitan area. Each participant who participated in the study received $40 in compensation. 5.2 Cognitive Interview Participants While we aimed to recruit participants with diverse demographic characteristics, there were nearly twice as many females as males in the sample. The majority of participants were either White or Black with a small number of participants identifying as either Asian, Middle Eastern, or two or more races. Eight of the 63 participants were Hispanic. The income distribution was close to being balanced across five income ranges. In terms of education, participants were almost evenly split between those with higher education (Bachelor’s and Post-Bachelor’s) and those without at least a Bachelor’s. The age distribution was fairly balanced. See Table 2 for a more detailed breakdown.
