20 5.3 Data Collection At the start of the interview, participants were told they were going to look at some envelopes, letters, postcards, and the questionnaire that they would get in the mail if their address had been selected to respond to a national survey called the American Community Survey. Participants were given a consent form to sign. Interviewers briefly explained the content of the consent form before giving the participant time to review the form and ask questions. Interviewers explained that participation is optional, all information participants provide is confidential, and that the form also asks for their permission to have this session audio recorded. When applicable, interviewers informed participants that the interview was being observed. Mockups of the mailing materials were used in the interviews. All materials were assembled as they would appear in production. For convenience, during the interviews, outgoing envelopes for mailings 1 and 3 were not sealed. However, the pressure-sealed mailings in mailings 2 and 5 were sealed and required tearing the perforated edges to open them. Participants were informed that mockups were being used for the interview and may not look quite as nice as they would if they received them in the mail. Each participant was initially shown materials from a single treatment. Before showing the first mail pieces, interviewers explained the format of the interview. The participants were told they would be shown different mail pieces one by one. Interviewers handed the participant each mail piece vertically, pointing towards the participant to avoid impacting which side the participant looked at first. After they finished with a piece of mail, the interviewer would take it back and hand them the next piece, explaining each mailing as it was introduced. Interviewers asked participants to “think aloud,” verbalizing their thoughts as they looked at the materials (Willis 2015). During this portion of the interview, interviewers observed how participants interacted with the materials, noting which way the envelope was facing when opened, which sides of materials they looked at and in what order, and whether participants appeared to pay attention to the content (see Appendix A for observation checklists). After participants had looked at all five mailings, interviewers administered a set of retrospective probes for each mailing. Interviewers handed each mailing back to the participant when asking probes specific to the mailing (see Appendix A). In addition to the scripted probes in the protocol, interviewers asked spontaneous probes in response to observations and comments made during the think aloud portion of the interview. Once all scripted and spontaneous probes were asked about the mailings in the participant’s treatment, there was a side-by-side comparison of all four treatments for selected mailings. In Rounds 1 and 2, the side-by-side comparisons were done on Mailing 1 (letter only) and Mailing 4 (postcard). In Round 3, the comparisons were done on Mailing 2 (open pressure seal mailer) and Mailing 3 (letter only). The four versions of each mailing were shuffled prior to the interview and placed down on the table in varying orders. Participants were instructed to take a minute to look over the four versions of the mailing, thinking aloud as they did so. After participants looked over the materials, interviewers asked scripted and spontaneous probes

21 similar to those used in the previous portion of the interview. Interviews concluded with debriefing questions about their overall impressions of the mail materials. It is important to note that one limitation of cognitive interviews is the back-to-back review of the mail materials. This may make features of the mail pieces stand out more than they would if they were received over a period of weeks in production. 5.4 Analysis After each round, interviewers completed individual summaries for each of the interviews they conducted using a standard template. Personally identifiable information (PII) such as names were not included in the summaries and participants were referred to using ID numbers. Summaries included interviewer observations on how the participant interacted with each material (e.g., what they looked at and how closely they read the materials), think aloud feedback from participants, and responses to probing questions. Researchers also provided high-level responses to the research questions for each participant. All summaries were compiled into one document which researchers independently reviewed. We then held a consensus meeting to answer the research questions, summarize results, and agree on a set of recommendations for production materials. The compiled summary document and discussion from the consensus meetings formed the basis of the cognitive interview findings. 6 COGNITIVE INTERVIEW FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS The sections outlining the research questions below (Sections 6.1 through 6.4.2) will be used to provide a brief high-level summary of findings for each research question across all three rounds of interviews. Subsections will then provide a more detailed discussion of each research question, presenting findings broken out by round. 6.1 Research Questions: Global Design features Q1. Does the use of color, images, and novel structure enhance the appeal of the letters? Does color affect readability or believability (perception of ‘official’ government mail)? Q2. Do the strategies of reducing the amount of text and using plain language in the bodies of the letters improve readability and clarity of letter content? Q3. Does Spanish messaging evoke any reaction? Q4. Does including “OFFICIAL U.S. GOVERNMENT MAIL” on the envelope increase “believability” (Mailing 1 and Mailing 3 only)? Q5. Do participants think that the treatment is a cohesive package? Do icons or the column and header/bullet format improve readability (CWT/TTP)? How do readers react to the sidebar design (FL)?

22 6.1.1 Research Question 1: Does the use of color, images, and novel structure enhance the appeal of the letters? Does color affect readability or believability (perception of ‘official’ government mail)? Overall, participants responded positively to the use of color, images, and novel structure in the letters. Feelings about these elements seemed to be a matter of personal preference. Of those participants that commented on these features, more made positive or neutral comments than negative. Any mention of the features affecting readability indicated that they improved readability. Previous research has shown that mail materials for government surveys can effectively use color and images judiciously to catch the eye and draw attention to important information (Dillman et al., 1996; Leslie, 1997; Whitcomb & Porter, 2004; Hagedorn et al., 2014; Reingold, 2014). However, one study on ACS mail materials found that "colorful, image-rich, or friendly designs” were less likely to be perceived as coming from the government than materials with straightforward designs and typeface (Walker, 2014, p.14). Since the newly designed materials incorporate the use of color, icons, images, and novel structure, the Design Team wanted to assess whether these features impacted readers’ perceptions of the new materials being official government mail. When explicitly probed, some participants did say that the use of these features made it seem less official than the version that does not use the features. However, many of these participants also indicated that other aspects of the mailing like the Census Bureau logo made the mailing seem official, so the novel features did not have a noticeable impact on believability. We continued to use novel structure and visual features in later rounds of interviews but made small changes to refine their use. 6.1.1.1 Round 1 Findings Five of the 16 participants in Round 1 commented on the use of color in the letter during the think aloud portion of the interview. Three of the five made positive comments, one wondered why green was used, and one noted the color and said the letter didn’t need to be “jazzed up.” Two participants commented on the use of images or novel structure while thinking aloud – one positively and one negatively. Four participants received the Classic with a Twist treatment in Round 1. Of the four, two participants commented on the color of the mailings during think aloud. None commented on the icons during think aloud. When asked what they noticed about Mailing 1, three participants made comments about it seeming official, being from Census, or from the government, conveying trust and legitimacy. Four participants received the Fresh Look treatment. One participant noticed and mentioned the color during think aloud, but the other three did not. This participant seemed to respond to the coloring on the instruction card. During probing, one of the other three participants added that color was one of the first things they noticed. The two participants who commented on the use of images and novel structure were both from the Fresh Look treatment. One commented on multiple mailings saying that he liked the pictures and the sidebar. The other felt that the use of the sidebar made them less likely to read its contents. “The box over here on the side - the words are little, they're in italics, they're separated from the body of this - I didn't even look at them. They don't interest me when they're little and separated. My eye just kind of... my

23 brain sort of filters them out. I don't even see them, almost, like they're decoration or something,” (Round 1, FL). Four participants received the To the Point mail treatment. One participant commented on the color of the mailings during think aloud. "I liked the green color. There's green on all of them, but this one you really notice. And the reason I like it is because it makes it non-government looking,” (Round 1, FL). The Outside Researcher materials were in grayscale so there was no color to comment on. There were also no icons used in the OR mail pieces. However, one participant said that the fact that the instruction card has green was odd since the rest of the mailings are in grayscale. Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes to the use of color, images, or novel structure after Round 1. 6.1.1.2 Round 2 Findings Seven of the 15 participants in Round 2 commented on color when looking at the materials in their treatment. Four of them commented spontaneously during the think aloud portion, and the other three commented on color in response to probes. Six of the participants commented on the use of icons or novel structure (column and header/bullet format or the sidebar). Of all of the comments on color, icons, and structure, all but one were neutral or positive. One participant who received the TTP treatment said she initially thought the use of green made the mail pieces look like junk mail during the think aloud. Once she opened it, she said it looks legitimate if you continue reading. The interviewer later probed on what she meant during think aloud. "Just because I saw this beginning of this green box… that just kind of stands out to me and it looks like those refinancing and those surveys that get sent to your house every day… that don't hold pertinent information or anything… that doesn't really stand out to me as something that the Census would have... I would think they're asking for money,” (Round 2, TTP). None of the participants who received the CWT treatment commented on color when looking at the CWT materials. Only one explicitly commented on the icons. For Mailing 2, when asked if she noticed anything in the letter about why she should respond, this participant said that she noticed the icons with reasons on why to respond. She did not comment on whether she liked or disliked the icons. Two of the participants who received the FL treatment commented on both color and the sidebar structure. When asked what she first noticed about Mailing 2, one participant mentioned the sidebar, "I noticed this little blurb on the side about the, it helps you plan parks and playgrounds and all that,” (Round 2, FL). When asked what she first noticed about Mailing 4, she commented on the color green and the picture of the community. Another participant commented on the use of color tying the mail pieces together. When reading Mailing 3, a participant in Round 2 (FL) said, “All the color schemes are the same,” and said this would help

24 him remember the previous mailings. He also noted that the green sidebar contained another reason to participate. Four of the five participants who received the TTP treatment commented on either color or the use of the column and headers/bullets. In addition to the one negative comment on color discussed above, two others commented positively about the use of color. One noted the use of color in Mailings 1, 3, and 4, saying it drew his eyes to the green text or green boxes in each mailing. He also said the use of green throughout the mailings made it clear that they were related. During probing on Mailing 2, when asked if there is anything in the letter about why they should respond, three of the five participants mentioned the bullet points drawing their attention to the reasons. "Well, these bullet points, these are things I care about. And in fact, these are things that people complain about if they don't get,” (Round 2, TTP). As in the previous round, although the mail pieces specific to the OR treatment did not contain color, the instruction card that was included in all treatments contains green. One of the five participants who received the OR treatment in Round 2 commented on the color of the instruction card. Though he questioned the use of color, his reaction was neutral. “This is the only thing that has green - what's the point?" (Round 2, OR). The use of color was spontaneously commented on much more in the side-by-side comparisons. All spontaneous comments on color during the side-by-side comparison were positive. Round 2, TTP: “The colors make it seem more inviting.” Round 2, CWT: [Comparing CWT and OR] "[The color] makes me want to read the letter a little bit more. I'm more likely to read the letter than throw it away because it catches my attention.” Round 2, OR: "This one [TTP]. The color, the separation into the paragraphs [in the FAQ style]. This definitely makes it easier on the eyes.” When probed on if the side-by-side letters look like official government mail, participants commented that the OR version looked more official than the others, but that the ones with color still look official. Round 2, TTP: "Honestly [OR] probably looks the most official because it's the most boring, but I think [TTP] is the most effective at communicating information and it still looks official enough.” Round 2, OR: "Yeah. I mean normally, I haven't seen official government mail that used color, I don't think I have. Normally there's not a lot of color. I mean maybe very little. But yeah, I mean it's still… usually what tells you that it's definitely official government mail is the envelope. I always feel that the most important thing is the envelope.” Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes to the use of color, images, or novel structure after Round 2.

27 6.1.2 Research Question 2: Do the strategies of reducing the amount of text and using plain language in the bodies of the letters improve readability and clarity of letter content? Efforts to improve the readability and clarity of the mail materials were successful. While there were no specific probes on the topic, interviewers were instructed to monitor for any indications that participants were having trouble reading or comprehending the letters. Aside from a couple of comments about one confusing sentence (discussed in section 6.7.2), participants did not indicate (explicitly or nonverbally) that the letters were difficult to read or comprehend. In every round, at least one participant from each treatment made spontaneous statements about the mailings being clear, easy to read, straight to the point, or understandable. 6.1.2.1 Round 1 Findings Participants in Round 1 appeared to read and comprehend the letters with ease. One participant expressed confusion about one set of sentences which was later revised for clarity (see section 6.7.2). There were no noticeable indications that participants were struggling to read or understand the content of the letters. Statements during the think aloud portion and responses to probes suggested that the content was interpreted as intended. In addition to the lack of comments about confusion or difficulty reading, participants made spontaneous comments about the readability of the letters. Three participants in the CWT treatment, and two each in the FL, TTP, and OR treatments commented on the readability or clarity of the letters. Some of these participants made multiple comments throughout the interview. Round 1, CWT: “I was able to read everything. The language was clear.” Round 1, FL: “I read it quickly. It’s straight to the point, has all the info right here. This is cool.” Round 1, TTP: “They're easy to read. They make sense.” Round 1, OR: “Everything was explained and understandable.” Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes to the amount of text or use of plain language after Round 1. 6.1.2.2 Round 2 Findings As in Round 1, efforts to improve readability and clarity appeared to be successful in Round 2. There was another mention about a specific set of sentences in Mailing 1 being confusing. These were revised after Round 2. There were no other comments or non-verbal cues suggesting that the letters were hard to read or confusing. Spontaneous comments were made about the readability and clarity of each treatment (one in CWT, two in FL, three in TTP, and one in OR). Participants referred to the letters as simple, straightforward, to the point, clear, and easy to understand.

28 Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes to the amount of text or use of plain language after Round 2. There was a separate recommendation to rephrase a confusing sentence after Round 2. This is discussed in detail in section 6.7.2. 6.1.2.3 Round 3 Findings Round 3 confirmed the findings in the previous rounds. Since the confusing sentences had been rephrased, there were no comments about the content being hard to read or comprehend. Participants in every treatment spontaneously commented on the readability (four in CWT, one in FL, five in TTP, and one in OR). Round 3, CWT: “Everything is easy to read, straightforward information.” Round 3, CWT: “It's very easy to understand for people." Round 3, TTP: "I kinda like the format. That is very precise and it's easy to look at and understand. But the questions are good questions, questions I would ask.” In Round 3, one participant was a native Spanish speaker who was in the United States to improve their English. This participant read every mailing very closely. They were able to comprehend the content fairly easily. They only expressed difficultly one time, asking if they could use their phone to translate the word “due.” The fact that a non-native English speaker was able to read and comprehend the mailings with relative ease is further proof that efforts to increase readability were successful. Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes to the amount of text or use of plain language after Round 3. 6.1.3 Research Question 3. Does Spanish messaging evoke any reaction? The team was interested in learning whether respondents had a positive, neutral, or negative reaction to the new use of Spanish on the letters.6 The use of Spanish messaging on English- language letters did not evoke any particularly strong reactions during the cognitive interviews. Those participants that did comment on the messaging either made neutral statements noting that it was there, or positive comments acknowledging that the language would be useful for those who need it. Since the messaging performed well without evoking any negative reactions, no changes were made to the Spanish messaging throughout the three rounds of interviews. 6.1.3.1 Round 1 Findings Overall, the Spanish messaging was perceived well in Round 1. Nine of the 16 participants in Round 1 commented on the Spanish messaging while looking at the mail materials. Many of 6 The 2017 production materials included Spanish only on the instruction card.

She understood that she could complete the interview in Spanish but said she would do it in English because she is in the United States to improve her English. Does including “OFFICIAL U.S. GOVERNMENT MAIL” on the envelope increase “believability” (M1 and M3 only)? Overall, the wording “OFFICIAL U.S. GOVERNMENT MAIL” on the envelopes of Mailing 1 and Mailing 3 did work to increase believability. However, the wording was not always noticed by participants. Other features like the Census Bureau logo and a box on the envelope that included the words, “YOUR RESPONSE IS REQUIRED BY LAW” seemed to draw most of the attention, increasing believability. Those that did notice the “OFFICIAL U.S. GOVERNMENT MAIL” wording when looking at the envelopes did say that it contributed to the legitimacy of the mailing. Since the wording did not draw much attention in Round 1, the font was made larger and bolded before Round 2. This change did succeed in drawing more attention to the wording, but other features on the envelope continued to make more of an impact on legitimacy. 6.1.4.1 Round 1 Findings Four of the 16 participants in Round 1 made unprompted comments about the words “OFFICIAL U.S. GOVERNMENT MAIL” on the envelopes while thinking aloud. Three of the participants who received the CWT treatment noticed “Official U.S. Government Mail” on the envelope and said that it did contribute to making the mailing look official. One of the three did not notice “Official U.S. Government Mail” until the third mailing, though. The fourth participant had not noticed that label and said it was too small to be noticeable

31 compared to other things on the envelope. They still felt the mailing was legitimate, but for other reasons, like the Census logo. None of the participants who received the FL treatment commented on the “Official U.S. Government Mail” on the envelope during think aloud. When asked during probing, three of the four participants said that they did notice the wording. Two of the participants that noticed felt that other wording/logos on the mailing made the mailing more official than this wording did, but the remaining two participants (one who noticed, and one who did not) felt that this wording did contribute to them considering the mailing as official. One participant who received the TTP treatment commented on the “Official U.S. Government Mail” label during think aloud and said the envelope “looks official.” Two other participants also mentioned the mailing looked official during think aloud, mentioning other things like the logo or that it is from the Census Bureau. None of the participants who received the OR treatment mentioned noticing this language on the mailing. However, during think aloud, one participant said they still felt the mailing looked official. When asked about the wording during probing, two participants in this treatment said the wording did increase the legitimacy of the mailing. Recommendation(s): Since not many participants saw the “OFFICIAL U.S. GOVERNMENT MAIL” wording in Round 1, we recommended increasing the font size of this wording and bolding it to make it more prominent. This change was incorporated for Round 2. 6.1.4.2 Round 2 Findings Two of the 20 participants made an unprompted comment about the wording while first looking at the envelope. When asked if they noticed the wording during probing, an additional eight of the 20 participants said they noticed it. Of the 20 participants, 11 indicated that the wording made the mailing seem official. The interviewer followed up with one of the participants who commented on the wording while thinking aloud by asking a probe about what she thought about the wording. She responded, “[This wording] makes it look more important. Also ‘Your Response is Required by Law’. I feel like I trust this box because it says, ‘Official U.S. Government Mail,’” (Round 1, CWT). Another participant said the envelope looked important. When asked what about it looks important, she said, “How it says, ‘Official U.S. Government Mail,’” (Round 1, FL). Six gave neutral responses, with most saying that the other elements of the envelope would let them know it is official mail. Three participants made comments about how it did not mean much to them, including sentiments such as anyone can put that there or scammers try to make their mail look like official government mail: “Oh yeah, I saw. I think in today’s world, anyone can put that on there. This is the unfortunate world we’re living in. It’s hard to know who to trust,” (Round 2, FL). Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes to the envelope after Round 2.

When asked if there was anything about the mailing that would make her more likely to respond, one participant said, “The ‘official U.S. government mail’ part makes it look legitimate, but I would definitely double check. Throwing it to the side, and ‘I can get back to that later, there’s no rush,” (Round 3, FL). Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes to the envelope after Round 3. 6.1.5 Research Question 5: Do participants think that the treatment is a cohesive package? Do icons or the column and header/bulleted format improve readability (CWT/TTP)? How do readers react to the sidebar design (FL)? Since participants saw each mail piece back-to-back and only saw one treatment prior to the side-by-side comparison, it was hard to gauge the extent to which they thought the treatment was a cohesive package. Some participants did make comments while looking at later mail pieces noting that there are certain distinct features that would clue them in to the fact that they had received previous mailings if they received them spaced out in the mail. These comments were usually about the Census Bureau logo and the use of the color green. Participants in the Classic with a Twist treatment generally seemed to like the icons and found them easy to read and understand. Participants in the Fresh Look treatment seemed to have a positive reaction to the sidebar. Participants in the To the Point treatment generally liked the column and header/bullet format of mailings and found the layout of this information easy to read and understand. While there were a few comments about some of these features being unnecessary or not personally appealing, no one expressed strong negative reactions or indicated that the features would make them less likely to respond to the survey. Since the design features of each treatment were consistent across all mailings and did not change across the rounds, this section discusses how each treatment performed as a cohesive design overall. Do icons or the column and header/bullet format improve readability (CWT/TTP)?

Do changes to mailings intended to increase trust and legitimacy actually convey that to the reader? Participants tended to perceive Mailing 1 as legitimate. There were no changes made to the mailing as a result of findings to this research question. 6.2.1 Round 1 Findings When reviewing Mailing 1 initially, eight of the sixteen participants made unprompted comments about the mailing looking official. After reviewing Mailing 1, participants were asked retrospective probing questions about what they noticed when reviewing. Seven participants commented that it seemed official, either noting that it was from the Census Bureau or from the government in general. Three of these participants were in the Classic with a Twist treatment and two participants each were in the To the Point treatment and the Outside Researcher treatment. Participants mentioned many aspects of the mailing that helped with legitimacy, including the Census logos, director’s signature, content on the envelope, and the content in the Frequently Asked Questions section.

35 The FAQs were on the back of the letter and fourteen of the sixteen participants had looked at the back of the letter during the think aloud. Participants especially liked the FAQs, as they thought they were clear and answered any questions they may have. Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes specific to this research question after Round 1. 6.2.2 Round 2 Findings When reviewing Mailing 1 initially during the think aloud, seven participants made unprompted comments that the mailing looked official. Does highlighting community benefits resonate with the reader? Does highlighting the use of ACS data by non-profit organizations resonate with the reader? Highlighting the ways in which responding to the ACS can benefit the community resonated with a majority of participants across all rounds. Participants often commented positively on the community benefits while looking at Mailing 2. The benefits that resonated most with a given participant seemed to be a matter of personal preference or connection. The use of ACS data by non- profits did not resonate with participants. Across all three rounds, only one person mentioned the use of the data by non-profits. 6.3.1 Round 1 Findings Three participants spontaneously brought up the community benefits when initially looking at the mailing – one in the CWT treatment and two in the TTP treatment. 37 that it “determined funding.” "I like that it's really explaining what the American Community Survey is. That it's going to help determine funding for local opportunities. Additionally, two participants in the FL treatment and one in the OR treatment mentioned community benefits in response to this probe. Participants did not indicate a strong preference for certain benefits, and no one mentioned anything they did not like. The words “it benefits the community” came up multiple times. Jobs, training, as well as infrastructure like roads and parks came up multiple times in the comments, as well as helping veterans and the elderly. So, this doesn't really apply to me, but I know I have an elderly neighbor, I know I have a disabled neighbor. So, these things would benefit them. So, I would definitely take the survey. 38 participant mentioned the benefits as a secondary reason after the fact that it was required by law. Does using messages about civic duty resonate with the reader? Or does reading about “jury duty” and “paying taxes” irritate the reader? Q9. Does using normative messaging resonate with the reader? 6.4.1 Research Question 8: Does using messages about civic duty resonate with the reader? Or does reading about “jury duty” and “paying taxes” irritate the reader? The following sentences about civic duty were used in each treatment at the start of testing: • CWT: “Responding is a civic duty much like paying taxes or responding to jury duty.” • FL: “Just as the law requires us to report for jury duty, pay taxes, and earn a license to drive, it also requires us to respond to this survey.” • TTP: “Responding to this survey is a civic responsibility-similar to voting or serving on a jury” There was no civic duty message in the OR treatment. The sentences about civic duty helped participants understand the importance of completing the ACS and understand why it is required by law. Participants generally liked the inclusion of the sentences. However, in Round 1, the phrasing used in the Classic with a Twist and the To the Point treatments was seen as a bit harsh. As a result, we recommended revising those

41 sentences using phrasing that is similar to the sentences in the Fresh Look treatment. The revised phrasing performed well in Rounds 2 and 3. 6.4.1.1 Round 1 Findings Participants generally seemed to like the sentence about civic duty and seemed to understand the importance of completing the ACS when it is compared to other duties that are required by law. A participant in Fresh Look said the following: Round 1, FL: "That's good. That makes it… I have never read anything like that. Now I would really sit down and be like ok, let me do this. Let's see what this is about." Interviewer: "What about that sentence would make you do it?" Round 1, FL: "Take it seriously? Because I see pay taxes, jury duty, and license to drive. So, they're basically stressing the point like it's really important to do this.” However, four of the eight participants in the CWT and TTP treatments felt that the language was a bit too harsh, even if they agreed that it presented examples of other civic duties. A participant in the Classic with a Twist treatment said the following: Round 1, CWT: "Now that seemed to be a little intimidating… 'or responding to jury duty' if you're not a registered voter, are you still eligible to be on the jury? When I hear or read ‘paying taxes’, that's like if you don't pay your taxes, we'll throw you in jail or we'll penalize you. That's the part I would say, that's what I correlate with. If I don't pay taxes like... If I don't fill out this form, will they put me in jail?" Recommendation(s): After Round 1, we recommended considering revising the civic duty sentences in CWT and TTP to soften the language. We suggested the sentence that was previously tested by CBSM in a 2017 Mail Test as a jumping off point when starting to think of how to rephrase them (Martinez et. al., 2018). The sentence in the 2017 Mail Test materials read, “Just as people are required to report for jury duty, get a driver's license in order to drive, pay their taxes, and report their income, they also have the obligation to respond to this Census Bureau survey.” The civic duty sentence in the Fresh Look treatment already used similar phrasing, so no changes were recommended for that treatment. In response to this suggestion, the following changes were made to the CWT and OR letters: To the Point Round 1 text: “Responding to this survey is a civic responsibility—similar to voting or serving on a jury.” Revised: “Just as we are required to report for jury duty, file taxes, and earn a license to drive, we are also required to respond to this survey.” Classic with a Twist Round 1 text: “Responding is a civic duty much like paying taxes or responding to jury duty.” Revised text: “Just as the law requires people to report for jury duty, file taxes, or earn a license to drive, it also requires people to respond to this survey.”

Because if this was just as important as jury duty or filing taxes, then it’s important,” (Round 2, CWT). However, as in Round 1, the civic duty sentence did not resonate with a few participants. However, as in the first two rounds, this did not resonate with a few participants. Three participants found this to be off-putting: one participant was in CWT, one participant was in FL, and one participant was in TTP. One participant, who was in CWT, said the duties listed are not comparable to completing the ACS. Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes specific to this research question after Round 3. 6.4.2 Research Question 9: Does using normative messaging resonate with the reader? Normative messages are intended to evoke normative beliefs, or “beliefs about whether important individuals or groups in a person’s life would perform the behavior and whether those individuals or groups would approve of them performing the behavior” (Oliver et al.,

43 2017, p.6). The following sentences are the normative messages that were used in each treatment: • CWT: “Many households across the nation have already responded to this survey. We need your response too.” • FL: “Millions of households participate in the American Community Survey every year.” • TTP: “Many households have already responded. We need your response too.” There was not a normative message in the OR treatment. Participants’ opinions on the messages that reference members of the community responding to the ACS were mixed. While a few participants did feel like the message would encourage them to respond, most reactions were neutral, and the messaging did not evoke strong reactions in any participants. 6.4.2.1 Round 1 Findings Participants’ opinions on the messages that reference members of the community responding to the ACS were mixed. This messaging resonated with a few participants positively when they were thinking about either the community or a specific group. One participant in CWT was thinking about their own community: Round 1, CWT: "It's encouraging. It's like why should I allow another community to have the heads up or the… the clout or whatever? It's like they completed it, I don't want all of the federal funding to go to them, I want it to go to my community as well." However, many participants seemed to feel neutral towards the sentence and did not have a positive or negative reaction. Some of the words and phrases participants used to describe the sentence included “ambiguous,” “redundant,” and “generic.” Another participant seemed to not think this sentence was true. Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes specific to this research question after Round 1. We continued to monitor whether the use of normative messaging resonates with the reader. 6.4.2.2 Round 2 Findings Participants were asked about their thoughts on sentences referring to ‘many households’ (CWT and TTP) or ‘millions of households’ (FL) completing the ACS. Although some participants found the sentence appealing, the majority of participants were neutral about this or did not seem to care about this sentence. Three of the five CWT participants did not care for this sentence, and three of the five TTP participants did not care for this. One participant in TTP said, “It wouldn't make me go 'oh my God my neighbors have done it, I got to get on it.' Because I don't care really if anybody else has done it,” (Round 2, TTP).

44 Of the four FL participants, only one participant seemed to not find it appealing. However, this still did not resonate too much. The FL participant said, “It’s a little bit encouraging that millions of households participate in it but that don’t necessarily mean I got to,” (Round 2, FL). Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes specific to this research question after Round 2. 6.4.2.3 Round 3 Findings As in Round 2, the majority of participants did not seem to find the ‘many’ or ‘millions’ sentences to be appealing. Of the seven participants in CWT, four participants were neutral towards this or did not seem to care for this. Of the four participants asked about this sentence in TTP, two participants believed they should respond since others did but two participants did not seem to care. In fact, one participant in TTP mentioned in the debriefing that they were not sure why should it matter and why they should care. Of the seven participants in FL, four participants were neutral towards or did not care for it while two participants felt they should respond since others did. However, one participant said there was no need to respond if others did: “Like I said, millions of households participated, so many people are doing it. Just me? They’re not going to miss just me. I’m sure plenty of people didn’t fill it out. They going to lock me up? What are they going to do?” (Round 3, FL). Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes specific to this research question after Round 3. The normative messaging was kept in because it’s a unique message that may apply to a different audience in the field test. 6.5 Research questions specific to Mailing 5 Q10. How does implementing a commitment device affect self-response? Does the commitment device make participants think they should circle or check an option and mail this piece back to the Census Bureau? One recommendation for Mailing 5 from the Strategic Framework report (Oliver et al., 2017) was to encourage recipients to make a commitment to respond to the survey. The Strategic Framework Mail Materials Design Team chose to include a commitment device in each version of Mailing 5. The commitment device asks participants to choose or select which mode they will use to complete the survey by the stated due date. As shown below, each treatment used slightly different formatting for the commitment device. Classic with a Twist used icons depicting each mode. The Fresh Look treatment used the same general format as CWT, but without the icons. The To the Point treatment used check boxes next to each mode. The Outside Researcher treatment placed a call-out box around the device. The OR version used slightly different wording throughout the mailing. No icons or checkboxes were used in this version. One concern with including the commitment device was that recipients may think that they need to respond with their answer. This was a particularly salient concern with the To the Point

45 treatment which included checkboxes next to each mode. For this reason, one focus for Mailing 5 during cognitive testing was noting any comments or indications that participants thought they may need to return the mailing after responding to the commitment device. Classic with a Twist: Figure 6. Commitment device in Classic with a Twist treatment Fresh Look: Figure 7. Commitment device in Fresh Look treatment

46 To the Point: Figure 8. Commitment device in To the Point treatment Outside Researcher: Figure 9. Commitment device in Outside Researcher treatment The inclusion of a due date as part of the commitment device in Mailing 5 was a strong motivating factor to respond to the ACS. Participants felt that the due date created a sense of urgency and would prompt them to take action quickly. Participants also liked that the commitment device mentions three ways to respond, noting that the new option to respond by phone that was not highlighted in previous mailings will be a positive to some people. The aspect of the commitment device that asks them to “select one” or “choose one way” to respond did not have much of an impact on participants. Most did not comment on this feature and those that did were simply noting it was there. While a couple of participants did say this feature made it seem like they should mail it back, they said it was also clear that they were not supposed to do so. 6.5.1 Round 1 Findings The most noticeable element of the commitment device seemed to be the inclusion of a due date. Thirteen of the 16 participants in Round 1 commented on the due date either during the think aloud or when asked what they first noticed about the mailing (four in the CWT treatment and three in each of the other treatments). Many commented that it was the first time they

47 noticed a due date in any of the mailings. Participants mentioned that the due date creates a sense of urgency. Some stated that they liked that they know how long they have to respond. Round 1, FL: “Uh, oh. Due date. Now I'll take it seriously.” Round 1, FL: “It's the first thing I see, bold and big, it's not in color, but the shading catches the eye.” Only one participant explicitly commented on the fact that the letter was asking them to commit to responding via one of the modes. Round 1, TTP: "I don't really know the purpose of it. This is just… having somebody check they're gonna do something online. So they still could not do it? So what good is this paper? To me, it's kind of a waste of postage for you guys.” No participants in Round 1 gave any indication that they thought they had to mail the letter back in after choosing which mode they were going to use to respond. Most of the other comments on the devices were just noting that the letter mentions three ways to respond. Some picked up on the fact that responding by phone had not been offered in previous letters. “It's different because on this one they have all 3 options. It should have been on [the] first one. The only thing different is due [date] and giving all 3 of options. I didn't know about [responding by] phone until last minute. If I knew that at first, it would have been helpful,” (Round 1, OR). Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes specific to this research question after Round 1. 6.5.2 Round 2 Findings In Round 2 the commitment device evoked similar reactions to Round 1. The aspect that received the most attention was the inclusion of a due date. Seventeen of the 20 participants in Round 2 noted the due date either during the think aloud or when asked what they first noticed about the mailing (four in CWT, four in FL, four in TTP, and five in OR). Most comments were neutral, just noting it as they reviewed the materials. Others responded positively, indicating that they like the due date so they know when they need to take action by. A few participants said they wished the due date was included in earlier mailings. Round 2, TTP: “Due date. That is the first thing I see. Yeah, that stands out in the upper left-hand corner.” Round 2, OR: “Oh, now I got a due date like a bill. I guess if you got the due date in the beginning maybe that would have kinda pushed you along to get it over with.” The second most commented on aspect was the fact that the commitment device listed multiple ways to respond. Some participants liked how the modes were presented in an easy-to-read format. Some participants also thought the modes should be presented in this format in an earlier mailing. Round 2, FL: "I like the way this letter is set up. It tells you where online to go, the phone, tells you all the options that you can access the information. You should send this letter first probably."

48 Round 2, CWT: “The letter is straight to the point. It tells you what will happen if you don't respond, and it still gives you the options to do the other two. So, either responding online or by mail if you want to. You can also do it by phone as well. It gives you a lot of different options. It targets the whole population.” Five participants explicitly mentioned that the letter is instructing them to choose one way to respond. Four of these participants were in the To the Point treatment that includes checkboxes. The fifth participant was in the Outside Researcher treatment. Three participants were just noting the language neutrally or saying that it specifies that you only have to respond using one mode. “The ‘one’ way is underlined so I don't have to do every single one,” (Round 2, TTP). The other two participants noted that the commitment device was a bit confusing because it seems like you have to let the Census Bureau know which way you are going to respond. Of these, one made it clear that he knows you are not supposed to send it back even though it looks that way. The other gave no indication that she thought she had to mail it back but did not explicitly say that she knows it is not expected. Round 2, TTP: “One thing that's puzzling on here is because of these boxes, it looks like you're supposed to tear something off and send it back, and you're not.” Round 2, OR: “It’s a little confusing because it's asking to select one on how to complete the survey, so you have to tell the Census Bureau to complete it by phone, mail, online or not do anything so someone comes to the house.” While there was some confusion mentioned, since no participants indicated that they would attempt to mail the letter back, no changes were suggested after Round 2. Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes specific to this research question after Round 2. 6.5.3 Round 3 Findings A smaller percentage of participants commented on the commitment device elements in Round 3, but the overall reactions remained the same. Nineteen of the 27 participants in Round 3 noted the due date either during the think aloud or when asked what they first noticed about the mailing (six in CWT, four in FL, four in TTP, and five in OR). Comments on the due date were mostly neutral or positive, saying that it was helpful or that it would push them to respond more quickly. One participant said that the due date would make her less likely to respond. She said this mailing seemed like a waste of time and that she would prefer to just wait for an interviewer to come to her house. The inclusion of the different response modes was viewed favorably by participants in all treatments. Some noted that the newly included phone option would be easier for them, while others noted that they think that option would be helpful for older individuals. Round 3, TTP: “They give you a lot of different options so hopefully one of these can accommodate somebody.”

49 Round 3, OR: “Huh, they come to your house. And then you can do it by phone. I don't remember if it said that you can do it by phone on the other ones. But that was a question that I asked you [after Mailing 3]. But it's nice. Lot of options. But maybe strange not to give you all the options to start with. I guess online collection is maybe the easiest for you guys as well.” Three participants in Round 3 explicitly commented on the “select one” or “choose one” language. One just read it aloud and commented on the urgency. The other two noted it and indicated that their next step would be to respond online. “Choose one way. Okay - online! I will go to online and respond,” (Round 3, TTP). None of the participants in Round 3 gave any indication that they thought they had to send the letter back after choosing a response mode. Since the commitment device performed well with little to no confusion across all rounds, no changes were made. Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes specific to this research question after Round 3. 6.6 Side-by-side comparisons Q1. What stands out to participants in a side-by-side comparison of all treatments? In the following sections, we describe features of the different treatments that stood out to participants. Overall, participants’ opinions varied based on their individual aesthetic preferences. There were few discernable patterns by treatment, although OR seemed to generate more negative comments than the other treatments. Color, format, and clarity of the text were frequent reasons given for liking a given treatment more than the others. We note that the counts mentioned below are not mutually exclusive-- some participants mentioned multiple versions as standing out to them. In Rounds 1 and 2, the side-by-side comparisons were done on Mailing 1 (letter only) and Mailing 4 (postcard). In Round 3, the comparisons were done on Mailing 2 (open pressure seal mailer) and Mailing 3 (letter only). 6.6.1 Round 1 Findings 6.6.1.1 Mailing 1 A few participants said that the color green really stood out to them in the materials. They did not mention this in reference to a certain mailing, but instead just said that they liked it in the versions it appeared in. Six participants mentioned liking CWT or the “icons” in particular. People felt the icons were great and one participant mentioned that it helps readers see where they needed to look for the necessary information to respond. Most participants generally liked the sidebar and colors in FL. However, only three participants seemed to feel strongly that FL stood out in the side-by-side comparison, and two of them mentioned also liking another version (CWT and TTP) equally.

50 Six participants mentioned liking some aspect of TTP. They mentioned liking the discussion of benefits in TTP, and at least one participant said they felt it was the most official-looking. People liked the color and organization and said that the design was not “too much.” At least two participants mentioned that it clearly gives them the information that they need to respond. Round 1, CWT: “I like [TTP] the most… I like the green contrast, the green and black. I like the green headers, 'Do I have to respond?' and 'Need a paper form?' more than the icons [on CWT]. It's more natural.” Round 1, CWT: “[I prefer TTP] Because of the wording. It says your response helps the community plan for projects such as new schools, health clinics, playgrounds, for the elderly and veterans.” The Outside Researcher treatment resulted in very mixed reactions. The majority of participants disliked it and felt it was too plain and said it did not particularly stick out in the side-by-side. The three participants who said it stuck out to them during the side-by-side felt strongly that they liked it. They felt it was more official and had less extraneous information. However, one participant expressed a preference for more color in OR, “I think the strongest one so far is [OR] and I think that's because the two things in bold that catches your eye first are ‘your response matters’ and ‘you're required by law to complete the survey’…I like [OR], but I wish that there was color in it. I really like how all of these things have green," (Round 1, CWT). One participant who preferred TTP expressed a strong dislike for OR, saying that, “This one [OR] just sounds like they're trying to get information from you. They're not really planning on using it,” (Round 1, CWT). 6.6.1.2 Mailing 4 Many participants had a difficult time identifying which version they preferred or what stuck out to them for Mailing 4 because they felt two or even more versions were really good. Four participants indicated that they prefer the CWT version for Mailing 4. Two of these people also liked another version equally. The other two participants mentioned that CWT grabs their attention and really sticks out from the others. An additional participant mentioned that although she prefers FL overall, the CWT version was the easiest to read and understand. Participants felt more strongly about FL in Mailing 4 than they did in Mailing 1. Seven participants mentioned FL sticking out the most to them. Participants mentioned liking the “how/when/why” bullets and the layout with graphics overall. At least two participants mentioned that “we need your response” resonated with them. The green color also came up as something a participant liked about FL. One participant said they liked, "’We need your response,’" the how/when/why bullets, and the ‘helping communities make informed decisions,’ [language]" (Round 1, FL). Six participants mentioned TTP as sticking out to them. Reasons included the bold heading and the “either/or” layout that presents two ways to respond. As with Mailing 1, at least one

51 participant brought up that TTP struck a good balance between using graphics and not providing too much information. One of the participants did not feel strongly but they mentioned TTP as somewhat sticking out to them from the others. As in Mailing 1, most participants felt negatively towards or did not mention anything in OR sticking out to them, but two felt strongly that OR was their preference. The two participants said that this was the best version because it was simple, and “stern” or official-looking. Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes specific to this research question after Round 1. 6.6.2 Round 2 Findings 6.6.2.1 Mailing 1 Seven participants mentioned something about CWT sticking out to them; for the majority of them, it was the icons. Several mentioned the “how/when/why” format. One participant mentioned liking the icons in CWT the best but felt that OR was the easiest to read. Another reason given in Round 2 for liking CWT was the mention of “saving taxpayer money.” Five participants mentioned FL sticking out to them, with most saying it was because of the side bar. However, another participant, who had no preference, said that, "I feel like it [the sidebar] makes it look less legit," (Round 2, CWT). One participant really liked the “colored box” on FL. Ten participants mentioned something about TTP that really stuck out to them, with the majority specifically mentioned liking the FAQ style. One of these participants was torn between TTP and CWT because he liked the pictures best. He said if that was combined with the “how/when/why” in CWT he would prefer that combination. Another participant was intimidated by TTP but felt it communicated clearly: "Do I have to respond? Yes. This is intimidating. All of them [say it] is required by law but [TTP] makes it seem like you'll be trouble if you don't respond. It's more clear and to the point," (Round 2, FL). Participants gave the same reasons as previous rounds including that it is to the point, easy to read, and looks official. Several participants mentioned liking the box as a way to draw their eye to the information, but overall said they preferred the colored box in FL. 6.6.2.2 Mailing 4 CWT stuck out to nine participants, and it inspired both positive and negative views. Several participants felt very negatively about CWT; they said that it was too pushy and had too much information. One participant who liked it said they felt that it still was in danger of looking like spam because of the use of lots of color. 52 As with FL, at least two other participants mentioned that TTP looked like spam and had too much going on. Two participants mentioned it sticking out to them in a positive way, however. One participant said they felt that TTP made them feel less of an obligation to complete the ACS than FL did. Two participants strongly felt that OR was the best version because it was cleanest and looked official. Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes specific to this research question after Round 2. 6.6.3 Round 3 Findings 6.6.3.1 Mailing 2 Nineteen participants mentioned CWT as really sticking out to them. The main reason given was the icons and visual layout of information. One participant pointed out how the icons quickly convey the needed information. Eleven people mentioned something about FL that stood out to them. For most participants, it was the sidebar and how FL conveyed the importance of responding and reasons to respond. Other common reasons were the color and visual layout. Six participants thought something in TTP stuck out to them. Reasons given were that it emphasized the benefits of responding and that they liked the reminder line at the top of the letter (“A reminder from the Director: Please complete the American Community Survey”). Several participants did not really say why they preferred TTP but just said it just stuck out to them in the side-by-side. Four participants mentioned OR sticking out for its simplicity and for how it motivated them to respond. One of these participants said that while he preferred CWT, he was more likely to respond to OR. 6.6.3.2 Mailing 3 Only five participants mentioned something about CWT sticking out to them. For this mailing, it was mostly the icons. CWT was often mentioned alongside other versions that stuck out to participants, rather than as the only treatment that stuck out. Fifteen participants mentioned something about FL sticking out to them. Most mentioned the layout and use of color, especially the images. One participant felt strongly the sidebar was distracting. Most of the fifteen participants both mentioned FL and TTP sticking out in a positive way to them. One participant said, “Because it's telling me why we need to respond for this survey because it's important to our community and our

53 nation and responding is required by United States law. Just as you're required to report for jury duty and pay takes or earn license to drive- it's giving me a good example. So - more easy to understand," (Round 3, CWT). Another participant pointed out that “response being required by law” was off-putting to her and said she preferred how TTP emphasized the benefits to your community as the reason to respond. Recommendation(s): There were no recommended changes specific to this research question after Round 3. 6.7 Recommendations not specific to research questions In addition to the research questions used to guide the overall approach to the cognitive interviews, interviewers were trained to note and probe on any confusion or issues participants may have had during the interviews. At times, the cognitive interviewing team noticed recurring issues that suggested a need to revise the mail materials. The following sections discuss recommendations that resulted from emergent issues or outside recommendations that were not tied to specific research questions. 6.7.1 Revisions to the Instruction Card and references to it In Mailing 1, the log-in ID that is needed to respond online is located on the instruction card. There is language in the letter explaining this, directing participants to the card to locate the ID. In Rounds 1 and 2, many participants were not immediately sure what the point of the instruction card was. They realized that they would need the instruction card to log in, but still were not sure what specific information they needed from the card. After Round 1, changes were made to both the instruction card and the language referencing the card in the letter. While these changes were an improvement, there was still confusion around the purpose of the instruction card and the location of the log-in ID. Additional changes were made to the instruction card after Round 2, which resulted in a marked improvement. In Round 3, we saw a big improvement in participants both understanding the purpose of the card and being able to find the log-in ID. We recommended proceeding with the version used in Round 3. 6.7.1.1 Round 1 Findings In Round 1, there were multiple instances of participants indicating confusion about the purpose of the instruction card included in Mailing 1. After coming across the instruction card, some participants who were confused by it went back to the letter in an attempt to figure out its purpose. They realized that they would need the instruction card to log in, but still were not sure what specific information they needed from the card. During the side-by-side comparison of the four treatments for Mailing 1, one participant asked for clarification on the language discussing the instruction card:

54 Round 1, TTP: “I have a question. Why does it say 'Enter the requested information. You will need the enclosed card to do this?' First time I'm getting confused [by the materials].” [The interviewer explained that the letter would come in an envelope with the instruction card that she saw in Mailing 1 and handed the card to her.] Round 1, TTP: "Okay, so you gotta put in that or this? Why is that not here for these two [other versions of the letter]? Where are [participants] getting that with these two [versions]? So we've gone through this three times now, and I'm just now picking up on the importance of this card now, that you have to pay attention to the mailing [address label portion]. That makes me really feel like this center set up [in the Outside Researcher version] is the best. 'Enter the requested information. You will need the enclosed card to do this," (emphasis added). Other participants made similar comments during the side-by-side comparison of the Mailing 1 letters. They commented on the box in the OR treatment, saying it makes more sense than the other versions. Some said that the treatment they initially saw did not include the information that the OR version has that explains the point of the instruction card. All treatments did contain this information, but it was included in different places and used different phrasing. Recommendation(s): As a result of the confusion, CBSM suggested that the CWT, FL, and TTP letters should be redesigned so that instructions similar to the ones in the OR treatment are in the "box" area or formatted so that the explanatory text near the area stands out more. After additional discussions about the issue, the Design Team also revised the language on the instruction card to clarify its purpose and explain how to find the 10-digit login ID on the card. 6.7.1.2 Round 2 Findings The changes made after Round 1 led to an improvement in Round 2. Eight participants made spontaneous comments that indicated they understood the point of the instruction card. There were no spontaneous comments indicating confusion about the point of the card. While participants understood the point of the card, those that looked for the 10-digit ID could not always easily find it. Five participants attempted to find the 10-digit ID on their own during the think aloud portion and one was prompted to look for it by the interviewer after expressing uncertainty while thinking aloud. Four who looked for it did not find the ID before moving on. Two who looked found the correct ID. They both found it easily after counting the digits in the number they assumed was the ID. While they found the ID easily, they seemed unsure throughout the process and said that the ID needs to be more apparent. Since participants still had trouble locating the ID on the card, we recommended revising the instruction card to make the 10-digit user ID easier to find. Recommendation(s): The following recommended revisions were made to the instruction card to make the 10-digit user ID easier to find:

55 • 10-digit ID was made larger and bolded • Revised the text explaining where to find the ID and removed “https://” from the URL (Note: The removal of “https://” was recommended by the NAS panel previously referenced) • Round 2: HOW TO RESPOND: (1) Go to https://respond.census.gov/acs (2) Log in with the 10-digit user ID below. • Revised: HOW TO RESPOND: (1) Go to respond.census.gov/acs (2) Log in with the user ID found in bold print below. 6.7.1.3 Round 3 Findings In Round 3, 12 of the 27 participants looked for or noted the ID during the think aloud portion of the interview without prompting. Of those, eight easily found the correct ID. "So just opening this up, looking at the card, pretty straightforward. Respond by going online to the [URL] and log on, User ID, pretty straightforward in bold, [Begins reading ID out loud.]…” (Round 3, OR). Four participants noted some uncertainty but eventually found the ID after counting the digits in the suspected number and/or reading that the ID was printed in bold. One of these participants looked through three sets of numbers before noticing instructions: “It does say in bold below, but I didn't read that. I just went as far as go to the web site because that's how I would respond to it. If I had read carefully, then yeah it's pretty clear in bold below. That information is there. I just wasn't attending to it,” (Round 3, FL). For 10 of the participants who did not look for the ID unprompted during think aloud, interviewers probed to see if they could find the ID before beginning a newly added task that consisted of navigating to the website and attempting to log in. This internet task was completed by all participants who indicated that they would respond online (see below for more detail). Of 10 participants who did not look for the ID unprompted, nine were able to easily find the correct ID when asked by interviewers. The tenth participant looked for the ID but was unable to find it. "Let's see…. No, I did not look into the 10-digit user ID. Log in with the 10-digit user ID found on the enclosed card… [looks] Um, I'm still confused, so I am not sure which 10-digit one I should use. Yeah, because it's not very clear for me,” (Round 3, CWT). Internet task In Round 3, we added an additional task to the interview to assess whether the changes intended to make it easier to locate the 10-digit ID worked. When individuals are sampled to respond to the ACS, the log in screen includes an image of the instruction card where the location of the 10-digit ID is circled and the text “Example User ID” is next to the image with an arrow pointing to the ID location. Since individuals would see this if they actually went online to respond, we wanted to see how navigating to the website impacted participants’ perception of the materials in Mailing 1. We also wanted to ensure that the removal of “https://” from the URL did not cause any difficultly navigating to the website.

56 The internet task was done after asking all probes on Mailing 1. If participants had not already indicated that they would respond to the survey online, they were asked if they thought they would respond online or go online to check out the website. All participants who indicated that they would either respond online or check out the website were asked if they would go online using their smartphone or a computer or tablet. If they said they would use their smartphone, they were asked if they were comfortable using their smartphone during the interview to do what they would do if they received the mailing at home. Participants who did not want to use their phone or who said they would respond using a computer or tablet were given a laptop for the task. The laptop screens were mirrored on a tablet for interviewers to watch as the participant completed the task. The text from the cognitive interview protocol is shown below: ➢ If R said they would go online with their smartphone: Would you be willing to use your smartphone now and do what you would do if you were at home? If yes: Please do that now and try to think aloud and say what you are doing as you do so. ➢ If no to smartphone or If R said they would go online with a computer or tablet: [Give R the laptop] Can you use this laptop and do what you would do if you were going online at home? Please try to think aloud as you do so. Twenty-one participants attempted the internet task. Eleven of those used the laptop we provided and 10 used their own smartphone. Interviewers observed the participant completing the task and noted whether they commented on any difficulty, and whether they commented on the example image pointing out where to locate the 10-digit ID. Navigating to the website Two participants indicated difficulty navigating to the website prior to probing. One was unable to pull up the site, possibly due to a typo when entering the URL. The interviewer could not see the participant’s cellphone screen to confirm what caused the issue. This participant was thinking aloud as she completed the task, so it was clear that she was attempting to type in the URL exactly as written. The second participant who experienced difficulties did so because they added “www.” before the URL, which results in a page that says, “This site can’t be reached.” Round 3, FL: "I'm assuming it's www even though it doesn't say that. [Types in URL with www. and comments on error page.] Let me try it again. It has to be 'www,' not just ‘respond by’…well let's try it. [Types in URL from card and successfully accesses page.] Oh, you don't have 'www'- I thought everything had to!" All participants were probed on whether it was easy or difficult to navigate to the site. Only one participant said it was difficult. She was referring to not having internet at first on the laptop because the Ethernet cord was loose. This participant had no difficulty navigating to the website once the internet connection was fixed.

57 Attempting to log in Four participants commented on difficulty finding the ID while attempting to log in. Three had not looked at the instruction card up to this point, the fourth (Round 3, CWT (mentioned below)) was the one who looked during the think aloud portion of his interview but could not find it when first prompted. All were eventually able to “log in” during the task. We did not have test IDs for the task, so success was defined as typing in the correct User ID in the appropriate boxes. At that point, the interviewer stopped them and informed them that they had completed the steps correctly. During the task, two participants referred to the letter which pointed them to the instruction card, where they easily found the ID. The participant (Round 3, CWT (mentioned above)) who had previously failed to find it earlier in the interview looked again after seeing the image on the website and was able to locate the ID. One participant never took the instruction card out of the envelope. He eventually found the ID by the barcode by looking through the address window on envelope. This participant did not mention noticing the image on the website but did read the text above the log-in box that read, “Enter the 10-digit User ID found below the barcode on the materials we mailed to you.” Eight of the 20 participants who completed the task commented on the image of where to find the ID while thinking aloud when completing the task. Round 3, CWT: “It actually has a picture of where you can find your User ID on it so that’s good.” Round 3, CWT (mentioned above): "At first I did not understand, but now when you go there [it looks] so similar like I would look at this one then. Because it shows on there the example where I can find it.” Individuals who did not mention the image while thinking aloud were asked if there was anything on the site that helped them figure out how to log in. Two mentioned the image. Round 3, TTP: "If you don't find [it] here [on the card] you can find here [on the website image].” Round 3, OR: [Looks back] "Oh, yep. Didn't even look at that! Maybe put that up higher for people like me." [This participant completed the task on their smartphone, so they had to scroll to see the picture.] Overall, the changes intended to make the User ID easier to find performed well in Round 3. The inclusion of the internet task provided some insight into how the instruction card and presentation of the User ID would perform in the real world. Although a few participants still expressed confusion about where to find the User ID when looking at the materials alone, all confusion was cleared up when those participants navigated to the website to log in and saw the image indicating where to find the User ID. Recommendation: No additional changes were recommended at this time. We recommended proceeding with the version of the instruction card used in Round 3 since we saw a big improvement in

58 participants both understanding its purpose and easily identifying the information they need. 6.7.2 Language about the upcoming paper questionnaire and contacting the Census Bureau In Rounds 1 and 2, a couple of older participants expressed some confusion about a particular set of sentences in Mailing 1. The wording varies slightly across treatments: Classic with a twist: "If you are unable to respond online, there is no need to contact us. You will receive a questionnaire in about two weeks. If you have questions or need help completing the survey, please call 1-800-354-7271." Fresh look: "If you are unable to answer online, you will receive a paper questionnaire in about two weeks. If you need help completing the survey or have questions, please call 1-800-354- 7271." Outside researcher: "If you are unable to respond online, you do not need to contact us. We will send you a paper questionnaire in about two weeks. [paragraph break] If you have questions or need help completing the survey, please call 1-800-354-7271." To the point: "If you are waiting to respond by paper questionnaire, you will receive one in about two weeks. You do not need to contact us. If you need help with this survey or have questions, call us at 1-800-354-7271." The sentences are intended inform participants who cannot respond online that a paper questionnaire will automatically be sent to them; they do not need to contact the Census Bureau to request one. However, multiple older participants misinterpreted the meaning. One participant said, “You do not need to contact us. Okay, hmmm…. I hope this is all legit. All I see here is… United States Census Bureau. I hope this is legit. It says I can’t contact them. Okay, so they chose me out of a hat, and then tell me I don’t need to contact them,” (Round 1, TTP). Recommendation after Round 2: The phrases “…there is no need to contact us” (CWT) and “you do not need to contact us” (OR and TTP) were the sources of confusion. The Fresh Look treatment did not contain either of these phrases. Therefore, we recommended replacing instances of this phrasing in CWT, OR, and TTP treatments with phrasing from the Fresh Look treatment. Round 3 Findings and Recommendation:

59 There were no additional mentions of confusion in Round 3. We recommended proceeding with the revised phrasing pulled from the Fresh Look treatment. 6.7.3 Alternate version of the questionnaire cover Between Rounds 2 and 3, the Strategic Framework Mail Materials Design Team presented the latest versions of the materials to a panel of experts at a National Academy of Sciences meeting on the American Community Survey. One recommendation was to revise the format of the front page of the ACS paper questionnaire. The original layout of the front page of the questionnaire created a “path” that draws the attention of the respondent to start reading at “You have two ways to respond…” (see figure 10 below). A panel member recommended re- designing the layout to change the path, drawing attention to the first box on the page where respondents begin filling out the paper questionnaire by writing in their name. The panel also recommended adding a tablet to the icons and wording about devices that can be used to respond online. As a result of this recommendation, the Design Team revised the formatting of the front page of the questionnaire to change the visual path. The newly designed questionnaire cover was cognitively tested in a split-ballot design in Round 3. Half of the participants received a version of the questionnaire with the original flow, and half received the new version with the revised flow. While working on the redesign, the team identified a few additional areas for improvement. To ensure that the split-ballot design isolated the effects of the formatting change on the flow, these other revisions were applied to both the original version of the questionnaire and the new version. Changes made to both versions of the questionnaire included adding a tablet to the icon and wording (discussed above), adding “US” before “law”, and revising the “Contact Us” section (see figures 10-12 below for all three versions of the questionnaire).
