These documents are appended to this report (see Appendix A. Testing Materials). 3.2 Participant’s General Knowledge of SNAP Information Before looking at the materials, participants were asked some general questions about information they received about SNAP, their understanding of the rules, and where they would go if they had questions about the program. All participants recalled receiving information about SNAP when they initially joined the program. Several participants said information was relayed via pamphlets/fact sheets sent via mail and email, telephone calls, and during their intake interviews. “All the information is always available. You will always get info that you need from over there. [They] have brochures. During the interview, they also tell you.” “They gave us a pamphlet of what was covered and not covered. I just printed it and mailed it in. It was a simple from what I recall.” However, one person noted that they did not receive the information again when they renewed their application.

3-2 “[I did not receive any rules or instructions] this last go round. The last time I got some paperwork. [This time] they just put it on my card – I didn’t even know I was approved. The first time I got a flyer.” From what participants could recall, the information they received discussed eligible and ineligible purchases, how to use your EBT card, who can use your card, and where you can use your card. They did not report that any of the information was unclear. “No alcohol, no tobacco. Common sense if you say you need food, don’t buy things that are not related to it. SNAP program covers a lot of food. Certain cooked food is also now allowed. They have it in the deli part as long as it is cold.” Participants also felt they had a good understanding of SNAP rules with a few noting that they were familiar with the program from family and friends. One participant noted that they did a lot of research when they applied to ensure they knew the rules, while another mentioned that stores also explain what can be bought with the SNAP EBT cards. “I feel like I do (understand the rules). I relied just on word of mouth.” “They tell you what you can do or not do, what you can buy or not buy. It was an easy thing to learn.” Most participants said they would call or make an appointment at the Alabama DHR county office with questions about benefits. Some participants said they would look online, and one person mentioned that they would call the SNAP hotline. “Call the DHR office. See if they can connect me to someone useful. They might send me some pamphlets.” “There are certain days you can call this office and talk with someone. You need an appointment, but it can be hard to contact anyone.” In general, participants were familiar with the SNAP program because they recalled receiving information, did their own research when applying to the program, or because they had family and friends in the program. Participants also knew to call, look online, or make an appointment with the local Alabama DHR office if they have questions about the program. 3.3 Card Management This section summarizes participants’ review of the Alabama Integrity Flyer EBT Card Security and Management section (Figure 3-1). This section included details about card management, who can use the card, PIN management, lost or stolen cards, and instructions for re-using the card every month.

Section 3 – Alabama 3-3 Most participants summarized this section of the flyer as providing information around the use and management of the EBT card such as keeping the PIN to oneself, not letting others use their card, keeping the card even when it is empty, and only using the card for food. “Basically, you are responsible for your card, and it comes back on you if you give it [EBT card] out or the PIN. Don’t use your card for anything else other than food.” “You never share your PIN number unless someone is shopping for you. You hold on to your PIN number and you don’t write your PIN number down. Don’t let someone else use your card. When SNAP balance is empty, don’t throw it [EBT card] away because the next month you get more as long as you are eligible. If you lose your card, you can call and they will deactivate it. They can send you another one. It takes 10 days. If you are a child or a low function adult, then you can use their card. Other than that it is their PIN and their card.” “If you are authorized user, you need a PIN number.” All participants correctly defined a PIN. “A password or certain number you use. It is a four-digit number that you choose and need to remember.” “Your four-digit code. Your private code to use the card. You definitely don’t write it on the card.” When probed whether there were situations in which someone would give their PIN to others, about half of the participants could see scenarios of that happening. Some participants described why they might share their PIN with family members. Figure 3-1 Information on EBT Card Security and Management from the Integrity Flyer

3-4 “I haven’t yet, but if it is a life and death situation, I will give it to my mom or brother. I live with my mom, brother, and two kids.” “You might need someone to get something for you.” “My sister could get groceries for me. Otherwise, I would never give this [PIN] to anyone.” Participants had one of two responses when asked about what they would do if someone knew their PIN and they did not want them to know: (1) change their PIN themselves or (2) contact the SNAP office for assistance. “Call and change it. The 1-800-number on the card. The app might give you that information as well.” “File and get it straightened out as this is a theft. I will call the SNAP office.” Some participants were unsure whether they could change the PIN themselves with one participant suggesting that the flyer could contain more information on how to change the PIN. “I would change that PIN. I don’t know how to do that. Maybe I will get a new card.” “I would contact the SNAP office about changing the PIN or getting a new card if it is stolen. It would be nice to know exactly what to do – that could be included here.” When asked whether there was information in this section of the flyer that was especially important, participants provided a variety of responses including information about the PIN and authorized representatives. Several participants said that the information about the PIN was the most important. “The PIN is very important. My aunt forgot the PIN and the card locked her out of it. She couldn’t get through to the people, so my mom tried calling but they didn’t give her any information.” “It is very important to not write down your PIN on your card. Very simple but needs to be there.” Some participants felt that the information about who can use the card and the authorized representative was especially important. While many participants said they understood the term “authorized representative,” it was not clear if all participants realized they need to add the authorized representative to their account.

Section 3 – Alabama 3-5 “An authorized representative is someone like my mom in case I am not able to go shopping.” “My household include three people. Let’s say my mom or dad visit, I would trust them to use the card. I would authorize one of them to use the card.” “I am my own authorized representative as I am of sound mind. If I give someone my permission, then they are authorized to use my card.” Other participants stated they were confused by the term “authorized representative,” indicating that some clarity around this information may be needed. Some participants did not understand who the authorized representatives were or how authorized representatives were designated. “Authorized representative is a full-time caregiver. I didn’t realize I can even name anyone.” “I’m hung up with authorized representative…’Authorized representative’ was difficult to understand. Is it as simple as naming your family member?” One participant noted that they were not aware of how the authorized representative was authenticated while using the card. “The one thing I found confusing with authorized representative is that we are not asked to show ID when we use the EBT card, so I am unsure why they need to know who the authorized representative would be.” Another participant expressed their confusion with the text “Do not use another household’s EBT card unless you are an authorized representative for their household,” because they thought it was referring to other household members and that more than one person in the household could be included in the program. “The one about not using another household member’s EBT card. For some reason, I was thinking that more than one person in the household could have EBT.” One participant noted that the statement “Do not pay off credit or charge accounts with stores with your EBT cards” was confusing because they do not get cash benefits. “‘Do not pay…’ was difficult to understand because I don’t receive cash benefits so I don’t understand that.” A single participant found the last item about using the same card each month confusing; however, all other participants understood that this item was saying not to throw away the card because it can be recharged in future months.

3-6 “The last item is confusing... how is it activated? What if I don’t use this for a considerably long time. Maybe I am out of the country, what do I do then? This is not explained here. Is it transferrable? Do you need to cancel it out or does the money remain on the card?... It is not told how it is possible to use it again. There should me more details here.” In general, participants understood the section on EBT card security and management to be about how to use and care for their EBT card. Several participants shared information about the PIN was the most important. Participants expressed confusion on how to change the PIN, what the term “authorized representative” meant, and how EBT cards can be used to pay for credit or charge accounts. 3.4 Eligible/Ineligible Purchases Participants were then asked to review a different section of the Alabama Integrity flyer that defined eligible and ineligible purchases and provided examples of eligible/ineligible items (Figure 3-2). Participants understood that this section of the flyer was describing what can and cannot be purchased with SNAP benefits. When interpreting the section, participants easily described examples of eligible and ineligible purchases. “You can buy anything at the grocery store other than hot foods and household items.” “What you can’t purchase. Anything that is not food, you cannot get. Anything that is food, you can get. This [EBT card] is for food.” “You are not allowed to buy cigarettes or alcohol. However, fruits, vegetables, and meats are essential items so those can be purchased.” “You can use your SNAP benefits for groceries and nothing else. No alcohol, cigarettes, no hygiene items. Nothing other than groceries.”

Section 3 – Alabama 3-7 When prompted about which information was the most important, some participants noted that the section on eligible and ineligible purchases was especially helpful in that it specifically lists what can and cannot be purchased. “Knowing what you can and cannot buy [is important]. I had learned this from experience and word of mouth.” One participant noted that the first three lines describing eligible purchases were the most important, whereas another participant said that the list of ineligible purchases was the most important piece of information. While this section on eligible/ineligible purchases was generally understood, three issues emerged during review of materials about eligible and ineligible purchases: learning new information, request for additional details, and suggestions for additional types of information. Several participants were not aware that seeds were an eligible item with the EBT card but learned this information from reading the flyer. One participant pointed out that this information is good to know as this could help save money. “I didn’t know you could buy seeds…I think it is important that you can buy seeds and plants. This is a money saving thing as you can grow your own food.” One participant noted that they were unsure where to purchase seeds. Another participant said they knew seeds were an eligible purchase but had not seen the information in SNAP materials before. “I have never thought of buying seeds and plants and it actually makes sense for the long run. I have seen seeds and plants at Lowe’s but I did not see the sign that the store accepts EBT.” Most participants said the information presented in the flyer was not difficult to understand. Several participants suggested including more detail around prepared and hot foods. Figure 3-2 Information on Eligible and Ineligible SNAP Purchases from the Integrity Flyer

3-8 “The part about ‘Prepared or hot food.’ This could be explained in more detail. Could you buy prepared cold food from the deli? That is a little confusing or could be explained better.” “You can’t buy foods from the deli. It is specifically for groceries. I think it needs additional description or examples.” “The prepared and hot foods could be better explained.” However, when asked to define prepared or hot foods, most participants provided an accurate description and knew they could not purchase these items. Some did distinguish between the rules for prepared hot food compared with prepared cold food. “For example, at Walmart – they have the hot chicken and you can’t buy that. However, I can buy the premade sandwiches.” “You can’t buy deli that’s already cooked.” Participants offered suggestions for additional types of information that would be useful in a SNAP flyer, including listing eligible items such as baby formula, baby food, Ensure, Glucose drinks, and nutrition drinks; a list of stores that sell seeds or plants and that would accept EBT; meal suggestions; and the use of EBT to pay for grocery pick-up. 3.5 Trafficking Participants were then asked to review a different section of the Alabama Integrity flyer that focused on trafficking (Figure 3-3). The Trafficking section of the flyer provided a definition of trafficking and included lists of prohibited actions and penalties for this misuse. Most participants summarized the definition of trafficking presented in this section to be about what someone can and cannot do with their SNAP benefits. “Not to be doing illegal stuff with your benefits. If you do, there are consequences for your actions. You’re not guaranteed benefits so they can be taken away.” One participant specifically noted that there are different types of trafficking violations when summarizing trafficking. “Selling, trading, reselling are things you can’t do.” Although most participants could define the term “trafficking,” many participants noted concerns around the term used in the context of SNAP EBT and others thought about the different meanings or types of trafficking (e.g., human trafficking). “‘Trafficking’ sounds a little scary.”

Section 3 – Alabama 3-9 “You have different meanings of trafficking. Trafficking is swapping it out, trading it out, you could use a different word. Somebody could think this is kidnapping your kid.” “I think of child / human trafficking…” One participant noted that they liked the use of the term “trafficking” saying that the term caught their attention. “I think of child / human trafficking. Trafficking is a great word to use here as it caught my attention. EBT is a privilege and a blessing. Section 3 – Alabama 3-17 3.8 Summary and Recommendations Overall, participants found that the materials were clear for the most part, and aligned with their understanding of the SNAP program, with some exceptions noted below. They agreed that the materials contained important information that was relevant to them and was worth communicating to program participants. However, there were some issues with how effective and clear they were with regard to integrity messaging. This section summarizes our findings by messaging domain across the materials that were tested for Alabama and, where appropriate, offers recommendations for improving their clarity and usefulness. Card Management While participants generally understood the intent of the information within the card management section of the Alabama SNAP flyer, participants shared some confusion on how to change their PIN and what the term “authorized representative” meant. Some participants were unsure whether they could change the PIN themselves and noted that the flyer did not provide enough information about how to change your PIN. While many participants said they understood the term “authorized representative,” some participants were unclear about the term. Relatedly, many participants demonstrated a lack of understanding about how to designate an authorized representative. Several participants described situations where they informally gave permission for someone else to use their card, but none were able to describe the process for adding an authorized representative to their benefits account (i.e., “named to the agency….”). Other participants were unsure how it is confirmed that someone making purchases is or is not an authorized representative. This appeared to be an instance where participants’ experiences did not align with the statements in the materials. Recommendations • Provide better definitions and descriptions of the procedures for identifying and formally adding authorized representatives that can use EBT cards. • Provide additional details about when an authorized representative is needed. • Provide more information about how PIN numbers can be changed. Eligible and ineligible purchases There was some confusion around the terminology “prepared or hot foods,” with some participants noting that they understood that prepared foods needed to be hot to be disqualified from eligibility. This reflected their experiences purchasing these items but is not aligned with the description of eligible items in the flyer, which says prepared or “hot foods.”

3-18 While discussing descriptions of eligible and ineligible purchases, participants shared that they learned seeds for growing food were an eligible purchase and noted that they found this to be valuable information. Recommendations • Clarify the eligibility of cold prepared food and hot prepared food and ensure this is clearly communicated in messaging. This clarification should consider that participants reported making purchases of cold prepared food with their EBT card, despite the materials saying these items were unallowable. • It would benefit future users of the SNAP program to more widely publicize the fact that seeds or plants to grow food are eligible purchases. Trafficking and Fraud It is noted that Alabama materials often present “fraud” and “trafficking” together, and often used the terms interchangeably. As such, these two domains are presented together for the state of Alabama. Participants shared their interest in providing consistent terminology when referring to SNAP fraud or trafficking. Many participants noted that the term “trafficking” to describe selling, trading, or misusing SNAP benefits was unexpected. Many participants did not feel “trafficking” was the most appropriate term to use when describing misuse of benefits. Instead, they thought that “trafficking” described much more severe behaviors such as drug trafficking or child/human trafficking. Participants noted the word sounded “scary.” Participants generally understood the intent of the Alabama SNAP application’s “Penalty Warnings and Perjury Statement” section that details the penalties for program violations, like fraud and trafficking. However, some participants asked for clarity on the statements about altering an EBT card, what “controlled substance” meant, what “fraudulent statement” meant, and whether there were inconsistencies in the penalties discussed on the Integrity Flyer and the application. Participants understood how they would report fraud, but most had not considered reporting fraud. If participants reported SNAP fraud, they would want to remain anonymous. Information about reporting anonymously was not included in the materials, but most indicated that they would not wish to leave their name. Recommendations • We recommend rephrasing references to trafficking or summarizing these behaviors in another way such as unauthorized uses or violations.
Section 3 – Alabama 3-19 • Prominently display text that reporting fraud anonymously is an option and include information about how to report fraud anonymously with fraud reporting messaging.

Participants understood that section to be about how SNAP benefits are only for food purchases (i.e., “anything other than food is not allowed”) and that they can call their caseworker if they need help protecting their benefits. “I can call on [them to learn] how to protect it [benefits] or what foods to buy.” “Not supposed to use for anything other than food. I used to break the law. I’m not a snitch. I’m not getting paid for it. What am I going to get out of it to report it. It’s not my job.” “No, I don’t want to be bothered in case it goes to court. SNAP benefit description within the Protecting Benefits Guide

4-18 because they have not had one and another wanting to know more about a portal for their benefits. “Case workers. That’s the biggest problem. They need to do their job so that I don’t get called into your office. Where have you been for the last 6 months to a year? I don’t have a case worker. Who am I supposed to see… I’m lost.” “I would like to know more about the portal because I read something, somewhere, about that. …a lot of the information for the people we contact, the codes...explanations about different benefits, uses, rules, rights...can they all be accessed from the portal? If they’re all from different websites, can I just click on something, and it sends me to that website?” One participant wondered why toiletries are not covered under SNAP benefits. “I would like to know why I can’t get toiletries. Even a little something for toilet paper, toothpaste, etc. Because this is allowed in other states.” Another participant thought there should be consistency across the materials shown. “No, just harmonize the language across materials. Looks like they are developed one at a time, so written by different people at different times, for different purposes.” If participants encounter issues, they all know what to do. Most participants would call their caseworker, local office, or the EBT general office. Some mentioned coming into the office, and some would visit the website. 4.8 Summary and Recommendations Overall, the materials tested well. Participants understood the content of the materials, with a few exceptions as discussed below. A few comprehension challenges emerged from the Washington D.C. cognitive interviews. In general, a review of the full SNAP application and materials is warranted to make sure consistency is achieved in terms of how details are being presented (e.g., uniformity in calling it the EBT card). It may also be beneficial to create documents with a larger print or font size to help readability. This is especially true for Exhibit 5: SNAP Integrated Application. Card Management During review of the out-of-state travel flyer, participants noted that they would not know if cards were blocked in a given location until they got there and had issues with their card. They also noted that they had never heard of blocking or the advisory about out of state travel.

Section 4 — Washington, DC 4-19 Recommendations • Provide this kind of advisory to all program participants to ensure travelers are aware of cards being blocked for out of state travel. Eligible and ineligible purchases Participants also cited issues in learning from materials about eligible and ineligible purchases. They noted information in the materials that described ineligible purchases that were inconsistent with their firsthand experiences with eligible purchases. Some cited experiences that precooked foods could be purchased using SNAP, as long as those foods were not hot. This conflicted with the guidance provided in the materials. Participants suggested that the phrase “Seeds and plants, produce food for the household to eat,” was confusing. When reading the phrase, participants were not sure whether “produce” was a verb (to create) or a noun (fresh vegetables). This is likely due to the phrasing. Further, confusion about the meaning of “Prepared food fit for immediate consumption” might be addressed by rephrasing with simpler terms. Recommendations • Some materials that discuss eligible and ineligible foods (Protecting Benefits Guide & SNAP website) could benefit from a review of language. There is an opportunity to provide more information using examples of allowable and unallowable foods, particularly those that are prepared and offered for sale hot or cold. Trafficking Participants also noted issues with comprehension of ‘trafficking.’ A few were unfamiliar with the term, while others did not understand how purchases of drugs and guns related to the SNAP program. In general, participants did not understand the third bullet listed in the food stamp penalty warnings of SNAP Approval Notice (Figure 4-7) on altering “authorization” (EBT) cards to receive food stamps they are not entitled to receive. Many had questions or were confused about how this could happen. Finally, at least one participant noted that materials (Figure 4-7 and Figure 4-9) used the terms “authorization cards (EBT)” and “electronic benefits transfer cards,” and it would be helpful to have an explanation about the differences between the two terms. Recommendations • Participants sought a different term for trafficking, or additional ways to refer to this behavior. •

4-20 • To increase comprehension around the example of altering an EBT card, consider adding some examples of altering a card. Other examples of trafficking could focus messaging on common behaviors. • A review of materials for consistency in terms could benefit comprehension. For example, consider whether materials should refer to either EBT cards, electronic benefits transfer cards or authorization cards. Fraud Reporting Participants generally understood materials presented in the section about fraud reporting and did not share any examples of confusion or misunderstanding. It is noted, however, that the section of the Protecting Benefits guide that outlined fraud reporting included an email address where people could report “misuse” but did not define fraud, use the term “fraud”, provide details about why it should be reported, or offer information about anonymously reporting. However, when probed, participants generally understood SNAP fraud to be misusing the benefits or supplying false information to increase their benefits. We also found that DC participants tended to indicate that they are unlikely to report someone for welfare fraud. Although most participants were unlikely to report welfare fraud, some participants would not have a problem sharing their name in the hypothetical scenario that they called to report SNAP fraud. Others shared that they would rather report anonymously or just provide an initial. Recommendations • Consider providing additional information about fraud, such as why it should be reported. • Prominently display text that reporting fraud anonymously is an option and include information about how to report fraud anonymously with fraud reporting messaging.

Pennsylvania Cognitive Testing Results 5.1 Materials We evaluated the documents shown in Table 5-1 provided by the Pennsylvania Department of Human Services (DHS), Office of Income Maintenance. We asked participants questions on the following topics: card management, eligible/ineligible purchases, trafficking, and fraud reporting. This chapter presents findings from our evaluation of the Pennsylvania SNAP materials and recommendations for improving the clarity and effectiveness of the materials. 5.2 Participant’s General Knowledge of SNAP Information Before looking at the materials, participants were asked some general questions about information they received on SNAP, their understanding of the rules, and where they would go if they had questions about the program. Participants were familiar with the SNAP

5-2 program, either because they recalled receiving information or because they had participated in the program for a long time. Most participants recalled receiving information when applying for food assistance. Only one participant did not recall receiving anything but said they are familiar with the system because they grew up with it. “No, I know what you can and can’t buy, I grew up on the system and know that it’s for food and not other things.” 5.3 Card Management Participants were first asked to review the Informational Flyer and the EBT Brochure, which contain information on EBT card security and management and who can use their EBT card. In general participants shared a consistent and correct interpretation of the materials, and few issues were found. A few participants noted areas where they would prefer additional information, and some noted that the materials had provided them with new information that they did not know before. Most participants lacked familiarity with the QUEST logo that indicates retailers who accept SNAP benefits. Most participants were able to share that the Informational Flyer provides information on how to activate their EBT card and how to protect it. “Your card is attached to this. You have to call a number to select your PIN. Your card will not be active until you select a PIN. Keep your card safe and keep your PIN very secret.” “You don’t want to throw your card out because it’s very difficult to get another one. You never give your PIN away or let anybody else have your information. Card won’t be activated until you pick a PIN.” Several participants thought information about not sharing their PIN was the most important in the informational flyer. “Selecting your PIN or you won’t be able to use your stamps and keeping it to yourself.” “Keeping the PIN secret is important. You don’t want anyone to know your PIN and the creation of the PIN are important. Your card is attached to this and it is the only way to get your benefits, by not throwing away the card.” One participant was surprised to learn that they are not supposed to give their caseworkers their PIN as well.

This page is about what not to do (giving false info, using someone else’s card).”

Section 5 — Pennsylvania 5-17 5.7 Debriefing Questions In wrapping up the interview, participants were asked if they have anything they’d like to add that was not previously discussed. Three participants would like a discussion on eligibility and the amount of benefits to which they are entitled. Participants shared some issues they’ve had with their benefits such as incorrect amounts of money, filling out forms, and issues with the end of the COVID-emergency funds. “I wasn’t getting the right amount of money in my direct deposit.” “When I was ill there are reporting forms and I was unable to do that and services were cut off.” “No, other than the cutback due to COVID. The prices are high so that’s hard.” “It is annoying. If you got a raise or a new job, if you don’t get your papers in then they will cut your food stamps off.” If participants encounter issues, they all know what to do. Most participants would call their caseworker. Some mentioned calling the 1-800 number, some mentioned coming to the state office, and some would use the Mycompass app. 5.8 Summary and Recommendations Participants described issues with comprehending messages as they reviewed the materials. Overall, the materials tested well. Participants understood the content of the materials, with some exceptions. There were some ambiguities that participants would like clarified in the exhibits PA Informational flyer, PA SNAP FAQs, and PA SNAP Application. The other exhibits tested well and were found to be clear among participants. Some recommendations are discussed below to help improve the materials that did not test as well. Card Management In the area of Card Management, participants did not widely recognize the Quest Mark logo, which indicates locations where an EBT card can be used. Two participants would like information on how to take care of their card. Another two participants wanted information on the do’s and don’ts of the card. Recommendations • Given unfamiliarity with the logo, consider either publicizing it more widely, such as on other materials.

5-18 Eligible/Ineligible Purchases As in other locations, participants continued to reflect on differences between their experiences in buying cold prepared food and the materials noting that these foods are ineligible. They shared inconsistent understandings of what was allowed for purchase. These inconsistencies were largely oriented around prepared cold food, such as a salad bar or premade sandwiches. Several participants had issues with the phrase “lunch counter items or foods to be eaten in the store.” Participants understood that they cannot buy “hot food” using their SNAP benefits. Many defined the phrase “lunch counter items or foods to be eaten in the store” as “hot food.” The Pennsylvania SNAP FAQs document covered eligible and ineligible purchases using the SNAP benefits. While reviewing this document, several participants who have been SNAP benefit users for some time learned for the first time that seeds to be grown for food consumption are eligible purchases. Recommendations • We recommend clarifying rules around eligible and ineligible purchases to address confusion. Specifically, we recommend clarifying the eligibility of cold prepared food versus hot prepared food. This clarification could align with participants’ experiences or address any discordance with those experiences. It could also disentangle hot foods from prepared foods. Provide additional examples of eligible and ineligible items, including deli items in these examples. • We also recommend publicizing information about the eligibility of seeds and plants more widely. It would benefit future SNAP program users to have this fact explained further by using examples such as using the phrase “seeds to be grown for food such as tomato, cucumber, lettuce, etc.” Trafficking Information about penalties related to trafficking in the Pennsylvania SNAP application document was the most challenging for participants. Although most participants understood that the document is about penalties for trafficking and prohibitions with the SNAP program, some participants struggled with the visual layout of the table and the font size. In this case, the amount of information also impeded understanding of the content. This table includes information on violations and penalties across programs which was not always clear to participants.

Section 5 — Pennsylvania 5-19 Recommendations • Arranging information by program would allow participants to focus their review on information about programs in which they take part. We recommend presenting information about different programs in separate tables that are clearly labeled. • We recommend moving away from a one-page table format to using two- to three- page format using headings and a larger font size. Fraud Reporting In general, participants had a good understanding of what constitutes welfare fraud and understood the information on the FAQ about how to report suspected welfare fraud. Most participants had not considered reporting fraud, citing a variety of reasons such as not feeling it is their “business,” never personally witnessing fraud, and not knowing how to report fraud. Only one participant noting they had reported fraud. Participants understood from the materials that while they can make an anonymous complaint, it is helpful to provide a name. However, many indicated they would prefer to stay anonymous when reporting fraud. Recommendations • No recommendations because participants thought materials presented were clear.

Second one is trying to find people to do it. First one is you found someone to do this with.” Some participants thought the difference between the two bullets was selling and buying. “Don’t sell them. They can use all the fancy words they want but it boils down to ‘Don’t sell them.’ The first one says don’t sell them, and the second one says to not buy them.” “The first one is you having the card and attempting to sell it and the other is you buying it.” When specifically asked about the fifth bullet, most participants understood the meaning with one participant noting that the bullet was too wordy. “It is a crime to use your card to buy a product and resell it for cash or some other kind of good.” “I can’t buy something for a $1 and sell it for $2. Can’t sell anything that you bought SNAP.” Only one participant was not sure about the meaning of the fifth bullet, saying, “Premeditating selling food stamps, maybe.” One participant noted that this section may get lost in translation because it is very long and contains a lot of information. Next, participants read a section from the Delaware SNAP application on penalties associated with different offenses for trafficking (Figure 6-9).

Section 6 — Delaware 6-15 Figure 6-9. Delaware SNAP application on penalties associated with different offenses Nearly all participants were able to describe that the material is about different ways of misusing their card and the consequences associated with them. “Right away I like the format. It’s the same as the others – it is clear, concise and tells you right away what’s going on…. If you give false statements, trade or sell, the different behaviors and the consequences.” “It tells you the penalties for the different crimes you can commit with EBT, with regards to selling benefits. I did not know how much you lose for each offense.” “This is the penalties in the EBT program and it is letting you know that if anything you include in your application that is not true or use the card illegally, there are punishments.” Most participants found the material to be clear and not difficult to understand. One participant noted that it was unclear if any of the penalties included jail time. Another participant found several of the offenses confusing, specifically the $500 associated with buying, selling, or trading food benefits. “Don’t understand ‘buy or sell or trade food benefits for $500 or more’. So, if it’s for less than $500, the penalty isn’t as much?”

6-16 This same participant was confused by the references to the school lunch and Medicaid programs in the material. “…Don’t know what ‘school lunch’ is. I have Medicaid. Don’t know about federal programs and federally aided state programs. That’s confusing—how are they different? The aid programs that I don’t understand, make them more clear.” It is important to note that Exhibit 4 is an excerpt from the consolidated application for other programs as well and is not just for SNAP. Those who receive the fill application may have more context that the application is for programs other than SNAP. Creating an excerpt of the larger document may have resulted in confusion for the participant. A participant noted that the text below the columns was wordy. “Just too many words at the bottom. Maybe put in bullets or something more concise.” Several participants shared that information provided in the material were all important. “As far as legality, yes, it is all important. It is important for the state to provide this information and make sure that people read and sign it at the end when completing the application. It may people stop and think about it. You won’t stop the fraud all together.” 6.6 Fraud Reporting This section summarizes participants’ review of the section on welfare fraud. These materials included details about how to report fraud, confidentiality when reporting fraud, as well as what fraud is and why to report it. Participants had different perspectives on this topic, including whether they would report fraud or whether they would prefer to remain anonymous. Participants were asked to review information on fraud reporting from the Delaware Health and Social Services website (Figure 6-10) in its entirety. All participants understood that this website was for reporting SNAP fraud. “To catch fraud is the main purpose. I think it is good so they can recoup money.” “To let an applicant know that they have an active office that investigates potential fraud with benefits. Any suspicion of fraud can be reported, and it lets the applicant know the guidelines for reporting. This is public information that can be accessed.”

Section 6 — Delaware 6-17 The webpage noted that those who report fraud can remain anonymous, which at least one participant noted they had not previously known. One participant thought the purpose of the document was snitching on other people and commented that people won’t do this unless there is a reward. “You’re also giving them an opportunity to throw their neighbor under the bus and all the information that they need. What motivation do people have for doing this? You don’t rat people out unless there is a reward.” Most participants also understood the overpayment of benefits mentioned in the “Overview” section, with only one participant noting that they had never heard the term overpayment in this context before. Some participants explained overpayment of benefits as a mistake in reporting income on the part of the participant. “You’re supposed to tell someone if you get overpaid.” “Like if I worked 20 hours in a week and you paid me for 30 and I didn’t step up and say that you paid me for 10 hours too much. Being honest is what is it saying.” Other participants explained the overpayment of benefits as committing fraud to obtain additional benefits. “You deliberately lied to get more benefits or you gave incorrect information.” “If people lie on the application to qualify for more benefits than they should actually qualify for.” Most participants thought the information on the webpage was clear. However, some participants thought there were unclear parts such as how one can interact with ARMS. ARMS did not appear to be salient for participants. “When do you interact with ARMS?” One participant asked for details about defrauding Medicare, which was an example of a program that could be affected by fraudulent behaviors. “How can you defraud Medicaid?” A third participant did not understand the reference to DHSS in the first sentence of the “Overview.” Many participants were not clear on how to actually report fraud when asked directly. This is an important finding, as the purpose of the website is to provide a vehicle for making such reports.

6-18 “Go to office locations list? I don’t know what the contact link is. I don’t know what phone or mail would be. It says phone, mail or email, but doesn’t give any of that information.” “Go online? Don’t know; never had to do it. I would figure it out if I had to do it.” “I don’t recall anything on this page but by knowing the name of the ARMS office, I could call DHSS.” Most participants noted that they learned something new from reading this information. Two participants noted that the reference to TANF was new to them. Two participants also said that they had never heard of ARMS. Three participants indicated that they now had a better idea of how to report SNAP fraud with two participants saying that they did not know they could remain anonymous. “I did not know there was a specific office for fraud and that you can remain anonymous under certain conditions.” Figure 6-10. Fraud Reporting Webpage

Section 6 — Delaware 6-19 Figure 6-10. Fraud Reporting Webpage Participants were then asked to review the fraud reporting flyer (Figure 6-11). All participants shared that the flyer was new to them and information provided was clear. When asked about the purpose of the document, all participants understood that it was to provide more information on reporting welfare fraud and provide motivation to do so. Participants appeared to vary in terms of whether they would report fraud. “To encourage people to report others who are defrauding the state benefits service.” “To let the public know that they will be rewarded if they have valid info about people committing fraud with EBT. It also includes a number to call. You do not have to reveal your name. These are offenses that are taken seriously because other people who need benefits are affected by welfare fraud.” “I would think it was silly if I walked by and saw this. This is to get people to turn people in if they are committing fraud.” When probing on the term “welfare fraud,” nearly all the participants were familiar with the term. Many different examples came to mind for participants such as lying about their work status, number of children, and using welfare for illegal things.

6-20 “I would think housing, in my situation, people lie about their work status.” “People with a lot of kids commit welfare fraud by saying they have more kids than they have. It’s usually people who need food. SNAP is considered welfare.” “People claiming extra kids. SNAP materials don’t use the term welfare. SNAP is food stamps. To me, welfare means food stamps, and Medicaid, etc. It’s a bunch of things.” “Somebody misusing benefits that could go to someone else legally. They’re using it to get not food, but maybe drugs or whatever and are defrauding the system.” About half of the participants did not know what “*TIPS” in the flyer meant. “I don’t know – is it a number to call?” “The asterisk would mean there is an explanation somewhere. Is there a charge for calling a 1-800 number? So, I am not sure what this means.” Most participants understood the connection between trafficking and welfare fraud and felt these were two terms for the same concept. “Yes this [welfare fraud] is trafficking – if they are doing this they are breaking the law.” “Yes, they are one and the same. Trafficking applies to fraudulent activity and illegal contraband. The two terms go hand in hand.” “They are the same. Trafficking may be a bit more broad; you can traffic a lot of things.” For several participants, it was not clear whether trafficking and welfare fraud were the same. “Don’t know if trafficking and welfare fraud are the same thing.” “Welfare fraud – I think of someone that gets benefits they don’t technically need. Trafficking in my mind is linked to drugs.” “I don’t think most people would put two and two together. There is not a clear connection.” One participant noted that SNAP materials should use either the term “trafficking” or “fraud” consistently to remove confusion.

Section 6 — Delaware 6-21 Although most participants liked the flyer, others provided some critiques on either the reward or how the flyer looked. “The reward; ‘up to’ sounds shady. Could be up to $1,000, but you could only get a penny and be technically within your rights.” “If you are anonymous, how do you get your money?” “The man with the hat on, doesn’t add up. Says Delaware Health and Human Services, but it doesn’t go with the picture.” “Why is Sherlock Holmes on the flyer?” Figure 6-11. Delaware Fraud Reporting Flyer Participants were also asked if they would have concerns about providing their name or other personal information if they were considering reporting fraud. Answers to this question were mixed. Several participants noted that they would feel comfortable providing

6-22 their name with some noting that although they would feel comfortable, it was good that someone could choose to remain anonymous. “I wouldn’t mind – I probably wouldn’t know the person in the first place. I think it is good that they could remain anonymous.” “I think anyone that would not provide [their name] should not have the opportunity to throw someone under the bus. Me, personally, I would [provide my name].” One participant added the caveat that they would feel comfortable as long as the government kept their name confidential from the person they were reporting. Other participants said that they would not provide their name if reporting someone for fraud. “I wouldn’t leave my name unless it was very messed up and I told the person I was going to call it in.” “I would not. I think the section about remaining anonymous should stand out.” Only one participant said that they had not seen that you could remain anonymous when they read this initially and thought that information should stand out more. 6.7 Debriefing Questions In wrapping up the interview, only three participants had recommendations from the materials discussed. Two participants had comments related to the dissemination of information. “[The materials are] good. It would be good for states to send out brochures or post them.” “There is a lot that DHS has added since I had SNAP. The Crimestoppers is awesome. When people apply, they should definitely get information about fraud.” The third participant commented that some information could be more direct and to the point, and they gave specific examples (which were described above ). One participant said that they gained a lot of information that they were not previously aware of from participating.

Section 6 — Delaware 6-23 6.8 Summary and Recommendations Overall, the materials tested well. Participants understood the content of the materials and the materials generally aligned with their experiences in the program. However, participants did note a desire for clearer language in a few places. Card Management Overall, participants understood the section on EBT card management to be about managing their EBT card. Several participants shared new information they learned by reading the information on the brochure such the card replacement fee, and methods of ordering a replacement card. Some participants wanted clarity on how the sun, magnets, and electronics can affect their EBT card. One participant wanted clearer language on how to replace their EBT card and specified highlighting the phrase, “If your card is lost, damaged.” They stated that the language on how to replace their EBT card could be clearer and specified highlighting the phrase, “If your card is lost, damaged.” Another participant wanted more clarity with regard to references to the EBT provider Conduent included in the material. The brochure on card management included references to manual transactions. Participants were not familiar with this and did not gather a complete understanding from their review of the materials. • Recommendations Review the description of manual transactions and consider providing examples or explaining this option more clearly. • Review the use of references to “Conduent” in the Program Information and Rights and Responsibilities material. This may be explained elsewhere in the material, but in the section that was reviewed during the interview this was a little confusing to at least one participant. A better explanation could be provided that Conduent is the EBT card service provider, including more detail about their role in delivering SNAP benefits. • Provide clear language on how to replace one’s EBT card. Eligible/Ineligible Purchases Within the eligible/ineligible purchases section, the interviews revealed some inconsistent interpretations of “foods prepared for immediate consumption” that were likely rooted in a conflict with participants’ experiences with making purchases under the program. Several participants shared that they learned seeds for growing food consumption were an eligible purchase during the cognitive interview. Recommendations

6-24 • Review the alignment of the definitions and descriptions of allowable purchases with participants’ experiences. • Include examples of seeds to be grown for food consumption in the materials, such as using the phrase “seeds to be grown for food such as tomato, cucumber, lettuce, etc.” In addition, the eligibility of seeds could be more widely publicized. Trafficking Within the trafficking section, most participants were explaining trafficking in the context of drugs and sex with several participants suggesting that a different word should be used in the context of EBT. Recommendations • Review descriptions of SNAP trafficking. Although participants understood most of the activities described as trafficking, they did not find that the term “trafficking” resonated with them. It would also be beneficial to use the terms consistently across documents. References to trafficking could be replaced using terms such as unauthorized uses or violations. Fraud Reporting While reviewing materials on how to report welfare fraud, we found many participants were not as clear on how to actually report fraud. Several participants shared that the acronyms “TANF,” “ARMS,” and “TIPS” were new to them. Several participants also shared they were unsure whether trafficking and welfare fraud were the same thing and requested consistency in the language used. Recommendations • The purpose of the Delaware web page (Exhibit 6-10) should be narrower, focusing on reporting fraud against SNAP or assistance benefits programs. It currently has a wider scope that is not relevant to those seeking information on reporting program fraud. • Review the website describing fraud reporting. Most participants had not heard of ARMS previously. Consider whether this new acronym is necessary to their understanding of the issues or the call to action to report fraud. Provide methods to report fraud on the website in a prominent location. • Consider the images and language in the Fraud Reporting Flyer. Few participants understood the *TIPS to be a phone number. Others commented on the role of the Sherlock Holmes character and its relation to the SNAP program. The flyer could be evaluated for adherence to SNAP branding.

Section 6 — Delaware 6-25 • Ensure that the information on the fraud reporting website clearly describes how people can report fraud and provides vehicles for doing so. The website should provide options for reporting fraud, such as phone numbers or email addresses. It should also provide an online form where one can submit reports.

7-1 7. Overall Summary and Recommendations Cognitive interviews in Alabama, Pennsylvania, Washington DC, and Delaware reviewed SNAP materials that are distributed to program participants in each state. Despite differences in the materials themselves, a few findings were repeated across states. These recurring findings are presented here, by domain. Recommendations are also included. 7.1.1 Card management In general, materials about card management practices were clear to participants. They understood the importance of keeping PIN numbers and cards secure, and they understood how to keep their card safe. Participants found the messaging important and relevant. Materials that offer card management guidance occasionally include state-specific program names (Quest and the Quest logo in Pennsylvania) or names of EBT service providers (e.g., Conduent from Delaware). Participants were not always familiar with these names, and some mentioned that they did not understand the role of these references in the materials. Participants identified suitable scenarios where they would allow others to use their EBT card to make purchases on their behalf. They cited examples of such scenarios, including when they might be too ill or busy to shop for themselves. They found this suitable despite limited knowledge of how to designate an authorized representative for their account. Some were not aware of how to designate such a representative while others did not understand why that would be needed. Participants expressed uncertainty on how to change their card PIN number. Across sites, participants were not familiar with instructions to keep their cards away from sun, magnets, and electronics. They were not aware that these could adversely affect their cards. Recommendations After reviewing the materials, participants were not in agreement about whether allowing someone to use their card to make purchases on their behalf was allowed. We recommend that language in card management materials clarify this rule and describe what is and is not allowed. In tandem, prominently displaying the role of an authorized user will allow participants to learn more about this feature. Descriptions of authorized users should include what they are able to access on the account, beyond making purchases. Most participants noted that an ID is not required to make purchases, so an authorized user didn’t seem necessary. Materials should provide clear instructions on how to change a PIN number, including contact information or website information as necessary.

7-2 In Washington, D.C., we recommend distributing the out-of-state travel flyer more widely so that participants can act upon the guidance to report their travel prior to departure. 7.1.2 Eligible/Ineligible purchases Information about eligible purchases often contradicted participants' understanding and experiences, leading to confusion or uncertainty about which items were allowed and not allowed under the program. Participants at every site noted that the description of ineligible purchases conflicted with their experiences. Recommendations Clarify, through definitions and examples, the eligibility rules. This will include clarifying the types of foods that are eligible and ineligible, especially which types of prepared or pre- cooked foods. We recommend reviewing descriptions of eligible purchases for accuracy, to ensure that they reflect the rules that participants encounter when making purchases. Emphasize that SNAP is meant to be used to buy "food that participants will prepare or cook at home." Include examples of eligible and ineligible purchases to illustrate SNAP policies. Feature cold and hot deli items in these examples to clarify persistent questions about these items. A separate list of what one can and cannot buy will be most helpful. Simplify language about these topics as well. For example, ‘prepared foods fit for immediate consumption’ is a complicated phrase that does not contribute to understanding the rules. Consider separating references to prepared and hot food if the eligibility rules for these are indeed separate. Finally, publicize more widely that plants and seeds are eligible purchases. 7.1.3 Trafficking Participants in general did not associate the term ‘trafficking’ with the buying or selling SNAP benefits. Instead, they associated this term with activities such as drug trafficking or sex trafficking. Some noted that they would prefer a different term to refer to the unauthorized buying and selling of SNAP benefits. Others felt as though examples of trafficking that included activities extreme or rare (i.e., trading benefits for guns or bombs) were not as salient as those that cited more familiar examples (i.e., buying or trading benefits). Participants were not familiar with altering a SNAP card. They could not produce examples of this activity nor could they cite motivations for altering a card.

Section 7 — Summary and Recommendations 7-3 Participants found the table in the Pennsylvania application (Figure 5-11) that lists penalties for trafficking to be confusing due to its visual design and choice of verbiage. On the other hand, participants commented on how the visual design of the penalties table in Delaware contributed to comprehension and understanding (Figure 6-9). When discussing penalties for engaging in trafficking behaviors, participants desired stronger language that denoted that those who engage in the behavior will face penalties. The materials often said people ‘may’ face consequences, but participants suggested language that indicated they ‘will’ face penalties. Recommendations Participants sought a different term for trafficking, or additional ways to refer to this behavior. We recommend that materials continue to provide examples of trafficking activities, while emphasizing common violations. Examples of common trafficking activities, such as individuals buying and selling benefits, resonated with participants. Describing rare and uncommon examples such as trading for bombs or bullets may not be necessary. Describe examples of or motivation for altering an EBT card to help clarify this example of trafficking behavior. Next, consider using more purposeful descriptions of penalties for trafficking, indicating more certainty that offenders will face penalties. Finally, review descriptions of penalties to ensure clear wording and to rearrange the visual layout of the information, using the Delaware table as a model (Figure 6-9). Penalties for different programs should be separated into different tables. 7.1.4 Fraud Reporting In general, most participants expressed opposition to the practice of defrauding the SNAP program. Some noted that this fraud affects those who rely on the program and were in favor of punishments for those who engage in these activities. Some shared examples of when they had reported fraud themselves. However, others noted that they were not motivated to report fraud, particularly if it did not affect them directly. The messages about fraud reporting were clear and well understood by participants. However, the findings suggest that better messages may be needed to convey the importance of reporting fraud and why individuals should report fraud if they see it.

7-4 Participants favored the ability to make anonymous reports, but on occasion noted that they would like to learn more about the details and terms of this promise of anonymity. In states where materials did not mention anonymity, such as Alabama, this should be added. We also suggest that materials should include clear methods of contacting and reporting fraud. In particular, the Delaware website should include a way to report fraud. Recommendations In general, materials should describe the purpose and importance of reporting fraud, with a goal of encouraging program participants to make these reports when they encounter these activities. The option to report fraud anonymously should be prominently displayed on materials related to fraud reporting. Materials should include all outlets for reporting fraud and should provide necessary links and online forms as applicable. 7.1.5 Challenges with clear and consistent wording In many cases, confusion was caused by wording that was unclear or needlessly complicated. We recommend reviewing the content of materials with an eye toward simplicity. This review could focus on whether information that is presented is necessary. For example, do forms contain references to too many agencies, or contain examples that are not relevant to end users? Revisions can focus on identifying and changing complicated phrases, complex syntax, and odd phrasing. Finally, revisions to materials can identify superfluous information that distracts from calls to action or critical information so as to present streamlined messages to end users. Examples of terms or concepts that participants reported as confusing or unclear included: • ‘Controlled substance’ (AL) • ‘Fraudulent Statement’ (AL) • ‘Intentional program violation’ (DC) • Overuse of acronyms (DE) • ‘If this happens without good cause’ (PA) • Descriptions of seeds and plants (DC) Participants flagged language that was inconsistent. Examples include: • References to EBT versus SNAP (multiple states) • Using fraud and trafficking interchangeably (AL) • “Authorization cards” versus “electronic benefits transfer cards” (DC)

Section 7 — Summary and Recommendations 7-5 Participants also flagged mentions of cash benefits or references to programs that provide cash benefits as being confusing. Beyond being not applicable, some participants were not aware of these programs and thus had questions about references to paying bills or using cash for purchases. Throughout the interviews, participants indicated that a phone call is often their first option when they encounter an issue or question about their benefits. Improving program materials and disseminating well-designed documents with clear and complete information could enable program participants to find answers on their own and avoid inadvertently violating program rules while also saving on the cost of telephone and in-office support.
