Any views expressed are those of the authors and not those of the U.S. Census Bureau. The U.S. Census Bureau reviewed this data product for unauthorized disclosure of confidential information and approved the disclosure avoidance practices applied to this release. CBDRB-FY24-0478

i Abstract The U.S. Census Bureau conducted focus groups to gather information about the feasibility of using an online individual census questionnaire in seven different group quarters (GQ) types. Taken in hand with the conclusions drawn from the GQ suitability survey (Piccirillo et al. forthcoming), we were able to confirm which types of GQs might be strong candidates for an internet self-response (ISR) option and which GQs to rule out. We recommend three GQ types for self-enumeration using an online reporting option which also matched the survey results: college housing, workers’ quarters and Job Corps centers, and religious quarters. We also recommend moving forward to test email as the notification mode for the residents. Finally, we recommend developing supplemental programming surrounding the census to promote why the census is important and why it is important to be counted at the group quarters. Keywords: Group Quarters, individual census questionnaire, 2030 Census, opinion, email notification, census programming, internet self-response Suggested Citation: Elizabeth Nichols, Piccirillo Alexandra, Rivas Alda, Tuttle Dave. (2024). Feasibility of Using an Online Individual Census Questionnaire in 2030: Focus Group Findings from Group Quarter Administrators. Research and Methodology Directorate, Center for Behavioral Science Methods Research Report Series (Survey Methodology #2024-07). U.S. Census Bureau. Available online at <https://www.census.gov/library/working-papers/2024/adrm/rsm2024-07.html>

1 1. Introduction Group Quarters or GQs are places where groups of unrelated individuals live together and where there is some oversight or management of the day-to-day lives of the individuals. The decennial census counts individuals living in Group Quarters as well as those living in housing units. In the 2020 Census, a paper questionnaire called an Individual Census Questionnaire (ICQ) was completed for each individual living in a GQ or data from facility records were compiled by the facility staff and delivered to the Census Bureau (Stempowski, 2021). In preparation for the 2030 Census, staff at the Census Bureau conducted focus groups with Group Quarters administrators to determine whether their residents would be able and willing to answer the census online and how best to notify the residents of their census online form. The focus groups were one of four separate exploratory studies to determine whether their residents would be able and willing to answer the census online and how best to notify the residents of their census online form. The other exploratory studies include cognitive interviews to explore the online questionnaire interface (Piccirillo et al., forthcoming (a)), a suitability survey with GQ administrators (Piccirillo et al., forthcoming (b)), and one-on-one task analysis and low fidelity usability testing with GQ administrators (Tuttle et al., forthcoming). The present report describes the methodology and main findings of the focus groups. The Census Bureau groups GQs into 30 different types depending on the population served and the level and type of support provided. Of the 30 GQ types, seven of them were selected to take part in the focus groups. They were selected based on Census Bureau institutional knowledge of the GQ types with the assumption that their residents might be able and willing to complete an online census questionnaire. The seven GQ types (including their Census Bureau type code number) included: • Residential schools for people with disabilities (GQ type code 405) • College/University Student housing (GQ type code 501) • Military installations (GQ type code 601) • Group homes intended for adults (noncorrectional) (GQ type code 801) • Residential treatment centers for adults (noncorrectional) (GQ type code 802) • Workers’ group living quarters and Job Corp Centers (GQ type code 901) • Religious group quarters (GQ type code 902)

2 2. Methods Seven separate virtual focus groups were conducted. Table 1 shows the number of participants for each GQ type. Table 1: Focus group participation by GQ type GQ type code and description # participants 405 – Residential school for people with disabilities 2 501 - College/University Student Housing (college/university owned) 7 601 - Military 3 801 - Group Homes Intended for Adults (noncorrectional) 3 (2 unique GQs) 802 - Residential Treatment Centers for Adults (noncorrectional) 2 901 - Workers’ Group Living Quarters and Job Corps Centers 5 902 - Religious Group Quarters 2 2.1 Recruitment Focus group participants were current administrators of Group Quarters. Administrators are individuals who have access to the list of residents by address and have the authority to use that information. From the 2020 Census, we had the list of GQ administrators by GQ type, their phone numbers, and for some, their emails. Census Bureau staff used several recruitment strategies for the focus groups: • The “GQ ISR Suitability Survey” collected information from 344 GQ administrators about the feasibility of an online census for their residents (Piccarillo et al. 2024). We emailed respondents from this survey who reported that they wanted to participate in additional Census Bureau research. Ten people responded to this email indicating interest. • A Bureau of the Census (BOC) email blast (see Appendix A) was sent to all Census Bureau staff asking for them to forward the group quarter focus group opportunity to people they knew who might qualify. Three individuals replied.

3 • Because these two methods failed to generate sufficient interest for participating in the focus groups, Census Bureau staff made cold calls to GQ administrators listed in the Census Bureau database of administrators from the 2020 Census. • Additionally, Census Bureau staff had regular meetings with the military and contacts with Job Corp Centers. Both the military and the Job Corp centers provided multiple names that the Census Bureau then contacted directly for the latter two focus groups. 2.2 Procedure Moderators from Census Bureau headquarters led the focus groups remotely using Microsoft Teams using a moderator’s guide (see Appendix B). Each focus group had one moderator and one note taker. Additional Census Bureau staff observed the focus groups. Focus groups ran approximately 1.5 hours. The moderator requested that participants be on camera and nearly everyone complied, except for the military. They did not have cameras on their devices. Focus groups were recorded with participant consent. We used Snagit 2023/2024 to record sessions. Participants received a copy of the consent form with the privacy notice before the session and were asked to sign the consent form electronically ahead of time. Oral consent was also obtained when one or more participants had not signed electronically. The data collection was approved by OMB under the generic clearance 0607-0725 on June 16, 2023. Results were summarized by reviewing the debriefing notes with observers, the notes of the session, and rewatching the recordings. 2.3 Research topics Since the Census Bureau has yet to collect census data online directly from GQ residents, there were several research topics to investigate. The focus group topics concerned internet access, resident abilities, notification methods, and administrator duties and preferences. To conduct a successful census enumeration online, we also wanted to get feedback on some logistical topics. The topics included: 1. Whether/how residents access the internet. 2. Whether residents can complete an online questionnaire themselves or whether staff can help them. 3. Best method for notifying residents of an online questionnaire. 4. Whether the administrator can provide residents’ emails to the Census Bureau. 5. Whether the administrator would prefer to send the notification emails to the residents.

4 6. Conducting the Special Sworn Oath virtually. This is an oath that needs to be taken if the administrator encounters census data. 7. Other topics. Some of the other topics discussed included: • How best to distribute the link and the access code (a credential) for the online questionnaire. The access code is assigned by the Census Bureau. The Census Bureau ties each access code to a particular residential address and allows each person to be associated with an address. There could be a unique access code for each resident. And since multiple people live in the same GQ, the GQ address would be associated with multiple access codes. An alternative is to have one access code per GQ address and that access code would need to be used over and over for each person. • How best to follow up if some of the residents do not respond online and what type of assistance would be reasonable to ask of the administrators. The census needs everyone to be counted. • Whether more outreach is recommended for their populations. The recommendations from these focus group include whether an online questionnaire would work for each GQ type based on the conversation, the notification mode preferences, and the willingness of the administrators to assist the Census Bureau in this process. 3. Results 3.1 Group quarter type code 405: Residential school for people with disabilities This GQ type includes schools that provide the teaching of skills for daily living, education programs, and care for students with disabilities in a live-in environment. Examples are residential schools for the physically or developmentally disabled. 3.1.1 Participants Two administrators provided information for this type of GQ. Three other administrators expressed interest in the focus group but ended up not joining. One administrator works for a large company with residential units (group homes, houses, and apartments) around the country. The company serves both adults and children. This administrator is responsible for several units within one state. The residents have a range of cognitive disabilities and in most cases, would not be successful in independently completing an online survey. However, there are some more independent individuals who could complete an online survey with staff support. The other administrator oversees several residential buildings where individuals with disabilities live. That participant said that while some residents are working toward

5 independence and completing the census would be a life skill, other residents did not have the cognitive skills to fill it out and still others would not fill it out because it would not interest them. 3.1.2 Internet access and resident ability Device ownership and device access is mixed. The first administrator said that the more independent individuals have their own devices. Centralized devices could be provided for those who don’t have their own device. Additionally, staff would be required help residents complete the census. One issue the administrator identified was that everyone uses the network associated with the company and the network blocks some sites. It is not clear whether a census survey webpage would be blocked but it sounded like the administrator had to have some sites unblocked in the past. The second administrator said that each of the residential buildings has a computer with internet access and an address-level email. The device and email are primarily used by the staff assigned to that home. 3.1.3 Notification modes Email would not work as a notification solution for either administrator. In the first GQ most of the residents do not have their own emails. Additionally, the company does not have a centralized database with the emails of the residents who have them. However, the administrator said it would be easy for them to ask the residents for their emails. For the more independent individuals, the administrator said they too could use a text message or a QR code with staff support. The other administrator also said that email notification would not work for their population, and it would be more efficient that the information comes to the administrators and that person distributes it to the homes. 3.1.4 Notification logistics Sharing emails with the Census Bureau would require resident consent. Upon reflection, the first administrator said that it might be easier for the organization to manage notifying residents – that is getting the link and access codes for the online census questionnaire and distributing them. They would like a template or letter that they could use to communicate with staff or drop in an email. The administrator spontaneously said this would allow them to use accurate messaging. When asked, this administrator said that for the more independent individuals a unique access code per resident makes it cleaner than one access code per address. The company knows how many residents live in each address and could assign a unique code for each person. However, for the addresses with children, there seems to be more fluctuation in living situations with children coming and going. The administrator said for addresses with disabled residents, it would be ideal if there was one code allowing a GQ administrator to enter all the residents at one time.

6 3.1.5 Staff cooperation If staff were to help residents answer their own survey or complete the survey as a proxy for others (particularly the nonverbal residents), the first administrator said that having an advance copy of the census ahead of time would be helpful, including information on what to expect, when to expect it, and when it needs to be done. This administrator was very willing to work with the Census Bureau, including communicating with the Census Bureau about who hasn’t responded, work with the residents to encourage them to complete it (a.k.a., “chase them down”), but also simply complete it for them, if allowed. For the 2020 Census, this administrator provided data over the phone. The administrator had some memory of the special sworn procedures but would have no issues with a virtual swearing in via Microsoft Teams. This company uses Excel and prefers that to Google Forms because it is more stable with their network system. The second administrator said that the staff could support some individuals to help them complete it online, but it would be more efficient that the information comes to the administrators and that person distributes it to the homes. This participant also completed a spreadsheet for the residents for the 2020 Census and that worked well for the facility. 3.1.6 Summary of findings for residential school for people with disabilities We conclude that, due to the disabilities associated with most of the residents, self-response (either electronic or paper) is not an option for most of this population. Staff in the residences would be best equipped to complete the census questionnaire for the residents and would like to know what to expect ahead of time. For one of the facilities, there was not a database containing all the demographic data in a centralized place. An online form where multiple people could be entered would work better for them than an individual form for each person. Staff are experienced with Excel documents and a spreadsheet with the residents’ information might be just as easy to complete, as it was in the 2020 Census for the other facility. For one facility, there would be multiple proxy reporters across the different addresses; for the other facility one administrator could report for everyone. For the residents who might be able to report online, staff assistance is needed. Most of these residents do not have emails and therefore if there was an online option, the information would need to be sent to the administrator who could then distribute it. Both GQ administrators were willing to work with the Census Bureau. 3.2 Group quarter type code 501: College/University Student Housing (college/university owned) This GQ type includes residence halls, and other buildings, including apartment-style student housing, designed primarily to house college and university students in a group living

7 arrangement either on or off campus. These facilities are owned, leased, or managed by a college, university, or seminary. Fraternity and sorority housing recognized by the college or university are also included in this GQ type as college student housing. 3.2.1 Participants Staff from a wide variety of college administration positions participated in the focus group. Three individuals were registrars. They have lists of all students registered for classes (whether they live on campus or not). Three were associated with college housing and know the students who live in campus housing. One individual was a student life dean. For the 2020 Census, the census task migrated to registrars at some universities because they had the lists of students and could communicate with them even though the student body was not living in university housing during COVID. 3.2.2 Online census thoughts Everyone agreed that they would like the next census to attempt to collect census information directly from the students themselves using an online questionnaire. Even staff from the smaller university said online was better than paper, especially if the students could answer with their phones. Paper questionnaires are more difficult to secure, and they are more time consuming to keep track of. One of the main reasons these participants wanted students to self-respond to the census is that the colleges and universities cannot share all the information the census requests due to Family Educational Rights Privacy Act (FERPA). They can only share “directory” information. The directory information appears to differ among colleges as well, but date of birth, race and Hispanic origin seemed universally off limits. One participant said they could not even share room number with the Census Bureau. 3.2.3 Notification modes The topic of how to notify the student body about the online questionnaire generated much discussion. While all the college administrators thought the best way (and really the only way) to individually reach students was through their email, they all acknowledged that students don’t always read and act on their emails. One smaller university participant said that they emailed students about the 2020 Census, and it was effective. Of the seven participants, three would not share their residents’ email address with the Census Bureau and said that the university staff would need to send any emails notifying students that they need to complete the census. Several participants said that having the university send the email makes the request more legitimate, implying it might be to the Census Bureau’s advantage to have the university send them. Several suggestions were made to optimize email notifications.

8 1. Participants warned against too many emails. Participants suggested sending up to three emails. They provided examples from their own universities of students drowning in emails and being “surveyed to death.” 2. Becoming email tone-deaf is an issue and they recommended changing the subject line of each email. 3. Participants warned against using a “Coming soon” email without the link to the census online questionnaire. Rather, they said that the resident assistant (RA) and other school communities could pass out fliers about the census email coming with the link to answer the census. The school could adopt programming surrounding the census to let the students know it is coming, and digital signage about the census coming would be more effective in getting the student body ready for the census. a. One participant said that it is confusing to answer the census at college since they live at home, not at college, so education around where to be counted is important. They would like canned information from the Census Bureau to explain the information. 4. Emailing in the month of April was met with approval from these participants. They said the start and the end of the term are not good times to email students as students are distracted during those times. 5. For a smaller college, a paper notification to remind them to look at their email might be helpful. It might not be physically feasible remind students at larger institutions. 6. They liked the idea of the Census Bureau providing a template for the emails. One participant noted that email templates are provided by the Census Bureau for students selected for the American Community Survey. All participants thought the Census Bureau should try supplemental notification in addition to email to get the word out about the census. One administrator brought up using a QR code. Several said that a QR code on a poster and on digital signage would work. Posters might get ripped down, so they strongly advised us to also consider social media messaging in addition to any paper. They all thought the QR codes should be used in the residence halls instead of the student center or classrooms. Only one administrator said that some students could be hesitant about QR codes. Texting students did not seem to be a viable notification option. The coverage and quality of cell phone numbers for students varies, even within universities. Additionally, none of the institutions would share phone numbers outside the university. 3.2.4 Access codes Administrator opinions were mixed on whether they would want a unique access code for each student or an access code for the residential hall, where all students in that hall would use the

9 same code. The participants who were not registrars said unique codes are a lot to keep track of and would have to hire someone to do that. The registrars in the focus group seemed more amenable to that idea of a unique code per student. One participant said that to help keep track of who has responded if one access code was used for the entire residence hall, the data collection should also collect room number. 3.2.5 Staff cooperation As far as following up on students who have not responded to the census, participants also expressed mixed emotions. All the participants understood the importance of having their students counted at college. However, many voiced concerns about the amount of work that would be needed to accomplish this task. One registrar described the task as “scurrying around.” If the Census Bureau wants this type of help, then the Department of Commerce would have to talk to the Chancellor to request this level of support. That is the strategy the Department of Education uses to successfully get the registrar “to do things.” Two participants said they would have to hire individuals to do this level of work. 3.2.6 Nonresponse Participants mentioned a different idea for counting students who had not responded. They said they (the university) could give the directory information for all the students to the Census Bureau and then have the Census Bureau deduplicate from the list against the people who have responded. All participants thought this idea was the best course of action for nonresponse. If the Census Bureau adopted this strategy for nonresponse, then they said there would be no need for them to see who has and hasn’t responded. Participants liked the idea of sending out email reminders to everyone, even if they had already responded. If administrators are to help remind only nonresponding students, they understood the need to see who has responded to know who hasn’t responded. They also understood that they would need to be special sworn if they saw who responded. They expressed no concern about themselves being sworn in by the census, and swearing in virtually also did not seem to be a concern. However, participants were not interested swearing in resident assistants. They are young individuals, with many responsibilities and participants uniformly agreed that asking them to be sworn in would be too much of a burden. 3.2.7 Other topics Participants brought up that students live in different types of housing. They said there needs to be census coordination in the different housing situations. For example, college housing can include nontraditional housing, like married student housing, fraternity or sorority homes. If we want to enumerate everyone, then the Census Bureau should coordinate with the registrar or bursar. They know all individuals who attend the school, which includes people who live in campus run housing and people who do not. It was not clear whether their databases included

10 where people live and if they live in campus housing. It was mentioned by a few participants that they did not know the children who live in married student housing. The registrar’s list does not contain information on the children in those residential units. (Additionally, it would be burdensome to list each household member in a married student housing individually in an ICQ.) A new topic was brought up by the participants. They expressed the importance of having events and promotion around the census. One participant described what their university did in 2020, including speakers, representatives visiting and other programs. This promotion helped students who live off campus learn how important the census is, especially international students who might not think the census applies to them. Having speakers, and educational events was critical they said, as the legislative process, and federal funding affects the local community. Another participant said having prepared activities like this from the Census Bureau would be helpful. 3.2.8 Summary of findings for colleges and universities College and university participants supported using an online census for 2030 in their group quarters. For legitimacy purposes and due to limitations on sharing information, universities said they (university staff) should send the emails notifying the student of their census obligation, versus the emails coming from the Census Bureau. These administrators recommended other supplemental notification tools be used too and were generally supportive of using a QR code on paper or on digital signage in residential halls. There was not universal agreement on whether one access code per residential hall or unique access codes for individuals would work better. For nonresponse follow up, the easiest solution for the institutions was provide the list of all the students with their limited data to the Census Bureau and have the Census Bureau staff deduplicate the list against who reported for themselves. This would remove any need for special sworn status for staff and simplify the process of sending reminder emails. Events for each university area should be developed and provided to the community to prepare for the census in advance, with special emphasis on explaining why to be counted at the university housing and why everyone at the school should be counted, including international students. 3.3 Group quarter type code 601: Military These GQs include military personnel living in barracks (including “open” barrack transient quarters) and dormitories and military ships. Students attending the U.S. Naval Academy, the U.S. Military Academy (West Point), the U.S. Coast Guard Academy, and the U.S. Air Force Academy are counted in military group quarters.

11 3.3.1 Participants Three individuals participated in the military focus group. Two were from the Army and one from the Navy. The three participants were all managers of residential facilities for single, enlisted individuals. Their titles were “Unaccompanied housing manager” or barracks manager. One individual oversaw one building with less than 50 people while the other two oversaw multiple buildings, housing between 800 and 5,000 enlisted individuals. None of the three participated in providing data for their units in the 2020 Census enumeration. They described the demographics of their residents as between 18 to 30 years old and single. There were no family units in their quarters. Seven administrators from other military GQs were invited to attend the focus group but ended up not joining. Not only did very few individuals participate, but those who were invited never contacted the Census Bureau saying whether they would attend. This lack of interest in the focus group made sense after discussing the idea of soldiers and sailors completing their own census questionnaire online in 2030. None of the focus group participants thought this was a good idea. They said asking the enlisted to complete their own census questionnaire online would not result in good data since the soldiers and sailors would probably not care and thus, they would not comply. One of the participants shared his own thoughts on the census and said that he never cared which state or geography received the money associated with the census and was not compelled to answer it because he moved so much. The same participant also said that a company leadership team will not take squad leaders away from their warfighting mission to fill out the census. 3.3.2 Online census thoughts All three participants said that for the enlisted to comply with completing an online census questionnaire, they would require commanders to instruct individuals to do it. Even so, the participants were skeptical they could get everyone to comply. One participant suggested an incentive to participate, but it was unclear what type of incentive would work best. Another participant said that even with an incentive the individuals would not complete the questionnaire if it was too long. One participant gave an example of a military Climate Survey which only results in a 50 percent response rate, after the managers begged for participation. Another example shared was the lack of compliance with a required inventory form associated with their job. This participant said that a battalion came back from deployment, and many wouldn’t even fill in their paper inventory sheet with 10 questions. The participant had to go to their commander to get them to comply. When asked whether a one-page paper questionnaire would work better than an online questionnaire, the participant associated with the smaller installation remarked that we would see the same response rate for paper as with an online questionnaire, but paper would be

12 easier for tracking and accountability. The other participant noted that with an online questionnaire, even if they bring personnel into a room and watch them, they couldn’t tell if someone was playing a game on their phone or completing the census. 3.3.3 Notification modes Using email to notify personnel about the census was not recommended by the participants. For the Army, not all personnel have a military email and the barracks managers do not necessarily have their residents’ personal email. The enlisted do not have to share their personal email with the government. All three participants also said that the junior enlisted personnel do not check their military emails, unless they are told to do so. One participant joked that the Census Bureau should create a census snapchat. Participants either could not share or were not sure whether they could share military emails with the Census Bureau. One participant doesn’t have the email for all the residents either. This participant has their leadership contact information and would have to tell that leader to push the email out to their individuals. The participant remarked that several rounds of reminders would be needed to make that happen. Participants seemed to like the idea of using a QR code to navigate to the online census questionnaire but mentioned that even QR codes cannot motivate all individuals to participate in required administrative tasks. Two participants said that their workorder form (for a problem with their barracks) is accessed via a QR code and that many enlisted residents fail to put in the workorder form. 3.3.4 Access codes When asked about what type of access code would work for the residents, participants recommended we investigate whether we could use their Department of Defense (DOD) ID number. Every service member is assigned their own DOD number, which is essentially a Social Security Number. This number could be tracked back to an individual and they all know their DOD ID number. 3.3.5 Address information The focus group moderator asked about the address of the barracks, but many of the participants focused on the mailing address for individual personnel. For these participants, the mailroom has an address, and each individual has a mail bin and their building has a number. For the Navy participant, each sailor gets mail from their own command, not through the building. However, this participant said that fliers are delivered to each room and the physical address is by building and room. For the Army, it was similar in that the physical address was the mailing address and the building. At the post, there is also privatized housing for families, and Senior enlisted or Senior officer quarters. For the Navy participant, their family housing is

13 off the base. The current participants only were responsible for the housing of the single enlisted personnel. 3.3.6 Staff cooperation When asked about their support for following up with soldiers and sailors who did not respond or for agreeing to becoming special sworn to help with that follow up, participants echoed earlier themes. For example, these participants did not think becoming special sworn would be an issue as long as it falls within duties, scope, and responsibilities of the unaccompanied housing manager. If the commander said to do this, then they would have to. It would have to be approved by the supervisor. As for following up on individuals who do not fill in the census questionnaire, one participant said that if we had a number to expect for each building and then check that number against how many questionnaires came in, that would be one way to see if we had everyone. 3.3.7 Summary of findings for the military There was very little support from these military participants for an individual online census for 2030. Their experience and struggle with enlisted personnel accomplishing administrative tasks, and the required follow up led them to this conclusion. If the Census Bureau really wants self- response from enlisted personnel, we would have to work with Command to require it, and these participants thought a paper questionnaire would be easier for them to confirm that the census was completed rather than an online questionnaire. Across both the Army and Navy participants, they said that if the census wanted accurate numbers, then we should contact the Unaccompanied Housing Office or some management within each individual post to get the lists of residents, which is basically the procedure we used in past censuses. 3.4 Group quarter type code 801 - Group Homes Intended for Adults (noncorrectional) Group homes are community-based group living arrangements in residential settings that are able to accommodate three or more clients of a service provider. The group home provides room and board and services, including behavioral, psychological, or social programs. Generally, clients are not related to the caregiver or to each other. Group homes do not include residential treatment centers or facilities operated by or for correctional authorities. 3.4.1 Participants Three individuals participated in the focus group, with two of them being from the same facility. Three other organizations expressed interest in the focus group but ended up not joining. The two facilities operated several different residential buildings, with different residents needing varying levels of support.

14 3.4.2 Internet access, resident ability, and online census thoughts One participant reported having more residents in skilled nursing facilities than in group homes. The majority of this participant’s residents would be unable to complete the online questionnaire themselves because of memory impairment issues. Only a small number of residents access the internet, and most of the residents are under a guardianship. For this participant’s facility, the internet option was not viable. The participant commented that if we had an internet option, a proxy would have to complete the questionnaire for each resident, defeating the purpose of self-reporting. It would also be more difficult to make sure everyone was counted, since the administrator couldn’t confirm whether each resident was helped. Due to the number of residents, different staff would be assigned to enter data for different residents. Instructions and monitoring would therefore be decentralized, and the administrator would be unable to verify that everyone’s data was entered. This participant added that they completed the 2020 Census for the facility by filling in a “giant” spreadsheet and spontaneously commented that the method worked well. The participant said that the data the census requested was already on her work file and added that as of October 1, 2023, all federal skilled nursing facilities would collect resident self-reported race and ethnicity. This participant was supportive of this rule change and said the data would be better. The participant’s only suggestion was to include a place to upload that spreadsheet to the Census Bureau. Two individuals participated from the other organization. That organization ran several residential buildings, including an emergency shelter, permanent supportive housing, family housing, and residential substance use housing. While there is a centralized computer for residents to use and completing the census is a life skill, participants said it might be easier to complete it via paper form, rather than online. The participants suggested that they would help residents fill in their paper questionnaire and then once the paper is complete, they could enter the data into a spreadsheet and send it to the Census Bureau. They added that some of the residents with mental illness would not want to complete the questionnaire online since they do not trust the internet. They also did not think email was good notification tool for their population. Many of their residents can’t get into their email since they have forgotten the password. It would take more oversight from GQ staff for residents to use their email. A QR code would not work either because only some residents might be able to use it. If the Census Bureau were to require an online questionnaire, the participants would rather have the facilities receive the link and then have the residents who are able complete the online questionnaire. The residential facility could keep track of who has completed the census.

15 3.4.3 Staff cooperation and release of information These two participants from the second GQ were very willing to help the Census Bureau with the census, whether this meant helping residents fill out the census or uploading the resident’s data into a spreadsheet. They had no problem with being sworn in or signing virtually. They have a Homeless Management Information System that houses data. These participants requested one point of contact with the Census Bureau for each GQ type. They can give collective data but for individual data on residents they need a release of information to allow them to send data to the Census Bureau. 3.4.4 Summary of findings for group homes intended for adults There was a lack of interest in participating in the focus group by this GQ type. While the individuals who participated were interested in helping the Census Bureau collect accurate information, it does not seem like a self-administered online questionnaire is efficient for this population or the administrators. A paper form would be easier to complete and more straightforward to coordinate across residents. For organizations with multiple GQ types, including skilled nursing care and other group homes, it appeared that centralized reporting by the administrator is most efficient, especially now that residents must self-report race and ethnicity and that self-reported data would be in the facilities’ data. 3.5 Group quarter type code 802 - Residential Treatment Centers for Adults (noncorrectional) These residential facilities provide treatment on-site in a highly structured live-in environment for the treatment of drug/alcohol abuse, mental illness, and emotional/behavioral disorders. They are staffed 24-hours a day. The focus of a residential treatment center is on the treatment program. Residential treatment centers do not include facilities operated by or for correctional authorities. 3.5.1 Participants Two individuals from two separate organizations participated in the focus group. Two other organizations expressed interest in the focus group but ended up not joining. One participant was the program manager for facilities for individuals who are mentally ill. Some programs in that facility have clients who live on the campus, but there were many more outpatient clients who live in the community. The other participant was program manager for the developmentally disabled (about 200 individuals in 20 buildings with one address). Both participants helped conduct previous censuses at their facilities. 3.5.2 Internet access, resident ability, and online census thoughts The participant from the first facility said that while many of the clients with mental illness have their own cell phones with internet, internet access is not universal in the facility. Specific

16 subpopulations of these facilities (e.g., older clients) do not use the internet. This participant shared that many of the individuals with mental illness are paranoid about the internet and about the government and would need support in filling out the census online. The participant expressed a willingness to support individuals filling out the census, especially for those who can’t read or write. Encouraging residents who can act independently was also important to this manager. This participant wanted to know if helping to fill out the census was a Medicaid approved chargeable service. The moderator later informed the participant that it was up to the state’s laws. Regarding the other participant’s facility, most of the clients are profoundly disabled and cannot use the internet. That participant mentioned that those clients cannot answer the census even with support, and there were only a handful of clients who could participate with support. The participant said that, for the last census, they provided a file with last name, first name, date of birth, age and sex of each person who lives there. The participant stated that providing the file with data for a particular date was not difficult because very few individuals change residence. 3.5.3 Notification modes Providing an email with a link and a code to the online would not be practical for either of the facilities represented during the focus group. If there was a desire for clients (who were able) to self-report, both participants said that a paper questionnaire for the facility manager to help fill out would work better than an online questionnaire. For the facility that houses clients with mental illness, the manager could monitor completion better working with them one-on-one. For the facility with disabled residents, while the participant said they could fill in a paper questionnaire for each individual, the spreadsheet worked well. 3.5.4 Other topics There was some confusion about when the next census will take place. One participant mentioned that they had been contacted by the Census Bureau recently. That participant also fills out other surveys for other organizations. Sending the information via the mail would work for both these managers, but they would be willing to send it electronically. Both participants wondered about releasing information to the census, specifically for those who filled it out themselves, whether they had to alert legal guardians about filling out the census. 3.5.5 Staff cooperation For the two individuals who participated, they both were very willing to work with the Census Bureau to make sure everyone is counted. Neither one had any concerns with using a virtual meeting and signing something electronically to become special sworn.

17 3.5.6 Summary of findings for residential treatment centers for adults For this GQ type an online questionnaire that residents would complete was not efficient for one participant and was not viable for the other participant. While the two participants were very interested in helping the Census Bureau any way they could, they identified a few roadblocks regarding with an online form. For one facility, the spreadsheet method used in 2020 seems to be the best option as most of their residents are incapable of self-reporting. For the other facility, while the residents are more able-bodied, a paper questionnaire was preferred for helping individuals self-report. The lack of participation in the focus group from the other two invited participants could also be an indication that the online reporting option is not something that resonates with this GQ type. There also was some confusion expressed during this focus group about different requests made by the Census Bureau. It seemed as if other Census Bureau staff had been contacting them for other surveys. The participant was slightly confused by the different contacts and did not understand the difference between the census and these other, what we assume to be, survey contacts. 3.6 Group quarter type code 901 - Workers’ Group Living Quarters and Job Corps Centers Job Corp Centers This GQ type includes facilities such as dormitories, bunkhouses, and similar types of group living arrangements for agricultural and non-agricultural workers. This category also includes facilities that provide a full-time, year-round residential program offering a vocational training and employment program that helps young people 16-to-24 years old learn a trade, earn a high school diploma or GED and get help finding a job. Examples are group living quarters at migratory farm worker camps, construction workers’ camps, Job Corps centers and vocational training facilities. 3.6.1 Participants A focus group was conducted with five Job Corp employees representing five different Job Corp centers from across the country. Job Corp centers offer job training, help with completing a GED, driver’s license, transitional services, and the like. 3.6.2 Description of typical resident Each center has both day students and residential students. There is a lot of mobility with the student population. Students stay with Job Corp an average of 12 months depending on the training program with some programs, like culinary, taking as little as 3 to 5 months to complete while other trades taking longer like 9 to 12 months. For a good proportion of students, they stay as little as 30 to 60 days either because there were disciplinary reasons or because they do not like the program. The maximum amount of time someone can live there is 2 to 3 years. New students arrive every week and students leave all the time. Summer is usually a slower time for residential moves and spring is a peak time for residential moves.

18 The five centers had different numbers of students living there, ranging from approximately 150 to 800 housed in multiple dorms. Most of the centers were not fully occupied and all the participants said they were still recovering from COVID, implying that no one lived there during that time, and they were just getting back their students. Several talked about how some of the dorms were closed currently but could reopen if the student population grew. Approximately 20 to 33 percent of the residents are minors (under 18) and the participants described that they must have parental permission to complete forms, like Census Bureau surveys. Center residents are on average between 16 to 24 years old with some older than that. 3.6.3 Internet access and resident ability All centers have internet access. Students have a student portal to access the internet and all students have access to Chrome books and computer labs in the dorms. The participants described students as individuals who can complete the census with a few individuals who might need support from staff. All participants said they had staff to assist residents if needed. 3.6.4 Notification modes Participants said that most of their students would comply and complete an online census. They acknowledged that the staff would have to encourage them, but that did not seem to be an issue. One center gave an example of a 20-minute Student Engagement Assessment survey, which is administered quarterly or every 6 months and has an 80 percent response rate. Another participant said they could do the census as part of their class on their Chrome books. None of them said a paper form was needed or preferred to an online questionnaire. They also said that email was the best way to notify the students as students have a Job Corp email, but they would also use other methods to encourage participation including: • post about the census on the media boards in each dorm hall and center wide, • spread the word in dorm meetings or weekly business meetings with students, • using QR codes on paper for some students with smartphones, • making sure it was on the student portal, and • having a census worker who could come in and help get residents enumerated. 3.6.5 Notification logistics They suggested that their organization sends the emails to the residents. They suggested the Census Bureau work with the Department of Labor and Job Corp Regional Directors to coordinate the data collection. (The moderator let participants know that this was how the present focus group was coordinated.) Once there is an agreement at that level, participants suggested the Census Bureau send the emails to the center director, who is the main contact, and that individual would make sure the emails were distributed residents. The primary reason

19 why they said they should send the emails was for accountability. They wanted to avoid any situation where the student said they did not get the email and the center is not able to verify that. When asked by the moderator, the participants said it was not difficult to separate non- resident students’ emails from the resident’s emails. 3.6.6 Access codes Participants said they could handle one access code per person, and several said that would help with tracking individuals who did not comply from those who did. The dorm buildings themselves vary by center. Some have wings; some have floors. One participant initially liked one code for the dormitory versus each student – saying that would make it easier to manage. They added that it is not hard to separate students by dormitories because that is the way their computer program is organized. So, it isn’t difficult to have either a unique code by student, or one code for the dorm. There is one address for the entire center, but then the name and the dorm is how they identify where they are. The post office delivers to the center, and a staff person distributes the mail. 3.6.7 Other topics When asked by the moderator, participants said they did not think most students would falsify their name on the census, but they added that several students don’t identify by their legal or given name. One participant said that students might not know their Job Corp address to enter it, but no one said that students would have a difficult time confirming their address. When asked, participants said the Job Corp Center data include all the basic demographic data needed on the census and the address of their permanent home. 3.6.8 Staff cooperation The participants were engaged with the focus group, everyone invited attended, and no one expressed concerns with virtually swearing in. 3.6.9 Other Census Bureau survey feedback Two participants said that their students were in Census Bureau surveys recently and provided feedback on the experience. • One survey was about employment and took 10-minutes to complete. We guessed it was the Current Population Survey (CPS). The Census Bureau administrator has a list of beds, and the computer picks a bed for her to survey. Then, the student calls the Census Bureau administrator, and they conduct interview over the phone. The participant added that this month is the last month, which makes sense for the CPS as it is a longitudinal survey. • The other participant described their experience with the American Community Survey. While the participant said that working with the Census Bureau representative was

20 positive and that the importance of the survey and how the data were used was explained well to the students, three barriers were mentioned. o For the minor students, they needed parental consent to comply. The survey had such a short window for data collection that it was difficult to get parental permission in that time frame. o One of the questions asks about schooling. The students consider themselves enrolled in school, but they are not in a K-12 school and they are not in college. There is no good response choice for Job Corp Center students. o The survey mode is by phone and not all students have a cell phone. This participant said that having a hybrid of phone or paper was important. 3.6.10 Summary of findings for Job Corps Centers Job Corp participants supported using an online census for 2030 in their group quarters. For accountability reasons, participants said they should send the emails notifying the student of their census obligation. They could support students completing the census in the classroom or in meetings. Like the college group quarter focus group, digital signage in residential halls is used and participants mentioned they would post about the census on the media boards. Participants said that a unique code for each resident could work and would be better for follow up. However, that doesn’t work if they post on the media board. The Job Corp centers have census-like data available for their students and were supportive of students answering for themselves. Challenges include the mobility of students in and out of the Job Corp Centers in the springtime and the requirement by the center to get parental consent for census reporting for a quarter of their population. Job Corp Centers also has umbrella oversight from the Department of Labor. Participants suggest the Census Bureau coordinates with the correct organization to receive support from Job Corp. The Census Bureau is aware of these coordination requirements. 3.7 Group quarter type code 902 - Religious Group Quarters These are living quarters owned or operated by religious organizations that are intended to house their members in a group living situation. This category includes such places as convents, monasteries, and abbeys. 3.7.1 Participants Two individuals from two different religious communities participated. One of the communities has fewer than 20 residents and lives in one building while the other community has around 100 residents living in multiple buildings. That community has one mailing address, but recently each building was assigned a 911 address.

21 A third participant was unable to attend the focus group. 3.7.2 Internet access and resident ability In both communities, there is internet access via phones, computers, and tablets. The participants said that most of their residents would be willing and able to complete the census online, with some of the older adults potentially having a little more difficulty. 3.7.3 Notification modes All residents have emails and both participants said that emailing would be the best way to communicate with the residents about the census. They also both agreed that they should send the emails and not the Census Bureau since their residents might not like them sharing their email with the government. 3.7.4 Access codes The two participants were not sure whether the access code should be at the residence or at the individual level. Both participants reported that they could keep track either way, with one explaining how he keeps track of serial numbers of the assigned phones by person. This participant whose residents only live in one building also said that it would be a little easier to send one email out to his distribution list with the details if it was one code. 3.7.5 Online census thoughts This participant remarked several times that even though his residents could complete their own census, the way he completed the 2020 Census would be easier. He had a spreadsheet and went around collecting data from each person and then sent in the spreadsheet. Because there were so few individuals, it was not a difficult task. The other organization has census-like data for the individuals collected at the organization level, but they seemed more receptive to individuals reporting for themselves since it is their own information. This participant also realized this might mean more work for him to make sure everyone reported. That participant said a combination of email and QR code and web address posted in a general location would work well. They have their residents’ emails since they are assigned by the community. Each resident gets their own email, except for the children. The participant as a distribution list for all members of community. He would want to send this information to that distribution list. 3.7.6 Staff cooperation Neither participant had any objection to be sworn in virtually and both were very willing to help the Census Bureau. 3.7.7 Summary of findings for religious group quarters While there was some lack of interest in participating in the focus group, based on feedback from these two participants, an online questionnaire that residents would complete themselves should be offered to religious group quarters. The residents are able-bodied and need little

22 support. They also have internet access and email that they read. Email along with QR codes should be offered as notification methods and we should allow religious communities to send out the email to their residents. Some religious communities might select the spreadsheet method regardless due to the ease of reporting using that method. Using the spreadsheet would mean that the administrator would not have to send out reminders to the residents or follow up on residents who do not respond. If an online self-response questionnaire is offered, we should be aware, that like the college housing, there could be children living in these communities. An ICQ might miss the children if they don’t have their own email and their parents do not complete an ICQ for them. Also, like college housing, there are advantages and disadvantages to one access code for the community or unique access codes for everyone. 4. Conclusion Based on the findings from the focus group conversations, an online individual census questionnaire would be a viable mode for collecting census data for residents of these group quarters: • College/University Student housing (GQ type code 501) • Workers’ group living quarters and Job Corp Centers (GQ type code 901) • Religious group quarters (GQ type code 902) Participants were globally supportive of having their residents provide their own census data online. Residents of these group quarter types have access to the internet, devices to complete the online questionnaire, the cognitive ability to complete a census questionnaire for themselves and are suspected by the administrators to be willing to complete it by themselves. For college and universities, they like the idea of a student completing the questionnaire for themselves because the colleges are unable to share detailed demographic data that is not in a public-facing directory. They suspect we will get more complete and accurate data from students than from a college list. Email notification (sent by the administrators of the three group quarters being discussed) was seen as the best method to communicate the census link and the access code needed to enter the online questionnaire. Email should be supplemented with other communication by the facility, whether orally in meetings, or on posters with a QR code to the online questionnaire, or through media events. Administrators liked the idea of email templates created by the Census Bureau to use. They cautioned against too many emails. The college and university participants also said to vary the subject line and include a call to action in every email. Sending email reminders to everyone

23 rather than just to those who haven’t responded is easier on the administrator. Census promotion before Census Day should occur by other means (rather than email). That might include print media, media boards, announcements, or events. The importance of being counted and where to be counted for individuals with other homes, such as a parent’s home, or a home outside the U.S. needs to be clearly communicated before Census Day. There are advantages and disadvantages to using individual access codes for each resident or having one access code for the residential building. While most of these facilities can handle assigning codes either way, if there is public display of the census URL or a QR code with an access code, then the access code cannot be individualized and rather it must be at the residence level. If there is follow up for non-responders, then individual codes are easier to track. Group quarters could also provide the list of residential names and census-like data to the Census Bureau to supplement for those who did not respond instead of following up on each person individually. Some of these types of GQs might prefer other enumeration options, like a spreadsheet, to coordinating each resident completing it for themselves. Allowing the administrator to choose which method to use to collect census data acknowledges that not all group quarters are alike. Children (whether dependents) living with adults also in the housing, or minor children who need a waiver to complete questionnaires could be challenges for enumeration in these group quarter types. The former situation would require the main resident to complete an ICQ for each family member, which could be seen as inefficient compared to the household form. The latter situation would require parental permission to be obtained before complying. All these GQs expressed approval for virtual swearing in for the Census Bureau Special Sworn Status. They understood that even if residents reported their own data, the GQ administrator would likely be involved in knowing who reported and who had not yet reported, thus needing the Special Sworn Status. We now turn to the other group quarters we investigated. Based on the findings from the focus group conversations, an online individual census questionnaire would not be a viable mode for collecting census data for residents of these group quarters: • Residential schools for people with disabilities (GQ type code 405) • Military installations (GQ type code 601) • Group homes intended for adults (noncorrectional) (GQ type code 801) • Residential treatment centers for adults (noncorrectional) (GQ type code 802) We did not find much enthusiasm for self-reporting for these group quarters, although our conclusions are based on a small number of participant’s experiences. Residents in type codes

24 405, 801, and 802 vary in their cognitive ability to complete a questionnaire for themselves. Residents in these facilities would require staff time to assist them. While the focus group participants seemed agreeable to assisting some of them, and there are life-skills involved in completing a census questionnaire for themselves, it would require more work and coordination from administrators. Several said a spreadsheet might be the easiest way to provide the data and to make sure it is complete. In large facilities where the support would be decentralized, there was a fear that some residents might get the support to answer online while others would not. For military group quarters (601s), administrators were skeptical they could get the soldiers and sailors to comply and if the Census Bureau required self-reporting, they wanted a paper form for each resident instead of an online questionnaire for ease of verifying that it was completed. 5. 2 Abstract In preparation for the 2030 U.S. Census, the Census Bureau is conducting a series of small experimental studies to improve self-response rates, data quality, and the respondent experience with the census data collection operation. In the Spring of 2023, the first study, the 2023 Census Test, was fielded. Roughly 15,000 sample addresses were sent up to four mailings that included a link to the 2023 Census Test landing page on the Census website and an individualized code to enter the survey instrument. On the landing page, individuals could read about the test, see answers to frequently asked questions, or press an English or Spanish “Respond Now” button to enter the survey login page. This report provides a summary of the landing page usage from February to April 2023, including devices and referral methods by which individuals arrived, and rates at which they navigated from the landing page to the survey instrument. Some of the results were as expected, with landing page hits generally mapping to the estimated mail delivery dates and many of those proceeding forward to access and complete the survey. Those who completed the survey tended to arrive by the expected method of typing or bookmarking the Census Test link that appeared on the mailings, and they predominantly arrived on a desktop or laptop. A more surprising result was the quantity of hits to the landing page (roughly 60%) that never resulted in trying to access the survey, which primarily occurred in visitors arriving via search engines on mobile devices. This pattern occurred throughout the operation, but especially later in the field period; it was unexpected, given that there was no communications campaign associated with this Census Test. It is unclear what motivated these landing page hits or whether these individuals were in sample. This finding suggests that even without an overt communication campaign, information is likely to spread about a web-based Census test and that landing pages are likely to be accessed by individuals not in sample. 4 1 Introduction There are numerous techniques to evaluate and improve the usability of websites, including usability testing, expert reviews, heuristic evaluations, card sorting, and collection and evaluation of usage metrics once sites are live (Hornbaek, 2006). This report summarizes the usage metrics for a Census Bureau website containing information and links to an online Census Bureau survey that was conducted between February and April of 2023. The webpage evaluated was www.census.gov/2023CensusTest. Figure 1 displays the top portion of the landing page the user sees first, and Appendix Figures A1-A3 display additional content (e.g., FAQs) the user sees if they continue scrolling down. Collectively these figures represent the landing page referred to in this report, and the survey is called the 2023 Census Test with the login page found in Figure 2. The goal of the investigation was to explore how the public used the website to access the survey to make improvements for future, similar websites so that survey access is easy and straightforward. Specifically, analysis focuses on the number of landing page hits over time by device type and referral method (whether they typed in the URL or came from a search engine or another website). The report also documents how many of those hits were from the same individual (duplicate visits) and how many translated into an actual survey completion. This exploratory research is the first time a survey landing page for the U.S. Census Bureau has been examined. Figure 1. Screenshot of 2023 Census Test landing page on a laptop.

5 Figure 2. Screenshot of 2023 Census Test login page on a laptop. 2. Background This research was motivated by the 2020 Census. In recent decades, respondents had multiple modes of completing the census (i.e., mailout/mailback forms, telephone, face to face visits), but in 2020 respondents could also self-respond on the internet for the first time. Mailed notifications for the 2020 Census provided a URL for the webpage from which the census questionnaire could be accessed (my2020census.gov, its “landing page”). That webpage (Figure 3) functioned similarly to the webpage for the 2023 Census Test, with users selecting the “Start Questionnaire” button to access the census login page (Figure 4) where they could enter their access code to begin the census data collection. The 2020 Census landing page also provided access to frequently asked questions and instructions and contained a language toggle to Spanish and eleven other non-English languages. In addition to the multiple languages offered in the 2020 Census, there was also a communications campaign associated with the 2020 Census that shared its URL widely across the U.S. in print, radio, and digital formats (Scheid, et al., 2024). The 2023 Census Test, on the other hand, only offered the instrument in English and Spanish and did not use a communication campaign, as the survey sample was relatively small.

6 Figure 3. Screenshot of 2020 Census landing page on a laptop. Figure 4. Screenshot of 2020 Census login page on a laptop. Although multiple rounds of usability testing were conducted on both the landing and login pages for the 2020 Census to improve the respondent experience (Hotchkiss et al., 2024), there was no quantitative evaluation of the metrics associated with the use of the landing page once it was live. For example, we do not know how many people accessed the landing page, which devices they used, or how many visitors accessed the page but never selected the “Start

7 Questionnaire” button. Such information might have had implications for future survey and census website designs. For example, if metrics indicated that people accessed a FAQ and then left the page, perhaps the FAQs were not sufficient, or they were confusing–either way, that finding would have led to more testing and evaluation of the FAQs so that they met user needs for the next round of data collection. Analysis of login pages for decennial tasks has also been limited, with research only showing spikes in the number of logins that match expected delivery of the mailed notifications and not the number of failed login attempts (Nichols, et al. 2019). The 2023 Census Test data provides the opportunity to perform these evaluations. Detailed user interactions data were collected for the 2023 Census Test landing page and for the 2023 Census Test login page. Thus, we can understand user behavior on these two pages at a granular level. While we do not expect the behavior to exactly match that of the 2020 Census, given differences in the operation, investigating current behavior patterns is useful for identifying aspects of the website and users’ interactions with it that could be improved—both for the user and as a baseline for future survey studies like this one. 3. Methods 3.1 Study description In preparation for the 2030 U.S. Census, the Census Bureau is conducting a series of experimental studies to improve self-response rates, data quality, and the respondent experience during the census data collection operation. The first study—the 2023 Census Test—was conducted in early 2023 with a sample of approximately 15,000 housing units nationwide. Manipulations of mailed survey notifications were tested, as were manipulations of some online census questions (Shagnea and Mathews, forthcoming). Other than the mailed notifications, there was no external communications campaign associated with this study. The mailed notification was bilingual – in English and Spanish and included: the requirement to complete the survey, web address of the landing page to access the survey (www.census.gov/2023CensusTest), and a code for logging into the survey. After the first letter, sent February 17, subsequent mailings—sent February 22, March 3, and March 10— reminded participants to complete the survey if they had not already done so. The webpage contained information about the survey, answers to frequently asked questions, and both English and Spanish “Respond Now” buttons to enter the survey login page. Once on the login page, users were requested to enter the unique access code provided in their mailing materials to gain access to the survey. In total, users logged in with 5300 unique codes. The landing page and survey were available from the date of the first mailing through April 4, after which they were decommissioned. The survey collected basic demographic data like a decennial census but was implemented using Qualtrics (Qualtrics, Provo, UT). This is in contrast

8 to the 2020 Census, which was implemented in a Census Bureau framework called Primus and had more flexibility and functionality in the interface design. The “landing page” as used below refers to the webpage found at the URL provided in the mailing materials: www.census.gov/2023CensusTest. The “login page” as used below refers to the Qualtrics survey entry page, on which users were requested to enter the unique survey code provided in their mailing materials. For the current paper, users were considered to have completed the survey if they made 100% progress through the survey. 3.2 Data Data on user interactions with the 2023 Census Test landing page were retrieved through Adobe Analytics and Google Analytics platforms and covered the time period from February 14 to April 9, 2023. Those data included: 1) the date and time of access to the landing page; 2) the user’s IP address; 3) the device used to access the page (“device type”)—a desktop or laptop computer, a mobile phone, or a tablet; 4) the method by which the user was referred to the webpage (“referral method”)—via typing the URL or accessing it through a bookmark; a search engine; a social network website; a news website; a government website; a security services website; a services provider website (i.e., the website of a company that provides access to internet, cable, and/or phone services); another kind of website; a link accessed in an email (generated by users—Census did not email links to the survey); or via an untraced method (“unknown”); 5) the amount of time spent on the webpage during the visit (a categorical variable ranging from “less than 15 seconds” to “over 30 minutes. A separate dataset included unique links, buttons, and page features, that were clicked on the landing page at a given date and time. Data about login page interactions, as well as data about survey completion, were retrieved through the Qualtrics platform. Those data included: 1) date and time at which the login information was input; 2) the user’s IP address; 3) the survey code input by the user; 4) the percentage of progress made through the survey prior to exiting; 5) the duration of time from login to exiting the survey. Unique visitor sessions were determined by dates and times associated with an IP address, although readers should note that an IP address does not unambiguously identify a single

9 individual. However, in this paper we make the assumption that multiple sessions with the same IP were controlled by the same respondent.1 3.2 Analysis The primary unit of analysis was the visit, a continuous period of time on the landing page website by an individual. Unique visits by users were determined by dates and times associated with an IP address. The analytics tools used to retrieve the data sometimes listed multiple consecutive entries, where the user’s interaction with the website (clicking accordion buttons, interacting with pop-ups, etc.) may have caused the tool to log a new entry. This creation of multiple entries makes it appear as if a single person is visiting multiple times, while in reality the multiple entries actually belong to a single continuous time period. Although these cases were the exception (about 7% of the data), we needed to consolidate them to accurately analyze visits. For the sake of determining the continuous time periods during which users were likely to have been interacting with the landing page, entries for a given combination of IP, date, device type, and referral method were grouped together. Device type and referral method were included in this list to allow for instances where users may have entered the landing page using multiple different devices or referral methods within a short time frame, which did occasionally occur in the dataset. Time was a categorical variable, which took the values: <=1 minute, 1-5 minutes, 10- 20 minutes, and >20 minutes. Grouping was performed such that any set of consecutive entries where each consecutive entry was within 20 minutes of the next were grouped. This process resulted in 973 groups of entries ranging from roughly 1 to 42 minutes long, averaging 5.6 minutes. For each of these consolidated groups, only one entry was kept—that with the latest date and time and longest time on page as listed by the analytics tool. Note that this grouping process may have affected reported group estimates of time on page; however, the effect is unlikely to have been extreme, given that the 973 consolidated sets of entries represent only about 7% of the total data. Unique IP addresses are used as a proxy for individual users in the current study.
