Research Questions The research questions were designed to explore aspects of user behavior that may help to improve user experience on census questionnaire webpages and to inform the expectations and design of future survey studies and online censuses. They were: 1. How do users navigate to the landing page—when do they arrive, which devices do they use, and what referral methods do they use? 2. Once on the landing page, how long do users remain on the page, and what links do they click on the page, if any? 3. How many users who navigate to the survey login page successfully log in to the survey? 4. How many users partially or fully complete the survey, and how long do they take to do so? 5. Do aspects of landing page navigation, survey logins, and survey completions differ by device and/or referral method? While the analysis is exploratory, we had some expectations given our experience with online survey completion. First, given that there was no communications campaign associated with this study, we expected that users would arrive at the landing page primarily by typing the link into the address bars of their web browsers and that those who received the mailed notifications would be the only ones to arrive on the landing page, given that the landing page was not linked to any other census page. However, it should also be noted that the landing page included a

11 button that allowed it to be shared on Facebook, Twitter, and LinkedIn (see Figure 1). Once posted on social media, anyone could follow the link, type the URL into a browser, and/or share it on other platforms, allowing those who did not receive the Census mailing to access the 2023 Census Test landing page (Figure 1). Notably, without a login ID these users would not be able to proceed past the login page (Figure 2). Because research comparable to the present study has not previously been performed on U.S. Census survey landing pages, we wanted to investigate which referral methods—e.g., search engines, social media, other websites, etc.—would be used to access, navigate, or complete the survey. Second, based on previous research, we expected that most English-speakers would navigate to the landing page using personal computers, whereas Spanish-speakers would use both PCs and mobile phones. Prior research examining the 2019 login data from Census Bureau’s American Community Survey (ACS) showed that PCs were the primary device used to access the questionnaire in English, with around 73% on PC, 18% on mobile phones, and less than 9% on tablet or other devices. By contrast, access to the ACS in Spanish was more evenly split between PCs and mobile phones (59 vs. 44%; Mills, Longsine, Sawyer, 2021). Finally, we expected that less than half of the 15,000 sampled households would complete the online questionnaire. Survey response rates in census tests prior to 2020 suggested that between 33% and 50% of the sample completed the survey online, varying by year and by geography (Nichols et al., 2015). We also expected that landing page visits would increase around the time the mailings arrived at the household with overall decrease in visits over time as fewer individuals responded to the survey request (Nichols et al., 2019). 5. Results 5.1 Research Question 1: Landing page arrival Figure 5 shows the number of landing page visits per day from the first date that mailing materials were sent, February 17, to April 9, roughly four weeks after the last mailing date. The first large peak of responses began about four days after the first mailing, on February 21st. This long runway is likely explained by the fact that February 17th was a Friday and the following Monday was a holiday—President’s Day. Peak visits to the landing page occurred roughly a week after each mailing date, and the number of visits per day steadily decreased over time. In total, there were 11,500 unique IP addresses that visited the site over this time period, with some visiting more than once, sometimes even using multiple devices or having multiple referrer types. Overall, there were 12,500 visits over this period from unique combinations of IP, date, device, and referrer type. Taking the 11,500 unique IP addresses as the numerator and the number of mailings sent to households as a denominator (15,000), this represents a visit hit rate of almost 77%, which is higher than we expected based on priors noted above. On average, the landing page hosted roughly 1,600 visits per week, with a peak in the second week of nearly

12 3,000 total visits. While the peaks of visits after the mailings and the slowly decreasing number of visits was expected, the overall number of visits to the landing page was higher than anticipated. The data suggest either that more of the sample visited the landing page, or more of the visitors to the landing page were not part of the original sample.

Roughly three out of five visits lasted a minute or less, and 90% lasted five minutes or less. While on the page, users clicked nearly 8000 times on the available FAQs—visitors were clearly interested in learning more about the survey, especially about why they were selected for the test and whether they were required to respond. Of primary interest was whether visitors proceeded from the landing page to the login page via the “Respond Now” buttons. Only about 40% of visits from unique combinations of IP, date, device, and referral type resulted in visitors clicking these response buttons, and 98% of those clicks were on the English, rather than Spanish, version of the button. This result means that 60% of visitors did not even attempt to access the survey. Those who did not click a response button tended to spend longer on the landing page, whereas those who clicked a response button tended much more often to spend less than a minute on the page (Table 2). A small number of users also interacted with other portions of the landing page, some even interacting with internet browsers in Spanish, Vietnamese, Chinese, or Russian (see Table A1).

Those who began but did not complete the survey spent roughly five minutes in the survey on average (mean=4.8 mins, SD=5 mins). Interestingly, a few users completed the survey twice on the same date (Table 5). We can only speculate as to why this may have happened, but it may have occurred because users had the mistaken impression that they had not finished the survey or because two individuals from the same household completed the survey. By the time that a month had passed from the day the first mailing materials went out (February 17, 2023), over 90% of the eventual amount of surveys had been completed. Users who completed the survey tended to spend very little time on the landing page, with 61% spending less than a minute and 81% spending less than 3 minutes on the page. Some multiple completions may have occurred because each address in the sample received at least three mailings between February 17 and March 3 asking and then reminding them to complete the survey. Not all addresses received the fourth mailing. Addresses were pulled from the printing for the fourth mailing if they had responded by a particular date. Although the second through the fourth mailings indicated that users needed not respond if they had already completed the survey, users may have received a subsequent mailing and forgotten about their first completion, leading them to complete the survey again. It could also happen that another person in the household opened the subsequent mailing and completed the survey. The mailings also emphasized that the survey is required by law. Recipients may also have felt compelled to complete the survey multiple times out of concern that their answers were not received after the first completion. Table 4. Conclusions Analyses of user interactions with the landing page of the 2023 Census Test and the survey to which it was linked provide a host of useful information for future surveys, especially those with a similar scope to the current experiment. The results provide takeaways concerning four domains: the design and content of future survey-related mailing materials, the design and content of future survey-related websites, the design and procedures for future surveys, and expectations for interactions with future survey-related websites and their associated surveys. 6.1 Design and Content of Mailing Materials The results show that users were confused about issues related to login codes and survey completion. Roughly 5% of users failed to login because they used incorrect codes. Some of these failures suggested that identifying one’s correct personal login code was difficult; other failures suggested that users expected that entering no code would be acceptable to enter the survey. Changes to the mailing materials might more clearly emphasize the location of the login code, its length, and its necessity. All of these changes may help to reduce future login failures and increase survey completion rates. Additionally, some users completed the survey multiple times, despite it only requiring one completion. Experiments might be performed on existing language in the mailing materials about only needing to complete the survey once, attempting to further clarify and visually emphasize the text. In large-scale Census Tests, users are only allowed to submit responses once, so there is not a risk of multiple completions. However, it is unknown how frequently users attempt to log in and complete questionnaires multiple times, and this creates an undue burden on them. In larger-scale operations, confirmation of completion may reduce such burden for respondents. In small-scale Census Tests that allow multiple completions, more strongly emphasizing certain text in the mailing materials might reduce duplication of responses. 6.2 Design and Content of Survey-Related Websites Regarding the design and content of survey-related websites—including the landing page and instrument login page—there are several important takeaways. Foremost is that future design of FAQs should be understood in the light of our results. The FAQs for the 2023 Census Test landing page were heavily trafficked, suggesting that many people sought the information they provided. Users interacted with all FAQs, but the most popular were those informing users why they were selected for the Census test and whether they were required to respond to the Census test, even if they already completed the 2020 Census. Furthermore, some FAQs or other information on the landing page should be geared toward users who were not invited to the survey. Contrary to our original expectation, it is clear from our results that, even in the absence of a paid media campaign, news of Census tests will get out

23 to the public—at least one user shared the landing page on social media via the website’s share button, and at least one news outlet wrote an original news story announcing that the Census test was being run. Thus, information on the landing page should make abundantly clear the purpose of the Census test and who is required to respond to it. It may also be prudent to set the expectation that although a visitor to the landing page may not have been invited to complete the Census test, their response will certainly be important for the 2030 Census. The issues mentioned previously relative to mailing material design are also relevant to website design: FAQs or other website content could reiterate that users are not meant to complete the survey more than once, and information on the login page can reiterate what an acceptable login code is, who should have it, and where it can be found. 6.3 Design and Procedure of Future Surveys Our results provide two small suggestions regarding the design and procedures related to future surveys. First, only about 2% of users clicked the “Respond Now” button in Spanish. This is not inherently a problem, and it is consistent with previous uptake rates of accessing Census Bureau surveys in Spanish. However, researchers could choose to include more Spanish speakers, especially those with limited English proficiency, if they wish to probe this population or more fully utilize both English and Spanish versions of webpage and survey materials. Second, the fact that some users completed the Census test twice on the same day may indicate that users were unclear about whether they had already completed the survey. To the extent that issues with the web content may have influenced this confusion, adjustments to web content may be a solution. For example, users might input an email address at the beginning of the survey and be notified automatically upon successful completion, in case the survey’s indication of completion is not otherwise received. Research around future census tests already plans to incorporate and test this idea. 6.4 Future Quantitative Expectations Other conclusions from our results are relevant to future researchers regarding quantitative expectations under similar survey circumstances. Our results indicate that users are likely to begin responding to mailed materials within roughly three days, though our results somewhat obscure this expectation due to the weekend and holiday after the first mailing date. Given a similar sample size and mail material regimen, roughly 32% of the sample (~4,900 completions/sample size of 15,000) are likely to complete the survey, and 90% of those are likely to have responded with 1 month. Over 90% of respondents in the current study who logged into the survey completed it, and roughly 75% of those who completed the survey arrived via typing/bookmark. Also, most users are likely to spend less than five minutes on the landing page, as 90% of users did on our Census test landing page. Finally, although it is difficult to estimate, some proportion of uninvited users are likely to try to “infiltrate” the survey, attempting log in to complete it despite having no code. In the current study, somewhere between 80 and

24 300 users (0.7-2.6% of users with unique IPs) may fit this category, given the amount of illegitimate login codes input by users who did not eventually log in to the survey. 6.5 Limitations Although the current study provides useful insights for identifying aspects of survey websites and users’ interactions with it that could be improved, our results do have some limitations. First, data about landing page interactions and logins/completions came from separate sources, which did not allow us to perfectly match the data together. Thus, our information about interactions with the landing page relative to users who logged into and completed the survey are only about 95% accurate and should be understood in this light. Second, based on the information retrieved from Google and Adobe analytics tools, referrals to the survey landing page were sometimes unknown (roughly 1% of data), limiting our understanding of the larger trends in referral type in our data. Finally, we are limited in the current study from drawing precise conclusions about individual users, as IP addresses had to be used as a proxy for individuals interacting with the webpage and survey. 7. RESEARCH REPORT SERIES (Survey Methodology #2024-09) Data Collection Quality Improvement (DCQI) at the Census Bureau: A Research Agenda Jessica Holzberg Jennifer Sinibaldi Renee Stepler Aaron Maitland Center for Behavioral Science Methods Research and Methodology Directorate U.S. Census Bureau Washington, D.C. 20233 Report issued: November 2024 Disclaimer: This report is released to inform interested parties of research and to encourage discussion of work in progress. Any views expressed on the methodological issues are those of the authors and not necessarily those of the U.S. Census Bureau.

i Abstract: Internet self-response and the use of auxiliary information are two potential methods for addressing the high nonresponse and data collection costs of in-person data collection for major federal surveys. However, it is not always clear how to best implement these methods. The Data Collection Quality Improvement (DCQI) initiative at the Census Bureau was created to address this gap. After reviewing existing research and consulting with survey directors and sponsors, the DCQI team identified four initial focus areas for its research agenda: 1) Implementing a contact strategy and sequencing modes, 2) Designing an internet instrument comparable to existing modes, 3) Ensuring data quality in a multi-mode context, and 4) Using auxiliary information instead of or as a supplement to traditional survey data. In this document, we describe ongoing and upcoming efforts in the focus areas. This research agenda will evolve over time. Future updates will report on research progress and offer guidance to survey programs looking to implement ISR and/or auxiliary information. The DCQI team will also continue to collaborate with survey directors and sponsors to ensure research addresses their most pressing needs. Keywords: internet self-response, modernization, auxiliary information, data collection quality improvement Suggested Citation: Jessica Holzberg, Jennifer Sinibaldi, Renee Stepler, Aaron Maitland. (2024). Data Collection Quality Improvement (DCQI) at the Census Bureau: A Research Agenda. Available online at https://www.census.gov/library/working-papers/2024/adrm/rsm2024-09.html

iii EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Most major household surveys conducted by the Census Bureau rely on interviewers to gain the cooperation of respondents and collect survey data in person or over the phone. Declining response rates and increasing costs have made this design less sustainable, therefore increasing interest in survey modernization through internet self-response (ISR) and use of auxiliary information. These methods open opportunities to produce quality statistics at a lower or equivalent cost, while potentially broadening the respondent pool, but more research is needed to determine how surveys can successfully implement them. In response to this challenge, the Census Bureau requested funding for a Data Collection Quality Improvement (DCQI) initiative designed to provide critical updates to the data collection methodology for major household surveys, develop expertise needed to modernize survey design, and enhance capacity for testing and evaluation to ensure data quality. As a first step, the DCQI team reviewed existing research and spoke with survey directors and sponsors of several major federal surveys. The review and conversations helped identify major research gaps and four initial focus areas, with the first three areas focusing primarily on internet self-response. In this document, we explain the challenges in each focus area and describe current and planned research efforts to address those challenges. • Focus 1: Implementing a contact strategy and sequencing modes New contact strategies are needed to recruit households to complete surveys via ISR. The DCQI team is conducting research in this focus area to determine how to best invite respondents to complete surveys on the web (e.g., the mode, sequencing, timing, and messaging of contacts). This also includes research on who should be targeted for online response and when to move from ISR to interviewer-based nonresponse followup. Use of incentives to encourage web response will also be explored. • Focus 2: Designing an internet instrument comparable to existing modes Interviewers can tailor the use of help text, probe on open-ended questions, and navigate complex multi-stage survey designs in ways that are difficult to replicate online. This major focus area includes efforts to minimize mode effects by replicating the role of the interviewer on the web. Examples of work in this area include questionnaire design and testing for the Current Population Survey, National Health Interview Survey, and Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement, an experiment on the presentation of data respondents previously provided, and a web questionnaire design mini course. • Focus 3: Ensuring data quality in a multi-mode context

iv Item missingness tends to be higher in ISR. Without an interviewer to motivate them, respondents skip more questions, say they don’t know the answer, and breakoff from the survey more easily; they also may satisfice by straightlining or speeding through the survey. Attention checks, requests for a best estimate, and selective implementation of “don’t know” response options may help alleviate these issues in ISR. The DCQI team collected lessons learned from survey programs that have already added ISR and/or are multimode. Other efforts include testing of attention checks in the Census Household Panel, an experiment on unfolding ranges for income, and a “don’t know” experiment. Another area for further exploration is how to best address mode effects in estimates. • Focus 4: Using auxiliary information instead of or as a supplement to traditional survey data Auxiliary information (AUX) includes government data, third-party data and supplemental sources of data internal to the Census Bureau). It has many potential uses throughout the survey life cycle. While there is extensive research at the Census Bureau on the use of large-scale AUX data sets, there has not been as much research on collecting AUX directly from respondents in a survey setting or using dynamic AUX (e.g., information respondents post on a website that could change over time). Initial research in this area includes exploratory qualitative interviews on asking respondents to upload health insurance cards and experiments asking respondents to provide job and mortgage information via uploading their own auxiliary information. This research agenda will be updated through the life of the DCQI program to report progress and refine focus areas as needed. Guidance will also be issued to survey programs interested in modernization.

1 U.S. Census Bureau 1. INTRODUCTION In addition to conducting the decennial census every ten years, the Census Bureau regularly collects survey data from the public on a variety of demographic, housing, and economic characteristics.1 Key metrics such as the unemployment and crime rate come from these recurring household surveys. The Census Bureau sponsors the American Community Survey (ACS), Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP), and the Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC), co-sponsors the Current Population Survey (CPS) with the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and conducts surveys such as the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS), American Housing Survey (AHS), Consumer Expenditure Surveys (CE), and the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) on behalf of other federal agencies. Historically, most of the Census Bureau’s data collection efforts have relied primarily if not exclusively on the use of interviewers (also referred to as field representatives, or FRs). Interviewers visit addresses sampled for household surveys in person and/or contact people living at that address via telephone to gain cooperation. Collectively, this is referred to as computer-assisted personal interviewing, or CAPI.2 Interviewers have numerous important roles in the data collection process—they address the concerns of reluctant respondents and convince them to participate, navigate complex survey instruments, help respondents understand and correctly answer questions with technical concepts, and ensure that respondents finish surveys that can often take a long time to complete. Unfortunately, this paradigm is becoming less tenable for most surveys, and sustainability is a major concern. Response rates to major surveys have declined in recent years, reflecting the increased difficulties interviewers have experienced reaching people and convincing them to respond. Larger societal trends such as advances in gatekeeping technologies (e.g., video doorbells), increases in telephone spoofing and spam telemarketing, decreased trust in government, and growing concerns about privacy and confidentiality are some of the factors that may contribute to increasing nonresponse (Brick and Williams, 2012; National Research Council, 2013). Because it is harder to get survey responses, interviewers are spending more time trying to reach and convince people to participate, and therefore the costs of data collection are also rising. Receiving fewer responses increases the risk of nonresponse bias and decreases the statistical power to produce valuable information. It also introduces particular challenges for longitudinal surveys that are dependent on returning to the same sample of respondents multiple times, since attrition, or further nonresponse, between data collections compounds the issue. 1 The Census Bureau also conducts establishment surveys. They are out of scope for this research agenda. 2 Some surveys also have a separate computer-assisted telephone interviewing (CATI) operation, while others incorporate telephone calls into CAPI. For the purposes of this document, we include CATI under the umbrella term of CAPI.

2 U.S. Census Bureau These challenges have led to an increased interest in alternative methods of data collection that are less expensive but still able to produce quality statistics. Many survey programs are interested in self-administered data collection as a supplement to current interviewer- administered data collection. Self-response via the internet is of particular interest because it does not incur interviewer labor or travel costs. It is increasing in feasibility as more and more people have access to the internet, use it regularly, and indicate it is their preferred survey response mode (Goldberg, 2024; Gelles-Watnick, 2024; Smyth and Olson, 2024). It is already used in the decennial census and in surveys such as the ACS, the National Survey of Children’s Health (NSCH), and the National Survey of College Graduates (NSCG). Internet self-response (ISR) also offers some distinct benefits compared to self-administered data collection via paper questionnaires. As is the case with the instruments used by interviewers in CAPI and CATI, ISR instruments can seamlessly navigate complex skip patterns and pathing without requiring interviewers to interpret instructions. Respondents can complete ISR surveys at times that are convenient to them. Additionally, processing of ISR responses is generally easier than processing of paper questionnaire returns. While ISR has several benefits, we anticipate survey programs will choose to become multi-mode as opposed to replacing CAPI entirely with ISR. For many surveys, offering ISR first and then gradually introducing more expensive modes if no ISR response is received can maximize cost savings while maintaining response and data quality. This “web first” or “web push” design is used in the ACS and is backed by the survey literature more broadly (U.S. Census Bureau, 2022a; Medway and Fulton, 2012). At the same time, a parallel interest in producing data in other ways has also received increased attention. Use of auxiliary information (AUX) external to the data collected in a survey is attractive because it could potentially increase statistical possibilities while reducing the burden placed on respondents. Questions could potentially be removed from surveys if auxiliary information can be used instead. AUX can also help inform adaptive survey design, assess measurement error, and improve modeling and estimation. However, it is not always straightforward to determine how to implement self-administered data collection and/or auxiliary information, even when there is agreement it is needed. There are numerous methodological challenges to consider and valid concerns about the impact of changes on highly visible, gold standard sources of data. In response, the Census Bureau requested funding for a Data Collection Quality Improvement (DCQI) initiative (U.S. Census Bureau, 2022b). 2. BACKGROUND The DCQI initiative team is charged with providing critical updates to the data collection methodology for surveys that produce vital statistical data on the U.S. population and economy. They also will develop expertise needed to modernize the designs of major household surveys and enhance capacity for appropriate testing and evaluation to ensure data quality. While each major survey collected by the Census Bureau is unique in its individual

3 U.S. Census Bureau methodology, there are many design features shared by multiple surveys, and therefore efficiencies that can be gained by studying challenges more generally, as opposed to a survey- by-survey approach. As mentioned previously, there are surveys at the Census Bureau that have already implemented ISR and/or use of auxiliary information, and it is important to acknowledge that these surveys offer many useful starting points. In particular, the ACS provides an example for mode sequencing beginning with the cheapest mode of ISR, messaging of contact materials, and exploring potential applications of auxiliary information. However, there are some important differences between ACS and other major interviewer-administered household surveys that limit the applicability of existing methodology, including the fact that response to the ACS is mandatory. Additionally, compared to other surveys, the ACS has a longer data collection period and a shorter questionnaire with fewer sensitive questions. ACS is not a longitudinal survey and it does not have strict requirements about selecting a household respondent or collecting responses directly from multiple household members. As a first step, the DCQI team reviewed existing research on implementation of ISR and use of auxiliary information and spoke with survey directors of several major federal surveys (Stepler et al., 2024). The review and conversations helped identify major research gaps and set priorities. The remainder of this document describes the initial DCQI research agenda, including four focus areas selected for maximum short-term impact and examples of work being undertaken in each of these areas. This research agenda is intended to be a living document and focus areas are not mutually exclusive. Future versions will provide updates on the status of this initial research and potentially expand the focus areas to address additional challenges. The four focus areas are: • Focus 1: Implementing a contact strategy and sequencing modes • Focus 2: Designing an internet instrument comparable to existing modes • Focus 3: Ensuring data quality in a multi-mode context • Focus 4: Using auxiliary information instead of or as a supplement to traditional survey data 3. FOCUS AREA 1: CONTACT STRATEGY AND MODE SEQUENCING Surveys that collect data via interviewers are also typically dependent on those interviewers to contact a potential respondent and invite them to participate. Interviewers visit sampled households in person and/or make telephone calls. The telephone numbers are either provided by the respondent in prior data collections or available to interviewers via tools at the Census Bureau that are compiled from auxiliary information. Generally, in-person contact via CAPI is used before telephone, but telephone is allowed if CAPI is unsuccessful and in later waves of longitudinal data collection after rapport has already been established with a respondent.

4 U.S. Census Bureau Often, advance letters are sent to an address before the interviewer first makes contact to describe the survey and lend legitimacy to the interviewer. If an interviewer is unable to make contact with someone at the sampled address, several different strategies can be employed, including sending more mailing materials through the regional office, leaving materials at the doorstep, and continuing to visit and/or call at different times. When an interviewer makes contact but the prospective respondent refuses to participate, the interviewer uses their training and optional paper materials to persuade and address specific concerns. In some situations, a difficult case may be reassigned to a more experienced interviewer or supervisor. Many surveys implement stopping rules that enforce a maximum number of contact attempts for a given case; these rules help control costs and reduce respondent burden (e.g., Coffey and Elliott, 2024). Severe instances in which there is concern for interviewers’ safety may also result in contact being discontinued. In a CAPI-only environment, using the interviewers as the primary method of contact allows for a seamless transition into collecting the data via the same mode. There are opportunities to replicate this continuity between contact mode and response mode in a web-push survey design while also saving money. When email addresses and mobile phone numbers are available (and respondents have opted in, as required for text messaging), links to surveys can be sent via email and text message. This allows respondents to directly click on the link and immediately begin responding instead of needing to type the URL into their browser. Quick Response (QR) codes in mailed letters can also make ISR easy for respondents. As previously mentioned, many multi-mode surveys employ a web-first methodology. In the ACS, all sampled respondents are first asked to respond online. Additional modes are gradually introduced over the course of a three-month data collection period, starting with a paper questionnaire and ending with a CAPI subsample. It may make more sense for some surveys to employ a targeted web-push methodology or to otherwise tailor data collection. In the 2020 Census, most households were pushed to web, but some households in tracts with hard-to- count or historically undercounted populations (e.g., lower ACS self-response, low internet response, higher population of people age 65 or older, or low internet subscribership) were given the choice between ISR and a paper questionnaire beginning with the first contact (Pennington, Bentley, and Walejko, 2018; U.S. Census Bureau, 2020). Some longitudinal surveys may choose to start with interviewer-administered data collection to gain initial cooperation and build rapport and then move to ISR. Information from the Census Bureau’s Planning Database (PDB) or prior waves (for longitudinal data collections) can help inform these kinds of adaptive design decisions and is also discussed in the fourth focus area. Mode sequencing is particularly challenging for surveys with short data collection periods, such as the CPS. Decisions will need to be made about the best time to transition from web-push to interviewer- conducted nonresponse followup to maximize cost savings and data quality, including situations where a respondent breaks off from web mid-survey. Offering respondents incentives for completing a survey early and/or via ISR is a promising area of research (Biemer

5 U.S. Census Bureau et al., 2017; Medway et al., 2024). Research in this focus area will continue to evolve to keep pace with changes in technology and respondent preferences. Current and planned efforts in this focus area 1) Modernized CPS contact strategy and mode sequencing The DCQI team is working collaboratively with other areas of the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics to design the contact strategy for a modernized CPS that includes ISR. This includes decisions about the timing, content, and mode of contact attempts and when to move to nonresponse followup. Experiments are being designed to compare different contact strategy conditions where feasible. In the future, we intend to revisit how to best connect text, email, mailed, and interviewer contact attempts together for CAPI as well as more broadly for surveys in general. 2) Collaboration with the Census Household Panel (CHP) on text message use The CHP sends survey invitations out through multiple modes, including text messaging. This analysis will examine who consents to text messages, the effectiveness of the text messages in gaining responses, and the data quality of responses collected this way. 3) Incentives testing We intend to test the impact of digital incentives on encouraging early web response in one of the upcoming CPS field tests. At the same time, qualitative testing and quantitative testing with a nonprobability panel will explore whether preferences for type of incentive (e.g., cash v. digital) vary by respondent demographics. 4. FOCUS AREA 2: DESIGN OF A COMPARABLE INTERNET INSTRUMENT Introduction of a new mode into a survey design will also inevitably introduce mode effects. For example, there are primacy and recency effects due to the differences in aural and visual presentation across modes. In visual modes such as ISR, respondents tend to select from the first options more frequently; in aural modes, they tend to select from the last options more frequently (Krosnick and Alwin, 1987). Respondents may be more reluctant to provide accurate responses to sensitive questions when in the presence of an interviewer, known as social desirability bias (DeMaio, 1984; Tourangeau and Yan, 2007). While elimination of mode effects entirely is impossible, thoughtful design can help make surveys as comparable as possible across modes. It is important to note that in some cases, changes to the interviewer- administered instrument may be necessary for comparability. The Census Bureau has guidelines to ensure the look and feel and question screen design in web surveys are useable and consistent across surveys, but these guidelines do not encompass technical decisions about

6 U.S. Census Bureau how questions should be worded and what information should be displayed to respondents (U.S. Census Bureau, 2024a). The DCQI team will communicate with the web design guideline team while conducting research in this focus area. One important design consideration is how help text is offered to respondents. For in-person and telephone data collection, interviewers are trained on the intent behind survey questions and what responses are acceptable. If a respondent struggles to respond or does not provide a sufficient answer, the interviewer can ask probing questions or provide additional information tailored to the respondent. This streamlined interaction is difficult to replicate in ISR. There are two primary ways to offer help text in ISR- as additional text on the screen with a question or behind a link. For help text on the screen to be useful, respondents need to read it before answering, but respondents do not always read instructions (Galesic et al., 2008; Conrad et al., 2006). Long lists of instructions can also require scrolling on mobile devices, which can increase response time and potentially the risk that respondents do not see all the information being presented (Horwitz, 2015; Couper and Peterson, 2016). The use of help text behind a link is reliant on respondents recognizing they do not know how to answer and being motivated enough to click on the link and find the relevant information. Both methods require respondents to accurately interpret the information and incorporate it into their responses, which can be difficult given the technical complexity of many survey concepts. Currently, CAPI help text is written for the interviewer and therefore is often informal or jargony (e.g., in the ACS, the help text on who to include in the household roster says: “The two-month period is not anchored by a specific reference date, but can encompass the two months prior to survey contact or the two months following the survey contact day.”). There are certain question types and interview designs that will be difficult to transition to ISR. Many surveys currently ask open-ended questions. Interviewers are trained on how to code responses and when it is necessary to probe for additional information. For example, in the CPS, interviewers ask respondents who are not working an open-ended question about whether they looked for work in the last four weeks. Based on the respondents’ description, the interviewer categorizes the activities into “active job search activities” (e.g., applying to a job) or “passive activities” (e.g., reading job postings). This distinction is a critical part of how the number of people in the labor force is determined, as only people actively looking for work are included. The challenge for ISR adaptation is to determine whether the respondent has engaged in active versus passive job seeking activities, but to do so in a way that avoids the labels “active” and “passive” and still conveys the meaning of those terms.. Another important ISR design decision is the presentation of dependent data, or information from prior waves of data collection in longitudinal surveys. When dependent data is shown, respondents can indicate whether their answer is still the same as it was in the previous month and therefore their burden may be decreased. Dependent interviewing is already used in CAPI, where interviewers can tailor their approach to strike the right balance between minimizing

7 U.S. Census Bureau burden and encouraging meaningful responses. When designed well, dependent data in ISR can facilitate faster data collection without increased measurement error (Jäckle and Eckman, 2020; Engstrom and Sinibaldi, 2023). Further research is needed on the best ways to design these types of questions. Surveys with more complex designs, such as multi-stage data collection, also face additional challenges in ISR implementation. Typically, the first stage of these surveys involves collecting a roster of household members and their demographic characteristics; one or more household members are then sampled for the longer second stage questionnaire. Interviewers have a substantial role in the process of implementing the household roster and ensuring that the correct household members are interviewed. In practice, this means that the person an interviewer initially makes contact with may not be the person they need to speak to for the subsequent data collection, thus requiring multiple visits and setting of appointments in CAPI. Surveys that need to conduct interviews with all members face similar issues. It may be challenging to prevent breakoffs in ISR without the finesse of an interviewer to navigate these situations. Self-administered surveys introduce challenges for respondents to understand who should be included on the roster and follow the respondent selection procedure in some household surveys (Olson and Smyth, 2017). Current and planned efforts in this focus area 1) Questionnaire design mini course The DCQI team designed a mini course on questionnaire design principles for ISR survey instruments. This was presented to several subject matter areas within the Census Bureau and at the 2024 American Sociological Association Conference. 2) Dependent interviewing experiment An experiment will be fielded on the Census Household Panel using dependent information for questions on factual (health insurance) and subjective (mental health) questions. Experimental manipulations include whether dependent information is shown or not, the framing of the question, and whether or not respondents are asked an anchoring question. Respondents will be debriefed, including on whether the dependent information was helpful and their enjoyment in answering the questions. The findings will inform how dependent interviewing affects item nonresponse and measurement error. 3) Questionnaire design and cognitive and usability testing for CPS and ASEC DCQI worked with program areas to create ISR versions of the CPS and ASEC. This required decision-making about how to adapt open-ended questions and implement help text.

8 U.S. Census Bureau Efforts to cognitive and usability test these questionnaires are underway. Similar work on the NHIS is also beginning. 5. FOCUS AREA 3: DATA QUALITY IN A MULTI-MODE CONTEXT After designing an instrument, it is important to assess the quality of the data it collects in the field. Based on this assessment, further changes to the instrument may be needed. Focus Area 2 and Focus Area 3 are closely related in this way. The Census Bureau monitors interviewer behavior in CAPI to ensure data quality and identify possible instances of falsification. Measures include unusually high item nonresponse rates or number of one person or no child households, contact attempts reported as occurring overnight, and short amounts of time spent in the instrument and between cases (Mahoney et al., 2024). Regular analysis of comparable metrics in ISR such as breakoffs, straightlining, and heaping can provide insight into respondent engagement and effort and inform necessary revisions to ISR instruments. Paradata can also be used to gain additional insight into responses. In ISR, information about the device a respondent is using allows for comparisons between data collected on mobile versus PC devices. Knowing the device, browser type, and browser language can illuminate differences in the way surveys are rendering for respondents that can impact response (e.g., Ellis, 2024). While ISR paradata have been used to examine data quality in the decennial census and some survey programs, there is no standing operation to do so like there is with CAPI. There are recent efforts at the Census Bureau to standardize collection and use of paradata; continued communication with the group leading this effort will be a priority for DCQI. Some of the ISR paradata metrics can also facilitate comparisons between modes. In interviewer-administered data collections, respondents will sometimes reply that they do not know the answer to a question. Interviewers use skills learned in their training to try to elicit a substantive response instead, but sometimes they are unable to do so. While respondents are not explicitly told they can select a “don’t know” (DK) response, interviewers can usually enter DK and move on to other questions in the survey. An explicit DK response option in ISR may risk undesirable respondent behavior because it offers respondents an easy way to complete the questionnaire quickly with minimal effort (i.e., satisficing, Krosnick, 1991). This may manifest through straightlining, or selecting the same response option across questions (Fricker et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2019). Therefore, an analogous approach to what is done in CAPI makes sense for most questions in ISR. This may look like not offering a DK response option but allowing respondents to skip questions that are not critical for estimates and/or instrument pathing. However, there are certain instances in which offering a DK may help reduce the likelihood of an even worse alternative in ISR- respondents breaking off entirely, especially when being asked highly sensitive or technical questions. This risk can be minimized in CAPI data collections through the interviewer in a way that it cannot be in ISR, given the lack of direct interaction. ISR breakoffs are also a risk for long surveys. Some of the surveys the Census Bureau collects data for take an hour or more to complete; ideally, these surveys would be shorter in ISR. One

9 U.S. Census Bureau technique for shortening an individual survey request is breaking a survey up into modules, although evidence is mixed for this method’s effectiveness (Peytchev et al., 2019). When breakoffs do occur in ISR, there are practical questions about whether to allow a person to come back and finish in ISR or whether to immediately followup with an interviewer, as mentioned in the first focus area of this research agenda. Without an interviewer present to motivate respondents, respondents in ISR also skip questions frequently (Tuten, Urban, and Bosnjak, 2002; Heerwegh, 2009). To combat this and other undesirable response behaviors and to assess data quality, researchers have used strategies such as attention checks, commitment devices, and consistency/edit checks (Mitterder, 2019). Attention checks can be implemented in a variety of ways, ranging from questions that instruct respondents to select a certain response option to questions that ask respondents to select the one true answer from a list (e.g., “Which of these is not a U.S. state?”) Commitment devices ask respondents to commit to putting forth effort in their responses (e.g., Cannell, Miller, and Oksenberg, 1981; Hibben, Felderer, and Conrad 2020). Respondents may also find attention checks and commitment devices odd in the context of major household surveys or interpret them in ways other than they are intended (i.e., believe that if they do not commit to putting forth effort they can satisfice). However, edit checks are more promising and are already used frequently in both CAPI and web surveys. They can be used to encourage a response to a skipped question (e.g., “Please answer this important question”), verify responses (e.g., “According to our calculations, John Doe received $2,329 from all income sources during the PAST 12 MONTHS. Is this correct?”) and correct nonsensical answers to questions (e.g., “You entered a year in the future. Please check your answer”). When using edit checks, it is important to strike a delicate balance between improving data quality and frustrating respondents. Respondents who encounter many edit messages may be more likely to break off from the survey (Mooney, Rogers, and Trunzo, 2003; Peytchev, 2009). A major concern identified by survey programs considering ISR is how to combine data from different modes into a singular estimate when there are known mode effects for certain types of questions. This challenge is compounded by the fact that respondents will generally self- select their mode of response (i.e., they will not be randomly assigned a mode) and there are demographic differences in who responds in what mode. For example, responses from people who are younger, more educated, and living in urban areas tend to be collected in ISR rather than in CAPI for the ACS (U.S. Census Bureau, 2023). While there are some statistical modeling methods that can help account for measurement error across modes (e.g., Elliott et al., 2009; Buelens and van den Brakel, 2014; Brick et al., 2021; Yu, Elliott, and Raghunathan, 2024), there are not many examples of it being implemented in the federal space. Notably, the ACS does not adjust estimates for measurement error across modes, though adjustments to weights are made to account for selection (Olson et al., 2019). It will likely be more practical for survey programs to conduct exploratory methodological studies of these types of methods as needed as a service to stakeholders and data users. More in line with Census methodologies, the

10 U.S. Census Bureau fielding of a bridge sample would provide a useful way to measure the impact of a new mode on estimates and communicate about changes with stakeholders and data users. As these early adopters of ISR implement bridge surveys, DCQI will develop additional guidance and recommendations. Current and planned efforts in this focus area 1) Testing of attention checks in the Census Household Panel An attention check was added to the baseline questionnaire in the CHP for a random half of respondents. It instructed them to select a specific answer to a question. Analysis looked at the demographics of who failed the attention check and differences in data quality metrics, such as straightlining, item missingness, and speeding between those who failed the attention check and those who did not (Stepler et al., 2024). 2) “Don’t know” (DK) and visual aid experiment The DK experiment will be fielded on the CHP using numeric and select one types of questions. In one treatment, “don’t know” will be offered in the initial question. In both treatments, if someone says they don’t know or skips the question, they will be asked a follow-up probe. The probe will either provide additional clarifying help text, a motivational statement encouraging response, or visual aids designed to provide additional information for respondents. Metrics will include item missingness and substantive responses. Respondents will also be debriefed on why they skipped the question and if they provided an answer after the probe, why they did so. 3) Mimicking interviewer encouragement experiment Several of the household surveys ask for discrete income, expenses, and amounts. If interviewers are unable to get the discrete value, a follow-up question asks the respondent to provide an estimate with ranges as the response options. DCQI partnered with ASEC, SIPP, and AHS to field a test on the Household Pulse Survey (HPS) that uses a nonsubstantive “I’m not sure” item versus using an instruction to imitate the interviewer asking a respondent to give their best estimate. Analysis of this experiment is ongoing to examine item missingness and data quality between the experimental groups. 5) Income range experiment This experiment, fielded in the Household Pulse Survey (HPS), unfolded a series of three income range followup questions if respondents skipped the initial question on income. With each unfold, respondents had the option to provide an exact amount by selecting the “I remember now” option and skip the additional range questions. Respondents were

11 U.S. Census Bureau debriefed on their experience. The results will evaluate item missing data on the followup questions to understand how fine of a range can be asked on income questions. 6. FOCUS AREA 4: USE OF AUXILIARY INFORMATION Researchers at the Census Bureau have a long history of conducting research with auxiliary information (AUX), which we define broadly as information from any source external to a survey. Some of the most common forms of auxiliary information used include administrative (government) records, third-party commercial data, and supplemental sources of data internal to the Census Bureau. Potential benefits of using AUX in lieu of or as a supplement to survey data include increased analytical possibilities as well as reduction in respondent burden. One of the most prominent and long-standing examples of AUX use at the Census Bureau is the Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) program, in which linked survey data and auxiliary information provide rich insights into trends in employment (U.S. Census Bureau, 2024b). There are some important limitations to using AUX, particularly with third-party data and government records. Acquiring, cleaning, and protecting AUX and assessing fitness for use can be a lengthy process spanning years. Because AUX data are not obtained from surveys, there is a great deal of variation in how they are collected, and methodologists have very little control over this process. This results in the potential for mismatches between AUX and survey data universes (e.g., household-level versus individual-level) and concepts (e.g., how a “job” is defined). There is also rarely opportunity to pretest administrative forms for respondent comprehension like the Census Bureau requires for surveys, making measurement error in AUX largely unknown (U.S. Census Bureau, 2021). Linking AUX to survey data that was collected differently further compounds potential measurement error. Quality comparisons of AUX are typically made against gold-standard survey data, but if survey data are replaced by AUX, these comparisons become impossible to make over time. There are also known coverage gaps for certain types of AUX; for example, people who do not file their taxes will not have AUX available from the Internal Revenue Service. Despite the potential drawbacks, there are many uses for auxiliary information throughout the survey life cycle. The Census Bureau Frames program is an agency-wide effort to gain efficiencies and reduce respondent burden by compiling multiple survey responses and sources of auxiliary information into one dataset (Ortman, 2024). This dataset can then be used to select targeted samples based on demographics and other characteristics. Additionally, AUX can be used in the early planning stages as a part of adaptive design to determine who is pushed to web, as discussed in the first focus area. During data collection, AUX can also be used in adaptive design to promote representativeness of the overall sample. At the Census Bureau, this work has been done in the NSCG and in SIPP, and similar work is planned for the NHIS (Coffey, Reist, and Miller, 2020; Tolliver et al., 2023). Use of AUX data in this way helps control survey costs while maintaining data quality. However, one consideration is that by focusing on people who are hard-to-count or have historically been undercounted, overall response during

12 U.S. Census Bureau followup may be lower than it would have been otherwise. While it may improve nonresponse bias, this reduction in overall sample can be challenging, especially for longitudinal surveys that have additional attrition between waves of data collection. This is an area for further research. There are also instances in which using auxiliary information in lieu of collecting survey data can be feasible. This is ideal in that quality statistics can still be produced without imposing burden on respondents. Research on the ACS acreage question serves as a model of how to successfully determine equivalency and implement this method. Third-party data was successfully linked to households and had sufficient household coverage and high match rates to survey responses; this allowed the question to be removed for respondents at addresses for which this information is available (Clark et al., 2023). There is ongoing research on whether data for an ACS question on agricultural sales can be similarly replaced with AUX (U.S. Census Bureau, 2024c). Auxiliary information can also be used in lieu of survey data for nonrespondents—it was used for households that did not respond to the 2020 Census or left some questions blank (Mule, 2021). After data collection, AUX can be used to improve imputation and modeling and provide additional context to survey data products (e.g., U.S. Census Bureau, 2018).This focus area is in an earlier stage of development for DCQI compared to the first three focus areas. There are two gaps in the research that we plan to address first, both concerned with respondent-provided auxiliary data. Existing Census Bureau efforts have required data acquisition, cleaning, and assessment of equivalency as critical, time-consuming first steps when working with large-scale AUX datasets. There has not been as much research on collecting AUX directly from respondents in a survey setting. Additionally, we note that there are some dynamic forms of AUX, such as information hosted online on sites like LinkedIn. Dynamic AUX increases both statistical possibilities and challenges. We intend to explore the implications of this compared to static AUX. Future DCQI efforts will also involve discussion and close collaboration with researchers at the Census Bureau already working with AUX. Current and planned efforts in this focus area 1) Exploratory qualitative interviews on health insurance As part of research for the modernized ASEC, respondents were asked open-ended questions in exploratory interviews about their willingness to provide photos of their health insurance card in lieu of answering survey questions about their health coverage. This provided an initial opportunity to assess respondent favorability towards providing their own AUX, although it does not address that health insurance cards cannot provide needed data to replace survey questions. 2) Job and mortgage information experiments As a followup to the health insurance research, DCQI researchers designed experiments on the Household Panel that will ask respondents to provide job and mortgage information. For the job experiment, respondents will be able to provide information via an uploaded

13 U.S. Census Bureau resume, a copied and pasted resume, a LinkedIn page, or survey questions. The experiment will assess whether the framing of this request makes a difference. In one condition, respondents will be asked to choose from the four options; in the other condition, respondents will be told they can choose from the first three “instead of answering [survey] questions.” Respondents will be debriefed about why they chose the option they did and there will be efforts to parse the AUX provided. For the mortgage experiment, half of respondents who are homeowners will be asked to upload an annual escrow analysis statement instead of being asked survey questions. We anticipate the mortgage information request to be more sensitive and difficult for respondents to complete than the job information request. Item missing data and compliance with the request will be analyzed and compared for both experiments. These experiments will also provide an opportunity to assess the amount of effort required to parse and use this type of respondent-provided AUX, and whether it is a viable substitute for comparable survey data. 7. CONCLUSION Increasing nonresponse and data collection costs have made in-person data collection for major federal surveys unsustainable. Internet self-response options and the use of auxiliary information are promising alternatives, but there are challenges to implementation and more research is needed. The DCQI initiative at the Census Bureau was created to address this gap. Following review of existing research and discussion with survey directors and sponsors, the DCQI team identified four initial focus areas for the DCQI research agenda. • Focus 1: Implementing a contact strategy and sequencing modes • Focus 2: Designing an internet instrument comparable to existing modes • Focus 3: Ensuring data quality in a multi-mode context • Focus 4: Using auxiliary information instead of or as a supplement to traditional survey data This research agenda is intended to be a living document. Future updates will report on progress of current and planned efforts in each focus area and provide guidance to survey programs interested in modernization. The DCQI team will also continue to work closely with survey directors and sponsors to ensure research addresses their most pressing needs. 8. REFERENCES Biemer, P. i Abstract This report presents findings and recommendations from cognitive testing of the computer assisted personal interview (CAPI) instrument for the 2023 National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) Internet Use Survey (also called “Computer and Internet Use”), a supplement of the Current Population Survey (CPS). The NTIA Internet Use Survey was shortened both in terms of (1) questionnaire length (e.g., removing questions) and (2) item length (e.g., removing words within retained questions) to meet a recommended standard to have CPS supplements be administered in under ten minutes. The Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) at the U.S. Census Bureau conducted cognitive testing to evaluate: (1) streamlined questions to ensure that comprehension and the question intention was maintained and (2) whether specific technology phrasing in revised and existing questions was well understood. Most of the streamlined and modified questions were successful; questions pertaining to Internet service and smart TV usage were still problematic. These findings and recommendations informed the final wording for the survey, fielded in November 2023. Future cognitive testing should continue assessing wording related to technological trends happening in real time. Keywords: interviewer-administered, cognitive interviewing, computer devices, Internet service, Internet challenges Suggested Citation: Jonathan Katz, Alexandra Piccirillo, Caitlyn Keeve, Jessica Holzberg. iv EXECUTIVE SUMMARY In an interagency project between the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) and the U.S. Census Bureau, the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) conducted cognitive interview research on the NTIA Internet Use Survey prior to its fielding in November 2023. The NTIA Internet Use Survey (also called “Computer and Internet Use”) is a computer assisted personal interview (CAPI) survey that is a supplement of the Current Population Survey (CPS) and it has been administered since 1994. Before cognitive testing, we conducted an expert review of the NTIA Internet Use Survey. The expert review primarily focused on streamlining questions that were taking a long time to administer in the prior data collection cycle in November 2021. When streamling the question text, CBSM and NTIA wanted to make sure the question text would still be easy to understand. Secondarily, we also modified questions thought to be potentially problematic, due to changes in terminology in Internet activities and unclear wording. Following expert review, one round of testing was conducted with 20 participants. We mainly tested the revised questions that were updated in the expert review phase. Overall, participants were able to answer most of the streamlined questions without much difficulty. Participants seemed to be able to answer questions with fewer examples listed than in 2021, with the lone exception being the use of financial services on the Internet question, where one participant forgot to include cash sending services like Venmo and PayPal. The other tested changes performed well, such as on questions about using the Internet when going from place to place and the accessibility of using devices connected to the Internet. However, participants still had difficulty answering about their household’s use of a smart TV (or a device connected to the Internet that played through a TV), their household’s home Internet service, and privacy and security concerns that stopped the household from participating in specific Internet activities. This testing informed the recommendations and final question wording for 2023 data collection.

1 U.S. Census Bureau 1. INTRODUCTION At the request of the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) conducted an expert review and cognitive testing of the 2023 NTIA Internet Use Survey, a supplement of the Current Population Survey (CPS), a computer assisted personal interview (CAPI) survey. The CPS collects data on the labor force but also has supplements on various topics in different months, such as the NTIA Internet Use Survey. The NTIA Internet Use Survey has been administered periodically since 1994. The survey asks questions about the household’s use of devices that connect to the Internet, use of Internet from various locations in the past six months, different applications used to connect to the Internet, and any privacy or security concerns using the Internet. A single household respondent answers questions on both the core CPS and any supplements. For the NTIA Internet Use Survey, select questions are asked about a randomly selected household member, so the household respondent in some cases may serve as a proxy respondent on their behalf. In recent years, the Census Bureau has requested most CPS supplements be completed in under 10 minutes in order to minimize respondent burden and stem the decline in response rates. Because of this new standard, NTIA needed to reduce the interview time for the Internet Use Survey. NTIA removed select questions but was also interested in streamlining current questions while maintaining clarity. NTIA asked us to conduct an expert review of the questionnaire to evaluate these questions. Following expert review, we were asked to cognitively test these streamlined questions to ensure participants were still able to interpret the questions with minimal difficulty. We also tested questions that were found to be problematic in either expert review, prior cognitive testing, or in the current cognitive testing. After the one round of interviews, we provided recommendations on the 2023 production wording to be fielded in November 2023; this report presents findings and recommendations from the one round of CAPI testing. Findings from self-administered testing conducted shortly after can be found in Katz, Piccirillo, Keeve, Holzberg, & Kohm (forthcoming). 2. LITERATURE REVIEW There have been three previous collaborations between the CBSM and the NTIA which included the cognitive testing of the NTIA Internet Use Survey for the years 2015, 2017, and 2021 (Terry & Fobia, 2017; Henderson, Luck, Katz, & Fulton, 2020; Terry, Rivas, Luck, Class, & Genter, 2022 ). Each testing evaluated both new and revised items of the NTIA Internet Use Survey to ensure both high data quality and minimal burden.

2 U.S. Census Bureau Each year of testing included two rounds of cognitive interviews, with the first round testing changes made to the questionnaire prior to testing and then the second round testing the changes incorporated after the first round. The results from the three different testing projects found that most participants had little to no difficulty comprehending and answering most of the survey questions. When participants had issues answering, it was typically due to unclear wording or technical terminology that was not widely understood (Terry & Fobia, 2017; Henderson et al., 2020; Terry et al., 2022). Terry et al. (2022) found participants were considering activities that were out of scope, for example some thought about their Wi-Fi connection when asked about how well their Internet connected devices worked. To account for this problem, an instruction was added reminding participants not to consider Wi-Fi speed. Earlier testing found that, for questions that asked participants to think about a particular timeframe, participants showed a tendency to consider a timeframe longer than the one specified in the question (i.e., thinking longer than a year when asked to only think about “past year”) (Terry & Fobia, 2017). For the most recent testing of the 2023 instrument, the full questionnaire was updated to increase comprehension by reflecting changes in technology and to shorten questions. The shortening of select questions was an attempt to stem declining response rates by shortening the overall interview. The types of issues found in prior cognitive testing aforementioned were also of focus in the most recent testing of the 2023 instrument. 3. METHODOLOGY 3.1 Expert Review In January 2023, three CBSM staff individually reviewed the questionnaire. To assist with the goal of keeping the overall supplement length under ten minutes, NTIA provided CBSM with information about survey questions that took a long time to administer in the 2021 data collection cycle. CBSM provided recommendations for these questions, including (1) shortening the question text and/or (2) modifying any terminology or wording that was potentially confusing. CBSM also reviewed other survey questions to ensure the terminology was up to date and that there were no other potential issues for participants. The team then had a consensus meeting to come up with recommendations to update the question wording. Following this consensus meeting, the project lead then met with NTIA to discuss the recommendations; NTIA accepted the majority of the recommendations with some minor modifications. These questionnaire changes were used to inform the questionnaire for cognitive testing and the design of the cognitive interview protocol.

3 U.S. Census Bureau Global changes made by CBSM to streamline the questionnaire included: 1. Reducing the number of examples (e.g., brand names) in the question wording. Cognitive testing and recruitment screening were conducted in English. 3.2.1 Recruitment Criteria and Strategy Our recruiting efforts aimed to achieve diversity in the types of respondents who typically participate in the NTIA Internet Use Survey, in terms of household relationship, household type, sex, ethnicity, race, age, education, and income level. We attempted to recruit participants with varying levels of computer and Internet use. We wanted a couple low or no Internet users in our study to see how these users would interpret

In the recruitment screener, we asked questions about Internet frequency (e.g., “how often do you use the Internet…”) and devices connected to the Internet the participant used, such as a desktop, laptop, smartphone, and tablet. Based on the interview data we collected and retrospective probing, we were able to recruit three participants who appeared to be a limited Internet user or did not use the Internet across many devices. One of these three participants was visually impaired and the other two participants were 65 and older. We did not have any participants who did not use the Internet at all. Before testing, all interviewers were trained on administering the NTIA Internet Use questionnaire and cognitive interview protocol. 3.5 The Cognitive Interview Protocol The cognitive interview protocol focused on testing revised questions to the NTIA Internet Use Survey; we also tested a few unchanged questions where NTIA wanted to confirm respondents were still interpreting the question as intended (See Appendix B for Round 1). At the beginning of the interview, participants were administered a shortened version of the roster asked in the main CPS. Participants were first asked to list all household members and then report the demographic characteristics of each person. Following the roster, the interviewer proceeded to the NTIA Internet Use Survey. There were six sections in the questionnaire. The first section included questions about the household’s use of various internet-connected devices, such as laptops, tablets, and smart phones. The second section included questions about where participants use the internet, such as at school, work, or public places. Questions from the first two sections were asked about everyone in the household. The third section asked about internet service plans—either home-installed or mobile—that the household may have subscribed to. The fourth section asked about participant engagement with various online activities such as email, social media, gaming, and health. These questions were asked about the participant, if it was a single person household; these questions were 4 Two participants did not report as a proxy for someone else since they were in single member households.

7 U.S. Census Bureau asked about another person in the house aged 15 years old or older, if multiple members were in the household. All questions relating to health were asked about the entire household. The fifth section included questions about various concerns the participant may have using the internet, such as privacy concerns and identity theft. The sixth section included questions about reasons why no one uses the Internet at home5 (if applicable) and if the household currently or ever had a cable or satellite TV subscription. These questions were only asked of the household in general and not of each individual. After completing the questionnaire, interviewers asked the participant retrospective probing questions to evaluate their comprehension of the survey items. In retrospective probing, interviewers ask follow-up questions about a group of survey questions after the participant has answered them. This technique allows participants to complete the survey without stoppage. However, participants may have some difficulty recalling their earlier thoughts about a survey response. (Willis, 2005). CBSM chose retrospective probing over concurrent probing (i.e., follow-up questions that are asked directly after a participant answers a survey question) to avoid biasing participants’ answers later in the questionnaire. To combat potential recall issues, participants were shown the questions again on in a powerpoint as each of the questions came up in probing. The probes asked questions such as what Internet behaviors participants were thinking of when answering the questions, requests for the participant to provide examples of the topics the question was asking about, and the difficulty participants had in answering the questions. In addition, for questions where we moved examples to be read only if needed, we showed the full question wording with all of the examples via screensharing in Microsoft Teams. Interviewers then asked if the examples would have been helpful when answering the question originally. Questions that CBSM expected to be universally understood or were not a target of the cognitive test had no probing questions. Finally, interviewers asked participants a set of debriefing questions about how easy or difficult it was for the participant to respond to the survey and if participants thought other people might consider any of the questions sensitive. Participants were then asked to share anything else they had not yet had a chance to mention. 5 All participants in this round had at least one person in the household use the Internet at home so nobody was administered this section of questions about non-Internet use.

CONCLUSIONS The expert review changes that were made to streamline the NTIA Internet Use Survey were mostly successful in cognitive testing. There was only one question where the streamlined version did not perform as well which was the question about using the Internet for financial services. As a result, we added examples of money sending services back into the question wording. Also, the streamlined text in three of the introductory paragraphs did not seem to affect comprehension of later survey questions. A later round of cognitive testing of the adapted self-administered instrument did find that some participants were only considering devices they had owned, so we added instruction for respondents to consider devices they used. Overall, the rest of the survey questions performed well in testing. The most problematic questions found in testing were about the type of home Internet service, the usage of a smart TV or other device that plays through a TV, and whether privacy or security concerns had stopped anyone from the household in engaging in specific Internet activities. However, some of these questions that were problematic in CAPI testing were found to be less problematic in self-administered testing (see Katz et al., forthcoming). Future testing of the NTIA Internet Use survey should continue to evaluate whether select technical terminology used in the survey questions is still widely understood. For example, during testing, the social media network ‘Twitter’ was renamed to ‘X’. Given that technology is always changing, it is imperative to keep the survey questions up to date with the current technological language used in everyday conversation. 6.
