ii Abstract: At the request of the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), researchers from the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) at the U.S. Census Bureau cognitively pretested new and revised survey questions for the interviewer-administered 2025 American Housing Survey (AHS). Tested questions included new topical modules on accessory dwelling units and climate risk and insurance. Other questions focused on updates to existing modules, which included topics such as reasons for doubling-up in residential units, household finances (such as taxes and fees), utilities, home purchasing, energy efficiency, and moving residences. Participants in 23 cognitive interviews, conducted remotely via Microsoft Teams from June 2024 to August 2024, generally understood most of the questions. Some of the more complex topics included why adults “double up” in residences, and whether customers have the option of choosing energy from renewable resources from their utility companies. In the former case, the questions produced inconsistent responses, and in the latter, respondents misunderstood the general meaning of the question, even after several revisions. These topics will be deferred from the 2025 AHS. 1 1 Executive Summary This report presents findings from cognitive testing of select questions and modules for the 2025 American Housing Survey (AHS), sponsored by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and conducted by the Census Bureau. The following five revised core modules were tested: Real Estate, Taxes and Fees, Utilities, Home Improvement, and Recent Movers. Additionally, a revised Doubling Up topical module was tested, along with two new topical modules: Accessory Dwelling Units and Climate Risk & Insurance. The Real Estate, Taxes and Fees, Utilities, Home Improvement, and Recent Movers core modules were last fielded in 2023. The Real Estate core module added and revised questions designed to improve estimates on ownership of real estate properties and covers payments, purchase price, and property acquisition. The Taxes and Fees core module has revised questions about rental costs. The Utilities core module is intended to provide data on the type, cost, and frequency of utility bills and adds new questions about the source of electricity in the home. The Home Improvement core module is designed to improve estimates on home improvement and remodeling projects by homeowners and added new questions about improvements done for energy efficiency. The aim of the revised Recent Movers core module is to better understand the reasons for moves and how movers find their homes. The Doubling Up topical module was last fielded in 2013. The revised module for 2025 includes questions intended to gather data on specific living arrangements in which a household has an additional adult in residence. The new Accessory Dwelling Units module is designed to capture additional living units located on or within the same property as a primary residence, but that are independent of the primary residence (such as an above garage apartment or a basement apartment). The intent of the new Climate Risk & Insurance module is to collect data on damages due to natural disasters and supplemental insurance, as well as information about electric vehicle charging access. In this study, Census Bureau researchers conducted 23 cognitive interviews virtually with participants via Microsoft Teams. We used a streamlined version of the AHS questionnaire containing test questions from the modules described above, along with questions from the Housing Unit and Demographics modules to provide the appropriate context for subsequent skip patterns and fills. We recruited participants at least 18 years old and who met certain criteria, ensuring they would likely follow specific paths in the questionnaire and arrive at the target questions for testing. We conducted two rounds of testing. For round 1 testing, we broadly recruited across the main areas of the tested modules. For round 2 testing, we adjusted our recruitment efforts to focus on recruiting more participants who lived in California, in hopes to capture more data on wildfire insurance. We offered recommendations for each of the modules. Modules included at least one new or revised question. All modules were tested across two rounds, with some questions requiring

2 revisions after the first round before finalizing recommended wordings. Recommendations across the modules included revisions such as rewording questions for clarity and grammatical accuracy, simplifying instructions, and question removal/replacement. Our interviews showed that most participants understood the questions, and they are expected to perform well in the AHS fielded survey, with minimal measurement error. In the doubling up module, questions about why adults share residences (whether due to economic hardship or other reasons) yielded inconsistent responses, even after two rounds of revisions. For instance, the reasons adult children live at home varied; some households reported economic hardship, while others gave unrelated reasons for similar situations. As a result, this module will not be included in the 2025 AHS, pending further testing. Similarly, several questions from the utilities module concerning whether utility companies offer renewable energy options and whether customers choose them also will not move forward in the 2025 AHS. Many participants misinterpreted these questions, and reported thinking they were about personal use of solar panels or renewable energy, likely because they had not encountered the choice from utility companies. The reframing of the questions did not improve performance, and additional testing will be conducted before they are added to the AHS. 2 Background on AHS At the request of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) at the U.S. Census Bureau conducted cognitive testing of new and revised survey questions for core and topical modules within the American Housing Survey (AHS). The AHS was first fielded in 1973 under the name of the Annual Housing Survey and was conducted annually until 1981. At this point, the survey’s name, was changed to the American Housing Survey, with data collected biennially due to budget constraints (Genter, Virgile, & Keeve, 2022). The AHS is currently administered by field representatives via in- person visit or telephone interview. Core modules of the AHS provide data on a wide range of housing subjects, including size and composition of the nation's housing inventory, vacancies, fuel usage, physical condition of housing units, characteristics of occupants, breakdown of household equipment (e.g., household appliances), home improvements, mortgages and other housing costs, persons eligible for and beneficiaries of assisted housing, home values, and characteristics of recent movers (Genter et al., 2022). The AHS also includes topical modules that are rotated, with some topical modules included/not included in a given year. These modules have focused on topics such as transportation, community involvement, emergency and disaster preparedness, health and safety hazards, and housing unit modifications made to accommodate disabilities. Select questions from both core and topical modules have been tested by the Census Bureau for prior versions of the AHS; the most recent of these was for the 2023 AHS (Genter et al., 2022). For cognitive testing of the 2025 AHS, select survey questions from the following ten modules were administered: Housing Unit, Demographics, Doubling Up, Accessory Dwelling Units,

3 Climate Risk & Insurance, Real Estate, Taxes & Fees, Utilities, Home Improvement, and Recent Movers. Prior to pretesting, we conducted an expert review of the questions and provided feedback to HUD. HUD provided the content to test after reviewing the expert review. We conducted cognitive testing via Microsoft Teams with 23 participants over two rounds of testing from June 2024 to August 2024. The results of these interviews will help inform the final version of a revised AHS instrument, which will be administered in 2025. Changes were made to the questions between rounds. 4 3 Study Methodology 3.1 Data Collection From June 2024 to August 2024, two rounds of cognitive interview testing were conducted virtually via Microsoft Teams. A total of 23 participants were included in the study. Interviews were conducted by three CBSM researchers. Each participant received a $60 cash incentive via Priority Mail after completing their session. Before participation, participants signed a digital consent form and after the session they signed an incentive voucher. The consent form included information about the study, personal identification protections, and a statement informing participants that the interview would be audio and video recorded (via Snagit recording software). Participants signed the consent form and reiterated their consent to participate and to be recorded verbally on the Snagit recordings. During interviews, the same version of the round- specific questionnaire was administered to all participants, with some following different paths of questions based on skip patterns within the survey. Participants were asked the questions orally by a researcher and answered orally. The researcher recorded the response. Participants did not see the questions but could see the researcher via the camera option in Microsoft Teams. During the first round of testing, we conducted cognitive interviews with 15 participants. We recruited participants who were aged 18 years or older and living in the United States. To ensure participants would be asked as many target questions as possible, we also focused our efforts on recruiting those who: • Lived with at least 1 other adult 18 years or older who was not a spouse or partner. • Had another residential unit or short-term or long-term rental unit on their property. • Lived in a home that has experienced damage from a natural disaster in the past year. • Moved residences within the past two years. • Knowledgeable about the insurance on the home they lived in. • Made any energy efficient home improvements. • Received government assistance for rent payment. • Had a mortgage or home loan. For the second round of testing, we conducted cognitive interviews with eight participants. During this round, we continued to recruit participants aged 18 years or older and living in the United States. Additionally, we adjusted the additional recruiting criteria in an effort to have the remaining participants pathed to target questions that had low frequencies during round 1 testing. Our second-round recruitment criteria included: • Lived with at least 1 other adult 18 years or older who was not a spouse or partner. • Lived in a residential unit that has another attached or detached unit on the same property. • Lived in a home that had experienced damage from a natural disaster in the past year. • Lived in a home located in a flood zone.

5 • Live in a home located in a high-risk wildfire zone. • Built their home on land they own. • Moved residences within the past two years. • Knowledgeable about the insurance on the home they lived in. • Made any energy efficient home improvements. • Received government assistance for rent payment. • Had a mortgage or home loan. The study was advertised with a Census Bureau wide broadcast email. (See Appendix A for the email text.) Interested participants either completed a self-administered online screening questionnaire or called the CBSM recruiter who administered the screening questions. These questions established eligibility for one or more of the testing modules. (See Appendix B for the full screening questionnaire.) 3.2 Participant Characteristics We attempted to recruit a sample of participants who met as many of the above criteria as possible (see Table 1 above for detailed counts). Our sample allowed us to successfully test all of the modules multiple times. In addition, we attempted to recruit a diversified sample across sex, age, education, and racial/ethnic identity. In our screening questionnaire, we asked participants to identify their gender. We used corresponding pronouns to align with participants’ self-reported gender identities throughout our findings and reports. We made efforts to include a mix of homeowners and renters to capture varying housing contexts. 7 The protocol was programmed into the survey software Qualtrics. Qualtrics allowed programming of fills for questions and skip logics to guide question pathing. This online protocol allowed the researchers to administer the AHS questions and cognitive testing probes orally and enter responses in real time as the interview proceeded. We informed participants that the purpose of the interview was to collect their thoughts and opinions on how the new questions worked. We also instructed them to answer the questions as if an interviewer had come to their home, and to “think aloud” as they answered questions by saying anything they were thinking about as they came up with their answers (Ericsson and Simon, 1980). We entered any issues participants experienced while answering survey items into the protocol. Issues included question misunderstanding, recall, and difficulties with response options. We primarily used concurrent probing to address issues participants had in answering survey questions. In concurrent probing, follow-up questions are administered immediately after a participant answers a specific question (Willis, 2005). The probes in our test protocols asked participant how they arrived at their answer, whether a question was easy or difficult to answer, to define what a specific term or phrase in a question meant to them or asked for other information that could be used to indicate possible issues with the survey questions. At the end of each interview, participants were asked three debriefing items, one asking if they felt any of the questions in the survey were sensitive, one asking if they felt any of the questions in the survey were difficult, and another asking about any last thoughts they might have had regarding the study. We posed different retrospective probes to some participants based on their previous answers and feedback to survey questions. This allowed us to further explore unanticipated responses and contexts (such as unique living arraignments, property ownership, and past experiences). In this vein, we also expanded retrospective probing with a few participants who noted that while they did not necessarily currently fit certain module pathing criteria, they had some experience with the topic in the past. For some of these participants, we posed modified versions of survey questions, including vignettes and example scenarios. For a few others who very closely aligned with criteria (but were not pathed due to small differences), we re-entered applicable modules and they answered the questions based on their experiences (despite being technically outside the original criteria range). This flexibility in the protocol allowed us to pose some of the questions that posed a recruiting challenge. To ensure data quality, we precisely noted and tracked when and how we expanded probing for specific participants beyond the existing scripted protocol probes. We utilized two versions of the interview protocol, one for each of our testing rounds. For round 1 testing, we developed the protocol using information provided by staff in the Associate Directorate for Demographic Programs (ADDP), who worked directly with the sponsor, HUD. After the first round of testing, we provided findings and recommendations for improvements to ADDP staff, who worked with HUD. HUD made decisions for round 2 question wording based on round 1 findings and recommendations. We then updated the protocol for round 2 based on

8 HUD’s decisions. The updates to the second-round protocol included question wording changes, removal of questions, and addition of new questions. 3.4 Analysis At least two CBSM researchers took notes during each of the cognitive interviews in the Qualtrics protocol. After the interviews, researchers would revisit and revise the summaries, if needed. This resulted in two to three interview summaries per interview/participant. At the end of each round, interview summaries were exported from Qualtrics to Excel, and into combined into a master document of all data from all participants/interviews. This master document was used by all three researchers during analysis. First pass analysis was divided by module across the three CBSM researchers working on the project. Once we completed an individual first pass analysis for our assigned modules, we reconvened as a group for a review and second pass analysis, discussing our findings and ensuring continuity in data interpretation across the group. Our analyses focused on whether and how questions should be revised to improve comprehension or otherwise reduce measurement error. We considered the number of participants who had an issue with a question, the nature of the issue(s), and whether CBSM could develop alternative wording that seemed to be an improvement over the original question. After round 1 testing and analysis, we shared recommendations with ADDP staff and HUD staff, who made the decision on whether and how to revise questions for round 2 testing. After round 2 testing and analysis, ADDP shared our recommendations with HUD staff, who made final decisions on whether and how to revise questions for the 2025 AHS. 4 Cognitive Interview Findings Our findings from the cognitive interviews are divided into sections for each tested module: Doubling Up (4.1), Accessory Dwelling Units (4.2), Climate Risk & Insurance (4.3), Real Estate (4.4), Taxes & Fees (4.5), Utilities (4.6), Home Improvement (4.7), and Recent Movers (4.8). 9 4.1 Doubling Up Module Doubling Up is a revised topical module that contains questions about living arrangements in which a household is (or recently was) comprised of a householder and at least one additional adult who is not the spouse or cohabiting partner of the householder. Doubling Up questions were last fielded in the 2013 AHS (Clark and DeMaio, 2012). HUD requested this shorter and more focused list of questions be tested for 2025. The purpose of this module is to capture data on combined households, including whether the reason they live together is associated with economic challenges. In addition, this module is meant to capture possible housing insecurity and risk of homelessness. Participants whose current households included at least one other adult who was not their spouse or partner began the module at question 4.1.1. Examples of these households included roommates, housemates, families with children over 18 living at home, etc. When participants received 4.1.1, names of all members of the household over the age of 18 were referenced in the question. Participants who lived alone, lived with a spouse/partner, and/or lived with children under 18 years of age began the module at question 4.1.7. The Doubling Up module was complex and participants had significant difficulty with the questions. Across both rounds of testing, participants had comprehension issues, especially with questions designed to capture information about people who may have recently moved out of the participant’s home. Participants reported feeling overwhelmed by the number of questions, that the questions were repetitive, and that they were unsure of the meaning of certain phrases. Additionally, participants with young adult children (such as college students) found the questions to be especially difficult and non-representative of their household’s context. We first recommended a major overhaul to this module, including combining some questions, removing some questions, and overall decreasing the number of questions in the module. After round 2 testing, we recommended this module not be added to the AHS without additional pretesting. HUD agreed with our recommendation, and this module will not be added to the 2025 AHS. 4.1.1 DB1 Round 1 and Round 2 Wording: REFERENCE PERSON NAME SPOUSE/PARTNER NAME OTHER ADULT NAME(S) The next questions are about adults who are living or staying here. Round 2 Findings: Five participants were asked this question, with one answering “Yes” and four answering “No.” There were some inconsistencies and confusion in how participants understood this question. While participants did, for the most part, appear to understand the question as attempting to capture possible economic hardship, there was uncertainty in the specific meaning of the question. As one participant asked, “I’m not sure if you’re referring to someone who doesn’t have housing? Does a dorm count? Is it economic hardship?” Similarly, one participant said he thought the question was trying to capture “maybe to see if people have financial troubles, or a divorce, losing a home, something like that?” Another participant was asked the question and responded by laughing. When asked to share what he was thinking, the participant told us “I’m trying to come up with what you mean by adequate place to stay.” One participant stated that he was “confused” and explained that he understood the question as asking him if he had a second/alternative place to live. The participant said that he has no second/additional home (beyond where he was living then), so he should choose “Yes” to the question (“are any of these adults staying here because they do not have a regular or adequate place to stay?”). If he did not have a second home, then yes, he must be staying here because he did not have a (alternative) regular or adequate place to stay. Additionally, participants understood “regular place to stay” and “adequate place to stay” as having two distinct meanings. For example, one participant told us that if someone did not have a “regular” place to stay, it would mean they would perhaps need to sometimes “couch surf” or “go to a hotel.” This participant contrasted this to their understanding of not having an “adequate” place to stay, explaining that “adequate sounds like they don’t have a roof over their head or in a situation where you’d need to take them in.” Another participant told us she understood the difference as being “regular would mean, let’s say, they can’t afford an apartment to live, and adequate might mean the only thing they could afford is rundown and unsafe.” Our recommendation for this question was to add clarifying optional help text that the interviewer could read if the participant struggled with the question. The clarifying text could use examples of situations that fit the meaning of "regular or adequate place to stay." HUD’s response was as follows: “Both concepts, 'regular' and 'adequate', are central to HUD focus on housing quality and housing stability. In terms of those at risk at homelessness,

This participant added that one of the reasons they are staying with them is because they “make a good price” implying that the cost of staying at the residence is reasonable. We did not suggest any wording changes for the second round but noted that HUD should consider if the answers to these questions are useful for what they are trying to capture with this module. Round 2 Findings: Five participants were asked this question, with two answering “Yes” and three answering “No.” Similar to the previous round, there was some confusion and inconsistencies in how participants understood and responded to this question. Upon hearing the question, one participant answered “No” (referring to his college-aged son who was living with him), but then stated that “younger kids need help in housing,” support while they are in college, and that it is appropriate for them to still “live at home” while they are trying to “get on their feet.” He said they are not in economic hardship, though, so his answer would be “No.” In contrast, another participant who similarly had a college-aged son living with him answered “Yes” and said, “maybe my oldest son would fall into that. He just graduated college and he’s

17 looking for a job right now.” While this appeared to be a similar situation as the previous participant, this participant ultimately gave an opposite answer to the question. Another participant had general confusion about the question. Upon hearing the question, the participant answered “Yes” and stated that they all (himself, his spouse, and his adult daughter) pay together “so it (this question) is confusing…” He continued by stating that they all stay at the home by choice. Upon further probing, the participant explained that he was thinking that the question was asking him if this (current home) is where they are living because they can't afford to stay somewhere else. He expressed some further confusion and stated let’s leave it at “Yes… let’s keep it simple.” The question failed several times. There were several scenarios that caused the question to fail (such as households with young adult children and households where people pooled their resources, but also wanted to live with each other beyond financial reasons). We recommended changing the question to tease out whether the people are "staying here" by choice or because of economic hardship. Two suggestions are: "Would any of the people staying here prefer to move out but can't because they can't afford housing of their own?" or “Would any of the people staying here prefer to move out if they could afford housing of their own?” We recommended further pretesting for this question, paying special attention to testing with households with young adult children and households who pool resources to afford a specific neighborhood, size of home, or amenities. HUD noted “they are interested in doubling up first in relation to economic vulnerability. There is also an interest in adult children and economic and life course factors related to household formation. The approach would be either to focus on economic vulnerability or to focus on both, but to have enough questions (that a respondent could answer) to measure both. The goal should be to develop clear questions that measure the distinct concepts and living situations.” We recommended that this question/module not be fielded without further testing. HUD adopted our final recommendation. This question will not be fielded without further testing. 4.1.6 DB4 Round 1 Wording: Since [date 12 months prior to interview date / you have lived here] who contributed to your rent or mortgage payment? Round 1 and 2 Findings: Across two rounds of testing, four participants were asked this question. Two participants answered “Yes” and two answered “No.” Participants showed no difficulties when answering this question. The two participants who answered “Yes” specifically mentioned that they had found their home on Zillow. HUD did not adopt any recommendations, as this question was not for review.

No DK Ref Final Recommendation: (Did you find your home) Through some other advertising by the owner? 1. Yes 2. No DK Ref HUD’s Final Decision: HUD adopted CBSM's final recommendation. Round 1 and 2 Findings: In round 1, eight participants were asked this question. Two participants responded “Yes” and five responded “No.” One participant changed her answer from “No” to “Yes,” stating that once she thought more about it, she realized the owner was the one who posted the house on Zillow (she had also answered “Yes” to the previous question, HEARSHSNET), so that must count as some other advertising, and she should answer “Yes” to this question (RMOVHS1). We believe this is a misinterpretation of the question. This question felt awkward for some participants who had just answered “Yes” to HEARSHSNET (for example, answering “Yes, I found it on Zillow.”) They wondered why they were being asked a second time about how they found their home and stated they already answered the question (“I just said I found it on Zillow.”) For round 2, we recommended adding an introductory sentence before this series of questions to let the participant know that they may answer “Yes” to all that apply. Such as: “The next set of questions is about how you found your home. Please answer Yes to all options that helped you to find your home.” This recommendation is similar to the recommendation for an introductory sentence about the reasons for moving. HUD did not adopt this recommendation for round 2. During round 2, four participants were asked this question, with all responding “No.” Participants appeared to answer this question correctly. When probed on their understanding of "some other advertising by the owner," participants gave the following examples: word of mouth, phone call/direct marketing, newspaper, homemade sign, local real estate groups. Two

95 participants also mentioned "the internet" and "craigslist," mistakenly repeating information meant to be captured in the previous question. These participants, however, also mentioned examples such as "a homemade sign" and "a friend of a friend." We did not recommend any changes to this question and HUD agreed to keep the question as tested in rounds 1 and 2. 5 Conclusion For this research study, we tested eight survey modules of the interviewer-administered AHS questionnaire planned for 2025. Many questions in the eight modules—Doubling Up, Accessory Dwelling Units, Climate Risk & Insurance, Real Estate, Taxes & Fees, Utilities, Home Improvement, and Recent Movers —performed well, but we also made several recommendations to reduce respondent burden, improve comprehension, and increase data quality. Our recommendations for the revised core modules (Real Estate, Taxes and Fees, Utilities, Home Improvement, and Recent Movers) primarily focused on wording clarification, consistency, and revisions to improve question comprehension. For the revised topical module, Doubling Up, participants experienced significant difficulties with burden, comprehension, and interpretation, thus our overarching recommendation was to not include the module in the AHS until further testing is completed. Our primary recommendations for the new topical model Accessory Dwelling Units focused on expanding and clarifying understanding of the term ‘Accessory Dwelling Unit’ so that participants could more accurately answer the subsequent questions throughout the module. Finally, for the new topical model Climate Risk and Insurance, our recommendations focused on the two most significant issues, addressing unfamiliarity with highly specified types of home insurance, and improving question wording regarding electric vehicle charging. 6 References Clark, A. & DeMaio, T. ADU_Intro Some properties have both a primary unit and a secondary unit, called an accessory dwelling unit. A primary unit is the main unit on a residential property. An accessory dwelling unit is an independent residence with its own entrance and exit, a fully functioning kitchen and bathroom, and is smaller than the primary unit. They are inside, attached to, or detached but on the same property as a primary residence. (Examples of secondary units include in-law suites, basement or garage apartments, guest houses, and manufactured or tiny homes on the same property as a primary residence. A secondary unit could be rented out by the owners of the primary unit.) Respondents should include rooms rented out if they have a bathroom and kitchen facilities, and direct access from the outside, (i.e., a large basement room). Respondents should not include spare bedrooms/rooms rented out. NOTE TO INTERVIEWER: BE AWARE THAT ADU DEFINITION INCLUDES KITCHEN AND BATHROOM. Accessory Dwelling Units Module 1. ADU_Intro Some properties have both a primary unit and a secondary unit, called an accessory dwelling unit. A primary unit is the main unit on a residential property. An accessory dwelling unit is an independent residence with its own entrance and exit, a fully functioning kitchen and bathroom, and is smaller than the primary unit. They can be inside the primary residence (for example, a basement apartment). They can be attached to the primary residence (for example, a converted attached garage apartment). They can be detached, but still on the same property as the primary residence (for example, a guest home or tiny home). Respondents should include rooms rented out if they have a bathroom and kitchen facilities, and direct access from the outside, (i.e., a large basement room). Respondents should not include spare bedrooms/rooms rented out. Universe: 1-unit detached, 1-unit attached, 2-unit buildings

i U.S. Census Bureau Abstract The Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the Current Population Survey asks respondents to report the annual earned income from their main job. Respondents can report their income in a periodicity that is convenient for them (i.e., for the year, monthly, twice a month, bi- weekly, or weekly). When redesigning the interviewer-administered questionnaire for web administration, the ASEC team was concerned that respondents would not know, or correctly enter, the total number of payments covering a full year without an interviewer present to help navigate any uncertainty. This experiment, on a preliminary version of the ASEC web questionnaire, tested respondents’ receptivity to a checkbox that indicated an “all year” response to the question asking how many paychecks were received during the year. In addition to taking away the need to know how may pay periods are in a year, the checkbox was intended to reduce burden and mitigate missing data for those who were paid for the entire year. Three-fifths of respondents were shown the checkbox version of the question and their response patterns were compared to a control version without a checkbox. Results showed that the majority of respondents offered the experimental version of the question used the checkbox, with nearly three-fourths of those minimizing their burden by using the checkbox only. The checkbox question significantly reduced item missing data, finding that the control question was three times more likely to have missing data. However, there was evidence that the checkbox may encourage satisficing: the mean number of “all year” responses for the experimental question (67.4%) is significantly higher than for the control (47.8%). Survey designers considering using the checkbox need to weigh the tradeoff between these two errors -- fewer responses or more data with more measurement error. As the checkbox question produced “cleaner” data with less variety of responses to recode, implementing it, but with some changes, is recommended. 1 U.S. Census Bureau Background The Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the Current Population Survey asks respondents to report the annual earned income from their main job. The respondent can report their earned income in a periodicity that is convenient for them (i.e., for the year, monthly, twice monthly, bi-weekly, or weekly). In the interviewer-administered ASEC, if the respondent provides their earned income for a time period that is less than a year, the interviewer can code the appropriate periodicity (e.g., monthly) and how many times they were paid that amount during the year (e.g., 12, if they were paid every month of the year) to get the total earned income for the year. Respondents who switched jobs during the year or routinely only work part of the year will report a number of payments that is less than a year. Respondents who stayed in the same job all year, and were paid for their vacation and sick leave, will report 52 weeks, 12 months, or 26 bi-weekly pay periods. If the respondent has difficulty recalling how many pay periods are in a year for their given periodicity, the interviewer can provide that information. When redesigning the interviewer-administered questionnaire for web administration, the ASEC team was concerned that respondents would not know, or correctly enter, the total number of payments covering a full year without an interviewer present to offer help. Previous testing on the American Community Survey found that, when asking for the number of weeks worked, respondents often miscalculated the total number of weeks in a year by multiplying four weeks by twelve months. Therefore, they based their response on 48, instead of 52, weeks in a year (Rothgeb 2007, p.20). To mitigate this error, a preliminary version of the ASEC web questionnaire experimentally tested the respondents’ receptivity to a checkbox that indicated an “all year” response to the question asking how many paychecks were received during the year. The experimental web questionnaire mimicked the interviewer-administered version, allowing respondents to report their earned income from their main job in a periodicity that is convenient for them (i.e., for the year, monthly, bi-weekly, or weekly). If the respondent choses a periodicity other than a year, a follow-up question asked how many times the respondent was paid that amount during the year. For respondents who stayed in the same job all year, and were paid for their leave, they could check the box to indicate “all [weeks/months/2-week periods]” instead of entering a number of payments. Selecting the checkbox would avoid misreporting due to miscalculating the total number of pay periods in a year, and reduce respondent burden, even for those who are confident of the number of pay periods in a year. An additional motivation was that the checkbox would make it easier to respond and therefore reduce missing data on the question. This analysis examined the use of the checkbox overall and by periodicity. Missing data rates between the control (no checkbox) and experimental (with checkbox) groups were compared to see if the checkbox improved item missingness on the number of payments question. Evidence of satisficing was examined by comparing the proportion of those reporting “all year” type responses in each group. Within the experimental group, the analysis looked at those who entered a number of pay periods representing the entire year (e.g., 52 weeks or 12 months) without checking the “all [weeks/months/2- week periods]” box, possibly indicating confusion as to the purpose of the checkbox or that the checkbox is redundant. These findings help determine whether the checkbox should be carried forward on the ASEC web instrument.

2 U.S. Census Bureau Data This experiment was appended to the end of the Census Household Pulse Survey (HPS), cycles 8 and 9 of Phase 4.2, which ran from 23 July through 16 September 2024. The HPS is a monthly cross-sectional survey of all 50 states that uses the Master Address File (MAF), maintained by the Census Bureau, to sample households. HPS draws a systematic sample of all eligible housing units, with adjustments applied to the sampling intervals to select a large enough sample to create state level estimates, including the District of Columbia, and estimates for the top 15 metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs). Independent samples are drawn for each cycle and matched to the Census Contact Frame. Of the 149 million addresses in the MAF, 77% of valid addresses are associated with at least one email, and 75% with at least one cellphone number. As a result, 88% of the housing units have at least one email or one cellphone. More complete information on sampling and weighting for HPS can be found at https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/household-pulse-survey/technical- documentation/source-accuracy.html. The 111,000 households sampled for cycles 8 and 9 were contacted by SMS text message and email, as available. The response rate was 5.7% for cycle 8 and 4.8% for cycle 9 (AAPOR RR2). Weights are available on the public use file but were not used for this analysis. No incentive is provided to respondents for HPS. Prior to the experimental questions, the HPS questionnaire included questions on the following topics, in the following order: demographics, employment, disability, mental health, childcare, inflation, food sufficiency, natural disasters, housing security, transportation, COVID-19, entertainment, health insurance, internet access, and household income. The first part of the experimental section (not reported here) pertained to mortgages or rent, and utility costs. The full questionnaire for cycles 8 and 9 can be found here: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/technical- documentation/hhp/Phase_4-2_HPS_Questionnaire_ENGLISH.pdf. Respondents eligible for the analysis were those who completed the survey in English (dropping 0.96% of cases who completed in Spanish), and answered “Yes” to the question: “Did you work at a job or business at any time during 2023?” In addition, they had to choose to report their earned income in weeks, 2-week periods, or months, rather than yearly. All respondents were asked their earned income for their preferred periodicity but the respondents not reporting yearly were also asked how many times they were paid that amount in 2023. See Figure A for screenshots of these questions. Of the 60,500 people who received the periodicity question, 1,100 skipped the question, and 30,500 answered “Yearly”. Additional cases were lost due to skips and breakoffs at the income amount question and breakoffs immediately after this question (see Table 1). Three-fifths of the remaining cases were randomly assigned to the experimental group and received the question asking for the number of times they were paid, with the checkbox option. These respondents could check the box for “All {weeks, 2- week periods, months}” instead of, or in addition to, entering data in the open-ended text box. The text box was not limited to numeric entries, for either the experimental or control groups. Tests of significance include Chi square tests of distributions and t- tests for pairwise comparisons. Simple logistic regression models are also used for paired comparisons and to estimate effect size. The analysis begins by assessing the popularity of the checkbox, within the experimental group. In addition to an overall percentage, significant differences in the popularity by periodicity are examined with a Chi square test and logistic regression predicting checkbox use. These analyses are duplicated for those cases who only used the checkbox and did not enter an open-end response. Since the cases that should have used the checkbox are those who were paid by their main job for the entire year, the open-end responses were coded within their periodicity to flag if they indicated an “all year” response. As the text entry was not limited to numbers, the data entered included numeric characters, letters, and symbols. Entries such as “52” for weekly responders, and “26” for bi-weekly responders, were coded as “all year”. Alphanumeric entries that were coded as “all year” included (but were not limited to): “1 year”, “12 months”, “Every week”, “All”, “All hear”, “For 2 years”, and “The whole year”. Open-end responses were also coded to flag cases that were not paid for a full year (i.e., paid for fewer than 52 weeks). Those that were left were coded as “irrelevant”. This category included numeric responses that were greater than a year for the periodicity (e.g., “56” for weekly respondents), income amounts (often noted with a “$”), explanations (e.g., “My job is part time”, “Varied week to week”), and ill-humored comments. Once coded, the analysis examined the number of people, overall and by periodicity, who “doubled down” on their all-year response by both checking the box and entering an “all year” open-end response. Likewise, the cases who could have used the checkbox but did not were analyzed. As above, these analyses included Chi square tests and simple logistic regressions.

Finally, the open-end responses were visually analyzed to identify the most frequent responses to look for evidence that respondents did not know how many pay periods are in a year for their chosen periodicity. Entering a number that is less than a full year appears contradictory. However, it could also be that respondents are selecting the checkbox to indicate that they worked all year but they did not get paid for every pay period. Is there evidence that people do not know how many pay periods are in a year for their chosen periodicity? Part of the motivation to provide the option of checking the “all year” box was to prevent measurement error from those who are not sure of the correct number of pay periods in a year and may miscalculate this number. As noted above, this is much less of a concern for those responding monthly. Analyzing all of the open-end responses for the bi-weekly responders in the experimental group (n=3,700) shows weak support for this hypothesis: 5.9% of cases entered “24”. This is the next highest proportion of responses, after “26”. This could be people who multiplied twelve by two. It could also

12 U.S. Census Bureau indicate a true response if people were not paid for two-weeks of vacation or sick leave or they were paid twice a month (instead of bi-weekly). Other spikes in the data, above 3%, for bi-weekly responders were at: “2”, “6”, “12”, and “20”. Of these, the highest frequency was “20” (5.5%), which is roughly 9 months and, once again, may be people in the education system. A visual review of the experimental question for the weekly responders (n=2,200) shows less support for this hypothesis: 3% of cases entered “48”. The most notable spike was for “40” (7%), which corresponds with 20 bi-weekly pay periods. Other responses provided by more than 3% of the cases were: “12”, “20”, and “50”. This review of open-end responses does not necessarily indicate that respondents confidently know the number of pay periods in year. It could be that many people took advantage of the checkbox as intended. To test this, a similar visual review was conducted on the control question. There are more cases with open-end responses in the control version, and these data are “dirtier”, meaning there is a wider variety of responses and most are at very low percentages. Despite this, the cut off of 3% was maintained for the comparison. For bi-weekly responders (n=5,800), a sizable 10% of cases reported “24” instead of “26”. This is twice the magnitude in the experimental version. Other spikes in the data were at: “2”, “12”, “20”, “25”, and “52”. The high proportion of “52” responses lends support to the hypothesis – it appears that people entered the number of weeks in a year rather than the number of 2-week pay periods. For weekly responders who received the control question (n=2,200), 5% of cases wrote “48”, which is a slightly higher percentage of cases than in the experimental group. Other spikes in the data (above 3%) were at “40” and “50”, both at 5%. It is not possible to draw firm conclusions from these data because we do not know if respondents were actually paid for fewer pay periods in a year or they did not know the total number of pay periods. To prevent this error carrying forward, the text in the question or checkbox could indicate the total number of pay periods in the year. For example, the checkbox could read “all 52 weeks” or “all 26 pay periods”. Conclusions This experiment, on a preliminary version of the ASEC web questionnaire, tested respondents’ receptivity to a checkbox that indicated an “all year” response on the question asking how many paychecks were received during the year. Results showed that the majority of respondents offered the experimental version of the question used the checkbox, with nearly three-fourths of those minimizing their burden by using the checkbox only. The checkbox question significantly reduced item missing data, compared to the control question. However, there was evidence that the checkbox may encourage satisficing. Survey designers considering using the checkbox need to weigh the tradeoff between these two errors -- fewer responses or more data with more measurement error. As the checkbox question produced “cleaner” data with less variety of responses to recode, implementing it, but with some changes, is recommended. The experiment intentionally allowed people to be able to both check the box and enter a text response to observe evidence of confusion. In addition, the survey allowed for data that are not purely numeric on this question. Once these settings are changed in production, respondents will only be able enter a numeric response with an appropriate number of digits or check the box (not both), resulting in cleaner data. Even so, respondents provided numeric responses that may have indicated confusion about the information requested or how many pay periods are in a year – things an interviewer would clarify on

13 U.S. Census Bureau the currently active version of the ASEC instrument. Therefore, an additional recommendation is that the text in the question, beside the text entry, or beside the checkbox indicates the total number of pay periods in a year for the preferred periodicity. E.g., the text beside the open end textbox could read: weeks (out of 52 weeks in a year). People who reported their income for the year did not receive the number of payments question. In addition, those who chose to report their pay monthly showed fewer problems reporting their number of payments for the year. The remaining cases, weekly and bi-weekly responders, were 39% of the respondents in these data. Therefore, if implemented thoughtfully, the checkbox could improve the data quality for these respondents, removing differential measurement error by periodicity. Respondents working in education may be introducing error by nature of their jobs. Analyses showed that some of the respondents who selected the checkbox entered a text response equivalent to 8 or 9 months. For educators, 8 or 9 months is a full year of work. For these and jobs that do not span a whole year by design, analysts calculating earned income will have to use the open-end response as the true response, and not the maximum number of pay periods implied by the checkbox. This concerns a small number of people -- 4.6% of all people who used the checkbox provided a text response of less than a year—but could introduce earned income bias for certain subpopulations. While restricting response to the text box or the checkbox might provide cleaner data, for these respondents, it seemed important to denote that they were employed all year. Further testing could be done to determine how these respondents would report the number of pay periods if restricted to the checkbox or text entry, especially once the question is edited to clearly state that all year is, for example, 52 weeks of pay. Finally, the web version did not include an option for people who are paid twice a month (not bi-weekly). If respondents looking for this option chose to report bi-weekly, the number of payments for a whole year would could be less than 26 and look as if they didn’t work all year. Including this option would clean up the these data and help respondents by providing the option that best fits them. Taken together, the checkbox was largely successful and seemed to be helpful to respondents. With the recommended changes noted above, and some further testing, this question feature is likely to be an asset to the ASEC and similar surveys. Caveats One caveat of this analysis which may have contributed to some of the irrelevant responses and alphanumeric responses (e.g., “50-52 weeks”), is that the questions asked about 2023 but the field period was seven to nine months into the 2024 calendar year. Respondents may have had trouble remembering how many times they were paid 2023, and this may have been worse for seasonal or hourly jobs that are paid weekly or bi-weekly. Some of the analyses above rely on the recoding of text responses. The paper details the decisions made as to what qualified as an “all year” response, and these decisions were always made within the selected periodicity. These analyses may turn out differently if the decisions as to what constitutes “all year” were more or less lenient. Bibliography

i U.S. Census Bureau Abstract The Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the Current Population Survey (CPS) includes a question on the amount of earned income from a person’s main job. In order to derive the amount for a full year, the respondent must provide the amount, designate the periodicity (yearly, monthly, bi-weekly, or weekly), and, for any periodicity less than a year, report how many times they were paid that amount during the calendar year. For those who do not provide all necessary information, this experiment tested a short series of unfolding categorical income follow-up questions. Respondents were asked three categorical income questions in total, with each subsequent question further narrowing the response provided in the previous question. Due to the narrower range for the middle income category, by the third categorical question, the response options had unusually small ranges. This specific pathway of unfolding questions was called the RSU (Really Small Unfolding) series. An additional element of the experiment was the option to choose “I remember the exact amount” on any of the categorical questions. Selecting this would prompt the respondent to enter an amount and not show them the rest of the income unfolding sequence. The experiment was conducted on the Household Pulse Survey (HPS) between July and September 2024 and analyzed unweighted. Results indicate that most people provided complete income information (91%) and were not shown unfolding categorical questions. Of those routed to the unfolding questions, the highest percent of people broke off at the first categorical question. In a debriefing question, a majority of these respondents reported that they did not want to provide income information, although a portion also reported not knowing the amount. Of those who were presented the first income unfolding question, 62% answered all three categorical questions, thereby, providing the missing income data. Response options with particularly narrow income increments (the RSU Series) and offering the option to provide a finite income amount (the “I remember” option) both resulted in more missing data and are not recommended. 1 U.S. Census Bureau Background The interviewer-administered Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the Current Population Survey (CPS) asks respondents detailed questions about income, health insurance, and other topics. One of the items asks respondents to report the annual earned income from their main job. When the respondent provides an amount, the interviewer asks if this is for the year, monthly, twice a month, bi- weekly, or weekly, and how many pay periods they received this amount. The combination of these three pieces of information allows for the calculation of total annual earned income from the respondent’s main job. If the respondent cannot provide an amount in the first question, the interviewer asks a categorical question with a choice of three income ranges representing earnings for the year from their main job. The categorical responses for the income question are: less than $45,000, between $45,000 and $60,000, and over $60,000. Note that the middle category has the narrowest range -- just $15,000. If the respondent chooses the lowest income category (less than $45,000), a follow-up categorical income question is administered to further refine their answer to a $15,000 increment. The other income categories do not receive a follow-up question. ASEC is undergoing a modernization process that includes the addition of a web-based instrument. The questions describe above were redesigned for self-administration. The series was altered slightly, in accordance with the Census Bureau Web Survey Design Guidelines, so that the respondent is first asked which periodicity (weekly, monthly, etc.) is most convenient for reporting earned income, then asked for the income amount, and finally how many payments. As in the interviewer-administered instrument, if the respondent does not provide complete information on these questions, they will be asked the categorical (annual) earned income question. In addition to testing the instrument for web administration, researchers also wanted to test if respondents would provide more precise income information than what is gathered from the single categorical income question, since more precise ranges would be helpful for the imputation models used in data processing. The experiment described below explores respondents’ willingness to answer additional categorical income questions which further narrow the earned income ranges beyond the first categorical question. This experiment implements the earned income series as described to test if respondents can/will provide all three pieces of information in web and if not, where they fail to do so. For those who do not provide all pieces of information, the categorical income question was presented and then unfolded two more times for all respondents, resulting in a total of three categorical income questions (see Figure 1 for an example). The analysis will assess the item missing rates when asking for this level of detail.

Prior to the experimental questions, the HPS questionnaire included questions on the following topics, in the following order: demographics, employment, disability, mental health, childcare, inflation, food sufficiency, natural disasters, housing security, transportation, COVID-19, entertainment, health insurance, internet access, and household income. In order to be eligible for the experiment, respondents had to be working in 2023. If they were working in 2023, they were asked two or three additional questions (called filter questions; see Figure 2) to report the income made at their main job in 2023. The first filter question asked what periodicity was most convenient for reporting earned income. If the respondent chose “yearly”, they were asked one additional filter question, which is the amount earned for the year. If they answered something other than “yearly”, they were asked two additional filter questions: the income amount for the periodicity (i.e., weekly, every other week, or monthly) and how many times they were paid that amount in 2023. If the respondent did not answer both/all of these filter questions, they were shown the experimental earned income unfolding series. Figure 2. Filter Questions Did you work at a job or business at any time during 2023? o Yes o No What is the easiest way for you to tell us how much you earned from your main job in 2023, before taxes and other deductions? o Weekly o Every other week (biweekly) o Monthly o Yearly

4 U.S. Census Bureau How much did you earn from your main job, before taxes and other deductions, in 2023? $_____ [if not providing a “Yearly” amount] For how many [weeks/2-week periods/months] did you earn $[fill amount] from your main job in 2023? ____ [weeks/2-week periods/months] The income unfolding series included three sequential questions which continually narrow the income ranges, depending on what was selected in the previous question (see Figure 1 for an example; see Appendix A for all possible sequences). The middle category of the first question ($45,000 - $59,999) is more narrow than the two other response options. Therefore, by the third unfold, the increments of the response options are less than $2,000. For this unfolding path, these questions are called the Really Small Unfolding (RSU) Series, because it is unusual to ask for ranges this narrow under normal circumstances. For each question in the unfolding series, respondents could choose the option labeled “I remember the exact amount” and enter an amount. This ended the unfolding sequence and skipped them to a debriefing question about why they chose this option, and then to the final section of the questionnaire. The questionnaire did not provide response options for don’t know or refused so respondents either selected a valid response or skipped the question. Any respondent who did not provide a valid response to all three unfolding questions was presented a debriefing question asking why they did not answer. The full text and response options for the filter, unfolding, and debriefing questions included in this experiment are detailed in Appendix A. Methodology The objective of the analysis was to document the points where respondents skipped or broke off in the initial earned income (filter) questions, and to do the same for the unfolding series. Therefore, the analysis is descriptive for the most part, reporting frequencies and percents. The only statistical tests are a Chi-square test when looking at missing data by periodicity, and a simple logistic regression model to further examine the pairwise comparisons. Respondents eligible for analysis were those who completed the survey in English (dropping 0.96% of cases who completed in Spanish) and answered “Yes” to the question: “Did you work at a job or business at any time during 2023?” Of the approximately 92,500 respondents who saw the work question, 1% skipped the question and 33% answered “No”. This left 61,000 cases eligible for the analysis. However, due to (700) breakoffs after the work question, 60,500 received the first filter question. Therefore, 1.2% of the eligible cases broke off when they saw that they were being asked a question about earned income.

Conclusions Results indicated that most people provided an income amount (91%) and were not shown the unfolding categorical earned income questions. Among the filter questions, the open-ended earned income question had the highest amount of missing data (5.8%) and therefore, this question routed more people to the income unfolding series than the other two filter questions. Missing data on this question varied significantly by periodicity: missing data was lowest on those who reported yearly and highest on those who reported bi-weekly. If we assume that those reporting yearly were salaried, it is mostly the non- salaried earners who were routed to the unfolding series. Due the regular occurrence of breakoffs, not everyone who had missing data on a filter question participated in the unfolding series. Of the 2,900 people presented the first income unfolding question, 61.5% answered all three categorical questions. The highest percent of people broke off at the first categorical question, indicating that they did not want to answer questions on income, whether open- ended or categorical. This was echoed in the debriefing questions, asked of those who skipped at least one categorical income question, where a majority of respondents reported that they did not want to

11 U.S. Census Bureau provide income information. Therefore, trying to make it “easier” for them by offering more questions on the same topic (income) was not a helpful solution. The RSU Series, with its narrow income increments, consistently showed higher missing data rates, especially at the third unfold. While significance tests were not conducted, it seemed to be that asking income questions with increments smaller than $5,000 could lead to higher missing data. Debriefing data on these questions showed the smaller increments were more confusing to people, compared to the non-RSU Series questions. The ”I remember” option was not very popular and, when it was used, it appeared that people were selecting it as a way to indicate refusal. Since respondents who chose “I remember” did not provide an income amount (for the most part), this option mostly generated unwanted missing data. Therefore, offering this option is not recommended. The unfolding questions provided an additional 1,800 cases over the 55,000 who provided data without the unfolding questions. However, this comes at a loss of 2,600 cases that either skipped the categorical income questions or broke off just before or during the unfolding series. At the end of a survey, this may be a worthwhile tradeoff but it’s probably too great of a risk earlier in the questionnaire. The primary caution from this research is when asking income on the web, it is best to ask it near the end of the survey to limit the amount of missing data on the subsequent questions from those who break off. This is in alignment with the literature on asking income and other sensitive questions. If income is asked early in the survey, those who refuse to provide the data should be identified and separated from those who need help estimating their income. Offering a don’t know /don’t remember option on the income question may help identify people who are more likely to respond to a follow-up categorical income question. Further testing is recommended to explore this suggestion, however. If the refusals cannot be disentangled from the don’t knows, follow-up questions offering categorical response options are not recommended. Caveats The respondents who received the earned income filter questions were more motivated than the full pool of respondents. As reported in the methods, 92,000 people received the question asking if they are currently working, but this was down from the 110,000 who started the survey (in English). That said, it is important to note that this experiment was conducted at the end of an already long web survey, taking up to 20 minutes. Therefore, respondents’ time and patience may have been short by the time they reached the earned income questions, exacerbating the missing data rates. ASEC is typically conducted in March and April of the calendar year, at a time when people have and are aware of their W2s for tax season. These data were collected later in the year when that documentation is not as handy and the information less salient. HPS does not offer an incentive. For some people, an incentive may have kept them from breaking off. However, it’s possible that the amount of skipped income questions would increase instead, essentially exchanging breakoffs for skipped questions. This should be experimentally tested. Due to an error in the survey programming, the results did not allow analysis of those least likely to respond to the earned income questions, whether due to motivation or lack of knowledge. Respondents who skipped the first filter question about preferred periodicity were not routed to the unfolding

12 U.S. Census Bureau questions. Therefore, the findings are limited and potentially more conservative than they would be if these cases had been included in the experiment. Finally, findings reported about the RSU series were confounded with the income amount. The narrow categories were not randomly tested on low, medium, and high earners. Instead this test was an artifact of the smaller middle income category in the first unfolding question. Therefore, the findings reported, such as the rate of missing data for these questions, may be due to the narrow categories, or attributes of people who earn mid-range incomes, or a combination of both.

Abstract A modernization effort is underway for the Current Population Survey (CPS), which is the premiere source of labor force statistics for the U.S. population. Currently, the CPS collects data via interviewers. However, declining response rates and rising data collection costs have motivated the development and addition of an internet self-response mode for the CPS. Interviewers play an important role in ensuring the CPS collects high quality data because some of the survey questions are complex requiring careful probing before the respondent can provide a complete answer. To evaluate how the internet self-response instrument performs, RTI International and Research Support Services Inc. (RSS) conducted two rounds of cognitive interviews with a prototype of the CPS instrument developed by the Census Bureau in Qualtrics. This report presents the findings from these interviews and recommendations for the CPS internet self-response instrument. Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 1-1 1. Project Background Sponsored jointly by the U.S. Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the Current Population Survey (CPS) is the premier source of data on employment and unemployment in the United States. It is a longitudinal survey conducted by trained U.S. Census Bureau interviewers, either by telephone or in person. The CPS comprises a core that asks the same employment, income, and demographic questions every month (see Questionnaires) and supplements that vary in sponsorship and content. The interviewer plays an important role in ensuring the quality of CPS data because the survey questions are complex, and careful probing may be needed before the respondent is able to provide a complete answer. The interviewer also plays an important role in maintaining the respondent’s motivation to complete the CPS survey, allowing item and unit response rates to remain high. Despite the importance of the interviewer for a successful completion of the CPS, there are compelling reasons to consider adding a self-administered web mode, including the potential to reduce data collection costs, improve response rates (both nationally and within demographic subgroups), and reduce the time required to complete data collection. To evaluate how well the CPS instrument performs in a self-administered web mode, RTI International and Research Support Services Inc. (RSS) provided support for cognitive interviewing. RTI/RSS conducted two rounds of cognitive interviews with a prototype CPS web instrument developed by the Census Bureau, programmed in Qualtrics. This report summarizes the recruitment efforts and findings from the first and second round of cognitive interviews.

2-1 2. Methodology 2.1 Introduction This section provides an overview of the recruitment efforts and interviewing methods for Round 1 and Round 2 of the CPS cognitive interviews. An overview of the recruitment strategies, eligibility criteria, cognitive interview participants, and the cognitive interview protocol and procedures are discussed in the sections that follow. 2.2 Recruitment Methods 2.2.1 Overview The RTI/RSS team recruited participants for Round 1 of CPS Core cognitive testing from December 1, 2023, to January 30, 2024, and participants for Round 2 from April 8, 2024, to May 11, 2024. For each round, the RTI/RSS team posted online recruitment advertisements in selected areas on Craigslist, releasing advertisements on a rolling basis to maintain a steady stream of prospective recruits for screening and scheduling. The Census Bureau programmed a web-based eligibility screener in Qualtrics. The RTI/RSS team also established a toll-free telephone line dedicated to recruitment purposes. The web link of the screening instrument and the toll-free phone number were presented in the online advertisements (see Appendix A) to support participant recruitment. During the data collection period, the RTI/RSS team provided the Census Bureau with a weekly recruitment and interviewing progress report. The weekly report displayed the number of interview participants with respect to recruitment goals and needed sub- characteristics. The results of Round 1 and Round 2 recruitment presented in Section 2.2.4 of this report reflect the final recruitment outcomes. 2.2.2 Recruitment and Advertising Procedures During Call Order 11 CPS cognitive testing for both rounds, the RTI/RSS team used Craigslist as the main venue for recruitment advertising. Craigslist is one of the best-known online bulletin boards and provides the most comprehensive coverage of metropolitan areas in the United States. To leverage Craigslist’s broad reach, RTI/RSS did not use targeted advertisements that focused on specific characteristics and used a customized general advertisement instead. Additionally, RTI/RSS also posted the general recruitment advertisement on Reddit under the subreddit “r/samplesize” to further expand the reach to prospective recruits during Round 2.

Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 2 — Methodology 2-2 The RTI/RSS team began the participant recruitment by posting the general recruitment advertisement on Craigslist under the “jobs/et cetera” sections. See Appendix A-1 for the text used in the recruitment ads. During Round 1, the first round of monthly paid advertising started on November 15, 2023, and expired on January 7, 2024. The team posted the first two general advertisements and received a few dozen completions within 24 hours. The team continued to receive completions at a consistent rate for approximately a week afterward. As completions gradually decreased, the team posted the third general advertisement on November 26 to boost the response to the web recruitment screener. The fourth and fifth general advertisements were posted on December 5, followed by the sixth posting on December 10. The RTI/RSS team recorded screening responses from more than 600 prospective participants from this first round of advertising. During Round 2, the first round of monthly paid advertising started on April 8, 2024, and expired on May 6, 2024. The team posted four general advertisements. Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 2 — Methodology 2-6 2.3 Cognitive Interviewing Methods 2.3.1 Overview Cognitive testing consists of one-on-one interviews and is often employed to assess functionality of questionnaires and surveys. For this effort, we employed cognitive interview methods to test an adapted internet self-response survey of the CPS Core questionnaire. The adapted internet self-response instrument was programmed in Qualtrics. The interviews assessed general comprehension and clarity of content and wording. The goal was to understand how well questions adapted for self-response are understood when administered without the aid of an interviewer. The interviews used a protocol with pre-scripted probes (as described in Section 2.3.2). Spontaneous probes were used as needed to better understand comprehension issues not addressed by scripted probes. Cognitive interviewing works best for the following: ▪ Learning about the thought process participants use when reading materials or responding to requests; ▪ Probing deeper into the response process; ▪ Observing nonverbal reactions; ▪ Testing navigation in forms or instructions; ▪ Examining new items for potential for measurement error; ▪ Examining all items for potential for comprehension issues; and ▪ Gauging opinions and reactions to the survey as a whole. 2.3.2 Protocol and Procedures Cognitive testing took place with 35 participants in each round (70 participants total) in English. All interviews were (1) conducted virtually using Microsoft Teams’ videoconference capabilities, (2) conducted within the Census Bureau’s Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) environment or on a Census Bureau–provided laptop, (3) audio-recorded or video- and audio-recorded, and (4) approximately 30–60 minutes long. Participants received a $40 digital gift card incentive. Census Bureau provided the RTI/RSS Team with the cognitive interview protocol to be used for data collection (see Appendix B-1 for the Round 1 protocol and Appendix B-2 for the Round 2 protocol). The cognitive interviews used a think aloud method and included additional retrospective scripted probing and spontaneous probing. To standardize the overall implementation of each test case, the test was carried out in the following sequence: 1. Obtain the participant’s consent (see Appendix C). 2. Start video and audio recording using Census Bureau–approved software and a backup digital recorder.

3-1 3. Findings 3.1 Introduction This section summarizes the findings from both rounds of CPS Core cognitive testing. The questions in the CPS Core instrument were divided into three topics: introduction questions, questions for participants not working during the reference period, and questions for participants working during the reference period. Within each topic, questions were divided into further subtopics; for each group of questions, the following are reported: Round 1 issues revealed while responding to the probes, Round 1 spontaneous issues, a Round 1 summary (including recommendations), changes made for Round 2, Round 2 issues revealed while responding to the probes, Round 2 spontaneous issues, and a Round 2 summary (including recommendations). 3.2 Introduction Questions The introduction questions included the following: BUS, BUS_OWNER, LABFOR, WORK, D_ANYWORK, BUS1, and BUS2. These questions asked about the household’s business ownership and work status. 3.2.1 Round 1 Issues Revealed as a Response to the Probes Reference period Each interview collected information about employment-related activity that took place within a specified 1-week reference period; the reference period was from the Sunday to Saturday that included the 12th of the month. Three reference periods were used during the 2-month period of conducting interviews in Round 1: ▪ 18 interviews conducted between December 1, 2023 (the date of the first interview), and January 8, 2024, used the reference period of November 12, 2023, to November 18, 2023. The average number of days between the last day of the reference period and when the interview was conducted was 27.5 (minimum=13; maximum=48). ▪ 3 interviews conducted between January 9, 2024, and January 13, 2024, used the reference period of December 10, 2023, to December 16, 2023. The average number of days between the last day of the reference period and when the interview was conducted was 25 (minimum=24; maximum=27). ▪ 14 interviews conducted between January 14, 2024, and January 30, 2024 (the date of the last interview), used the reference period of January 7, 2024, to January 13, 2024. The average number of days between the last day of the reference period and when the interview was conducted was 9.8 (minimum=3; maximum=17). After participants answered the CPS survey questions, the first retrospective probe they answered was whether they could recall the reference period used in the survey. Most participants could recall the reference period dates with no issues. However, there were some participants who either had issues recalling the reference period dates during
