These issues will be described below, but they seem to be an artifact of the cognitive interviewing process and may not be an issue in CPS production. Participants who were not working began the interview with questions about the standard reference period. However, they were then asked questions with different reference periods. For example, one question asks, “Have you been doing anything to find work during the last 4 weeks?” (variable LK) while another asks “Did you look for work at any time during the last 12 months?” (variable DWLK). They were also asked to discuss when they last worked. Therefore, retrospective probes about the reference period were not as successful with this group because they had reported on numerous time periods throughout the interview. A few participants did not have any issue recalling the reference period dates during the retrospective probing but expressed some confusion about the dates during the interview. All of these participants completed interviews in December, but the instrument used the November reference period, which caused some confusion. One participant was confused both about what the current month was and what year the questions were referencing, explaining “I was thinking last year… because I was thinking that we were still in November and no, we're in December, so, that's the reason why it didn't really match the dates for December but I didn't realize that it was December and that the question was saying November, so it was my mistake” (P153). These issues are likely caused by the context of the interview protocol, which used a reference period sometimes referring to the previous month. During CPS production, because the instrument will use a reference period closer in time to when the interviews are conducted, this is less likely to be an issue. Interpretation of BUS During the retrospective probing, when participants were asked whether they could describe what they thought BUS was asking in their own words, most participants answered that the question was asking if anyone in their household owned a business or farm and did not express any difficulty with interpreting the question. We believe that these are cases where participants are underemployed, as opposed to unemployed. Most participants did not have any difficulties determining their answers to these questions; however, the phrasing of “or do ANY work for pay” in WORK caused confusion for two participants. One of these participants, who works in real estate, thought aloud while answering the question, “So a lot of my business activities, I don’t get paid for. They’re all like development-type activities. So yes, I did work, but did I get paid or make money? No, I did not. So, this would be tough for me to answer. When the interviewer asked what they thought the question was asking, they said, “Did I receive a paycheck? Or did someone make a payment to my business?” (P1234). Because the participant interpreted WORK in this way and because they did not receive any payment for work in the prior week, they reported in the introduction questions that they were not working for pay during the reference period.

Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 3 — Findings 3-9 At the end of the interview, the interviewer asked more probing questions about WORK. For example, the interviewer asked how would the participant answer if the wording of WORK only asked, “did you work at a job” and did not say “or do ANY work for pay.” The participant said that if that was the wording, they would answer yes. Because of these responses to the introduction questions, the survey path then asked this participant questions about being absent from work, which was very confusing to them and not appropriate for their situation. In addition, when the participant was asked questions about the details of their employment (e.g., IO1INT), the question stem used a fill to ask about their “last job” because the survey responses indicated that they might have been absent from work, which made the participant think about the previous job that they had before they were an artist. Although the wording of “or do ANY work for pay” in WORK only caused confusion for two participants during Round 2, it led one of these participants to answer incorrectly and took them down the wrong survey path, which had a large impact on their survey data. 3.2.7 Round 2 Summary Changing the wording of the cognitive interviewing probe and changing the reference period to be more recent resulted in fewer issues around the reference period during Round 2. In general, participants did not have any major issues with the reference period during Round 2. Similar to Round 1, most participants overall did not have difficulty with answering BUS. However, some participants interpreted BUS as only referring to incorporated businesses, which resulted in them answering no, although some participants included non-incorporated businesses into their answer and answered yes. If these different interpretations led to incorrect responses from participants, then BLS could consider providing a definition or rephrasing the question. In addition, although some participants questioned why the survey was asking about a farm or a business, this did not impact their understanding of the question and how they answered. Lastly, although some participants questioned why this was the first question being asked or wondered whether there would be follow-up questions about a business or farm, most participants did not have a strong reaction to the fact that BUS is the first question asked. Although participants did not have issue with this during Round 1, the phrasing of “or do ANY work for pay” in WORK caused confusion for two participants and led one of these participants down the wrong path in the survey. This participant seemed to interpret WORK as asking if they worked AND received pay; because this participant worked but did not receive pay during the reference period, they answered “No” to WORK and were led down the unemployed path in the survey, which was very confusing for them since the questions were not applicable to their employment status. BLS could consider rephrasing the question to only ask if respondents worked at a job or further separate out the concept of pay.

Her discussion also raises a consideration of how employers categorize employee leave, as opposed to participants’ own justifications for activities during the absence. When participants add this consideration to their response, this can further complicate reporting. For example, some employers provide personal time off for most types of leave and do not differentiate between sick time and vacation time. Multiple participants were thinking about their employers’ categorization of the leave when answering the question. Another participant (P295) was not sure whether to select the option “Vacation or personal time off” or the option “Caring for family or personal obligation.” She did not note what the leave was for but noted that she used her employer’s leave category of personal time off to attend to a personal obligation. Other participants identified response options that might be missing from the list. These include the following: ▪ Religious observations ▪ Bereavement leave/attending a funeral ▪ Jury duty ▪ Playing hooky (providing a reason to your employer that is not the real reason) ▪ Mental health leave ▪ Healthcare appointments ▪ Lack of transportation BLS may intend for some general reasons for work absence to be categorized as “personal obligations.” However, we note that this category is combined with “caring for family.” Furthermore, it is in the middle of a long list of response options and as a result may not serve as a catchall general category. An “other (specify)” response option is provided on the current list. Some participants were confused by the hypothetical nature of this probe. The question as displayed during the interview asked about absence during a specific week, but they were instead asked to imagine the last time they missed work. Those who did not have absences during the displayed reference period were confused by the probes and the hypothetical nature of the question. Furthermore, interviewers asked all participants to think about the last time they were absent from work and to answer ABSRSN1. However, this was intended for participants who had worked in the past 12 months, which led to additional confusion among those who had not worked in the past 12 months.

Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 3 — Findings 3-12 In future interviewing rounds, we recommend tailoring the question to actually ask about the last time the participant was absent from work so that participants do not have to interpret the question beyond what is shown on the screen. We should also review the procedures to aid interviewers in identifying the appropriate audience for this probe (i.e., those who have worked in the past 12 months). Round 1 spontaneous issues Fourteen participants reported that they were not working during the reference period, while only one reported having an absence from work during the reference period. This response pattern limited the findings for these variables. Another participant (P09) discussed his unique circumstances and revealed misreporting in response to three survey questions. While responding to probes in the interview, this person (P09) revealed that he was laid off from his full-time job on the Monday of the reference period. As described in Section 3.2.2, this participant reported in WORK that he was not working during the reference period. He went to work on Monday, was informed that he was permanently laid off, and spent the rest of the day working on tasks related to his layoff. The participant confirmed that he was paid for work on the Monday of the reference period. WORK asks, “Last week, between [reference period] did you work at a job, or do ANY work for either pay or profit?” Here, the participant conflated the concepts of being paid for work with performing typical duties. Given that his last workday (the Monday of the reference period) was spent on tasks related to his termination, he responded “no” to this question. This conflation of being paid for work and performing typical duties influenced the participant’s responses to the questions in the absence and layoff section. The participant approached ABSNT (left) in a similar manner as WORK. He did not include his last day of employment in his reporting and said “no” to this question. In response to whether they were on layoff from a job (LAY), this participant, who had been laid off from their job permanently, answered “yes.” Round 1 summary Very few participants met the criteria to report about their own absences from work. Therefore, additional testing of these questions will be important. Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 3 — Findings 3-14 Round 2 issues revealed as a response to the probes As a result of changes to the interview protocol in advance of Round 2, participants were only asked about the absence and layoff questions if they reported an absence or layoff from work. Two participants reported experiencing an absence from work during the reference period. The first participant (P1018) worked a part time job and took time off during the reference period to attend to errands. When asked about the reason for her absence in ABSRSN1, she selected “vacation or personal days.” She did not report any issues with the response options and thought that the response options made sense. The next participant also had a part-time job in retail. She reported that she did not work during the reference period. When considering ABSRSN1, which asks about the main reason for the absence from work, she indicated “day off” as the most appropriate response. Later, during discussion of this item, the participant revealed that she had not worked in a few weeks because of shoulder surgery. She acknowledged that her response to ABSRSN1 did not align with this response. She said that she had been thinking that she does not work on Sundays. When asked about the reference period, she seemed confused: “Well, it said between the 14th and 20th so that lands on a Sunday, so yeah, it is my day off” (P971). Upon revisiting ABSRN1, the participant noted that the list contained many response options. She edited her response to “sick” indicating that the option “sick, injured or had other medical reason, including being pregnant” was the best fit. Through probing, it was not clear whether confusion about the reference period or confusion about the response options in ABSRSN1 contributed to the misreporting for the item. No one reported experiencing a layoff during the reference period. Round 2 spontaneous issues No spontaneous issues were detected in Round 2. Round 2 summary Fewer participants answered these questions because of changes in the protocol for Round 2, which allowed us to draw fewer conclusions about the performance of the items. However, one of the two participants who received the question incorrectly answered ABSRN1, which asks about the reason for work absences. This item contains a long list of response options, which one participant noted as she reviewed the list and edited her response. She noted that she should have put sick or injured, but “there were so many.” (P971)

Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 3 — Findings 3-15 3.3.2 Looking for Work Questions included in this section: LK, LKM, D_LKACTIVE, LKAVL, LKAVR, LKLL1, LKLL2, LKLW, LKDATY, LKDR1, LKDR2, LKDR3, and LKFT These questions are administered to participants who are not working during the reference period. They assess whether participants have done anything to look for work, activities participants have done to look for work, if they are either actively or passively looking for work, activities before the participants were looking for work, when the participant last worked, and the length of time the participants have been looking for work. In response to LK (“Have you been doing anything to find work during the last 4 weeks?”), seven participants said “Yes” and five participants said “No” in Round 1 interviews. During Round 2 interviews, three participants said “Yes” and two participants said “No.” Round 1 issues revealed as a response to the probes Anything that might be considered work If participants reported in the instrument that they were not working during the reference period and not looking for work (i.e., “No” to LK), they were asked during retrospective probing if there was anything they did during the reference period that might be considered work, even if for just an hour. One participant, who is retired, thought about gig jobs that they occasionally do, like participating as a mock juror or counting houses in a gated community. Another participant said that they find odd jobs from Craigslist that they can complete online. This participant considers participation in surveys to be a “job.” Another participant explained that they participate in activities every day that they consider to be “work”; they participate in a brain health study, do games offered by the New York Times, and have hobbies. However, they noted that this is not work for pay and said if we wanted to know about paid or volunteer work, they would answer differently. This participant was somewhat confused but ultimately felt we were referring to work for pay. Although this probe was intended to reveal if participants misreported not working during the reference period (if they failed to report any work during the reference period), it is not clear whether participants were discussing work that they did during the reference period or discussing work that they do outside of the reference period.

Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 3 — Findings 3-23 Length of time looking for work Participants did not have trouble recalling the length of time they were looking for work because they had been looking for work recently. One participant (P1147) used COVID-19 as a reference point. However, one participant had some confusion about LKDR1 and explained, “It says weeks, month, year, so I’m thinking you’re looking for time…I think that’s what you mean. I’m not sure what this question means, with the answers” (P1147). Once this participant saw the next question (LKDR2), which asked them to give a number, LKDR1 made more sense to them, and they were able to answer the question. When asked if the participants did the same activities to look for work over this period or whether they varied, two of the participants said they did the same activities. However, the other participant (P1147) explained that she did different activities during this time, as she said some activities were not as productive anymore. For example, she never used to use LinkedIn, and now she uses it more. She used to rely a lot on Craigslist, but now she does not use it much anymore as a source for job openings. Calculations based on usual start time and end time The most common strategy employed among participants was to think about when they usually start and end their workdays. This was very straightforward for participants who have relatively consistent schedules: “It's exactly on the dot. I go in at 8:30, I leave at 5pm and I have a one hour lunch break that's not paid. Ease of providing “usual” hours Most participants said that it was easy to answer HRUSL1_1 & HRUSL1_2, either because they knew how many hours they usually work or because it was not difficult to estimate. A few participants did say they found it difficult, citing the fact that they do not have a consistent work schedule, so their hours vary. For example, one participant explained, “It was a little difficult, because like I said, it varies so sometimes it’s [kind of] hard trying to figure out how many hours I'm [going to] get” (P255). During this exchange, the interviewer pointed to the second bullet (“Consider the LAST 4 MONTHS”) and third bullet (“If hours vary from week to week, give the number of hours worked in a typical week”) and asked whether these instructions were helpful or not helpful. The participant responded, “it was okay. It really [kind of] depends, the last 4 months it varies... It was still kind of difficult. If it varies, how can you really say the average number of hours? It’s kind of contradictory” (P255). One participant who has a second, part-time seasonal job preparing tax returns commented that it was more challenging to answer about their usual hours for that business: “For the second one kind of, because it can vary, because the season hasn't started I can't really account for a whole lot of work. I usually just go to meetings or do marketing and that can be, honestly it's not determined. It can be any time of the day or night, as needed so…It was just a little bit more difficult with the second one” (P153). Round 1 summary Participants with full-time or consistent jobs had the easiest time answering these questions. Some tended to report on their agreed upon hourly schedule or on the number of hours for which they are paid. In most cases, they acknowledged that they work more than this number of hours they reported because they are unpaid hours and thus, they underreported their total hours. We recommend that future testing probe to see if participants tend to work more or less than their expected number of hours.

Hours they work most of the time Another related but slightly different strategy that did not come up in Round 1 was that four participants in Round 2 spoke about how they based their usual hours on the number of hours they work most of the time: "I counted them. Less consistent schedules and average hours Another very common strategy for answering the usual hours questions came from participants who have less regular schedules and told interviewers they had to average their hours. This was also consistent with our findings in Round 1: “I said 4 because the first one… sometimes I work a lot during the week and sometimes not at all … it varies… I would say… This is more of an average…” (P1124). Job specific ways of counting usual hours One type of strategy for responding to the usual hours questions that came up in Round 2 that we had not heard in Round 1 came from participants who spoke about how they thought about something specific to their job to count their usual hours. For example, a psychotherapist spoke about how they see individual clients and knows they typically see 23 to 25 clients per week for 1-hour sessions. They told us they took those client hours and added 5 or so more hours to account for documentation, emails, meetings with colleagues, and any other administrative tasks they might do in a week. This brought them to 30 to 33 hours, and they entered 33 hours (P983). Another participant who works backstage for a performance company explained their strategy, “I was going by show. So each show is about 5 hours. I can do between 3 and 4 shows a week so I went with 20 part-time hours, like a goal that I try to hit. That's how I broke it down in my head” (P1012). Other examples of this included an educator who counted student observations, a shopper for an app that counted shopping trips, and a hairdresser who counted the hours their salon is open for customers.

Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 3 — Findings 3-39 Thinking about the reference period for usual hours One participant told the interviewer that they were actually focusing on the reference period of last week when they answered about their usual hours, even though it was not particularly representative of how things typically are for them, “So my work, believe it or not, is highly seasonable [seasonal], we have seasons where we are busier than other times. So if we’re in the middle of a busy spring market, which is technically where we are now, I just happen to not be that busy, I would be working many more hours. What I find on average, or looking specifically at that week, I have 3 clients, I’m doing about the same activities for them every day, and that averages to 6 hours. But I did really kind of look more to that one-week period that you had asked about to help” (P1267). Round 2 spontaneous issues No spontaneous issues were detected in Round 2. Round 2 summary The usual hours questions seemed to work well in Round 2. Participants used varied strategies for providing their usual hours but seemed to interpret the question as intended. Round 2 summary These questions again performed well in Round 2. The addition of the transition statement did seem to improve understanding of the difference between the usual hours questions and the actual hours questions. However, several participants reported excluding unpaid hours from their actual hours worked during the reference period. This included time commuting, evenings answering email or phone calls, and time they considered “non-billable.” We also found some additional uncertainty among two participants about what should or should not be included as time “lost” or that they “took off,” particularly when they do not have set schedules but rather do work that depends on client needs in a given period. Some clarification on what is meant by “did you lose or take off any hours from work, for ANY reason such as illness, vacation personal obligation, or because business was slow?” in HROFF1 for those who are self-employed could be considered. 3.4.4 Part-time Work Questions included HRFTPT, HRWANT, HRRSN1, HRRSN2, HRRSN3, and HRAVL.

Changes made for Round 2 Because of the findings from Round 1, we made some changes to IO1IND/IO2IND. Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 3 — Findings 3-59 Round 2 issues revealed as a response to the probes Twenty-eight participants reported working for pay or having a job during the reference period and were asked these questions. Overall, the changes made to the instrument helped participants feel more confident about the answers they provided and about the level of detail they were being asked for when they provided information about the business or industry. Participants were generally able to provide clear and concise answers to these questions. Some were very general responses like “media,” “retail,” “consulting/communications,” “healthcare,” and “manufacturing”. Others were more specific but still brief: “counseling practice,” “performing arts production,” “childcare/daycare,” “greeting card company,” “hair salon,” “elementary school,” and “law firm.” Yet others were somewhat less concise: “It's a sales textile industry, we basically produce and sell clothes,” “Real Estate Industry/Real Estate services buying and selling,” or “Mystery shopper, grocery shopping for customers of various retailers. Shopping and delivery.” Difficulty responding about business or industry (IO1ND and IO2IND) Again, as in Round 1, most participants found answering IO1IND and IO2IND easy. The addition of examples helped them figure out how long and detailed their answers should be in most cases, as illustrated here: “It wasn't that difficult, especially since they had examples, so that helped, just figure out what exactly they were looking for” (P905). Some participants explained how they reached their answers based on the examples. One who answered, “performing arts production,” explained, “…there's not really a full name for what I do when I am working so seeing the kind of language in the examples, I kind of mirrored it in terms of that this is just the area, the function, that I do” (P1012). Another participant followed the example to know not to include the company name. “Well, I noticed that they don’t use any proper names of businesses…so I decided not to put [business name] and just decided to put greeting card company because all of the examples were just generic categories…” (P1066). There were some exceptions. Two participants were still unsure how much detail to provide (P1018, P1235), and another who answered “retail” reflected in probing that they should have provided a longer answer because there was a large space for the response and because retail may encompass many different things (P971). Three other participants thought of ways in which the examples could have been more helpful. One person (P1267) who had answered “real estate sales” said that they hesitated about giving their title (broker) or the function (sales). They said, “When I was looking at the examples, I chose to say sales versus what the title was. If I look at this even closer, I probably should have just said real estate.” This person went on to explain that the question asks for business/industry, but the instructions say to include the “main activity” and that some examples are providing one or the other. Another participant (P1234) thought the examples were not expressed consistently: “I think to make the examples more parallel,

Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 3 — Findings 3-60 though, would be helpful. Right now, it’s giving a place, then a thing, then a place, then a duty…” Finally, another participant thought the examples should include more common businesses: “They were helpful but…I guess I would say…things more common would be more helpful, for example: …retail store…grocery store. Places that are more common... The examples listed you need special training or a special degree…” (P1124). Issues responding about occupation (IO1OCC and IO2OCC) The occupation questions worked well. All but two participants answered the question, providing an occupation in one to four or five words in line with the examples provided. The two exceptions were participants who restated the business or industry/activity in which they work rather than providing their own individual occupation. One answered “retail” and the other answered “sales.” Eliciting how they describe to others what they do was more consistent with how they answered their usual activities at work in IO1DT1/IO2DT2, although a few would instead give the activity in which they work. Issues responding about usual activities at job (IO1DT1 and IO2DT1) Participants found these questions easy to answer but were not always sure how much detail to provide. Some did not actually read the examples provided but most did and used them as models for the amount of detail to provide: “I think that they gave me the indication that I should just write a simple sentence” (P960) and “…I feel like it did a good job of modeling how you wanted the question to be answered” (P983). For others, it was more difficult to know how detailed to be. One (P1012) suggested asking for the top three activities or including a character limit to indicate how brief or detailed the response should be, whereas another would have liked to see a number of tasks required for the description (P1039). A genetic counselor (P1224) gave a long list of activities but indicated that it was hard to succinctly describe their job as in the examples. Finally, one participant thought that listing usual activities for more than one job, as the examples provided, may be confusing and that a better way to provide an example would be to list multiple activities for a single job (P1234). Conclusions and Recommendations 4.1 Round 1 Conducting cognitive interviews to pretest CPS questions allowed us to gather valuable insight into how well respondents comprehended CPS survey questions. As the CPS transitions to a self-administered internet mode, developing clear measures is paramount. Respondents will no longer have the presence of a field representative to serve as a resource when answering questions. Furthermore, field representatives will no longer be available to motivate respondents’ participation in the survey. The interview protocol reviewed several complex topics related to employment. Participants with unique employment situations were most likely to misreport or have difficulty answering the questions. These include participants with the following criteria: ▪ Are retired but are interested in small jobs occasionally, ▪ Own a business that performs work seasonally, or ▪ Conduct freelance work in addition to a full-time job. The CPS survey uses skip patterns to present participants with questions based on their answers to earlier questions. This allows the interview to be tailored to a given participant’s circumstances. However, this can create confusion when participants misreport gate questions early in the interview. We encountered this during the cognitive interviews with participants who misreported being self-employed, not working, or having multiple jobs. Questions later in the interview confused participants because they did not find them to be appropriate for their situation. We recommend embedding instructions into questions where appropriate. Although field representatives received training on which items allowed multiple responses, respondents will lack this context. Adding instructions such as “Select all that apply” or including response options such as “None of the above” will provide additional guidance on the response process. Several terms and concepts caused confusion for participants during Round 1 interviews (e.g., layoff, non-profit). During Round 2, we have an opportunity to add definitions or examples into these questions and test the performance of these additions. Round 2 interviews also afforded the opportunity to test revised questions and response options. We recommend revising questions to leverage the testing findings presented in this report. As necessary, we could test multiple versions of the same question (with the same participants) to determine how alternate wording affects comprehension and reporting. The Round 1 interview guide featured retrospective probes that the interviewer administered after the participants answered the survey questions on their own. This

Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 4 — Conclusions and Recommendations 4-2 approach limited the interviewer’s ability to discuss inconsistencies and misunderstandings as they occurred. Structuring an interview guide to include concurrent probes will allow for a more comprehensive account of challenges that participants encounter. Testing revised questions, response options, and instructions in Round 2 will allow the team to assess the performance of these revisions. 4.2 Round 2 Overall, the changes that we made to the instrument and the protocol for Round 2 eased some of the confusion participants had during Round 1 and resulted in most questions working well for participants. Furthermore, we did not see many new issues that we had not seen in Round 1. However, there are a few issues that participants had in Round 2 that could continue to be monitored in the field test. First, several of the changes that we made in Round 2 worked well for participants: ▪ In Round 1 during probing, some participants could not recall the key reference period that was used in the CPS Core instrument. For some participants, the reference period used in the CPS Core instrument referred to the prior month. Changing the reference period to be more recent and changing the wording of the cognitive interview probe resulted in fewer issues around the reference period in Round 2. ▪ In Round 1, in response to HRUSL1_1 (which asks, “How many hours per week do you USUALLY work at your <MAIN> job?”), one participant was confused about the instruction to “Consider the LAST 4 MONTHS.” Rather than providing an answer for the hours per week, this participant provided a total answer for the last 4 months. In Round 2, removing the instruction to “Consider the LAST 4 MONTHS” in this question worked well for participants and eased confusion that a participant had in Round 1. ▪ In Round 1, some participants could not tell the difference between the usual hours question (HRUSL1_1/HRUSL1_2) and the actual hours question (HRACT1/HRACT2). Adding a transition statement and removing the word “ACTUALLY” from the actual hours question (HRACT1/HRACT2) worked well for participants in Round 2 and eased confusion that participants had in Round 1. ▪ In Round 1, when asked about their business or industry (IO1IND/IO2IND) some participants were not sure how to categorize their work and others felt the question was unclear. In Round 2, adding examples to this question was helpful to participants, and they understood how detailed of an answer we were expecting. ▪ In Round 1, one self-employed participant was unsure if their business was incorporated (IO1INC/IO2INC). In Round 2, adding a “Not sure” response option to this question was helpful for two participants to express their uncertainty. However, both participants indicated that they would have felt more confident in answering “Yes” if the question had been clear that an LLC should be counted as an incorporated business. Next, we saw a few new issues in Round 2 that we had not seen in Round 1:

Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 4 — Conclusions and Recommendations 4-3 ▪ Two participants had difficulty answering WORK because of the phrase “or do ANY work for pay”; this caused one participant to answer incorrectly and led them down the wrong survey path. This participant seemed to interpret WORK as asking if they worked AND received pay, causing them to answer “No” to WORK and were led down the unemployed path in the survey, which was very confusing for them because the questions were not applicable to their employment status. BLS could consider rephrasing the question to only ask if respondents worked at a job or further separate out the concept of pay. ▪ One retired participant had difficulty with the phrase “line of work” in the response options for the question asking the main reason why they were not looking for work during the last 4 weeks (DWRSN); however, this was a minor issue. ▪ Some participants had difficulty answering the question about hours that they lost or took off from work (HROFF1/HROFF2), particularly when they did not have set schedules. BLS could consider rewording this question, particularly the wording of “because business was slow,” as this was difficult for self-employed participants to answer. Lastly, there are some remaining issues and confusion that participants experienced in Round 2: ▪ Participants still had some difficulty understanding what was considered a business when responding to BUS, specifically if this only included incorporated businesses. BLS could consider adding a definition of “business” to BUS or rephrasing the question. ▪ One participant incorrectly answered the question about the reason for being absent from work (ABSRSN1), possibly because of the long list of response options; however, this was a minor issue. ▪ Participants were unsure what “Professional register” refers to in LKM. BLS could consider providing a definition of “professional register.” ▪ Participants were also unsure how to incorporate looking for jobs on sites like Indeed, LinkedIn, or Craigslist into the available response options in LKM because they were looking for a response option to more clearly indicate looking “online.” BLS could consider either rewording the response option “Looked at job ads” to include looking for jobs online or adding another response option to more clearly indicate looking for work online. ▪ In response to the actual hours question (HRACT1/HRACT2), several participants reported excluding unpaid hours from their actual hours worked during the reference period. This included time commuting, evenings answering email or phone calls, and time they considered “non-billable.” ▪ BLS made a major change to the response options in MJ, which asks if the participant has one job or multiple jobs. Although these revisions did seem to reduce the number of participants who incorrectly answered “Yes” (that they have more than one job), there were several participants who were confused about the two “No” responses (indicating that they have one job). If BLS intends to ultimately combine the two “No” responses (as is used in the skip pattern), this may not be a major issue. However, if BLS intends to use the responses to MJ in data analysis, then the

Final Briefing Report — Rounds 1 and 2 Section 4 — Conclusions and Recommendations 4-4 results from Round 2 indicate that there may be some measurement error in the responses to this question. – BLS could consider removing the instruction “If you do similar work across multiple clients or apps, count as one <job/job or business>,” because this was confusing for participants in combination with the second response option. – BLS could consider adding instructions to include irregular or gig work because we found that not all participants included this while answering MJ. The Census Bureau and BLS could consider monitoring these new and remaining issues in the field test.

1 RESEARCH REPORT SERIES (Survey Methodology #2025-04) Targeting At-Risk Households to Understand and Reduce the Undercount of Young Children: A Research Agenda Joanne Pascale Center for Behavioral Science Methods Research and Methodology Directorate U.S. Census Bureau Washington, D.C. 20233 Report issued: April 2025 Disclaimer: This report is released to inform interested parties of research and to encourage discussion. The views expressed are those of the authors and not those of the U.S. Census Bureau. The U.S. Census Bureau reviewed this data product for unauthorized disclosure of confidential information and approved the disclosure avoidance practices applied to this release.

2 Abstract The goal of the decennial census is to count every person living in the United States. Inevitably, some individuals are omitted, while others are counted more than once. These two types of errors can, in some cases, cancel each other out and result in a net count that accurately reflects the population. If the number omitted is higher than the number of duplicates, the result is a net undercount. There is a well-established literature going back decades indicating that young children (under age five) and racial and ethnic minorities are systematically undercounted at higher rates than other groups. For example, in the 1940 Census males aged 21-35 were undercounted by about 3%, but Black males in that same age group were undercounted by about 13% (Price 1947). Indeed, the net undercount for the Black population overall has persistently tracked higher than for the non-Black population. In 1940 the undercount estimates were 8.4% and 5.0%, respectively – a gap of 3.4 percentage points – and in 2010 that gap was 3 percentage points (O’Hare et. al 2020). By age, the net undercount of young children has tracked higher than any other age group over the past several decades, and in 2020 hit a historic high of 5.4% (Jensen 2022). Over the decades, numerous causes and correlates have been identified as contributing to the undercount and attempts to implement operational changes that address those causes and correlates have met with varying success. One such contributing factor that persists is trust: some people are missing because they want to be missed. This paper outlines a research proposal designed to address the trust issue in a novel way (at least for the Census Bureau) by leveraging a community- based participatory research approach. The agenda includes an exploration of how to identify and recruit staff members from community-based organizations (CBOs) to participate as co- researchers along with census staff. The collective research team of CBO and Census staff would then conduct qualitative research exploring the reasons young children were omitted from the census form. The research agenda incorporates one more novel feature: using administrative records to identify a targeted sample of individuals in households where young children actually were omitted from a household roster. Research goals, detailed protocols, site selection and hypothetical schedules are offered in the spirit of a road map for a future project. Suggested Citation: Joanne Pascale. (2025). 3 I. INTRODUCTION There is a well-established literature indicating that young children (under age five) are systematically undercounted in censuses and surveys around the world, and the U.S. decennial census and American Community Survey (ACS) are no exceptions (O’Hare, 2015). Furthermore, analysis of the 2020 Census shows that certain groups were undercounted at higher rates than other groups, including the Black or African American population, the American Indian or Alaska Native population living on a reservation, and the Hispanic or Latino population (U.S. Census Bureau, 2022). This project aims to reduce the differential undercount of young children and other groups through engagement with community-based organizations (CBOs) in research on collecting household rosters. While urban historians have documented a differential undercount going back as far as the 1840s (Sharpless and Shortridge, 1975), the modern era of survey statistics only came into its own in the 1930s and a systematic differential undercount was observed soon thereafter in the 1940 Census. Since then, the Census Bureau has been examining the magnitude and characteristics of undercounted groups, the causes of the undercount, and conducting research to attempt to reduce it. Through the 1950s and 1960s research focused on the extent and nature of the undercount, exploring alternative data sources as a means of estimating the undercount, and scrutinizing internal processes and procedures to identify correlates and patterns of the undercount of what is currently called historically undercounted populations (HUPs). In the early 1970s the Census Bureau turned to ethnography, which produced a seminal study by Valentine and Valentine of a Black inner-city neighborhood. The two ethnographers selected 25 housing units in a single inner-city block and conducted their own enumeration of residents of those households. Then, in a blind comparison, they matched their own household rosters case by case to the rosters collected via a traditional “interviewer-survey research” method. They calculated an overall census undercount of 17% and the undercount of Black males over age 20 was 61%. In terms of causes, one finding that has since been corroborated in numerous other studies was related to material poverty. The vast majority of study participants were recipients of public benefits, which led respondents to deliberately omit certain household members for fear of losing their benefits. The study went further to contextualize the findings from that particular site and population, and noted the unique contributions of the ethnographic method. One of their conclusions was that “No basic national survey, such as a census, should be planned without conjoining ethnographic research on at least one urban and one rural community of Afro-Americans, of Hispano-Americans, of Native Americans, and of poor Whites in two or more geographic regions for each group….it should be possible to express many social statistics in terms of survey results accompanied by adjustments, extrapolated from ethnographic samples for many ethnic, socio­economic, and regional segments of the national population.” Indeed, in the late 1980s the Census Bureau began sponsoring more ethnographic research along these lines, and during the 1990 census a series of ethnographic studies in 29 sites focusing on HUPs throughout the country was conducted. High-level findings were that the HUP undercount did not have a single cause, and three main themes were identified. One was housing unit coverage error; that is, housing units were missing from the Master Address File because there were no externally visible indicators of housing units available to the canvassers and listers on the ground (e.g. converted basements; subdivided rowhouses; rural roads with difficult access or vague markers). A second major theme was within household undercoverage, and within that theme were two main patterns of living arrangement contributing to the undercount. First were individuals who

4 cycled among one or more residences or places, and no one residence was their “usual home.” These individuals (and sometimes families) were at risk of not being listed by the household respondent as “living or staying” there since they came and went. Second were those who were in transition and neither they, nor their host, would consider them to really “live” there; they were just staying “temporarily” but, in fact, would not be enumerated at any other location at that moment in time. A third theme that cut across both housing unit and within household undercoverage was trust. This included general distrust in government and Census Bureau motives, disbelief in promises of confidentiality, concerns about misuse of data, and fears over deportation and/or losing public benefits (e.g., when the number of household residents violated terms of lease and/or housing vouchers). These findings may have contributed to the initiation of the Partnership Program in the 1990s in which the Census Bureau works with tribal, federal, state, and local governments as well as commercial partners at the local, regional and national level to encourage participation. Over the decades the Partnership Program has grown in size and scope, and in more recent decades it has been enhanced with an integrated paid advertising campaign. In spite of all the Census Bureau’s efforts over the decades to measure, understand and reduce the undercount, the problem persists and for some groups it reached a historic high in the 2020 Census. This grim fact, and the very brief history above, bring us full circle back to the Valentine work. In their closing remarks titled “A Proposed Solution” they suggest that “Optimum completeness of information can be achieved only through intensive, long-term resident participation in the life of the community by independent researchers. This ethnographic approach is the only means by which researchers can come to be regarded as trustworthy, for it is the only way to give people convincing experience that they will not be compromised or injured by revealing themselves…” (Valentine and Valentine, 1971, page 36; for a complete account see Appendix A). Subsequent ethnographic research conducted in the 1980s and 1990s corroborated the Valentines’ findings on trust being a crucial aspect of census participation. Indeed, more than 50 years later, these same issues of trust and concerns about how the data will be used are still observed. For example, in interviews with Census Bureau Partnership staff conducted in 2020, they reported that respondents expressed fear that census data could be used against them (e.g., threats to their immigration, tax, housing or green card status). That same research project also involved interviews with staff from population-serving organizations, and they reported that distrust of government was a barrier to participation among some of their constituents (Terry et al, 2023). In 2023, focus groups with a general population sample were conducted to explore public opinion about a new database that would combine administrative record data from multiple government agencies, with data from both public and private surveys to produce statistics. Researchers found “The issues most commonly raised…involved wanting more details about the reason or purpose for the database, specifically how the data were going to be used.” (Blackburn et al, 2023). In addition to addressing the issue of trust, the Valentines stated that an ethnographic approach “…also maximizes opportunities for direct observation of actual behavior…a great deal of such direct knowledge may be accumulated through experience by persons who are known to live under the same conditions as those whom they study…This could also be a means to increase opportunities for members of minority groups to become social scientists and contribute to the understanding of their own and other communities.” They went on to suggest that the Census Bureau’s “devices” (such as public relations campaigns and hiring a temporary workforce of enumerators from the local community), are all “ineffective because they do not deal with the basic

5 problem of the relationship between those who are seeking the information and those asked to provide it.” (Valentine and Valentine, 1971, page 36). More than 50 years later, in January 2025 the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) issued a report on social and behavioral science and specifically called out the value of what is now called “community-based participatory research” (CBPR), stating that it: “…has a distinct focus on creating collaborations between scientific organizations, government agencies, the private sector, and the communities they serve. CPBR also focuses on combining knowledge with action to bring about positive outcomes – especially among populations that have been and continue to be under-resourced and underserved. CBPR…involves all partners in the research process and recognizes the unique strengths that each brings to the table…Research indicates that CBPR, although more time- consuming, results in more effective and sustainable outcomes. Agencies should equip their personnel with skills to effectively engage with individuals, groups, and organizations impacted by the problems the agency is tasked with solving. Scientists in all disciplines need to be aware of best practices in recognizing and responding to the lived experiences of the populations they are studying…True partnerships ensure community input and ownership and lead to more effective evaluation and policy impacts.” (President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, 2025, page 26). In this spirit, what follows is a research proposal for a novel approach for building trust within the community and leveraging local knowledge: hire staff not just from the community as temporary enumerators, but hire staff from community-based organizations (CBO) to conduct Census Bureau pretesting field work on an ongoing basis, throughout the decade. The potential benefits are many, including: 1. Builds trust by inviting individuals who have a relatively stable, consistent presence in the community into the process of the production of data at the “ground floor.” This could help demystify the data collection and analysis process, and help community members gain a more grounded understanding of uses of the data, and spread the word to their constituents about the benefits of census participation; 2. Provides the opportunity to gain unique insights on pretesting protocols, data collection and analysis by tapping the experiences of “persons who are known to live under the same conditions as those whom they study” as noted by the Valentines; 3. Provides CBO staff the opportunity to contribute to the narrative of research findings; 4. Builds data literacy and capacity to enable community members to pursue their own priorities (e.g. via data analysis and grant applications for local programs and initiatives); 5. Provides CBO staff with transferable, marketable skills for their own career advancement; 6. Provides CBO staff with a paid wage, rather than burdening them with volunteer work on behalf of the Census Bureau; and 7. Maintains contact at community-level throughout the decade. 8. To the extent the above benefits are manifest, such an approach establishes the potential to even the playing field across states in terms of get-out-the-count efforts by giving all communities the opportunity to have semi-permanent staff participating in Census research activities.

6 The proposal involves recruiting CBO staff to become co-researchers in field work designed to examine the role of the questionnaire and other data collection materials in the undercount as specified in the 2030 Research Design Proposal: “Improving the Coverage of Young Children in the 2030 Census: Research on Why Young Children are Missed” (Project 108/Subproject #10). Specifically, the aim is to identify and recruit research participants at-risk of being undercounted and to use focus groups and cognitive interviewing methods to explore any features of the data collection materials (e.g. question wording, layout) and/or census processes (e.g., mode availability; non-English language access) that are contributing to the omission of individuals who should be listed on the form. The aim is also to assess effective messaging that could be used in a communications campaign. Outlined below is the basic research plan. I begin with a summary of research that was intended to inform the 2020 Census but was stalled due to the pandemic, and lessons learned from the pre- pandemic work. I then discuss plans for adapting the original 2020 research for the 2030 census, incorporating the CBO approach, which would consist of three phases. Phase 1 would be dedicated to the development of a method for community-based engagement, leveraging all in-house expertise and knowledge we have and blending that with other entities with CBO experience (university-based; foundation-funded; state and local agencies, etc.). Phase 2 would be a limited scope study in the DC metro area involving 5 focus groups and 24 cognitive interviews. Pending proof of concept during Phase 2 (meaning that the basic approach is implementable and yields useful findings), in Phase 3 the basic approach would be refined as needed and scaled up to other sites throughout the country in subsequent years. Section II summarizes the research intended for the 2020 Census, and lessons learned regarding the identification of sample “at risk” for being undercounted. Section III describes in more detail the rationale and approach of the focus groups and cognitive interviews and an innovative sample method for identifying research participants. Sections IV-VI describe the three phases of actual research noted above, and Section VII provides a high-level timeline and milestones. II. CENSUS 2020 RESEARCH A. The 2019 Pilot In 2019, staff from the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) conducted a pilot study exploring the long-standing issue of the undercount of young children (UYC) in the decennial census and ongoing surveys. The goal was two-fold: first to identify households at risk of omitting young children from the household roster; and second to conduct field work with individuals in those households using qualitative methods to explore features of the data collection operation that contributed to the erroneous omissions, such as question wording, instructions and layout. The pandemic put the field work on indefinite hold, but the pilot experience proved useful for assessing the viability of using conventional methods of recruiting and screening for identifying households at risk of omitting young children. Typically, these conventional methods include a mix of paid advertisements, social media posts, flyers and word of mouth. The ads/posts/flyers usually describe some basic characteristics of participants being sought (e.g., adults 18-35, high school students, Medicaid enrollees) and indicate a dollar amount of a paid incentive provided

7 after participation. Potential recruits are encouraged to be screened for eligibility for the study, either by calling a recruiter or filling out a screener questionnaire. The pilot used these conventional methods, enhanced by additional community outreach. Guided by the literature to date, we developed a screener that asked about key characteristics of households at-risk of an undercount, and then used multiple methods of outreach to encourage individuals to call in for eligibility screening. These methods included: • Subject Matter Experts and Advocacy Organizations: given their long-standing relationship with the Census Bureau, we solicited input from several stakeholders who work for child advocacy organizations. The “ask” was for the stakeholders to reach out to individuals who worked directly with at-risk individuals and families. We developed a 2-page description of the study for agency staff, and a 1-page flyer intended to be posted and distributed to potential study participants. • Multi-Generational Housing Communities: we made contact with two housing complexes in DC that explicitly serve low-income families where grandparents live with grandchildren (often with no parent present); we requested that staff post flyers advertising the study. • Community Outreach: We used direct outreach in the local community surrounding the Census Bureau headquarters in Suitland, MD. Over the course of two weeks, CBSM staff made contacts and distributed flyers on three different occasions at community centers, libraries, day care facilities, recreation centers, churches, laundromats, hair and nail salons. Wherever possible, we spoke with staff at these facilities. In total, we posted flyers at 24 facilities or businesses and spoke with staff at about half of them. • Craigslist: We posted an ad on Craigslist under all eight categories of “temporary gigs” that described the study and the types of households we were seeking. • Census Staff in the Local Community: We sent a broadcast message to the entire Census Bureau staff at headquarters asking for volunteers to promote the study within their local communities (e.g., at PTA meetings, church gatherings, sporting events). • Census Partnership Specialists: We reached out to three Partnership Specialists (covering DC, Northern Virginia and the nearby Maryland suburbs), provided them with flyers about the study and asked them to distribute at local events. Results were disappointing. Given the level and breadth of effort (roughly 6 months of a wide range of outreach activities), we did recruit the goal of 9 subjects for a small pilot study, but the yield was simply inefficient for main stage data collection. Furthermore, though many of the living situations of our nine participants were complicated, none failed to list young children on the roster. Details of the pilot study can be found here: https://www.census.gov/library/working- papers/2022/adrm/rsm2022-01.html One take-away from the 2019 pilot exercise is that relying simply on the correlates or profile of at-risk households is insufficient to yield a sample that will provide useful results from qualitative work; MANY households fit the at-risk profile but do NOT under-report children. Overall, the net undercount of young children in 2020 was about 5% and the omission rate was about 10%. While this is of great concern, it means that about 90% of respondents DO appear to report young children on the form. The target sample is also elusive. Screening mechanisms that ask respondents if they live with young children are likely to elicit the types of people who WOULD report those young children on forms. In other words, the target population is both rare AND elusive and we seem to be looking for a needle in a haystack.

8 B. Administrative Records Linked to Self-Reported Household Rosters Given the challenges of using conventional recruiting methods demonstrated in the pilot, I turned to an alternative approach for identifying and recruiting at-risk sample. At earlier meetings of the Decennial Research Objectives and Methods (DROM), Census Bureau Chief Scientist John Abowd suggested I pursue a method that was more likely to produce a “sure thing.” Specifically, he suggested using an amalgamation of administrative records (adrecs) matched to self-reported household rosters. Households where one or more child was found in the adrecs but not listed in the roster would be deemed at-risk (that is, a “needle” from the haystack). Due to the timing of this work (2019) I was unable to exploit the expertise of decennial staff who were conducting similar adrec-roster matching work for the 2020 decennial census. The next best option was to use a slightly more limited set of adrecs from the Production Environment for Administrative Records Staging Integration and Storage (PEARSIS) system, matched to the most recent vintage of the American Community Survey (ACS), which was 2018. I conducted this exercise and limited the sample selection to households in the DC metro area, given the goal of conducting local qualitative field work in the next stage of the study. The adrec matching exercise began in the fall of 2019 and continued into early 2020, at which point the project came to a stand still on account of the pandemic. In the spring of 2023, I revived the analysis of the PEARSIS-ACS matched file as an exercise to assess the general viability of the approach, the yield and characteristics of the at-risk sample. Results were presented in the summer of 2023 at the European Survey Research Association conference and are summarized here. In the final matched file, we identified about 650 households in the DC Metro which contained about 4,000 person records. Among those 4,000 people, about 58% were found in the adrecs but not listed in the ACS. Among those 58% of individuals, the age distribution was as follows: • Under 5 years old: 31% • 5-9 years old: 13% • 10-17 years old: 7% • 18 years and older: 49% With regard to type of household, we developed three categories of interest based on the limited data available in the matched file and on the prior literature. These household types, and the distribution, was: • SubFamily: at least one child under 18 and at least one adult 18+ missing: 65% • KidsOnly: Only kid(s) under 18 missing from ACS (no adults missing): 24% • SkipGen: Only kid(s) under 18 missing and adult(s) in household seem to be grandparents (skipping the parent generation): 4% The exercise demonstrated proof of concept for the general approach, as these distributions are in line with expectations based on prior literature.

9 III. RESEARCH FOR 2030 CENSUS As noted above, much has been learned over the decades about the causes and correlates of the undercount, but questions remain about how to implement changes to procedures that effectively reduce that undercount. The conundrum with some of the research to date is the “diluted” sample. Without a method to target the rare and elusive respondent who actually under-reports a young child on the census form, the findings are of limited use. In other words, conducting research with a general sample – even a sample of households where young children reside – is unlikely to produce actionable findings because most respondents DO report young children. Given the novel approach described above which leverages adrecs to produce a targeted sample of respondents in households where young children actually were omitted from the census forms holds promise for qualitative research to discover the reasons respondents omit those children. Below is a detailed description of the methodology and protocols for such qualitative research. A. Focus Groups Focus groups would be composed of individuals from various types of households that were identified through the adrec matching method, but using more current and comprehensive data. Topics and techniques to be explored and employed include: • Past experience with the decennial census o Awareness: any recollections about how participants learned the decennial census was coming; thoughts/reflections on general sentiments about census participation o Participation: household-level discussions/negotiations over who would complete the census for the household o Self-completions (where applicable): Any recollections about their living situation at the time, mode of completion; who they listed and why; questions/confusion/issues at the time, etc.; whether they had help with understanding and/or responding to any of the questions (if so which questions, who helped, etc.) • Activity: each participant to complete a mock decennial census form as if it was Census Day; group discussion who they listed and why; questions/confusion/issues that came up, etc. • Vignettes: provide hypothetical scenarios of the types of housing arrangements and living situations that often result in undercounted young children and probe respondents for who they would list and why. • Young children focus: o Do participants express any confusion or doubt about whether babies and young children should be counted? If so why (e.g., do they think children need to be of age for certain activities, such as going to school, working, voting, and having a driver’s license)? Probe on research findings indicating that the younger the child, the more likely the undercount (e.g., infants are more likely to be missing than 1-year-olds, who are more likely to be missing than 2-year-olds). o Are there issues of privacy/sensitivity, particularly with regard to listing babies or young children of other people (such as distant relatives, renters, neighbors). That is, do participants feel children are more vulnerable and need to be “protected” in some way? o Are there issues of deliberate omissions of subfamilies with young children, due to fear of consequences (e.g., loss of lease if the number of residents exceeds the lease; loss of benefits based on household composition and income; immigration officials if individuals are undocumented).

10 o Given the empirical finding that the youngest of the young are most likely to be undercounted, and the relationship is linear (i.e.: newborns are most likely to be missed, then 1-year-olds, then 2-year-olds, etc.), there could be respondent fatigue at work. That is, in particularly large households, respondents may report their own nuclear family first, and then a subfamily, starting with the adult, then their oldest child, then the next oldest, etc. In households with multiple and/or particularly large sub-families, perhaps the younger children simply do not get listed out of sheer respondent fatigue. To explore this, participants could be asked in what sequence they would report household members and subfamilies, and whether age is a factor. Alternative wording could also be explored, e.g., asking respondents to start with the youngest child, and the next-youngest, etc. • Discussion of alternative wording: o Based on consultation with other Census staff who are actively conducting research on rostering methods for both decennial and ACS we expect to develop a “state of the art best practices” version of the rostering questions to get participants’ reactions. o Given the “cyclers” and “transitioners” (discussed more above and below), explore participants’ reactions to a departure from traditional enumeration. One approach is to ask the household respondent to list all household members, and then ask if there are any “tenuously attached” members. If so, the household respondent would be asked to convey to the tenuously attached individual/family the opportunity to fill out their own form (e.g., pass a census form and/or household ID with some kind of suffix and/or url with a link to the non-ID census path). • Messaging: if time allows, we will discuss how participants get their news, information and updates about what is going on the community and in the country, and their reactions to various messages about the purpose and importance of the decennial census, and other topics. • Mode: What modes are available to respondents (e.g., in households with no or limited internet access, web may not actually be an option to choose from). Which mode do they consider their “default”? If they do have multiple modes available, how do they choose which mode to use? What are the barriers to accessing their preferred mode? B. Cognitive Testing Cognitive interviews would be conducted with individuals in at-risk households, ideally with two respondents in each household (e.g., from two different generation within the household). The objective is to assess whether the household roster produced by each of the two household members is the same, and if not, why not. The overarching goal is to identify any disconnect between the “true” list of household members, and the individuals that respondents listed on the form. If there are disconnects, the objective is to identify specific features of the stimuli (question wording, instructions, layout, etc.) of the census form that are contributing to the disconnect, and examine modifications to reduce underreporting. In terms of the baseline questionnaire/instructions/layout to use as stimuli in the testing, the aim is to learn all we can from other studies to date (e.g., the ACS roster research) and consult with decennial and ACS staff regarding what stimuli to use in the testing and what modes, given what is known at the time of the specific instrumentation being developed for the 2030 Census. Once the stimuli are determined, the high-level protocol for cognitive testing would be developed based on results from the focus groups, and include probes on: • the individuals listed, and the rationale for including and excluding them

11 • underlying reasons or causes for omissions – specifically probing on: o privacy/sensitivity around reporting of young children, particularly if the respondent is proxy-reporting for a non-relative staying temporarily, or a neighbor o deliberate omissions tied to concerns or fears (e.g., losing benefits, child protective services, abusive family members, custody disputes) o confusion about whether young children “count” and should be listed o burden and respondent fatigue; do respondents essentially run out of steam after listing numerous household members • the relationships between the respondent and those listed, and relationships between those listed to each other • the “pop count” question and any disconnect between that number and the number of individuals listed on the roster • the “undercount questions” (asking if anyone was missed) • the “overcount questions” (asking if all those listed have a “usual residence elsewhere”) In addition to those general plans for probes, probes would be developed that target two broad categories of people who are at risk of undercounting: • Cyclers: those who cycle among more than one residence or place. This goes beyond children in shared custody (who go back and forth between divorced parents’ residences) and college students (who go back and forth between their student housing and parents’ residences). In those instances, the children may actually be more likely to be overcounted than undercounted. There are, however, other types of cyclers more likely to be undercounted. For example: o New immigrants who have resettled in a large housing complex may “float” among individual units of fellow new immigrants within the larger complex. o In many communities with a deep-rooted culture of extended family and “fictive kin” networks, individuals cycle among multiple residences (e.g., a few days at a girlfriend/boyfriend’s house; a few days at a parent’s house; a few days at a friend’s place). o Some individuals may stay most of the time at one or two specific residences (e.g., a friend’s place, and/or a family member’s house) but they may also spend some nights in their car, a shelter, a treatment facility and the street – sometimes just for a night or two and sometimes for longer stretches. o Apart from joint custody issues, children may cycle between multiple households of working parents and caregivers in order to cover child care. • Transitioners: those who are “temporarily” staying with family or friends but have no defined timeline or plan for where they will go next or when. In many cases these would be considered complex households because the “transitioners” (and/or the people they are attached to) would not all be related. For example: o An adult child with a new baby whose relationship with the other parent is on/off so they are staying with a parent or friend for the time being o A new immigrant who is staying with family friends from the same village in their country of origin until they get oriented to life in the U.S. o A young single person (usually male) staying with family or friends for employment opportunities until he can get established enough to send for his wife and family who are living in another state (or another country)

12 C. Sample The PEARSIS-ACS exercise yielded very promising results, and the next step is to replicate the approach on more recent data and conduct field work. Two discreet goals are: (1) to validate that the adrec-roster match method does, based on ground-truthing, identify households where individuals have been erroneously omitted from the roster and (2) learn from qualitative field work why those individuals were left off the roster and assess the potential for feeding into data collection operations with the aim of reducing the undercount. The adrec-ACS matching process described above is currently being replicated with more recent, comprehensive data (Chapman and Pascale, 2025). On the ACS side, key ACS staff were consulted to request permission to use the ACS data in this way, and to ensure all policies and procedures were followed. Staff granted permission, pending the outcome of certain follow up steps, specifically: • Avoid sampling cases from the ACS that have already been sampled for the National Survey of College Graduates (NSCG), the National Training, Education and Workforce Survey (NTEWS) or for reinterview. ACS staff gave instructions to proceed with sample plans and later consult with them on the best way to cross-check our MAFIDs with those cases selected for other studies. If any cases do overlap, they are to be deleted them from the caseload. • The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in conjunction with the Census Bureau established the Interagency Council on Statistical Policy Subcommittee on the ACS (ICSP- SACS) to advise the Chief Statistician on policies and practices for the ACS from the perspective of the federal statistical system. As of mid-August 2024, ACS staff was planning to reach out to the ICSP to determine what, if any, procedures need to be followed to request approval the use of ACS data for this project. They foresaw no barriers and regarded this is mostly a formality. • Conduct due diligence on how to approach ACS respondents sampled for follow up surveys. Consultations with key staff from the NSCG and NTEWS were conducted to discuss how to approach respondents with regard to the sample method and its relationship to the ACS. Staff explained that those surveys do not mention ACS at all in any of their recruitment or survey introductory materials; they approach the interview as in a cold call. Unless advised otherwise, the plan for this research would be to follow the precedent used in these other surveys. In terms of geography, for data collection in the DC metro area, the sample selection would be limited to cases from the adrec-ACS matching to addresses located within driving distance of the DC metro area, specifically: • District of Columbia • Montgomery County, MD • Prince George’s County, MD • Fairfax County, VA Finally, it should not be ruled out that that CBO staff could also help identify and recruit “at risk” households to capture those individuals who do not appear in adrecs at all.

13 IV. PHASE 1: IDENTIFYING AND APPROACHING COMMUNITY-BASED ORGANIZATIONS The first step is to develop a general approach/strategy/method for identifying and recruiting CBOs to partner with, and to identify a list of specific CBOs in the DC Metro area to approach for pretesting. Specific activities include: A. Brainstorm with the offices/teams/individuals below. B. Produce a list of CBOs to recruit for focus groups to discuss the general research plan. C. Organize a series of focus groups with CBO staff and meetings with experts, advocates and stakeholders; integrate feedback from each meeting and focus group and conduct more in an iterative fashion. D. Products coming out of the focus groups include: 1. A general approach/strategy/method for identifying and recruiting CBOs (at the agency-level) to partner with on pretesting research on the undercount. 2. A set of recruiting materials (e.g., a slide deck) for Census staff to present at CBO offices that would explain the pretesting research opportunity. 3. A list of ~10 specific CBOs in the DC Metro region to approach to participate in the pretest research project. In addition to this discrete goal of Phase 1, the goal would be to explore how to partner with CBOs more generally. While some HUPs (e.g., young children) have established teams within the Census Bureau focused on issues particular to that group, other vulnerable groups (particularly low literacy and disabled) have a less-established team to examine and address barriers to their inclusion in the census. Advocates and experts familiar with these vulnerable groups are included here as a start toward filling that gap. Thus, a secondary objective of Phase 1 is to augment the CBO focus groups with informal meetings, brainstorming sessions and/or focus groups with advocates, experts and stakeholders who are knowledgeable about these vulnerable groups to help inform efforts on data collection and messaging to avoid undercounting these groups in ongoing operations census and survey operations. STEP 1: ASSEMBLE PARTICIPANTS 1. Census Bureau Outreach Staff Many staff are already connected in some way with the Census Bureau community outreach infrastructure and have a wealth of expertise and knowledge.
