15 F. Census 2030 “Project 110” leadership: this team is working on ways to identify and recruit partners using methods such as relational organizing to identify high-value stakeholders. The team has produced a draft list of “must have” partners, by state, county and city, which can be used as a starting point. G. Office of the Director of the U.S. Census: the previous director conducted a series of “listening sessions” among under-represented communities around the country from 2022- 2024. Lessons learned from these sessions should be gathered and there may be opportunities to follow up with same communities and contacts. H. State-level Complete Count Committees: these are state-level groups (i.e., not officially part of the Census Bureau) that work to “get out the count.” Given heterogeneity across states (in terms of challenges, tactics, outcomes and budget) the experiences of staff from these teams could inform the research approach. California and New York were particularly active and well-funded in 2020, and experiences from less-well-funded states should also be included to provide a well-rounded picture and insights from the ground-level. 2. Community-Based Participatory Research Practitioners and Experts The growing field of community-based participatory research could be tapped to learn from academics as well as practitioners in the field who are taking a deliberate steps to fully engage with CBOs and other groups that directly serve vulnerable populations. A. Harvard Catalyst Community Engagement Program: In the fall of 2022, CBSM staff made contact with researchers from the program, which has established a coalition for integrating a CBPR approach in research. CBSM staff gave a talk to the coalition in October 2022 on the undercount, and later co-presented on the undercount with a researcher and a coalition member on a panel at AAPOR in the spring of 2023. https://catalyst.harvard.edu/community- engagement/community-coalition/ B. West Virginia University Health Affairs Institute MATCH team and Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond: At AAPOR 2023, staff from the team of the “MATCH” study (“Mountain State Health Assessment of Trends in Community Health”) presented on the project which they described as a kind of “mini-ACS” at the state level. Excerpts from the abstract explain: “Substate, population-level mental and behavioral health data in West Virginia (WV) are scarce due to WV’s difficult-to-reach population, characterized by rurality, low internet coverage and subscriptions, and cultural nuances. This data gap limits healthcare practitioners, researchers, policymakers, and the general public from understanding and addressing health concerns across WV. In response, an inter-bureau collaboration…was formed to conduct the…MATCH survey…to better understand the health of West Virginians and match community health needs with resources specifically designed to meet those needs.” https://wvmatchsurvey.org/ The presentation sparked a very engaged floor discussion, particularly around the concentrated efforts the MATCH team has undertaken regarding community-based engagement. The discussion spawned an impromptu meeting at the conference between MATCH and Census staff. Follow up discussions included staff from the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, given their work in community engagement in the West Virginia region. Their role is to strengthen the economies of the region’s communities through research, surveys and data analysis. They also engage regularly with business leaders, community leaders and policymakers to understand and address economic challenges and identify opportunities in low- and moderate- income and underserved communities. Based on the nature of the West Virginia population, which encompasses many of the characteristics of historically undercounted populations (HUPs), the depth and breadth of the MATCH study, the focus on community engagement,

16 and the proximity of West Virginia to Census Bureau headquarters, staff are continuing discussions about collaborative research on the undercount and HUPs. 3. Advocates, Experts and Stakeholders Working with Vulnerable Populations These individuals will be identified on a rolling basis, and each meeting/conversation it is expected to generate recommendations for more individuals to consult with and/or more issues or groups to consider. Efforts on this exploratory phase will continue until saturation is reached, or time and budget run out. STEP 2: DEVELOP A METHOD TO IDENTIFY CBOs There is no pre-determined “eligibility criteria” for CBOs to participate. However, because one of the goals is to establish ongoing relationships with CBOs that have a relatively permanent, stable presence in the community, CBOs with a longer track record may be more desirable than those that are less established. Another consideration is input from an external stakeholder (Ed Kissam) with experience on the California Complete Count effort, who suggests: • “Restrict the CBOs to those that provide direct high-demand services, ideally with counseling and/or home visits (e.g. food distribution programs, community health clinics, legal service providers, after school programs, Headstart). Lots of CBOs do not have direct contact with the most persistently undercounted populations.” • “The national organizations have almost zero on-the-ground presence. They may be good intermediaries, but they really know very little about persistently undercounted populations. We learned a lot about the ‘distance’ between the CBOs that are linked in to state and national networks and the local ones that are actually linked into the community itself. I can’t over-emphasize the need for screening alleged CBOs for actual in-field knowledge and cultural competency and strength of their social/constituent/client networks.” This latter point is consistent with findings from the pilot (see Section II.A above). STEP 3: DEVELOP AN APPROACH TO SOLICIT CBO INTEREST AND RECRUIT STAFF AS CO-RESEARCHERS Working with the staff noted above under “Assemble Participants,” the goal would be to develop an approach/strategy/method for identifying CBO candidates in the DC Metro region to approach as research partners (note this aim, on a very small scale, overlaps with some of the goals of Project 110). Once a small set of CBOs is identified, initiate contact (ideally via one of our established partner organizations or contacts). The content of the initial contact would include: • Brief summary of the undercount issue and consequences for local and state programs • The research project for the DC Metro area • The invitation to participate in a focus group to discuss the undercount issue, the research approach, and the ultimate “ask,” which is to allow Census staff to make a presentation to CBO staff to solicit their interest in a “side gig” as a co-researcher on the Census Bureau pretesting team. The focus group protocol itself would cover three main themes. First would be the topic of how to identify and recruit CBOs who work with HUP communities. In other words, for a project like this

17 it is necessary to “start somewhere,” and the above resources on Census Bureau outreach infrastructure is a starting point for identifying some CBOs to start the conversation. Once a small number of CBOs staff are at the table, the idea would be to have an open discussion about the entire “universe” of CBOs who should be considered for participation in the research project – keeping in mind transparency and representation. One concept to solicit feedback on is the notion of a lottery system. The second main theme of the focus groups would be getting CBO input on the approach for soliciting their staff to participate in the research. The default starting point is to discuss the feasibility of Census Bureau staff visiting CBOs on-site to present to the staff a ~ 30 minute slide show followed by Q&A to solicit their interest in participating in the research project. The contents would include: • Census mission • The role of Census data in public funding and Congressional representation • The undercount problem and how it affects distribution of funding and political representation • The DC metro area research project, goals and tasks • Basic overview of pretesting, focus groups and cognitive testing tasks • Overview of project-specific materials (e.g., baseline focus group and cognitive interviewing protocols) • Logistics, wages, hours, etc. • Security clearance procedures The third theme is to assess interest on the part of participating CBOs in the research project and to gather their suggested candidate CBOs. In other words, to gather feedback and perspectives on both a process for identify and recruiting CBO participation, and also their interest in actually participating themselves. The final goal is to develop a list of at least 10 specific CBOs who could commit to a later presentation by Census Bureau staff to solicit CBO staff interest in being part of the research team for the DC metro area project. The basic strategy is to begin with one focus group and iterate the method for selecting the next set of participants and the materials, and to repeat as necessary until “saturation” is hit or until time and budget run out. “Saturation” is loosely defined as the point at which little or no substantive findings are emerging from additional focus groups. The final deliverables from Phase 1 would be: a. A general approach/strategy/method for identifying and recruiting CBOs (at the agency-level) to partner with on pretesting research on the undercount. b. A list of ~10 specific CBOs in the DC Metro region to approach to participate in the pretest research project. The goal would be to identify two CBOs who each designate two CBO staff (for a total of 4 CBO staff) to conduct the research. c. A set of recruiting materials (likely a slide deck) for Census staff to present at CBO offices that would explain the pretesting research opportunity. d. A final report for the Census Bureau’s Decennial Research Objectives and Methods group (DROM). See Appendix B for a sample OMB package and focus group protocol.

18 V. PHASE 2: SMALL SCALE DATA COLLECTION IN DC METRO AREA The plan would be to conduct data collection in the DC metro area (perhaps extending to West Virginia), given the proximity to Census staff and the goal of minimizing travel and lodging costs. The 2018 PEARSIS-ACS exercise was limited to DC and adjacent counties in Maryland and Virginia and yielded about 650 households. Thus, there is reason to believe that the replicated exercise will yield sufficient sample for the planned field work, which will consist of focus groups and cognitive interviews. A. Training of CBO Staff CBO staff would participate in focus groups as observers, and they would also provide logistical support and take notes. The experience is intended to orient CBO staff to the issues and themes regarding the differential undercount, and to essentially provide background training for the cognitive interviewing task. Census staff (perhaps in conjunction with a contractor) would also provide a one-day generic training in cognitive interview methods for CBO staff. They would become part of the paid research team and participate in development, review and finalization of the research protocols and reports. B. Focus Group and Cognitive Interviewing Protocols Pre-pandemic protocols would be used as a starting point (see appendices here): https://www.census.gov/library/working-papers/2022/adrm/rsm2022-01.html Census would update these protocols taking into consideration all the background materials noted above, stakeholder input and discussions with decennial and ACS (focusing on staff with experience on rostering and coverage issues) and taking into consideration the latest research findings from the ACS roster cognitive testing. Once the protocols are updated to reflect all the research to date and stakeholder input, we would consult with CBO staff and iterate as needed until all are in agreement that the protocols reflect our best starting point. C. Recruit and screen for focus groups and cognitive interview participants Starting with the list of households generated from the ACS-adrec match, and perhaps augmented with sample generated from CBO suggestions and initiatives, we would recruit and schedule participants for research (focus groups first, then cognitive interviews). D. Conduct data collection For the focus groups, Census staff (perhaps in conjunction with a contractor) would take the lead, with CBO staff facilitating (e.g., organizing logistics, taking notes). For cognitive interviews, Census staff would conduct the first “batch” of interviews. Census and CBO staff would meet to listen to the recordings after the fact to assess the protocols and adjust as needed, and to further train CBO staff. When all parties feel CBO staff are adequately trained, they would begin to conduct their own interviews, with Census staff listening to recordings and providing feedback and additional training as needed.

19 E. Summaries Census staff would take the lead on transcriptions and summaries. Each interviewer would be responsible for creating summary spreadsheets of the contents of the interviews (with cases in rows and themes in columns). F. Analysis and Report Writing Census staff would take the lead on analysis and report writing, iterating with CBO staff input. G. CBO Staff Engagement To assess the component of partnering with CBO staff as co-researchers, debriefings with CBO staff along with a pre-post survey of attitudes toward the Census Bureau. That is, at the very beginning of the project, CBO staff will complete a short survey asking about their own trust in the Bureau. At the conclusion of the project, the same survey will be administered to gauge whether the experience of acting as co-researchers with CBSM staff has served to “move the needle” on their trust in the Bureau. The survey will also borrow methods from respondent driven sampling to assess network size; that is, the survey will include a measure of the “reach” of the CBO staff and the size of their networks – both in their capacity as CBO staff working directly with vulnerable populations, and in their own lived experience in the community. These findings – from the debriefings and the two measures from the survey (change in the trust of the CBO staff and their reach in the community) will inform the effectiveness, feasibility and scalability of the basic approach of partnering with CBO staff as co-researchers to address the chronic distrust faced the Census Bureau.

23 APPENDIX A: Excerpt from Valentine and Valentine (1971) Charles A. Valentine and Betty Lou Valentine. 1971. Missing Men: A Comparative Methodological Study of Underenumeration and Related Problems. Report prepared under contract for the U.S. Census Bureau. Washington, D.C. Pages 34-39 “A Proposed Solution” “Optimum completeness of information can be achieved only through intensive, long-term resident participation in the life of the community by independent researchers. This ethnographic approach is the only means by which researchers can come to be regarded as trustworthy, for it is the only way to give people convincing experience that they will not be compromised or injured by revealing themselves. This method also maximizes opportunities for direct observation of actual behavior which is inevitably more revealing than any system of verbal requests for information. Much that is easily omitted from responses to any interview or questionnaire is semi-public knowledge to observant neighbors. Even the most cautious devices for self-protection are often largely inoperative against intimate acquaintance and systematic observation. It is within the ethical code of the community described earlier to accept tacitly the fact that a great deal of such direct knowledge may be accumulated through experience by persons who are known to live under the same conditions as those whom they study. Participant ethnography itself remains imperfect and cannot be expected to yield absolutely full and accurate information, even on the small scale to which it is unavoidably confined. Nevertheless, the comparisons cited earlier strongly suggest that this approach is markedly more successful than other common techniques. The major advantage of surveys is the large number of people they can reach. For obvious practical reasons, ethnography cannot match this coverage in quantitative terms. Participant observation therefore cannot be a substitute for mass interviews or questionnaires. What is needed is rather a combination of the two approaches which will capitalize on the strengths of both in order to reduce the weaknesses of each. To this end we propose that the research design of survey programs should regularly include independent ethnographic checks or controls. This proposal can also be viewed the other way around, suggesting that ethnographic research should regularly be made more useful by matching some of its data gathering against relevant surveys. Considerations of cost, availability of personnel, against relevant surveys, and other matters of feasibility clearly will require that the proposed controls be highly selective, in relation to the massive coverage of survey work. This would presumably mean that ethnographic control studies should be strategically placed to cover samples of populations already known or suspected to pose serious methodological problems which are beyond the capacity of survey techniques alone to solve. In this respect there is the fortunate circumstance that ethnographers, anthropologists of complex societies, and other similarly inclined scholars tend to be interested in urban and rural minorities and the poor. It is beyond the scope of this report to suggest in detail the scale of such efforts that might be possible. For the sake of discussion, however, it might be reasonable to establish that no basic national survey, such as a census, should be planned without conjoining ethnographic research on at least one urban and one rural community of Afro-Americans, of Hispano-Americans, of Native

24 Americans, and of poor Whites in two or more geographic regions for each group. This would suggest a tentative initial program of sixteen or more ethnographers to accompany any basic nationwide demographic survey. Starting now, it should be quite within the realm of possibility to organize such a minimal program for a census in 1975 or earlier. Extensions of the essential idea would not be difficult to devise. Before long it should be possible to express many social statistics in terms of survey results accompanied by adjustments, extrapolated from ethnographic samples for many ethnic, socio­economic, and regional segments of the national population. The organization and operations of such an effort could begin by envisioning extensions and adaptations of the project described here. A double-blind independence between ethnographers and enumerators would be a methodological essential. The ethnographies would have to be long- term intensive, resident participatory efforts guided by the purposes of community studies and testing sociocultural hypotheses, by no means confined to gathering demographic data for matching against the census. Some anthropologists and others already carrying out or planning relevant research should be available and amenable to arrangements for cooperation along the lines suggested. Additional personnel might be commissioned and, where necessary, trained for this work. This could also be a means to increase opportunities for members of minority groups to become social scientists and contribute to the understanding of their own and other communities. In any such program it would be of utmost importance to dissociate the ethnographic work from either actual or suspected reporting of individual data to authorities or organizations which might use the information in any way against the people concerned. Ethnographers must be fully convinced that they actually control their data in this respect, and they must be prepared to demonstrate this if individuals or groups within the communities under study should ask. The sense of being under official and non-official surveillance is too well developed and too strongly resented in many relevant populations to be dealt with effectively by pro-forma declarations of dedication to confidentiality. Perhaps some special system for sharing data with surveyors without divulging individual identities would have to be devised. While experience in Blackston has convinced us that communities with much hostility toward outsiders are nevertheless open to genuinely participant inquiry, we are equally convinced that the time is past when any such inquiries could proceed without being accountable to the people under study. Some ethnographers and other scientists will be convinced, as we are, that this accountability extends beyond concern for individual confidentiality to responsibility for broader social and political effects flowing from their work. This means, first of all, that any publication of or access to information such as that reported here from Blackston must be arranged so as to protect the interests of the community, as defined from a community viewpoint. For example, efforts must be made to prevent published reports and deviant behavior from leading to special crackdowns by agencies of social control or discriminatory punitive legislation from various levels of government. Thus at a time like the present when major political efforts are being made to reduce public assistance benefits by stigmatizing welfare recipients, any conscientious ethnographer of the poor must be troubled by the possibility that his work may be used in support of these inhumane political initiatives. Yet this whole problem area is full of ambiguities, dilemmas and indeterminate complications. It is difficult at best for researchers to maintain anything approaching reliable control over the use of

25 material once it has been published or otherwise shared. Particularly when dealing with vulnerable groups whose trust in the ethnographer makes the work possible, abstractions about the scientific value or professional obligation of publication are insufficient to resolve these dilemmas. It may often be necessary to make difficult and uncertain judgements as to the balance of positive and negative consequences likely to flow from various decisions in this realm. If any such program as that sketched above should be instituted, it would be vitally important that participating ethnographers have maximum freedom of judgement in these matters, as well as full responsibility for their own data. Many decisions in this area will no doubt be heavily conditioned by one's evaluation as to the benevolence or otherwise of both public authorities and private powers toward the peoples and communities most concerned. It must be noted that participatory experience in ghetto communities is not conducive to sanguine expectations in this regard. On the other hand, it also seems plausible to posit substantial positive consequences - quite beyond scientific benefits -- if the quality of our basic social statistics can be significantly improved. A successful program along these lines could greatly increase the accuracy of the basic perceptions and images of society and its component communities referred to earlier. Nothing could be of more fundamental significance than the possibility of correcting systematic errors in generally accepted statistics which discriminate against minorities and the poor in the deepest sense of distorting and falsifying their nature as human groups. To the extent that these distortions perpetuate stigmatizing stereotypes, they help to rationalize the discriminatory oppressions of inequality and to justify an unjust status quo. To the extent that the program sketched in outline here might validly counteract these justifications and rationalizations, it would be worth considerable risk.”

There is also concern that other groups may be at-risk of an undercount, including those with low literacy and those with a disability. One key objective of this research is to address one of the chronic contributors of the undercount: distrust. By partnering with staff from CBOs whose mission is to serve HUP constituents, the goal is to build trust within the community and leverage local knowledge. 1 U.S. Census Bureau Abstract Several interviewer-administered U.S. Census Bureau surveys, like the Annual Social and Economic Supplement of the Current Population Survey and the Survey of Income and Program Participation, collect income and expense data via open-ended numeric questions. These questions are essential to producing accurate statistics about the financial health of the United States, but they can be challenging for respondents to answer. Respondents may not know the exact amounts, can view the information as highly sensitive, or may prefer to answer using range options since reporting discrete amounts can be cognitively burdensome. Currently, interviewers play a vital role in encouraging respondents to provide precise values for these questions. As major U.S. Census Bureau household surveys prepare to integrate web survey response modes, it is crucial to explore effective methods for displaying these questions online in ways that motivate accurate responses, maximize data quality, and reduce respondent burden. Using data from the web-administered Household Pulse Survey, this experiment tested three approaches for reporting discrete values for mortgage, rent, utilities, and the down payment for home purchases. The control group received the interviewer-administered wording requesting respondents to provide a dollar amount in a write-in box. The first experimental group was given an additional instruction telling them to provide their best estimate if they were unsure. The second experimental group had an “I’m not sure” checkbox below the write-in box they could select instead of reporting an answer. This study shows that an instruction on the item encouraging respondents to estimate if they are unsure is an effective way to reduce item missingness and the risk of breakoffs on cognitively burdensome items when compared with a control question without instructions. There is also evidence that the “I’m not sure” checkbox and the instruction to estimate may reduce the risk of survey breakoffs when compared with a control group that does not provide motivational or encouraging statements; however, this pattern was less clear when breakoffs were compared between the checkbox and the instruction- to-estimate treatments. As survey practitioners consider adding instructions or using nonsubstantive response options, careful considerations should be made to these tradeoffs in data quality and respondent burden. Keywords: item nonresponse, respondent burden, income data, web survey, survey methods Suggested Citation: Renee Stepler, Abbey Nawrocki, and Lisa Cheok.(2025). 4 U.S. Census Bureau INTRODUCTION The Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the Current Population Survey and the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) are actively designing web self-response instruments to add web data collection as an additional response mode alongside computer- assisted personal interviewing (CAPI) (Cheok 2024; Fields and Bennett 2024). In CAPI, these surveys ask respondents detailed income and expense questions using an open-ended numeric write-in format. While interviewers are able to enter a “Don’t know” or “Refused” for these types of questions, they are trained to encourage respondents to provide these detailed data by motivating them to share the value or probing for an estimate when a respondent seems unsure. But in a self-response web survey, it is difficult to replicate these probing techniques used by interviewers to motivate reporting. Additionally, many of the Census Bureau’s household surveys rely upon proxy reporting where the household respondent may not truly know the answer to these detailed questions or may not be able to provide a good estimate. From a respondent burden perspective, it may seem attractive to give respondents the option to enter nonsubstantive answers like a “Don’t know” in order to reduce the risk of breakoffs or frustration with the survey. However, prior research has shown that offering nonsubstantive options like these may encourage satisficing, increase item nonresponse, and diminish data quality. To inform survey program decisions on how to incorporate this style of question in a web survey, we conducted an experiment on the Census Bureau’s Household Pulse Survey (HPS) using several expense questions from the American Housing Survey (AHS) and SIPP. This study compares two experimental groups to the a control group which replicates the CAPI question in a web format. The first experimental group uses an instruction to encourage respondents to report an estimate if they are unsure of the answer. The second experimental group allows respondents to select an “I’m not sure” checkbox below the numeric write-in field instead of reporting a value. This paper examines the data quality and respondent burden associated with each of the treatment groups and control group by analyzing item nonresponse, rounded responses, average completion time of the series, and breakoff rates. 1. BACKGROUND Several U.S . Census Bureau household surveys ask respondents to report detailed income and expense information in a numeric open-ended format (see Figure 1). If the interviewer records a “Don’t know” or “Refused” response in the CAPI instrument for the open-ended numeric write-in, the respondent is then asked a follow-up questions that contains range response options (see Figure 2).

5 U.S. Census Bureau Figure 1: SIPP CAPI Numeric Open-end Question – Mortgage/Rent Note: “^RENTMORT” fills with “rent” or “mortgage” depending on the household tenure status. “^CALENDAR_YEAR” fills with the year prior to the interview. Figure 2: SIPP CAPI Range Follow-up Question – Mortgage/Rent Note: The range follow-up question shown here is only asked when the interviewer enters a “Don’t know” or “Refused” response into the numeric open-end in Figure 1. “^RENTMORT” fills with “rent” or “mortgage” depending on the household tenure status. “^CALENDAR_YEAR” fills with the year prior to the interview. Moving these types of questions to web merits careful consideration. Developing web survey instruments requires balancing the need for the detailed data while considering data quality concerns and respondent burden. Generally, past research has shown higher item nonresponse on the web than interviewer-administered surveys (Lesser, Newton and Yang, 2012; Heerwegh and Loosveldt 2008). This is a particular concern as U.S. Census Bureau surveys begin to integrate web survey components into their traditionally interviewer-administered surveys. Maintaining data quality when integrating an web mode is of utmost importance for ensuring accurate estimates. There are a few reasons why we may expect higher levels of item missingness on these numeric write-in question for income and expense data on the web versus in interviewer-administered surveys. First, interviewers are able to probe respondents with follow-up questions or motivate them to report answers – a feature that is difficult to replicate in the web survey. For example, Lipps and Monsch (2022) showed “Don’t know” answers were given in the web mode more often than those on the telephone for questions that required respondents to calculate information, suggesting that interviewers served an important role in helping respondents provide substantive responses for these types of questions. Secondly, while requesting open- ended information provides more detailed and granular information to calculate federal statistics, it is also more cognitively demanding for respondents. Retrieving historical

6 U.S. Census Bureau information, calculating an answer, and verbalizing an answering without preset categories tend to be a more burdensome tasks for respondents than when they are presented with categories to choose from. It is well-known that providing “Don’t know” or other nonsubstantive options on the web can lead to increased item missingness (de Leeuw et al 2016; DeRouvray and Couper 2002). However, there are three reasons why using a “Don’t know” response may be important for these types of numeric open-ended questions. First, income and expense questions can be particularly sensitive questions for respondents (Tourangeau and Yan 2007). Many of the Census Bureau surveys that have these discrete value questions are asking several questions about types of income the respondent or another household member received (e.g. salary/wages, commissions, 401K distributions, dividends, social program amounts, etc.) or expenses and purchases made by the respondent or another household member (e.g. utilities, purchases of goods, investments in real estate, etc.). Asking respondents to provide this sensitive detailed information on the web when there does not appear to be option to indicate they are not sure of the answer or an obvious way to opt-out of answering that item could increase breakoffs. In the interviewer-administered environment, the interviewer can provide additional details on the importance of the question and encourage the respondent to continue despite this request for sensitive information; however, in the web environment, sensitive questions like these could encourage higher levels of survey breakoffs. Second, many of the Census Bureau household surveys are completed with a household respondent who provides proxy information for other household members. There are situations where the household respondent may not have a good estimate of the income or expenses for another household member. In this case, the survey may become particularly burdensome and there is concern for breakoffs when respondents are not presented with an option to indicate their lack of ability to provide a good answer to that question. During an in- person or telephone interview, the interviewer can encourage the respondent to continue the survey, but we lack the dynamic ability to motivate respondents to continue in a web survey. Third, receiving a “Don’t know” for these question formats would allow us to route the person to a range follow-up to attempt to collect some information about the income or expense type, mimicking what is done in CAPI. Receiving a “Don’t know” and probing respondents to provide a range in the follow-up versus having someone breakoff at the numeric write-in screen due to the burden of the survey is preferable. An alternative to providing respondents with a “Don’t know” option would be to try to replicate motivational messages that an interviewer may use in the field. Motivational messages in web surveys encouraging respondents to answer specific questions have been shown to reduce item missingness for some questions (see Al Baghal and Lynn 2015; de Leeuw et al 2016). Because respondents may be apprehensive to report numeric open-ended values either due to the

7 U.S. Census Bureau complexity of the task or not being certain of an accurate answer, adding an instruction to the question text may encourage respondents to provide an estimate if they are unsure. This could mitigate the risk of higher item missingness. This would largely mimic the training we give to interviewers to use probes to encourage the respondent to provide an answer. While this does not directly address the sensitive nature of the question, encouraging an estimate may put the respondent at ease when providing a response knowing that it is not required to be exact. It also may encourage the respondent to give us something slightly more precise in the numeric open-end than we would receive if they skipped the item and were subsequently routed to one of the range follow-up questions. There could be potential downsides to adding an instruction to estimate in the web environment. First, many of these questions are about complex topics and have instructions of what to include or not include. Adding an additional instruction to these questions can clutter the screens and could increase the burden of that question by requiring the respondent to read more and make another consideration about the extent to which they want to estimate for that particular question. Another risk of adding this instruction is that it may cause changes in response behavior that could reduce data quality. Respondents who may otherwise have provided a more precise answer in the numeric write-in may be influenced to round their answer when presented with an instruction to estimate. If this is prevalent, we may expect to see more response heaping (e.g. more rounded answers) in the data. Timbrook, Olson and Smyth (2022) tested an instruction to estimate in a telephone and mail survey and found that it did reduce nonsubstantive responses for mail surveys and simplified interactions between the interviewer and respondent for telephone response, but did not significantly change rates of item nonresponse or rounded answers in either the telephone or mail mode. An alternative to adding the instructions to the question text for the numeric write-in would be to add a soft check if the respondent skips without answering. The soft check could encourage the respondent to estimate if they were unsure. While this would reduce clutter on the screen compared to adding the instructions directly to the screen for all respondents, it could become burdensome and frustrating to the respondent if many questions in the survey have soft checks to encourage an answer. Because there are range follow-ups for this question used to collect additional information for producing national estimates, we did not test this design feature as part of the experiment. For the aforementioned reasons, we designed an experiment to assess data quality and respondent burden when presenting respondents with an “I’m not sure” checkbox against using an instruction encouraging the respondent to provide an estimate if they are not sure. We test these designs against a control group that replicates the CAPI version of the question.

8 U.S. Census Bureau Research Questions and Hypotheses This paper examines data quality and respondent burden to evaluate the best course of action for ensuring data quality for open-ended numeric responses on the web. As such we have the following research questions and hypotheses: RQ1: What effect does adding an instruction to estimate or adding an “I’m not sure” checkbox have on item missingness? Based on prior research, we would expect the “I’m not sure” checkbox group to have higher levels of item missingness on the initial numeric write-in question than the control and instruction to estimate. We also expect the instruction to estimate to encourage response and have lower levels of item missingness than the control group. However, in combination with the range follow-ups we may expect that the level of item missingness overall to be somewhat equal across the treatments. RQ2: Are there signs of heaping or more rounded answers in the instruction-to-estimate treatment versus the control and “I’m not sure” checkbox group? While adding an instruction to estimate could reduce item missingness, it is also possible that this instruction could degrade the quality of the data we receive. For example, someone receiving this question may be discouraged from looking up information when they normally would have done so. Therefore, we expect that we would see more heaping of responses in the instruction-to-estimate group than in the control and the “I’m not sure” checkbox groups. RQ3: How does the time spent answering the numeric write-in, follow-up range question, or the combination of the numeric write-in and follow-up range question differ by treatment group? On the numeric-write in questions, we would expect more satisficing with “I’m not sure” checkbox treatment. Therefore, we might expect shorter response times as this group may quickly assess that they do not have a good response for this numeric write-in and select the “I’m not sure” checkbox. Similarly, we suspect that the group encouraged to provide an estimate via the instruction may also move more quickly than the control group. This instruction may encourage people to quickly estimate versus looking the information up or thinking more carefully about their response. However, it is possible with additional text, we may see slightly increased time for this group as they read more information on the screen. Among people who receive both the numeric write-in and range follow-up, we suspect if more people are satisficing in the “I’m not sure” checkbox treatment that they could spend longer on the range follow-up as they reflect upon the value. However, people who

9 U.S. Census Bureau skipped the numeric write-in in the instruction-to-estimate group may have spent time considering their answer already and may have an estimate they are able to provide when asked in a range format. Therefore, the instruction-to-estimate group may move more quickly on the range follow-up question than the “I’m not sure” checkbox group. RQ4: Is there any evidence that breakoffs are higher for those who receive an instruction-to- estimate or the control group compared with the “I’m not sure” checkbox group? It is possible that respondents could become frustrated when being asked these detailed expense questions, especially if they are not familiar with the expenses for their household. The “I’m not sure” checkbox may offer respondents an opportunity to express that they do not know the answer to the question and encourage them to continue in the survey without breaking off. Conversely, not having a way to express that they do not know the answer may lead to greater frustration and eventually cause a respondent to breakoff in the survey for control group. The instruction to estimate may potentially reduce the likelihood for frustration and encourage the continuation of the survey leading to lower breakoffs for this group than the control group. 2. METHODOLOGY Data and Experimental Design This paper uses data from the Phase 4.2 HPS, cycle 8 and cycle 9. Cycle 8 data was collected from July 23 to August 19, 2024 and Cycle 9 data was collected from August 20 to September 16, 2024. This series came at the end of a survey with a total median completion time of 18 minutes (the mean completion time is 38 minutes and the mode completion time is 15 minutes).1 As part of the HPS questionnaire, respondents were asked a series of questions about their demographics, employment, education, housing security, food sufficiency, household spending, inflation concerns, physical and mental health, social isolation, child care arrangements, chidren’s mental health treatment, transportation, participation with the arts, internet access, COVID-19 vacinations and long COVID symptoms, and impact of living through natural disasters. The unweighted AAPOR Response Rate 2 is 5.7% for Cycle 8 and 4.8% on Cycle 9. 2 Three questions on expenses were part of this experiment. Each of these questions asked the respondent to provide a numeric write-in value. RESULTS RQ1: Item missingness Item Missingness in the Numeric Write-in First, we examine item missingness for the five questions across each of the treatment and control groups. Item missingness is defined as viewing the numeric open-ended question but either skipping the question without entering an answer or selecting the “I’m not sure” checkbox without entering an amount in the numeric write-in if they are in the second treatment. Table 2 shows percent of item missingness for each of the numeric write-in questions by the treatment and control groups. Pairwise comparisons are tested between each of the experimental groups. DISCUSSION This study examined data quality and respondent burden metrics associated with adding an “I’m not sure” checkbox or instruction to estimate for numeric write-in questions on household expenses. The goal was to understand the tradeoffs each of these designs have when it comes to data quality metrics – item missingness and rounded answers – and respondent burden – completion time and breakoff rates. We found consistent and substantially higher levels of item missingness on the numeric write-in questions when using the “I’m not sure” checkbox than the other treatments. The instruction- to-estimate treatment was associated with lower levels of item missingness than the control group for four of the the five items tested and the “I’m not sure” checkbox across all five of the items tested. When respondents were offered the range follow-up question after skipping or selecting only the “I’m not sure” checkbox, most did provide an answer. This means the overall item missingness for the series of questions (numeric write-in and the range follow-up) had small differences when examined together; however, the share of responses that came from the range follow-up were much higher in the “I’m not sure” checkbox treatment, some of which were up to 20% to 25% of responses. Offering the “I’m not sure” checkbox will limit the granularity of the data collected from the respondent, meaning a substantial amount of the reported answers would be in a range format versus a discrete value. 25 U.S. Census Bureau burden compared with the “I’m not sure” checkbox since fewer respondents would receive a range follow-up question if they provide a response in the numeric write-in. When exploring how reports of rounded answers differed by treatment, the instruction-to- estimate treatment did have slightly higher percentages of rounded answers for three of the four items examined than the control and “I’m not sure” checkbox treatments. This suggests that adding the instruction does encourage respondents to provide more rounded answers or estimated amounts. However, it is important to keep in mind that this treatment also led to lower levels of item missingness on the numeric write-in question, which means fewer people were routed to a range follow-up question and forced into answering with the range options provided. Interestingly, the “I’m not sure” checkbox was associated with substantially higher completion times on average across each of the items tested for those who skipped or only selected “I’m not sure”. The mean completion times of the instruction-to-estimate and control groups were similar. This seems counterintuitive to what we might expect if respondents were quickly satisficing with the “I’m not sure” checkbox. It is possible the longer time spent on this question series for respondents in the “I’m not sure” checkbox treatment could be an indicator that they are spending time interpreting what the question is asking them to do. There are two tasks on the screen: provide a value and/or report that they are not sure. From this perspective, the checkbox may be creating greater respondent burden. Alternatively, the “I’m not sure” checkbox may cause respondents to overthink their answer. For example, they might spend time developing an estimate but the “I’m not sure” checkbox leads them to believe the estimate they calculated or recalled is not good enough. This hestitation may lead to increased completion times as they think through how to proceed. For four of the five items tested, the “I’m not sure” checkbox was associated with lower breakoff rates than the control group; however, this was only true of two of the five items when comparing the checkbox breakoff rates to the instruction-to-estimate group. The instruction-to-estimate group had lower breakoff rates for four of the five items tested than the control group and for one item it had a lower breakoff rate than the “I’m not sure” checkbox. Overall, either of these interventions (using instructions or providing the “I’m not sure” checkbox) seemed useful in reducing the risk of breakoffs on these types of numeric write-in questions on expenses. There are a few caveats and limitations to the experiment and results. First, these questions were tested at the end of the HPS which is on average shorter and less burdensome than some of the Census Bureau interviewer-administered surveys that collect these types of data. The questions in this study were household level expense questions; however, this question structure is used for income and expense questions at both the household and person level in the Census Bureau interviewer-administered surveys. In particular, this study does not address collecting person-level information in a proxy interview. Finally, there is no way to determine

26 U.S. Census Bureau the accuracy of the data reported in the numeric write-ins and we did not evaluate the level of confidence respondents had in the values they reported in any of the treatments. Examining the instruction to estimate and “I’m not sure” checkbox on these questions in the context of proxy reporting and evaluating the respondent’s confidence in the values they provide would be two recommendations for future testing. This study shows that a motivational instruction on an item encouraging respondents to estimate if they are unsure is an effective way to reduce item missignness and the risk of breakoffs on cognitively burdensome items. Providing users with an “I’m not sure” checkbox may be enticing to ensure respondents who are unsure of the answer have an option to select; however, the increase in item missingness and average completion time on the series are tradeoffs that should be considered. There was evidence that the “I’m not sure” checkbox and the instruction to estimate reduced the risk of survey breakoffs, compared with the control version that offered neither of these enhancements. However, when comparing breakoffs between the “I’m not sure” checkbox and the instruction-to-estimate treatments there was not a clear pattern on which format offered lower risk of breakoffs. As survey practitioners consider adding instructions or using nonsubstantive response options like “Don’t know” or “I’m not sure”, careful considerations should be made to these tradeoffs in data quality and respondent burden.

i Abstract In the 2020 Census, households were offered several different ways to answer the census: on paper, over the phone, in person with a census worker, or online. The online option was new for the 2020 Census and very effective. People living in group quarters (GQs) did not have the opportunity to answer for themselves online. GQs are places where people live or stay in a group living arrangement, such as college dormitories, nursing homes, etc. For these types of living quarters, often the administrator of the GQ fulfilled the census obligation by providing a list of residents and their demographics to the Census Bureau. The quality and detail of the data provided in the lists depended on the demographics available in the GQ’s original files and their own rules about sharing those data with other entities, like the Census Bureau. Given the success of the online data collection for households in 2020, in preparation for the 2030 Census, the U.S. Census Bureau is considering allowing residents living in certain group quarters to complete their census questionnaire online. As part of the research investigating whether an online questionnaire would work for GQ residents, the Census Bureau fielded an online feasibility survey to gather information from group quarters administrators in six different group quarter (GQ) types. Email notification with a link to the survey was sent to a sample of group quarter administrators selected using a 2020 Census frame of emails. Response was low across many of the group quarter types. Taken in hand with the conclusions drawn from the GQ focus groups (Nichols et al., 2024), we were able to determine which types of GQ might be strong candidates for an online self-response questionnaire option for the 2030 Census. Those include college housing, workers’ quarters and Job Corps centers, and religious quarters. 1 Executive Summary The census is conducted at the household level for most of the population, but for those living in group quarters there is a separate census operation. Group quarters, such as college dorms and nursing homes, differ from households in that they house many residents in an institutional setting. For the group quarters operation, the census relies on administrators in these facilities to provide information on the number and characteristics of residents living in the facility. Typically, GQ administrators complete the census on behalf of their residents through a variety of methods, none of which rely on residents reporting their information for themselves. In 2020, the primary method was for the GQ administrator to send a list of residents to the Census Bureau using a secure Census Bureau portal, but they could also complete an individual paper questionnaire for each resident, they could ask their residents to complete a paper questionnaire themselves, or there could have been in-person interviews conducted, to name a few methods. For 2030, the Census Bureau is exploring using an online questionnaire for a select group of group quarter types, with the thought that the online questionnaire would be completed by the resident, instead of the administrator. While this enumeration method might not be ideal for all GQs, it could be one of several different enumeration methods offered. In 2023, an online survey gathered feedback from group quarters administrators on whether they thought an online census questionnaire would be a feasible solution for their residents to self- report and for administrators to promote. While there are over 20 types of GQs, subject matter experts at the Census Bureau identified six of them to participate in this survey. The six types identified were possible candidates for an online reporting option where the residents could answer for themselves. A sample of GQ administrators from these six types were selected to participate and were emailed a link to this online survey. Those six GQ types included: • Residential schools for people with disabilities • College/University student housing • Group homes intended for adults (non-correctional) • Residential treatment centers for adults (non-correctional) • Workers’ group living quarters and Job Corp centers • Religious group quarters Response rates varied across the group quarter types with a 16% overall response rate. In part those response rates were due to the large number of bounce backs to the email distribution. The bounce back finding suggested that there was substantial employee turnover among group quarter administrators between 2020 and 2023. Data were not available to determine whether the bounce backs affected one GQ type more severely than another.

2 A total of approximately 300 group quarters administrators responded. Based on those responses, we were able to recommend three of the six group quarter types for further study: college housing, workers’ quarters and Job Corps centers, and religious quarters. This report summarizes findings and recommendations from the feasibility survey. Its purpose was to help identify which group quarters might be good candidates for an online census questionnaire data collection mode. The Census Bureau will focus on these group quarters for further qualitative research in preparation for an individual online census questionnaire for the 2030 Census. 1. Introduction The 2020 Census offered an online reporting option for households in addition to more traditional reporting options such as a paper questionnaire, over the phone, or with a census worker. However, the online reporting option was not available for residents of Group Quarters. Group Quarters (GQ) are places where groups of unrelated individuals live together and have some oversight. In preparation for the 2030 Census, the Census Bureau conducted a series of exploratory studies with GQs administrators to determine whether their residents would be able and willing to answer their census questionnaire online and how best to notify the residents of the online census. These exploratory studies including focus groups (Nichols, et al., 2024), cognitive interviews to explore the interface, and a feasibility survey. The present report describes the methodology and main findings of the feasibility survey. 2. Methods 2.1 Survey topics The topics addressed by the feasibility survey aimed to better understand internet access, resident abilities, notification methods, and administrator duties and preferences. The survey questions were developed to elicit the following information from GQ administrators: 1. How residents access the internet. 2. Whether residents can complete an online questionnaire themselves or whether staff can help them. 3. Best method for notifying residents of an online questionnaire. 4. Whether the administrator can provide residents’ emails to the Census Bureau. 5. Whether the administrator would prefer to send the residents emails. 6. Concerns with conducting the Special Sworn Oath virtually.

3 2.2 Sample selection and notification schedule Group quarters administrators, those who have access to the list of residents by address and hold the authority to use that information, were recruited to participate in the feasibility survey. Some examples of the 20+ types of GQs include college or university housing, residential treatment centers, skilled nursing facilities, group homes, military barracks, correctional facilities, maritime and military vessels (U.S. Census Bureau, 2021, pp. B11-B16). Subject matter experts at the Census Bureau identified six GQ types they thought would be most likely candidates to have residents who could complete an online census questionnaire by themselves. These six GQ types were eligible to be included in the feasibility survey sample. They included: Code Description 405 Residential schools for people with disabilities 501 College/University student housing 801 Group homes intended for adults (non-correctional) 802 Residential treatment centers for adults (non-correctional) 901 Workers’ group living quarters and Job Corp centers 902 Religious group quarters To sample GQ administrators, we relied upon a 2020 Census list of GQ administrators emails for these six GQ types. In total, approximately 2,100 GQ administrators were selected to be part of the sample. This sample size was determined by an initial list of email addresses we obtained. We put forward that initial number to OMB when we sought approval for this data collection. However, after the data collection was approved by OMB, we were provided a much larger list of email address – approximately 14,500 from the Census Bureau’s Master Address File from the 2020 Census. From this list, we selected all GQ type 405 – residential schools for people with disabilities since there were so few administrator emails for that GQ type. For the remaining GQs we sorted the list by GQ type and took a systematic sample to reach our sample size of 2,100. Up to four emails were sent to encourage response. Those were sent June 14, June 20, and June 26. Emails that bounced back and emails where a response was received were removed from reminder emails. The survey was open for 17 days: from June 14 through June 30, 2023, In total, we collected approximately 300 responses for a response rate (RR2) of 15.7% (AAPOR, 2023). For an RR2 response rate, completed and partial surveys are counted as responses and that number is divided by all cases in sample, whether they were eligible or ineligible. The distribution of the sample and response rates for each GQ type are presented in Table 1.

Four participants answered the survey as they would if they received it in their inboxes while thinking aloud with a Census Bureau researcher over a Microsoft Teams meeting. The participants included a religious group quarters administrator, a Job Corps administrator, and two university administrators. A few minor changes were made to the survey based on pretesting, including adding “Don’t know” as a response choice for some of the questions. The specific wording of the questions in the final survey, as well as the survey flow can be found in Appendix A. Topics in the feasibility survey included whether residents had internet and email access, the administrator’s opinion of email notification about the census for their GQ residents, whether residents knew their address, whether residents would need assistance in completing an online questionnaire, willingness of staff to assistant in the census process - including whether staff would be able to conduct follow up with nonresponders and record their data, along with willingness to take the Title 13 confidentiality oath over the internet so that they could collect census data, which is Title 13 protected. We included a question about whether residents knew their GQ address because one of the questions in the online census questionnaire asks respondents to confirm or provide their address. Not knowing their GQ address would lead to data quality issues in responses in an online self- response questionnaire. We assumed that the GQ address might be more difficult to know than other basic census information, like their name, date of birth and race, and therefore we included this address knowledge question in the feasibility survey, and did not include questions about resident knowledge of their own demographic data. In the feasibility survey, the same questions were administered to each GQ type with one exception. College and university housing administrators were not asked if their residents had internet access, as we assumed they had access. We also assumed college residents would not need assistance in completing an online questionnaire, and did not ask those questions either.

34 3.7 Email findings Sending notification emails with the link to the feasibility survey provided some insight into the turnover rate in the GQ administrator position across all six GQ types. Of the 2,100 emails initially sent on June 14, approximately 24% bounced back. In most cases, this meant that the selected respondent no longer worked for the organization. For that first email, approximately 36% of the emails were opened. It is not clear whether the remaining 40% of emails reached individuals who still worked in their position. While email addresses that bounce backed for the first email were not sent subsequent emails, and nor were emails to administrators who answered the survey, we continued to monitor the percent of emails opened. The percents hovered around the original 36% rate, with 36% for the second email; 35% for the third email; and 30% for the final email. We do not know whether the same or different administrators opened each email. Nonetheless, since less than 50% of the emails were opened in any one time, it could be that the inboxes were not being monitored by the original GQ administrator. While we could not determine whether a particular GQ type had more bounce backs or fewer opens then another email type, the level of both bounce backs and not opened emails suggests that turnover and nonresponse of GQ administrators will be significant hurdle in 2030, regardless of the enumeration method chosen. 4. Conclusions While the response rates to the survey were low across group quarter types, the findings can still be used in planning for more research for the next census. In 2030, GQ administrators will select the census reporting option for their residents. These data provide evidence to the Census Bureau on which GQ types should be offered an online reporting option that the residents answer for themselves. Even though subject matter experts initially thought six GQ types might be good candidates, this research suggested that three of the six appear to be viable candidates for a self- administered online reporting option. Findings from the feasibility survey indicate that college housing (501), workers’ quarters and Job Corps centers (901), and religious quarters (902) are good candidates for an online self- response census questionnaire. Residents living in these GQ types typically have access to internet and email, know their address, and would need little by way of GQ staff assistance in completing an online census on their own. Further, while staff were divided about whether they could provide the Census Bureau with their residents’ emails, almost all were willing to send emails on the agency’s behalf. Additionally, they were generally willing to become Title 13 sworn online and conduct nonresponse followup as needed. Conversely, residential schools for people with disabilities (405), group homes for adults (non- correctional) (801), and residential treatment centers (802) are likely not strong candidates for an

35 online self-response census questionnaire. While some of the residents of the GQ types had access to the internet, few had access to an email account. Their support needs were also high, with most likely needing staff assistance to complete an online census questionnaire. This is an important consideration because even though staff were generally willing to assist the Census Bureau with nonresponse followup and be Title 13 sworn virtually, the support needs of residents outweigh other considerations. These summarized findings are corroborated through focus group results (Nichols et al. 2024). 5. 36 Appendix A: Feasibility Survey Q1 Greetings, and thank you for taking our Group Quarters Feedback Survey. The Census Bureau is responsible for enumerating all persons living in the United States, including those persons living in various types of group quarters. i Abstract When implementing a large survey redesign, we found a simple question template to be a useful tool for sharing detailed information about the goals of the question and the concerns that should be explored in cognitive testing. The template, in its basic form, reported the research question, question universe, question text and responses, and information to be reported back from testing. Some teams further adapted the template to include more information, creating a comprehensive record of all information relevant to the programming and testing of each question, and the connections between questions. The template was a success and helped facilitate communication between subject matter experts and the methodologist. We recommend this template for any size redesign. 1 Introduction To develop the best questionnaires possible, the Census Bureau routinely conducts expert reviews and a variety of qualitative testing: exploratory, cognitive, and usability interviews, eye-tracking, and focus groups. Most commonly, methodologists receive a pre-existing survey instrument and take the lead on identifying potential stumbling blocks in the survey response process. They suggest a small or moderate number of improvements in collaboration with the survey sponsor, conduct qualitative testing, and provide recommendations on potential changes and next steps. Currently, several of the Census Bureau’s flagship computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) surveys are undergoing a modernization process that includes developing a web-based instrument for self-administration. This is a significant undertaking, especially since many of these surveys are long, complex, and ask about difficult or sensitive topics. The question revision requires substantial collaboration between the methodologist and teams of subject matter experts (SMEs). While the SMEs are the authority on substantive topics and the reporting requirements, question design and testing methodologies are not necessarily part of their backgrounds. The methodologist must balance the SMEs’ redesign goals with methodology principles to produce a final instrument for testing. One of the surveys that is modernizing is the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the Current Population Survey (CPS) (see https://www.census.gov/programs- surveys/cps/about/modernization/asecmodernization.html). ASEC covers the following topics: health insurance, out-of-pocket medical expenses, earned income, other income sources, and poverty indicators. Besides the fundamental goal of adjusting the current questions for self- administration, the ASEC modernization managers and SMEs wanted to test changes that aim to lower respondent burden, as well as leverage the visual medium and technology of the web to introduce different question formats. Redeveloping and thoroughly testing an ASEC web instrument, from exploratory interviews to field testing, will involve four years of effort and over thirty SMEs within the Census Bureau. Qualitative testing, particularly cognitive interviews, is critical to developing a web instrument comparable to the CAPI questionnaire. However, the complexity of the ASEC CAPI instrument, scale of the redesign, multiple stages of qualitative testing, and central role of multiple teams of SMEs, demanded a heightened level of documentation and coordination. The survey methodologist needed an organized method of collecting detailed information about each question from the SMEs to better prepare for cognitive testing. Therefore, a question template was devised to gather and organize the SMEs’ question changes and testing goals and provide a structured platform for iterative communication between the methodologist and SMEs. Template The template was simple. For each question, the SME should first report the Research Question which provided information about changes to the question and the SMEs’ concerns about the effectiveness of the question without an interviewer present. The concerns could pertain to specific vocabulary, overall comprehension, the potential need for help text or instructions, and usability concerns for new question formats. Next, the question text with response options and fills was provided. Finally, the template asked for what was to be reported back from the cognitive testing.

2 SMEs were encouraged to ask for things like: situations where the question failed, alternate wording provided by the respondent, and counts of certain behaviors or responses. This sequence of information was to be applied to every question included in the revised questionnaire, even if the question was the same as in the CAPI version and/or the SME had no concerns about the respondents’ abilities to understand and answer the question. The template was initially presented in a kick-off meeting with SMEs as a PowerPoint slide (see Figure 1). Since we knew that the questionnaire may be too long for the time allotted for cognitive testing, the presentation also encouraged SMEs to designate “low priority” questions that could be dropped from the test questionnaire, if needed. These questions and the corresponding information were designated by light grey, rather than black, font. Figure 1. Template as originally proposed and presented The SMEs were receptive to the template and grateful to have some structure to their task. The presentation was converted to a guidance document with additional examples and instructions (e.g., using an automatic table of contents, inserting horizontal lines to separate the questions). The examples provided were from another Census Bureau survey, so as not to influence their efforts (see Figure 2). As the SMEs worked with the template and guidelines, further improvements were suggested (e.g., universes and instructions on question fills were included for each question). The template became an essential document, recording all relevant information about the survey questions.

Does the overlap in “State or Federal Marketplace,” “Healthcare.gov,” and/or the state-specific portal name confuse people? The content of the template was passed between the SMEs and methodologist several times for each section of the survey in order to continually refine the questionnaire and goals for testing. As originally envisioned, the methodologist used the template to guide her question revisions as well as to develop meaningful probes for testing that would give the SMEs the information they needed. The final version was provided to the contractor conducting the qualitative data collection so that they too could understand the testing goals of each question and what information was required from the interviews. Additional Applications of the Template Beyond the development of the questions and testing protocol, there were a couple additional, unintended, outcomes of the template that supported other steps in the cognitive testing process. With the universes included and heavily scrutinized by the SMEs, the templates were used as the specification documents for the programmers. Also, the templates became the backbone of the cognitive testing report prepared by a contractor. For each question, the contractor included the Research Question and question text. When reporting the findings from each question, the contractor used the information from the Report request or the specific probes (which closely mimicked the Report requests) as subheadings. See the appendix for an example showing the format of the section documenting the findings for each question. Conclusions The template was straightforward for the SMEs to use and motivated them to thoughtfully consider each question and what was important for the ASEC redesign. It provided essential support to the development and testing process, and facilitated communication and cooperation across teams. While the Census Bureau is currently conducting several redesigns as part of their broader modernization effort, this is a unique experience for the staff involved. Therefore, regardless of the SMEs’ inexperience with qualitative interviewing or questionnaire design, this trial found that the template is an easy tool for non-methodologists to apply. Even though the magnitude of the ASEC redesign effort is unique, we would recommend the template for any size project. In our experience, it fostered communication between the sponsor and methodologist and provided helpful documentation. As methodologists, we also found it advantageous that the template moved the questionnaire from Excel, where the SMEs had started working, to Word. It was easier to comment on specific words or segments of the questions, track changes, and visualize the instrument.

5 One lesson learned during this process was that the subtle difference between the Research Question and the Report request was not immediately clear to everyone. An effective clarification was that the information in the research question is a succinct communication of the main concern(s) with the question. The Report request provides specifics of that concern and many of those are translated into probes. Furthermore, by also knowing the Research Question, the methodologist can suggest additional probes and reporting, or alternative question wording. The template has established its place in the ASEC modernization effort’s toolkit and is being implemented for the next round of cognitive testing. The SMEs have noticeably improved both the format of the templates and their questionnaire design skills. The template, used in conjunction with the methodologist’s comments and edits, has imparted some basic questionnaire design principles, providing for a more efficient and harmonious redesign process. i Abstract This report presents findings and recommendations from cognitive testing of two new select-all that apply questions about traffic measures (e.g., speed safety cameras, raised intersection crossings) and bike infrastructure (e.g., sharrows, bike lights, buffered lanes) surrounding schools for the School Pulse Panel (SPP). The response options for these questions used highly technical terminology that may not be easily understoold by all participants. Images were added to each of the response choices to provide a visual example for each transportation feature alongside the description. There is limited prior research in using images on online surveys to help with questions that require technical terminology. During cognitive testing, researchers focused on determining whether the images assisted participants in understanding the response options and if there were any usability issues with the images, focusing on the image size and clarity, length of descriptions or the number of response options and images per page. Twenty school staff participants took part in the remote pretesting. They were asked to think- aloud while answering the online survey. Researchers noted any spontaneous comments and participant behavior on these two new questions. After completing the survey, participants were asked whether they found the images and item descriptions helpful and how they would have responded if the images had not been provided. Participant feedback confirmed that the images were helpful when selecting their answers and that the questionnaire design was successful. Our recommendations for online surveys looking to include images are the following. Select images that are high resolution, bright, and that accurately depict the topic- specific terminology. During the questionnaire design phase, consider the number of images per page, image size, and ensure images look different from each other, which may assist participants in distinguishing between similar items. These findings and recommendations informed the final production survey, fielded in March 2025. Future cognitive testing should continue assessing images as a tool to assist participants with answering topic-specific and technical questions. Keywords: cognitive interviewing, qualitative research, questionnaire design, images, transportation infrastructure Suggested Citation: Caitlyn Keeve, Kristen Kohm, Alexandra Piccirillo, Jennifer Pace, Kelyvette Ortiz Fontanez, Jonathan Katz, Erin Tanenbaum.
