iv EXECUTIVE SUMMARY This report presents findings from cognitive pretesting of select questions from the March 2025 content of the School Pulse Panel (SPP). The SPP is an online self-response questionnaire that surveys public K-12 schools on high-priority, education-related topics once a month during the school year. This project is sponsored by the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) within the Department of Education's Institute of Education Sciences (IES), with data collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. In fall 2024, researchers pretested using images with item descriptions for two new school transportation questions for fielding in March 2025. Generally, past research on the topic of images in surveys focuses on surveys collecting images from participants, rather than how images may help respondents in questions with highly technical information. Images were added to the response choices for a question about traffic measures (e.g., speed safety cameras, raised intersection crossings) and another question about bike infrastructure (e.g., sharrows, bike lights, buffered lanes) surrounding participants’ schools. Images were pretested with response option text descriptions. Using images to assist participants in answering questions is one method of questionnaire design that may help participants answer topic-specific questions. Images were presented for each response option with the assumption the images would help participants understand what the term meant. Since differences in transportation options across areas may impact how participants respond to the questions, the Census Bureau recruited pretesting participants from schools across the country. Researchers conducted twenty cognitive interviews remotely with participants via Microsoft Teams. Participants were school staff, principals, assistant principals, deans of students, and other knowledgeable front office staff from public and charter K-12 schools. They worked at schools with a variety of grade levels, and their schools were located in different states. During the session, participants were asked to think-aloud while answering the questions. During the think-aloud, interviewers noted usability issues (e.g., image size and clarity, length of descriptions, items per page) and/or difficulty with the questions that appeared to affect the survey experience. After completing the survey, participants were asked whether they found the images and item descriptions helpful and how they would have responded if the images had not been provided. This report documents the methodology, design, and qualitative results of using images and item descriptions in questions with technical terminology in the SPP. Participant feedback confirmed the images were helpful when selecting their answers and that the questionnaire design was successful. Our recommendations for online surveys looking to include images are the following. Select images that are high resolution, bright, and that accurately depict the

v topic-specific terminology. During the design phase, consider the number of images per page, image size, and ensure images look different from each other, which may assist participants in distinguishing between similar items. These findings and recommendations informed the final questions on the production survey, fielded in March 2025. Future cognitive testing should continue assessing images as a tool to assist participants with answering topic-specific and technical questions.

INTRODUCTION The School Pulse Panel (SPP) is a study sponsored by the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), part of the Institute of Education Sciences (IES), within the United States Department of Education, to collect extensive data on current and emerging issues concerning students and staff in U.S. public primary, middle, high, and combined-grade schools. SPP has become one of the nation’s main sources of timely and reliable data on issues concerning the education environment, as reported by school district staff and principals in U.S. public schools. The SPP is an online self-administered questionnaire answered by a panel of public K-12 school staff, including front office staff, principals, heads of school, and assistant principals. Between 2021 and 2025, the survey was fielded once a month during the school year with existing and new question content. Before data collection, new question content is pretested with school staff to make sure the questions are easily understood and not too burdensome. Staff in the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) within the Census Bureau has regularly conducted cognitive interviews to test content for SPP since 2021. In the round of testing for the March 2025 survey, new questions about transportation were tested as shown in Table 1. One question was about traffic measures surrounding their school (e.g., speed safety cameras, raised intersection crossings) and the other question was about bike infrastructure (e.g., sharrows, bike lights, buffered lanes) surrounding their school. The response options for these questions were technical and images were added for each response option (See Figures 1 and 2). Traffic Measures

Bike Infrastructure Wording and Images While there are a variety of other studies that show including images in a survey may affect participant’s answers (Couper et al., 2004; Witte et al., 2004), little is known about how participants may perceive the use of images to illustrate highly technical content on surveys. Generally, past research on the topic of images in surveys focuses on surveys collecting images from participants, rather than providing images to improve the survey experience. For instance, research shows that asking participants to provide their own images on a survey significantly increases likelihood of item nonresponse and increases survey completion times (Bosch, 2022). Another study found that participants asked to take a picture on their smartphone and upload it to a survey, are less likely to find the question easy to answer (Ilic et al., 2022). Less recently, a study by Couper et al. (2007), explored the visual context effects of varying image complexity, including image size, content, and placement, on participant’s interpretations of their own health. This study cautioned the use of images for questions that are ”straightforward” self- assesments (e.g., participants’ self-rated health) due to images playing a role in “shaping” participant’s answers to self-assesment survey questions. For this testing of SPP, the survey sponsor suspected some of the terms in the traffic measures and bike infrastructure questions might not be understood by all participants and collaborated with CBSM to provide images that correspond with the transportation features. During the prestesting we explored whether providing relevant images may assist participants in answering the survey questions.

METHODOLOGY 2.1 Data Collection In fall 2024, cognitive testing was conducted with 20 participants virtually using Microsoft Teams. Since the School Pulse Panel is completed by school staff or principals, researchers focused recruitment efforts on participants aged 18 years or older who were school staff, principals, assistant principals, deans of students, or other knowledgeable front office staff from public and charter K-12 schools. Participants were from the Midwest, Northeast or South. Conducting interviews with school staff from different regions of the country was a priority due to differences in language used to describe traffic control measures.

6 U.S. Census Bureau The study was advertised with a Census Bureau wide broadcast email. Census staff also recruited their networks of relevant participants for the study. Interested participants completed a screener via a web self-administered link or called our recruiter to complete via telephone. The screener consisted of two parts. First, there was pre-approved universal questions to collect demographic information, including questions asking if they work in K-12 and whether their school is a public school, a charter school, or a private school. Next, supplemental questions were administered to collect information criteria, including past research participation and access to a laptop to complete the survey to establish eligibility for one or more of the testing modules. Each participant received a $75 cash incentive via Priority Mail after completing their session. All participants were asked to sign a digital consent form to participate in the research study and to allow the researcher to audio record the session (using Snagit) and video record their screens. All participants agreed to the recording, and sessions were led by one of five CBSM staff researchers. All the participants used a personal computer to complete the survey during the interview. 2.2 The Cognitive Interview Protocol At the start of the interview, participants were told that the purpose of the interview was to gain their thoughts and opinions about the survey questions and talk to the interviewer about whether the questions made sense and how they understood the questions (Willis, 2005). After obtaining consent for recording the interview, participants were asked to complete an online survey programmed in Qualtrics. At the beginning of the survey, participants were instructed to answer the questions as if they were completing the survey by themselves without the researcher present. They were also asked to “think aloud” as they answered questions to allow the interviewer insight into their thought process (Ericsson and Simon, 1980). The survey had 57 questions across 10 modules, including topics such as mental health and well-being, drug overdose prevention, school and district vaccine requirements, transportation, housing instability, crime and safety, and learning strategies and recovery. This report focuses on a subset of the interview, the two transportation questions with images and text descriptions that were as part of the 19-question Transportation module (see Appendix A). All participants received the two transportation questions displayed in Figures 1 and 2. High resolution stock images were received from NCES and uploaded to the survey. All images adhered to the standard resolution of 72 PPI for web images and were approximately 1.79 x 2.5in, which prevented blurry or out of focus images from being presented to participants (See Figures 1 and 2). The “Traffic Measures” and “Bike Infrastructure” questions displayed seven images per page, one for each substantive answer choice. Two additional response options were displayed

7 U.S. Census Bureau without any images at the end of the response list: “Other, please specify” and either “There are no traffic calming measures immediately surrounding our school” or “We have no bike infrastructure surrounding our school” depending on the question. The “Traffic Measures” and “Bike Infrastructure” questions were each displayed on their own page. The item description, which participants selected as an answer choice, appeared above the image on the screen. Survey questions were evaluated in terms of participants’ understanding of the questions and their ability to respond to the questions and/or access the necessary information to respond to the questions. Participants were asked to think-aloud while answering the survey including the two new select-all-that-apply questions about traffic measures and bike infrastructure. During the think-aloud, interviewers noted usability issues (e.g., issues with the image size and clarity, length of descriptions, items per page) and/or difficulty with the response option text and questions that appeared to affect the survey experience. Researchers also noted any issues during the session, which included response hesitations, misunderstanding of the question, difficulty selecting a response, and comments on the images displayed on the screen. During testing, researchers kept track of spontaneous comments participants made about the questionnaire as well as noted non-verbal reactions by watching them on the video web camera, when available. To the extent possible, response errors (i.e., either missing data or incorrect responses) were captured based on participant verbalizations and observations. Participants were debriefed at the end of the session so researchers could clarify any responses or answer participants outstanding questions about the survey. Scripted retrospective probes in the protocol focused on if participants found the included images to be helpful in answering the questions, and if the images were not provided, did they think their answers would have changed (See Appendix A). If so, they were asked which answers would have changed if the images were not provided next to the item description. 2.3 Analysis CBSM staff prepared written summaries for each interview they conducted. Once all summaries were completed, CBSM staff discussed whether and how questions should be revised to improve comprehension or otherwise reduce measurement error. Consideration was given to the number of participants who had an issue with a question and the nature of the issue. After these internal discussions, CBSM shared recommendations with NCES staff, who made the final decision on whether and how to revise questions. 3. USABILITY FINDINGS The “Traﬃc Measures” and “Bike Infrastructure” questions displayed seven images per page, one image for each substantive answer choice. This number of images did not appear to be an issue for participants. However, it did require them to scroll down the page to see the images in their entirety and scroll up when they wanted to revisit an image previously viewed. All participants used a personal computer to test these questions, which perhaps contributed to no one commenting on scrolling between images being burdensome. For participants who selected the “Other, please specify”, “We have no bike infrastructure surrounding our school”, or “There are no traffic calming measures immediately surrounding our school” options at the bottom of the screen, they did not seem to have any issues finding those given all the other information on the screen. While screen sizes and browser settings diﬀered across the participants, Figure 10 displays an example of the questions on a computer screen. Mobile Display Example The succinct item description with the image appeared to work well for participants by providing enough detail, while not overburdening them with excess text on screen. While one participant suggested that a detailed deﬁnition of each transportation measure may be able to help them improve their understanding of the terminology, walls of text have not been received positively by participants. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS For this research CBSM tested two transportation questions that provided images for response options and item descriptions to assist participants in selecting their answers on the School Pulse Panel survey. During cognitive testing, researchers focused on determining whether the images assisted participants in understanding the response options and if there were any usability issues with the images, focusing on the image size and clarity, length of descriptions or the number of response options and images per page. Participant feedback confirmed that the images on both questions performed well in helping participants understand each response option and select their answers. Data from these interviews suggest that the images may be an effective approach for aiding respondents when they are faced with questions about highly technical concepts that may not be best described in words alone. One potential concern associated with using images on web response is the risk of usability issues. There was not any major usability issues found in this study for each question, where there were seven images per page for each response option. However, the design did require

18 U.S. Census Bureau scrolling up or down the page to see the images vertically. One caveat to the pre-testing results is that all participants used a PC to test these questions; and none said scrolling was burdensome. Our opinion is that if these questions were tested on mobile devices, scrolling to revisit an earlier image on a small screen may have shown to be a usability issue. Our recommendations for online surveys looking to include images are the following: • Select images that are high resolution, bright, and that accurately depict the item. • Design should be consistent in showing images; do not display images for some response options but not others. • Public Domain or “stock” images should be unique and clearly distinguish key features. which may assist participants in distinguishing between similar items. School transportation is one topic where participants’ environments and knowledge about terminology may vary. With future testing, online surveys may consider the methodology and design decisions discussed in this report. In addition, there are a number of alternative methods to be explored for utilizing images to assist participants in answering survey questions. The following are recommendations for future testing: • Consider providing images for response choices in a pop-up modal or link, only when those items are not well known. • Test using multiple images for each concept. • Consider offering a brief video if the item changes (such as the flashing lights). • Test images with participants on a mobile device and larger screen to watch for issues with scrolling due to the number of images on a page or the image size. • Evaluate how the inclusion of images may impact respondent burden and completion time. We used an image for each item, but future testing could offer an image only for items that are not well known. If some response choices in a question have an image and others do not, consider offering those images in a pop-up modal with a link to the image next to the response choice. The link would not take up as much real estate and unfairly emphasize one response choice over the other. Overall, we recommend that the design choice is consistent throughout the survey. As discussed, terms like “sharrow” and “chicane” were among the most common unknown items where participants appreciated having images. However, other terms like “bike lane” and “speed safety camera” were easier for participants to identify without an image. One recommendation for improving usability and eﬃciency is to test allowing participants to hover or click on the item description to view the corresponding image. This design would allow for the participant to control which individual image they’d like to view, rather than seeing all

19 U.S. Census Bureau images at once. This increased personalization may help researchers better understand where participants are having diﬃculty comprehending an item. This may also eliminate any extra “noise” on the screen. Others may also consider using multiple images to depict a technical term in their survey. Utilizing multiple images, perhaps with a slide show feature that presents the items in diﬀerent angles or in diﬀerent geographies may oﬀer more variety for participants and increase likelihood of recognition. Another option may be to embed a brief (e.g. 5 second) video instead of an image to show how real people usually interact with a transportation measure. For example, instead of a static image, a brief video of a bicycle in motion turning into a bike lane may better show the diﬀerences between similar terms. Finally, images in our survey did not include descriptive text embedded within images for accessibility software. However, this is a feature we recommend adding in future versions of images on the SPP. Future research should also examine timing data and how images contribute to overall burden in surveys. Generally, topic-specific survey questions may lead participants who are unfamiliar with terminology to spend excess time thinking about their answer or trying to imagine what the question is asking about. These participants may also prefer to select “don’t know” or skip the question, rather than provide a substantive answer. A study that compares timing and non- response data between participants who receive images and those who do not may provide insight into how using images may affect response efficiency and data quality in an online self- response survey.

RESEARCH REPORT SERIES (Survey Methodology #2025-09) Global Versus Decomposed Questions: How Does Decomposing a Global Utilities Expense Question Impact Data Quality and Respondent Burden? Renee Stepler Center for Behavioral Science Methods Research and Methodology Directorate U.S. Census Bureau Washington, D.C. 20233 Report issued: June 2025 Disclaimer: This report is released to inform interested parties of research and to encourage discussion of work in progress. Any views expressed on the methodological issues are those of the authors and not necessarily those of the U.S. Census Bureau. The paper has been reviewed for disclosure avoidance and approved under CBDRB-FY25-0311.

1 U.S. Census Bureau Abstract One consideration when writing survey questionnaires is using a global question that asks respondents to report a measure in one question versus decomposing the question into a series of items. Currently several U.S. Census Bureau household surveys are undergoing modernization efforts to add web self-response modes to their interviewer-administered surveys. Some of these surveys use global questions that contain definitions or details about what to include or exclude in their response. While an interviewer may use their judgement to explain these instructions or definitions to the respondent as needed, these global questions with complex instruction text could cause frustration in the web self-response mode leading to more breakoffs or satisficing that could harm data quality. This study tests a global utilities expense question against two formats of a decomposed utility expense series to examine data quality and respondent burden. The global utilities question contains examples of utilities that should be included and excluded from the amount. The decomposed versions use two questions: the first identifies the types of utilities the household pays and the second asks for the expense amounts for each of the types of utilities reported in the first item. While the global utilities expense question is completed faster by respondents, the respondents in this question version reported including fewer utility types in their answer than in the decomposed versions and reported including utility types that the instructions directed them to exclude. Conversely, item missingness was higher for the decomposed versions than the global version. This experiment suggests that survey managers and subject matter experts should carefully weigh the tradeoffs between different measures of data quality and response time when deciding whether to use global or decomposed questions for complex concepts. Keywords: decomposition, survey methods, data quality, respondent burden, expenses Suggested Citation: Renee Stepler. (2025). 3 U.S. Census Bureau 1. INTRODUCTION Writing survey questions to elicit precise and accurate responses from respondents can be a challenging endeavor, especially when the question measures complex concepts and requires technical definitions. Some features added to questions to help communicate this complexity include providing a definition of the survey concept, adding a list of examples about what to include or exclude, or including language modifiers as cues to the respondent about the threshold for reporting (e.g. “did you do ANY work for pay, even for as little as one hour?”) (Schaffer and Dykema 2011). When implemented well, these question features can reduce measurement error and improve data quality. However, it can be overwhelming for respondents to receive so much information at once. One alternative to a global question that asks respondents to report a measure in one question is decomposing the question into a series of items or subtasks that can be collapsed for analysis. A common example of a global versus a decomposed question series is collecting information about household income. A global income question may look something like “In 2024, what was your total household income before taxes?” Alternatively, income can be decomposed into a series of items asking about different types of income the household or people in the household may have received, such as salary or wages, earnings from interest or dividends, income from rental property or other investments, and so forth. Global questions can be attractive because they reduce the number of total questions in a survey, which may reduce respondent burden as measured by completion time compared with decomposing a question into several shorter or simpler items. However, decomposing an income question into several questions enables the survey to ask more details about income and helps to engage the respondent in producing a more accurate response by reporting each type of income step-by-step. Decomposition is also a common way to easily provide the respondent with a definition of what types of income the survey is interested in and reduce the single task into a series of less cognitively burdensome subtasks (Schaffer and Dykema 2011). Decomposition of questions may be particularly important as major Census Bureau household surveys, that are primarily interviewer-administered, undergo modernization efforts to add a web self-response mode (Cheok 2024; Fields and Bennett 2024). Many of these surveys ask about complex topics, such as income and expenses, requiring detailed instructions, definitions, and/or help screens. In efforts to reduce completion time in the interviewer-administered modes, some questions are asked in a global format that contain interviewer instructions or help text that detail what to include or exclude in the recorded response. An interviewer can use their judgement to explain these instructions or definitions to the respondent as needed or as the respondents asks questions about the thresholds for reporting. But as these questions transition to web self-response, the cognitive burden associated with additional instruction text and the complexity of a global item could cause frustration that leads to breakoffs or satisficing that may harm data quality.

4 U.S. Census Bureau To better understand the impacts of decomposition on a web self-response survey, we tested a global question on utility expenses with detailed instructions of what to include and exclude. We compare the global question to two decomposed versions to examine the reliability of the answers and the respondent burden associated with each question format. 2. BACKGROUND The global utility expense question tested comes from the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP). Figure 1 shows an image of the question in the computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI) instrument. The question stem asks specifically about how much the household paid in December for electricity, gas, basic telephone services and “other utilities”. Interviewers are given an instruction with other types of examples to be included and some examples of utilities to exclude (cable TV or internet). The interviewer instructions are not designed to be read directly to the respondent. Other surveys at the Census Bureau decompose utility expenses into a series of questions. Figure 2 shows one example of a decomposed utility series from the American Community Survey (ACS) paper form, which asks about the cost of electricity; gas; water and sewer; and cost of heating fuel, etc. separately (note that the reference period also varies for the questions). Figure 1: Survey of Income and Program Participation utilities question in CAPI Figure 2: American Community Survey utilities questions on the paper form Note: On the ACS form, Items c and d are displayed directly below a and and b.

5 U.S. Census Bureau Reporting utilities in a global single item may be complex for many reasons, especially when using a particular month as the reference period. First, utilities can vary month-to-month due to changes in seasons that require different use of some types of utilities (e.g., heating). Utilities may also have different payment cycles (e.g. monthly, quarterly, seasonally, annually). When asked about how much is spent in a particular month, it is not clear how respondents may answer for utilities that they used that month but did not pay for in that month due to the billing cycle. Finally, the instructions do give examples of what to include or not include; however, in the web environment instructions can be easily overlooked by respondents or become overwhelming leading to satisficing. When the instructions only provide a limited number of examples, it is left to the respondents’ judgement about what other types of utilities they should include or not include. Leaving these decisions to the respondent makes the question more cognitively burdensome, which is further compounded by any calculations they must do to add their utility expenses from multiple sources into one number and/or prorate expenses for non-monthly billing cycles. Decomposing questions about utilities eliminates several of these issues, but increases the number of questions added to the survey. Research Questions This paper examines an experiment that tests the CAPI version of the global utility expense question (Figure 1) against two decomposed versions that ask the respondent to report the expense amounts for each utility they have separately. Debriefing questions were asked to assess the accuracy and data quality of the global question against the decomposed questions and timing data is analyzed to assess respondent burden. This paper seeks to answer the following research questions: • Research Question 1: Are there differences in the data quality between the global and decomposed question series? • Research Question 2: How does the response time for the global question compare to the decomposed question series? Is there a difference in the amount of time it takes to complete the two versions of the decomposed question series? 3. METHODOLOGY Data and Experimental Design The data for this experiment came from the Census Bureau Research Panel. The Census Bureau Research Panel is nonprobability sample of participants who were recruited when they agreed to be contacted about future survey opportunities at the end of the Census Household Pulse Survey (HPS). An online survey was administered via Qualtrics from December 3-15, 2024, in English. The sample for the December data collection included panelists that were recruited from the Phase

6 U.S. Census Bureau 4.2 HPS administered from July to September 2024 (n=30,000).1 The Census Bureau Research Panel aimed to collect approximately 10,000 responses over a two-week period using an email invitation and up to three reminders. No incentives were offered. Due to a high-level of response only two emails were sent, with the last invitation sent on December 6, 2024. The total number of responses (completes and partials) was 9,900. The survey topics included: basic demographics, ages of children in the household, receipt of school breakfasts or lunches, habits around carrying and spending cash, preferences for incentive payment methods, utilities expenses, and amounts for select income types. This experiment contained a control group and two treatment groups. A random third of respondents were assigned to each of the experimental groups. The control group replicated the CAPI question wording and instruction text and is referred to as the “global” version (see Figure 3). Figure 3: Global Version Treatment 1 and treatment 2 decompose the global version into two questions. The first question for treatment 1 and treatment 2 was the same. It asked the respondents to select the types of utilities that they paid for in their homes (see Figure 4). The treatment 1 and 2 types- of-utilities response options were designed to be congruent with the examples of utilities to report in the global question stem and instructions (electricity, gas, basic telephone service, water, heating oil or wood, trash or recycling, mobile telephone service. This was to help encourage a closer comparison between the global and decomposed questions. In treatments 1 and 2, the next screen displays write-in numeric boxes for respondents to report the amount they paid for each utility they selected in the prior question (see Figure 5). Only the items the respondent selected are displayed and asked about on the second screen asking for expense amounts. Treatment 1 repeats the question stem (“How much did this household pay for [utility type] in November?”) for each utility they selected. In treatment 2, the question stem is listed at the top of the screen “Please enter how much this household paid for each of the following types of utilities in November.” followed by numeric write-in boxes labeled with the utility type. It is expected that the treatment 2 would enable the respondent to move more quickly through the series than in the treatment 1 format. DISCUSSION This paper examined the data quality and respondent burden associated with asking about utilities expenses by comparing a global question to two different kinds of decomposed questions. Overall, the study shows that the global question is completed faster than the decomposed question series; however, there are some cautions about the quality of the data in both the global question and decomposed series. Overall respondents reported fewer utilities in the expense amounts in the global question than the decomposed versions and substantial shares reported expense amounts that they were explicitly directed to exclude in the global version. On the other hand, the decomposed versions contained higher rates of item missingness for the utilities amount. In terms of data quality, the two versions of the

16 U.S. Census Bureau decomposed treatments performed similarly, but the treatment 2 version had advantages in reducing the completion time for respondents compared with the treatment 1 version. The treatment 2 version of the questions seemed to best balance the data quality concerns while limiting the respondent burden and completion time. One concern for using the two-step decomposed series is that item missingness was higher when compared with the global question. However, it is possible that there were reasons people may not have been able to answer the utilities expenses in November specifically. First, we did not ask about whether people paid these utilities as part of their HOAs/condo fees or as part of their rent. It is possible that people may report that they pay these utilities, but that they do not have a good estimate of how much of their rent or condo fees go towards specific utilities. In addition, the first question asked whether they paid for the utilities – but did not specify the reference month. Only the follow-up question contained the reference month of November. It is possible that a portion of the respondents with the missing data were part of the group who paid the utilities on a non-monthly basis and did not provide a prorated amount for the utilities in November. Nevertheless, one future recommendation for testing may be to use a one-step decomposed series that asks the expense amount for the specific utilities of interest, without asking a question about the types of expenses first. This would need to contain an instruction to enter zero for utilities that they do not have or a checkbox to allow respondents to report that they do not have the utility; though recent research suggests the instruction to enter zero or the filter question is more optimal than a checkbox (see Schulzetenberg et al 2023). The timing data also suggests that this one-step approach could make a decomposed version of the question more comparable to the global version. It should be noted, however, that this one-step approach may also have drawbacks. For example, respondents may not follow an instruction to enter zero if the utility does not apply to them, which could make it difficult to distinguish whether it is a true zero or they skipped the item. Among those who did report their utility expenses, respondents tended to report fewer utilities in the global question than when they were asked a two-step decomposed question about the types of utilities they had and then were asked the amounts for those utilities in November. This suggests that the global utilities questions may result in underreporting of the utility expenses since respondents generally tend to report fewer utilities than the instructions suggest they should include. The global question was also associated with respondents reporting other utilities that we may not want them to include (such as internet, cable TV, home security systems, pest control services, and so forth). From this perspective, the decomposed question does provide respondents with a clear definition of the types of utility expenses to report compared with the global version and would likely lead to more accurate estimates of the utility expenses that are of interest for the question series. One interesting note is that each group was asked whether they included a prorated amount for utilities they used in November but were billed at a different cycle than monthly. There were not any significant differences among the experimental groups for this item. This suggests

17 U.S. Census Bureau that some respondents in the global group seem to be making a series of calculations that include prorating amounts paid for utilities on non-monthly cycles and adding these expenses together with their other utilities. Given that about a third of respondents reported having utilities that are billed on a non-monthly cycle, subject matter experts may consider testing in the future whether including an instruction for handling these types of billing cycles may be useful for their estimates based on monthly reference periods. This type of instruction is likely to work best in the decomposed format that did not require other instructions advising the respondent about the types of utilities to include or exclude. Subject matter experts may consider some additional cognitive testing to get a better feel for how people are calculating utilities on non-monthly billing cycles as it is possible that the web probing item as written in this survey may not have been clear to respondents. Focusing on the completion time of the global versus decomposed items, the results show that the global version is completed by respondents more quickly and that the decomposed version without the repeating question stem is quicker for respondents than the decomposed version with the repeated question stem for each utility. It is possible that there is some degree of satisficing occurring on the global question where respondents provide an answer that is “good enough” without calculating each utility in their homes or fully calculating the cost of each utility combined. In other words, survey managers and subject matter experts should carefully consider the need to balance respondent burden, as measured by completion time, with their needs for high quality data. Among the two decomposed series, this study did not show any major quality differences, but the treatment 1 series had a larger average completion time than the treatment 2 version. It seems likely that respondents are spending extra time identifying which utility the treatment 1 series is asking about since there was no formatting (e.g., bold text) applied to the question text to help differentiate the utility for each question. Because there were not any data quality differences detected between the treatment 1 series and the treatment 2 series, using the decomposed treatment 2 series seems more beneficial to collecting these types of data. There are a few limitations and caveats that should be noted for this study. First, this experiment was conducted on a nonprobability panel, which likely includes more attentive and motivated respondents than general population surveys. Additionally, the study did not provide options for respondents to report that their utility payments were made as part of their HOA or condo fees. As a result, some of the missingness in the decomposed treatments may be associated with this lack of ability to report this. Future studies on global versus decomposed questions may consider examining how these formats influence breakoffs. This study did not examine this since it was conducted on a nonprobability sample who were mostly motivated to complete the study to its fullness. In addition, this study did not evaluate the amounts reported to see if there were any differences in the distribution of utilities expenses across the experimental groups. Because the design of the decomposed treatments limited responents to reporting only utilities listed as examples to

18 U.S. Census Bureau include in their answer in the global question and instructions, the comparison between the global and decomposed series would not have been congruent. Future studies could provide an “other” option in decomposed types-of-utilities questions to enable this type of analysis and consider altering the instructions on the global question to remove instructions about what utilities to exclude. A decomposed question for the utility expenses with the question stem at the top followed by a series of labeled write-in amounts seemed to best balance the priorities of collecting high quality data with limiting the time spent on the question series. While this decomposed version took slightly more time than the global question on average, the global question had some disadvantages when it came to the count of utilities respondents reported and inconsistencies between the types of utilities respondents included versus the types of utilities the instructions directed to include or exclude. The two-step nature of the decomposed series did lead to some higher item missingness compared with the global version. For this reason, future testing may include a one-step version of this question and may allow respondents to report that utilities were part of their HOA/condo fees to deconflict some of the item missingness that showed up in this test. This testing would help deduce whether item missingness concerns could be rectified using a one-question series in a decomposed format.

i Abstract The 2023 Census Test is the first iteration of the Small-Scale Response Testing (SmaRT) program that is part of the Census Bureau’s Small-Scale Testing Initiative. In preparation for the 2023 Census Test, the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) at the Census Bureau carried out cognitive and usability testing of the online questionnaire. Seventeen participants provided feedback during the pretesting, and the online questionnaire was tested in English and Spanish. The questionnaire was programmed in Qualtrics and followed the 2020 Census online questionnaire design with few exceptions. The research questions included observing any issues related to a redesigned address collection screen, observing for any issues with a new question related to whether respondents are answering the census questionnaire for their entire household, and observing for any cognitive or usability issues related to the flow of the questionnaire, especially for reporting vacant housing units. In this paper, we present our findings and recommendations based on respondent feedback and spontaneous reactions, as well as observational, behavioral, and satisfaction data. INTRODUCTION The 2023 Census Test is the first iteration of the Small-Scale Response Testing (SmaRT) program that is part of the Census Bureau’s Small-Scale Testing Initiative. SmaRT is our primary small- scale testing vehicle and how testing is being conducted this decade (complementing our two major census tests: the 2026 Census Test and the 2028 Dress Rehearsal) (United States Census Bureau 2025). The Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) at the Census Bureau carried out pretesting, including cognitive testing of the 2023 Census Test mailing materials (Feuer et al. 2023a), as well as usability testing of the online census questionnaire. This pretesting took place in the fall of 2022 with 17 participants in preparation for a field test in March 2023. Nine participants tested the mail materials and online questionnaire in English and eight in Spanish. Some interviews were conducted virtually, and others were conducted in person. This report focuses on the usability testing of the online questionnaire for the 2023 Census Test. The online questionnaire included typical decennial census questions such as address collection, whether the home was owned or rented, names of individuals living at the address, the name of the householder, demographics for each household member, and relationship to the householder. The focus of the usability testing was on three key revisions to the 2020 Census online questionnaire. 1. The address collection fields were modified from the version used in the online 2020 Census questionnaire to separate the address number from the street name (in 2020 the address number and street name were collected in one field). 2. A new question to the questionnaire asking whether or not the respondent included everyone in the household on the roster, referred to as the Whole/Partial roster question. We looked at responses to this question as well as placement of this question. 3. A new path to collect whether the address was vacant and new vacancy questions. Based on the findings from this usability testing, we recommended some changes to the question order and the wording of questions and response options. In the following sections we outline the research questions, the methodology used in the pretest – focusing on the usability testing of the internet instrument, findings, recommendations and whether those recommendations were adopted in the March 2023 field test. 2. RESEARCH QUESTIONS One research question in this pretesting was related to a redesigned address collection screen. In the 2020 Census, respondents were asked to enter their address number and street name into separate fields. Previous usability testing recommended that the address collection question be changed to ask for address number and street name in a single field. The current testing further investigated whether there were any issues related to the redesigned address collection screen.

2 U.S. Census Bureau We also tested a new question that asks respondents who they are including in their responses on the census questionnaire, and whether that encompasses everyone who lives at that address or only some of the people. Since this is a new question, our testing was looking for any cognitive or usability issues with that question. Part of our testing was also looking at the flow for questions about reporting vacant units. Participants recruited for this study were not recruited based on having a vacant residence, so we created vignettes to test whether there were any apparent cognitive or usability issues with the questions. Finally, we had an overarching research goal of identifying any potential general issues with the wording, instructions, layout, or display of any portions of the online instrument. The research questions for this study were answered based on participants’ answers to the questions, combined with their spontaneous and think-aloud responses, as well as observational, behavioral, and satisfaction data. 3. METHODS 3.1 Session methodology Testing was conducted one-on-one with a test administrator (TA) and individual participants, though sessions were occasionally observed by a notetaker or other observers who were members of the project team. Some sessions were conducted virtually, and others were conducted in person, as part of separate research into the effects of interview mode after the coronavirus pandemic saw a surge in remote virtual interviewing (Feuer et al. 2023b). The entire session was 90-minutes in length, both in person and virtually. The cognitive testing of mailing materials portion occurred during the first 45 minutes, with the cognitive and usability testing of the internet instrument taking the latter 45 minutes of the session. We obtained oral consent to collect data from each participant, and each participant received a monetary incentive of $60 for their participation. The TA trained participants how to “think aloud” during the session to provide us spontaneous comments as they completed the online questionnaire. Virtual sessions were conducted using Microsoft (MS) Teams, a free videoconferencing application. MS Teams allows for screen sharing, audio, and webcam use. Prior to the session, the TA led the participant through a brief “tech check” to familiarize the participant with the technology, specifically how to share their screen and access the chat feature. Practicing how to use these features in the tech check saved time during the session itself. Virtual session participants used their own laptop, tablet, or smartphone.

3 U.S. Census Bureau For the in-person sessions, the participants joined an MS Teams meeting so that other project team members could observe the session. While in-person participants generally also used their own laptop or mobile device, the TA would provide a laptop if the participant encountered technical problems. Each session also had a notetaker, when available, to assist the TA in capturing the participants’ comments and behavior. Some sessions had other members of the project team observing the session. These observers could provide the TA with additional questions for the participant at the end of the session. The TA recorded the session using the Snagit recording application. The online questionnaire was tested in English and Spanish. The questionnaire was programmed in Qualtrics and followed the 2020 Census online questionnaire design with a few exceptions. Full results from this segment of the testing can be found in Feuer et al. 2023a. • Task 2: Participants completed the online 2023 Census Test questionnaire. • Task 3: Participants completed a satisfaction questionnaire about their experience with the 2023 Census Test questionnaire. • Task 4: Participants answered TA debriefing questions about the questionnaire they had just completed.

The knowledge check asked participants’ about their understanding of topics related to the census. • Task 6: Participants were asked for any final comments or reactions on anything they encountered during the session. Data used to answer the research questions for this study included spontaneous verbalizations elicited during the think-aloud portion of the session and participant feedback obtained during the debriefing portion of the study that included directed probes. Observational data was based on what the test administrator and notetaker observed participants doing throughout the session while answering the online questionnaire. 3.2 Participants Seventeen participants (9 English-speakers and 8 monolingual Spanish-speakers) from across the country participated in the study. The study was split into both virtual and in-person sessions, where the in-person sessions were conducted in the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area and the virtual sessions were with participants from across the country. Participants completed the interview using the device they would normally use to respond to a questionnaire. We aimed to recruit participants who would complete the questionnaire using different devices, either a computer or a mobile device such as a smartphone or tablet. Seven English speakers completed the study on a laptop and two on a smartphone. For Spanish- speakers, three completed the study on a laptop, four completed it on a smartphone, and one participant completed it on a tablet. Participants with different household compositions were recruited, including those from unrelated households, such as roommates or unmarried partners, people living alone, and people living with nuclear family members. Approximately half of households for both English and Spanish participants had all members related to each other, and about half had at least one unrelated member. RESULTS 4.1 Usability findings 4.1.1 Address Screen After logging into the online questionnaire, participants saw an address collection screen. The address screen tested was updated from the 2020 Census address screen. In the 2020 Census instrument, the address screen asked respondents to enter their address number and street name in separate fields (see Figure 2). Previous usability testing had revealed that the separate fields did not work well and recommended a combined field. The proposed new address screen asked participants to enter their address number and street name in the same field (see Figure 3). Since the combined Address Number and Street Name fields were a recommendation of previous testing, the goal of this testing was to confirm that there were not unforeseen usability issues with the new design. The separate fields that were used in the 2020 Census were not tested again in this research. Figure 2. 2020 Census Address screen with separate fields for address number and street name

6 U.S. Census Bureau Figure 3. 2023 Census Test Address screen with a combined field for address number and street name. Most English-speaking participants entered their address information accurately and did not have any issues with the new address screen. These participants found the layout of the screen to be similar to other address screens they had completed before. Some Spanish-speaking participants, however, struggled with the address screen. Some of these participants had to look up their address. Four Spanish speakers included portions of their address information in the wrong field. For instance, one Spanish speaker included the city and state in the Street Address field and put the ZIP code in the Apartment field, and another Spanish-speaking participant included the city and ZIP code in the Street Address field and repeated the address number in the Apartment field. These issues all occurred on mobile devices. However, it is not clear that the errors were due to device type. Because we did not want to point out respondent errors, we did not probe respondents on why they entered their information this way. Two English-speaking college students did not know where to count themselves and counted themselves in the wrong place. However, their errors were not associated with the address field design, but about the concept of where they lived. Based on our testing, we recommended that the 2023 Census Test continue to use the combined address number and street name field. Since the apartment field appeared to cause some confusion, we recommended that there be some kind of indication that the Apartment/Unit field is optional. We also recommended that the Spanish screen not use “apto.” as an abbreviation for “apartamento” (apartment). Finally, since there was some

7 U.S. Census Bureau confusion about where to count college students, we recommended including clarifying instructional language on where college students should count themselves. In the 2023 Census Test that followed this cognitive and usability testing, both address screens (one with the combined address number and street name fields and one with the separated fields) were tested in a split ballot experiment. The response fields and labels in that test did not change based on this qualitative testing. Results of the 2023 Census Test are forthcoming. 4.1.2 Whole/Partial Screen Instructions on the census questionnaire for the 2023 Census Test ask the respondent to list everyone living or staying at an address as of a particular date. Most respondents provide an exhaustive list of every person living or staying at an address. However, sometimes multiple questionnaires are submitted for the same address and sometimes those questionnaires have different people listed on them. This indicates that, in some cases, respondents are not completing the questionnaire for everyone living or staying at an address. The primary purpose of the Whole/Partial question (Figure 4) is to indicate whether the Census Bureau should expect an additional census questionnaire with different people for that address. If the respondent reports that they did not list everyone at their address and another questionnaire also arrives for that address, but with different people, then the Census Bureau would know that the two households should both be recorded as living at that address. During pretesting, the Whole/Partial question came early in the questionnaire, after the question asking how many people live or stay at the address as shown in the questionnaire flow above in Figure 1. These participants then decided that they only wanted to report for themselves. Based on the results of this pretesting and our recommendations, the Whole/Partial question and the response options were redesigned for the field portion of the 2023 Census Test. The new question (Figure 5) was more similar to the one used in the 2020 Census User Experience Survey (see Nichols, Olmsted-Hawala, Feuer, 2021). The response options were changed to “I” statements, the reference date was removed, and a response option was included specifically for respondents who live alone. Respondents are asked the total number of people living at the address, their name, the names of the other individuals, and a final question trying to make sure they did not leave off people inadvertently. During probing, some English-speaking participants wondered if they should answer about the people staying in the household for that specific day or where people spend most of their time. In general, they asked questions about the intent of the roster questions and wondered how long someone needs to stay with them before they should be included. The knowledge check also indicated that some participants did not know how to define who was staying in the household for the census. In the knowledge check, five of the seven English-speaking participants and one of the eight Spanish-speaking participants said that the Census Bureau wants people to be counted where they live on a particular day while the other two English- speakers and seven Spanish-speakers said that the Census Bureau wants people to be counted

Another issue was that some participants did not feel comfortable entering the answers for other people in their household, particularly among those who lived with people who were not related to them. 19 U.S. Census Bureau Some highlights from this section of the debriefing include: • While all 15 participants who responded to this question (8 English, 7 Spanish) correctly understood that the law requires answering the census, they were not sure whether they must answer each question in the census. • Another question in the knowledge check asked whether you can leave the answer to a question blank and move on to the next question on the census if you do not know the answer. Of the 16 participants who responded to this (8 English, 8 Spanish), 10 said that they did not know, while five said that you could leave a question blank and one said that you could not. When asked about where people should be counted – whether it is where they live most of the time or where they live on a specific day – there was a marked difference between English- and Spanish-speaking participants. Of the seven English speakers who responded to this question, five believed they should count people where they live on a particular day, while only two answered that they should count people where they live most of the time. Conversely, of the eight Spanish speakers who responded, only one said that they should count people where they live on a particular day, while seven said they should count people where they live most of the time. Although it is not immediately clear why this would differ by language, it appears to not be clear to participants where people should be counted given these two options. 5. SUMMARY RECOMMENDATIONS Three changes to the online census questionnaire design used in 2020 were pretested in the fall of 2022 in preparation for the field portion of the 2023 Census Test. Those included: • Address field changes where street number and street name were combined into one field called street address. • The addition of a path for vacant addresses. • The addition of a question asking whether the respondent had included everyone on the roster. Participants struggled with entering their address accurately in both languages, but not because of the combined street number and street name field. We recommend keeping the design of entering the house number and street name in one field and to indicate that filling in the Apartment field is not required. For the Spanish version, we recommend not abbreviating the term "apartamento" (apartment). The address instructions also proved to be confusing for college students, so clarifying instructional language on where a college students should count themselves is advised. We did not identify any critical usability or cognitive problems with the new questions and question order for identifying housing units that are vacant. However, we were only able to test this path using a vignette.

20 U.S. Census Bureau We identified high priority usability and cognitive issues with the Whole/Partial question asking whether the respondent listed everyone or only some of the people. Because of this misunderstanding of the question, the question will be placed at the end of the questionnaire for the field test so as not to influence how many people are listed. Additionally, the response choices were confusing, especially for single-person households. Tuttle Center for Behavioral Science Methods Research and Methodology Directorate U.S. Census Bureau Washington, D.C. 20233 Report issued: September 2025 Disclaimer: This report is released to inform interested parties of research and to encourage discussion of work in progress. 1 U.S. Census Bureau Abstract Group quarters (GQs) are places where people live or stay in a group living arrangement provided by an organization that may also provide services for the residents. Examples of GQs include university student housing, residential treatment centers, and correctional facilities. The U.S. Census Bureau has developed special procedures to enumerate residents of GQs during the decennial census, and is currently exploring the development of a new enumeration method to enable residents of select noninstitutional GQ types to complete their Individual Census Questionnaires online (also known as internet self-response or ISR). The use of this method would require GQ administrators to use a web-based instrument to provide residents’ names and email addresses and to provide information about the GQs themselves (e.g., expected population on Census Day). After GQ administrators complete this process, the Census Bureau would then send email invitations to residents with links to access the questionnaire. Administrators would also be able to use the instrument to monitor response rates at individual GQs and identify nonrespondents that need encouragement to respond. To support the requirements gathering process for the administrator instrument, we conducted usability interviews with GQ administrators to assess their reactions to an initial design of the interface of the instrument using nonfunctional wireframes. The wireframes approximated the page layouts of the administrator instrument and presented questions/instructions, response fields, buttons and links for various functions, etc. We presented the wireframes to administrators to explore their understanding of the expected tasks presented on each screen and identify potential problems that might interfere with correct understanding. We also asked administrators for their opinions about the appearance of the interface, workflow and expected tasks, and asked them to describe their processes for obtaining requested data. This report details findings on the administrators’ reactions to implementing internet self-response for their GQs and recommendations on improving the design of the instrument for collecting information from GQs administrators. 4 U.S. Census Bureau 1. Introduction The 2030 Group Quarters (GQ) Internet Self-Response (ISR) Team is developing plans to offer an option for residents in select GQ types to complete an online census questionnaire in the 2030 Census. The GQ ISR option entails coordination between the Census Bureau and GQ administrators to facilitate residents’ access to the ISR instrument. The GQ ISR Team’s current plans include development of the GQ ISR Administrators Dashboard, a web-based instrument that would enable GQ administrators to facilitate GQ residents’ access to the online questionnaire. Previously, field staff delivered a paper questionnaire to GQ administrators, the GQ administrators filled out the questionnaire, and field staff returned later to pickup the completed questionnaire. The development of the ISR option for GQ residents was initiated in part in response to requests from GQ administrators and stakeholders for a convenient, web- based mode to enable GQ residents to complete their own census forms (Arenas-Germosen, 2024). This report documents findings and recommendations from usability testing of wireframe mockups of the GQ ISR Administrator Dashboard instrument (indicated hereon as the Dashboard). At the time this study was conducted, five options1 were being considered for enabling GQ residents to access the ISR instrument: Option 1 – GQ administrators provide residents’ contact information to the Census Bureau and the Census Bureau sends email invitations to residents. Options 2–4 – GQ administrators send email invitations to residents containing login credentials provided by the Census Bureau. Option 2 – The Dashboard provides a generic URL to the ISR and unique Census IDs for each resident to log into the ISR instrument. Option 3 – The Dashboard provides GQ-specific URLs to the ISR containing embedded GQ identifiers. Option 4 – The Dashboard provides a generic URL to the ISR and GQ-specific Census ID for residents of the same GQ to log into the ISR. Option 5 – GQ administrators distribute paper letters and questionnaires to residents, and residents may complete the paper questionnaire or use log-in credentials in the letters to complete the ISR instrument. 1 Since this research was conducted, Options 2-4 have been removed by the GQ ISR Team.

5 U.S. Census Bureau In summary, the purpose of the Dashboard as of this stage of development was to enable administrators to either provide residents’ contact information so that the Census Bureau can contact residents directly by email or to obtain links and login credentials to distribute themselves by email to residents.2 URLs and login credentials would be provided in Excel spreadsheets downloaded from the instrument. The Dashboard would also identify residents who have responded to enable administrators to identify nonrespondents and encourage them to respond. To support administrators’ follow-up actions, the Dashboard would provide email templates that administrators could use to remind nonrespondents to complete the census. GQ administrators would be asked to select from among these options during the Group Quarters Advance Contact (GQAC) operation that precedes the Group Quarters Enumeration (GQE) operation. GQ administrators’ choices would enable the Census Bureau to anticipate how residents’ data would be collected in the Enumeration operation and plan accordingly. The purpose of this study was to assess the initial requirements for the Dashboard and look for opportunities to improve them prior to development of a functioning prototype. This study had two main goals. The first goal was to understand administrators’ opinions about email as a communication mode to invite their residents to complete an online census questionnaire. The second goal was to get feedback from GQ administrators on the planned design of the Dashboard instrument, including: • The design and workflow of the interface • The tasks they would be expected to perform on each screen as indicated in the wireframe • The functionality intended to facilitate the tasks they would be expected to perform Administrators’ feedback on the screens allowed us to assess the effectiveness of the design. We also sought to identify any reasons that GQ administrators may not understand the expected tasks on each screen to inform improvements to the interface. To evaluate the Dashboard’s intended use and functionality, a subset of screens was selected for testing that is representative of the workflows for: • Reviewing and updating GQ-level information, such as their name, address, and expected number of people residing in the GQ • Selecting one or more options for providing resident contact information • Providing residents’ names and email addresses • Obtaining resident login information • Monitoring residents’ response status 2 Paper letters and questionnaires would be obtained through a different procedure not involving the Dashboard.

6 U.S. Census Bureau Participants in this study also reviewed wireframes for an instrument being developed for the GQAC operation. The two instruments present similar tasks related to reporting or confirming GQ-level information, and two teams working independently developed different designs for these screens. Administrators were asked their opinions about the two designs and whether they preferred one design over the other. These findings are included in this report (see section 4.4.1) 2. Research methods We conducted usability interviews with individual administrators using wireframes representing initial conceptions of the screens of the Dashboard. Wireframes (similar to mockups, paper prototypes, or storyboards) are used in the development and evaluation of software to determine and assess the flow of screens and presentation of user tasks. They can be used to identify potential problems early in the development process so they can be addressed before a functional prototype is created (Brinck et al. 2002, pp. 238-243). The wireframes used in this study were created using Microsoft Excel to map out the entire Dashboard instrument and its functional requirements. A subset of wireframes were selected for inclusion in this study that represented the core path through the Dashboard and key tasks and functions. Some screens were also selected because they present novel questionnaire design features such as data entry fields located in otherwise static tables presenting GQ-level data. The wireframes generally approximate individual Dashboard pages and present questions/instructions, data entry fields, navigation and help buttons, and other functionality such as downloading Excel spreadsheets containing GQ-level data. Administrators were informed that the wireframes were part of the early development stage and represented an approximation of the instrument’s interface. The wireframes used in this study are presented in relevant sections throughout the report. It should be noted that any names or addresses presented in the wireframes are fictitious. Usability interviews were conducted with seven GQ administrators from around the United States who are potential users of the Dashboard. These administrators represented the following types of GQs: • GQ Type 501, College/University Student Housing • GQ Type 901, Workers’ Group Living Quarters and Job Corps Centers • GQ Type 902, Religious Group Quarters Most participants were interviewed virtually using Microsoft Teams and the wireframes were presented to them through screen-sharing. One participant was interviewed in-person at their work site and shown the wireframes on the interviewer’s work laptop. Participants reviewed one wireframe screen at a time and were asked to comment on what they thought was the purpose of each screen and anything that may have caught their attention. Then they were

7 U.S. Census Bureau asked follow-up probes about specific features of each screen and, after reviewing all screens, about the overall workflow. They were also asked their opinions about the tasks they would be expected to perform in the course of using the Dashboard, and about the feasibility of email for delivering census invitations to their residents. Most participants were recruited from a list of GQ administrators who had participated in previous research conducted by our group and who said they were willing to participate in future research. Some participants were recruited from a list of stakeholder contacts provided by the Decennial Census Management Division. Interviews typically took 60-90 minutes, and participants were not provided an incentive to take part in the study. This study addressed the following research questions: 1. What do GQ administrators think of the tasks that would be expected of them – providing residents’ contact information, distributing login information to residents, monitoring response and sending reminders – and how would they carry out these tasks? 2. Do GQ administrators understand the tasks as they are presented in the Dashboard wireframe, and what are reasons the tasks may not be clearly understood, if any? 3. Do GQ administrators want any additional functionality not offered by the current Dashboard design? 4. Do GQ administrators think email is feasible for delivering census invitations and facilitating response from GQ residents? The remainder of this report presents findings and recommendations from the usability interviews. Recommendations are included in the final section. 3. Assumptions and Limitations The main limitation of this study is that it was conducted with a small, nonrepresentative sample of GQ administrators, and thus the findings may not generalize to the broader universe of GQ administrators and GQ types. Also, the wireframes used in this study were developed for the purpose of documenting requirements and not with usability testing in mind. Although they were deemed fit for usability testing, they do not perfectly replicate the appearance of web pages; thus their draft appearance may have resulted in some biased or confused reactions from participants.

8 U.S. Census Bureau 4. Results 4.1 Administrators’ opinions about the ISR enumeration option Most administrators found the idea of sending email invitations to their residents to complete an online questionnaire acceptable. For example, one administrator said, “I think that would be great… I'm really cool with Option 1… Take out the middleman. I think my role is to present that the Census Bureau needs to get this information and how they're going to do it, that they're sending an email, please do it, and just leave it at that.” Another administrator who provided residents’ data using eResponse3 in the 2020 Census commented that offering the option for residents to complete their own census form would lead to more-complete data: “It would have an improved accuracy over filling out the census by the administrator, especially for some of the ethnic self-identification components. It will be a little bit more work on the part of myself as the administrator, making sure that people complete it, but I think that that extra work is probably worthwhile in terms of providing better data.” An administrator of a facility with younger residents commented that they are comfortable with online forms and would be more likely to respond to email with a link than a paper letter: “I think Option 1 would probably be the easiest to do… Because their email address is something simple [to provide], and… if they [can] click on a link and go to it, it'll definitely be the easiest for them… For our residents… there's more chance they're going to do it [if they can click a link to a web questionnaire].” All administrators described personal experience with internal surveys of their residents and several had experience coordinating with the decennial census, the American Community Survey, or other federal surveys. Their experiences informed their opinions about the likely efficacy of applying ISR procedures in their organizations, optimal strategies for maximizing self- response to the census, and the potential burden associated with coordination. Several administrators commented on their experiences with surveys and their use of various strategies: “We have about a thirty percent return rate for online questionnaires, so you’re going to miss a lot of people that way.” “We do annual surveys with our students, and there are some that log in right away and do it, and there are some that have to be reminded a few times to do it, and then there's a 3 eResponse is a web-based instrument introduced with the 2020 Census which enables GQ administrators to provide residents’ data from organizational records via Excel spreadsheets.

There would be students who do not understand the importance of what they're doing, so we've got to communicate that.” Administrators said they would communicate with their residents about the census to motivate them to complete their questionnaires, using personal and other means of communication. Several administrators said they would provide advance notice to their residents to expect the census request, saying things like, “I think having an email coming directly from the census, with forewarning from us [is best].” “It might be appropriate for our housing officer to send a note saying the Census Bureau is going to be contacting you in the next week, and you have to respond. We'd meet with the students just to let them know, hey, this is coming, and this is what you need to do when you get it. If you get it and you want help doing it, these are the people you see and we'll walk you through it. All of those options, we'd make sure they knew in advance it was coming.” Some administrators said they would explain to their residents what the census is and why it is important that they respond: “I would send out an email and say, hey, the census is about to send you an email with a survey. We would like one hundred percent completion because by doing so you provide resources to our community.
