The first concern they shared was that expecting residents to type a code to log in to the ISR instrument is potentially problematic: “For students to have to type in that number, you're reducing your response rate, the more difficult it is.” “Why would you send a unique ID if you don't have to? Option 1 you don't need the unique ID and Option 2 you do. And 3 looks like you just go straight to a questionnaire.”

11 U.S. Census Bureau One administrator said their residents would be likely to respond by smartphone and such devices would have a higher risk of input errors: “There's a lot of chances that a student will put in a Census ID wrong… [and] they end up getting [an error message] and they just, they won't take any effort to do it over again… Most of them will be doing this on a cell phone, which, when you're doing links and typing in a lot of numbers, it becomes much more complicated.” Another administrator thought residents would have trouble keeping track of a Census ID, although he appeared to be thinking of it as something that residents would need to retain rather than the credential needed to access the online questionnaire: “Option 2, sending a unique ID by email, that could be confusing, you want to avoid that one. If folks have a number that they've got to write down, you're going to lose a lot of people that have to write down that number. They're going to know their social security number, they're not going to record their census ID number.” Administrators with younger residents said some of them would likely have concerns about the legitimacy of the request and security of their data. One administrator said, “There's definitely some questions that are going to be coming up about privacy, protecting your privacy and things when you're putting in that kind of information, especially when you're putting it online. There's a lot of people that are going to be having some questions about it… I think the biggest thing will be my students looking at it and thinking it's a scam, it's spam or something like that. That's why I think actually sitting down and talking to them or telling them hey, you're getting this, it's an official email [would be important].” Another administrator shared this opinion based on experience with coordinating the American Community Survey: “I occasionally get pushback from students asking if the monthly Census thingy is a legit thing.” Two administrators indicated that their housing includes family housing and expressed confusion with regard to whether and how they would be expected to coordinate communication with such residents: “My question would be that, because we do have family student housing… For partners, spouses, children, I don't know how we would do that.” “So a family of five is going to get five letters (i.e., emails)?”

12 U.S. Census Bureau 4.1.1 Opinions of administrators at large universities In contrast to the administrators described above, two administrators at large universities did not readily embrace the ISR option. Both of these administrators had served as the points-of- contact for their universities during the 2020 Census and used eResponse to provide residents’ response data. Both said they would prefer to continue to use eResponse because they would expect it to be less burdensome and more efficient than ISR and it would ensure their ability to enumerate all residents. Both also cited the potentially extensive follow-up with nonrespondents as a concern: “I think it just depends on my workload, how feasible it would be… A part of me says it might be easier to let the students complete their own form, and at the same time… there may be more follow-up that needs to be done, and I don't know who would manage that, if it would be me or if it would be the folks from the U.S. Census Bureau, and so it might be more efficient and easier for me to provide all the data.” “I don't love this whole approach, because to me the electronic data transfer is the best answer that I've seen in terms of being sure to get information, not having to rely on students… Students just aren't going to do it. Am I as the administrator responsible for sending this one out and then I'm done? Or are you putting on me the responsibility to follow up with everybody, send a second, third reminder, so then I somehow have to know who's completed it, who hasn't completed it? If you place that burden on the administrator, I'm running far away from you and changing my phone number.” The latter administrator in particular anticipated that getting self-responses from thousands of residents at their university would be extremely challenging and time-consuming, and he wondered what would be expected of them with regard to those students who would not respond at all in spite of their efforts: “Chasing down 15,000 students, maybe 6,000 of them do it the first time, you know, and maybe half do it, maybe 10,000 do it, I don't know. So I've still got maybe 5,000 students I've still got to [follow up with], first just figuring out who [has not responded]... Slowly you'll get diminishing numbers of people who say yes, and finally you'll get the ones who just won't do it, so… what's the next step? Do you knock on the door, and call them? I think it's a nonstarter… I'm just so repulsed by the possibility of having to take on this full-time job for weeks... There's just no way.” Another concern expressed by these two administrators is about the sharing of students’ information. They both noted that the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) would not allow them to share students’ email addresses if they opted out of sharing. For example, one said,

13 U.S. Census Bureau “Our students are given the option to have confidential records... So it's possible, even using this method, I wouldn't be able to give you the full list of our residents for that census.” Both administrators noted prior requests from the Census Bureau for which information was unavailable for substantial numbers of students who had opted out of FERPA directory information sharing. One cited their experience with the 2020 Census: “Around a quarter of our students opted out of directory information [sharing].” The other administrator shared their experience with the American Community Survey: “I have to provide a list of ten students per residence hall every month, and usually from that list of ten students, I would say three, maybe four have directory confidential records… It seems like a small number but that could be up to like thirty or forty percent (of all students).” One administrator thought providing information for all students who had not opted-out would not be feasible and was potentially risky from the university’s perspective: “I don't think we're giving you [all] the email addresses… I used to provide information to census takers on the American Community Survey, ten a month in a building… That's different from handing you 15,000 email addresses, for every student living on campus. Some administrators commented spontaneously on the links to help videos on various screens, and reacted in various ways: “I like the ability to watch the video there.” “Watch a video on how to do this, boy that sounds like a fun video.” Some administrators indicated they may watch help videos if they had a problem with the instrument that they could not figure out or get past. For example, when asked whether they ever watch help videos when using a new application, one administrator said they do “when it won't go to the next step.” Another administrator expressed a similar thought:

34 U.S. Census Bureau “I do look at video tutorials, and I think my choice to watch a video like that would be based on how intuitive the system appears to be. If it looks really clear, I'd be confident that I would be able to navigate it without watching the video. But if I look at a system and I think, I'm not sure, then I might be more inclined to watching the video.” One administrator expressed an aversion to help videos and said they prefer telephone support or written guidance: “If I'm desperate I might do that. I think I'd be more inclined to call my contact, if I'm really flummoxed and I don't know what's going on… When I'm browsing in other contexts, I don't have a lot of patience for videos… I'd much rather have a popup that gave me a very brief sentence or two on, this is how you do this or that... I'd be more inclined to go to a written set of instructions than I would to kind of watch videos.” Some administrators emphasized that help videos for the Dashboard would need to be short and concise because their time is limited. For example, one commented, “Usually it tells how long the video is. If it's a long video, no, because I don't have time. But if it's a three- to five-minute video, yes, I will watch it really quickly… So the shorter it is, the more apt I am to click on it and get the information I need, so it would have to be as concise as possible, or bite-sized pieces.” Another administrator commented that it would be better to have numerous short videos rather than fewer, lengthier videos, and that they are clearly labeled with regard to specific procedures: “I would make sure with each video you put the amount of time and be specific about what it's going to tell you. If you have to break them down into bite sized pieces to keep from having a really long video, that's helpful too. I'd rather see 10 one- or three-minute videos than two 15-minute videos listed.” 5. DISCUSSION Most administrators liked the idea of enabling their residents to complete their census questionnaires online, and preferred to allow the Census Bureau to send email invitations rather than take on the distribution of emails themselves. These administrators also said that they would be willing to send their own notifications to residents to expect the census request and to encourage and assist them with responding. All administrators described having previous experience with conducting and/or coordinating surveys of their residents, and their experiences informed their opinions about the most efficient ways to maximize responses and expectations about efficient strategies and likely

35 U.S. Census Bureau outcomes. They anticipated issues like having to identify nonrespondents for targeted follow- ups and the potential for greater burden if they chose to send invitations and reminders themselves. However, most also described automated methods for mass distribution of emails including use of institutional email systems and Microsoft Word mail merge that would make such hands-on coordination feasible, if not necessarily more attractive. The ready availability of resident contact information and willingness to share it with the Census Bureau also made ISR an acceptable enumeration option for most administrators. By contrast, the administrators from two larger universities, each responsible for dozens of GQs and thousands of residents, preferred the option to provide residents’ information themselves from institutional records via eResponse. They thought this method would be more efficient and would result in a more complete enumeration than relying on students to self-respond. One suggested that GQ ISR could be used to supplement eResponse; students who opted-out of allowing their data to be shared – and therefore were not reportable through eResponse – could be sent ISR invitations by the administrator. This study accomplished its goal of getting feedback on the initial plans for the ISR Dashboard instrument in the form of wireframes. The wireframe enabled users to provide feedback on the screens and enabled us to test whether users would understand the purpose and the expected task on each screen. Generally, the intended uses of most screens were clear. The one screen with an intended use that was not clear to several administrators – selecting a GQ for which to enter resident contact information via online spreadsheet on a subsequent screen (Figure 7) – presented the first task in a sequence that spanned screens. This more complicated task appears to require a clearer instruction but otherwise the tasks themselves were comprehensible. Administrators also indicated comfort with using Excel to send, receive, and manipulate information. Although some administrators expressed ambivalence or even reticense to use help videos, most indicated they might be willing to watch videos to clarify confusing aspects of the instrument if the videos were short (three to five minutes at most), focused, and clearly labeled with topic addressed and duration. 6. Recommendations 6.1 General recommendations for screen design 1. We recommend that the Dashboard screens maintain a simple and consistent page design to facilitate comprehension of the purpose of each screen. 2. Place questions and instructions above data entry fields and other task-oriented features using a clear and consistent format. 3. Include a simple title/header above the question text that describes the response tasks for a given page. 4. Use simple questions/statements to communicate response tasks, and use clear, plain language to describe the expected ISR coordination tasks and in items asking for data.

36 U.S. Census Bureau 5. Avoid the over-use of all-caps to emphasize important information. All-caps may be used to call attention to specific words or short phrases, but should not be used for for more than a few words in a given question. 6. Remove extraneous text that is not needed for understanding the tasks on a given page. 7. Avoid the use of jargon that is not generally understood outside of the Census Bureau. 8. Avoid placing additional text or other features in the upper-left to prevent obscuring or distracting from the question/instruction text. 9. Place buttons related to on-screen functions and navigation buttons on the bottom of the page below the response fields. 10. Use simple and accurate descriptions for button labels. 11. Keep all help-related buttons in the top-right corner of the screen. 6.2 GQ review/update page We recommend that the single-screen design for reviewing and updating GQ-level information be used in the Dashboard rather than the multi-page version. 6.3 Select option to provide residents’ contact information We recommend that users be allowed to explore both options (Excel template and online spreadsheet) before deciding which they want to use, rather than requiring them to choose one before they are able to try it. 6.4 Select GQ to go to online spreadsheet page 1. We recommend that a more detailed instruction that describes the purpose of the screen be provided. For example: Click on each Group Quarters in the list below to go to an online spreadsheet that you can use to provide contact information for the residents of that Group Quarters. 2. We recommend that GQ names be presented as clickable links. 3. We recommend that list the of GQs be presented in a format that looks different from that used for tables intended for data entry. 4. We recommend that the “save and continue” button be grayed out until all GQs have been completed. 6.5 Online spreadsheet pages 1. We recommend that users be allowed to paste multiple cells/rows/columns and that an instruction be provided indicating that this feature is available. 2. We recommend that users be able to specify a number of rows needed.

37 U.S. Census Bureau 3. We recommend that examples of GQ-level or resident-level data be formatted differently from the corresponding data entry fields and that they be clearly labeled as examples. 6.6 Report Dashboard page 1. We recommend that users be able to obtain lists of ID’s in Excel that have not been used, to make identifying nonrespondents easier. 2. We recommend providing concise instructions for using basic functions in Excel to compare two spreadsheets and identify duplicates and unique records. 6.7 Help videos 1. If help videos are provided, we recommend that they be short (no more than 3 minutes) and each one focused on a specific task for a given page, to make it easy for Dashboard users to find solutions to problems they encounter. Video links should have clear labels indicating the tasks they address and their length. 2. We recommend creating a separate button or link for videos in the help bar in the upper-right corner of the Dashboard pages to make them easy to find. If possible, hovering over the link should open a drop-down list of the videos and clicking a video link should open the video in a pop-up window to avoid having users leave the page for which they are seeking help. 7. ii US Census Bureau Abstract When developing a questionnaire for web administration, respondent burden is a major concern. It may be tempting to condense multiple questions into a single grid or other format to reduce the number of screens shown to the respondent. However, this may not accomplish its intended purpose. As time spent answering a single survey question varies by the question’s complexity and the cognitive burden placed on the respondent, condensed questions may not actually save time in some circumstances. Using a question about which children in the household eat what school-provided meals, this experiment aims to test if more screens do take more time, even if the questions being asked are simpler to answer when kept separate. The decomposed version asks first which children eat school-provided meals (with an option for none) and then shows a simple grid listing only the relevant children and the two possible school meals (breakfast and lunch). The analysis compares the time to answer this series to the time to answer a comparable “condensed” survey item which uses a single grid to list all children in the household, and options for both possible school meals and “No meals”. Findings indicate that the decomposed version appears to be faster, but this is partially due to the number of households with no children who eat school-provided meals. In this case, the first question of the decomposed version is significantly faster than the condensed question. However, the condensed question is significantly faster for respondents with at least one child eating a school meal. The time saved in the decomposed version is greater than the time saved in the condensed version though, leading to the overall efficiency of the decomposed question. 1 US Census Bureau Introduction Several Census Bureau household surveys, such as the Current Population Survey (CPS), Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the CPS, and Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) are introducing web-based data collections to complement their existing interviewer-administered modes. As various experts work together to develop the new web questionnaires, decisions must be made concerning respondent burden, specifically, whether condensing and combining questions to reduce the number of screens results in quicker survey completion times. As time spent answering a single survey question varies by the question’s complexity and the cognitive burden placed on the respondent, time may not be saved in some circumstances. While qualitative testing can help identify questions that require more thought or elicit confusion, a controlled experiment could help quantify the effect. The test below was designed to determine if the completion time of a condensed question is significantly faster than a comparable, but less cognitively burdensome, decomposed question. The “condensed” survey question captures response(s) in a single grid and asks for data that could reasonably be collected by two separate survey questions. Its comparable “decomposed” version has two simpler questions that must be combined during analysis to determine the same information. The experiment captures the time per question, with the time summed across the two questions for the decomposed version. The comparison of the question times and multivariate analyses exploring what factors contributed to longer or shorter times, evaluate whether more screens take more time, even when the questions are simpler to answer. Data The experiment was hosted on a web survey of Census Bureau Research Panel members. Participants were recruited into the Panel database when they agreed to be contacted about future research opportunities at the end of the Census Household Pulse survey (HPS). The sample for this data collection included respondents recruited from the Phase 4.2 HPS administered from July to September 2024 (n= 30,000). The online survey was open from 3-15 December 2024 and available in English only. The survey asked some basic demographics, ages of children in the household, questions about carrying and spending cash, preferences for incentive payment method, cost for utilities, and the questions in this experiment. It took approximately 15 minutes. No incentive was offered. The Panel aimed to collect approximately 10,000 responses and used two reminders, beyond the initial email invitation, before ending data collection because the goal was reached. The 500 bounce backs were assumed eligible, for an AAPOR RR2 of 33%.

2 US Census Bureau Questions in the experiment The questions in the experiment asked which school-provided meals the children in the household routinely ate. Respondents were randomly assigned to only one version—condensed (Group C) or decomposed (Group D). The condensed question asked this as a grid listing all children in the household and checkboxes for each meal (breakfast and lunch) and no meals (see Figure 1). This question mirrored the format of a condensed question tested in the first round of cognitive testing of the ASEC web-based questionnaire. The decomposed version of the question asked which children usually ate school-provided meals, with an option for “none”, and then followed up with a simpler grid including only the relevant children and the two meals (see Figure 1). If no children ate school-provided meals, the second question was not shown. The grids for both questions appeared the same on computers and mobile phones, and hence, were not reformatted for smaller screens. For respondents with only one child, the question wording was slightly different for both the condensed and decomposed versions. Both versions read: “Does [child’s name] usually eat a complete breakfast and /or lunch prepared by the school?” The condensed version was followed by the same four-column grid as for multiple children (but with one row only). The decomposed version of the question was followed by radio buttons for Yes and No (instead of the multiple response list of all the children). The follow-up question showed the grid with checkboxes for breakfast and lunch but with a single row. While the questionnaire did not collect a household roster, parents were asked how many children under 18 lived in the household and then asked to provide initials or nicknames for up to five children. These abbreviations were used as fills for the questions about school-provided meals. Dependent variable To compare response times for the two versions of the question, “page submit” times were recorded from the Qualtrics instrument. “Page submit” measures the total amount of time, in seconds, the respondent spent on a page or screen. The instrument displayed one question per screen. All time estimates were trimmed at the 95th percentile to omit the influence of extremely high values. Short times were considered valid and not trimmed. Trimmed times were summed to generate a total time for the decomposed question. Respondents who broke off or skipped the experimental questions were omitted from the analysis. The model included an indicator for the cases that were trimmed. The distributions of the response times for each question version, after trimming large values, are shown in Table 1. In Group C, 4.9% of cases were trimmed. Of these, 73% had times under 60 seconds and 94% had times below two minutes. Times were trimmed to a maximum of 30.4 seconds. Across the two questions in the decomposed version (Group D), 6.2% of the cases were trimmed. Of the 50 cases trimmed for the first question, 82% had times under 60 seconds and

Respondents’ highest level of education was recoded into an indicator for having graduated college or not. Device type was self-reported as “phone”, “laptop or desktop computer”, or “tablet”. Missing data for device type were imputed using paradata that captured the operating system, indicating phones, tablets, and computers. The analysis controlled for the number of children who could have eaten school meals. Respondents reported having up to nine children under 18 in the household but the school meals question asked about no more than five children, using the up to five nicknames provided in an earlier question. Therefore, the <15 cases with more than five children (approximately evenly split across the two question versions) were recoded as “5”, and the variable is interpreted as the number of children included in the school meals questions. For the condensed question, this number corresponds to the number of rows shown in the grid. For the decomposed question, it corresponds to the number of response options in the first survey question in the series. This count was also recoded into an indicator for one-child households. Supplementary analysis examined the effect of reporting no school-provided meals for any children versus at least one child eating at least one meal. This variable was recoded from the responses to the condensed question and the first decomposed question.

5 US Census Bureau Methods Chi square tests of independence were used to evaluate differences in demographics between the two question versions, and an independent samples t-test was used to compare the mean response times. Differences in the response times were modeled first with a reduced regression model and then using four multiple regression models. In the reduced model, question type was the only covariate used to predict response time. The full models incorporated controls for the respondents’ level of education, sex, device type, number of children included in the question, and an indicator of trimmed timing data. There are two versions of the full model that vary how the number of children is treated—as a continuous count or a dichotomous variable for one-child households. The model with the indicator for one child is used to explore interaction effects between the experimental group and the indicator for one child in the household, and between the experimental group and the indicator for no children eating any school-provided meals. Results There were 2,000 respondents who had children and answered all of the questions in the version of the question to which they were assigned. The cases were evenly split between the condensed (49.1%) and decomposed (50.9%) versions. Within each version, a similar proportion of respondents reported having only one child in the household (44.8% in Group C; 41.4% in Group D). In addition, there were no significant differences between the groups in the distribution of sex, college graduates, and device used. Evaluating the mean times, the decomposed version of the school meals question took significantly less time to complete than the condensed version: 11.8 vs. 12.8 seconds (t(2,000) = 3.321; p < 0.001). Despite the decomposed question containing two parts, respondents completed this question, on average, one second faster than the condensed, single question. The speed of the decomposed question was also evident in the regression analyses of the reduced and full models showing only main effects. Before introducing the indicator for no meals selected (see Table 2, Models 1-3), respondents to the decomposed version were roughly one second faster to respond compared to those who answered the condensed question (e.g., β = -1.3; p < 0.001 for the full model with an indicator for only one child under 18 (Model 3)), on average, even after controlling for other characteristics. Models 2 and 3 also show that having more children to answer for lengthened the time to answer, with each child taking, on average, 1.8 seconds longer (see Table 2, Model 2), controlling for other factors. College graduates, those completing the survey on computer or tablet, and respondents reporting for only one child all had significantly faster response times. An interaction between the experimental group and the indicator for one child was not significant (not shown).

7 US Census Bureau Half (50.6%) of the respondents who answered the decomposed version had children who did not eat a school-provided meal, and therefore, did not receive the second question in the series. These respondents were still included in the analysis since they did not break off or skip questions, and they are comparable to the Group C respondents who also had children who did not eat any school-provided meals (40.3%). With only one non-grid question to answer, a short response time is expected for these cases and that may be driving the shorter overall response times for the decomposition version. To explore this, supplemental analyses were conducted to see how much more quickly respondents answered the decomposed version when no children ate school meals. When a variable indicating that none of the children ate any school-provided meals was added to the model, it was strongly significant (see Table 2, Model 4). The coefficient indicates that, on average and controlling for other factors, respondents with no children who ate school-provided meals answered the question nearly five seconds faster! (β = -4.7; p <0.001). Overall, the decomposed version is still faster than the condensed, controlling for other factors, but the difference is reduced to -0.8 seconds. So, answering only the first decomposed question explains some of the efficiency of the decomposed version but not all. Other notable results of Model 4 are the increased adjusted R2 and the significance of sex, showing that males take more time to answer than females, on average, controlling for other factors. Model 5 (see Table 2) introduces a significant interaction effect between the version of the question and the indicator for no meals selected. This model and the corresponding plot of the interaction (see Figure 2) show that, when at least one meal is selected, the decomposed version takes 1.5 seconds longer, on average. However, if no meals are selected, the decomposed version is 3.5 seconds faster to complete, more than accounting for the time lost if at least one meal is selected. The difference in these times seems to drive the overall faster completion time of the decomposed version and illustrates that the simpler questions can be answered quickly.

8 US Census Bureau Figure 2. Plot of interaction between no school-provided meals indicator and question version Conclusions Several factors seem to influence how quickly a respondent completed the questions about school meals. Being on a computer, having a college degree, having only one child for whom to answer, and reporting that no children ate school-provided meals all significantly decreased the time to answer either version. Taken together, the decomposed version had faster completion times but that seemed to be moderated by the number of respondents who reported that no children ate school-provided meals. In this situation (where no children ate school meals), the decomposed version, with its single radio button question, was significantly faster than the condensed version, with the grid. The grid used in the condensed version takes time to comprehend and is more cognitively burdensome than the first question in the decomposed version. In addition to navigating the format, simplification of the wording of the question stem and grid’s column headings could make the condensed question easier to comprehend. Given these features, even when no child eats any school meals, there is a minimum time investment to understand both the question and the grid. The interaction effect allows for a rough quantitative measure of this extra time to comprehend the grid over a non-grid question: 3.5 seconds. That is, if a respondent does not receive the second question in the decomposed version, their response times are 3.5 seconds faster, on average, than a respondent reporting no meals in the condensed version, controlling for other factors.

9 US Census Bureau This saved time is larger than the time difference between the two versions when at least one child eats at least one school meal; the condensed version is 1.5 seconds faster, on average, which is half the time savings for the decomposed question. The success of the decomposed question is an artifact of the distribution in the data. If most of the children in both groups had eaten school meals, the decomposed version may be significantly faster overall. The decomposed question is more respectful to respondents’ time and cognitive burden in other ways. Not only is the grid in the follow-up question easier to comprehend, the respondent also spends less time on each page compared to the single page of the condensed version. Being able to advance to the next question quickly contributes to a perceived sense of moving quickly through the questionnaire. This keeps respondents engaged and prevents breakoffs. The decomposed version of the lunch question is still a grid, and it could have been decomposed even further, resulting in three (or more) questions in total. Given the time to read the additional question(s) and advance to the next screen(s), a more decomposed question lunch question would probably not be more efficient than the condensed version. In addition, given the simplicity of the topic (school meals) and the limited number of response options (essentially a Yes/No for two meals), it seems unnecessary to decompose the question further. Depending on how different respondents prefer to recall this information (i.e., focusing on the child or the meal), they either need to see both meals on the screen for the child they are thinking about, or all children listed for a particular meal. The format tested provides the desired cross-section for both preferences. Separating either the children or the meals into additional questions would cause additional cognitive burden, undermining the goal of decomposing the question. Furthermore, separately asking about breakfast and lunch may introduce a confusing repetitiveness which could lead to measurement error or breakoff. While this experiment did not test this type of further decomposed question, even without empirical evidence, I caution against overly decomposing questions. The value of this analysis is not the outcome for this single decomposed question—saving one second on one question is fairly insignificant compared to the overall time to complete the survey. However, decisions throughout the survey, balancing burden and timing, are additive, thereby potentially resulting in significant time savings. In addition, decisions about a single question must be considered in the context of the whole questionnaire. E.g., if the same type of question is asked repeatedly, a series of condensed questions may be more efficient, with the respondent exerting extra time to learn the format on the first question and then moving more quickly through the similar questions. Overall, the goal is to provide questions respondents can answer easily and keep burden, both in terms of time and cognition, to a minimum.

1 U.S. Census Bureau Abstract The 2023 Census Survey was the planned second iteration of the Small-Scale Response Testing (SmaRT) program that is part of the Census Bureau’s Small-Scale Testing Initiative. In preparation for the 2023 Census Survey, the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) at the Census Bureau carried out cognitive testing of the mail materials intended to be sent to respondents who would participate in the survey. Nineteen participants provided feedback during the pretesting, and because the mail materials are bilingual in English and Spanish, testing was conducted in English and Spanish. The research questions included identifying any major comprehension issues with any of the mail materials, investigating how participants responded to the use of plain language, and testing the use of text message reminders to respond to the survey. In this paper, we present our findings and recommendations based on respondent feedback and spontaneous reactions, as well as observational and behavioral data. 4 U.S. Census Bureau INTRODUCTION The 2023 Census Survey was the planned second iteration of the Small-Scale Response Testing (SmaRT) program that is part of the Census Bureau’s Small-Scale Testing Initiative. Although the 2023 Census Survey itself was postponed, this paper documents the pretesting that was carried out in preparation for the survey. SmaRT is the primary small-scale testing vehicle and how testing is being conducted this decade (complementing our two major census tests: the 2026 Census Test and the 2028 Dress Rehearsal). The Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) at the U.S. Census Bureau carried out cognitive testing of the mail materials, as well as usability testing of the internet instrument. This report focuses on the cognitive testing of the different mail materials that respondents would have received as part of the 2023 Census Survey operation had it not been postponed. Previous testing of the 2023 Census Test mail materials are also documented in Feuer et al. (2023). This pretesting took place in June and July of 2023, in preparation for a field test in November 2023 (although this field test was delayed until the spring of 2024). 1.1 Research Questions The main objectives of this pretesting for the 2023 Census Survey were to test the use of plain language in the mail materials, as well as a test of the use of a text message reminder in an A/B test. To test these mail materials, we conducted cognitive interviews in both English and Spanish. Some interviews were conducted virtually, and others were conducted in person. For the remote virtual interviews, all four mailings were sent in advance to the study participant in a United States Postal Service Flat Rate Priority Mail envelope. For the in-person interviews, the materials were presented in person to the participant. The final mailing containing the Final Letter, FAQ insert, paper questionnaire, and prepaid return envelope, was enclosed in an envelope to mimic how these materials would have been sent during the 2023 Census Survey.The research questions for this study were answered by how participants interacted with and responded to the different mail materials. The test administrators (TAs) noted spontaneous verbalizations, observed how participants reacted to and read the materials, and asked probing questions about the materials during debriefing. Our primary research question was to identify any major comprehension issues and review spontaneous feedback of the mail materials, especially looking at the use of plain language and the use of a text message reminder to respond to the survey. We also aimed to suggest revisions to address any comprehension issues. 2. Methods 2.1 Session Methodology The pretesting for the 2023 Census Survey used a series of four mailings. After the initial invitation letter asking them to respond online, respondents who had not answered the survey

5 U.S. Census Bureau would continue to have received the remaining mailings until they respond or until they had received all four mailings. Each mailing contained both English and Spanish for all text. This test also included testing of two text messages incorporated into the schedule of mailings. The mailings and text messages in the testing were: • Invitation Letter inviting the respondent to participate in the 2023 Census Test1 (Appendix A) and FAQ insert (Appendix B) • Reminder Letter (Appendix C) • First text message reminder (Figures 9a-b below) • Reminder Postcard (Appendix D) • Final Letter (Appendix E), FAQ insert, paper questionnaire (Appendix F), mailing envelope (Appendix G), and prepaid return envelope • Second text message reminder (Figures 10a-b below) For this study, we conducted 90-minute cognitive and usability sessions, both in person (n=8) and remotely (n=11). The portion of the session relating to the mail materials took up approximately the first 45 minutes of the 90-minute sessions, while the latter half was devoted to the participant answering the online 2023 Census Survey. We provided the participants with information about the privacy and confidentiality of their responses prior to the interview, and we obtained oral consent to collect data from each participant. Each participant received a monetary incentive of $60 for their participation. Participants were trained by the TA in how to “think aloud” during the session to provide us with spontaneous comments as they read through the mail materials. Remote virtual sessions were conducted using Microsoft (MS) Teams, a videoconferencing application. Prior to the session, the TA led virtual participants through a brief “tech check” to familiarize the participant with the MS Teams application that would be used during the session, in order to save time during the session itself. Remote session participants used their own laptop, tablet, or smartphone to complete the interview and debriefing. For the in-person sessions, the participants were still asked to join a MS Teams meeting so that other project members could observe the session. While in-person participants generally also used their own laptop, tablet, or smartphone to complete the tasks, the TA also had a laptop with them that the participant could use in case of technical problems. Many sessions also had a notetaker to assist the TA in capturing the participants’ comments and behavior. Some sessions had other members of the project team observing the session as well. These observers could provide the TA with additional questions for the participant at the end of the session if time allowed. The TA and notetaker (if applicable) recorded the session using the Snagit recording application. Data used in this analysis were spontaneous verbalizations elicited by the use of a think-aloud protocol, as well as participant feedback obtained during the debriefing portion of the study that 1 The materials for this pretesting were created at a time when the test was still called the 2023 Census Test. 7 U.S. Census Bureau 3. Results 3.1 Findings 3.1.1 Due Date On the Final Letter, as well as the envelope the Final Letter materials were enclosed in, we included a Due Date. On the envelope, the Due Date appeared to the left of the address window (Figure 1), and appeared in both English and Spanish. On the Final Letter, the Due Date appeared in the upper left portion of the letter (Figure 2), below the Census logo and address. The Due Date appears in the same location on both the English and Spanish sides of the Final Letter. Figure 1. Final Letter mailing envelope with address window

8 U.S. Census Bureau Figure 2. Final Letter top half All the English-speaking participants noticed the Due Date on both the envelope and letter, and commented positively on it. Comments from participants included that the Due Date stood out, was the first thing participants noticed, and helped them prioritize what needs to get done. Some participants also spontaneously mentioned on earlier mailings that they would like to know when the deadline was to complete the survey, before even seeing the final mailing. Other participants suggested adding the Due Date to the information in the FAQ document. Some Spanish speakers did not notice the Due Date on the envelope. One Spanish-speaking participant reasoned that since there were so many people responding, they would need to complete the survey earlier than the Due Date. Another Spanish speaker thought that the Due Date was an approximate date, saying “Me están avisando que tengo que hacerlo antes de esta fecha… yo pienso que eso es como una fecha falsa porque… es como para darme una idea.” (They are telling me that I have to do it before this date… I think that this is like a false date because… it's like to give me an idea). Overall, we recommended that the fourth mailing keep the Due Date on the materials, and that the Due Date also be included on earlier mailing materials, such as the first and second mailings, on both the letter and the envelope. We also recommended continuing to test the timing of when to alert respondents about the Due Date. Although participants say they want a Due Date, one that is too far in the future may also depress response. 3.1.2 “Required by Law” There is language on the first mailing, both on the envelope and the Invitation Letter, informing respondents that their response is required by law. All of the English-speaking participants and some Spanish speakers spontaneously noticed and commented on this language on the Invitation Letter. Some participants noted that this language meant that it was “serious”, while another said that it made them anxious. Multiple respondents (1 English, 2 Spanish) spontaneously wondered what would happen if they did not respond, noting that there was no penalty listed.

9 U.S. Census Bureau In general, we recommend keeping the “required by law” language. Although some participants expressed fear and dislike for the messaging, it is not clear that it would depress response. We recommend further testing looking into response rates for different demographics when this language is used. 3.1.3 “10 minutes” The Invitation Letter and the FAQs also included bolded messaging that the survey would only take 10 minutes. Some English-speaking participants noticed the messaging and commented positively. Others, including all Spanish-speaking participants, did not spontaneously comment, but when they were directed to the messaging, they also commented positively. Participants said that they appreciated having the information, and that the short length would make them more inclined to complete the survey immediately. A couple of participants noted that the mention of 10 minutes was not on other mailings, and they would like to see it elsewhere too. We recommended keeping the “10 minutes” language on the Invitation Letter and FAQs, and adding it to other mailings as well. 3.1.4 Reminder Letter The second letter participants received was a Reminder Letter (Appendix C). In general, participants in both languages understood the purpose as a simple reminder, although some participants in each language expressed confusion about receiving a second letter if they had already responded to the first letter. One participant mentioned the toll-free number and that they would call to make sure that their response was received, stating “I might wonder why was the letter generated if my responses were received. So I’d think maybe my responses were NOT received, so I would call the toll-free number and I don’t know if they would know me by my Census ID number.” Several participants stated they were inclined to disregard the Reminder Letter due to the similarity to the Invitation Letter. One participant pointed out that if someone was against the contents of the Invitation Letter, they couldn’t see what the Reminder Letter was doing differently to incentivize them to respond. Another indicated that they would throw the letter away because it seemed identical to the first letter. Because of this, we recommended making the Reminder Letter look sufficiently different from the Invitation Letter to seem intentional to respondents. 3.1.5 “Please do so today” On the second letter, there was new messaging that says “If you have already responded, thank you. If not, please do so today by following these two steps:”. Some participants commented that the bolded text in this sentence meant that the due date is “today.” Other participants commented on the polite nature of the sentence, especially the inclusion of “please.” The polite urgency of the sentence seemed to encourage prompt response. As a result, we recommended keeping this sentence.

10 U.S. Census Bureau 3.1.6 Plain language One of the primary research questions for this round of SmaRT testing was to test plain language in the mailing materials. The language used in the letters was inspired by the American Community Survey (ACS) Strategic Framework research (Martinez et al. 2023), which aimed to reduce repetition in mailing materials and improve their readability as a primary research goal. This testing borrowed heavily from the simplified language used in the ACS Strategic Framework materials. The plain language appeared to work well with participants in this testing. There was no apparent confusion about the messaging in the letters, and participants understood the call to action in each of the mail materials. We recommend continuing to use plain language. 3.1.7 “Help your community” We tested the inclusion of text stating that responding would “help your community” on the Invitation letter, the Reminder Letter, and the second reminder text message. There seemed to be mixed reactions to this messaging. Some participants did not feel like the “help your community” language would inspire them to complete the survey more than the “required by law” language would. One participant said helping their community sounded “too cheerleader-y,” while another thought that it sounded too political. Some also said that they would like more details about how their response would help their community. Conversely, some other participants said that the polite language and messaging about helping their community would inspire them to complete the survey. They mentioned that it made them feel excited to participate. One participant said “If you don’t speak up about your neighborhood and community, how can others know what it needs?” Overall, we recommended maintaining a mix in the mail materials of the “required by law” language mentioned earlier, and the “help your community language,” since the former works well for some respondents and the latter works well for others. We also recommended further testing about including the types of ways that responding could help a community, for example with parks, roads, community centers, schools, hospitals, or prisons. This would provide insight into what types of community assistance matters most to respondents. 3.1.8 Confidentiality The Reminder Letter includes bolded language that “your answers are confidential (Title 13, U.S. Code).” Some participants in both English and Spanish spontaneously commented on this messaging, saying that it was good and important. Some participants said that they would look up what Title 13 was, while some others suggested including language about confidentiality on all the mailings.

11 U.S. Census Bureau While the Reminder Letter itself had language reading “your answers are confidential,” we also asked participants how they felt about alternate wording “your answers are protected.” All English-speaking participants understood both, but preferred “your answers are confidential.” Spanish-speakers also understood the term confidential, with one participant stating that it meant “que mis respuestas, no es que no las van a divulgar, pero por ejemplo, mi nombre no va a aparecer” (that my answers, it’s not that they aren’t going to share them, but for example, my name is not going to appear). Generally Spanish speakers did not have a preference between the two options, although one participant felt that “your answers are protected” would be better because they felt more people would understand that than “your answers are confidential.” When asked if they believed there was a difference between “confidential” and “completely confidential” in this context, participants in both languages said that there was no real difference. We recommended that the confidentiality language remain the same as the current mailing in the Reminder Letter, and that it be added to all the mail materials. 3.1.9 Census ID “missing” from mailings The Census ID was only indicated on the Invitation Letter and the Reminder Letter. This led several English-speaking participants to spontaneously note that the other mailings (the Reminder Postcard and the Final Letter) were lacking a Census ID. This was not spontaneously mentioned by any Spanish speakers. Participants said that they would have had to have saved earlier mailings to know that information, and they were not sure whether they would have saved them. Although participants noted the Census ID was missing from the last two mailings, the ID was included, but not identified as such. Shown in Figures 3 and 4 below, the Census ID appears below the barcode. On the Reminder Postcard (Figure 3), the Census ID 1234-1234-1234 is not identified because it is fully visible and not inside an envelope. Similarly, on the final mailing (Figure 4), the same Census ID is below the barcode on the Paper Questionnaire. The barcode, Census ID, and address all show through the window of the envelope, and because this is fully visible (not obscured by the envelope), the Census ID is not identified as such.2 2 Note: The figures in this paper use test data for demonatration purposes only and do not represent actual participant data.

The front of the envelope (Figure 1, repeated here as Figure 7) showed the “Your response is required by law” language, as well as the Due Date. Some participants also noticed the URL on the reverse side of the envelope and commented positively on that as well. No Spanish speakers spontaneously commented on the envelope. Reverse side of the final mailing envelope 3.1.11 Paper Questionnaire Generally, participants said that they liked that the Paper Questionnaire was included in the final mailing. Participants had mixed responses about how they would complete the questionnaire, with some saying that they would fill out the Paper Questionnaire, and others saying that they would still complete the survey online. There did not seem to be any preference for paper versus internet related to age or language spoken in our sample. Participants noticed and appreciated that the mailing came with a postage paid return envelope. Some participants said that they would expect to receive the Paper Questionnaire earlier, such as in the third mailing. One participant said they hoped to receive it earlier because “If I hadn’t responded already, it’s because I wanted the paper questionnaire.” Another participant, a Spanish speaker, said they would wait for a Paper Questionnaire because they pay all of their bills by mailing things back in postage paid return envelopes. We recommended in future testing that respondents be provided with a way to request a Paper Questionnaire, such as by calling to request one. 3.1.12 Sampling Information Several English-speaking participants spontaneously asked about how they were selected to participate in the survey. One participant mentioned not seeing any information about sampling in the FAQs. Others mentioned that they would ask their neighbors or family members whether they had also received the letter from the Census Bureau. One participant said that if it is required by law, they assume that everyone in the neighborhood would be equally required to complete the survey. We recommended that information about sampling and selection be included in the FAQs for respondents to reference. We recommended the following language as an example of an FAQ that could be included to address this: Q: Why has my household been contacted to participate in a survey?

15 U.S. Census Bureau A: Your household may be selected to participate in a survey. The U.S. Census Bureau randomly selected your household through a process of scientific sampling. We collect information from a smaller group to produce estimates for the entire population. 3.1.13 Enumerator at the door Some participants, both in English and Spanish, pointed out the sentence that if they do not respond by the due date, a Census Bureau interviewer may come to their home to complete the survey in person. Most participants, either spontaneously or when probed, said that this would motivate them to complete the survey online. In particular, one Spanish-speaking participant said that it would make them nervous to complete the survey with someone at the door. A few participants said that they would welcome, or even prefer someone coming to their door, and therefore would not complete the survey online or on paper. One participant said “I might just not respond so someone will come to my home. I’m 70 years old and retired. I enjoy visitors.” Because this was a small minority, we recommended no change, and that the language about an enumerator coming to their home stay in the mailing materials. 3.1.14 Language of materials Most Spanish speakers had no trouble finding the Spanish language side of the materials, although some had difficulty finding it. One participant said that they would wait for their children to get home to translate the materials for them. Another participant said they would call the phone number listed on the letter to try to get information in Spanish. These participants had to be instructed by the interviewer to flip the letter over to be able to continue with the interview. Another participant had a difficult time figuring out how to fill out the paper questionnaire in Spanish. They said they felt like they had to complete the form in English. Even though they felt like there was a way to respond in Spanish, they did not know how. Currently, on the letters, the instruction on the English side to flip the letter over to see the Spanish text is found at the bottom of the letters. Spanish-speaking participants were not reading all the way through an English letter to look for such a message at the bottom of the letter. We recommended that future testing investigate whether the instruction were more effective at the top of the letters. 3.1.15 Text messages Part of our testing included getting participant feedback on text message reminders. Participants were shown text message reminders after the Reminder Letter (mailing 2) and again after the final mailing. Each of these text messages had two versions, one that included a link to the survey (Figures 9a and 10a) and one that did not (Figures 9b and 10b).

Second reminder text messages For both the first and second text messages, we asked participants for their preference between the A and B versions (with and without the link to the survey). All participants who expressed a preference preferred the text with the link, although several participants preferred that the link be in the middle of the text message instead of at the beginning. Some participants said that they would ignore the message either way. In English testing, some participants said that they would click the link to respond to the survey. One participant in particular assumed that including the link in the text message meant that the survey must be short and easy. Another participant said that they would respond ‘HELP’ to get more information. Yet another thought that the “short survey” mentioned in the text message was not the Census Survey itself, but rather a satisfaction survey. Several English-speaking participants felt that the tone of the first text message was rude, demanding, and not polite. Participants mentioned that they wanted more of a preamble to the message and for the language to be more polite. Generally, we recommended including the link to the survey in all text messages. We also recommended future split panel testing with the link

18 U.S. Census Bureau in different places (e.g. at the beginning of the text, in the middle of the text). This will allow the team to analyze whether there is a bump in responses related to the position or possibly length of the link. We also recommended changing “short survey” to the name of the survey, for example “the 2023 Census Survey.” The text messages in this study were only provided in English, but they were still tested with Spanish-speaking participants. Spanish speakers said that they had a difficult time with the text messages being in English. Some Spanish-speaking participants said that they would assume the texts were a scam and would ignore them. One in particular said that they would ignore the texts because they do not know why the Census Bureau would be sending text messages. We recommended that the text message include a brief instruction in Spanish, such as “Para español, responde ESP”, meaning “for Spanish, respond ESP.” If the technology to provide Spanish information is not available this way, we recommend researching other options to reach the Spanish-speaking population. 4. Conclusion The goal of this project was to identify any major comprehension issues and review spontaneous feedback of the mail materials, especially looking at the use of plain language and the use of a text message reminder to respond to the survey. We also aimed to suggest revisions to address any comprehension issues. Generally, we found that the plain language used in the mail materials was well-received, and participants in this study understood the purpose of the mailings and the call to action. Participants liked having a Due Date on the mailings so that they had a deadline to complete the survey by. They also liked some of the messaging that was included in the letters, such as the survey taking 10 minutes to complete, their answers being confidential, and helping their community. We recommended changes to the mail materials and text messages. We recommended including FAQs with an explanation of the selection and sampling process, and another with a phone number for respondents to receive more information. We also recommended that the letters include a way for respondents to request to receive a paper questionnaire rather than just having them wait until the final mailing. We also recommended some avenues for future testing. Because participants had a hard time locating their Census ID on the Reminder Postcard, we recommended testing the possibilityof a sealed Reminder Postcard so that the Census ID could be printed inside and labeled. We also found that some participants preferred to fill out a Paper Questionnaire, so we recommended testing a letter that allows for respondents to request a Paper Questionnaire over the phone. Some Spanish-speaking participants did not realize that they needed to turn the letter over for Spanish language content, so we recommended testing the effectiveness of versions of the

19 U.S. Census Bureau letters where the message to turn over for Spanish content was at the top of the letter rather than the bottom. Finally, based on participant feedback in this test, we recommended testing text messages with a link to the survey in the middle of the test against text messages with the link at the beginning, to see whether one is more effective than the other. 5. CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 1-1 1. Project Background In addition to providing data on employment and unemployment, the Current Population Survey is the vehicle for several important supplemental question modules, including the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC). The ASEC collects data on income sources, health insurance, and participation in various economic support programs. ASEC data also support the creation of the Supplemental Poverty Measure and are thus critically important to a broad array of data users. To support development of new questions on health insurance and income/public assistance topics for the ASEC supplement, RTI International and Research Support Services (RSS), conducted 50 one-on-one exploratory qualitative interviews. Interviews were split (i.e., 25 each) across two topic ASEC topic areas—health insurance and income. The purpose of the exploratory interviews was to learn more about how respondents think about these topics, identify possible issues that may hinder a respondent’s ability to respond to questions about these topics, and gather feedback that can be used to draft easily understandable questions that can be answered accurately. This report details the study methods, including the description of the target population and participant eligibility criteria, the strategies of participant recruitment and screening, and the interviewing procedures. Findings from exploratory interviews are also presented in detail, with recommendations offered where appropriate.

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 2-1 2. Methodology This section provides an overview of the recruitment and interviewing methodologies used during ASEC health insurance and income exploratory interview data collection. Specifically, this section includes an overview of recruitment strategies and targets, presents participant characteristics for each topic area, and provides details about the protocols and procedures that were used during interviews. 2.1 Recruitment Methods The RTI/RSS team recruited participants for the ASEC exploratory qualitative interviews from November 15, 2023, to January 16, 2024. The recruitment for the exploratory interviews for health insurance and income topics began by identifying multiple metropolitan areas across all four Census regions that have relatively large and diverse populations for a potential larger proportion of residents who met the recruitment criteria of both subprojects. The RTI/RSS team then posted online recruitment advertisements in the selected metropolitan areas, releasing advertisements on a rolling basis to maintain a steady stream of prospective recruits for screening and scheduling. The Census Bureau programmed a web-based eligibility screening in Qualtrics. The RTI/RSS team also established a toll-free telephone line dedicated to recruitment purposes. The web link of the screening instrument and the toll-free phone number were presented in the online advertisements (see Appendix A) to support participant recruitment. During the data collection period, the RTI/RSS team provided the Census Bureau with a weekly recruitment and interviewing progress update report, reflecting results to date. The weekly report sought to present the diversity of interview participants with respect to recruitment goals and needed sub-characteristics. The results of ASEC exploratory interview recruitment presented in Section 2.1.3 of this report reflect the final recruitment outcomes. 2.1.1 Implementation of Recruitment Advertising The RTI/RSS team used Craigslist as the main venue for recruitment advertising. Craigslist is one of the best-known online bulletin boards and provides the most comprehensive coverage of metropolitan areas in the United States. Based on past experience with previous call orders, RTI/RSS has been able to successfully recruit participants for qualitative research with diverse demographic and socioeconomic characteristics from Craigslist, with the exception of identifying some hard-to-reach sub populations such as those with racial or ethnic backgrounds that account for small percentages of the general population. To leverage Craigslist’s broad reach while recruiting general population samples, RTI/RSS did not use targeted advertisements that focused on specific characteristics and

2 – Methodology CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 2-2 used a general advertisement instead (see Appendix A for recruitment materials and advertisement text). The RTI/RSS team began the participant recruitment by posting the general recruitment advertisement on Craigslist under the “jobs/et cetera” sections for the six metropolitan areas across all four Census regions. RTI/RSS staff also reached out to their personal networks to solicit participation from those who may fit our recruitment criteria and asked their personal contacts to refer others who might be eligible for the participant recruitment screener (i.e., word of mouth). The first round of monthly paid advertising started on November 15, 2023, and expired on January 7, 2024. The team posted the first two general advertisements for the metropolitan areas of Columbus, Ohio, and Dallas/Fort Worth, Texas. The recruitment screener had received a few dozen completions within 24 hours and continued to receive completions at a consistent rate for approximately 1 week afterward. As the receipt of completions gradually decreased, the team posted the third general advertisement for Orlando, Florida, on November 26 to maintain the momentum of recruitment screening. The fourth and fifth general advertisements for Salt Lake City, Utah, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, were posted on December 5, followed by the sixth posting for San Diego, California, on December 10. RTI/RSS team recorded screening responses for more than 600 prospective participants from this first round of advertising. 2.1.2 Participant Selection Strategy To facilitate efficient screening review and participant selection between health insurance and income exploratory interviews, the RTI/RSS team created three automated spreadsheets. First, the team created a main intake sheet to import the screening responses from Qualtrics. The main intake sheet was used to determine the main eligibility criteria (i.e., adults age 18 or older, lives in the U.S., and meets one or more recruitment criteria outlined in Tables 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, and 2.4 presented in Section 2.1.3) for ASEC exploratory qualitative interviews health insurance and income topics. Within the main intake spreadsheet, the RTI/RSS team employed a two-step review strategy to determine topical interview assignment and participant selection priority. The spreadsheet first calculated and presented the number of eligible respondent characteristics for both health insurance and income interviews. The lead recruiter then selected and assigned prospective recruits to the topic area (i.e., health insurance or income) for which they had the most eligible characteristics or represented a criterion relatively more difficult to fulfill (see Tables 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, and 2.4 presented in Section 2.1.3). Next, the lead recruiter reviewed the tentative assignment of all prospective participants on the intake sheet, focusing on contact information self-reports and the IP addresses in the paradata for de-duplicated entries from the same individuals and excluding ineligible entries from foreign IP addresses.

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 2 – Methodology 2-3 After reviewing and cleaning the tentative assignments, the records of eligible recruits were exported to either health insurance or income specific recruitment tracking sheets. The allocation of eligible recruits is determined by (1) the fulfillment status of the required quota of the primary criteria and (2) the balance of the household and demographic characteristics in the secondary criteria. The interview assignment–specific spreadsheets served as the main reference for recruitment and interview progress for the entire project team, including for the recruiters and interviewers. For ASEC exploratory qualitative interviews, the team used the ASEC Health Insurance recruitment tracker and ASEC Income recruitment tracker to account for different needs of topics and support the recruitment effort for the interviews. During data collection, RTI/RSS team processed and reviewed the screening data at least once a week to select eligible participants for an interview. After a batch of screening data were reviewed, about 1 week would elapse before new assignments would be made to allow recruiters sufficient time to contact their existing assignments. How quickly interviewers contacted a selected participant after their assignment varied based on several factors, including the interviewer’s case load at the time of assignment, the number of scheduled interviews, and the speed with which other participants responded to the interviewer’s contact attempts. 2.1.3 ASEC exploratory qualitative interview recruitment outcomes During the data collection, RTI/RSS received 836 screening responses, including 13 respondents who were screened by phone. A total of 667 recruits were considered eligible to participate in the study based on their screening responses. Sixty-four recruits were excluded during the selection review process. These potential recruits were excluded after examining responses to screener questions and fell into one of more of the following exclusion categories: (1) they were unwilling to share their screen, (2) provided inconsistent responses over multiple screening attempts, or (3) completed the screening from a questionable IP address (i.e., a foreign IP address). The RSS team completed 25 exploratory qualitative interviews for the health insurance topic while the RTI team completed 25 interviews about income. Across both health insurance and income interview efforts, RTI/RSS also selected and contacted 40 eligible participants who did not complete the interview; 26 participants did not respond to our invitation, 11 of them did not show up for their scheduled interview, and another three decided to withdraw their participation after they were scheduled for an interview. CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 2 – Methodology 2-7 one for income (Appendix C). RTI/RSS provided input and reviewed each protocol. Both protocols included a mix of open-ended “exploratory” questions designed to assess participants’ general knowledge and understanding of different domains under each topic area (i.e., health insurance; income) and questions designed to evaluate participants’ understanding for a subset of specific draft ASEC questions. Both protocols were designed to be completed in 1 hour or less. On average, health insurance topic interviews took 46 minutes to complete and ranged from 27 minutes to 65 minutes. Income topic interviews took an average of 49 minutes to complete and ranged from 18 minutes to 78 minutes. For the income interview that lasted over 1 hour, the observer had additional questions at the end of the interview. Once finalized, interview protocols were programmed in Qualtrics to facilitate virtual interviewing. Respondent-facing instruments that contained the draft ASEC health insurance and income questions being tested were also programmed on the web. During the interview, participants were either provided a link to ASEC topic–specific questions (i.e., health insurance or income) and asked to respond to questions while sharing their screen, or the interviewer displayed the web instrument containing ASEC questions on screen and asked participants to respond while entering responses for them. All interviews were conducted remotely using Microsoft Teams within Census Bureau’s secure Virtual Desktop Interface (VDI) environment or using a Census Bureau issued laptop. With permission from participants, interviewers recorded all sessions using handheld audio recording devices or, when available, SnagIt software. Recordings were saved to the designated deliverable folder in the Census Bureau file share location. After each interview, interviewers completed the appropriate case summary template for the topic area (i.e., health insurance or income). At the end of the interview, interviewers offered participants a $40 Visa digital gift code as a thank you for their time. Although the two protocols and respondent-facing instruments differed, each interview was conducted in the following sequence to standardize implementation: • Explain the purpose of the study. • Confirm participant had reviewed and signed the online consent form to participate in the study and be audio/video recorded (Appendix D). • Start audio recording using an external audio recorder or SnagIt software. • Re-confirm verbal consent to participate and be recorded once recording has started. • Ask open-ended “exploratory” questions. • Share the respondent-facing instrument ask participants to answer ASEC questions shown on screen. • Administer probes to ASEC questions. • End the interview and send the participant the incentive.

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3-1 3. Findings 3.1 Health Insurance This section presents results and recommendations, where appropriate, for ASEC Health Insurance questions by topic area. The interview consisted of an exploratory section where participants were asked in a semi-structured interview format about their health coverage and general knowledge about health insurance, the coverage of others in their household, and terminology used to refer to different aspects of health coverage. They were asked to provide some information from their insurance cards and probed on their preference for how to provide Census Bureau with information about their health insurance plan. All participants were then asked to complete ASEC health insurance questions (Set A) and were probed to better understand their responses and understanding of the questions. Findings in this section are presented by topic, with findings from exploratory questions first followed by cognitive testing questions. 3.1.1 Exploring Coverage and General Knowledge about Health Insurance At the beginning of each interview, participants were asked a series of questions to establish where they go for medical care and how they pay for such care, followed by an exploration of their understanding of what health coverage involves and the varied terms that refer to it. 3.1.2 Medical Care and Coverage Access to Care Usual place for care. Participants were asked where they usually go when they want to see a doctor or other medical professional. Nine of the 25 participants reported going to see a doctor. Several of these participants used a variation of the term primary care physician or PCP, including: “PCP” (P212 and P445), “primary care physician” (417), or “primary physician” (P332, P620). Others used the terms “physician” (P56), “general practitioner” (P340), or “doctor’s office” (P500 and 549). Six participants said they usually go to a hospital or emergency room, six reported usually going to an urgent care center, and four reported usually going to a local clinic. Overall, there was little relationship between participants’ health coverage and their answer to this question, but some participants did connect the two. For example, one participant explained that they had recently been going to the emergency room for care because they were uninsured but that the hospital recently helped them sign up for “emergency Medi-Cal” so they now have Medicaid coverage. “More recently I’ve been having to go to the ER to seek medical care, I haven’t gone to an actual doctor’s office in a bit just because of my insurance.” (P405)
