CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3 – Findings 3-15 Participants whose household members had the same health coverage were asked if these household members shared their plan or if they had their own. Participants who lived with family members typically reported sharing the same plan, while those that lived with roommates mentioned having their own. However, two participants who lived with direct family members (brother and father, respectively) shared that they each had their own plan. Participants were asked how knowledgeable they felt about the coverage of others in their household when it was different from their own. In general, participants did not feel very knowledgeable about others’ health coverage, except for one participant. “I’m quite knowledgeable…a lot more than my own because he uses his a lot more because of his disability and he has more health issues… but I’m the one that makes most of his appointments and transportation…” (P313) One participant said they were “just assuming” in terms of being knowledgeable about the health coverage of others in their household (P658). Another said they were not sure because their boyfriend does not typically get sick, so he has not had to seek medical help (P549). One participant said they felt somewhat knowledgeable about their girlfriend, mentioning what it covered and referring to copays or premiums, but were not at all knowledgeable about their roommate (P445). “Not too much, I know she always talks about a $50 copay. She’d be going to the doctor’s a lot; I don’t know too much about it.” (P405) “Not very knowledgeable, I know for a fact that one is under 26 and covered with parents, the other two I believe is probably through work as well.” (P340) Finally, participants were asked if there was anyone outside of the household who shared coverage with them or other people in the household. All respondents answered no, except one participant who was under 26 and on their parent’s health plan and who lived with unrelated roommates who were also on their own parents’ plans, although none of the parents lived in the shared household (P718). Terminology Participants were asked for their interpretation of four terms used in relation to health insurance. These terms were premium, subsidy, co-pay, and policyholder. Of the 25 participants who answered these questions, only 10 provided answers that were consistent with the intended meaning of health insurance premium. One of these included employer- paid portions of a premium, while others did not. “A fee you pay per year for the insurance. Some Medicare plans have premiums.” (P76)

3 – Findings CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3-20 Recommendations As shown previously, several participants either did not know the meaning of the terms premium and subsidy or showed a mistaken understanding of the terms when putting them into their own words. For this reason, we recommend that definitions of the two terms be included when those terms are first used in a questionnaire. With regards to “health coverage,” “health plan,” and “health insurance” and given the substantial variation in the way participants viewed these as similar or different, we recommend using the term health insurance, which was most familiar and well understood by participants whenever possible, or that descriptions be used in place of these terms. 3.1.4 Alternative Methods of Collection In this section, participants were asked to retrieve their insurance card to provide the interviewer information from the cards. Seven participants either said that they do not have a card or that they could not find it right then. All others produced the card and either the interviewer was able to see it on screen and record the information or the participant read it to the interviewer if it was not clear on screen. Of the 18 participants who had the card with them, three were unable to find the name of their plan on the card, but 13 could answer what type of plan it was, whether HMO, HAS, PPO, or Medicaid. Not all participants were knowledgeable about what their insurance plan covers or does not cover, and the information on the card was not great help. Many felt it covered everything, all types of medical needs. “For everything. Dentist, eye doctor, the dudes that pop all your bones and that. For meds. They give you a Walgreens card as well.” (P11) “Primary care specialist, telemedicine, urgent care, outpatient hospital, inpatient hospital, of course there’s different price to all that, emergency room.” (P47) “Free emergency CareSource, urgent care and stuff around the city, that’s free, I have to get picked up by the ambulance, that’s free. Vision, they help me out with the vision and I’m not sure about what’s going on with dental.” (P108) Four were unsure regarding coverage for dental, mental health, or vision. One participant specifically mentioned that cosmetic procedures were not covered. “Pretty much everything. Though electives are not, cosmetic procedures. But all necessary things are covered, including prescriptions. It’s got pretty broad coverage… Dental is also covered.” (P76)

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3 – Findings 3-21 Participants were next asked how they would prefer to provide their health insurance information to Census Bureau. An introductory statement explained why it is important for Census Bureau to collect such information and why it can amount to a lot of questions to make sure the person’s coverage is clear. For this section, participants were offered three hypothetical options for providing the information: (1) answering a lot of questions about their coverage, (2) inputting basic information from their insurance card, or (3) uploading a photo of their insurance cards. Fifteen participants selected the option of uploading a photo of the card. They generally agreed that this preference was based on it being the easiest option. “Just upload it and you don’t have to do anything else. It’s just quick and easy.” [I: “would you have any concerns about uploading a picture?”] R: “There’s always concerns anytime you do anything online, so I cannot be scared all the time. Cause I’m always concerned whenever you have to upload a driver’s license or a social security for jobs and different things, but my husband works for [redacted] so my network is pretty secure, so I think it’s pretty safe for now.” (P47) “Yes. It would be easier. Personally, I do think navigating healthcare can be very challenging. I have a master’s degree and a bachelor’s... it’s hard. For everyday people, it’s... whenever you have an issue you call your insurance company… Uploading a card would be easier for me.” (P205) “It’s just a whole lot simpler. If they’re taking the information they need just from the back of my insurance card, I don’t mind the U.S. Census Bureau having a copy of that.” (P313) “It just makes it so that all the accurate information is taken from the picture and there’s no confusion as to in case you put in the wrong information in the wrong box or fill out the wrong box.” (P405) “Because that’s what I’ve done before, and it seems to be the easiest option.” (P576) Two participants selected the second option to input the basic information from their card. They felt this would be easier. “Because if I got it right here now; that means it will be a little bit easier.” (P108) “That’s how I would prefer to do it, it seems easier.” (P340) Eight participants selected the first option to answer a lot of questions about their coverage. “That’s how I would prefer to do it, it seems easier.”

3 – Findings CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3-22 Their stated reasons varied from security concerns to information control and fear of technology. “Because of security reasons, not wanting to upload or input my information somewhere.” (P76) “The list of questions… I just feel like somebody is trying to infiltrate my information or something like that, I don’t know, it just feels wrong, something too wrong to ask.” [I: What feels wrong to ask?] R: “I don’t want to say wrong, I don’t know, that’s an inappropriate question to give someone like, I don’t know, I just don’t feel like, I don’t know, the feeling I just get, honestly a bad feeling, I don’t know.” [I: Regarding which question?] R: “Like asking, like somebody say what provider are you with right off the bat, I don’t think nobody gonna tell them, but they might tell you stuff about the plan, not who the plan is coming from you know. That’s why I would rather answer the questions (inaudible) just telling them I’m with such and such.” [I: You feel like it’s uncomfortable to give information about the name of the plan or upload a photo? Or both?] R: “Photo. Both, both, both, yeah.” (P175) “Because it makes the process easier, sometimes with electronics you try to open this, and that becomes an issue, and then you spend more time. Quicker.” (P181) “To me that one seems more secure in a way, like if I’m giving my ID number or showing my insurance card, I’m not sure how that information is getting stored so if it’s not used for something with a direct health benefit I guess then, that’s just not really something I feel comfortable floating out there.” (P445) Recommendations Participant preferences for how this information should be collected varied. Most participants either preferred uploading a photo of their ID card because of its ease or preferred to answer questions about their coverage because it felt more secure to them or gave them more control. A minority of participants preferred the option to input basic information from their card because it seemed easy. In light of this, we recommend that survey respondents be given the option to either answer a set of questions or to upload a photo of their insurance card, as those were the most preferred methods. This way both types of respondents will be served, and the information needed can be collected from the maximum number of respondents.

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3 – Findings 3-23 3.1.5 Cognitive Testing of Question Set A Part two of the interview protocol shifted from open-ended discussion to a more focused discussion about specific questions. Participants were asked to answer a set of questions via a web survey and were probed about their answers after the first three questions and again after completing the rest of the question set. The first subset of questions were as follows. Q1) Do you NOW have any type of health plan or health coverage? o Yes o No (DONE WITH QUESTION SERIES) Q2) How do you get the coverage you have now? o Through your job o Through a spouse/partner or parent’s job o Government or state o Some other way Q3) Are you covered by any of the following? Mark all that apply. o Medicare (for 65+ and people with disabilities) o Medicaid, State Medicaid, Medical Assistance, or CHIP o State exchange plan or other state health plan If Q2 = Through your job or through a spouse/partner or parent’s job, go to Q4 If Q2 = Government or state, go to Q5 If Q2 = Some other way, go to Q6 Deciding on coverage categories in questions 2 and 3 and confusion around ‘Mark all that apply’ Twenty-three participants selected “yes” to question 1 and were subsequently asked questions 2 and 3. Participants were able to answer question 1 without any issues. Question 2 also seemed to be straightforward for most participants, but a few indicated that they selected their answers through a process of elimination. “Just based off of the type that it was, and process of elimination also.” (P405) “I know the coverage I’m getting is provided by the government. I know that; I can’t give you any other reason why, since I’m not working, it’s not through my job. I don’t have a spouse or partner so, it’s also some sort of process of elimination, but I just know that Medi-Cal and Medicaid are government, that’s clearly what I have.” (P417)

3 – Findings CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3-24 “Well, I knew it wasn't going to be my job because I don't have one really. And I knew it wasn't going to be a spouse, partner, or parents’ job because none of those give me health insurance. Government or state because it's Medicaid and some other way I'm assuming is like a private personal insurance and that's not me either. So, government or state seem to be most descriptive.” (P658) Question 3 was generally more problematic for participants. One issue was that they thought they had to select one of the responses: it was not clear to some participants that they were not required to select any of the answers to the mark all that apply question if none of them applied to their situation. For example, one participant selected “Medicaid, State Medicaid, Medical Assistance, or CHIP” after selecting “Through your job’” in question 2 and explained the following: “I really don’t know. I just chose the answer because I don’t think I have any of them, can I choose not any of them? Do I have to choose one?” Later in the interview, at probing, this participant then changed their answer but still thought that they were required to select an answer, “I guess the best answer would be number 3 because I don’t have Medicaid or Medicare but I do have coverage so I guess it would be state exchange plan, health plan.” (P175) Another participant seemed to misunderstand what was meant by “other state health plan” in question 3. This participant selected “Through your job” at question 2 went on to select selected “State exchange plan or other state health plan” at question 3. “Because it’s through my company and it is state, Blue Cross Blue Shield Florida, so state, Florida.” (P181) Another participant who had recently become covered under Medi-Cal, California’s Medicaid program, mistakenly selected “State exchange plan or other state health plan” as their answer to question 3 but commented that they were not confident in their answer. “Honestly that one’s a little confusing, that potentially sounded correct, but not 100% sure.” (P405) Perhaps also because of confusion around believing that they needed to select an answer to question 3, two participants who selected “Through a spouse/partner or parent’s job” at question 2 also selected “State exchange plan or other state health plan” at question 3. One of these participants was clear in their think-aloud that the selection was based on the other two response options clearly not applying to their situation. “Since we don’t have Medicare or Medicaid, it must be the third option.” In probing, this participant did not know what the state exchange plan option meant (P620). The other participant said of their partner’s plan through their employer, “I think it’s a

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3 – Findings 3-25 federal plan through the state,” which seemed to lead them to choosing “State exchange plan or other state health plan” in questions 3, but they may have believed they had to find an answer among the options provided. Only one of the participants in our testing chose more than one option to question 3. This participant, who has Medicaid coverage, selected both “Medicaid, State Medicaid, Medical Assistance, or CHIP” and “State exchange plan or other state health plan.” “Because I know I got it through the state, I know it’s Medicaid, I just figured the bottom two were the right ones and it says State Medicaid, Medical Assistance, State Exchange plan or state health plan. I know it’s through the state, so that’s why it’s called Keystone. I don’t know. That’s how I came up with it.” (P283) Only five participants did not select any option for question 3, with think-alouds making clear that they understood that they did not need to select any answer if none applied to them. One participant even suggested that adding a “None of these” option to question 3 to make it clear for people who may believe they need to select an answer (P212). Understanding of Questions 1–3 In probing, participants were also asked to explain in their own words what questions 1–3 are asking. Most participants were able to explain that the questions were generally asking about health coverage and the type of coverage that one has. “Ok, first and second, do you know have any type of health coverage, it’s just plain and simple, yes or no. Within each section, participants were first asked exploratory questions to gather general information about that topic area. All participants were then asked to complete ASEC questions for each of these topic areas, and corresponding follow- up probes were then administered to better understand participant responses and understanding of draft ASEC questions. In addition to sources of income, participants were also asked to answer ASEC questions about different types of programs and expenses, including free or reduced-price school meals, WIC and SNAP participation, participation in energy assistance and housing programs, medical expenses, and childcare expenses. For each domain in this section, general findings from exploratory questions are presented first, where applicable, followed by question specific findings.

One participant (P8) explained that they rent a room in a group home, and they may consider other people in that home as part of their household. All participants were asked how easy or difficult it was to respond to these questions. Of the participants who responded “No” to Q20 and Q21, a majority confirmed that the questions were easy to answer. “I am familiar with SNAP and food assistance, so it wasn’t an issue for understanding what they were.” (P211) “Easy, nothing with food or anything for us.” (P180) “Since I don’t have the programs, it was easy for me to respond right away.” (P420) For participants who responded “Yes” to either Q20 or Q21, two confirmed that the questions were easy to answer, but five experienced issues responding to these questions. After probing, it was noted that three of these participants should have responded “Yes” to Q21. Two of these participants did not think that SNAP was a state program, with one not reading the instructions to include SNAP benefits in their response. One of these participants received food stamps and answered “Yes” to Q20, but they did not know what SNAP was and that it included food stamps, so they responded “No” to Q21 because it did not include the term “food stamps.” One participant (P46) responded “Yes” to 20, and “No” to 21 because they did not think that SNAP is a state program. They did not see the instruction to include SNAP. This participant should have responded “Yes” to Q21. Note that no additional participants reported missing this instruction, but participants were not directly probed to determine if they were reading instructions in italics. One participant (P2) responded “Yes” to Q20 but “No” to Q21. This participant was confused about the term “state program” explaining that SNAP is federally funded, but the money is given to the state and the state reviews eligibility, issues the card, and provides the benefit amount. When responding to Q20 they were thinking about food stamps, they get an EBT card in Texas called the Lonestar card, so this participant should have responded “Yes” to Q21.

3 – Findings CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3-56 One participant (P211) was initially confused about Q21, explaining that they did not receive food assistance from the state. When they re-read the question, they saw that this question includes SNAP, which they receive, so they responded “Yes.” One participant (P54) noted that the format of Q20 is confusing and not conducive to reading. This participant thought the question should say “receive SNAP benefits” or simply “receive SNAP” and remove “benefits from.” This participant responded “Yes” to Q20 and Q21. One participant (P363) responded “Yes” to Q20 but “No” to Q21. This participant receives food stamps but did not know what SNAP was and that it includes food stamps. They responded “Yes” to Q20 because they receive food stamps but responded “No” to Q21 because it did not include the term food stamps. This participant should have responded “Yes” to Q21. Participants who responded “Yes” to Q20 were then probed about the benefits received from SNAP, how the benefits were obtained or received, and what types of benefits they were including in their answers. Six participants confirmed that they receive SNAP, which is food assistance. Participants explained that they receive an amount monthly that is loaded onto a card to buy groceries and food. Four participants were thinking about SNAP, and one participant was thinking about SNAP and a food pantry. These participants were then asked if they have an EBT card as part of their benefits, and if they included the EBT card in their answer to these questions. All six confirmed that they have an EBT card. Participants who responded “Yes” to Q20 or Q21 were asked if they included benefits from WIC in their answers to these questions. Three participants who responded “Yes” to Q20 or Q21 confirmed that they did not include WIC in their responses to these questions. Of these three, two confirmed that they do not receive WIC. For other participants who answered “Yes” to Q20 or Q21, this probe was skipped for time. All participants were asked if they were aware of any nutritional assistance programs in their state that were not mentioned in these questions. Eleven participants were not aware of any other nutritional programs in their state. One participant (P496) noted that their insurance offers a food program, but they have never used it. Another participant (P52) explained that people can call “211,” which directs the caller to nearby soup kitchens and other resources. One participant (P220) also mentioned different food pantries from churches whereas one (P180) mentioned assistance for the elderly, explaining that they sometimes pick up magazines that have two to three pages of information about state agencies and private help. Recommendations Because of the confusion around Q21, which led three participants to respond “No” when they should have responded “Yes,” we suggest either adding text that reads “This includes

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3 – Findings 3-57 SNAP (Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program) and the Food Stamp program” in bold, not italic, to Q21 Alternatively, we suggest only asking Q20, as participants that responded “Yes” to this question were receiving SNAP, had EBT cards, and did not receive any other assistance from their state. When asked about any other nutritional programs in their state, participants mentioned food programs through insurance or calling “211,” which directs the caller to soup kitchens and other resources, food pantries, and assistance for the elderly. Because some of these are not programs sponsored by the state, if Census Bureau would like to capture this assistance, they could include a question asking, “Did you receive any assistance from other food programs such as soup kitchens or food pantries?” Energy Assistance All participants were asked Q27, shown below. Of the 25 participants, three reported receiving energy assistance to help pay heating and cooling costs from the federal, state, or local government. Q27) In 2022, did you receive energy assistance to help pay heating and cooling costs from the federal, state, or local government? This assistance can be received directly by the household or it can be paid directly to the electric company, gas company, or fuel dealer. o Yes o No All participants were asked how easy or difficulty this question was to answer. A majority of the participants confirmed that this question is clear, straightforward, and easy to answer. One participant (P496) asked if this question includes solar panels, noting that you can get allowances for installing solar panels and that everyone can get these allowances, not only low-income individuals. This participant (P496) responded “No” to Q27. When asked if there is anything about this question that is confusing to them or that they think other people might not understand, 13 confirmed that there is nothing about this question that is confusing to them or that they think other people might not understand. “Easy. We pay every month for energy bills.” (P180) "Very easy, all my bills are included in rent. I don’t qualify for that [energy assistance]. If I did qualify, I still wouldn’t because of my income from Social Security, there's an income cap.” (P8) “Oh, I think this question is very clear. You either get money to help pay your utility bills or you don’t.” (P372)

3 – Findings CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3-58 The participants who reported receiving energy assistance were then probed about the type of energy assistance they receive, how the energy assistance was obtained or received, and what types of energy assistance they were including in their answers to the question. One participant (P52) received assistance from a state program called Texas Utility Help, another (P1) received assistance from a program called PIPP, which pays a portion of the respondent’s energy expenses, and one participant (P420) indicated that they applied for energy assistance when they were unemployed through the gas and electric company. One participant (P52) who received assistance from a state program explained that assistance is applied for on a website. To qualify you must be in a certain income range. The program takes your income and reviews past bills and determines an amount to be paid directly to the light company and water utility. Another participant (P1) who received assistance from a program called PIPP explained that you apply for PIPP online. The program automatically deducts an amount from their bill so that the participant only has to pay a portion of it. One participant (P420) who received assistance through the gas and electric company explained that it was a reduction in their energy bill. Another participant (P52) was thinking about electricity and water while two (P1, P420) were thinking about their energy bills. Participants who did not report receiving energy assistance were asked if they use anything other than their regular income to pay their heating and cooling costs. Eight participants did not use anything other than their regular income to pay their heating and cooling costs. One (P8) explained that their heating and cooling costs are part of their rent in their group home, and they pay their rent with Social Security money. Another (P2) mentioned that they asked their energy provider if they offer assistance for low-income customers, but they do not. This participant explained they pay bills from Social Security money or using virtual gift cards from focus groups and interviews. They indicated that they keep their energy expense to a minimum. One participant (P279) noted they pay their energy bills with their credit card, which is paid off with money from their job. One participant (P180) does not use anything other than their income to pay their energy bills, but they mentioned that they are on a budgeting plan with their energy company. Recommendations Participants that received energy assistance correctly responded to this question and were able to explain the energy assistance received. Participants who did not report receiving energy assistance believed this question was straightforward and easy to respond to. Because of this, we do not recommend any changes to this question. Housing Assistance All participants were asked to respond to Q28 and Q29, shown below.

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3 – Findings 3-59 Q28) Is this public housing, that is, is it owned by a local housing authority or other public agency? o Yes o No Q29) Are you paying lower rent because the Federal, State, or local government is paying part of the cost? o Yes o No None of the participants in this round of interviews reported living in public housing owned by a local housing authority or other public agency (Q28). One participant (P52) responded “Yes” to Q29 asking whether they are paying lower rent because the federal, state, or local government is paying part of the cost. This participant receives Section 8 through Dallas Housing Authority. All participants were asked how easy or difficult it was to answer Q28 and Q29. Fourteen participants confirmed that these questions were very easy to answer. One participant (P28) indicated that they were not certain of their responses to these questions and that they felt these items were confusing and was not sure how they would know this information. “I mean I was confused because the question just came out of nowhere asking about housing, I didn’t understand why it was there. It was kind of random and I didn’t know how to answer because I was like ‘how would I know this?’” (P28) Three participants indicated that they were confused by either Q28 or Q29, specifically by the term “public housing.” One participant (P399) did not know what public housing was. Another (P507) noted that the way the questions is worded implies that they live in public housing, and one (P599) was not sure why they needed to reply to Q29 as they responded “No” to Q28, which asks about public housing. “I don’t know how you could be confused. If you don’t know that you live in public housing you got issues besides not being able to fill out this survey, and the same with the rent, either you know you get rent subsidized or you know you don’t get rent subsidized.” (P372) "Very easy, I don’t live in public housing, I live on a ranch." (P8) “Easy. For Q28, it’s a private house and we are not renting anything for Q29.” (P180) “Q28 was a bit difficult. I don’t really get it. That is why I went back.” [It is noted that the participant went back to the previous question to try to

3 – Findings CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3-60 understand, thinking they had responded “yes” to something to get this question because it says, “is this public housing.”] (P599) “Q28 I am not going to lie was a little confusing. Q29 I am definitely certain.” [And why would you say Q28 is confusing?]: “Because it’s asking if it’s public housing or owned by a local housing authority or other public agency. I answered no, maybe it’s the way it’s worded. I am guessing that housing authority is the state? I have no idea to be honest.” (P399) When asked if there is anything about these questions that was confusing to them or that that they think others may not understand, 10 participants confirmed that there was nothing confusing to them. However, some participants were confused by these items. One participant (P151) believes that there should be a “not applicable” response option for Q28. Another participant explained that when Q28 asks “is this” some people may not know what “this” is and that it should ask if the person resides in public housing. One participant (P402) reported that they were confused because the question implies that they live in public housing. Another (P28) was confused because these questions seem different than the other questions in the survey. The last (P2) was not familiar with these programs. They explained that there may be a housing assistance program in their city, but it has to be housing in certain areas. They noted that housing is a little cheaper for them because they live in an older building. Their county did have some rent assistance, but they checked about this a year ago and the money is gone. “Well, it did kind of confuse me [Q28] because I thought ‘wait I don’t get any public housing, so it almost kind of assumes that you do receive public housing, at least that’s how I took it when I first read it. For Q29, that wasn’t confusing, so I just said no.” (P420) “I mean I was confused because the question just came out of nowhere asking about housing, I didn’t understand why it was there. It was kind of random and I didn’t know how to answer because I was like ‘how would I know this?’” (P28) When asked what “public housing” means to participants in Q28, seven participants considered “public housing” to be Section 8 housing. Eight participants explained that “public housing” is subsidized housing paid for by the government and that the government either pays for or pays for part of the rent based on a person’s income and family size. “Well, you know I have been aware of public housing since I was 5 years old. They were called projects a lot when I was growing up. There’s one a few miles away from where I live. And it’s housing that the government owns and it’s for low-income folks and they pay a much lower rent to live there than they would pay in private housing.” (P372)

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3 – Findings 3-61 “Public housing to me is subsidized housing. The government will assist in paying your rent.” (P211) "Public housing is Section 8. The government pays either the full rent or a portion of rent in Section 8, based off of the recipient’s income and family size." (P1) “My taxes going to the government to pay for other people’s places of residence to help them out.” (P180) When asked what “Section 8” means to participants, six participants thought that Section 8 is the same as public housing, three participants did not know what Section 8 is, and three participants explained that with Section 8 individuals can choose where they want to live and the government pays for all or part of the rent. “Well, they say public housing assistance is different than Section 8, like they are both housing but it’s different forms of it. Like Section 8 is where you get assistance, you can find your own home and get assistance with paying, but then public housing is housing and developments that are built, and you have to pick the area you want to live in.” (P399) “I really don’t know, I’ve heard the term, but I don’t know. My guess is that you have to meet a minimum of income to get Section 8.” (P211) "It’s a program where people can live wherever they want but the government pays 80% and you pay 30%, something like that." (P8) “It has to do with housing. I think it is a program to assist low-income families or the disabled.” (P599) Recommendations A couple of participants noted that the way that Q28 is worded implies that the participant lives in public housing, which led to confusion, and one participant noted that the phrase “is this” in the question could cause confusion because participants may not know what “this” is. We recommend looking for other ways to word the question. For example, asking “do you live in public housing, that is, is it owned by….” Many participants did not know what public housing or Section 8 is. Providing examples of this type of housing may help participants understand the question. Several participants reported that Section 8 and public housing are the same thing. If the Census Bureau is trying to determine participants that live in Section 8 housing vs. public housing it is suggested that public housing and Section 8 are asked about separately. If they are trying to determine participants who live in public housing or Section 8 housing it is suggested that Section 8 be added to Q28.

3 – Findings CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3-62 Medical Expenses All participants were asked to respond to Q23–Q26, which ask about insurance premiums, co-pays and medical care, and out-of-pocket costs. Several participants had trouble responding to one or more of the questions in this set. Some were uncertain about what questions were asking about, what should be included, or what the differences were between some of the questions, and many noted they were not certain about their answers or provided “guesses” in their responses. These issues are discussed in more detail for each question in the following section. Premiums. All participants were first asked to respond to Q23, as shown below. Q23) Last year, how much did you pay out-of-pocket for ALL health insurance premiums covering yourself or others in the household? Include both comprehensive and supplemental plans (such as vision and dental insurance). Do NOT include Medicare deductions from any Social Security or Social Security Disability payments mentioned earlier. [Dollar field] Participants provided a range of responses to Q23. Ten participants entered “$0” for this question and indicated they either did not have insurance or were on Medicare or Medicaid and did not have to pay a premium. Fourteen participants provided an answer, with one respondent (P278) indicating they have premiums but were not sure of an amount and were not able to provide a response. Dollar amounts provided had a range of $200 to $33,000, an average of $4,789, and a median of $2,000. The participant (P496) who reported $33,000 indicated they had a health savings account, which was the figure they were reporting. When asked how easy or difficult it was to answer this question, 13 participants reported some difficulty responding. Five participants noted it was difficult because they did not have the information or would need to consult others in the household to provide more accurate responses. “This was quite difficult. I had to give a rough estimate. I would have to calculate to give an answer.” (P599) “It was challenging to answer because I had to think about how much I paid each month.” (P220) “I don’t keep track. Most of that is taken out already.” (P278) There was also some confusion observed with the term “out-of-pocket” used in this question, which resulted in some participants including other “out-of-pocket” expenses. Six participants considered other “out-of-pocket” expenses, such as what they paid at the

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3 – Findings 3-63 doctor for co-pays or what they paid after insurance covered their portion of the cost. One participant (P363) entered the amount paid out-of-pocket braces last year. Four participants (P151, P55, P211, P506) were uncertain if they should include co-pays they paid at the doctor in their response. Another participant (P507) said the term “out-of-pocket” was confusing because insurance premiums come out of a person’s paycheck before it is dispersed, and they don’t think about premiums as “out-of-pocket” expenses. “This is a confusing question because the [term] ‘pay out-of-pocket’ for all healthcare insurance premiums.’ So, it’s asking me about how much I paid for insurance. It’s also asking me how much I paid out-of-pocket after insurance covered paying for something. I still paid out-of-pocket after insurance paid for a procedure and the doctor didn’t get all of his money.” (P211) “[I] would have to try and remember all doctor visits and how much they cost. No way." (P506) “Does this include monthly payment and what you pay when seeing the doctor?” (P55) “These expenses were low because no one in the household was very sick or needed to go to the hospital last year.” (P138) Related, one participant provided their plan’s yearly deductible amount, not their premium, because they met their deductible and that is what they paid “out-of-pocket.” “It is a tough question. I think my deductible on my plan was $2,500, so if you’re comfortable with that response that is what I’d go with.” (P90) Two participants (P279, P220) were initially unsure if they should include the monthly payment amount or the amount for the entire year. One of these participants (P279) decided to calculate the total by multiplying monthly payments, and one participant (P220) provided the amount that was deducted from their social security each month for their insurance. When asked how certain they were of their responses, eight reported not being certain about the figures they provided, with five reporting they estimated or “guessed.” “It is kind of a wild estimate actually.” (P180). “It's a total guess. Could be totally wrong – not even close.” (P506) “I don’t know the answer to that because it’s taken out [of my paycheck] already.” (P278)

3 – Findings CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3-64 Finally, participants were asked what the term “premium” meant to them. Although there was some confusion about what costs to include in Q23, 16 participants generally described premiums correctly (e.g., amount paid to maintain insurance coverage). “Premium is what you pay every month to have insurance.” (P48) “A monthly rate that someone pays for insurance.” (P52) “Premium is the price of your insurance.” (P211) “What you pay to an insurance company to cover you for your benefits.” (P180) However, others provided descriptions that did not align with the meaning of “premium” as it is intended in this question and instead described deductibles or something that insurance pays. “It is a little bit of a tougher word for most people. Premiums can be something in addition to, or a bonus. When I think of premiums I think of a bonus or incentive offer through insurance.” (P54) “What does your insurance costs to meet your deductible.” (P90) “[That] insurance covers some of the cost” (P363) Co-pays and Medical Care. Participants were then asked to respond to Q24, which asks about “out-of-pocket” expenses for their own medical care. Q24) Last year, how much was paid out-of-pocket for your OWN medical care, such as copays for doctor and dentist visits, diagnostic tests, prescription medicine, glasses and contacts, and medical supplies? Include any amount paid out-of-pocket on your behalf by anyone else in this household. [Dollar field] Four participants provided “$0” responses. One participant (P278) noted they would not know how to answer this question and did not provide a response. Twenty participants provided responses with a range of $20 to $7,000, an average of $1,691, and a median of $500. The participant (P399) that reported only $20 provided their co-pay amount. When asked how easy or difficult Q24 was, seven participants reported having some difficulty or were uncertain about how to respond. Two participants also reported providing “guesses.” "Oh my god! I'm sorry, but this would be my real-life reaction. I have no idea." (P220) “Again, a wild estimate. I don’t have that many medical bills.” (P180)

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3 – Findings 3-65 Two participants (P48, P211) noted it was difficult to think about expenses for co-pays in addition to all the other costs for other medical expenses (e.g., tests). Related, one participant (P507) was uncertain if they should include over the counter medication under “medical supplies.” “There’s too many things in there, like the prescriptions, the glasses, the diagnostic tests, the dental, etc. to group it all together. You’re going to get more of an estimate than a proper number. My eyecare covers up to $2,000, anything out-of-pocket I wouldn’t know. Separate them into not such a broad group.” (P211) “Easy to put the number, but difficult to think about all copays plus tests, visits…”. (P48) “When I hear medical supplies, I also think of first aid stuff and over the counter medication I use to help my skin condition, but I am not including these things in this number.” (P507) When asked about the difference between Q23 and Q24, seven participants had trouble discerning the difference between the two items, and what information each was requesting, and three participants felt they were asking similar things. “I really don’t see a difference, because they are both asking out of pocket expenses for medical care.” (P90) “There doesn’t seem to be a whole lot of difference to me.” (P180) One participant (P278) described Q23 as what is paid by health insurance, and Q24 as what is paid by an individual/household. Two participants felt the only difference between Q23 and Q24 was that Q24 asked just about the participant’s own expenses, whereas Q23 asked about the entire household. “[In Q23] if you have family, include what you pay for everyone. [In Q24] Include just your own. That’s the only difference.” (P279). “Well in 23 you are asking for everybody in the household and in 24 you are just asking about me.” (P28) Out-of-pocket costs. Participants were then asked to respond to Q25–Q26 and report their out-of-pocket costs for non-prescription healthcare products (Q25) and their total out- of-pocket costs for medical care (Q26).

3 – Findings CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3-66 Q25) Last year, how much was paid out-of-pocket for your non-prescription healthcare products such as vitamins, allergy and cold medicine, pain relievers, quit smoking aids, and anything else not yet reported? Include any amount paid out-of-pocket on your behalf by anyone in this household. [Dollar field] Q26) Last year, how much was paid out-of-pocket for your OWN medical care (e.g., copays for doctor and dentist visits, diagnostic tests, prescription medicine, glasses and contacts, and medical supplies) AND non-prescription healthcare products (e.g., vitamins, allergy and cold medicine, pain relievers, quit smoking aids, and other expenses)? Include any amount paid out-of-pocket on your behalf by anyone in this household. [Dollar field] For Q25, four participants provided $0 responses. Twenty participants provided responses with a range of $20 to $2,000, an average of $360, and a median of $200. For Q26, six participants provided $0 responses. One of these participants (P28) noted in subsequent probing this figure was actually $700–$1000. Eighteen provided responses with a range of $50–$10,000, an average of $2,225, and a median of $2,200. One participant (P278) noted they would not know how to answer either of these questions about out-of-pocket costs. Participants were then asked how easy or difficult it was to respond to Q25 and Q26 and how certain they were about their responses. Eleven participants reported some difficulty with questions, and 12 reported providing estimates. One participant (P52) who is not insured felt the term “out-of-pocket” made them think the questions were only for those who are insured. Another (P55) noted the questions were long, and they had to read the items “2 or 3 times” before responding. Five participants noted it was difficult because they did not have the information available in the moment or noted they would need to consult others in the household. One participant (P151) suggested using the term “over the counter” instead of “non-prescription” would help some participants better understand what these questions were asking about. Three participants felt the two questions sounded alike, or were asking for similar data, which caused some confusion. Participants were then probed about the differences between Q25 and Q26. Although some understood that Q26 was asking them to report totals from both Q24 and Q25, six had difficulty discerning the difference between these items and felt they were the same. “This is the one (Q25) I had to go back to…, so I guess it was a little confusing. It felt like I was answering the same question twice but looking at them next to each other I see that one was the total amount, and one was just myself.” (P420)

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3 – Findings 3-67 "One is about medicine over the counter, and the other is about over the counter stuff too." (P8) “It is getting confusing to me because it [Q26] doesn’t seem to me any different from the $2,500 [reported in Q23 and Q24]. To me it seems redundant.” (P90) “They seem to run together.” (P180) “No, they are the same.” (P211) "Isn't Q26 the same as Q25?" (P506) Four other participants focused on the differences between the medication/healthcare products listed in each item, not mentioning the other medical care expenses (e.g., co-pays, doctor visits, tests) asked about in Q26. “One [Q26] is referring to nonprescription and prescription. Q25 is only asking about nonprescription expense (P52) “Q25 is asking about expenses for prescriptions only while Q26 asks about non-prescription items.” (P138) “Q25 is over counter. Q26 is prescription doctor gives you” (279) “Well 25 says non-prescription and 26 says prescription and non- prescription.” (P28) Five participants recognized that Q26 was asking them to report values from Q24 and Q25. However, three participants (P496, P507, P372) were confused why Q26 was asking them to provide data they felt they had already included in Q24 and Q25. “I think it would be these two amounts (Q24 and Q25) added. This is confusing. It is awkward because I already did this, and doing math off the top of your head can throw people off. If I am understanding this is asking about Q24 and then the last question (Q25) and I think it is the combination, but it almost looks like a math problem. I would assume it would do the math for me.” (P507) “Well, Q26 is basically a combination of Q25 and Q24, and it seems redundant. I already broke down Q24 for you, I already broke down my premiums for you, I already broke down my out-of-pocket for copays and prescriptions, and I already broke down my out-of-pocket for OTCs, so why do I need to do that again?” (P372) Related, some participants reported that it would be generally burdensome to calculate these figures.

3 – Findings CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3-68 "I understand what each of these things are, I just would have to go look up doctor bills and credit card bills, and I don’t even know if I have those things. Logistically, not very convenient for whoever is taking this." (P506) Recommendations The use of the term “out-of-pocket” expenses appeared to result in misreporting for Q23. Several participants focused on the term “out-of-pocket” and reported expenses that are more commonly associated with “out-of-pocket” medical costs, like co-pays, deductibles, and other expenses that insurance does not cover and must be paid by the recipients of care. A few were also confused because premiums for employer-based plans are typically taken out of pay before it is dispersed, so they did not equate premium payments as coming “out-of-pocket” in a traditional sense. We suggest avoiding this term as it relates to premiums and instead providing a definition of “premium” and instructions on what should be included. This would also help address the confusion with the term “premium” that was reported by some participants. Several participants also had trouble differentiating between questions in this set and generally reported high levels of burden when responding. We recommend simplifying these questions to the extent possible and avoid asking respondents to sum across questions where data have already been provided as in the case of Q26. Instead, Census Bureau may consider computing these totals for the respondent and asking them to confirm the amounts. Childcare Expenses Participants were asked to answer ASEC questions related to childcare care expenses (Q30– Q32). Q30) Now we want to ask about some of your expenses for children. Did you or anyone in this household PAY for the care of any children while you or they worked, searched for work or were in training/education in 2022? o Yes o No Q31) Do you or does anyone in this household currently use any of the following types of child care for [CHILD]? Select all that apply. o Pre-kindergarten or 3-K o Head Start o Preschool, nursery school, or daycare center o Family daycare or paid care provided in someone else’s home o A paid babysitter or nanny in the home o Free care with a relative

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 3 – Findings 3-69 o Paid care with a relative o Any other type of child care, specify: ____ Q32) Do you or does anyone in this household receive government assistance, for instance a voucher or child care subsidy, to help pay for [CHILD]’s child care? o Yes o No Twenty-three participants reported not paying for childcare expenses in Q30, with only two participants (P48, P599) responding “yes” to this item. The majority of participants (22) skipped Q31 without selecting any responses as the question did not apply to them and there were no appropriate options for them to select (e.g., “not applicable”). However, one participant (P28), selected the “Any other type of childcare, specify” option and entered “I do not have children” in the text box. Only two participants (P599, P363) endorsed items in Q31. One of these participants (P599) indicated they pay for childcare in Q30 selecting “A paid babysitter or nanny” and “Free care from a relative” and another participant responded “No” to Q30 but selected “Free care from a relative” in Q31. All respondents selected “No” to Q32 and had no issues responding. When asked how easy or difficult it was to respond to this set of questions, the majority of participants reported the items were “easy” and had no difficulty answering. “I thought that they were extremely clear and concise, there shouldn’t be any issues answering them.” (P372) However, note that this series of items was administered to all participants, regardless of whether they had indicated having children. As a result, several participants who reported not having children were confused when they received these questions. In particular, some participants were uncertain about how to respond to Q31 given there were no applicable response options for them to select. “Again, this one (Q31) is not relevant to me, but there is no “not appliable.” I would just skip the question or I would click “any other” and specify that I don’t have children.” (P507) Given these items will only be administered to households with children once in the field, this issue should not be a problem.

CBDRB-FY24-SEHSD003-095 D-1 Appendix D: Participant Informed Consent Form What is the purpose of this interview? The U.S. Census Bureau is conducting interviews to help with the design and content of the Current Population Survey (CPS). The CPS is an important source of information about our nation on topics such as employment, health insurance, and income. It’s important that the questions make sense, are easy to answer, and that everyone understands the questions in the same way. You are one of about [ASEC Exploratory Interviews: 50; ASEC Cognitive Interviews: 120] people who are being asked to participate in these interviews. Findings from these interviews will be used to clarify survey questions and instructions on the CPS. What will happen if I take part in this interview? If you agree to take part in this study, you will be asked to answer questions about your household, including yourself and other people that live with you. Abstract The Current Population Survey (CPS), which is currently conducted via face-to-face and telephone interviewing, is the primary source of monthly labor force statistics in the U.S. Because of increasing costs of interviewer- administered surveys and lower response rates, the CPS is undergoing a modernization initiative to add an Internet self-response mode to its data collection. Designing the survey questions in web is a major change and requires extensive pretesting. RTI International and Research Support Services Inc. (RSS) conducted two rounds of usability testing to evaluate how respondents interacted with the prototype instrument in the Census Bureau’s production environment. Testing focused on how participants navigated through the prototype instrument and whether they encountered any issues with the design and usability of the instrument when answering the survey questions. This report documents the findings and recommendations from the usability testing of the CPS prototype instrument. 1-1 1. Project Background Sponsored jointly by the U.S. Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the Current Population Survey (CPS) is the premier source of data on employment and unemployment in the United States. It is a longitudinal survey conducted by trained U.S. Census Bureau interviewers, either by telephone or in person. The CPS comprises a core that asks the same employment, income, and demographic questions every month (see Questionnaires) and supplements that vary in sponsorship and content. The interviewer plays an important role in ensuring the quality of CPS data because the survey questions are complex, and careful probing may be needed before the respondent is able to provide a complete answer. The interviewer also plays an important role in maintaining the respondent’s motivation to complete the CPS survey, allowing item and unit response rates to remain high. Despite the importance of the interviewer for a successful completion of the CPS, there are compelling reasons to consider adding a self-administered web mode, including the potential to reduce data collection costs and improve response rates (both nationally and within demographic subgroups). To support this effort, RTI International and Research Support Services Inc. (RSS) conducted cognitive interviews to evaluate how well the CPS instrument performs in a self- administered web mode (see Cognitive Testing Results Report). RTI/RSS conducted two rounds of usability testing interviews with a prototype CPS web instrument programmed in the Census Bureau’s survey production environment to determine whether there were any issues with the usability that would result in errors or confusion or would otherwise hinder respondents from accurately completed the CPS internet instrument. This report summarizes the recruitment efforts and findings from the first and second round of usability testing interviews.

2-1 2. Methodology 2.1 Introduction Since the CPS is a longitudinal survey, usability testing was also conducted using the same participants in Round 1 and Round 2. The first interview instrument (Month in Sample 1 or “MIS-1”) was tested in Round 1 and the MIS-2 instrument in Round 2. In the MIS-1 instrument, the respondent is asked to roster their household, provide demographic information about themselves and their household members, and then complete the labor force section of the instrument for all household members ages 15 and older. In the MIS-2 instrument, the previously collected roster is presented to the respondent for any updates or revisions and the respondent proceeds to the labor force section for all eligible household members. Dependent interviewing—providing respondents with their previously reported responses—is used in some questions within the labor force section in the MIS-2 instrument. In the Census Bureau’s production environment, logging into the instrument differs for those who are logging in for the first time and those who are returning users. Due to differences in login procedures and instrument functionality, this usability study tested both the MIS-1 and MIS-2 instruments using the same participants in each round of testing. This section provides an overview of the recruitment efforts and interviewing methods for Round 1 and Round 2 of the CPS usability testing interviews. An overview of the recruitment strategies, eligibility criteria, usability testing participants, and the usability testing protocol and procedures are discussed in the sections that follow. 2.2 Recruitment Methods 2.2.1 Overview The RTI/RSS team recruited participants for Round 1 of Call Order 11 CPS Usability testing from June 25, 2024, to August 19, 2024, and participants for Round 2 from October 15, 2024, to November 13, 2024. Round 2 participants were individuals who had previously completed a Round 1 interview; no new individuals were recruited for Round 2. The RTI/RSS team posted online recruitment advertisements in selected areas on Craigslist, releasing advertisements on a rolling basis to maintain a steady stream of prospective recruits for screening and scheduling for Round 1 interviews (see Section 2.2.2 for details). The Census Bureau programmed a web-based eligibility screener in Qualtrics. The RTI/RSS team also established a toll-free telephone line dedicated to recruitment purposes. The web link of the screening instrument and the toll-free phone number were presented in the online advertisements (see Appendix A) to support participant recruitment. During the data collection period, the RTI/RSS team provided the Census Bureau with a weekly recruitment and interviewing progress report. The weekly report sought to present

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 2-2 the status of interview participants with respect to recruitment goals and needed sub- characteristics. The results of Round 1 and Round 2 recruitment presented in Section 2.2.4 of this report reflect the final recruitment outcomes. 2.2.2 Recruitment and Advertising Procedures During Call Order 11 CPS usability testing, the RTI/RSS team used Craigslist as the main venue for recruitment advertising. Craigslist is one of the best-known online bulletin boards and provides the most comprehensive coverage of metropolitan areas in the United States. To leverage Craigslist’s broad reach, RTI/RSS did not use advertisements that focused on specific characteristics and instead used a customized general advertisement. Additionally, RTI/RSS also posted the general recruitment advertisement on Reddit under the subreddit “r/samplesize” to further expand the reach to prospective recruits. The RTI/RSS team began the participant recruitment by posting the general recruitment advertisement on Craigslist under the “jobs/et cetera” sections. See Appendix A-1 for the text used in the recruitment ads. During Round 1, the first round of monthly paid advertising started on June 14, 2024, when we posted two advertisements. As completions gradually decreased, the team posted the second general advertisement (two new advertisements) on July 10 to boost the response to the web recruitment screener. The third general advertisement (three new advertisements) was posted on July 24, followed by the fourth posting (one new advertisement) on August 2. The RTI/RSS team also pursued avenues outside of Reddit and Craigslist during recruitment. We leveraged personal connections to contact potential participants who may fit the study criteria. We also posted advertisements to Facebook groups geared toward sharing job or work listings. The RTI/RSS team recorded screening responses from more than 950 prospective participants from all the advertisements in Round 1. For Round 2, the RTI/RSS team selected a subset of participants from Round 1 to complete a Round 2 interview. During Round 1 interviews, interviewers assessed participants’ interest and availability to complete a Round 2 interview. If participants were interested in participating in a second interview, interviewers made note of the participant’s availability/schedule for the Round 2 interviewing period (i.e., October and November). Interested participants were marked in the recruitment tracker as either a priority to schedule for Round 2 or a backup; priority participants were selected for Round 2 to achieve a sample that varied on employment status and device (e.g., cell phone, laptop or desktop) used to complete the Round 1 interview. Priority participants were sent a reminder in September about the Round 2 interviews and in early October, recruiters contacted those interested Round 1 participants to schedule them for their Round 2 interview.

2. Methodology 2-3 2.2.3 Participant Selection Strategy To facilitate efficient screening for the Round 1 CPS usability interviews, the RTI/RSS team created two automated spreadsheets to process screening data to determine participant eligibility for the required characteristics of interest. First, the team created the main intake sheet to import the screening responses from Qualtrics and to determine whether participants were eligible. Within the main intake spreadsheet, the RTI/RSS team employed a two-step review strategy to prioritize participants for selection. The spreadsheet first calculated the total number of eligible participant characteristics (recruitment criteria are displayed in Table 2.1). Next, the lead recruiter proceeded to review the screener responses of all prospective participants in the intake sheet, focusing on the self-reports of the contact information and the IP addresses in the paradata. Entries were screened for duplicates, and those with a foreign IP address were excluded. After reviewing and cleaning the tentative assignments, we exported records of eligible recruits to the CPS recruitment tracking sheet, which served as the main reference for recruitment and interview progress for the entire project team, including recruiters and interviewers. This recruitment tracker displayed which primary and secondary recruitment characteristic each participant represented (see Table 2.1 and Table 2.2). In this recruitment tracker, we created formulas in Microsoft Excel to make these eligibility criteria mutually exclusive; for example, self-employed participants were not also counted as employed full time. During the CPS usability testing data collection in Round 1, the RTI/RSS team processed and reviewed the screening data at least once a week to select eligible participants for an interview. After reviewing a batch of screening data, about 1 week would elapse before new assignments to recruiters/interviewers would be made to allow recruiters/interviewers sufficient time to contact their existing assignments by phone or email. How quickly interviewers contacted a selected participant after their assignment varied based on several factors, including the interviewer’s case load at the time of assignment, the number of scheduled interviews, and the speed with which other participants responded to the interviewer’s contact attempts. 2.2.4 CPS Usability Testing Participants For the first round of usability testing, the RTI/RSS team completed 80 interviews. During Round 1, RTI/RSS selected and contacted an additional 71 eligible participants; 27 participants did not respond to our invitation, four refused to participate, 18 did not attend their scheduled interview, and another 22 decided to withdraw their participation after they were scheduled for an interview or experienced severe technical issues that prevented them from being able to participate.

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 2-4 The 80 Round 1 participants served as the participant pool for Round 2. During Round 2, RTI/RSS completed 47 interviews. RTI/RSS selected and contacted an additional 13 eligible participants; six participants did not respond to our invitation, three did not attend their scheduled interview, and four decided to withdraw their participation after they were scheduled for an interview. RTI/RSS did not attempt to contact the remaining 20 participants. See Appendix A for all materials that recruiters used when contacting eligible participants and scheduling interviews, including the initial contact email (Appendix A-2), the scripts for speaking with eligible participants on the telephone (Appendix A-3), the template for the calendar invitation (Appendix A-4), and the template for the reminder emails (Appendix A-5). During Round 1, participants were asked to complete the interview on either a smartphone or a computer. Early in the data collection period, one participant participated in the interview on a tablet; however, as tablets were not a focus of this usability testing effort, no other participants were permitted to complete the interview on a tablet. This participant who completed on a tablet was counted as a computer interview for recruitment purposes. The recruitment team was flexible on the device that participants used (i.e., asked if the participant would prefer to participate on a desktop/laptop or a smartphone) until we got to the end of the interview period and asked participants if they were able to complete the interview on a specific device to meet recruitment goals. Device assignment had no observable impact on the pattern of results. During Round 2, we asked participants to use the same device that they used in Round 1 and all participants were able to do so. CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 2-8 2.3 Usability Testing Methods 2.3.1 Overview Usability testing consists of one-on-one interviews and is often employed to assess the functionality of web-administered questionnaires and surveys. For this effort, we employed usability testing methods to test an internet self-response survey of the CPS Core questionnaire, programmed in the Census Bureau’s production environment. The focus of this testing was to determine whether there are any issues with usability that would result in errors or confusion or would otherwise hinder respondents from accurately completing the revised CPS Core instrument. The interviews used a protocol that included both observing the participants as they interacted with the website and survey as well as using retrospective pre-scripted probes (as described in Section 2.3.2). Spontaneous probes were used as needed to better understand usability issues not addressed by scripted probes. 2.3.2 Protocol and Procedures All interviews were (1) conducted virtually using Microsoft Teams’ videoconference capabilities, (2) conducted within the Census Bureau’s Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) environment or on a Census Bureau–provided laptop, (3) audio-recorded or video- and audio-recorded, and (4) approximately 60 minutes long. Participants were asked to complete the interview using either a desktop/laptop computer or a smartphone. Participants received a $50 digital gift card incentive during Round 1 and a $60 digital gift card incentive during Round 2. Census Bureau provided the RTI/RSS Team with the usability testing protocol to be used for data collection (see Appendix B-1 for the Round 1 protocol and Appendix B-2 for the Round 2 protocol). The interviews used a think aloud method and included additional retrospective scripted probing and spontaneous probing. To standardize the overall implementation of each test case, the test was carried out in the following sequence: 1. Obtain the participant’s consent (see Appendix C). 2. Start video and audio recording using Census Bureau–approved software and a backup digital recorder. 3. Ask the participant to share their screen and log in to the survey (the login steps are detailed in Section 3.2.1 and Section 3.2.5). 4. Ask the participant to answer the survey questions in the web instrument while thinking out loud. During this step, the interviewer observes and makes note about any issues. 5. (Round 1 only): Share their screen and open a satisfaction questionnaire programmed in Qualtrics (see Appendix B-1). The participant then told the interviewer how they would answer each question, and the interviewer filled this out for them.

2. Methodology 2-9 6. Ask retrospective probes after the main interview (both scripted and spontaneous) while the interviewer shared their screen with screenshots of the survey for reference. 7. Complete the payment voucher. 8. Save the recording locally within Census Bureau’s secure network environment. 9. Indicate on a tracking sheet the time on the recording that the interview began and ended. 10. Complete the summary template provided by Census Bureau following each interview on a flow basis and no more than 5 business days after each interview. These summaries contained exact words/phrases/sentences (when this information was important for the study goals) and included quotations that may be useful in illustrating a finding along with spontaneous verbalizations from the participants.

3-1 3. Findings 3.1 Introduction This section summarizes the findings from both rounds of CPS Core usability testing. These findings are first presented by topic (i.e., the sections of the CPS survey that were of most interest in the testing protocol). Within each section, findings are presented separately for Round 1 and Round 2. Miscellaneous usability and cognitive findings are presented last. During usability testing, programming errors were found, since an early version of the instrument was still in development. These findings are not included in this report. All screenshots included in this report are test images and do not represent any participant information. 3.2 Survey Invitation Letter and Login Process 3.2.1 Round 1 Login process During Round 1, the login process included the following steps. Once the participant reaches the survey website, they must enter information at three different screens (screenshots below) to log into the survey. 1. Access the survey: Desktop/laptop: Interviewers sent the survey invitation letter (a PDF document) to the participant via email as an attachment (see Appendix D). This letter included the web address to access the survey and the participant’s unique user ID. Sending the PDF helped to replicate the information respondents would receive via a postage mailing and/or email the first time they are invited to complete the CPS on the internet. Interviewers asked participants to access and log in to the survey using steps in this invitation letter as a guide. Smartphones: Because reading a PDF document is difficult on the smaller smartphone screen and switching between the PDF and the survey login screen can be challenging on smartphones, these participants were not sent the survey invitation letter. Instead, interviewers gave the participants the web address for the survey either verbally or in the chat on Microsoft Teams. As a result, the study did not evaluate the usability of accessing the website on smartphones. If the participant struggled, the interviewer asked what they would do if the interviewer was not there; the interviewer only provided instructions if the participant was unable to access the survey or log in. As described in Section 2.2.4, in Round 1, participants generally chose whether to use a desktop/laptop or a smartphone to complete the interview. As we neared the end of the interview period, interviewers asked participants if they were able to complete the interview on a specific device to meet recruitment goals.

Participants then accessed their email to get the verification code and entered this code into the text box on the second screen (Figure 3.2). Figure 3.1. Findings 3-15 3.2.4 Round 1 Recommendations The recommendations that follow could potentially make the login process clearer to participants because some were not expecting the multiple steps required to log in. The recommendations could also make the login process easier for participants, as some thought that the process was burdensome. • Consider making the web address more prominent on the survey invitation. When sent to participants over email, consider making this a hyperlink. Also consider ensuring that participants can copy and paste their User ID from the invitation when it is sent through email. • Because of the study limitations, we did not evaluate the usability of accessing the website on smartphones. More usability testing of accessing the survey on smartphones should be done before conclusions can be made. • Consider adding a QR code that links to the CPS web address if the invitation is sent in the mail. • Consider describing the three steps of the login process in the survey invitation. o Recommendation for survey invitation wording for email: Please respond by the end of this week. Follow these steps to login to the survey: 1. Click here to log in: access.census.gov/cps 2. Enter your email address and check your email to get the verification code. Please make note of the email address you use to complete this month’s survey as you will use the same one each month. 3. Enter your User ID: XXX-XXX-XXXX o Recommendation for survey invitation wording sent in mail: Please respond by the end of this week. Follow these steps to login to the survey: 1. Enter this web address into your browser: access.census.gov/cps OR scan this QR code: [IMAGE] 2. Enter your email address and check your email to get the verification code. Please make note of the email address you use to complete this month’s survey as you will use the same one each month. 3. Enter your User ID: XXX-XXX-XXXX • On the login screen, consider labeling the User ID text box with “User ID,” similar to how the email box and verification code box are labeled. 3.2.5 Round 2 Login Process When a respondent is a returning user to the Census Bureau’s survey site, the login process is only two steps. Once they arrive at the website, they must enter the same email they

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 3-16 used to log into the website originally. Next, an 8-character verification code is sent to that email, and they must enter the verification code to enter their survey. They are not asked for their User ID as a returning user. These login screens were modified due to feedback received in Round 1 that the User ID and verification code were confused with one another. On the first screen requesting the user’s email address, “8-digit” was added as a descriptor of the verification code in the instructions: “You will receive an 8-digit verification code in your email” (see Figure 3.5). On the second screen where users are asked to enter the verification code, the introduction text was revised to: “Please enter the 8-digit verification code sent to you by email. This is not the same as the User ID in your survey invitation.” The label for the write-in box was modified to “Verification Code (8-digit)” (see Figure 3.6). During Round 2 of the usability testing, participants were not given a survey invitation letter regardless of the device they were using (as described in Section 2.2.4, we asked participants to use the same device that they had used in Round 1, that is, either a smartphone or a computer/desktop). Interviewers gave all participants the web address to access the survey either verbally or in the chat on Microsoft Teams. Once accessed, participants would enter their email address, receive an email with the verification code, and enter the verification code on the next screen. Like in Round 1, if the participant struggled, the interviewer asked what they would do if the interviewer was not there; the interviewer only provided instructions if the participant was unable to access the survey or log in. Round 2 Second Login Screen Requesting Verification Code 3.2.6 Round 2 Login Process Findings Overall, participants had fewer usability issues with the login process in Round 2 than in Round 1. As this was the second time that participants were logging into the survey, this could be due to familiarity with the process and learning that took place during the first login. Of the five participants who experienced major issues with logging into the survey in Round 1 and required assistance from the interviewer, three participated in a Round 2 interview. Only one of these participants experienced major issues with logging into the survey in Round 2, indicating that these participants’ familiarity with the login process and assistance from the interviewer in Round 1 could have contributed to experiencing fewer issues in Round 2. Across all of the Round 2 participants, 39 participants had no usability issues with the login process and were successfully able to log in to the survey, 7 participants had minor issues but were easily able to navigate these issues on their own, and 2 participants who had major issues and required the interviewer’s assistance to log in. Most participants who did not have any usability issues logging into the survey thought that the process was easy. “This looks really similar to a lot of the pages that I have encountered that asks for a code. It seems like everyone is doing a two-step verification now so it has a place to enter in a code that was sent to my email and then click submit so it looks really standard from things I've seen on other sites or logins that ask for a verification code” (P1429, computer). “This is pretty easy. I feel like a lot of websites have done this kind of thing before where they send a code to my email and I plug it in for security. This is, you know, the usual what I expect” (P1470, computer).
