However, a few recommendations, described below, could potentially make the process easier for participants. • Consider making the “Resend email” button larger to make it more visible to participants. • If participants attempt to use the back button in the browser on this screen, a message such as the following could appear: “Confirm form resubmission.” 3.3 Household Roster 3.3.1 Round 1 Household Roster Functionality During Round 1, participants were asked to list everyone that lived in their household (see Figure 3.7). To ensure that the CPS instrument did not take up too much time during the usability interview, interviewers asked participants to only add up to three individuals to the household roster (if applicable) and to list individuals who were age 15 years old and older (if there were children younger than 15 years old in the household). Participants could add children under 15 years old if there were not three people in the household ages 15 years old or older.

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 3-24 3.3.3 Round 1 Recommendations CPS respondents including themselves in the household roster is a major data quality issue. Therefore, we recommend making it clearer that respondents should add themselves to the household roster. • Recommendation for wording on the household roster screen: What are the names of all persons living or staying here? Enter one person on each line. Enter names until you have listed everyone who lives or stays here, then click next. Please start by entering your name. Findings 3-27 3.3.5 Round 2 Findings As described in Section 3.3.2, some participants did not enter themselves in the household roster and had to be instructed to do so by the interviewer during Round 1; other participants did not list themselves first. We note that the Round 1 instructions asked users to start with the person who owns or rents the home, which could have caused some participants to not enter themselves first. Some participants also did not realize they needed to enter themselves at all. In cases where the interviewer instructed them to do so, they were listed last in the household roster. In the Round 2 instrument, on the household roster screen, Person 1 was programmed to be the participant; therefore, there is no “Remove” button (see Figure 3.9 above). This caused some routing and fill issues later in the survey during usability testing where some questions were directed toward “you” but were referring to Person 1, a different member of the household. This has been revised in the CPS instrument and any issues found in testing due to this error have not been included here. Adding and Removing Household Members Overall, most participants did not have any major usability issues adding or removing individuals from the household roster (Figure 3.9). Only three participants spontaneously added or removed people from their household roster without instruction from the interviewer to do so (P1616, smartphone; P1804, computer; P1980, smartphone). A few participants were unsure if they needed to add individuals to their household roster. One participant (P1733, smartphone) shared that they started renting a room in their house to a tenant and asked if they should be added to the household. When the interviewer asked what they would do on their own, the participant said, “I would probably be inclined to not to add him just because a) it's easier for me and then b) because I don't know his birthday off the top of my head so I would have to… look up what his birthday is and so it's obviously a lot easier to skip it and not add him. Especially if I know he is just here temporarily.” Later in the interview, this participant also mentioned that their daughter occasionally lived with them and if this interview had happened during that time, they would add their daughter to the household roster. Similarly, another participant noted that a definition of “living with you” would be helpful: “It's very easy. You just click on Add another person. One thing that you might add to the screen that I don't know if it matters is what's your definition of someone that's living with you. Are they staying there a week? That's their only home? Are they staying there at least a month? That might need to be cleared up a little bit. If somebody is staying with me, they could be here for two weeks on vacation, do I add them? I don't think I do because

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 3-28 they're not resident, but if somebody lost their place to live and they need to stay with me until their new apartment is available, that I might consider them living with me” (P1658, computer). Whether they did it spontaneously or because they were instructed by the interviewer, most participants did not have any usability issues with adding or removing participants. “It was pretty easy, it shows what to do, it shows 'add another person' and a plus sign so that's pretty self-explanatory and then it asks the basic questions that it did initially for me and the other person in my household so that was easy” (P1429, computer). “Yes, it was either confirm that, that it is, that's who is in the household or if you had to remove them, it has that 'Remove' button. Or if needed to add someone it had, did have the 'Add' button. So it was basic, very clear” (P1591, smartphone). Remove Person Confirmation Pop-Up Most participants said that they appreciated this pop-up asking them to confirm (Figure 3.10). “Well I think it's good because they want to make sure that you're aware that you're about to remove someone. So that's just a reminder. Are you sure you want to remove this person? Yeah, that was pretty cool” (P1328, computer). “I like that because if you made a mistake the person would be gone and this is asking if you are sure and you can say no and change your mind, so those things are pretty important,” (P1721, smartphone). “I like the pop up. I like that it does ask you, are you sure you want to do this, because sometimes you can accidentally click on something, I've experienced that, where I didn't want to click that and then I have to click all the way back and put it in. So knowing that this is something where you have to do some work before deleting it, just to be sure” (P1760, computer). “I always like a confirmation though, so I was glad it was there. However, the recommendations below could potentially reduce the usability issues that participants experienced with other aspects of the household roster section. • Consider rewording the response options on the question that asks why a household member is being removed to better differentiate between “Person moved out,” “Person left – usual residence elsewhere last month,” and “Person has a usual residence elsewhere this month.” Due to sensitivity, consider moving the option where the household member died as the last option. • Consider realigning the edit buttons to match the categories on the same line and removing or reducing the size of the “No Issues Found” column, as this may crowd the screen (see Figure 3.14, left). For one participant (P1716) who had a warning message in the issues column, the warning message was nearly unreadable and made the edit screen very difficult to navigate (see Figure 3.14, right). Although few smartphone participants accessed the “Edit” screen, consider reformatting this so that it is easier to read on mobile devices.

However, BLS and the Census Bureau could consider using dropdown menus that allow text input to make this process easier for some participants. However, because some participants did not know the date of birth for some household members and one participant did not want to enter the date of birth for any household members because of the sensitivity, we do have several recommendations to improve the Help functionality on this page (described below). The text included in the “Help” pop-up used during Round 1 testing is shown in Figure 3.16. • Instead of the link text “Help,” consider changing this to “Don’t know this person’s date of birth? Click here.” • Consider making the Help text more succinct. Because participants do not receive an error message if they leave only date of birth blank, consider removing this text from the Help screen. For example, this Help text could include the following: This question consists of two parts: the person’s date of birth and the person’s age. I do not know the person’s date of birth: o If you know only part of the date of birth (month, day, and/or year), enter as much as you know. Then confirm or enter the person’s age. o If you don’t know any of the date of birth, leave the date of birth blank. Then enter the person’s age. o It is okay to estimate the person’s age, but please do not estimate the month, day, or year. • Consider making the “How is date of birth data used?” section of the Help text a separate pop-up. Instead, these participants only saw the first few words of the prefilled text and did not click into the textbox to view the complete description before confirming that no changes had been made. I like to see everything on one page” (P1238, computer). One participant said that the font could be slightly darker to contrast more with the white background (P1383, computer). One participant (P1935, computer) commented on the Yes/No radio button questions early in the survey and the gray bar that appears when the cursor is over one of the response options: “So for selecting the options I feel like maybe, um, I don't know. I'm just wondering, so there's this gray bar that's included with each of the options and I feel like it would be easier to use if the gray bar was slightly more visible.” Figure 3.52 below shows an example of what these comments refer to, where the “Current Population Survey” banner takes up much of the screen real estate on a laptop screen (as mentioned by P1238, computer). Furthermore, it shows that when the mouse is hovering over a response option, the gray highlighting could have further contrast with the white background (as mentioned by P1935). However, we do note that the gray and white contrast issue could potentially have 508 compliance implications.

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 3-74 Figure 3.52. Example Screen on a Laptop Recommendations Although some participants had some suggestions for improvements of the visual design of the survey, there were no major usability issues related to the visual design. Therefore, there are no recommended changes. However, we urge that designers consider the participant views presented here when they design a final version for implementation, including any 508 compliance implications. 3.11.3 Error Messages Findings In Round 1, a few participants received error messages that seemed to indicate an issue with the server. However, they were able to refresh the page and continue with the survey without issue. One participant (P1429, computer) received an error message when they reached the screen asking for telephone number. The message stated, “Your current session has gotten out of sync with the server, this is most likely due to another user working on the same thing you are. We need to reset your session to the last known good state.” The participant clicked “Ok” and the page refreshed, taking them back to the previous question that asked about phones in the household. This participant did not have any further reaction to this error message. Another participant (P1754, smartphone) received two error messages while completing the survey. A first error message popped up when the person was responding to employment questions about the first person in the household, but the participant clicked okay too quickly and the interviewer could not see it. It did not show on the recording because the

3. Findings 3-75 Teams icon was covering it, but the screen refreshed and the participant was able to continue without any problems. The second error message appeared while the participant was answering the disability questions. It said “Something went wrong! We were unable to save your latest data. We need to reset your session to the last known good state.” It was unclear why they received this error. They clicked “OK,” the page refreshed, and they were able to continue with no problems. During the debriefing probes, this participant mentioned these error messages when asked how the CPS survey compared to other surveys they have completed, saying, “I kept getting an error.” Otherwise, this participant did not have any other reactions to these messages, as they were able to refresh the page and continue on with the survey each time. Finally, one participant (P1578, smartphone) received a “Session out of sync with the server” error that occurred at the level of the education screen for Person 1. The participant had to re-enter the date of birth questions. This participant did not have any further reaction to this error message. Recommendations Receiving these error messages did not cause any usability issues for these participants. Without being sure about the reason for the errors, we have no recommendation to make. 3.11.4 FAQ/Progress Bar Findings About a dozen participants across rounds wished the survey had a progress bar to know how much more they had ahead, along the lines of the following quotes: “…Oh, by the way, it would have been nice to have some sort of progress bar. I know it’s hard because some questions are skipped… that would be really nice because they know I’m making progress” (P1800, computer). “…There wasn't even a progress bar that kind of showed that you're X percentage of the way through or you're on this section and there are five sections total. So I guess if someone didn't have a lot of time and they thought it was going to be quick and then they got part-way through it and they're like, 'well, I've got to go do something' they don't have any idea if it's going to save” (P1563, computer). “What I did like is that many surveys it tells you that you are at question 11 out of 80, 12 out of 80, it tells you how many screens you've done and how many you have left, I didn't see that on yours and I like that. It doesn't make me think that I have 15 more pages, 20 more pages, I just do it until I am done” (P1721, smartphone).

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 3-76 “I mean my overall thoughts it’s a little cumbersome. It's like a lot of short questions and also I kind of wish, going on, that I knew how many more questions there were going to be like a little tracker bar” (P2019, computer). While answering the satisfaction survey, one participant mentioned that there was no hover-over text for additional information on any of the questions to give more information in case the respondent needed help answering a question, including knowing if a partial survey could be saved. “So, I guess if someone didn't have a lot of time and they thought it was going to be quick and then they got part-way through it and they're like, 'well, I've got to go do something' they don't have any idea if it's going to save” (P1563, computer). Recommendations Participants’ comments showed that they did not know some basic information about the survey (such as approximate burden) or where to go if they had questions. We did not observe any participant click or comment on the FAQ button or the Save and Log out button. The current position of the FAQ and the Save and Log out buttons can be seen in Figure 3.53. Current Location of the FAQ/Save and Log Out Buttons The survey methods literature generally does not recommend including a progress bar, and programming one would be nearly impossible given the varied skip patterns. Nonetheless, making it more evident for participants where to get answers to their questions would be useful, particularly in production to reduce possible breakoffs. We recommend looking for a

3. Findings 3-77 way to make these buttons more visible, to make them stand out. For example, the buttons could have labels in blue font inside white frames in that same upper-right corner of the screen. 3.11.5 Accidentally Exiting Out of the Survey Findings In Round 2, a few participants exited out of the survey by mistake. These were people answering the survey on smartphones, where they accidentally used the back button on their phone (i.e., clicked back in the browser). This logged them out of the survey, and they had to login again. They were pleasantly surprised to see that the survey had saved their previous answers and took them back to where they had left off. For example, after the interviewer asked one participant to return to the household roster screen, the participant (P1616, smartphone) hit the browser back button on their phone instead of the back button in the programmed instrument. This took them out of the survey and back to login page where they were asked to enter their email. The participant then had to complete the login process again before getting back to the survey. Another participant (P1754, smartphone) had a similar situation. When they were logged out of the survey they said: “I can’t believe you can’t go back one, that’s not good... that’s not helpful.” During probing, the interviewer asked the participant what made it easy to complete this survey on their smartphone, and they said, “Definitely going back to where you were if you got bumped off, that was a lot of help, because if I had to do it over and over again, I would have been very frustrated and I might not have gone through with it… I think that was a good failsafe for them to put in.” Recommendations The recommendation provided in Section 3.2.7 could also be applicable here, to discourage respondents from using the back button in the browser. If participants attempt to use this back button in the browser rather than the back button on screen in the CPS survey, a message such as the following could appear: “Confirm form resubmission.” 3.11.6 Submit Page Findings In Round 2, a few participants commented on the fact that they cannot review or edit their answers once they get to the submit page, unless they click the back button. “The only thing that really did make me feel if anything uncomfortable, it’s not like these questions are doctor’s questions, where it’s like life or death, but like I said, at the end where I click the last page and suddenly I can’t go back anymore and I’m told once I hit submit, that’s it and you can’t go back anymore, I’m being told this,

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 3-78 but I don’t really have a way to review what I’ve said. So the way it’s worded… it’s like oh, should I really review what I just wrote?... Especially if you might be conversing with these people in the future. If you’re going to show the survey and what I answered before is going to pop up, I’m already going to trust you that what I answered before is already there. But if I wasn’t going to go back, I’d get nervous… so especially if you’re going to be talking to these people for a long time, more than once, maybe make sure that the first answers are the right answers. That’s definitely something that I would see as a red flag in getting the right data” (P1760, computer). While reviewing the submit screen, one participant (P2158, smartphone) said that they were assuming that once they submitted, they would be shown a confirmation page, noting that it says you cannot change anything. This person said that they wanted to be able to see their answers without having to back through the whole survey. However, they were not sure what to do if they wanted to review something and change something. There were a few additional comments about the submit page: “…And also the submit, the last couple of screens was, you were, I wasn't submitting at that point. Other than that, there, you know, it seemed pretty easy” (P1716, smartphone). “No everything was pretty much straightforward and other than, you know, it said 'you are almost completed' until you had to keep clicking on 'next' to get to the end, the confirmation” (P2133, smartphone). “The last, on the very last page, when we finish, it would have been nice to see like 'thank you' written in like big bold letters and just a really brief summary from like one to four sentences of the importance of filling out the survey, so that people will leave with, knowing, feeling that they've contributed to the US Census” (P1364, computer). Recommendations Implement a feature that would allow respondents to review their answers before submitting. 3.12 Miscellaneous Cognitive Issues 3.12.1 Don’t Know/Unsure Option Findings Although already discussed in the usual/actual hours worked section, it is worth mentioning that some participants were vocal about needing an option to indicate they did not know certain information for other household members. They were looking for a “Don’t know” or

3. Findings 3-79 “Unsure” response option for many questions. Some examples include the following situations. One participant (P1367, smartphone) rented rooms to others in their home and reported them as household members, but they did not know many of the answers to the questions asked about the renters. This participant explained their frustration with not having any options to indicate “Don’t know” on any of the questions. Another participant (P1568, smartphone) was filling out the certification/license question for the second household member and said they would not be sure how to proceed if they did not know the answer for the other household member. “Questions like this I'm kind of like, what if I don't know? Is there an option to, like, skip and come back to it? That would be nice.” This participant also said they weren’t sure about the number of hours that their household members worked: “Yeah, again, this is like, because I'm answering on behalf of someone maybe it's a best guess.” Another participant (P1754, smartphone) wrote in “IDK” in answer to the question asking for usual activities or duties at a household member’s job. Recommendations Consider if any questions could include a “Don’t know” response option, particularly when asked about other household members. We understand the risk of giving respondents an easy way to avoid estimating (or feeling they are providing information about others without their permission) in proxy responses, but there may be some items where missing data for proxy responses is a well-known occurrence and a “Don’t know” answer might be more useful than a blank. 3.12.2 Unique Employment Situations Findings Some participants had unique employment situations and went down a survey path that they thought did not necessarily match their situation. One participant (P1549, smartphone) was not working but currently looking for work. They answered “yes” to the question asking if they had done any work for pay last week, thus routing down the “single job” display logic. The participant indicated that in the week prior they had participated in a research study and received an incentive for doing so but they were not employed. When they saw the question asking about the usual number of hours worked, they were confused: “Umm, how would I answer this? Would I just put '0' if I am currently unemployed?” … “Yeah, I mean, I did a research study. I participated in a research study which, I mean, I consider work for pay because they did pay me” (P1549, smartphone).

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 3-80 One participant (P1297, smartphone) used the back button in the Looking for Work section. They were actively looking for work while already employed, but they were asked why they had stopped working. They used the back button to see the previous question but did not change anything and then returned to the reason for stopping work question. They had not stopped working but chose Temporary Job Ended: “I was looking for something part time as I'm working. … I don't know about this one. I'll just say ‘temporary job ended’.” Last, another participant (P2141, computer) indicated during the interview that their wife is retired but does small jobs/gig work for extra money. Therefore, they indicated that their wife worked for pay in the prior week, but when asked how many hours she usually works, the participant responded “0” because their wife is retired. Because of this combination of responses, the participant was taken down a path that was very confusing to them and indicated that there was no way to report that their wife is retired but does small jobs for extra money. Furthermore, there were five participants who owned businesses but did not work in the business in the prior week. Therefore, the survey took them down the path of being absent from work, which was very confusing to them. These participants’ experiences with the CPS survey are described in Section 3.8.1. Recommendations Consider these situations and their likely prevalence in the overall survey population. Depending on the potential impact of these, there may be a need to make design changes in the survey. 3.12.3 Miscellaneous Additional Cognitive Issues One participant made an interesting suggestion that may be useful to respondents in general. They said that they wanted the introduction to the employment section (“These questions ask about work-related activities last week”) to include a specific range of dates for the week in question: “Maybe it would be clearer to put actual dates on it, depending on when the person is taking the survey, because thinking back, I'm like okay what day is it today, like what does last week count as? Is it Sunday through Thursday? Or is it Sunday through Saturday of last week? What are the actual boundaries I should be thinking about?” (P1568, smartphone). However, this was intentionally programmed in this manner (i.e., without specific dates) for usability testing, as interviews continued on a rolling basis throughout two months. This will not be the case in CPS production. One participant (P1328, computer) wanted more information about why the survey was asking questions about their work history: “Certain portions of it I was, didn't see the necessity of the questions as far as income and if we're working and I didn't like that part. I didn't think it had any relevance but that's just my opinion.”

Findings 3-81 One participant (P1563, computer) had some difficulty reporting whether they and another household member (Person 2) were working during the previous week; both had been away on vacation together. To the question “LAST WEEK, did you do ANY work for either pay or profit?” the participant answered Yes for themselves, but No for Person 2. Neither reported any hours worked the previous week. This impacted the follow-up questions that were displayed for Person 1 because they were shown questions about being absent from work (they selected “vacation or personal time off”). However, they did report 0 actual hours worked for both household members. It is unclear why this participant answered differently for each person. It would probably go faster if we just had the question itself because the first time it was mentioned, that's fine, but each. I found myself, after awhile, not wanting to read that part because I already knew what it was” (P1591, smartphone). Recommendations No recommendations at this time.

4-1 4. Conclusion 4.1 Round 1 In summary, the major findings after Round 1 usability testing include the following. For each section, the usability issues are listed in order of relative severity, with any other observations (including findings of functionality that worked well) listed last. Survey invitation letter: • Minor issues with the letter included the following: (1) a few participants had trouble finding the web address for the survey, likely because it does not start with “www”; and (2) although they did not view the letter during testing, a few smartphone participants mentioned the use of a QR code rather than a web address to access the CPS survey. • When asked about the survey invitation letter, most participants thought that the letter was easy to understand and said that they could easily find the information that they needed. Login process: • Some participants who completed their interview on the computer and were sent the survey invitation letter attempted to enter the User ID into the verification code field. Ten of these participants (all computer) were able to figure out the difference on their own, but five of these participants (4 computer, 1 smartphone) had to be guided through this process by the interviewer. • Two participants had issues with navigating to the web address. Some participants had some trouble with copying and pasting or entering the verification code or the User ID. • Sixteen participants (9 computer, 7 smartphone) thought that the login process was burdensome because it had more steps than what they were expecting. • Eight participants commented that either the verification code or the User ID was longer than what they were expecting or what they were used to. • The recommendations listed in Section 3.2.4 could potentially make the login process clearer to participants, because some were not expecting the multiple steps required to log in. The recommendations could also make the login process easier for participants, as some thought that the process was burdensome. • The following findings indicate further observations (i.e., not usability issues) of the login process:

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 4-2 o Sixteen participants used another device during the login process, specifically, to access their email to get the verification code. Many of these participants said that they did this so that they could keep the CPS login screen open in their browser and not have to go to another window/tab to check their email. o Eight participants mentioned that they did not mind getting the verification code over email but wanted the option to receive it via text. o Many participants thought that the login screens were clear and felt that they understood what to do on each page. Participants also thought that the email containing the verification code was clear and appreciated that the verification code was displayed in large font. Furthermore, some participants commented that they were expecting or used to a two-step verification login process, which is used on many other websites and apps. Household roster: • The major usability/cognitive issues with the household roster include: o It was unclear to some participants that they needed to add themselves to the household roster. Some participants asked the interviewer to confirm that they should add themselves on the initial household roster screen, and other participants did not add themselves to the household roster until the interviewer instructed them to do so. If participants were instructed to add themselves to the roster, they had no issues completing this. It should also be noted that some participants did not list themselves first because of the instruction on the page, “Start with the name of the person, or one of the persons, who owns or rents this home.” The recommendation listed in Section 3.3.3 could make it clearer to respondents that they should add themselves to the household roster. o A few participants had some trouble deciding who they should include in the household roster. • Overall, most participants did not have any usability issues with the household roster screens and thought that the process of adding household members was easy. Demographics (date of birth): • A few participants were unsure of some household members’ complete birthdays and were unsure what to do next. Some participants asked the person if they were present (i.e., in another room, in the household at the time) and some participants made their best guess. Only one of these participants clicked on the “Help” link but could not figure out what to do; this participant entered an age for each person but

4. Conclusions 4-3 not date of birth. One participant did not want to give the full date of birth for each member of her household and preferred to only state their ages. • Because some participants did not know the date of birth for some household members and one participant did not want to enter the date of birth for any household members because of the sensitivity, the recommendations listed in Section 3.4.2 could improve the Help functionality on this page. • Many participants commented that they liked the format of entering month, day, and year as separate dropdowns, especially preferring this method over a calendar method. However, other participants noted that the dropdowns were easy to use, but being able to type into the dropdowns would have been faster. Usual and actual hours: • As had been the case in cognitive testing, some participants objected about being asked both usual and actual hours, because they work the same number of hours every week and are not allowed to work more hours. Others thought the question may need to be answered with the number of hours they get paid for, regardless of how many hours they actually work. • We recommended using the instructions that were tested in the second round of CPS cognitive testing, as described in Section 3.5.2. • Sixteen participants who reported multiple jobs for themselves or a household member were probed on their preference about seeing the usual hours questions (and later about the actual hours questions) for the main and other job on the same page or across different pages. All but one of the 16 participants preferred reporting them on the same page. • Survey designers had wondered if the labels for “hours” or “hours per week” were understood to be labels rather than clickable buttons. None of the participants tried to click on a label, and all understood what the labels were for. Questions for those who are self-employed: • No recommended changes at this time. Questions for those who are not working: • As there were 5 participants who were confused about being taken down the path of being absent from work if they reported owning a business but not working in that business in the prior week, we recommend considering this unique employment situation.

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 4-4 • There were no major usability issues found during Round 1 for any of the “not working” series of questions. • However, when answering the question that asked how long they had been looking for work (Figure 3.42), one participant (P1754, smartphone) entered in the number and did not select the unit of time from the dropdown. When they clicked next, they got the error message (Figure 3.43). After this participant saw this message, they were easily able to understand that they needed to select “Weeks” from the dropdown. They were able to fix this error and continue with the survey, indicating that the error message was helpful to them. • Because there were no usability issues with the questions in the “not working” section, no changes are recommended. • Last, a few participants were confused about the wording of the question that asked how long they had been looking for work, specifically because the question specified “As of the end of LAST WEEK” (Figure 3.42). Disability questions: • There were no major usability issues for the disability section during Round 1, nor any major differences between the smartphone and computer cases. Participants felt that the questions were generally easy to answer, and a few found the format of the question particularly effective. • We recommend adding a “Help” or “More information” button to address privacy concerns (listed in Section 3.9.2). Nativity dropdown: • Although many participants found it helpful to type in partial responses before selecting the country from the dropdown, some were unsure how to interact with the textbox. Some participants experiencing delays when they clicked on the dropdown, which caused confusion. Other issues stemmed from participants entering things like “USA” or “US” into the textbox without selecting the “United States” option from the dropdown. This led some participants to answer additional questions about their citizenship status, which caused confusion. • A few participants searched for countries that had several names listed (e.g., China). • Some participants also found the sequence redundant and bothersome because the sequence asked about each individual and each individual’s mother and father. • The recommendations listed in Section 3.10.2 could improve the functionality of this dropdown.

4. Conclusions 4-5 • The interactive dropdown list of countries was generally well-received, with almost all participants using a combination of typing and selecting the country from the predictive dropdown list or selecting the pinned option, United States, from the top of the dropdown. No participants scrolled through the entire list in search for their desired country. The placement of “United States” as the first option on the list was appreciated among several participants. Miscellaneous usability issues: • A few participants received error messages that seemed to indicate an issue with the server. However, they were able to refresh the page and continue with the survey without issue. • About a dozen participants across rounds wished the survey had a progress bar to know how much more of the survey they had left to answer. Participants’ comments showed that they did not know some basic information about the survey (such as approximate burden) or where to go if they had questions. We did not observe any participant click or comment on the FAQ button or the Save and Log out button. The survey methods literature generally does not recommend including a progress bar, and programming one would be nearly impossible given the varied skip patterns. Nonetheless, making it more evident for participants where to get answers to their questions would be useful, particularly in production to reduce possible breakoffs. • Some participants, across different equipment, commented that the font size could be bigger or the buttons could be larger. • Participants were asked which of the persons listed by the participant owned or rented the home where the household lives. This question was set up to accept a single answer, but some participants did not understand why the question only allowed one response so some attempted to select more than one. Miscellaneous cognitive issues: • Some participants wanted a “don’t know” or “unsure” response option in many sections, as proxy reporting was difficult for these participants. • Some participants had unique employment situations and went down a survey path that they perceived to not necessarily match their situation (details listed in Section 3.12.2). 4.2 Round 2 In summary, the major findings after Round 2 usability testing include the following. Overall, participants were easily able to answer the questions and had no major usability issues with the visual design of the survey. For each section, the usability issues are listed

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 4-6 in order of relative severity, with any other observations (including findings of functionality that worked well) listed last. Login process: • One participant did not see the “Resend email” button on the login screen and clicked “Back” in the web browser to enter their email again. This caused confusion for them when the screen refreshed to the same page, and they were unable to enter their email a second time. • The recommendations listed in Section 3.2.7 could potentially make the process easier for participants, although the few issues that participants experienced were minor. • Participants did not have any major usability issues with the login process. However, (similar to Round 1) some participants wanted the ability to receive the verification code over text because this would have been easier for them. Household roster: • On the question that asked the reason why the person is removed (Figure 3.11), many participants said that some of the response options were confusing or unclear and thought that some of the response options were overlapping. However, some participants noted that the formatting of the edit screen was confusing. • The recommendations listed in Section 3.3.6 could potentially reduce the usability issues described above. • Overall, most participants did not have any major usability issues with adding or removing individuals from the household roster. 4. Conclusions 4-7 Demographics (education): • Most participants did not have any issues on this screen, whether they received this screen during the CPS instrument or were shown this question in probing. • Several participants noted that they appreciated having the education question prefilled with dependent data. • A few participants mentioned during probing that they thought the number of response options was excessive (see Figure 3.18). • Because participants did not have any major usability or cognitive issues that prevented them from answering this question, no changes are recommended. However, the list of response options for this education question could be reduced, if desired. Usual and actual hours: • As had been the case in Round 1, some participants appeared unhappy or impatient about having to report both usual and actual hours, and a few mentioned that these questions seemed repetitive to them. In addition, proxy reporting was difficult for some participants. • In probing, we collected participants’ reactions to the instructions added to the usual hours’ question: to estimate the usual and not actual hours, to consider the previous 4 months, to report on a typical week if hours varied, and to give best guess if not known. Although some participants had no issue with this set of instructions, with others it yielded mixed results. Although the instructions added to the usual hours’ question appeared to work well, the instruction to “consider the past 4 months” was confusing to some participants. During Round 1 cognitive testing of this instrument, this instruction to “consider the last 4 months” was confusing to participants and was removed for Round 2 cognitive testing, where it tested well. We recommend to remove this instruction and use the below version of the question (i.e., the version used in Round 2 cognitive testing): How many hours per week do you USUALLY work at your job? • Estimate the USUAL number of hours worked per week, not the actual hours worked • If hours vary from week to week, give the number of hours worked in a typical week • If you do not know your usual hours, give your best guess Industry and occupation: • The recommendation listed in Section 3.7.2 could reduce the burden required to answer several confirmation questions. For smartphone participants, we also recommend implementing textbox wrapping so they can review the entire entry without having to click into the textbox and scroll.

CPS Usability Report: Rounds 1 and 2 4-8 • All participants who saw questions IO1DP1 (Figure 3.35), IO1DP2 (Figure 3.36), and IO1DP3 (Figure 3.37) (see Section 3.7.1) understood that the textboxes were prefilled with their responses from Round 1 and generally did not struggle to confirm or update the information as needed. Some participants specifically appreciated the use of the dependent data because it made the response process more efficient. • Some participants needed to update information, and they were able to do so without major issues. • Overall, participants generally felt that the sequence was easy to answer and geared towards people who might have been promoted or changed jobs since the last interview. Questions for those who are not working: • A few participants had some issues with determining responses to questions in this section and they thought they potentially received questions that did not apply to their situation). • Because there were no major usability issues with the functionality of these questions, no changes are recommended. Disability questions: • The recommendations from Round 1 were not applied during Round 2 of testing; however, almost all participants found the prefilled disability questions in Round 2 easy to confirm and answer. • Despite the ease of answering the questions, a few participants found the sequence annoying and unnecessary. • There are no additional recommendations aside from those in Round 1. However, as some participants found these questions to be redundant and burdensome, consider whether it is possible to identify changes in disability status more efficiently or through fewer questions. Nativity dropdown: • Very few participants saw the nativity sequence in Round 2 because it was only asked of participants who either had missing data from Round 1 or added new household members during Round 2. Of those who saw the questions, all recognized that the data were prefilled from Round 1 responses and noted that they were satisfied with the sequence. • There are no additional recommendations aside from those in Round 1.

4. Conclusions 4-9 Miscellaneous usability issues: • A few participants exited out of the survey without intending to. These were people answering the survey on smartphones, where they accidentally used the back button on their phone (i.e., clicked back in the browser). This logged them out of the survey, and they had to log in again. They were pleasantly surprised to see that the survey had saved their previous answers and took them back to where they had left off. • A few participants commented on the fact that they cannot review or edit their answers once they get to the submit page, unless they click the back button. Census Bureau and BLS could consider implementing a feature that would allow respondents to review their answers before submitting. • Some participants had mixed reactions to the visual design of the survey. i Abstract The Current Population Survey (CPS), which is currently administered entirely as a computer assisted personal interview (CAPI) survey, is exploring adding a self-administered mode option to its data collection later this decade (Linse & Johnson, 2023). As a result, many supplemental surveys that are fielded as part of the CPS may also be impacted; one of these supplemental surveys is the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) Internet Use Survey (also called the “CPS Computer and Internet Use Supplement”). In summer 2023, following cognitive testing of the CAPI instrument, the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) at the U.S. Census Bureau conducted exploratory cognitive and usability testing of an adapted self-administered NTIA Internet Use Survey web instrument. There were a series of global changes incorporated in the self-administered questionnaire prior to testing, including modifying household-level questions where a participant had to report household members who engaged in specific Internet behaviors, changing the conversational language typically found in CAPI instruments, formatting the question-level instructions, and shortening the text in introductory sections. These global changes were made to reduce respondent burden and take advantage of the features of the Internet mode and were mostly successful in testing. We also evaluated select questions, to see if there were any changes in comprehension between CAPI and Internet. Overall, questions that participants did not struggle with in CAPI testing were also not difficult for them to answer in the Internet mode. Many questions that participants struggled with in CAPI testing also were difficult in the Internet mode; however, there was one question that was easier to answer in Internet. This exploratory cognitive and usability testing was a successful first look at how the question types and topic areas of the survey perform in a new mode. iv EXECUTIVE SUMMARY In an interagency project between the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), under the Department of Commerce, and the U.S. Census Bureau, the Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) conducted cognitive interview and usability research on the NTIA Internet Use Survey. The NTIA Internet Use Survey is a computer assisted personal interview (CAPI) survey that is a supplement to the Current Population Survey (CPS). In preparation for the November 2023 fielding of the CAPI survey, CBSM conducted cognitive testing of the current CAPI instrument (see Katz, Piccirillo, Keeve, & Holzberg, 2024). CBSM also conducted exploratory testing to evaluate a self-administered instrument version of the survey. There is a current initiative to add a self-administered component for the CPS, and later this decade, CPS supplements may also add a self-administered component. When developing the self-administered instrument, CBSM incorporated various changes, including but not limited to updating the format of the questions and instructions.. One round of cognitive and usability testing was conducted with 20 participants to evaluate the ramifications of these changes on data quality, participants’ comprehension of the questions, and burden. Participants were able to complete the adapted self-administered component of the NTIA Internet Use Survey without much issue and the changes that were incorporated were mostly successful. Select questions that were difficult in prior CAPI testing of the survey were also found to be difficult in the self-administered component. However, one question was found to be much easier to answer for participants in the self-administered component, the home Internet service question. Although testing of the adapted questionnaire was successful, future research should continue to evaluate how the CAPI and newly adapted self-administered survey perform. The research approach described in this report can also be a useful first step for other surveys exploring implementation of a self-administered mode.

1 U.S. Census Bureau 1. INTRODUCTION The Center for Behavioral Science Methods (CBSM) conducted cognitive and usability testing of an adapted self-administered version of the 2023 NTIA Internet Use Survey, a supplemental survey of the Current Population Survey (CPS). The CPS collects data on employment and labor work force but also conducts supplements on various topics in different months, such as the NTIA Internet Use Survey. The NTIA Internet Use Survey, a computer assisted personal interview (CAPI) survey, has been administered periodically since 1994 and was last fielded in November of 2023. The survey asks questions about the household’s use of devices that connect to the Internet, use of Internet from various locations in the past six months, different applications used to connect to the Internet, and any privacy or security concerns using the Internet. As part of data collection, one household member is randomly selected for additional questions about different Internet application uses. The household respondent may need to serve as a proxy respondent on behalf of the randomly selected household member during this section of the questionnaire. The CPS is exploring a modernization effort that includes adding a self-administered component to its data collection (Linse & Johnson, 2023). In the years following, select supplemental surveys to the CPS will add a self-administered component as well. We wanted to evaluate whether participants would be able to complete a version of the NTIA Internet Use Survey adapted for the Internet. CBSM adapted the existing CAPI survey to a self-administered Internet mode prior to testing. This required changes to various survey questions for both practical reasons and also to maintain comparability in the question wording. After modifying the questionnaire, we conducted cognitive and usability testing of the adapted self-administered instrument. 2. BACKGROUND Many computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) surveys are starting to consider adding a self-administered web survey component to their data collection due to concerns about costs and rising nonresponse rates. The introduction of a new mode requires changes to the survey’s contact strategy, questionnaire, interviewer training, processing, and statistical processes. In this section, we highlight some of the existing research focused on adapting a CAPI questionnaire to an Internet response mode. Surveys that move from a CAPI design to a self-administered design should be visually appealing and easy to use (Betts & Cubbon, 2015). Further, web surveys in particular might be accessed on different platforms including smartphones, tablets, and computers. Therefore, the survey should display similarly across platforms (Dillman et al., 2014). Adapting a CAPI

2 U.S. Census Bureau instrument for a self-administered response also requires that some questions be reformatted to lessen respondent burden. For example, a list of Yes/No questions administered in an interviewer instrument can be modified to ‘Select-all-that-apply’ style questions in a self- administered instrument. However, this can increase satisficing as Callegaro et al. (2015) and Nicolaas et al. (2015) found there are more positive endorsements in a Yes/No format compared to ‘Select-all-that-apply’ format. For survey questions asking for a numeric or dollar amount, Dillman et al. (2014) suggest formatting the size of the response text box to fit the answer to the question (i.e., not providing an overly short or overly long text box). Further, providing other cues such as a dollar symbol next to the response box can guide respondents on how to answer the question without providing extra written instructions. Dillman and colleagues (2014) also indicate that including yes/no filter questions before asking a series of follow-up questions can lessen respondent burden. This can make skip instructions difficult for respondents in paper surveys, but in web surveys yes/no filters can ensure respondents do not need to answer questions that are not applicable to them. The handling of interviewer instructions in self-administered instruments also needs to be considered. Some instructions give the respondent information about what to expect in the coming questions; this can be easily mirrored in a web-administered version but the instructions can be reduced (Campanelli, 2021). Introducing a self-administered web survey raises concerns about data quality. Respondents may interpret questions differently depending on whether they read the question on screen or if an interviewer reads them the question. This can affect the comparability of estimates between self-administered and interviewer-administered data collections. A switch in data collection mode can have major impacts on data trends for topics that have been measured for decades. Jackle et al. (2015) found that item non-response increases in cases where surveys include a self-administered option; Cernat and Revilla (2020) also found higher item nonresponse in the web mode compared to CAPI. However, Loomis and Paterson (2018) found that the item nonresponse between CAPI and self-administered web was not significantly different. When “don’t know” is offered as a response option, it is more likely to be selected in self-administered web surveys than in face-to-face surveys (Lipps and Monsch, 2022; Wolf et al. 2021). Similarly, Breton et al. (2017) found “don’t know” and “refused” responses increased in web. For this study, we wanted to explore the possible effects of a mode switch on the NTIA Internet Use Survey by cognitive and usability testing the adapted Internet version. This testing was conducted in summer 2023 and followed cognitive testing of the CAPI 2023 NTIA Internet Use Survey in spring 2023.

CBSM drafted a recommended version of the self-administered instrument and then NTIA reviewed the questionnaire to provide feedback. NTIA accepted most of the recommended changes to the instrument to make it self-administered. These questionnaire changes were used to inform the focus of the cognitive and usability protocol. Global changes made across the questionnaire for the Internet mode included: 1. Adapting select household level questions from two questions to one question. In the CAPI survey, respondents are currently asked if anybody in the household currently uses specific devices connected to the Internet and at which locations they use the Internet. If it is a single-member household, the question is simply phrased as “Do you use…” For multi-member households, it is modified to “Does anyone in this household…” When respondents in multi- member households report ‘Yes’, they are then subsequently asked who in their household participates in each Internet activity. After respondents report the names of the household members that did each behavior, the interviewer marks each name retrieved from the roster completed earlier in the interview as applicable. For self-administered testing, the wording for single-member households remained consistent with the CAPI mode. For multi-member households, we combined the two questions and modified the wording to be “Who in your household uses...” with each name auto-populated from the roster as a response option. Participants were instructed to mark the name of each person who did that activity. If no one participated in the activity, they were supposed to select “None of the above.” Therefore, participants only had to answer one question for each topic in Internet rather than the two questions in CAPI testing. RESULTS We will first provide findings for the global changes outlined in Section 3.1 (Expert Review) and then we will discuss cognitive interview findings of the individually tested questions. The questions in the survey are divided into the following sections: Types of Computing Devices Used, Location of Internet Use, Type of Internet Service Used, Computing Applications and Services Used, and Challenges and Concerns with Internet Use. 4.1 Global changes to wording in the self-administered instrument The following global changes, mentioned earlier, were made for the self-administered instrument: • Adapting select household level questions from two questions to one question (e.g., selecting household member’s name(s) for each Internet activity). • Changing conversational language that was specific to CAPI.

13 U.S. Census Bureau • Moving ‘if needed’ instruction text from the question stem to its own line in bullet format and also changing the font to be italics. • Making decisions about questions per page. With these changes, participants generally were able to navigate and complete the self- administered instrument without much problem. At the beginning of retrospective probing, participants were asked if the survey was easy or difficult to complete. Almost all of the participants reported that the survey was easy to complete: • “Everything was responsive and it didn’t halt in any place.” • "The questions were simple. They weren't long winded. I pretty much got an idea on what goes on in my house to answer the questions. They didn't have multiple sentences and the survey really wasn't that long and that's what made it easy." Regarding the global changes, combining the two-part household level questions into one question seemed to ease the user experience since there was less questions to answer. Participants were asked how easy or difficult it was to select names for survey questions that displayed a list of names for who participated in which Internet activity. Most of the participants who were asked this question said this process was easy. A couple of participants noted that it was difficult knowing what other people in the household were doing at times. This seemed to be more of a knowledge issue than an issue with the question wording (which included a “Select all that apply” instruction) or display itself. Almost everyone seemed to find the process of selecting each name easy. Two participants noticed that a square button that was next to each name indicated to them it was a ‘Select all that apply’: • “When I see square, I think check box. You can always check multiple options.” Only one participant seemed to struggle with selecting names in the survey as it sometimes required them to make multiple clicks to mark the name. Although the participant did not mention this, we think it may have been a function of the participant’s mouse/touch pad as we have rarely seen this problem in the Qualtrics software used for testing. Modifying the conversational language to be more direct eased the participant experience as they were able to understand who the question was asking about in each instance. Some participants did overlook reading the italicized instruction at first but generally would return to reading the instruction later while answering. One participant mentioned that some people may overlook a ‘Do not include’ instruction that was included in one of the questions. Otherwise, the italicized instructions seemed to be informative to participants.

14 U.S. Census Bureau Participants did not comment on the number of questions per page but it did not seem to hinder their experience in completing the survey. Participants were also told in retrospective probing that this survey is also administered via face to face/by telephone and were asked whether they would rather have completed this survey in one of those modes instead. Of the twenty participants asked, 16 said they preferred the web, three participants said face-to-face/phone, and one participant said either option was sufficient. Participants generally said they liked reading the questions and in certain circumstances, re-reading them if necessary: • “I’m able to see and read questions and click on the answers.” • “I wouldn’t want someone reading the questions to me and having them repeat themselves.” Of the three participants who preferred face-to-face/telephone, two of them mentioned having an interviewer present to answer questions would be helpful to them: • “If I have some doubts, you can answer the doubts.” Overall, participants were able to answer the adapted self-administered NTIA Internet Use Survey successfully with few usability issues. 4.2 Types of Computing Devices Used These questions cover the different types of devices a household uses, the performance of these devices, and the accessibility of these devices. CONCLUSIONS The goal of this exploratory testing was to explore the feasibility of a self-administered NTIA Internet Use Survey. Exploratory testing showed that global changes that were incorporated across the self-administered instrument were successful, including adapting the conversational language for self-administered and moving ‘if needed’ CAPI instructions to be on its own separate line in self-administered. Most of the individual survey questions tested well in self-administered mode. Select questions that were found to be problematic in CAPI testing were also problematic in self-administered testing. This included questions asking about households using a smart TV, using household devices that are connected to the Internet like a smart thermostat or security system, and concerns using the Internet. However, the question that asked about home Internet service was found to be less problematic for participants answering the survey in a self-administered mode compared to the CAPI mode. The home Internet service question may be complex to answer in a CAPI mode due to the extensive length; however, with the self-administered mode, it may be easier for the participant to comprehend by reading the question on screen. The question asking what concerns households the most in terms of online privacy and security risks had been an open- ended coded question in CAPI and was adapted to a mark all that apply in self-administered.

41 U.S. Census Bureau Participants understood this question in the new mode, but this question will still need to be monitored in the future to evaluate the data quality, given the change in question type. Although the changes from CAPI to self-administered performed well in the exploratory testing, this is just the first step in exploring an Internet mode of the survey. For this study, we did not test a mobile version of the questionnaire as the goal was mainly to see how these questions would perform in a self-administered mode on a laptop/desktop computer. However, it is essential that surveys are now designed to be completed by mobile users; 32% of responding households completed the American Community Survey (ACS) on a mobile device in 2023 (Mills, 2024). Future research should explore cognitive and usability testing of adapted self- administered changes on mobile devices. In addition, field testing should be conducted to evaluate any potential mode differences between self-administered and CAPI. Overall, other surveys should consider starting with similar exploratory cognitive and usability testing if they are thinking of adding a self-administered web component. This is a successful first step in understanding any possible differences in comprehension and reporting when adapting question wording across modes. 6. REFERENCES Betts, P., & Cubbon, B. (2015). 1-1 1. Executive Summary This report details the results of 60 cognitive interviews which were conducted during the first round of cognitive testing for the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC). The cognitive interviews tested the ASEC instrument which includes questions about health insurance coverage, medical out of pocket expenses, moving, earned income, income sources and amounts, poverty, and child care. The instrument and tests were divided into two sections, broadly categorized as the “health insurance” and “income” sections. Health insurance includes the medical out of pocket expenses and moving questions. Income includes the remaining sections. Interviews were conducted by RTI International (RTI) and Research Support Services (RSS). Findings and recommendations from the cognitive interviews will be used to revise the questions for the second round of cognitive testing to take place in the Spring of 2025. Cognitive testing consists of one-on-one in-person interviews to assess a questionnaire in terms of general comprehension, clarity of question and response wording, effectiveness of skip logic, and visual aids. Census Bureau provided two separate and distinct cognitive protocols: one for health insurance and one for income. Both protocols included the full set of questions tested in each interview, concurrent probes on most questions, designation of the motivation for testing the question, and the desired output to be reported for each. Interviews were designed to take no more than 90-minutes. The Census Bureau programmed each questionnaire in Qualtrics to facilitate virtual interviewing. All interviews were conducted remotely and were recorded by interviewers. Following each interview, participants were provided with a $40 Visa digital gift card as a token of appreciation for completing the interview. Participants were recruited and selected based on pre-established targets/quotas. All efforts were made to reach these targets while providing an even distribution among demographic characteristics such as sex, age, education, race/ethnicity, and household composition, among other criteria. The RTI and RSS team used a systematic approach to analyze the cognitive interview data and address the research questions. Each team coded data with a combined approach of coding in the raw data, as well as developing iterative codes for questions with significant feedback. Once the data were organized and coded, the teams wrote up their findings in a standardized format, including question-level responses from participants, key findings, a summary, and recommendations for questions that performed poorly. These provided the basis of this report. There were several overall recommendations that came from the research which included the following:

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 1-2 Health Insurance Module • Questions in the Health insurance section need to be reviewed for how best to address the issue of respondents who are covered by insurance of a non-household member, in particular young adults not living at home and covered until age 26 under their parents’ insurance. Participants with unrelated household members also found it difficult and sometimes impossible to proxy report for their roommates. • Medical out of pocket expenses that ask for a dollar amount of expenses includes a field to enter the amount, but also allowed for text entries. Those who entered text entries were treated as having answered the question with a value, and therefore skipped out of the follow up questions offering ranges for non-respondents. It is recommended to either not allow text responses or route respondents in a similar fashion as nonresponders. • Migration questions asking the 1-year and the 10-year time frame use the structure "x year(s) ago, that is, September 1, 2014/2024." The date was provided as a fixed date, not as it related to the interview date. In addition, all but one participant focused on the month and year or the number of years, or both, but not on the specific date. For these reasons it is recommended to restructure the time frames as "1/10 year(s) ago, that is, <CURRENT MONTH>, <1/10 YEARS AGO>. Income Module • Include instructions within the Introduction. The prenotification letter should describe the survey and the data we are collecting so participants can be prepared. In addition, the introduction of the survey would be a prime location to explain that some financial records would be helpful to have during completion of the survey. • Allowing estimates. If SMEs believe that an estimate is acceptable, that instruction could be included in the introduction as well. Alternatively, the instruction could be included as a soft check prompt if respondents try to go to the next question without responding. We may also consider including this instruction on certain questions that are more likely to need to be estimated, such as income from interest-earning accounts. • Section introductions / Transition statements. As respondents progress through various income and finance topics, it can be somewhat confusing or disorienting as to the content being covered. It is highly recommended to include a short instruction or transition statement at the beginning of new sections. These transitions could be included on the same screen as the question text. • Additional definitions. Several questions may benefit from the addition of definitions of key terms to ensure respondents are consistently presented the same information. Adding definitions may also be helpful for proxy reports, in which respondents may not know the term themselves, but seeing a definition could help them remember and report for someone else in their household. • Overall summary screen. During cognitive testing, it was evident that some participants responded to several questions while thinking of the same source of income or account. In essence, this led to “double-counting.” One consideration to help aid respondents would be to include an overall summary screen which would allow participants to review each of the accounts that they noted to ensure they did not double-count items. Moreover, this screen might help respondents to determine that an income source was not listed.

Section 1 — Executive Summary 1-3 • Validations / Confirmations. Another approach to increase data quality and reliability would be to include various validations and confirmations. This can be done through the inclusion of programming logic around key questions that may contribute to respondents providing duplicate information. We would not recommend consistency logic to be included on all questions, but the survey would benefit from inclusion on some items, where respondents are likely to get confused or double report. A standard message could appear on specific questions confirming with respondents that this information was not already reported on a previous question. • Respondent burden and reducing breakoffs. It was clear during cognitive testing that respondent burden associated with answering many of the questions is quite high. Knowledge is not available or would require review of financial documents. While some participants will take the time to report accurately, others will either provide an estimate, leave the question blank, or breakoff entirely. To mitigate these concerns, we suggest the following: ○ Consider removing questions that pose the highest respondent burden and lowest data quality (See Section 6.2.2 for further details). ○ Consider allowing a “Don’t know” response option for a few key questions, where “don’t know” could improve respondent experience and provide more complete data (See Section 6.2 for further details). ○ Consider allowing response ranges. ○ Consider providing additional context to tie previous questions together. ○ Consider additional features to improve reporting such as including labels outside of the response boxes and adding a “$” when looking for a monetary value. ○ Ensuring consistency throughout the questionnaire by placing the reference year at the beginning of the question. Finally, there were many challenges in conducting cognitive testing cognitive during the first round of testing as the questionnaire is quite long at 90 minutes. One issue that contributed to challenges in collecting data was due to programming errors. We were unable to assess the performance of several questions due to incorrect or broken skip logic and problems with fills. We assume that these will be corrected during the second round of interviews to fully assess the questions.

2-1 2. Introduction The Current Population Survey (CPS) is an important source of data on U.S. employment and unemployment. Collected within the CPS is the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC). The ASEC collects data on income sources, health insurance, and participation in various economic support programs. ASEC data also supports the creation of the Supplemental Poverty Measure and are thus critically important to a broad array of data users. To support development of new questions on health insurance and income/public assistance topics for the ASEC supplement, RTI International and Research Support Services (RSS), conducted 60 one-on-one cognitive interviews in each of two rounds of cognitive testing. Interviews were split (i.e., 30 each) across two topic ASEC topic areas—health insurance and income. The purpose of the first round of cognitive interviews was to learn more about how participants interpret and respond to the questions and response options, identify possible issues that may hinder a respondent’s ability to respond, and to gather feedback that can be used to revise the questions. This report details the cognitive methodology, including the description of the target population and participant eligibility criteria and interviewing procedures, participant recruitment and screening, question findings and recommendations, and overall recommendations for the Health Insurance and Income modules. Findings and recommendations from the cognitive interviews will be used to revise the questions for the second round of cognitive testing to take place in the Spring of 2025.
