3-1 3. Cognitive Methodology This section provides an overview of the interviewing methodology used during ASEC health insurance and income cognitive interview data collection. Specifically, this section provides details about cognitive methodology, as well as the protocols and procedures that were used during interviews. 3.1 Methodology The cognitive testing consisted of (virtual) one-on-one in-person interviews to assess the questionnaire in terms of general comprehension, clarity of question and response wording, effectiveness of skip logic, and visual aids. The goal was to gain an understanding of how well the questions work when administered to a sample of the survey’s target population. The interviews followed a protocol with pre-scripted probes, administered after most questions. Cognitive interviewers also used spontaneous probes to gain a better understanding of questions. Cognitive interviewing was used to: • Learn about the respondents’ thought processes while answering the questions; • Measure the response process, including comprehension, retrieval, judgement, and response; • Observe non-verbal, human reactions; • Test navigation of the instrument; • Assess the potential for measurement error in survey items; • Examine potentially big or complex issues; and • Gauge opinions on the survey as a whole. 3.2 Protocol Census Bureau developed two separate and distinct protocols that focused on each of the two topic areas being explored in this study: one for health insurance (Appendix D) and one for income (Appendix E). RTI/RSS provided input and reviewed each protocol. Both protocols included the full set of questions included in each interview, along with concurrent probes on a subset of questions. Due to the large number of questions included in each interview, scripted probes were only utilized on a subset of questions to maintain the required 90-minute timing for the interview. Interviewers were instructed and trained to collect spontaneous feedback on other questions as needed. Census Bureau programmed the protocols in Qualtrics to facilitate virtual interviewing. However, there were some identified issues with the programming when interviews started (see Appendix F for the list of programming issues, both those known before interviewing started and those discovered during interviewing). During the interview, the desired protocol was to provide a web survey link to participants to review the ASEC topic–specific questions (i.e., health insurance or income). Participants were then asked to respond to

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 3-2 questions while sharing their screen. In most cases this was the approach, however, as a back-up, the interviewer could display the web instrument containing ASEC questions on screen and ask participants to respond while entering responses for them. 3.3 Interviews All interviews were conducted remotely using Microsoft Teams within Census Bureau’s secure Virtual Desktop Interface (VDI) environment or using a Census Bureau issued laptop. With permission from participants, interviewers recorded all sessions using handheld audio recording device. Interviews were also recorded using SnagIt software, which records both audio and video. Recordings were saved to the designated deliverable folder in the Census Bureau file share location. At the end of the interview, interviewers offered participants a $40 Visa digital gift card code via email as a thank you for their time. Following each interview, interviewers or note takers completed the appropriate case summary template for the topic area (i.e., health insurance or income). Although the two protocols and respondent-facing instruments differed, each interview was conducted in the following sequence to standardize implementation: • Interviewers explained the purpose of the study. • Confirmed participant had reviewed and signed the online consent form to participate in the study and be audio/video recorded (Appendix C). • Started audio recording using an external audio recorder and SnagIt software. • Re-confirmed verbal consent to participate and be recorded once recording has started. • Shared the respondent-facing instrument and asked participants to answer ASEC questions shown on screen. • Administered probes to ASEC questions. • Concluded the interview and sent the participant the incentive. • Saved the recording within the Census Bureau’s secure network environment in the designated file share folder. • Completed the interview summary and saved it in the designated file share folder no more than 5 business days following each interview. Before conducing cognitive interviews, all RTI/RSS interviewers were trained by Census Bureau on protocols for each topic area (i.e., health insurance; income) and other key procedures, including Title 13 requirements. Because each topic area used different protocols, two interviewer training sessions were held: one that focused on the health insurance protocol and one that focused on the income protocol. Due to the length and complexity of the interviews, all interviewers also completed a recorded practice interview before beginning interviews with participants. This practice interview was reviewed by RTI’s lead researcher, and feedback was provided to interviewers directly to prepare them for the main interviews.

Section 3 — Cognitive Methodology 3-3 3.4 Analysis The RTI and RSS team used a systematic process to analyze the cognitive interview data and address the research questions. The case summaries were recorded in Excel to provide a thorough data set for analysis, with participants presented in each row and interview probes presented in each column. Both teams coded data with a combined approach of coding in the raw data, as well as developing iterative codes for questions with significant feedback. Once the data were organized and coded, the teams wrote up their findings in a standardized format, including responses from participants, key findings, a summary, and provided recommendations for questions that performed poorly. For the Income section, RTI also developed substantial overall recommendations based on trends across questions, as well as suggestions for question order.

4-1 4. Participant Recruitment This section provides an overview of participant recruitment used to screen and select participants for the ASEC health insurance and income cognitive interviews. Specifically, this section includes an overview of recruitment strategies and targets and presents participant characteristics for each topic area. The RTI/RSS team recruited participants for the first round of ASEC cognitive interviews from September through November 2024. The concurrent recruitment for these two testing tasks began by leveraging the participant recruitment for the CPS usability testing conducted from June through August 2024. First, the RTI/RSS team identified 115 prospective participants who were selected based on their eligibility for the CPS usability testing but were left uncontacted for solicitation. The team planned an email outreach campaign, inviting them to complete the ASEC online screener to determine their eligibility for ASEC cognitive interviews based on their demographics and current employment status. Following the outreach campaign with the previously screened individuals, the RTI/RSS team identified multiple metropolitan areas across all four Census regions (i.e., Northeast, Midwest, South, West) that have relatively large and diverse populations for a potential larger proportion of residents who met the recruitment criteria of both subprojects. The RTI/RSS team then posted online recruitment advertisements in the selected metropolitan areas, releasing advertisements on a rolling basis to maintain a steady stream of prospective recruits for screening and scheduling. RTI/RSS team also conducted word-of- mouth outreach with the staff’s personal networks specifically screening for individuals with the rarer primary characteristics that seemed to fall behind after approximately 8 weeks of data collection. The additional effort helped improved our recruitment outcome with those who live with unrelated individuals and those who received income from unemployment benefits or worker comp. The Census Bureau programmed a web-based eligibility screening in Qualtrics. The RTI/RSS team also provided a toll-free telephone line dedicated to recruitment purposes. The web link of the screening instrument and the toll-free phone number were presented in the online advertisements (see Appendix A). During the data collection period, the RTI/RSS team provided the Census Bureau with a weekly recruitment and interviewing progress update report, reflecting results to date. The weekly report sought to present the diversity of interview participants with respect to recruitment goals and needed sub-characteristics. The results of ASEC cognitive interview recruitment presented in Sections 4.3 and 4.4 of this report reflect the final recruitment outcomes.

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 4-2 4.1 Implementation of Recruitment Advertising The RTI/RSS team began the participant recruitment by launching the email outreach campaign to contact those previously recruited through Craigslist posts and screened but not contacted in September 2024. For the main online recruitment strategy, the RTI/RSS team used Craigslist as the primary venue for recruitment advertising. Craigslist is one of the best-known online bulletin boards and provides the most comprehensive coverage of metropolitan areas in the United States. To leverage Craigslist’s broad reach, RTI/RSS did not use targeted advertisements that focused on specific characteristics and used a customized general advertisement instead (see Appendix B for recruitment materials and advertisement text). The RTI/RSS team posted the general recruitment advertisement on Craigslist under the “jobs/et cetera” sections for ten metropolitan areas across all four Census regions (further details below) over the entire duration of data collection. At the same time, the RTI/RSS staff reached out their personal networks to solicit participation from those who may fit our recruitment criteria, and also asked their personal contacts to refer the participant recruitment screener word-out-mouth to others who might be eligible in their broader social circles. The first round of monthly paid advertising started September 2023, and expired November 2024. RTI/RSS team recorded screening responses for more than 650 prospective participants from the first round of advertising. 4.1.1 Participant Selection Strategy To facilitate efficient screening review and participant selection across subprojects, the RTI/RSS team created two spreadsheets. First, the team created a main intake sheet to import the screening responses from Qualtrics. The main intake sheet was used to determine eligibility for the first round of the ASEC cognitive testing. Interested participants were reviewed to ensure they met the main eligibility criteria (e.g., Age 18+ and met one or more of the recruitment criteria outlined in the exhibits). Within the main intake spreadsheet, the RTI/RSS team employed a two-step review strategy to determine subproject assignment and participant selection priority. The spreadsheet first calculated and presented the number of eligible respondent characteristics. Participant screening responses were reviewed to determine whether they fit within one or more of the quotas which were established. Next, we reviewed all prospective participants on the intake sheet, focusing on contact information self-reports and the IP addresses in the paradata for de-duplicated entries from the same individuals and excluding ineligible entries from foreign IP addresses. After reviewing and cleaning the tentative assignments, the records of eligible recruits were exported to each of the two subproject-specific recruitment tracking sheets (i.e., ASEC Income or ASEC Health Insurance). The lead recruiter reviewed the participants to ensure fulfillment of key quotas and selected participants for the RTI/RSS recruiter to contact.

Section 4 — Participant Recruitment 4-3 During data collection, RTI/RSS team processed and reviewed the screening data at least once a week to select eligible participants for an interview. After a batch of screening data were reviewed and released to recruiters, about 1 week would elapse before new assignments would be made to allow recruiters sufficient time to contact their existing assignments. Once recruiters contacted participants, they scheduled an interview for each of the interviewers, sending a confirmation email with all the information needed to take part in the interview. At that point, the interviewer took over the case, sending reminders and communicating with the participant, as needed. 4.1.2 ASEC cognitive interview recruitment outcomes The RSS team completed 30 cognitive interviews for the health insurance module while the RTI team completed 30 interviews for the income module. Across both efforts, RTI/RSS selected and contacted an additional 88 eligible participants; 58 participants did not respond to our invitation, 6 participants refused during recruitment and 14 of them did not show up for their scheduled interview. Another 10 decided to withdraw their participation after they were scheduled for an interview. 4.2 Health Insurance Participants Exhibit 4-1 details the distribution of the completed interviews with the primary recruitment criteria for the topic of health insurance for the ASEC cognitive interviews. Do people read and understand the instructions (about drug, vision, etc.)? • Most participants (n=19) noted that they read the instructions, although many did not comment on the impact they had on their answer. • Three participants [P2538, P2647, P2260] did not read the instructions, one of whom [P2647] noted that it was helpful to consider after the interviewer pointed them out. • Three participants [P2279, P2507, P2589] noted that they were uncertain about whether dental, vision, and drug were included in their health insurance plans. • One participant [P2707] stated that the instructions did not impact their response at all. Participants generally understood this question and were able to easily answer it. Most recognized “private health insurance” as employer-provided insurance, however some participants questioned whether their employee insurance would be considered private or under “something else.” The submenus for Medicaid and Medicare options were generally well received, although they were not interactive, which led to some confusion. Some observations suggest that the submenus for Medicaid and Medicare would have been more effective in confirming a participant’s decision had they been shown immediately rather than appearing upon selection. Recommendations: Consider testing additional information for the “Private Health Insurance” response option. For example: 1. Private Health Insurance ▪ A plan provided through an employer or union ▪ A plan purchased by an individual from an insurance company This may help clarify participants’ understanding of what “private health insurance” means and whether it applies to them. We suggest testing a version in which the submenus for Medicare and Medicaid are shown in full rather than expanding upon response selection. This may help participants make a clear decision and avoid hiding key information.

If they have employer sponsored insurance, is the value provided before or after any contribution from their employer? • Of 13 participants that answered Q18 (Did employer or union help pay for the health insurance?) only 4 received this probe with 7 accidentally skipped. Two others were not probed because they did not know anything about the employer- paid insurance someone else covers them under. • One participant [P2256] provided the portion that comes out of her boyfriend’s paycheck, i.e. after employer contribution. • Three other participants [P2344, P2589, P2718] reported the amount after employer contribution. As in previous questions asking about “ten years ago, on September 1, 2014,” we recommend asking it as “ten years ago, on [CURRENT MONTH], [YEAR 10 YEARS AGO].

6-1 6. Question by Question Results – Income This section presents results and recommendations, where appropriate, for ASEC Income questions. Findings in this section are presented by topic, with findings from the cognitive interviews listed first followed by recommendations. Each question is formatted with the following elements: • Research question provided by Census Bureau with the goals of testing each question, as well as background about changes made to the question. • Question text and response options that were shown to the participants during cognitive interviewing. • n, representing the total number of participants who were exposed to the question, and thus could provide feedback. • Responses provided by participants during the interview. • Findings detailing the answers to key research questions provided by Census Bureau. • Summary with an overall summary of the findings, especially for questions that included significant findings. • Recommendations for question changes, when appropriate. The goal of cognitive interviewing is to collect qualitative feedback from participants about their response process when providing an answer to each question. We have included a report of the responses to each question (i.e., the quantitative data) to provide context for the findings. This response data comes from a combination of the Qualtrics data entered by either the participant or the interviewer, and the response recorded in the notes during the interview. Participants are not required to provide an answer, and thus the total sample who saw the question (“n”) may differ from the total number of responses. 6.1 Employment Questions Question 29a Research Question: Does revising question impact respondent’s understanding? What do respondents consider as “work”? Does adding the phrase, “even if for one day” capture additional work? Q29a. Did you do any work for pay or profit at any time during 2023, even for one day? ▪ Yes ▪ No n = 30

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-2 Findings: Would respondents answer differently or think of different kinds of work if the question asked about a “job or business” instead of “work”? • Of the 30 participants that received this question, many felt that there was a difference in how they would interpret the question if they thought about work as opposed to a job. • Several participants (n=10) would answer differently if the question asked about a “job or business” instead of work. They explained that work would also encompass things like charity work you don’t get paid for, work that you do not get a W-2 for, odd jobs or “gig” work (n=4). ○ Reflecting on how adding “job or business” would narrow their understand of the question, one participant (P2245) explained, "Yeah, I would think that would really narrow what they're asking… Because you'd think that you'd have to be employed, there'd be like a W-2, you get paid by somebody else, you know, direct deposit." ○ Another participant (P2709) added, "Yes it would. It would make it feel like that would be a more regular position. This is a more on-off gig type work." Did respondents include work in 2023 that they did not get a paycheck for, such as managing a rental property or sell something online? • Three participants (P2245, P2303, P2595) included work that they did not get a paycheck for when answering this question. • One participant (Pp2464) thought of "freelance" work such as doing the cognitive interview, focus groups, and odd jobs such as this as "work." ○ One participant (P2245) explained, "I do sell things sometimes online that isn't furniture, un… I would include that as well. I have a friend that does, like, babysitting before the bus comes and after the bus drops them off. I would think that, you know, it would include her work because she does get paid for it. So, I think this is very, like, it's a wide berth of what could be included in this question." Did any respondents not include short-term work when answering the question? • [Participants were not asked directly about short-term work] • Participants had a narrower interpretation of “job or business” as opposed to “work.” They interpreted the term “work” as including odd jobs or “gig” work in addition to standard W-2 job roles. This could also include making money from informal economy jobs (e.g. babysitting) and freelance work such as participation in a focus group. If the question were to ask about a “job or business”, participants thought the question was only asking about regular/formal types of job where they received a W-2. Recommendations: Depending on the intention of this question, consider whether to change the wording. For example, if only W-2 jobs should be considered, then changing to “job or business” may be more appropriate. Regardless, the question might benefit from inclusion of some examples to ensure respondents are interpreting the question in a standard way.

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-4 Findings: How did respondents interpret ‘on layoff’, were they confused by this term? (Note: on layoff is different than laid off. On layoff means they will be called back to work). • Only four participants received this question but did not seem to be confused by the term ‘on layoff.’ • Participants considered ‘laid off’ as being permanent, such as losing your job or that you’re unemployed. One participant (P2351) contrasted ‘on layoff’ with ‘laid off’ explaining that ‘on layoff’ is temporary, while “laid off” is more permanent. ○ One participant (P3022) explained, “…say he was working, and then he got laid off from his job, or he was unemployed, if he was trying to go back to work, he would be trying to find a job, so that time, then the answer would have been yes." ○ Another participant (P2261) added, “I wouldn't say confusing, but 'On layoff' you can still look for work when you're on layoff, so… I don't think 'On layoff' is a reason to not look for work." ○ One participant (P2710) felt that it is awkward and suggested two separate questions, suggesting, “Did you spend any time trying to find a job/ and/ did you spend any time on layoff?” While only 4 participants received this question, they seemed to understand what was being asked and understood the term ‘on layoff.’ Recommendations: While participants did not seem to be confused by the term ‘on layoff’, the question seems to be asking about two different things, that is, it is double barreled. Double barreled questions pose a higher respondent burden and can lead to more misreporting than questions about a single topic. People could be ‘on layoff’ and not looking for a job. It is unclear whether the analytic value of this question is to determine how many people are looking for a job, are on layoff, or both. Consider separating the question into two questions: Q30. If they did work for more than one employer at a time, how did they come to choose their response? • Of the participants that worked for more than one employer at the same time, some counted them as one and others counted them separately. This may have been a reflection of the confusion they had over the instruction within the question. ○ One participant (P2246) explained, "Another self-employed tricky one because I do work with two employers so maybe that's what I should focus in on. I think that's what I would do… So, I do work with two employers who I contract with. But I also provide services for a number of clients. But I do, now that I'm saying that out loud, I do think that's separate from 'employer'. So, I think I would just focus on the two instead of answering three or more." Earlier, the participant explained that he worked for these employers at the same time. There was a lot of confusion among participants in how to interpret the instruction, “If you worked for more than one employer at the same time, only count it as one employer.” This likely resulted in error when participants had more than one job, which often overlapped. Recommendations: Respondents do not understand the instruction consistently and this is resulting in significant misreporting. We recommend the SMEs reconsider the target of interest with this question and how to better conceptualize a shift in employment over the span of a year that better aligns with how the majority of Americans work. SMEs should consider what they are trying to measure here and whether we could ask about it in a different way. However, another participant (P2332) believed that tips were payments they received directly from the client for doing a good job. ○ These issues stem from the question wording asking about “income that you received from [employer].” While participants have different understandings of who pays out tips, they seem able to select the appropriate response option without much difficulty. • One participant (P2283) volunteered that they were confused about the response option “tips.” This participant wondered whether the question was asking about tips that come from their company. They talked through an example of being a delivery driver and receiving tips but did not think that tips applied in their case in an office setting. The wording of the question seemed to have made them uncertain about whether tips could be paid out by an employer. Overall, this question is easy for participants to understand. They were able to review the response options and select which options apply for themselves and others in their household. However, there was some minor confusion around the response option “tips” because of the question wording of “income that you received from [employer].” Unfortunately, we have limited data on “tips” since only three participants reported any tipped income. These participants varied on their understanding of who pays out tips, however, all of them selected the response option “tips” without major issues. Recommendations: Due to the limited data, we recommend consulting with SMEs about whether the language of “tips” could be confusing in this context. We may want to consider altering the question text to exclude the direct reference to participants’ employers. However, with the current evidence, those who do have tipped income are able to report this accurately. We can continue to monitor this question during the second round of interviews, as is or with SME- suggested changes.

Two of these participants entered other amounts than yearly; one (P2646) entered weekly amount, and the other (P2286) entered hourly amount. Another participant (P2253) questioned whether overtime pay should be reported as hourly or yearly but decided it should be yearly and responded appropriately. ○ For example, P2286 asked "Is this hourly or a total do you know? Do I put hourly?" This participant entered “15.00 hr” into the text box, which triggered an error that said, “Please exclude commas and if necessary, use a point as a decimal separate.” The participant realized that the text “hr” may be triggering the error and removed it for his final response of “15.” He also reported a yearly amount for his bonus. ○ One participant (P2434) reported 2,100 for the year, which did not seem to match with her description of the job; a full-time job which she worked for 40 weeks in the year. It is unclear whether she reported a periodic amount instead of yearly or omitted a “0.” ○ One participant (P2417) struggled to respond because they did not work the entire year, sharing, "Since I didn't work the whole year, I'm trying to figure out how I would calculate that." This response reflects the high respondent burden of this question. • A few participants struggled with the wording of the question “before taxes and other deductions.” ○ One participant (P2283) was stuck on understanding this phrase and after rereading several times seemed to understand. They thought that “Gross pay, I think, that's probably more straight forward." ○ One participant (P2770) pulled up their W2 statement during the interview but saw that the W2 reports total with taxes taken out. The participant was not sure how to get a total “before taxes and other deductions” (per the wording of the question) and thought that if it was too hard, they would just skip the question. Do respondents notice and understand the checkbox for reporting for different time periods? • Eight participants were unclear what the checkbox was used for. Even those who understood that the checkbox could be used to report in a different way were sometimes surprised by the format of the second screen, as discussed below. • Four participants (P2595, P2332, P2283, P2770) did not see the checkbox until probed by the interviewer. If the current format is retained, two participants (P2283, P2246) preferred for the checkbox to be featured higher up on the screen. P2283 thought that it would make it easier for people to see and consider reporting in a different way before trying to use the first question. P2246 shared,

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-34 “I noticed [the checkbox] before I started entering in the digits up there, but I think it would really jump out at me more if it was up top." ○ Additionally, P2283 did not realize at first that he needed to click the arrow to view the alternative response options and was confused when he clicked the checkbox, and nothing happened. • Two participants thought the checkbox would give them the option to refuse to answer (P2310) or indicate they did not know the answer (P2646). Would they prefer being asked how they want to report the amount first? • Fourteen participants indicated they would prefer to pick the way to report first. These participants more often have irregular pay, multiple jobs, and are not salaried, which make reporting yearly totals more difficult. ○ One participant (P2595) completed calculations on their phone to report a yearly total and would prefer to report monthly and have the total calculated automatically. ○ A few participants who are salaried yearly indicated it would be better to ask for everyone, even though in their case they would prefer to report yearly. This indicates that participants do not see asking about how to report first as significantly increasing burden. ○ One participant (P2770) stated they would prefer to respond with a range rather than a single number, sharing “I feel like I'd be a lot more confident in just reporting a range… Even in overtime pay I think I would feel more confident giving a range… Number feels very… have to be more correct than a range where there's a little more forgiveness." How do respondents feel about reporting income amounts separately? Would the respondent prefer to report some of these all together? • Seven participants found the types of income difficult to report separately. Of these seven, four participants (P2253, P2285, P2770, P2595) found overtime pay especially difficult to report. These participants store their hourly rate in their memory, but do not have the ability to recall their total overtime pay. The question does not match how participants have the information stored in their minds. Many would not look for records to answer this question, and even if they did, it would find it difficult to find records that have a single number for total overtime pay before taxes and deductions. ○ One participant (P2770) shared, "I don't really know if I can remember. Especially the breakdown with overtime pay. Like, I would have to check my tax pay… I know I got overtime pay, but I could not tell you what that would be." This participant did pull up their W2 during the interview and shared that the W2 didn’t have overtime listed. He stated he has the total easily available but not the breakdown. ○ Another participant (P2595) described that overtime was difficult to report about because the number of overtime hours varied drastically throughout the year. He knew the amount he was getting paid for overtime but could not estimate the number of overtime hours he may have worked in the year. He would rather report all of his income as one number rather than separately. ○ The other three participants mentioned that reporting one single number would be easier, though they could produce estimates of the individual types of income.

Section 6 — Question by Question Results – Income 6-37 • Six participants (P2332, P2434, P2285, P2709, P2361, P2283) suggested additional changes that they wanted to make to the question wording and display. • One participant (P2283) thought that “gross pay” would be clearer than “net pay.” ○ One participant (P2434) preferred to have the word “yearly” in the question rather than just “in 2023.” ○ Another participant (P2709) wanted to be able to easily toggle between the different reporting options to see what the options were rather than having to use the checkbox and the next arrow. Can the respondent “make corrections”? If it’s difficult, explain why. • No data to support analysis. Response difficulties for this question seemed to stem from issues with how participants think about and store information about their income, as well as issues with recall for pay of short-term, irregular work. The question was easy for those with only a full-time salary to report, but more challenging for those with other income categories. Many store in their minds information about their income in hourly or weekly amounts rather than in yearly amounts. Additionally, for some forms of pay, the records of their yearly income may not exist, for example, overtime pay separated from other types of pay and reported before taxes and deductions. When the question is more difficult to answer, participants were more likely to skip it. Participants with varying types of income preferred to report one total for the entire year, which they would have in their records, if they chose to access them. The checkbox was also not working as intended. It appeared too far down the page for participants to notice it before starting their response process to the question on screen. Additionally, the wording (“I want to report monthly or in a different way.”) was not clear enough to match participants’ expectations of what will happen when they click the checkbox. The format for reporting by different time periods was also not clear for all participants, since the blank drop downs are not populated with any instructions or indications of how to use them. Over half of participants preferred to be asked how they want to report rather than the current question set up. Recommendations: In combination with the findings from other income amounts questions (See Section 6.4.3), we recommend moving forward with only the alternative question, which includes reporting periodicity. Any changes to this format should be retested in the second round of cognitive interviews, with a focus on mobile testing. Some improvements should be made to the periodicity question including grey text instructions in the drop-down bars (e.g., “How often”), formats should be hard coded for dollar amounts, instructions should be added on how to report number of payments, and clear indication that the total is automatically calculated (e.g., all other boxes are white and

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-38 total is greyed out). Switching to the language “How often” instead of “Choose frequency” should be easier for respondents to understand. Discussions with SMEs should explore how important it is to separate out income categories, especially overtime, which are difficult for participants to accurately report. We recommend not splitting out income types since participants lack records and do not have a clear idea of how much they made in each category. Instead, we recommend asking for “total income.” If tipped income is especially important for SMEs, then the second round of cognitive interviewing could target those with tipped income for additional testing. However, we are concerned that respondents may lack records about tipped income as well, which will make reporting accurately very difficult. Consider the following revision: Q48a_alt. Please reference the table below for number of payments in a year to report how often you were paid. Section 6 — Question by Question Results – Income 6-39 Findings: Do respondents like reporting the amount yearly or would they have preferred to report it differently? • A total of three participants received this question. ○ Two of the three participants (P2283 and P2245) prefer to report yearly. One participant (P2332) preferred to report monthly because income can change drastically from month to month; this participant may have thought they would have reported income for each month rather than one value for all months of the year. ○ P2283 and P2245 preferred yearly because it would be less confusing, more straight forward, and more burdensome. Would they prefer being asked how they want to report the amount first? • Participants did not like the option of reporting by other time periods for business earnings, and so do not want to be asked how to report first. They preferred to report by year. Would it be easier for them to report net earnings directly or is reporting gross earnings and expenses separately easier? • One participant (P2332) preferred to respond with gross earnings and take-home since expenses can vary over time. This participant thought of their business earnings in terms of the total rather than split out as earnings and expenses. • One participant (P2245) would report whatever their tax statement said. This participant did not find the total helpful in catching errors. • This question about gross earnings for their businesses was mostly easy for participants to understand; however, we have limited data from this round of cognitive interviewing. One participant disliked the term “expenses” since those vary over time, however, we were unsure whether changing the question text to “net earnings” would improve clarity. Recommendations: Testing supports annual reporting for business income. However, we may want to try different wording during the second round of cognitive interviewing. We should consult with the SMEs and confirm whether they would like to try the suggested revision below. This revision would lower respondent burden by asking for only one number but may increase misreports if participants accidentally report gross earnings instead of net earnings. This participant explained, “I'm going to say ‘no’, because my mother-in-law had already been for -- since the mid-90s, so it wasn't stopping her in 2023." • One participant (P2332) thought the question was repetitive since they already reported one member of their household as receiving disability benefits. While there were no research questions for this item, there were significant problems with the current question wording, which was not consistently understood by participants. Participants were making guesses about the level of severity of health issues that the question was asking about, and the question was not currently working well as a good filter to find households where members are receiving disability income. Recommendations: SMEs need to weigh in on these findings with the wording issues for this question. The goal of the question is to identify people who may be receiving disability income; however, the question was not currently consistently understood, and more people may screen into the follow up questions than should, increasing respondent burden.

Section 6 — Question by Question Results – Income 6-61 Are respondents able to provide proxy responses for household members receiving survivor benefits? • No data to support analysis. Did they read and consider all the options or decide after the first few that these weren’t relevant to them? • Most participants (approximately 23) read or skimmed all of the response options. Those who did not read the options knew right away that the question did not apply and looked immediately for “none of the above.” Did they find the “none” response, if applicable? • No participants experienced issues finding the “none” response option. • This question is complex because of the wordy response options and can pose a high respondent burden. Some participants did not understand what “survivor benefits” are, even those who receive some survivor benefits. Additionally, the response options “Regular payments from estates or trusts” and “Regular payments from annuities or paid-up insurance policies” are unclear and omit the word “survivor.” Recommendations: Consider adding additional text or an instruction to explain what “survivor benefits” are. While we only had one person who received benefits question what “survivor benefits” means, there was evidence that others are also unclear. This could pose issues with data quality if respondents are moving quickly and do not take the time to read all the response options. Additionally, providing a definition could be helpful for proxy respondents who may not be familiar with this term. A potential instruction is included below but should be reviewed with SMEs and included in the second round of cognitive testing. We also recommend moving response options 8 and 9 to a new, separate question. This change will result in an increase in response burden for those receiving survivor benefits, but cognitively, the question should be easier to answer by grouping these payments together topically. See proposed revision below, which also includes an explanation of what “regular payments” means. Consider the following revision: Q58a. Which types of survivor benefits, if any, did (^anyone in this household/you) receive in 2023? Exclude Social Security and VA benefits. Survivor benefits are benefits paid to eligible family members after an individual has passed.

Was the ending of the question understood (“that were designated specifically for retirement savings”)? • Most participants found this phrase clear and easy to understand. However, three participants (P2646, P2278, P2770) indicated the phrase was only clear when they read the response options. What were the “other” responses? • Four participants selected “other” for various reasons, including one with a legitimate other type of retirement account, two with other accounts that could be used for retirement, and one who did not know which type of retirement account she has. ○ One participant (P2710) used “other” because she knew she had a retirement account but was not sure what type of account it is. ○ One participant (P2286) had a general investment account invested in stocks and bonds. ○ One participant (P2246) reported a high yield savings account that he could use for retirement. It sounded like this was a savings account that could be used for anything, including retirement. ○ One participant (P2709) indicated they had a thrift savings account from working for the federal government. There were some problems with this question due to low knowledge among the general population about retirement accounts. Several participants struggled to answer and select the appropriate retirement account type. Additionally, participants had questions about some of the account types, most commonly about a 403b account. Recommendations: While there are cons to adding a “don’t know” or “not sure” option, the data supports that this could be a legitimate response from the general public for this question. Respondents may know they have a retirement account, but not know what type of account; this is especially true for proxy reporting. Allowing for a “not sure” option should improve data quality by increasing the consistency with which these participants answer this question. Additionally, providing a “not sure type of account” response option will allow the follow up amounts question to be asked even in cases where respondents do not know the type of account. Otherwise, we risk respondents with unknown retirement accounts skipping this question and missing data on the amounts in the account. We recommend either 1) adding a “not sure” option or 2) adding an instruction to select “other type of retirement account” when someone is unclear about the type of account. If we move forward with this option, the follow-up amounts question should fill appropriately when this response option is selected.

Ten participants were not clear on what a pension plan is and confused pension plans with other retirement accounts, such as a 401k. There was also low general knowledge about pension plans which may impact how accurately respondents can report for their entire workplace. Recommendations: While there are cons to having a “don’t know” response option, it is a legitimate response for this question. Combined with the lack of knowledge about pension plans, it may be best to present a “don’t know” option so that respondents can accurately and consistently report about pension plans at their workplaces. Having a “don’t know” response for this question may improve the respondent experience by recognizing it as a legitimate response. Alternatively, this question may be best asked about only the respondent and other people in their household rather than the entire workplace. If this question is retained to ask about the entire workforce, it may be useful to add a definition of a pension plan to increase the consistency of respondent answers. A potential definition is included below. Adding the definition should improve data quality and reduce respondent burden for those who may answer “yes” and be asked the follow up questions when the workplace does not have pension plans. What did the R report for “other”? • The other accounts reported included a stock market account, mutual funds, money market account, a high yield savings account, cryptocurrency, a brokerage account, and acorns. • One participant (P2710) had loaned money to a friend and was being paid back with interest, so included that as an “other” asset for this question. • One participant (P2595) had a severe misunderstanding of the question and reported an “other” account when they were thinking about paying loans with their associated interest. This participant explained, "For me student loans and, um… yeah, I'd say student loans and car payments." If “none”, do they have bank accounts? Clarify - these don’t earn interest or the interest rate is very low? • Only one participant (P2277) reported “none of the above” because they were not sure. They do have a checking account but no savings account and believed they do not earn any interest. • Another participant (P2512) initially reported “none of the above,” but when probed about her bank accounts realized she does have two checking and a savings account that do earn interest. It is unclear why this participant did not originally report these accounts; however, this is likely due to these accounts earning so little interest that she did not think it was of interest to the Census Bureau.

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-80 While straightforward for many participants, there are some concerns with measurement error for those who misunderstand the question or those who do not realize their accounts generate interest. The “other” category was also being used for a wide range of account types which may be better captured by other response options already available. However, low financial knowledge may make it a good idea to retain the “other” response option for those who do not recognize their interest-generating accounts as one of the options listed, such as a high yield savings account. Recommendations: The wording of “assets” seems to imply a large account generating a lot of income, which is not true for the majority of Americans. Consider changing this word to “accounts” and retesting this question in round two of cognitive interviewing. While “accounts” may not match perfectly for the response option “savings bond,” the benefits of this more inclusive word with a lower monetary bar than “assets” could be worth the change. This recommendation assumes that the SMEs are interested in ALL interest-generating accounts, no matter how small the monetary value. This question is cognitively complex and with retirement accounts already reported in previous questions, it may be worthwhile to consider moving “besides retirement accounts” to an instruction. This approach matches the format of many other questions with instructions and reduces the cognitive burden for respondents. If this recommendation is followed, it should be retested in round two of cognitive interviewing to confirm that participants do not attempt to report retirement accounts. Consider the following revision: Q99Ar. In 2023, which types of accounts, if any, did (^you/anyone in this household) have that may have paid interest? Do not include retirement accounts. Continue to monitor this question during the second round of interviews. 6.2.3 Income Amounts Research Question: These questions are created by combining several periodicity and amount questions. For example, public assistance combines Q59ep, Q59e, Q59e2 and Q59e3. The goal is to reduce cognitive burden by grouping together related income items, and to reduce burden by reducing the number of screens and the amount of text respondents must read through. The amount of text seen will vary depending on how many sources they reported and whether they follow the default periodicity. Description of how questions will function: All the following income amount questions will function this way unless otherwise specified. Income amount questions that don’t have a commonly selected periodicity will initially ask amounts using a grid format. The grid format will have a row for each source reported in the corresponding source question. The frequency, amount and number of payments will be entered. The frequency column will have a drop-down with options of:

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-94 ▪ weekly ▪ monthly ▪ yearly The ‘number of payments received’ box will only be fillable if something other than yearly is selected. There will be a total line for the year that is auto populated based on these entries. The respondent will be able to change fields entered to render a new total amount, if needed. If this can’t be programmed in the instrument for the cognitive interviews, then a printout of what it would like with probes could be used instead. Income amounts that have a commonly selected periodicity will initially ask for the amount using a default periodicity. There will be an option for the respondent to check if they prefer to report the amount in a different way. If they select this, they will then be taken to a screen with the grid format of asking for amounts. This screen will be the same that is used for income amounts that that vary in the way periodicity is reported. See example question (Q59) below). Section 6 — Question by Question Results – Income 6-101 Did the respondents report the periodicity requested or make a mistake? • Only one participant (P2332) misreported weekly amounts instead of monthly amounts on the default screen for Q59amt (unemployment) because they only thought about unemployment in weekly payments. They did not realize the question asked about monthly values. Do respondents like reporting the amount monthly or would they have preferred to report it differently? Would they prefer being asked how they want to report the amount first? • Preference for the default or alternative screen seems highly dependent on the income topic, with participants preferring the format that works best for them for a given question. • When asked, two participants (P2286, P2332) indicated they felt the set up of the default screen first worked well. P2286 thought this on both Q62E1 (pension) and Q65d (rental income). P2332 thought this on Q59amt (unemployment) and shared that he didn’t think there was any way to report differently because they pay out unemployment weekly. When the amount they want to report matches the default screen, then participants think it is working okay. • However, five participants (P2245, P2283, P2351, P2770, P2961) indicated a preference to be asked about reporting period preference before being asked to report the amounts. Several of these participants preferred the alternative version of the question where they could choose the time period themselves. ○ P2245 thought the alternative format was more convenient but was slightly concerned that some people might not understand the dropdown menu. He shared, "I like the drop down and I like this box better than the checkmark... this feels a lot more efficient, and this seems more intuitive... Doesn't look very cluttered. Sometimes with the checkbox it's like visual clutter, but this is very clear." ○ P2961 thought about his unemployment income in weekly amounts rather than monthly and preferred the alternative question so he could report weekly. When reviewing the default screen he shared, "So this is asking the amount you received each month from state and federal unemployment so I would love to just report this, you know, here's my weekly amount... I don't see that as an option. The number I think of... I think weekly." • However, some participants preferred to have the alternative screen first because the time period they wanted to report for did not match the default screen. For example, P2283 wanted to report RETIRENEW1 (Retirement accounts – interests and dividends) yearly and so preferred the alternative screen. Another example was P2770 who liked that at Q72cp (regular financial assistance) they could report 12 payments of $50 right away without having to click the checkbox; the alternative screen (which is the only option for regular financial assistance) worked better for their reporting needs.

Section 6 — Question by Question Results – Income 6-103 ○ The automatic calculation is not always obvious to participants. ▪ One participant (P2734) did not initially understand that the total would be automatically calculated and was worried about having to do the math herself. ▪ Another participant (P2434) revealed that the automatic totaling was not obvious when she tried to enter a one-time payment into the total box for Q72cp (regular financial assistance). ▪ Another participant (P2770) thought that when she reported payments biweekly (i.e., chose biweekly in the dropdown) that the grid would automatically calculate the total for the year without having to put in the number of payments. She got confused about how many biweekly payouts she received for Q63cp (Nonretirement accounts – interests and dividends) and decided to skip the question altogether rather than provide a response. Does having the confirmation of the total annual amount help respondents to catch errors? Do they even know this amount to check the total (i.e., is the total meaningful to them)? • Six participants (P2245, P2246, P2278, P2286, P2434, P2646) thought the automatic total was helpful, while four (P2332, P2351, P2770, P2734) thought it was not too helpful. Those that liked the automatic total thought it was convenient, could help prevent errors, and was overall helpful. Those who did not think the total was helpful were neutral about it and did not feel it obstructed their response process, but just did not need it to respond. For example, P2351 stated “Having the total box doesn’t hurt, but not sure it helps. But it certainly is simpler for calculation purposes, so I see nothing wrong with this.” Can the respondent “make corrections above”? Are there situations (like one month is different from the others where this won’t work? • There are no data to support analysis about making corrections. However, there were several instances when participants struggled to fit irregularly, inconsistent amounts into this reporting structure. ○ One participant (P2734) struggled to answer Q63cp (Nonretirement accounts - interest and dividends) because the amount varies from month to month. They shared, “For me personally that amount fluctuates…It would be really hard [to answer]." This participant said even with records it would be difficult to report this on a monthly time frame because of the variation in interest. ○ One participant (P2710) reported on Q58E1 (survivor benefits) that the question was difficult to answer because she gets several yearly payments from several separate accounts, which places burden on her to add them up and report in one number. ○ One participant (P2961) struggled with Q59amt (Unemployment) because the payment came every two weeks but was a weekly amount. There were some significant issues with the income amounts questions, both the topic of income and the display of the questions. Participants struggled to report exact income amounts and many preferred to skip the questions than spend time to retrieve their records. Some were willing to guess, but others were hesitant to do so without explicit

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-104 instructions. The income amounts questions pose extremely high respondent burden due to these factors. Recommendations: We recommend considering a reduction of income amount items to focus on key topics. The questions that should be considered for removal are RETIRENEW1 (Retirement accounts – interests and dividends) and Q63cp (Nonretirement accounts – interests and dividends). See next sections for question-specific findings about these two questions. We believe these questions could be replaced by RETIRENEW2 and NONRETIRENEW12, respectively. Removing these two questions should help reduce respondent burden and improve data quality. These questions had the highest number of missing responses, and most misunderstandings about the topic. We also recommend adding instructions to encourage respondents to estimate their responses, preferably both at the start of the interview and on key questions, such as RETIRENEW2 and NONRETIRENEW12. We recommend changes to the order of questions (see Section 7. Overall Recommendations) so that these amounts questions follow their filter question directly. This should help improve data quality by maintaining consistency for respondents across questions and reduce respondent burden by grouping questions about the same accounts together. Finally, we recommend moving forward with the alternative version that asks periodicity for all amounts questions alone, without first showing the default question. Asking the periodicity for reporting first may increase burden for those who want to report using the most commonly used time period; however, it should decrease confusion for those who need to report in a time period that is uncommon for the given type of income. We recommend some changes to the alternative grid, as follows: • Some improvements should be made to the periodicity question including grey text instructions in the drop-down bars (e.g., “How often”), formats should be hard coded for dollar amounts, instructions should be added on how to report one payout per year, and clear indication that the total is automatically calculated (e.g., all other boxes are white and total is greyed out). • We also recommend providing a reference guide to report the number of payments by frequency. This should be tested in the second round of cognitive interviewing to ensure that it is understood. Any changes to this format should be retested in the second round of cognitive interviews, with a focus on mobile testing. If we decide not to move forward with periodicity as the only amount question, then each income type should be reviewed for the most common reporting period and updated. For example, the unemployment question should ask about weekly payments instead of monthly.

Select all that apply. ▪ Mortgage or similar ▪ Second Mortgage ▪ Home Equity Loan ▪ None n = 16 Findings: How many respondents had difficulty? What would make more sense, if they were confused? • Of the thirteen participants who reviewed this question, there were two issues identified. • Two participants (P2710, P2734) raised questions about their understanding of the question. Both of these participants were unsure what “this property” referred to in the question text. ○ One participant (P2710) was unable to provide an answer and asked “What property? I mean are you talking about my home, or other things and stuff?" ○ Another participant (P2734) had a similar concern, asking, “What property am I talking about?” This participant was able to select the response “home equity loan” after reading through the response set. When probed, the participant thought that having the address of the property listed in the question would help to improve clarity, especially when someone owns multiple homes. ○ While participants did not struggle to respond to the question, one participant (P3022) shared, “All paid for…no car loan, no house loan”, illustrating that his

Section 6 — Question by Question Results – Income 6-117 first thought was about “property” in general, including vehicles, and not solely focusing on his residence. • Due to the question order, MORT_YN was asked over half-way through the questionnaire, following questions about income. Therefore, the question was missing the context of previous questions about their home or residence which might help respondents understand what “this property” meant in the context of other questions. The question text itself is not specific enough and could refer to many different types of property, as evidenced by one participant’s (p2710) reaction to the question. Furthermore, this may result in increased respondent burden as participants only understand the question meaning, and specifically the meaning of “this property,” after they read through the response options. • Another two participants (P2277, P2595) found it difficult to respond as they do not own the home they are living at. Both participants answered “none” but indicated their parents may have loans on the property they live in, but they personally do not have a loan. Note that this response issue could potentially impact other people who are not knowledgeable about their home’s financial status, such as a cohabiting partner. Did anyone confuse home equity loans and mortgages? • Most participants seem to understand the differences between home equity loans and mortgages, especially when the options apply to their situation. • When asked about the difference between home equity loans and mortgages, none of the participants thought that home equity loans were used to purchase a home. Of the 12 who were asked, six participants (P2261, P2253, P2961, P3022, P2417, P2369) stated that they understood home equity loans as being taken against the equity one already has in the home, and two participants (P2710 and 2417) stated they would use home equity loans for a repair or renovation. Two participants (P2310 and P2734) said they generally understood or were familiar with the difference between the two, without elaborating. • However, one participant (P2710) was somewhat unclear about the distinction and said a home equity loan and second mortgage could be the same thing. This did not impact their response process as they skipped the question due to confusion about what property was being asked about and not due to lack of clarity surrounding what loans they have on their property/ies. • Generally, the participants found the response options clear and did not confuse home equity loans and mortgages, but there was evidence that the wording “this property” was too vague. Without the context of a prior question defining ‘residence’, participants thought of many different types of properties and response burden was increased because the question text cannot stand alone without the response options. • Since many of the other questions ask about the entire household, it may be helpful to emphasize that the question is only referring to the respondent themselves so that people who live in properties for which others have loans are not confused about how to answer, such as those who live with parents.

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-118 Recommendations: SMEs should be consulted to determine the preferred option to move forward, but there are two ways to reduce confusion about the phrase “this property.” We recommend as the first option, to consider filling the address respondents reported earlier in the survey into the question text. This fix will address the ambiguity of “this property” for those who may own multiple homes, as well as reduce respondent burden by clarifying the question meaning. For cases when the respondent has refused to provide an address or the address details are missing, we recommend wording that will refer to the respondent’s current residence. Additionally, SMEs should consider whether we can simplify the question by asking about whether the respondent themselves has a loan on the property. This will reduce respondent burden and improve data quality in cases where the respondent cannot proxy report about their home’s loan status. We recommend adding “yourself” to the question text to get a more accurate report of the respondent’s loan status. The second option to consider is the question order for this item. If the wording is not changed, placing the question immediately following questions about the respondent’s home should help improve clarity, especially if placed immediately following the question asking for the respondent’s address. Placement of this question may improve data quality regardless of changes to the text of the question and should be considered whether a fill is added or not. Note that these recommendations assume that this is an individual-level question and not household. If the intent for this question is household level, we recommend using “…do you or anyone in this household…” and including a “don’t know” response option. Finally, these findings should be taken in tandem with Q65A2 where we posed the potential for an additional question about whether anyone in the household owns a property. If the SMEs decide to move forward with a new question about property ownership, then those who answer negatively can skip this question (MORT_YN). Consider the following revisions: [IF ADDRESS PROVIDED BY RESPONDENT:] “Which of these loans do you, yourself, have on this property: [FILL_STREETADDRESS]?” [IF NO ADDRESS PROVIDED BY RESPONDENT:] “Which of these loans do you, yourself, have on the property where you currently live?”

People refer to SNAP as a variety of things, so we provide a list of everything they might call it, but we don't actually need to know these separately. People also likely refer to them as more than one thing but know that it's all the same program. In the past, we’ve asked two questions for this. The first one has SNAP and food stamps. The second has the state program fill, which is just SNAP or food stamps in the vast majority of states, and the phrase “even for one month.” A bunch of people in states where the fill is SNAP or food stamps say yes on the second question after saying no on the first. We have no idea if this is because they needed to be prompted a second time or if “even for one month” is making the difference. Regardless, we know that SNAP is underreported, so it’s not an issue of people being bullied into over-reporting. We really want to be sure that this question works and that we aren’t going to lose those people who need to be asked twice. We’ve also moved these questions in the survey.
