We have to know whether or not students USUALLY (more than half the time) ate at school, regardless of whether they received free or reduced-price meals. We also need to get the count of kids in all the different meal categories (didn’t eat, had breakfast, got lunch for free, etc.), so we need the follow up question of which kids which meals and which meals they got for free. SMEAL_YN: During 2023, did any of the children in this household usually eat a complete breakfast and/or lunch provided by the school? ▪ Yes ▪ No n = 8 Findings: How many respondents had difficulty? What would make more sense if they were confused? • Of the eight participants who reviewed this question, two (P2961 and P2289) had difficulty, indicating that clearer question wording regarding the age of children being asked about and the definition of “provided” would have helped with comprehension and retrieval. • One participant (P2961) originally clicked “no” after reading the question multiple times. When probed about his rereading by the cognitive interviewer, the participant shared "I did…my daughter goes to... my son, he usually brings his lunch, he's a first grader. My daughter… she's in daycare, and so, yeah so, she might qualify for that... So, I would say maybe yes for her... the school feeds her." At that point he changed his answer to yes, and the interviewer noted that he was at first thinking of his older son. The participant said that was correct, because he doesn't usually think of the daycare as a school; however, he also shared that sometimes his son eats a school lunch. • Another participant (P2289) has two children, one of whom is school-aged. He answered “no” to this question and stated that his wife provides breakfast and lunch money for that child to buy lunch at school. He shared that the phrase “provided by” means that the school provides everything.

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-128 If not done in think aloud, have them think through each child and note if they eat at school or not to check their answer and where the question might go wrong. • None of the participants had more than one school-aged child in 2023; however, two participants (P2961 and P2289) had one school-aged child and one younger child who attended a childcare program. One participant responded “yes” and one of these responded “No” to SMEAL_YN, despite both having similar situations where their older child purchased meals at school. Did the respondent notice the word “complete” in the question? Did the inclusion of “complete” change their answer to the question? • Of the 7 participants who were asked this probe, three (P2303, P2369, P2283) noticed the word ‘complete’, one did not (P2961), and three participants (P2245, P2289, P2332) did not directly address whether they noticed the word. No participants said it would have changed their responses, with four (P2961, P2369, P2289, P2283) specifically stating it would not have changed their response. • When receiving this probe, one participant (P2303) seemed to interpret the word “complete” to be referring to all meals instead of complete meals: “Yeah, I know like morning, afternoon, evening… Like, breakfast, lunch, and dinner." • Another participant (P2245) stated they don’t exactly know what a complete breakfast or lunch refers to and speculated that it likely includes a drink and sides. However, this participant has a homeschooled child and answered “no” to SMEAL_YN, so this did not impact their response. Does “provided” mean the same as “prepared”? • Participants were probed about their understanding of the terms “provided” and “prepared” to better understand which term might fit the intent of the question. Of those asked, only one participant (P2289) said these words mean the same thing. Four participants (P2303, P2245, P2961 P2369) thought the meanings of ‘prepared’ and ‘provided’ were different but struggled to clearly verbalize the differences. • One participant (P2303) said ‘prepared’ is “future” tense. • One participant (P2245) described how schools may provide a wrapped Smuckers peanut butter and jelly which they did not prepare. • Three participants (P2283, P2303, P2245) preferred the word “provided,” two participants (P2961, P2310) prefer the word “prepared,” and one (P2332) would prefer “free” instead of either of these terms. • Those participants who preferred the word ‘prepared’ (P2961 and P2310) had that preference because ‘provided’ implied ‘free’ to them, which made it confusing for them to answer. However, some of this interpretation of “provided” may have been influenced by question order effects of the preceding items about food assistance. Recommendations: Due to question order effects of this question being presented immediately after the one about SNAP, respondents may be primed to think this question is asking about government benefits or subsidized lunch programs when reading the word “provided.” We recommend

Section 6 — Question by Question Results – Income 6-129 changing the order of questions so that this item does not immediately follow questions about SNAP. See Section 7. Overall Recommendations for more details. We also believe that adding language to the question text to include meals sold by the school is important because purchased lunches are currently underreported. Additionally, although this question was only supposed to be presented to participants with children aged 5-18, two participants, who only had children under 5, were presented this question. Even with correcting this programming error, we may want to consider including language to specify what age children should be included when answering. It is possible that households with multiple children, such as P2961, screen into SNAP_YN, but only the younger child is provided food by their preschool. There may also have been some confusion over the word “usually,” though there was not a direct probe about the word. We may want to consider specifying what “usually” means or changing the wording of the question to use the definition “more than half the time.” Finally, it should be considered whether the universe is respondents with children aged 5-18 during the current year or the year being asked about in the survey, as those children who were 5 years old this year likely did not eat a school meal last year except in a preschool or daycare program. Consider the following potential revision, which should be reviewed by SMEs for what is most in line with their analytic goals: Please think about all the children aged 5-18 years in this household. During 2023, did any of these children eat breakfast and/or lunch provided or sold by the school more than half of the time? • Yes • No Question SMEAL_ROST Research Question: See above (SMEAL_YN). SMEAL_ROST: For each child, please indicate which school-provided meals they usually ate in 2023. Select all that apply. Child Breakfast Lunch None [Child 1] [Child 2] [Child N] n = 4

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-130 Findings: Does the question make sense? What is confusing? • Three of the four participants who reviewed this question had some challenges understanding or answering it, partially due to unclear wording and partially due to being presented the question when they should not have been. • For one participant (P2961), the question only was presented for his son, despite discussing both his son and daughter in SMEAL_YN. His son typically brings (packs) his lunch but sometimes buys a lunch; it is his preschool-age daughter who is provided breakfast and lunch every day. It is unclear if the participant did not see the term “usually,” if the term was too vague to map his response correctly, or his focus on his daughter in the preceding question is why he listed his son. • One participant (P2310) only selected “breakfast” even though his child eats both breakfast and lunch at school; his child gets breakfast for free and pays for lunch. This participant thought aloud about whether “provided” meant free and had decided that it does when choosing to only answer “breakfast.” • Another participant (P2369) could not choose meals because she was answering about her 4-year-old (see below). Does the format work? Note if the respondent should have selected more than they did, or they did not choose “none” and instead left the row blank. • The format was understood by participants. However, the programming error affecting both SMEAL_YN and this question led to it being asked of parents who have children under age 5. This created confusion for those without school-aged children. If the respondents don’t check any meals, probe as to what went wrong in the previous question. • One participant (P2369) was unable to check any meals as her 4-year-old child was not listed in the instrument. This was a result of the participant being screened in for this question and the former (SMEAL_YN) despite not having any school-aged children. This participant verbally stated that her child received both breakfast and lunch at preschool. • The primary challenge with this question was that parents whose children were under age 5 during the year of inquiry were presented the question incorrectly. The instrument had not prompted them in the prior question to only think about school-aged children, so they could not answer this follow up. Recommendations: Adjust the programming to correctly present the filter question SMEAL_YN to those with children ages 5-18, along with the changes to the question text in SMEAL_YN to prompt respondents to only think about their school-aged children. If SMEAL_YN is changed to include the text “more than half the time,” then this language should be duplicated in SMEAL_ROST.

Section 6 — Question by Question Results – Income 6-131 Question SUBMEAL_YN Research Question: We need to know which kids got free or reduced-price meals and for which meals. We have previously not asked about breakfast, so that part is new. SUBMEAL_YN: During 2023, did [any of these children/this child] receive free or reduced price school meals? ▪ Yes ▪ No n = 8 Findings: Does the question make sense? What is confusing? • The question made sense to most participants, but one participant (P2303) did not immediately understand the phrase “free or reduced price,” and another participant (P2332) seemed to be answering about their own experience instead of their child who is not school-aged. • One participant (P2303) said they needed to read the question twice to understand what was meant by “free or reduced price.” • Another participant (P2332), who did not have school-aged children, answered “no” to SMEAL_YN but “yes” to this question and seemed to be answering about her own experiences receiving free or reduced price lunch in childhood, stating that they had qualified. Would it be clearer if we specified breakfast and/or lunch again? • It would be clearer if breakfast and/or lunch was spelled out again. One participant (P2310) said that he only considered lunch, but that if the question asked about meals, he would have said “yes” for both children. This participant had noted that the children’s schools give them breakfast in SMEAL_YN. Do we need to note that we want people to say yes if the kids are getting free meals because everyone at the school is getting free meals (versus schools where individuals have to apply)? • Two participants had children who receive and eat free meals at schools where at least one meal per day is provided free for all students. One (P2369) clicked “yes” and another (P2310) clicked “no” for this question. Therefore, based on limited data available, it would likely improve the judgement and retrieval process to be clear that those whose children receive a free meal along with all other students should still say “yes” to this question. Are people thrown off by the phrase “reduced price” vs. “free or reduced school meals”? • Generally, participants were not thrown off by the phrase “reduced price” and preferred it to the phrasing without the word “price.” • One participant (P2332) shared that they did not know there was a “reduced price” option, thinking it was either free or paid. This person was the only participant probed who preferred the phrase “free or reduced school meals.”

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-132 • Of the other seven probed, participants either had no preference or explicitly preferred the current phrasing: “free or reduced price school meals,” over options like “free or reduced school meals,” or “free or reduced lunch.” • One participant (P2310) noted that without the word “price” included, the phrase “reduced meal” could mean a “small” meal. • For this question, in addition to the programming error, the question wording can also be improved to assist with data accuracy. Recommendations: This question was presented to all participants who received SMEAL_YN, not just participants who answered “yes” to SMEAL_YN. Presenting to the correct universe of respondents will be important in reducing confusion for this question. If the words breakfast and lunch were spelled out, this may have avoided. This language of breakfast and/or lunch is already used in SMEAL_YN, so it could be used here for consistency as well. We may infer based on the limited data available that specifying that schools where free meals are provided for all students should be included. Consider the following revision: During [2023], did [any of these children/this child] receive free or reduced-price school breakfast and/or lunch? Section 6 — Question by Question Results – Income 6-141 • A total of five participants selected “Free care with family, friends, or neighbors” as a response and reported that this care occurred in their home and outside of their home. ○ Two participants (P2332, P2961) said this care was provided both in home and outside of home. ○ One participant (P2245) said this care was provided outside of their home. ○ One participant (P2303) said this care was provided in their home. What was confusing? • Participants were asked about whether the option “Care by a parent/guardian at home” made sense to them, and 5 participants indicated the option made sense and understood it to mean something like a stay-at-home parent or “homemaker.” • None of the 7 participants who received this question reported any confusion with the question or any other response options. However, one (P2961) seemed to think the question and response options were redundant, saying "Care by parent/guardian… That's always free." Additionally, despite indicating having children, two participants (P2283, P2269) selected ‘none’ for both paid and unpaid forms for childcare. If the respondent answered “other,” what types of care did they use? • None of the participants who received this question answered “other” so there is no data to answer this research question. Are we missing any types of care that people think are common? • Most of the participants (P2245, P2283, P2369, P2961) who received this question did not think any other types of care were missing. • However, one participant (P2332) thought that an option for ‘Churches providing free childcare’ was missing, and explained, "Some churches have free child care throughout the week.” Are they selecting more than one option for the same kind of care? • No data to support analysis. Do respondents understand “unpaid” and “free” as the same? • Two participants (P2245, P2369) believed that “unpaid” and “free” have different meanings. For them, “unpaid” meant there was no cost to the parent/guardian for the care, but someone was getting paid for providing care via taxes or a grant. Comparatively, “free” care would be care that no one was paying for. For example, one participant (P2369) noted this “unpaid” care is different from family and friends doing child care for free because no one is paying them. • Three participants (P2245, P2332, P2961) indicated some preference for “free” over “unpaid” since it seemed like a clearer word. ○ One participant (P2245) preferred “free” because the types of care listed in the response options are free to the parent, even if the caregivers are getting paid. They shared, "I think in a parent's mind it probably makes more sense to say free."

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-142 ○ Another participant (P2332) could see benefits of both, but “free” is very clear, explaining, “I think unpaid sounds more professional, but free is, like, straight to the point.” ○ One participant (P2303) preferred “unpaid” over “free.” Are there other “unpaid” arrangements, like trading services? Do respondents also call those “Free”? • Most participants (P2303, P2332, P2369, P2961) said they could not think of any other “unpaid” childcare arrangements. • However, one participant (P2245) did report trading child care with others, and said they sometimes watch the other person’s child as a trade. This participant thought that trading child care with others was a fairly normal practice. Overall, the participants found this question easy to answer. Participants understood the question was asking about unpaid care only and were able to differentiate this question from the previous question about paid care. However, it is possible that respondents may not think of the daily care they provide for their own children as a form of unpaid child care, potentially leading to misreporting. Two participants viewed there to be a difference between free and unpaid care, suggesting that free care means ‘no one’ is being paid, but all participants understood the intent behind the question about free care. The majority of participants preferred the term “free” over “unpaid,” as it was clearer and straight to the point. One participant mentioned engaging in other “unpaid” arrangement of taking turns with another parent in watching each other’s kids. Recommendations: To help reduce the chance of respondents misreporting unpaid care, we suggest revising the “Care by a parent/guardian at home” response option to reflect the SMEs’ intent more adequately. Currently, most participants interpret the question to mean having a stay-at- home parent with a few participants not seeming to think of the daily care they provide as a form of child care. Consider the following options for clarifying the intent behind this response option: Option 1: If the intent is to capture stay-at-home parents only: “Care by a parent/guardian at home (for example, stay-at-home parent or homemaker)” Option 2: If the intent is to capture all care provided by parents: “Care by a parent/guardian at home (for example, everyday care provided by parent/guardian) Additionally, although participants perception of free vs. unpaid care did not impact their response process, if desired, to clarify the meaning behind “free care,” an italicized definition can be added to the question. SMEs should review this instruction and tweak as needed.

Of the five participants who received this question, most had no trouble with the grid format and preferred the periodicity dropdown option as the best way to report amount of money spent on child care. One participant did use different dropdown options when reporting on amount spent on child care for different members of their household, suggesting that having a variety of ways to report will work best for respondents. One participant did have some confusion using the grid when reporting a yearly amount when it came to amount of payments, because she didn’t actually make one payment so entering “1” as number of payments felt slightly counterintuitive. There was also not a direct probe asked about complicated child care arrangements, such as more expensive care during the summer compared to the school year. Section 6 — Question by Question Results – Income 6-149 • How participants interpreted the question also impacted whether or not they included ‘using paid time off’ to watch their children when answering. What situations did people think of? Did they think of isolated situations (babysitter was sick one day and parent had to stay home) or chronic problems (can’t get care after 3pm so reduced their hours)? • There was an even split between participants who thought of isolated situations and those who thought of chronic situations when answering the question. Two participants (P2369, P2961) thought of more chronic problems that extended for more than one day. ○ For example, one participant (P2369) thought of issues similar to what was encountered during the pandemic, where child care places were closed, and it was struggle for her to work her full amount of hours due to not having child care. ○ Another participant (P2961) interpreted the question as, did not having child care prevent them from having a different work schedule overall (e.g., working additional hours or turning down work) rather than working less than their normal hours for a day or two because their child is sick. Specifically, P2691 says, “You know, did anybody turn down work… Did our kids prevent us from working any more additional hours at our job, in terms of getting child care for our kids. Did we have any problems getting child care… So we could work more hours." • On the contrary, two participants (P2245, P2303) thought of infrequent situations, having difficulty finding care for only a short period of time. ○ Thinking broadly about any situation rather than only about struggling to find child care for an extended period of time, P2245 interpreted the question to mean “If you don’t have anyone to watch your kid, you can’t go to work.” Do they count using their vacation time (paid time off) when answering? Or just unpaid time? • One participant (P2303) did count using their vacation time when answering whereas two participants (P2369, P2961) did not count this time. For one participant (P2961), while he did not think of using paid time off when answering the question, he did recall there was a time when his wife was sick and he had to take PTO to watch their child. However, this situation did not come to mind when he first read the question, so he did not think that situation applied to the question. • One participant (P2245) is self-employed so the question of using time off was not applicable to them. Overall, there was some inconsistency in how participants are interpreting the question. While some participants understood the question to be asking about any time where they might have missed work due to not having child care (e.g., short and infrequent situations), other participants were only thinking about chronic problems that have made finding child care difficult, such as day care closures during the pandemic or not taking on additional work or certain job opportunities because it would interfere with child care. As a result, not all participants are thinking about moments where they might have used their paid time off

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-150 to watch their kids. Updating question wording to clarify whether question is referring to infrequent or chronic situations would help alleviate confusion and promote more consistency in how respondents interpret the question. Recommendations: Due to inconsistencies in interpretation, we recommend discussing with SMEs which type of situations (infrequent vs. chronic) they are hoping to capture with this question and updating question wording accordingly. Depending on the intent of the question, we recommend updating the question wording in one of the following two ways: If the intent is to include infrequent situations, consider the following revision: Did [you / anyone in this household] have to work fewer hours in 2023 because of problems obtaining child care? Please include infrequent instances of missing work, such as, child was sick from school or usual care provider was not available and parent and/or guardian had to take time from work to watch their child. If the intent is to only focus on chronic situations, consider the following revision: Did [you / anyone in this household] have to work fewer hours in 2023 because of chronic problems obtaining child care (e.g., can’t get care after 3pm so reduced their hours or turned down opportunities for more work/overtime)? Section 6 — Question by Question Results – Income 6-153 • None of the 27 participants who received this question struggled with the grid format. Are their children living with someone other than a parent/ guardian? • None of the participants who received this question reported having any children living with someone other than a parent/guardian. Overall, none of the participants struggled with the grid format and the majority of the participants understood the question was asking about whether they had additional children who were not already listed in the household roster. A point of confusion for a few participants though was whether or not their adult children should be considered. While this did not impact the validity of their responses (e.g., none of the participants considered their adult children as the intended subjects of the question and answered “No”), the confusion did require participants to re-read the question a few times for clarification, suggesting there is some response burden. Due to a programming error that resulted in question asking about the child’s “other parent” and not “other parent or guardian”, two participants noted the exclusion of guardian did impact their responses and led to some confusion about whether or not they should consider a child who is living with someone other than a parent (e.g., foster care). These comments confirm the importance of using the phrasing “parent or guardian” for this question. Finally, a few participants did make a note that they don’t have any children whatsoever, indicating potential confusion as to why they were being asked this question. Recommendations: To help reduce confusion for respondents who only have adult children, we recommend updating the wording to include “any children under the age of 18” as it is the traditional cutoff of child support in most states. However, there are situations where child support may be paid for children over the age of 18 (e.g., if a child has disabilities). Further discussion with SMEs may be beneficial for finalizing question wording to ensure the target of measurement will be captured by this question. We also recommend adding a “Not applicable” option to the grid. This can help reduce confusion for respondents who do not have any children. 7-1 7. Overall Recommendations This section presents global recommendations for issues that impact multiple ASEC Income and Health Insurance questions. We provide several considerations to improve the questions prior to the conduct of the second round of cognitive testing. 7.1 Income 7.1.1 Introduction with instructions During cognitive testing, several participants asked whether they should have their financial information and records available. They explained that they were unsure what to expect going into the interview. As a result, participants were not prepared to answer many of the questions. The prenotification letter should describe the survey and the data we are collecting so participants can be prepared. This may be somewhat challenging as we will want to balance the need for more accurate reporting with the increased perceived respondent burden that would be associated with such preparation. However, respondents deserve to have some context before entering the survey. In addition, the introduction of the survey (initial introduction screen) would be a prime location to explain that some financial records would be helpful to have during completion of the survey. Furthermore, instructions should be provided to respondents to only report each income source one time. We could include testing of prenotification and/or introductory text in the second round of cognitive interviewing. 7.1.2 Allowing estimates If SMEs believe that an estimate is acceptable, that instruction could be included in the introduction as well. This raises a larger question as to whether estimates are acceptable. It was determined during cognitive testing that many participants were already providing estimates, so prompting for this would lead to more complete data and reduce item nonresponse. As explained by one participant (P2361), "In all honesty, if I was taking this survey, I may not answer this question [RETIRENEW1] because it would take me a lot of time to like find my log-ins for my accounts and yeah I... wouldn't do that... If it said... an estimation, a ballpark figure... I'd be more comfortable answering it personally." If SMEs would prefer that this instruction is not included in the introduction, the instruction could be included as a soft check prompt if respondents try to go to the next question without responding. We may also consider including this instruction on certain questions

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 7-2 that are more likely to need to be estimated, such as income from interest-earning accounts. 7.1.3 Section introductions / Transition statements As respondents progress through various income and finance topics, it can be somewhat confusing or disorienting as to the content being covered. We would highly recommend including a short instruction or transition statement at the beginning of new sections. We believe this will improve the survey experience, along with the suggested reordering of questions described next. 7.1.4 Additional definitions While comprehension of financial terms is not key to the response process for many items, there are several that may benefit from adding instructions to define terms. In some cases, respondents may look up definitions on their own, which could lead to measurement error if they review incongruent definitions. Adding definitions may also be helpful for proxy reports, in which respondents may not know the term themselves, but seeing a definition could help them remember and report for someone else in their household. 7.1.5 Reordering of questions The order of the questions seemed to increase respondent burden because they were not organized logically, especially questions about income sources and amounts. Participants found it challenging to move back and forth between very different types of income when responding. Reordering of questions should help align topic areas to establish context and improve the survey experience. We recommend reordering the questions to present more common sources of income before less common sources. For example, we recommend asking the overall pension question (Q62Ar) first before other questions that also include the word “pension,” such as survivor benefits (Q58a) and military pension (Q60A88). When participants saw “pension” as an option in the survivor benefits and the military pension questions, some tried to select it to report their pension income. Participants are looking for the type of income they have to report and try to fit it into the categories presented, even when not appropriate. Exhibit 7-1 below presents an abbreviated list of the question order changes by topic, with the income questions first asked of sources of income, then amounts of income. We provide a full list of all questions and their recommended order in Appendix G, presenting each question, a summary of the topic, and both the original and new order. These question order changes should be tested in the second round of cognitive interviews. Another option we could consider is reordering questions with a responsive design based on the reported age of the respondent. If the respondent reports they are 65 years or older, we could first present questions about pension, retirement withdrawal, and social security. If the respondent is under 65, then we could present employment sources of income first, and ask questions about pensions, retirement withdrawal, and social security later in the survey.

In essence, this led to “double-counting.” One consideration to help aid respondents would be to include an overall summary screen which would allow participants to review each of the accounts that they noted to ensure they did not double-count items. Moreover, this screen might help respondents to determine that an account was not listed. The premise of this summary screen is similar to the approach TurboTax includes on their platform, allowing the individual

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 7-4 to review what was entered for accuracy. If an error is found, they can return to the question to make adjustments. While this will involve additional programming, we do believe this will result in more accurate data reporting. This may also increase respondent burden since it will take more time to review and confirm their sources of income; however, many participants in the cognitive interviews indicated a desire to accurately report data. Respondents may feel positively about being given the opportunity to review the data they have reported and make corrections. We believe this summary screen should appear directly after the section about income, before any other questions (e.g., food assistance, childcare). 7.1.7 Validations / Confirmations Another approach to increase data quality and reliability would be to include various validations and confirmations. This can be done through the inclusion of programming logic around key questions that may contribute to respondents providing duplicate information. For example, if a respondent selects “Veteran’s pension” in question 60A88 and “yes” to “U.S. Military retirement survivor pension” in question 58a, a soft check could pop-up to ensure that the respondent is referring to different accounts. We would not recommend consistency logic to be included on all questions, but the survey would benefit from inclusion on some items, where respondents are likely to get confused or double report. A standard message could appear on specific questions confirming with respondents that this information was not already reported on a previous question. Specific validation logic could be programmed to look for similar values or trigger a consistency check if the respondent previously selected or entered data in a previous question. These checks can be overridden by the respondent if the information is correct. However, if the information entered was incorrect, they can return to a previous question to make a correction, then return to the last unanswered question. These validations/confirmations require some additional programming and testing but should result in more accurate data reporting. 7.1.8 Respondent burden and reducing breakoffs It was clear during cognitive testing that respondent burden associated with answering many of the questions is quite high. Knowledge is not available or would require review of financial documents. While some participants will take the time to report accurately, others will either provide an estimate, leave the question blank, or breakoff entirely. To mitigate these concerns, we suggest the following: 1. Consider removing questions that pose the highest respondent burden and lowest data quality. Some questions might be unnecessarily burdensome considering they have low analytic value (e.g., amount of income from interest-earning accounts,

Section 7 — Overall Recommendations 7-5 Q63cp). For example, most participants estimated the amount of interest they received in an Interest-earning savings account or standard savings account. In most cases, the amounts are going to be quite low. It may be worth considering whether it is analytically useful to ask for this level of information, considering the added burden. One participant (P2310) refused to answer question 63cp based on both burden and privacy concerns explaining, “I would need to really go through my accounts to figure this out… I’m not going to do that to fill out a Census form.” 2. Consider allowing a “Don’t know” response option for certain questions, as specified on the question-specific findings in earlier sections. While Census Bureau treats all nonresponse in the same way analytically, providing a “don’t know” response can improve the respondent experience by allowing respondents to indicate their true response – that they do not know the answer. This may help to minimize break- offs, encouraging respondents to review more questions and provide the information they do know. Another option to immediately offering the “Don’t know” option is to suppress the option unless the respondent attempts to go to the next question, leaving the current question unanswered. In this case, we allow “Don’t know” as a legitimate response in lieu of item nonresponse. 3. Consider allowing response ranges of questions with less importance. Another option to address item nonresponse would be to provide ranges when a respondent attempts to go to the next question, leaving the current question unanswered. This would allow us to gather some information, although not as precise as a specific value, but analytically preferable to item nonresponse. This format is already employed in the question series about energy assistance (ENG_RNG and END_RNG2) and could work well for other items in the survey. 4. Improved question context. Consider providing additional context to tie previous questions together. One way to do this would be to change “who had X account” questions from “the account” to “this type of account” as recommended in the discussion of Question 99Ba. Another option would be to include a statement prior to asking the follow-up question, for example: “In the previous question you reported [fill account type name]. Who had this type of account?” 5. Consider additional features to improve reporting. All questions asking for numeric values should include a label outside of the response box. For example, add a “$” when looking for a monetary value. Add “Weeks” when asking about the number of weeks. Furthermore, decrease the response box to be the width of the maximum numerical value allowed. For example, if asking weeks that the respondent was

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 7-6 looking for a job in a specific year, the response box should only allow two numbers. This will avoid inadvertent alpha-numeric responses, resulting in errors, as we found during the cognitive testing. 6. Ensuring consistency when referring to the year throughout the instrument. Consider using standard language and formatting when referring to the year throughout the questionnaire. This helps “train” the respondent and increases data quality. For example, we found an inconsistent format in how the time frame ”2023” was presented. In some cases, “In 2023,” preceded the question and in other questions, we found “…,in 2023.” at the end of the question. We recommend consistently beginning the question with “In 2023,” to make it easier for respondents to understand the time frame. Furthermore, there were some child care questions that did not include a time frame. We recommend ensuring that all questions requiring a time frame have one clearly specified. 7.1.9 Recommendation for format of grids As discussed extensively in Section 6.2.2, we recommend moving forward presenting only the alternative version of the grids, allowing respondents to report in the time period they prefer for all financial amounts questions. Additionally, we recommend several tweaks to the presentation of the grid questions to improve functionality. See Section 6.2.2 for further details about these recommendations. 7.1.10 Programming of instrument for the second round of cognitive interviews Cognitive testing was difficult to complete during the first round of testing, in many cases, due to programming errors. We were unable to assess the performance of several questions due to incorrect or broken skip logic and problems with fills. We assume that these will be corrected during the second round of interviews in order to fully assess the questions. 7.1.11 Information sharing from government Finally, while this is outside the scope of this project, it is a finding that is worth noting. Some participants expressed confusion that the Census Bureau would need this level of detailed financial information since it would already be available within tax data reported annually to the IRS. While sharing of this level of data poses additional challenges, there have been other Census Call Orders that have investigated the sharing of data between government agencies. This may be a long-term answer to the data collection challenges faced on the ASEC questionnaire, and potentially lead to better quality data.

Section 7 — Overall Recommendations 7-7 7.2 Health Insurance 7.2.1 Health insurance Questions in this section need to be reviewed for how best to address the issue of respondents who are covered by insurance of a non-household member, in particular youth not living at home and covered until age 26 under their parents’ insurance. 7.2.2 Medical out of pocket expenses In the questions that asked for a dollar amount of expenses, the field to enter the amount also allowed for text entries. Those who entered text entries were treated as having answered the question with a value, and therefore skipped out of the follow up questions offering ranges for non-respondents. We recommend either not allowing text responses or routing them the same as for blank responses. 7.2.3 Migration For the 1-year and the 10-year time frame for questions, the current formulation mentions "x year(s) ago, that is, September 1, 2014/2024" The date was provided as a fixed date, not as it related to the interview date. In addition, all but one participant focused on the month and year or the number of years, or both, but not on the specific date. For these reasons we recommend reformulating the time frames as "1/10 year(s) ago, that is, <CURRENT MONTH>, <1/10 YEARS AGO>.

8-1 8. Conclusions The first round of cognitive testing uncovered several issues with the questions in both the Health Insurance and Income modules. As noted, the Income section was challenging for many participants due to contextual issues resulting from the order of questions. As a result, we highly recommend the reordering of questions. Furthermore, consistency in formatting (e.g., placing the year time frame at the beginning of the question, and standard formatting of numeric responses) is recommended to reduce respondent burden. Consider whether to allow “Don’t Know” responses on questions that are highly burdensome or require data retrieval. This should help to reduce item-nonresponse or potential breakoffs and could improve the respondent experience. Finally, it is highly recommended that the programmed instrument is thoroughly tested following any changes that result from the Round 1 findings to ensure that Round 2 testing is not influenced by programming issues. The recommended changes outlined in this report are grounded in survey methodology best practices and should help to both improve the respondent experience and generate more complete and accurate reported data.

C-1 Appendix C. Cognitive Interview Participant Consent Form What is the purpose of this interview? The U.S. Census Bureau is conducting interviews to help with the design and content about a portion of the Current Population Survey (CPS). This module, called the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) is an important source of information about our nation on topics such as employment, health insurance, and income. It’s important that the questions make sense, are easy to answer, and that everyone understands the questions in the same way. You are one of about 60 people who are being asked to participate in these interviews. Findings from these interviews will be used to clarify survey questions and instructions on the survey. What will happen if I take part in this interview? If you agree to take part in this study, you will be asked to answer questions about your household, including yourself and other people that live with you. The interview will be conducted virtually by a staff member from RTI International or Research Support Services, who are doing this study for the U.S. Census Bureau. We would also like to audio and video record the interview. Only the people who work on this study will review the recording. It will help us make sure we accurately capture your answers. If you don’t want to be recorded, that’s okay – you may still participate in the interview. How much time is required to participate? The interview will last approximately 90 minutes. Do I have to take part in this interview? No, participation in this interview is voluntary. You can stop the interview at any time, and you don’t have to answer a question if you don’t want to. You will not lose any rights you would normally have if you choose not to join this interview. What are the possible risks and benefits from participating in this interview? There are no direct benefits to you from doing this interview. Your involvement in this study will help us improve the questions for the Current Population Survey. There is no more than minimal risk in participating.

ii Abstract Common wisdom in survey methodology is that cash is the most persuasive form of incentive payment. Since the establishment of this guideline, however, the world has become more digital. Restaurants and retailers have started to move away from accepting cash payments, a trend accelerated by the pandemic. Gift cards, especially those issued by online retailers, are often digital. Smart phones allow people to leave their wallets at home and instead use their phones to pay-- either digitally with an app or with a credit card tucked into a card holder stuck to the phone. Given these shifts in how people pay for things, is cash still enticing to all subpopulations? Data collected from a large nonprobability survey asked about people’s use of cash and their preferred form of incentive payment for $5 and $40. Incentive types offered in the vignette were: cash, digital gift cards, physical gift cards, check, and electronic bank transfer. A small number of people preferred cash incentives for either amount (5%), with most opting for electronic bank transfers and digital gift cards. The small subpopulation preferring cash was mostly young, low-income, and without a college degree. It seems that cash is no longer king but digital cash (i.e., digital gift cards and bank transfers) now reigns. Keywords: incentives, incentive preference, digital incentives Suggested Citation: Sinibaldi, Jennifer. 2026. “Is Cash the King of (Promised) Incentives for All Subpopulations?” Research and Methodology Directorate, Center for Behavioral Science Methods Research Report Series (Survey Methodology 2026-05). U.S. Census Bureau. Available online at: <https://www.census.gov/library/working-papers/2026/adrm/rsm2026-05.html>

1 Overview The common wisdom among survey methodologists is that cash incentives are more effective at gaining response than alternative monetary incentives (e.g., gift cards) and non- monetary incentives (e.g., Gajic et al. 2012, Birnholtz et al. 2004, Singer and Ye 2013). This research has led to the mantra that “cash is king” in the incentive world. While cash is more motivating than a pen or magnet, in a post-Covid world, how does it compare to alternative monetary incentives? It may be time to update the mantra. Changes to consumers’ relationship with cash were accelerated with the ubiquity of contactless payment methods that arose during Covid (Dickler 2021). Beyond handing over a credit card, using one’s smartphone as a digital wallet can eliminate the need to carry a physical wallet, and therefore perhaps the ability to carry cash. So, is it now inconvenient to respondents to offer cash if their habits have changed such that they don’t carry it or use it? There is evidence that the enthusiasm to abandon cash is likely not evenly distributed across the population, and may vary by income, race, and age. Studies conducted by Pew Research in 2015, 2018, and 2022 (Perrin 2018; Faverio 2022) reported that low-income households are more likely to use cash, compared to mid- and high-income households. Black consumers are more likely to use cash than White consumers, and people ages fifty and older are more likely to pay with cash, compared to people younger than fifty. Given this, receptiveness to a cash incentive may vary by demographics, leading to different preferences for different subpopulations. This research collects information on respondents’ relationship with cash and asks vignette questions about how they would like to receive $5 and $40 promised incentives for completing a web survey. The results will show respondents’ incentive preferences and characterize those who still prefer a cash incentive. Research Questions 1. Are people carrying cash? Of those carrying cash, what are their characteristics? 2. Are they using cash? Of those using cash, what are their characteristics? 3. What type of incentive payment is preferred for $5 vs. $40? 4. What are the characteristics of those who prefer cash incentives? 5. Overall, is cash, as a promised incentive, still enticing for all subpopulations? Data The experiment was hosted on a web survey of Census Bureau Research Panel members. These 30,000 panel members were respondents to Phase 4.2 of the Census Household Pulse survey (HPS), administered from July to September 2024, who agreed to be contacted about future research opportunities. The web survey was open from 3-15

2 December 2024 and available in English only. The survey asked about demographics, household composition, carrying and spending cash, preferences for incentive payment method, costs of utilities, school lunches, and income from property rental (in that order). It took approximately 15 minutes. Two reminders were sent, beyond the initial email invitation, resulting in approximately 10,000 responses and 500 bounce backs (assumed eligible), for an AAPOR RR2 of 33%. There were about 9,200 cases still active in the survey for the questions about incentive preference and having and using cash. No incentive was offered for completing the survey. Applicable Survey Questions Respondents were randomized into two groups to determine which incentive vignette they were shown first. For illustration, a screenshot of the $40 incentive vignette question is shown in Figure 1 (the other group would see the same question but with “$5” instead). The respondent could choose to receive cash, digital gift card, physical gift card, check, or electronic bank transfer, or decline payment. Note that incentive options include how the incentive would be delivered, in case that is a factor in the respondent’s decision. The survey length of an hour is included in the vignette to encourage respondents to take a payment for their time (and to avoid confusion about receiving an incentive for the shorter survey they were currently answering). After answering about either $40 or $5 (depending on their group), they were asked if their answer would change for the other incentive amount. If yes, they were asked their preference for the new amount.

The analysis found that although people carry cash, they are not using it often. Also, those who do use it often have different characteristics than those carrying it often. Promised cash incentives were preferred by only 5% of respondents, with digital gift cards and electronic bank transfers being most popular. Of those who wanted to receive a cash incentive, they were more likely to be young (19- 35 years old), not have a college degree, be low-income (<$35,000), and use cash often. Analysis of the propensity scores for different demographic groups revealed that having a low income was the most consistent factor. The incentive options provided to respondents in the vignette were all forms of monetary payment, with only one option being physical dollar bills (i.e., cash). Therefore, this study provides clarification as to respondent preferences for receiving monetary incentives. Cash, in the form of dollars, is not king but digital money is appealing (i.e., digital gift cards and bank transfers). It seems that the mantra should be updated to, “Digital cash is king”, at least for promised incentives. References Birnholtz, Jeremy P., Daniel B. Horn, Thomas A. Finholt, and Sung Joo Bae. 2004. 1-1 1. Executive Summary The Current Population Survey (CPS) is an important source of data on U.S. employment and unemployment. Collected once a year within the CPS is the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC). ASEC collects data on income sources and amounts, participation in various economic support programs, health insurance, medical expenditures, child care, and moving. ASEC data support the creation of the Supplemental Poverty Measure and thus, are critically important to a broad array of data users. In an effort to decrease costs while maintaining data quality, the Census Bureau set a goal to develop an internet self-administered (web) version of ASEC. A web version of this questionnaire presents many challenges, particularly with regards to respondent burden and data quality. To support the development of revised and new questions for web- administration of the ASEC instrument, RTI International and Research Support Services (RSS), previously conducted 60 one-on-one cognitive interviews, separately testing the health insurance and income sections of the instrument. This report details a second round of cognitive testing with similar methodology to further refine and revise the questions. The cognitive interviews focused on participants’ interpretation of the questions and response options, and the accuracy of their response. The testing aimed to identify possible issues that may hinder a respondent’s ability to select an answer, and gather feedback that can be used to revise the questions prior to fielding. There were several cross-cutting findings and associated recommendations that came from this research, which are summarized below: Health Insurance Module • As a result of prior exploratory and cognitive testing, questions where participants had trouble interpreting items or response options as intended were modified to include clarifications and examples. Although these generally worked well, for some participants the parenthetical examples or qualifications proved somewhat confusing. This was the case, for instance, in a question asking about type of insurance coverage where a response option read, “Medicare (including Part B, or any Advantage or Supplemental plan).” • Another issue was found with a term that performed well for most participants but was not understood by one: “uninsured.” This was a finding in the question “Were you uninsured for part of 2024?” Although this appeared not to be a common problem, the data the question elicits are very important and it is crucial to have everyone understand and answer this item as intended. • The response choice “Private health insurance not through a job” presented some difficulties. Some participants reporting coverage from “the Marketplace” or from “Obamacare” did not think this response applied to them. A participant without a job thought this option could not apply to them because it mentioned a job, which they did not have.

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 1-2 • Medical out of pocket expenses: An important issue remains in the Medical Out of Pocket Expenses section with possible double reporting of certain expenses between the question about coverage costs and other out of pocket costs. The transition sentence into this topic is necessary, but it could be simplified. In its current form it may be contributing to the double counting. Migration Module • Reference dates: The version of the item tested in this round did not include a reference date, and some participants were unsure about the reference period the question was asking about. Although most participants were able to interpret and answer the question without the inclusion of a reference date, a couple of participants either had trouble with recall or expressed they would have found the inclusion of a reference period date helpful. • Reasons for move: For the ‘reasons for move’ migration questions, findings suggest that the list of response choices should be reviewed to identify any possible reductions and clarifications, as participants often found the list dauntingly long and some had difficulty selecting the option that best fit their situation. In addition, for those items that include the “No other reason” response choice, consider more prominently displaying this option through emphasis or spacing the response option to make it stand out. Income Module • Proxy reporting: Almost half of the participants in Round 2 indicated that they did not know the answer to a question at some point during the ‘income sources’ section of the interview when considering others in their household. This finding was also seen in Round 1. To address this, the response option “Someone in the household got [INCOME SOURCE], but I’m not sure what type” was added to items in this section. In Round 2 of testing, this response option was rarely used when participants were uncertain about income sources of others in their household, so it did not aid in their response process. • Double reporting instruction: Round 1 of interviewing found that double reporting was a common problem, which was not an issue found in Round 2. To address the issue of double reporting found in Round 1, several items in the ‘income sources’ section included the instruction “Do not include anything you already reported.” This instruction does appear to be helpful on some items (e.g., when an income source is likely to have been reported in a previous question) and appears to have addressed earlier issues with double reporting. However, this instruction is repeated on all items and, overall, participants found this instruction to be confusing and repetitive, especially when they were asked about an income source they had not been previously asked about in a prior question (e.g., unemployment). A few participants also interpreted this instruction to refer to reporting on taxes, which introduced additional confusion for them.

2-1 2. Introduction This report details the results of 60 cognitive interviews that were conducted during the second round of cognitive testing for the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC). The instrument and tests were divided into two sections, broadly categorized as “health insurance” and “income”, with 30 interviews for each topic. The health insurance instrument included questions about health insurance coverage, medical out of pocket expenses, and moving (migration). The income instrument included questions about earned income, income sources and amounts, poverty (program participation), housing, child care, and child support. This section also included questions on moving (migration) when time allowed. Interviews were conducted by RTI International (RTI) and Research Support Services (RSS). Cognitive testing consists of one-on-one in-person interviews to assess a questionnaire in terms of general comprehension, clarity and completeness of question and response wording, effectiveness of skip logic, and availability of help information. Census Bureau provided two separate and distinct cognitive protocols: one for health insurance and one for income. All protocols included the full set of questions tested in each interview, concurrent and retrospective probes for most questions, designation of the motivation for testing the question, and the desired output to be reported for each. Interviews were designed to take no more than 60 minutes. The Census Bureau developed PowerPoint slide decks for each questionnaire that included jump-to navigation features to facilitate virtual interviewing. All interviews were conducted remotely and were recorded by interviewers. Following each interview, participants were provided with a $40 Visa digital gift card as a token of appreciation for completing the interview. Participants were recruited and selected based on pre-established targets/quotas approved by the Census Bureau. All efforts were made to reach these targets while providing an even distribution among demographic characteristics such as sex, age, education, race/ethnicity, and household composition, among other criteria. The RTI and RSS team used a systematic approach to analyze the cognitive interview data and address the research questions. Once the data were organized and analyzed, the teams wrote up their findings in a standardized format, including question-level responses from participants, key findings grouped by ‘report back’ questions provided by the Census Bureau, a summary of any overarching findings (where applicable), and recommendations for questions where issues were identified. These details provided the basis of this report.

3-1 3. Cognitive Methodology This section provides details about the cognitive methodology, protocols, and procedures that were used during the ASEC health insurance and income cognitive interviews. 3.1 Methodology The cognitive testing consisted of (virtual) one-on-one in-person interviews to assess the questionnaire in terms of general comprehension, clarity of question and response wording, effectiveness of skip logic, and visual aids. The goal was to gain an understanding of how well the questions work when administered to a sample of the survey’s target population. The interviews followed a protocol with pre-scripted probes, administered either concurrently (i.e., directly after the question was answered) or retroactively (after a section of questions were completed), depending on the module. Cognitive interviewers also used spontaneous probes to gain a better understanding of participant feedback, when needed. Cognitive interviewing was used to: • Learn about the respondents’ thought processes while answering the questions; • Measure the response process, including comprehension, retrieval, judgment, and response; • Observe nonverbal, human reactions; • Test navigation of the instrument; • Assess the potential for measurement error in survey items; • Examine potentially big or complex issues; and • Gauge opinions on the survey as a whole. 3.2 Protocol Census Bureau developed two separate and distinct protocols that focused on each of the two topic areas being explored in this study: one for health insurance (Appendix D) and one for income (Appendix E). Additionally, questions on migration were included as part of both protocols. RTI/RSS provided input and reviewed each protocol. Both protocols included the full set of questions included in each interview, along with probes on a subset of questions. Interviewers were instructed and trained to collect spontaneous feedback as needed. Census Bureau developed a series of PowerPoint slide decks for each section of the health insurance and income instruments to facilitate virtual interviewing. Slide decks included with jump-to navigation programmed on question response options that allowed the interviewer to skip to the next appropriate slide in route to that response option. During the interview, interviewers shared their screen of the slide deck and asked participants to respond to the

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 3-2 questions shown on screen. Interviewers then ‘selected’ responses for the participant and navigated the slide deck instrument forward during the interview. 3.3 Interviews All interviews were conducted remotely from June 11, 2025, through September 15, 2025, using Microsoft Teams within Census Bureau’s secure Virtual Desktop Interface (VDI) environment or a Census Bureau issued laptop. Participants were assigned to either the health insurance protocol or the income protocol, depending on characteristics reported during screening. Questions on migration were included in both protocols. With permission from participants, interviewers audio recorded all sessions using handheld devices. Interviews were also recorded using Snagit software, which records both audio and video. Recordings were saved to the designated deliverable folder in the Census Bureau file share location. At the end of the interview, interviewers offered participants a $40 Visa digital gift card code via email as a thank you for their time. Following each interview, interviewers or notetakers completed the appropriate case summary template for the topic area (i.e., health insurance or income). Although the two protocols and respondent-facing instruments differed, each interview was conducted in the following sequence to standardize implementation. The interviewer: • Explained the purpose of the study. • Confirmed the participant had reviewed and signed the online consent form to participate in the study and be audio/video recorded (Appendix C). • Started audio recording using an external audio recorder and Snagit software. • Reconfirmed verbal consent to participate and be recorded once recording has started. • Shared the respondent-facing instrument and asked participants to answer ASEC questions shown on screen. • Administered probes to ASEC questions. • Concluded the interview and sent the participant the incentive. • Saved the recording within the Census Bureau’s secure network environment in the designated file share folder. • Completed the interview summary and saved it in the designated file share folder no more than 5 business days following each interview. Before conducting cognitive interviews, all RTI/RSS interviewers were trained by Census Bureau on protocols for each topic area (i.e., health insurance or income) and other key procedures, including Title 13 requirements. Because each topic area used different protocols, two interviewer training sessions were held: one that focused on the health insurance protocol and one that focused on the income protocol. Due to the length and complexity of the interviews, all interviewers also completed a recorded practice interview before beginning interviews with participants. This practice interview was reviewed by RTI’s

Section 3 – Cognitive Methodology 3-3 lead researcher, and feedback was provided to interviewers directly to prepare them for the main interviews. 3.4 Analysis The RTI and RSS team used a systematic process to analyze the cognitive interview data and address the research questions. The case summaries were combined in Excel to provide a thorough data set for analysis, with participants presented in each row and interview probes presented in each column. Both teams analyzed data and wrote up their findings in a standardized format, including responses from participants, key findings, a summary of general findings (where applicable), and recommendations for questions that presented issues.

4-1 4. Participant Recruitment This section provides an overview of participant recruitment strategies used to screen and select participants for the second round of ASEC income and health insurance cognitive interviews. This section includes 1) an overview of recruitment strategies across both the income and health insurance tasks and 2) targets and participant characteristics. The RTI/RSS team recruited participants from June through September 2025. The income recruitment began by leveraging the participant recruitment for the Current Population Survey (CPS) usability testing conducted from June through August 2024. First, the RTI/RSS team identified 151 prospective participants who were selected based on their eligibility for the CPS usability testing but were left uncontacted for participation. The team emailed each, inviting them to complete the ASEC online screener to determine their eligibility for ASEC cognitive interviews based on their demographics and current employment status. Following this outreach, the RTI/RSS team identified numerous metropolitan areas across all four Census regions for recruitment: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; Houstin, Texas; Toledo, Ohio; Albuquerque, New Mexico; Detroit, Michigan; Charleston, West Virginia; Cleveland, Ohio; New Orleans, Louisiana; Phoenix, Arizona; Cincinnati, Ohio; Grand Rapids, Michigan; Kansas City, Missouri; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; Portland, Maine; Tucson, Arizona; Baltimore, Maryland; Boston, Massachusetts; Chicago, Illinois; Florida Keys, Florida; Las Vegas, Nevada; New Haven, Connecticut; San Diego, California; St. Louis, Missouri; Indianapolis, Indianna; Jacksonville, Florida; Providence, Rhode Island; Sante Fe, New Mexico; Milwaukee, Wisconsin; Omaha, Nebraska; Scranton, Pennsylvania; and Worcester, Massachusetts. The RTI/RSS team then posted online recruitment advertisements in these selected metropolitan areas, releasing advertisements on a rolling basis to maintain a steady stream of prospective participants for screening and scheduling. The team also conducted word-of-mouth outreach with the staff’s personal networks specifically screening for individuals with the rarer primary characteristics that were underrepresented after approximately 8 weeks of data collection. The additional effort helped improved our recruitment outcomes with those who live alone or with unrelated individuals and those who are self-employed. The Census Bureau programmed a web-based eligibility screening in Qualtrics. The RTI/RSS team also established a toll-free telephone line dedicated to recruitment purposes. The web link for the screening instrument and the toll-free phone number were presented in the online advertisements (see Appendix A). During the data collection period, the RTI/RSS team provided the Census Bureau with a weekly recruitment and interviewing progress update report, reflecting results to date. The weekly report tallied the interview participants with respect to recruitment goals and needed

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 4-2 sub-characteristics. The results of ASEC cognitive interview recruitment presented in Sections 4.3 and 4.4 of this report reflect the final recruitment outcomes. 4.1 Implementation of Recruitment Advertising For the main online recruitment strategy, the RTI/RSS team used Craigslist as the primary venue for recruitment advertising. Craigslist is one of the best-known online bulletin boards and provides the most comprehensive coverage of metropolitan areas in the United States. To leverage Craigslist’s broad reach, RTI/RSS did not use targeted advertisements that focused on specific characteristics and used a customized general advertisement instead (see Appendix B for recruitment materials and advertisement text). The first round of monthly paid advertising started on May 22, 2025. The sixth and final round of general advertising was posted for Milwaukee, Wisconsin; Omaha, Nebraska; Scranton, Pennsylvania; and Worcester, Massachusetts on August 20, 2025. 4.1.1 Participant Selection Strategy To facilitate efficient screening review and participant selection across subprojects, the team created a main intake tracker sheet to import the screening responses from Qualtrics. Interested participants were reviewed to ensure they met the main eligibility criteria (e.g., Age 18+) and one or more of the recruitment criteria (outlined in the Exhibits). Participant screening responses were reviewed to determine whether they fit within one or more of the quotas that were established. Next, the team reviewed all prospective participants on the intake sheet, focusing on contact information self-reports and the IP addresses in the paradata. RTI removed duplicate entries from the same individuals, any entries identified as past participants, ineligible entries from foreign IP addresses, and any potentially fraudulent cases that were identified during recruitment (e.g., IP addresses did not match city/state the respondent reported in screener). The RTI/RSS team determined protocol assignment (e.g., Health Insurance or Income) and participant selection priority. Within the main intake spreadsheet, the ASEC Health Insurance recruitment tracker and ASEC Income recruitment tracker were separated to account for different criteria and separate recruitment efforts. The lead recruiter reviewed the participants to ensure key quotas were fulfilled and selected participants for the RTI/RSS recruiters to contact. During data collection, RTI/RSS team processed and reviewed the screening data at least once a week to select eligible participants for an interview. After a batch of screening data was reviewed, about 1 week would elapse before new assignments would be made to allow recruiters sufficient time to contact their existing assignments. Team members contacted participants and scheduled interviews, sending a confirmation email with all the information needed to take part in the remote interview. Because access to Qualtrics was lost in June 2025, the RTI team front-loaded recruitment efforts as a way to build an ample screener sample to draw from later in the interviewing period. To retain participants who screened into the study early in the data collection period but would not be invited to participate in an interview until later in the data collection time frame, RTI/RSS sent email communication in June 2025 letting them know that they could expect to hear from a recruiter in July or August.

Findings in this section are presented by topic, with findings from the cognitive interviews listed first followed by recommendations. Each question is formatted with the following elements: • Question text and response options that were shown to the participants during cognitive interviewing. The goal of cognitive interviewing is to collect qualitative feedback from participants about their response process when providing an answer to each question. We have included a report of the responses to each question (i.e., the quantitative data) to provide context for the findings. Health insurance may include insurance through a job, Medicaid, Medicare, or insurance purchased from healthcare.gov. 1 Yes (29) 2 No (1) 3 No response (0) Findings: No probes were administered for this question. • Of the 30 participants, 29 answered without any issues. A second participant initially answered “No” to the question about additional insurance; however, they recalled previously mentioning their Veterans Affairs (VA) insurance and corrected their response to “Yes.” Because the participant had referenced VA insurance earlier (Q2) but appeared confused when asked again, the interviewer probed further to determine if it was confusing to be asked about it again.
