6-1 6. Question by Question Results – Migration This section outlines findings from the migration module. We first present findings for the 1- year and 5-year migration questions, followed by findings from associated ‘reason for moving’ items. Globally, we recommend filling the reference date (1 or 5 years ago today, as relevant) on questions to orient respondents to past time periods without negatively impacting others’ response process. In MIGPLC1, for example, a participant asked the interviewer to remind them what month it is right now to help them figure out the start of the reference period so they could think back to last year at this time. This request for clarification indicates that the respondent was seeking to benchmark their response within the reference period. This finding and subsequent recommendations are discussed in more detail in this section (see MIGSTAT1). MIGSTAT1 (n=36) Were you living at your current residence 1 year ago today? 1 Yes (28) 2 No (8) Findings: How many respondents found this question challenging, confusing, or potentially ambiguous? • Generally, this question was not challenging or confusing to participants. However, of the 36 participants who received this question and were probed, 9 said they would prefer the question to include the exact date fill from “1 year ago today.” The lack of a reference date was the primary source of confusion for respondents. When asked if it would be helpful to include the reference date in the question, 9 participants said it did not matter or did not express a clear preference, and 22 preferred to leave the question as tested (i.e., version presented above). (Totals do not add up to 36 as some answers were coded in two categories). What did the respondents who found this question to be challenging, confusing, or potentially ambiguous actually find to be challenging, confusing, or potentially ambiguous (and why they found that to be the case)? • Of the nine participants who would prefer to have the date filled, seven had a general preference for inclusion because it would be more specific, or because the specificity might help others, but did not express difficulty answering with the original wording. However, two participants indicated that having a date would help them with recall, and in one case, change their answer. • On participant [P3515], who had a history of homelessness, stated a specific date would have aided their memory of where they were residing at the time. When probed if they knew exactly where they were living last year, they stated: “Um,

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 6-2 no. I actually don’t. No. I might have been either homeless or staying with someone, or I wouldn’t say, yeah, I wouldn’t know. I wouldn’t know for sure. I don’t know.” On further probing as to whether having a date helps them think back, the participant confirmed: “Yeah, it makes me think back. It’s easier to recall.” • Another participant [P3667], who had last moved in March 2024 but was interviewed in July 2025, answered “No” to MIGSTAT1. Probing revealed this answer to be incorrect. When probed as to whether they would prefer the date being listed in the question, they said it would have been “easy,” and “My attention was on the beginning of the last year.” They said that having the date “would make a very big difference.” This participant should have answered “Yes” to MIGSTAT1, but they answered “No” because they were thinking about early 2024 instead of exactly 1 year ago. • Another participant [P3246], who preferred to keep the wording as is, thought it would be harder to remember the specific date: “Some people might not be able to remember exactly from a year from now, that’s just more simpler [sic].” • Notably, one participant [P3665], who reported living at their current residence 1 year ago, stated they didn’t prefer whether the question wording included the date or not but thought that changing the wording to a specific date would change the meaning of the question: “Maybe I actually went for a business trip, and I was not actually home that particular month.” This participant may have misunderstood what was meant by the phrase “living at,” and interpreted it to mean “staying at,” such as where they were sleeping when they were traveling. Because this issue only arose upon probing and no similar confusion arose during Round 1 of testing, we consider this to be rare. Recommendations: (Any suggestions for improvement that ensued, either directly from respondents or interpretationally via report writers) During Round 1 there was some confusion about the date that was filled on screen, but this was because the date was static and did not align with the actual reference date at the time of the interview. In this round of cognitive testing, the question did not include a reference date. Most participants were able to interpret and answer the question without the inclusion of a reference date; however, some participants’ experience suggests that including a specific reference date could reduce measurement error. Presenting the reference date below the question may aid the recall of respondents who may have moved at or around the time of the reference date, or who are transient (e.g., Date 1 year ago: February 3, 2025). Although this specific presentation was not tested in the current round of cognitive interviews, similar formats that display fills below questions were tested in the Health Insurance module and performed well. Based on those findings, we expect this format to function well and should address the few issues we found with recall and comprehension (due to lack of reference period) observed in this round. We also recommend including this item in a future round of cognitive testing to assess performance.

Because there aren’t 50 United States, there’s only one United States.… I’m sure most people don’t get worried about the grammar.… There aren’t 50 United States.…” ○ P3444 said: “Yeah, the Washington, D.C., threw me off.…It should say, ‘Were you living in any of the 50 states?’” [PROBE: What about that Washington, D.C. part? 7-1 7. Question by Question Results – Income This section presents results and recommendations, where appropriate, for ASEC Income questions. Findings in this section are presented by topic, with findings from the cognitive interviews listed first followed by recommendations. Each question is formatted with the following elements: • Question text and response options that were shown to the participants during cognitive interviewing. Each question is followed by the total number and the counts for each response option. • Summary findings, where applicable (e.g., questions that included significant or overarching findings or recommendations). • Findings grouped by and detailing the answers to key research questions provided by Census Bureau (i.e., from the report back templates). • Recommendations for question changes, when appropriate. The goal of cognitive interviewing is to collect qualitative feedback from participants about their response process when providing an answer to each question. We have included a report of the responses to each question (i.e., the quantitative data) to provide context for the findings. This response data comes from the response recorded in the notes during the interview. Participants are not required to provide an answer, and thus the total sample who saw the question (“n”) may differ from the total number of responses in some cases. 7.1 Employment (I&O) Questions Q29a (n=30) Did [you/^name] do any work for pay or profit at any time during 2024, even for one day? 1 Yes (25) 2 No (5) Findings: There were no specific probes for this question. • Two participants, who worked odd jobs/side gig work, were initially uncertain whether odd jobs should be considered as “for pay or profit.” Both participants ultimately selected “Yes.” • One participant noted they are retired but they earn extra money doing surveys, mock jury trials, and gambling studies. This participant answered “Yes” after giving it some thought. • One participant initially was uncertain as to whether he should answer “Yes” to this question. This participant explained: ○ “I don’t get a paycheck.… I work under the table as they used to call it. I don’t know what they call it these days, but I work for cash for different

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 7-2 places.” The participant was unsure if this should count as “work for pay or profit” but decided that he would say “Yes” to this question. (P3313) Recommendations: No change recommended. Q29b (n=4) Did you do any temporary, part-time, or seasonal work, even for one day during 2024? 1 Yes (0) 2 No (4) Findings: Did respondents include any Military Reserves or National Guard work? • No participants were in the Military Reserves or National Guard, so we could not determine whether participants considered this as work when responding to the question. • None of the four participants who received this question answered “Yes.” Recommendations: No change recommended. Q30 (n=5) Did you spend any time trying to find a job or on a temporary layoff during 2024? 1 Yes (0) 2 No (5) Findings: How did respondents interpret “on temporary layoff”; what does the term “on layoff” mean to them? • All participants interpreted “temporary layoff” to mean the employer could bring you back at another time. • However, when asked specifically what “On layoff” meant (n=5), three participants thought it meant the same as temporary layoff, while another two thought it meant that you were permanently cut from your position or that the company has “let you go.” Recommendations: No change recommended. If not, did the additional text next to the response box help? • The participants all read the instruction, but several (n=8) felt that it did not apply to them as they do not take vacations or get sick. • Other participant(s) (n=4) mentioned that their job was part time and that they do not receive paid vacations. • One self-employed/1099 employee felt the qualifying statement did not apply to them as they do not receive “paid vacations or sick leave” like those who work for an employer. Section 7 – Question by Question Results – Income 7-5 • Another participant wasn’t sure how long she was on unemployment and whether this should be included or not. ○ She explained, “I think the part I am not totally clear on is the paid leave portion.” This participant explained that if this had an instruction to NOT include unemployment, she would have answered differently. This participant answered “All 52 weeks,” which included her unemployment. [P3172] Did respondents follow the instruction to count any work at all during the week as a full week of work? For example, if they lost their job on a Monday, that’s a week of work. • Some participants (n=4) found it a little burdensome to calculate the response as they worked part-time in 2024. However, they ultimately provided a response as they counted weeks that they worked, even if only a few hours. • Another participant excluded weeks where they did not work a full week as they would not consider working 1 or 2 days a week as a “week worked.” ○ This participant explained, “For somebody working part-time, these questions are a little … they’re not necessarily straightforward for how you answer them and is going to be a little mentally challenging on the math on this.” This participant said that at his last week in the first job, he got laid off midway through the week and didn’t work that full week, but he tried to accurately estimate the number of weeks he worked there the best he could. The interviewer clarified that if you only worked 1‒2 days in a week, would they consider this a whole week worked. The participant responded that they would not consider that a whole week. [P4958] • Most participants followed the instructions and counted any work completed in a week as a full week of work. Recommendations: Overall, the question performed well but may benefit from additional testing and revision to determine what changes might be helpful for respondents who may not consider or count partial worked weeks (e.g., 1‒2 days) when responding to the question. For example, a version of the question that revises the label to “weeks of any work...” or just “weeks” could be tested to determine if this would address issues with respondents who wanted to report only “full” weeks of work. We also recommend considering a more robust instruction on this item to count any weeks of work at all, even if less than a standard week or only a few hours were worked in that week. For example: Count any weeks of work as a full week, even if only for a few hours during that week. A new question could also be considered prior to this item that states: Did you work every week in 2025, even if only for a few hours certain weeks? This item would also include an instruction about paid leave and expanded instructions

Section 7 – Question by Question Results – Income 7-23 Findings: For those who reported multiple sources in the preceding question, how did they think about combining these different sources on the fly? Was it difficult for them? Would it have been easier if any items were broken out separately? • Eight participants reported multiple types of income on EMP_INC_TYP. There were four participants who reported multiple types of income on EMP_INC_TYP but were not asked this probe and it is unclear if they thought this was easy or difficult. • Of the participants who were asked this probe, all but one had multiple jobs/employers in 2024. Some of these participants expressed difficulty with answering this question, but their difficulty was not in combining income sources or types. Instead, they struggled with deciding whether they should be reporting income from one or all jobs in 2024 (see “Other findings” below). However, these participants knew their monthly or gross income for each job and could calculate an estimated answer. • Other participants (n=3) said this question was difficult to answer: ○ One participant, who received salary or wages, bonuses, overtime pay, and commissions, opened an ADP payroll app and found the answer. They noted that without the app, it would have been “impossible” to calculate this himself. ○ One participant preferred to report income separately for each source. This participant added her monthly income across all jobs and then multiplied by 12 to arrive at the answer. ○ One participant wanted to have the option of reporting income by year, week, or month, as a salary would be easier to report annually but other sources of income like bonuses or overtime pay would be easier to report by week or month. If earnings are variable (e.g., different each month), is there an easier way for them to report info to allow an annual amount to be determined? • Seven participants said that their earnings varied each paycheck. • Of the four participants who were asked if they would prefer to report for a different time period, all said that it was easier to report their annual income than for another time frame because other time frames would be more time consuming to calculate. For example: “Some people know exactly how much they get paid each pay period, but if you’re in a variable situation, it’s not gonna be the same, so I would just keep it at the annual level.” (P4766) Was the instruction to provide their best estimate helpful? What does “best estimate” mean to respondents? • Most participants said that this instruction to provide their best estimate was helpful, explaining that it was encouraging to them that they did not have to provide a precise answer. ○ “Yes, because, you know, I was trying to do quick math in my head.” (P4302) ○ “Best estimate is letting people round it off.” (P4613)

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 7-24 • Two participants said they would have given an estimate even without the inclusion of the instruction. ○ “I would give my best estimate anyway because I wouldn’t remember anyway, the exact figure unless I grabbed ahold of my tax, um my tax folder, that my CPA has prepared.… I’m used to government forms or questions like these where they want your best estimate. I just assume that’s what they want.” (P5339) • Two participants said they would prefer that this instruction was placed immediately after the question stem, as it was displayed underneath the bullet points of income sources and therefore was easy to miss. • The meaning of “best estimate” was not specifically probed. Other findings: • Some participants with multiple jobs in 2024 mentioned that this question was confusing because it said “this employer” and they were not sure which employer they were being asked about. • One participant gave the answer for their annual salary, but during probing, realized that they retired in September 2024 and changed their answer to account for this. • One participant gets paid hourly and said that it is difficult to calculate annual income for an hourly worker and that this question is designed for a salaried worker. Recommendations: Recommend further testing of this item to determine the extent that participants who have multiple types of income have difficulty reporting. Similar to EMP_INC_TYP, although participants with multiple jobs differed in whether they thought about their main job or all jobs in 2024, using “(^your/their) employer” appeared to be the primary source of confusion and may have been a limitation of testing. We recommend using a fill for the employer name in production (e.g., Employer: [FILL]). Section 7 – Question by Question Results – Income 7-27 Were the concepts of positive earnings or loss ones that respondents were familiar with? Were there other words they might use to describe earnings being greater than expenses or earnings being less than expenses? • All participants except for one said that these phrases were clear and were terms that they are familiar with. ○ Only one participant was not as familiar with these terms; however, this participant chose their employment type as self-employed because they are a contractor, but they do not consider themselves self-employed. Did respondents know this information at an annual level or would they have preferred to report a lower periodicity (monthly, quarterly)? • All participants said that it was easy to report this information at an annual level. • Three participants noted that while answering at an annual level was easy for them, it might be easier for others to report a lower periodicity. They, however, did not have a preference themselves. • Three participants preferred to report at an annual level. • One participant would prefer to report at a quarterly level: “Ideally, yes, it would be better quarterly. Because of the holidays, there are times when people are spending less throughout the year.” (P4152) How did respondents think about variable earnings or expenses (e.g., different every month or quarter) when answering this question? • No data to report. This was not specifically probed. Other findings: • Two participants were confused by the visual formatting of this question. One participant thought that they needed to choose one of the types of income in the bullet points in addition to selecting an answer for positive/even/loss. The other participant thought it was asking them for the same information as the previous question, before seeing the response options of positive/even/loss. ○ This finding might not be an issue in the field, if there is better visual differentiation between bullet points and choosable response options. Further, due to the limitations of testing, we were not able to fill the income types listed in the previous question. As this question will not list all income types in the field, this finding may not be relevant. However, we should monitor this in usability testing. Recommendations: As noted above, none of these participants owned their own businesses and were all contractors or freelance workers. Therefore, the way that this question is phrased (i.e., comparing earnings to expenses) wasn’t applicable to their employment situation. SMEs should ensure that the skip logic for this question is being asked of the correct population.

For example, when asked if it was easy or difficult to answer a question on behalf of others in their household, one participant explained: ▪ “Oh, extremely difficult. I know nothing of their business. I don’t know if they have one cent to their name or if they have millions of dollars to their name. I know nothing, they tell me nothing, they’re not gonna tell me nothing…. They’re just other renters.” (P5339) ○ Seven of these participants live with family. For these participants, they could answer most questions for others in their household but came across at least one question where they did not know the answer for others. The questions

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 7-32 they did not know the answer to were mostly questions that required more of a specific knowledge of someone’s finances (e.g., interest-earning accounts, annuities, dividends). The “Someone in the household got [INCOME SOURCE], but I’m not sure what type” response option was rarely used when participants were uncertain about income sources of others in their household (see distributions for each question below). Choosing this response option would indicate that the respondent confidently knows that someone else in their household received income from this source, but that they just did not know the type of income received. However, for the participants described above, most were not confident or had no idea if others in their household received that income source at all. Therefore, this response option was not appropriate for them to indicate that they didn’t know the answer for others in their household. We recommend rewording this response option on all questions as follows: I am not sure if someone else in the household received [INCOME SOURCE], or I am not sure what type they received. 2. “Do not include anything you already reported” instruction This instruction was added to all income source questions following the findings from Round 1, where some participants were reporting the same income source on multiple questions. • Overall, participants found this instruction to be confusing and repetitive, especially when they were asked about an income source they had not been previously asked about in a prior question (e.g., unemployment). • A few participants interpreted this instruction to refer to reporting on taxes, which was also confusing to them. • In general, we recommend including this instruction only when relevant (i.e., when an income source is likely to have been reported on a previous question). We have listed this recommendation where applicable in each associated question below. However, we note that for some questions, this instruction is helpful and important to keep if respondents are likely to “double report.” We have noted this where applicable in each section below. Do not include WIC or TANF. 1 Yes (4) 2 No (7) Findings: Did respondents notice the “even for one month” instruction? • All participants confirmed that they noticed the instruction, “even for one month.” Only one participant (P4958) provided an additional comment. This participant questioned why food stamps are called the more complicated “Supplemental Nutrition” program name. Did they understand that all these programs refer to the same thing? • Of the 10 participants who received this probe, more than half (n=6) did not understand that SNAP, the Food Stamp program, and the state assistance program referred to the same thing. • Four participants reported that SNAP, the Food Stamp program, and the state assistance program are the same thing. Of these participants, one participant (P3128) endorsed receiving benefits from a food assistance program for at least 1 month in 2024. • Four other participants reported that SNAP, the Food Stamp program, and the state assistance program are different programs. Of these participants, three (P5215, P4206, P4896) endorsed receiving benefits from a food assistance program for at least 1 month in 2024. ○ One participant (P5215) noted that these are different programs with different paperwork. ○ Another participant (P4896) shared that “state assistance program” is a vague statement considering there are a lot of state assistance programs, including SNAP, which is a specific state assistance program. • Two participants, who both did not endorse receiving benefits from a food assistance program for at least 1 month in 2024, expressed uncertainty. One participant (P3373) explicitly stated they did not know. The other participant (P4958) stated “to me, it’s the same thing, but I don’t know if it is exactly the same thing or not.… I don’t know if the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program is different from the Food Stamp benefit card.”

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 7-64 Did they find the presence of the state card fill helpful or confusing? • Of the three participants who received this probe, no one mentioned the presence of the state card fill to be confusing and two participants (P3128, P3373) thought the presence of the state card fill was helpful. Of these, one participant (P3128) reported the programs in the question stem are the same thing, whereas the other participant (P3373) reported not knowing if the programs are the same or different. • The other participant (P3269) who stated the presence of the state card fill was not helpful also reported that they believe the question stem referred to different programs. If they didn’t know what WIC or TANF were, did they try to access the help text? • Four participants (P3128, P3373, P4958, P5215) expressed uncertainty about TANF specifically. Three of these participants acknowledged the help link and understood this survey feature would display additional information about WIC and TANF. For example, one participant explained, “If you click it, it will tell you what WIC is and what the other one [TANF] is.” (P3128) Recommendations: Although participants who received SNAP_YN did not express any difficulties with selecting a response, many participants—including those who endorsed receiving benefits from a food assistance program—did not understand that SNAP, the Food Stamp program, and the state assistance program or a SNAP, food stamp, or state benefit card all refer to the same thing. It is unclear if providing a list of everything a participant may identify as the food assistance program received is causing participants to doubt their understanding of these programs. This item is also positioned toward the latter half of the interview, directly following detailed employment and income items that required great cognitive effort from participants. It is unclear if participant fatigue, or something else, impacted participant understanding that all food assistance programs included in the question stem are referring to the same thing. SMEs should consider revising the question stem to reduce the level of cognitive effort required from participants to provide a response. Consider the following revision: The next questions are about food assistance programs. [NEW HELP LINK] At any time during 2024, EVEN FOR ONE MONTH, did anyone in this household receive benefits from a food assistance program such as SNAP? Do not include WIC or TANF. [EXISTING HELP LINK] If the question stem is simplified, information about the specific food assistance programs should be added to a help link message that participants may access if needed. Specifically, the help message would be revised to include the information about SNAP, the Food Stamp program, and the state assistance program as well as the SNAP, food stamp, and state benefit card.

8-1 8. Conclusions and Overall Recommendations The following section presents global findings and resulting recommendations for issues that impact multiple ASEC Income and Health Insurance questions. We provide several considerations to improve the questions prior to the conduct of any additional testing or fielding. 8.1 Health Insurance 8.1.1 Parenthetical Examples and Other Terminology As a result of previous exploratory interviews and cognitive testing of the Health Insurance module, questions where participants had trouble interpreting items or response options as intended were modified to include clarifications in parentheses. Although these generally worked well, for some participants the parenthetical examples or qualifications proved somewhat confusing. In light of the findings outlined in this report, we recommend that this section be reviewed to see whether all the clarifications are needed, and if it is best to keep them in parentheses or make them part of the question stems. We also offer specific item- level recommendations for revising examples in Section 5.1. The term “uninsured” was also not fully understood by some. Although no issues were found in Round 1 cognitive testing with the term “uninsured” and participants were split in their preference of “uninsured” or “without insurance,” and despite the small evidence that the term “uninsured” could possibly be problematic, we recommend rewording as “Were you without health insurance at any point in 2024?” This is important data and this change will ensure clarity for everyone. 8.1.2 Medical Out of Pocket Expenses An important issue remains in this section with possible double reporting of certain expenses between MOOP_PREM and MOOP_NONPREM. The transition sentence into this topic is necessary, but in its current form it may be contributing to the double counting. We recommend the wording be simplified as an introduction only as follows: The next questions are about what your household paid for health costs in 2024. Then, prefacing the MOOP_PREM question with “First…” may make it clearer to the participant that this question is just about the amount spent on premiums. As further assurance that respondents will not double report expenses, MOOP_NONPREM could be reworded as: Not counting any amount reported in the last question, in 2024, how much did your household pay out-of-pocket for medical care and other nonprescription medical expenses?

ASEC Cognitive Interviews 8-2 8.2 Migration 8.2.1 Reference Periods The lack of a clearly stated reference date appeared to be the primary source of confusion for respondents on 1-year and 5-year move items. Presenting the reference date below the question may reduce measurement error and aid the recall of respondents who may have moved at or around the time of the reference date, or who are transient. We recommend filling the date (i.e., 1 year ago; 5 years ago) below the question (e.g., Date 1 year ago: February 3, 2025). Although this specific presentation was not tested in this round of cognitive interviews, similar formats that displayed fills below question text were tested in the Health Insurance module (e.g., Q15job or 15m as presented in slide 19 in Appendix D) and performed well. We also recommend retesting this format in future rounds of cognitive testing to assess performance. 8.2.2 Reasons for Moving The questions on reasons for move should be reviewed to identify any possible reductions and clarifications of response choices, as participants often found the list dauntingly long and some had difficulty deciding what option best fit their reason for moving. In addition, for those items that include the “No other reason” response choice, this should be more prominently displayed, through the use of highlighting or by separating the line to make it stand out more. 8.3 Income 8.3.1 Proxy Reporting Similar to Round 1, several participants in Round 2 had trouble reporting for others in the household on income source items. The inclusion of the new instruction allowing estimates seemed to address some of the issues involved with reporting income amounts that were found in Round 1. Following the findings from Round 1, to address issues with proxy reporting of income sources, the response option “Someone in the household got [INCOME SOURCE], but I’m not sure what type” was added to several questions in the “Income Sources” section. However, almost half of the participants in Round 2 indicated that they did not know the answer to a question at some point during the “Income Sources” section of the interview. The “Someone in the household got [INCOME SOURCE], but I’m not sure what type” response option was rarely used when participants were uncertain about income sources of others in their household (see distributions for each question below). Choosing this response option would indicate that the respondent confidently knows that someone else in

Section 8 – Conclusions and Overall Recommendations 8-3 their household received income from this source, but that they just did not know the type received. However, for the participants described above, most were not confident or had no idea if others in their household received that income source at all. Therefore, this response option was not appropriate for them to indicate that they didn’t know about income sources for others in their household. We recommend rewording this response option on all questions as follows: I am not sure if someone else in the household received [INCOME SOURCE], or I am not sure what type they received. 8.3.2 Double Reporting Instruction To address issues found in Round 1 with double reporting, most items in the “Income Sources” section included the instructions: “Do not include anything you already reported.” Overall, participants found these instructions to be confusing and repetitive, especially when they were asked about an income source they had not been previously asked about in a prior question (e.g., unemployment). A few participants also interpreted this instruction to refer to reporting on taxes. In general, we recommend including this instruction only when an income source is likely to have been reported on a previous question. We have listed this recommendation where applicable in each associated question in Section 7.2.2. We also note that for some questions, this instruction was helpful in reducing double reporting on items where respondents were more likely to do so (e.g., pensions), and thus it is important to keep this instruction on those questions.

C-1 Appendix C. Cognitive Interview Participant Consent Form What is the purpose of this interview? The U.S. Census Bureau is conducting interviews to help with the design and content about a portion of the Current Population Survey (CPS). This module, called the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) is an important source of information about our nation on topics such as employment, health insurance, and income. It’s important that the questions make sense, are easy to answer, and that everyone understands the questions in the same way. You are one of about 60 people who are being asked to participate in these interviews. Findings from these interviews will be used to clarify survey questions and instructions on the survey. What will happen if I take part in this interview? If you agree to take part in this study, you will be asked to answer questions about your household, including yourself and other people that live with you. The interview will be conducted virtually by a staff member from RTI International or Research Support Services, who are doing this study for the U.S. Census Bureau. We would also like to audio and video record the interview. Only the people who work on this study will review the recording. It will help us make sure we accurately capture your answers. If you don’t want to be recorded, that’s okay – you may still participate in the interview. How much time is required to participate? The interview will last approximately 90 minutes. Do I have to take part in this interview? No, participation in this interview is voluntary. You can stop the interview at any time, and you don’t have to answer a question if you don’t want to. You will not lose any rights you would normally have if you choose not to join this interview. What are the possible risks and benefits from participating in this interview? There are no direct benefits to you from doing this interview. Your involvement in this study will help us improve the questions for the Current Population Survey. There is no more than minimal risk in participating. How will my privacy be protected? By law, we are required to keep your answers confidential. The U.S. Census Bureau is conducting this study under the authority of 13 U.S.C. Sections 131, 141, 182, 193, and 196. Your privacy is protected by the Privacy Act of 1974 (5 U.S.C. Section 552a). i Abstract In this study, we explored the extent to which the design of date-entry fields (e.g., text entry, dropdown, and calendar) interacts with characteristics of the task (e.g., knowing the day of the week, relying on memory) to affect the usability (effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction) with which participants complete date-entry tasks for near dates. A total of 1000 participants completed different tasks using one of the three date-entry designs. For some of the tasks, knowing the day of the week was required to provide a correct response. Our findings indicate an advantage of the calendar design over the text entry design in terms of effectiveness and over both text entry and dropdown designs for most tasks in terms of efficiency. No difference across designs was observed for perceived difficulty, with most participants rating all date-entry design conditions as “extremely easy”. Based on our findings, we recommend implementing a calendar date-entry design for near dates, particularly for tasks requiring the day of the week. Future studies can expand these findings by exploring whether the advantage of the calendar design over the text entry and dropdown designs holds for distant dates. iv EXECUTIVE SUMMARY This paper examines how three common date-entry designs—text entry, dropdown menus, and calendar interfaces—perform when users enter dates that are close to the current date. Using two separate experiments with a combined sample of 1,000 U.S. residents, the authors assess each design’s effectiveness (accuracy), efficiency (time-on-task), and satisfaction. Across both studies, the calendar design consistently demonstrated the strongest overall usability for near-date tasks. It produced the highest average accuracy, though statistically significant differences were limited to specific tasks. More notably, the calendar design delivered the fastest performance on nearly all tasks, outperforming dropdowns and text entry even when tasks differed in structure—whether framed as an actual date, a day of the week, or a date recalled from memory. Satisfaction ratings showed that participants generally found all designs easy to use, with no statistically significant differences across conditions. Although the calendar showed a slight trend toward higher ease-of-use ratings, the study’s satisfaction results were not robust enough to establish clear superiority. Overall, the findings indicate that for online forms requiring respondents to enter near dates, the calendar design offers meaningful advantages—particularly in efficiency. The results also highlight how specific task characteristics influence usability outcomes and reinforce that date- entry design cannot be evaluated independently from the nature of the task itself.

INTRODUCTION Online forms collect factual data on a wide range of topics (e.g., a person’s age, last time they visited a doctor, etc.) and the answer to some of these questions require respondents to provide a date (Bargas-Avila et al., 2011; Persson, 2020; Wang, 2022). Some of the most common date-entry designs include text entry boxes, dropdown options, or calendars. The characteristics of these designs may interact with the characteristics of the date to be entered. For example, whether the date to be entered is close to the date of the study (a near date) or farther away from it (a distant date). One aspect that has been overlooked in the literature is the fact that some date-entry tasks may be easier to complete when respondents know the day of the week. For example, a patient trying to select a doctor’s appointment may prefer to select “next Wednesday” instead of “the 15th of January.” In this study, we explored the extent to which some date-entry designs (e.g., text entry, dropdown, and calendar) affect the usability, including the effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction with which respondents enter near dates. We vary this based on questions that may or may not require them to know the day of the week (e.g., entering the date for “last Friday” or entering the date “April 21, 2022”) or may require them to rely on their memory (e.g., “your last doctor’s appointment”). 2. BACKGROUND 2.1 Date-entry Designs In this section, we present a description of some of the most common date-entry designs (text entry, dropdown, and calendar) along with a short summary of the research that has explored their effectiveness and efficiency. Because different authors may use the same label for different date-entry designs (e.g., date picker for calendar and spinner for a dropdown on mobile

2 U.S. Census Bureau devices; Antoun et al., 2017; Persson, 2020; U.S. Web Design System, 2025), this section provides a label, a description, and an image to help the reader visualize the design being described. 2.1.1 Text entry Design The text entry design allows respondents to type the desired date, typically into a fixed- length field where an underline is presented with a pre-specified number of spaces for character entry. One potential issue with this design is that respondents may not enter dates in the desired format (Bargas-Avila et al., 2011; Wang, 2022). For example, users may either switch the order of the numbers for day and month (e.g., entering 01/06 instead of 06/01 to report June 1st), or may not enter the requested number of digits (e.g., entering “1” as opposed to “01” for January or entering “24” instead of “2024”). To solve these potential problems, designers may use a mask format, where the response field contains format cues about the information to be entered. Figure 1 provides a visualization of a text entry design with a fixed-length field without masking (left) and with masking (right). Figure 1. The text entry design may not specify the format (left) or may include a mask to specify the format for date-entry (right) 2.1.2 Dropdown Design This design consists of three fields with pre-specified values for month, day, and year. The “month” field can be the month names, the month number, or a combination (e.g., 1- January). The “day” field provides the numbers 1-31 (depending on the selected month), and the year field provides a range of years, typically in four-digit format (except for credit card

3 U.S. Census Bureau expiration dates, which typically require only the last two digits). This design allows the user to select each value by scrolling through the list and then selecting the applicable choice. For mobile device operating systems, the equivalent of a dropdown design may be called a “spinner,” “picker,” or “spin wheel” (Antoun et al., 2017). In this paper, we refer to all these designs as “dropdown.” The advantage of the dropdown over the text entry design is that it prevents users from entering the data in the wrong format or in the wrong order. One potential disadvantage of this design is the amount of scrolling needed for a year in the distant past, such as the year of birth for an older individual. Another disadvantage is that, as can be observed in Figure 2, an expanded dropdown box may conceal other information in the screen. Figure 2. Dropdown design with the month field collapsed (left) and expanded (right). 2.1.3 Calendar Design The calendar design includes a pop-up display of the current year and month, and a highlighted current day. Common calendar designs include buttons or arrows that allow respondents to change the month or the year, as shown in Figure 3.

LITERATURE REVIEW Studies that have explored the usability of different design options for entering dates have found conflicting results for both effectiveness and efficiency outcomes. Regarding effectiveness, although some studies have found no difference in number of errors between the text entry and calendar designs (Persson, 2020) or text entry and dropdown designs (Waloszek et al., 2020), others have found that text entry leads to a higher number of errors than both calendar and dropdown (Myka et al., 2019). However, other studies have found

5 U.S. Census Bureau that the higher number of errors observed in the text entry design is limited to errors involving the participants switching the numbers for day and month (Bargas-Avila et al., 2011), or when the date to be entered is a near date (a day in the same month; Drygielski et al., 2018). When focusing on differences in effectiveness between the calendar and dropdown designs, some studies have found that these two designs lead to similar number of errors (Myka et al., 2019; Türkcan & Durdu, 2018), but other studies have found that the calendar leads to a higher number of errors than the dropdown design (Bargas-Avila et al., 2011). Yet, other studies have found that the calendar design not only outperforms the dropdown design, but it also leads to no errors (Waloszek et al., 2020), although this advantage of the calendar design may be limited to tasks involving near dates (Drygielski et al., 2018). Furthermore, Türkcan and Durdu (2018) found that the number of errors committed by participants using the calendar design for distant dates was so high that this was the only condition where some participants did not complete the task. Regarding efficiency, although some researchers have not observed a difference in time- on-task between text entry and calendar (Persson, 2020) or text entry and dropdown (Drygielski et al., 2018), other researchers have observed that text entry outperforms both the dropdown and calendar designs (Bargas-Avila et al., 2011; Myka et al., 2019; Türkcan & Durdu, 2018; Waloszek et al., 2020). However, the higher efficiency of the text entry design may be limited to distant dates (Drygielski et al., 2018). When comparing the dropdown and calendar designs in terms of efficiency, some studies have observed no difference in time-on-task between these two designs (Bargas-Avila et al., 2011; Myka et al., 2019). Others have observed a shorter time-on-task for the calendar than for the dropdown design (Waloszek et al., 2020), yet others have observed the opposite pattern

6 U.S. Census Bureau (Türkcan & Durdu, 2018). However, studies that have manipulated the date to be entered (near or distant) have observed an interaction between date-entry design and the date: When the date to be entered is near, the calendar design performs better than the dropdown design in terms of efficiency. However, when the date to be entered is distant, the pattern is reversed, and the dropdown design results in lower time-on-task than the calendar design (Drygielski et al., 2018). Some of the conflicting findings in the literature may be explained by differences in methodology in terms of sample size, and manipulation of different factors. For example, the study conducted by Myka et al. (2019) consisted of 10 participants per design, and no inferential analyses were conducted. Therefore, it is not clear whether the differences in time and errors between the designs are due to random variability or due to specific characteristics of the designs. The lack of difference in number of errors between text entry and calendar design observed in the Persson (2020) study is contrary to the findings of Myka et al. (2019) and Türkcan and Durdu (2018). The conflict between these studies may be explained by the fact that Türkcan & Durdu, included both near and distant dates in the task, while the task in the Persson (2020) study did not require participants to change the year. In fact, Persson (2020) acknowledged that the results may have been different if the task would have required participants to change the year. Finally, the conflicting results between Drygielski et al. (2018) and other studies (Myka et al., 2019; Persson, 2020; ; Türkcan & Durdu, 2018; Waloszek et al., 2020) is due to differences in operationalization of outcomes. The Drygielski study is the only study where the operationalization of errors takes into consideration whether the numbers for day and month were switched, while other studies did not make this distinction.

7 U.S. Census Bureau Regardless of these limitations, the studies described above have expanded our knowledge by allowing the conclusion that there is not a “one size fits all” when it comes to date-entry designs. The current literature drives attention to the importance of not only considering the design for date-entry, but also considering the characteristics of the stimuli (e.g, near and distant dates: Drygielski et al., 2018) and the operationalization of outcomes (e.g., different types of errors: Bargas-Avila et al., 2011). One characteristic of the stimuli that has not been explored in the literature is the day of the week. Although the day of the week may not be necessary for some type of dates (e.g., date of birth), it may be indispensable for other situations. For example, a patient may ask the staff at the doctor’s office to reschedule their appointment for “next Wednesday”. For tasks when knowing the day of the week may be advantageous, the calendar design may be the most effective and efficient given that the day of the week is visible to the respondent; that visibility is a design characteristic not included in any other design. To the best of our knowledge, no study has compared the text box or dropdown menu designs to the calendar design in situations where knowing the day of the week would be helpful to select the correct date. The Present Study The purpose of the present study is to add to the existing literature by exploring the usability associated with three common date-entry designs (text entry, dropdown, and calendar), focusing on entering near dates. The study investigates whether the usability of the design (effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction) depends on whether the day of the week is part of the date-entry task (e.g., entering last Friday), when the date relies on memory (e.g., entering your

8 U.S. Census Bureau last doctor’s appointment), or a date either in the immediate future or close past. For this purpose, we developed the following research questions: 1. Is there a difference in effectiveness as measured by data entry accuracy between text entry, dropdown, and calendar designs when entering near dates, when the day of the week is provided (e.g. last Friday), or when the actual date is provided (e.g. April 21, 2022)? 2. Is there a difference in efficiency as measured by time-on-task between text entry, dropdown, and calendar designs when entering near dates, when the day of the week is provided, when the near date is from memory, or when the actual date is provided? 3. Is there a difference in satisfaction for the three designs for near dates? To answer these research questions, we conducted two studies that required participants to enter near dates using either a calendar design, a text entry field, or a dropdown menu to complete tasks that may or may not have required them to know the day of the week. 4. METHODOLOGY 4.1 Sample The data for both studies were collected in 2022. The Office of Management and Budget reviewed and approved the materials and methodology for this study. The first study was conducted in April and May and the second study was conducted in July. Two separate quota samples of 500 U.S. residents from a nonprobability panel completed each study (for a total of 1000 participants). All participants received informed consent prior to the start of the study. The first study oversampled bilingual participants (English-Spanish; for a separate research objective) which resulted in more Hispanic participants. The second study required participants to use a

Some dates were in the same month as the study completion, some were in the next month, and some were in the previous month. 4.4 Outcomes of Interest and Analysis 4.4.1 Effectiveness Effectiveness for this study was defined as accuracy and it was recorded as a binary variable (accurate or not accurate). For the one week from today task in Study 1, accuracy was based on whether the date entered was one week from the date the participant completed the study, which was data recorded by Qualtrics. We calculated average accuracy by dividing the number of correct responses by the total number of participants that answered the question and conducted a t-test to determine significance. The same type of calculation was used when determining accuracy for entering last Friday’s date and entering two Monday’s ago in Study 2. For the other two tasks in Study 1, the date entered was accurate if it was April 21, 2022, for the

12 U.S. Census Bureau second task and May 21, 2022, for the third task.Task 4 (entering the date of the last doctor’s appointment) is not included in this analysis since we do not know the true answer. Analysis for each study was conducted separately but used the same mixed-logistic model with a random effect for the participant, each of which responded to multiple date-entry tasks: πi = β0 + β1[condition]i + β2[demographics]i + β3[question]i +β4[condition*question]i + ei, where π is the success probability of an accurate response, i is the respondent level indicator, and β0 = γ00 + µ0,. The three conditions are text entry, dropdown, and calendar. The demographic variables are the participant’s age, sex, Hispanic origin, race, and, for study 1 participants only, the device used. 4.4.2 Efficiency Efficiency was measured by time-on-task (seconds) for each correctly completed task. Time was measured from the time the page loaded until the participant advanced to the next page. We used a mixed-linear model with the log of time as the dependent variable, the condition as the independent variable, and the same covariates as were used in the accuracy model. Again, a random effect for the participant was added to account for the number of date-entry tasks. For both effectiveness and efficiency, we report significant pairwise comparisons after using a Bonferroni correction where the F test of the interaction between the condition and the task was significant. 4.4.3 Satisfaction Satisfaction was measured by the ease-of-use question in Study 1. The three lowest scores were combined into one response choice since very few participants reported that the

13 U.S. Census Bureau tasks were difficult, then a Chi-Square statistic was calculated to determine if the ease of use was independent of condition. 4.5 Hypotheses Hypothesis 1- Effectiveness: The date-entry design will be a significant predictor of accuracy. Answers using the calendar will be more accurate for the tasks indicating the day of the week (tasks 1, 5, 6) compared to the text entry or dropdown. Answers for the tasks with a date only (tasks 2 and 3) will be more accurate in the calendar and dropdown condition than the text entry as suggested by earlier studies. Hypothesis 2 - Efficiency: The date-entry design will be a significant predictor of time- on-task. As observed by Drygielski et al. (2018), and given that the current study involves near dates, the calendar will be faster to use than dropdown and text entry for all tasks. Hypothesis 3 - Usability: Given support for hypotheses 2 and 3, the calendar design will be reported as easier to use than the other two designs. 5. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITATIONS We assume that participants’ report of their last doctor’s appointment was reported accurately and did not verify this information. It is possible that participants may have just estimated this date. 6. RESULTS 6.1 Effectiveness The calendar design had the highest average accuracy across all five tasks. However, it was only significantly higher for a few of the tasks. There was no significant difference in accuracy between the calendar and the

Error bars represent the standard error of the mean. 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS Many online forms require respondents to enter dates. Some dates, such as birthdates, can be a long time ago while others, such as reservations or appointments, can be close to the current date. There are multiple designs available to collect this information, each with their benefits and drawbacks. This analysis aimed to determine which design has the highest accuracy and efficiency in situations where the date is near the current date. The results from both experiments indicate that the calendar design is overall the best option for entering near dates between the three designs tested. These results are consistent with prior findings from Waloszek et al. (2020) and Drygielski et al. (2018). The first hypothesis was that the calendar would result in more accurate entry for tasks indicating the day of the week compared to the text entry and dropdown, and that text entry

17 U.S. Census Bureau would result in lower accuracy compared to the other two designs when a date was given. While there was a trend suggesting the calendar design results in more accurate data for near date tasks that involve day of the week and dates, there were few differences that were statistically significant, and this hypothesis was only partially supported. Participants completed three tasks referring to a day of the week (rather than a date). The calendar resulted in more accurate entry for two of those three tasks compared to text entry. There was no statistical evidence that the calendar resulted in more accurate entry compared to dropdown. There was also no statistical evidence that accuracy diminished with text entry compared to the calendar or the dropdown when a date was provided in the task. This finding matches the Persson (2020) finding but is contrary to Myka et al. (2019), Waloszek et al. (2020) and Drygielski et al. (2018). Those three papers found that text entry results in more inaccurate entry. In the present experiment, the mask used in the text entry fields and the label above the fields likely helped participants understand the desired format. It could be that these features supported participants so that they entered data as correctly as those who received the dropdown or the calendar design when the task included the date. The second hypothesis was that the date-entry design will be a significant predictor of time-on-task and that the calendar will be faster to use than dropdown and text entry for near dates, similar to the findings by Drygielski et al. (2018). In all six tasks, participants used the calendar more quickly than the dropdown design, supporting the second hypothesis. Furthermore, in five out of six tasks, participants were able to answer with the calendar more quickly compared to text entry. This finding was consistent no matter if the task was presented as a day of the week, an actual date, or a date from memory.

18 U.S. Census Bureau Repetition could have been the reason the calendar and text entry timing were not different for one task. In Study 1, participants completed two similar tasks, one after the other: “enter April 21” and then, on the next page “enter May 21.” The calendar was quicker to use for the April 21 task than text entry, but not for the May 21 task. We suspect that the participants who received the text entry design became more efficient, eliminating any difference in task completion time between the text entry design and the calendar. In fact, they sped up so much in the second task that they were significantly faster than the participants who received the dropdown design. The final hypothesis was that the calendar would be reported as easier to use than the other two designs. While the satisfaction data suggests the calendar might be easier to use, the results were not statistically significant. Thus, our hypothesis was not supported. Our satisfaction measure did have some limitations; it was only asked in one of the two studies, and had satisfaction been recorded after each task, that might have been more useful to tease out the difficulty of the task compared to the difficulty of the design. Previous literature showed that calendars performed better than text entry and dropdown for date-entry on online forms, particularly for near dates. These experiments support those findings, with participants entering data into the calendar significantly faster than the other two designs and establishing a trend of having higher accuracy. For near date entries involving day of the week, we find some evidence that the calendar improves accuracy compared to the other two designs, but it is not as strong as the efficiency finding. Interestingly, the text entry condition performed better in the present experiments compared to what had been reported in the literature, both in time-on-task and accuracy. This is likely because a label was above the field and masking was used in the text field, which alerted the respondent to the desired format, thereby reducing

19 U.S. Census Bureau errors. This finding showcases how the evolution of designs can improve performance. Future research can explore whether small changes to existing designs, such as including a calendar icon next to the text field, can lead to additional gains in performance (U.S. Web Design System, 2025), or whether the advantage of the calendar design over the text entry and dropdown designs holds for distant dates.

i Abstract As data collection efforts face concerns about declining response rates and rising costs associated with participant recruitment and follow-up, further research is needed to understand how different contact strategies may benefit survey researchers confronting these challenges. Text message invitations present an opportunity for data collection efforts – especially longitudinal efforts with repeated contact – to adopt a potentially faster and less expensive contact strategy compared to other commonly-used contact strategies (e.g., mail, in- person visits, telephone). This study extends the literature by using nationally representative data from a unique data source: the Census Household Panel (CHP). The CHP was a probability-based nationwide survey panel that regularly fielded surveys to panel members as monthly “topicals”. Once enrolled, panelists were invited to the topical surveys via email and text messages. Panelists must provide a mobile phone number and consent to receive text message invitations. This research uses paradata and survey responses from the May 2024 topical (i.e. Topical 7) with approximately 10,000 respondents to explore the impacts of text messaging. More specifically, we examine four central research questions: (1) How do text message reminders contribute to response in the topical 7 survey?; (2) Are there demographic differences in who clicks on the survey through text message invites versus email invites?; (3) What are the consent rates for receiving text messages?; and (4) Are there demographic differences in who consents to receive text messages? Insights from this research help extend the field’s knowledge and understanding of the impacts of sending text message invitations. Findings from this research show that: (1) text message invitations appear to contribute to survey response by bolstering initial response rates in the hours immediately following receipt of these text messages; (2) there are demographic differences by age, race/ethnicity, education level, family income, and respondent type in the propensity of panelists to access a survey through text message invitation; (3) text message consent rates for Topical 7 of the CHP are comparable to the existing literature (i.e. ~50%); and (4) there are demographic differences by race/ethnicity, age, family income, educational attainment, marital status, region, and respondent type in panelists’ consent behaviors. In sum, this paper’s findings suggest that the use of text messages as a contact strategy is advantageous for reaching certain demographic groups and is a promising tool for increasing response rates to national data collection efforts. INTRODUCTION As U.S. Census Bureau surveys are modernizing and adding internet self-response data collection to historically interviewer-administered surveys, better understanding the impacts of mixed-mode contact strategies becomes even more vital for encouraging response. Best practices in contact strategy designs emphasize the necessity of using multiple modes (i.e. mail, email, text messages, phone calls) to invite and remind potential respondents to complete the survey to boost response rates (Dillman et al. 2014; Millar and Dillman 2011). While postal mailing invitations add authenticity and legitimacy to the survey request (Dillman et al. 2014), they are not as timely as electronic contact modes and are more costly. Electronic contact modes, such as emails and text messages, provide opportunities for reaching respondents more quickly and may better signal the time sensitivity of the request. While emails and text messages both provide the advantages of speedy delivery, text messages provide a few advantages over emails for web surveys. First, text messages can be perceived as more immediate or time-sensitive than emails. This has been reflected in studies that have shown response comes more quickly via text message invites than via other types of contact modes (Mavletova and Couper 2014). This is particularly important for sequential multimode surveys as they try to push respondents to complete in the less expensive mode – web – and for those with shorter field periods, like the Current Population Survey. Gathering responses on the web quickly before progressing to the next mode produces savings in nonresponse follow- up in a more costly survey mode. Using text messages can provide other advantages over sending emails. Cell phone numbers provide additional alternative contact information for cases where the email address was not recorded accurately. Text messages may also be beneficial for potential respondents who do not regularly check their emails or pay close attention to their emails. Similarly, text messages may be advantageous in cases where potential respondents do not have email accounts or where potential respondents ignore or overlook contact attempts via email (e.g., when emails are thought to be spam) (Cabrera-Álvarez and Lynn 2023). Spam filters or inbox rules can be set up to filter messages from senders not known to them – sometimes by the email service and not by the user themselves. While some spam filters exist for text messages, they tend to be used less and require more deliberate set-up by the user than email spam filters. Despite this, text messages do have some drawbacks. First, text messages do not offer as much space to build rapport or convey a message to persuade the potential respondent to complete the survey as a letter or an email (Hansen and Pedersen 2012; Mavletova and Couper 2014). Additionally, text messages may reach people at times when they are unavailable to respond or in a place where it is not easy to respond (i.e. in a public setting where they are uncomfortable responding or unable to due to accessibility to the internet). Finally, some studies have shown lower response rates from text messages indicating that text messages may not necessarily be

2 U.S. Census Bureau an efficient contact mode alone (see Hansen and Pedersen 2012). Further, requirements by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) present additional considerations regarding the use of text messaging as a contact strategy for data collection efforts. While the FCC has clarified that the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA) does not restrict the federal government (or contractors acting at its direction) from using autodialers or sending unsolicited text messages to cell phones in the conduct of official business (because the government is not considered a “person” under the Act) these exemptions do not apply to other survey organizations (Federal Communications Commission 2016). Private entities must comply fully with the TCPA when using texting as a contact method (Federal Communications Commission 2016). In addition, cell phone carriers and industry groups often impose their own rules: carriers may refuse to transmit large volumes of unsolicited texts, even if such messages are legally permissible, to protect their networks and subscribers (Federal Communications Commission 2016). These limitations restrict when and how text messaging can be used as a respondent communication strategy in survey operations. In practice, mass texting is almost always limited to opt-in lists of recipients (which is further constrained by the availability and accuracy of sample phone number information). Government surveys have only recently begun to use text message invites and reminders. For example, the Household Pulse Survey (HPS) invited potential respondents to complete their survey via text message starting in 2020. Other examples of government surveys that have used text messages include more specialized populations, such as the National Survey of College Graduates (Horwitz et al. 2024) and a survey of principals and teachers which used texting as a two-way survey response mode (Spiegelman et al. 2024). As federal surveys continue to adopt web response and optimize survey instruments for mobile devices, understanding the impacts of implementing text message invitations and reminders becomes more important. According to Pew Research Center (2024), 91% of Americans own a smart phone, including 15% of Americans who depend upon smartphones for their internet use and have no home broadband service. With high smartphone ownership rates and increasing technology use, text message invitations have the potential to reach a large portion of Americans who can actively complete the survey on their devices. Furthermore, reaching those who rely upon smartphones for their internet use is particularly important for response as Americans who are younger (ages 18-29), not White, have lower incomes, and have lower levels of educational attainment are more likely to be smartphone dependent (Pew Research Center 2024). This study uses Census Household Panel data to examine who consents to receiving text message invitations and reminders, how text message reminders impact response, and who is responding to email and text message reminders. Findings from this study can help inform future contact strategies for federal surveys, particularly those that are longitudinal in nature, and can give us insight on how this type of data collection scheme may look for others who incorporate text messages in a longitudinal design.

BACKGROUND 2.1 Impact of sending text messages invites and reminders on response Research so far suggests that text message invitations and reminders do not appear to substantially impact overall response rates (Christian et al. 2024). In an experiment comparing email invites and reminders to text message invites and reminders, de Bruijne and Wijnant (2014) did not find a significant difference in the response rate by the invitation type for their panel respondents. Similarly, in an experiment comparing postal, telephone, and text message recruitment in Denmark, Hansen and Pedersen (2012) found the initial response rates before reminders were sent were lower for those receiving text message invites versus telephone invitations, but no difference with postal mailings. However, Horwitz et al. (2024) found in an experiment comparing unsolicited text only invitations versus text message and email invitations for the Census Bureau’s Household Pulse Survey that the text only contact strategy resulted in a slightly higher response rate overall and higher response amongst younger age groups and females than the email and text message contact strategy. Studies have shown that response to text message invites does occur rapidly, which makes text message invites an important tool for gaining responses. This rapid response is important for surveys that use sequential mixed-mode design by lowering the costs associated with nonresponse follow-up in another mode or for surveys with short field periods. For example, Christian et al. (2024) found that sending earlier text messages in the data collection period (vs. later in data collection) resulted in respondents completing the survey more quickly, which meant fewer respondents required follow-up reminders in the mail. McGeeney and Yan (2016) noted that 15% of the panelists who responded did so within 30 minutes when both an email and text message invitation was sent versus 6% when only an email invitation was sent. Andreadis (2020) found that half of the survey links in a text message reminder that were clicked occurred within one hour, including 25% that occurred within about 3.5 minutes of the text message reminder delivery. 2.2 Consent to Text Currently the Census Bureau only sends text message invitations and reminders to those who have previously consented to be texted when they provide their mobile phone numbers. In a longitudinal design this means the Census Bureau can collect the individuals’ mobile phone number and obtain their consent for future text messages in their initial interview or survey completion and send invites and reminders for later survey periods. Prior work has shown consent rates for text messages to be around half of respondents. In a study on Pew Research Center’s American Trend Panel, about 54% of their respondents consented to text message (McGeeney and Yan 2016). In a panel study in the Netherlands that conducts weekly online questionnaires, 59% of smartphone users provided their mobile phone number when asked to consent to receiving text message for a main questionnaire invitation (de Bruijne and Wijnant

4 U.S. Census Bureau 2014). Among a survey of teachers and principals, Spiegelman and Zotti (2021) found that about half of the principals and teachers who provided their cell phone numbers consented to receive text messages. Prior studies have found that those who do consent to receive text messages differ demographically from those who have not consented to receive text messages. McGeeney and Yan (2016) found that text message consenters in Pew Research Center’s American Trend Panel tended to be younger, have higher incomes, live in urban areas, and more likely to be non- White or Hispanic than those who did not consent. There were not any statistically significant differences between consenters and non-consenters by sex or education. Similarly, Spiegelman and Zotti (2021) found that non-White or Hispanic principals and teachers were more likely to give their cell phone number and consent to receive text messages than White principals and teachers. Interestingly, higher likelihood of providing a cellphone number and consent to text also increased with age for these principals and teachers. De Bruijne and Wijnant (2014) did not find any significant differences in providing a phone number for text message consent by sex, age or education in their study in the Netherlands. Horwitz et al. (2024) found in an experiment for the National Survey of College Graduates that those who consented to be texted were older, more likely to be White, and had higher levels of educational attainment. Obtaining consent to send text message invites, especially among subgroups that have traditionally had lower self-response rates, is important for ensuring invitations and reminders are effective in encouraging response. Evaluating the share of respondents who consent to future text messages and how these respondents may differ from those who do not consent is valuable for developing and implementing effective contact strategies. 3. RESEARCH QUESTIONS The Census Household Panel data used for this study did not include an experimental design. This study is an exploratory study that examines the following four research questions (RQ): RQ1: How do text message reminders contribute to response in the Topical 7 survey? RQ2: Are there demographic differences in who clicks on the survey through text message invites versus email invites? RQ3: What are the consent rates for receiving text messages? RQ4: Are there demographic differences in who consents to receive text messages?

5 U.S. Census Bureau 4. METHODOLOGY 4.1 Data We use data from the Census Household Panel (CHP) recruitment survey and the Topical 7 survey. Invitations for the recruitment survey were distributed via postal letter that included a $5 prepaid incentive to encourage participation. The recruitment survey was administered September 12 to October 10, 2023, in English and Spanish, and the first replenishment operation was conducted from March 5, 2024, to April 9, 2024. Responding households received a $20 cash incentive to complete the recruitment questionnaire. Participants could complete the web questionnaire in Qualtrics or call to complete the questionnaire on the telephone. There was also a nonresponse follow-up outbound telephone operation. A total of about 18,500 respondents completed the recruitment surveys. Once enrolled, panelists are invited to respond to monthly topical surveys via emails and/or text messages. Up to 4 emails and 4 text messages are sent each month, inviting the panelist to respond to the survey via the web or telephone. Outbound telephone operations are conducted for select cases. Participants received a $10 incentive upon the completion of their survey. The Topical 7 survey was administered from May 21 to June 4, 2024. Table 1 shows the sample size, number of respondents, and response rates for recruitment and Topical 7 surveys. The sample for the Topical 7 survey was about 18,500 respondents who completed the recruitment survey1 and a total of about 10,000 responded to the Topical 7 survey. The weighted response rate (AAPOR RR2) for Topical 7 was 10.2% (American Association of Public Opinion Research 2023). Table 1.
