We examine the timing of the response by which type of link was clicked. This analysis is descriptive in nature. For significance testing for RQ2 and RQ4, this paper includes two main outcome measures. First, clicking on text messages is a binary measure of whether someone clicked on/accessed the survey through a text message invitation instead of an email invitation (0 = No; 1 = Yes). Second, consent is a binary measure of whether someone consented to receive text message invitations/reminders when enrolled in the panel (0 = No; 1 = Yes). The analyses for RQ2 and RQ4 include a total of 9 control variables to account for compositional differences which may influence survey engagement and response behaviors. Age group is categorized into eight mutually exclusive categories: 18-24; 25-34; 35-44; 45-54; 55-64; 65-74; 75-84; and 85+. Sex is a binary variable denoting if respondents identify as male or female. Race/ethnicity is a nominal-level variable that consists of five mutually exclusive race/ethnicity groups: White, non-Hispanic; Black, non-Hispanic; Asian, non-Hispanic; Some other race/Multiracial, non-Hispanic; and Hispanic/Latino. Marital status is divided into now married, domestic partnership, widowed, divorced, separated, and never married. Education level is divided into five mutually exclusive categories: less than a high school diploma/GED; a high

7 U.S. Census Bureau school diploma/GED; some college; an associate’s degree; a bachelor’s degree; and a graduate degree. Family income consists of seven ordinal categories classifying respondents’ annual family income: less than $25K; $25K-39.9K; $40K-59.9K; $60K-74.9K; $75K-99.9K; $100K- 149.9K; and greater than or equal to $150K. Region is a categorical variable denoting if respondents reside in the Northeast, Midwest, South, or West. Language is a binary variable denoting if the respondent completed the survey in English or Spanish. Lastly, respondent type is categorical variable classifying respondents as: regular responder (if they completed 5 or more topical surveys); irregular responder (if they completed 4 or fewer topical surveys); and replenishment sample member (if they were first included in Topical 7 as part of the replenishment sample). Using Stata 18, descriptive statistics were calculated to establish Topical 7 response rates, consent rates (i.e. RQ3), and sample demographics. Chi-square tests of statistical significance were performed to identify bivariate associations between demographic variables and outcomes of interest (e.g., consent behaviors). Binary logistic regressions were performed to ascertain: (1) How do consent rates to receive text messages differ by respondent characteristics?; and (2) Who is clicking through on the text message invites versus the email invites? We present the odds ratios from these binary logistic regressions and interpret them as percent increases and percent decreases. For missing data, pairwise deletion is employed to preserve sample size across models depending on the outcome variable of interest. All analyses are based on unweighted data and we report significant differences at the 95%, 99%, and 99.9% confidence levels. In the Appendix, we also include findings from supplemental analyses where we performed chi- square tests of significance for different consent behavior patterns (e.g., consent to receive neither texts nor emails, consent to receive only texts) by respondent demographics (Table A1) and then we performed binary logistic regressions to assess the influence of respondent demographics on specific consent behavior patterns (Tables A2-A4). For these analyses, the sample size is further restricted to respondents who provided phone number information as well as respondents who provided email information (where applicable). 5. RESULTS RQ1: Response to Survey Via Text Message and Email Survey Links In the Topical 7 survey, a majority of responses came from clicking on the email link (77.9%), compared with 22.1% that came from clicking on the text message link. Figure 1 shows the percent of response coming from the email and text message links throughout the 15-day survey period. Response from the text link grew most notably on days text messages were sent and remained relatively static on days without the text message reminders. By contrast, responses via email links grew most greatly on days when email reminders were sent, but response continued to come in steadily on days in-between email reminders.

Significance testing via chi-square tests suggests that all of the demographic variables in Table 3 (with the exception of region) are statistically significantly associated with the distribution channel selected by respondents. In brief, Table 3 provides insight into how several key demographic characteristics differ descriptively by distribution channel – differences which we examine in a multivariate model in Table 4. Table 4 outlines the odds ratios for a respondent clicking on text links over email links – taking into account all of the demographic measures outlined in Table 3. For clarity of interpretation, we discuss these odds ratios as % increases and % decreases. Looking at Table 4, we see several statistically significant differences emerge. First, consistent with the descriptive findings on race/ethnicity in Table 3, we see that identifying as Black, non-Hispanic or SOR/Multiracial, non- Hispanic is associated with a 53% increase and 48% increase respectively in the odds of clicking on text links over email links – compared to identifying as White, non-Hispanic (OR = 1.53, p < 0.001; OR = 1.48, p < 0.01). Similarly, compared to non-Hispanic White respondents, Hispanic/Latino respondents experience a 31% increase in the odds of clicking on text links over email links (OR = 1.23, p < 0.05). However, we do not see significant differences by the language that surveys are completed in (i.e. English or Spanish). Also mirroring findings from Table 3 are the findings by family income and education level. More specifically, we see evidence that those with lower family income or lower educational attainment are more likely to click on text links over email links. Compared to those with a bachelor’s degree, those with less than a high school diploma and those with a high school diploma/GED experience a 48% increase and 24% increase in these odds respectively (OR = 1.48, p < 0.05; OR = 1.24, p < 0.05). Compared to those with a family income of >$150K, we see that all income groups lower than >$150K experience statistically significantly greater odds of clicking on text links over email links – with the exception of $75K-99.9K where the association is non-significant (OR = 1.11, p > 0.05). As mentioned earlier, these significant findings corroborate the earlier discussion of descriptive trends in Table 3, where a greater share of respondents with higher income or higher education are observed clicking on email links versus text links. Continuing with Table 4, we see several novel differences that were not initially noted in the discussion of descriptive findings in Table 3. First, we see a significant age effect, where increases in age are associated with decreases in the odds of clicking on text links over email links. More specifically, all age groups above 55-64 experience statistically significant decreases in these odds. Compared to those who are ages 55-64, respondents ages 65-74 experience a 21% decrease (OR = 0.79, p < 0.01), respondents ages 75-84 experience a 23% decrease (OR = 0.77, p < 0.05), and respondents ages 85+ experience a 47% decrease (OR = 0.53, p < 0.05) in the odds of clicking on text links over email links. Examining respondent type, replenishment sample respondents do not significantly differ from the regular responders who were already enrolled in the sample. However, irregular responders experience a 32% increase in the odds of clicking on text links over email links – compared to regular responders (OR = 1.32, p < 0.01). This finding appears to corroborate prior research showing that panelists with “irregular” response patterns are more likely to respond from text messages (Carbrera-Alvarez and Lynn 2024). Additionally, we observe one statistically significant coefficient for marital status – with

12 U.S. Census Bureau widowed respondents experiencing a 34% increase in the odds of clicking on text links over email links compared to now married respondents (OR = 1.34, p < 0.01). The reasoning for this singular difference for marital status is not immediately clear, but it is important to note that the sample size for widowed respondents is comparatively small – which may be influence findings in this instance due to statistical power. In brief, we do find evidence of demographic differences in who is clicking on text links versus who is clicking on email links, with race/ethnicity, family income, education level, age, respondent type, and marital status all being statistically significantly associated with the likelihood of clicking on text links over email links (as outlined above).

17 U.S. Census Bureau RQ3: Consent Rates for Receiving Text Messages Table 5 provides insight into the share of panelists who consent to receiving text messages and provides phone number information. Looking at Table 5, we see that the overall text messaging consent rate for the analytic sample is ~52.6%, with ~5,000 respondents consenting out of ~9,500 respondents total. For Topical 7 of the CHP, the text message consent rate appears to be comparable to those documented in the existing literature (i.e. ~50%). RQ4: Demographic Differences in Text Message Consent Behaviors Tables 5-6 also provide insight into: (1) the demographics of who consents to receiving text messages and provides phone number information (Table 5); and (2) the odds of a respondent consenting to receive text messages when taking into consideration all of the demographic variables (Table 6). Beginning with Table 5, we see that the demographic distribution of who does or does not consent to receiving text messages is fairly similar across each demographic measure. However, several differences do emerge. First, we observe descriptive differences by income and education, with a greater share of respondents with lower income or lower education consenting. For example, 13.8% of those who consented to receive text messages had a family income less than $25K whereas 10.8% of those who did not consent had a family income less than $25K. Consistent with this, 20.4% of those who consented to receive text messages had a family income greater than $150K, whereas 26.1% of those who did not consent had a family income greater than $150K. We observe a similar education gradient where respondents reporting higher educational attainment compose a larger share of those not consenting compared to those consenting to receive text messages. More specifically, 54.8% of those who consented to receive text messages had a bachelor’s degree or higher whereas 60.3% of those who did not consent had a bachelor’s degree or higher. We also observe a potential sex disparity in Table 5, with 57.1% of those who consented identifying as female versus 54.9% of those who did not consent. Significance testing via chi-square tests suggests that all of the demographic variables in Table 5 (with the exception of language) are statistically significantly associated with respondents’ consent behaviors though. In brief, Table 5 provides insight into how several key demographic characteristics differ descriptively by consent behavior – differences which we examine in a multivariate model in Table 6. Table 6 outlines the odds ratios for a respondent consenting to receive text messages – taking into account all of the demographic measures outlined in Table 5. For clarity of interpretation, we discuss these odds ratios as percent increases and percent decreases. Looking at Table 6, we see several statistically significant differences emerge. First, consistent with the descriptive findings on family income and education in Table 5, we see that across all family income brackets, any family income below $150K is associated with a statistically significant increase in the odds of consenting to receive text messages – with the exception of $75K-99.9K where the association is non-significant (OR = 1.11, p > 0.05). Less stable are findings by education level. More specifically, while we saw preliminary evidence of higher education being potentially associated with lower odds of consenting, we see that both education above and below a bachelor’s degree is significantly associated with increases in the odds of consenting. Compared to those with a bachelor’s degree, those with a graduate degree and some college experience a

18 U.S. Census Bureau 14% increase and 22% increase in these odds respectively (OR = 1.14, p < 0.05; OR = 1,22, p < 0.01). Yet, having an associate’s degree is not significantly associated with these odds compared to those with a bachelor’s degree – suggesting a potential nuanced education gradient and underscoring the importance of testing observed descriptive trends in multivariate models. Continuing with Table 6, we see several novel differences that were not initially noted in the discussion of descriptive findings in Table 5. First, we see significant age effects, with mixed evidence on how increases and decreases in age are associated with the odds of consenting to receive text messages. For example, we see that most age groups above 55-64 experience statistically significant increases in these odds. More specifically, compared to those who are ages 55-64, respondents ages 65-74 experience a 15% increase (OR = 1.15, p < 0.05) and respondents ages 75-84 experience a 28% increase (OR = 1.28, p < 0.01). However, we also find that respondents ages 85+ experience a 40% decrease (OR = 0.60, p < 0.01) in the odds of consenting – suggesting a potential threshold effect. Additionally, we see that those ages 45-54 experience a 13% decrease in the odds of consenting to receive text messages (OR = 0.87, p < 0.05). Regarding race/ethnicity, we also see that (compared to non-Hispanic White respondents) non-Hispanic Black respondents experience a 28% increase in the odds of consenting (OR = 1.28, p < 0.001) while non-Hispanic Asian respondents experience a 25% decrease in the odds of consenting (OR = 0.75, p < 0.001) – suggesting that there may be racial/ethnic differences in who opts into receiving text messages. We also observe statistically significant associations by respondent type, with irregular responders experiencing a 62% decrease (OR = 0.38, p < 0.001) and replenishment sample members experiencing an 11% increase (OR = 1.11, p < 0.05) in the odds of consenting to receive text messages – compared to regular responders who were already enrolled in the panel. Lastly, we observe several isolated statistically significant coefficients for marital status and region. More specifically, respondents who are widowed (compared to those who are now married) experience a 43% increase in the odds of consenting (OR = 1.43, p < 0.001) and respondents from the Northeast (compared to respondents from the South) experience a 13% decrease in the odds of consenting (OR = 0.87, p < 0.05). However, we again need to be mindful of sample size (particularly for widowed respondents) and statistical power before we generalize from these findings – particularly given the lack of empirical support in the broader literature for theorizing differences by marital status and region. In brief, we do find evidence of demographic differences in who is consenting to receive text messages, with race/ethnicity, family income, education level, age, respondent type, marital status, and region all being statistically significantly associated with the odds of consenting to receive text messages (as outlined above).

23 U.S. Census Bureau 6. DISCUSSION This paper aimed to answer four research questions using data from the Census Household Panel (i.e. a national panel survey): (1) How do text message reminders contribute to response?; (2) Who is clicking through on the text message invites versus the email invites?; (3) What are the consent rates for text messaging?; (3) What are the consent rates for receiving text messages?; and (4) How do consent rates differ by respondent characteristics? Looking at how text message reminders contribute to survey response (RQ1), we observe rapid initial response when text message invitations are sent – consistent with prior literature. We also see that response declines sharply as the number of hours since text messages are sent increases. These findings suggest that text message invitations contribute to survey response by bolstering initial response rates in the hours immediately following receipt of these text messages. This paper contributes to the available literature by quantitatively examining and documenting demographic differences in the likelihood of clicking on or accessing a survey through text invitation (as opposed to email) (RQ2). More specifically, this study documents demographic differences by age, race/ethnicity, education level, family income, and respondent type in the propensity of panelists to access Topical 7 of the CHP through a text message invitation. In sum, these findings suggest that certain sociodemographic characteristics are associated with greater propensity of panelists to click on text links as opposed to email links (and vice versa). This paper also quantitatively documents consent rates for receiving text messages among enrolled panelists (RQ3). Looking at this paper’s findings, we observe text message consent rates for Topical 7 of the CHP that are comparable to the existing literature (i.e. ~50%). Further, this paper quantitively examines and documents how these consent rates differ by respondents’ characteristics (RQ4). Consistent with the available literature, we find evidence of demographic differences in consent behavior (McGeeney and Yan 2016; Spiegelman and Zotti 2021; Horwitz et al. 2024). More specifically, this paper’s findings corroborate documented differences by race/ethnicity, age, and income. We also find novel differences by educational attainment, marital status, region, past response behaviors (e.g., regular vs. irregular responders), and survey language. However, while past research found no significant differences by select demographics (i.e. age, sex, education) in providing phone numbers for consenting to text messages (de Bruijne and Wijnant 2014), this study finds evidence of demographic differences in providing phone numbers for consenting to receive text messages. There are several limitations that should be considered when evaluating the results from this research. First, all analyses presented are observational and exploratory in nature. Consequently, we cannot speak to causal relationships. Additionally, the data used for this paper come from a panel survey. Panelists may differ from other survey respondents in non- panel surveys in ways that are consequential for findings on text messaging as a contact strategy. Lastly, consenting to receive text messages does not necessarily mean that

24 U.S. Census Bureau respondents will receive text messages. For example, text message recipients can block or unsubscribe from receiving these messages that they previously consented to receive. Consistent with this limitation, prior research has shown that some demographic groups are more likely to block numbers (Christian et al. 2024). Findings from this study indicate that text message invites were responsible for a substantial portion of responses. Compared to some contact modes, such as mail or interviewer- administered follow-up, it remains to be a relatively low-cost contact mode. This paper’s findings suggest that the use of text messages as a contact strategy is advantageous for reaching certain demographic groups and is a promising tool for national data collection efforts to bolster initial survey response. Future work may consider evaluating the use of text messages via an experimental design to investigate not only their effectiveness in encouraging response, but also the best time and day to contact potential respondents. In addition, further evaluation could examine the impact of text message invitations (and response to text message invites) by evaluating the data quality of responses to text message links and the impacts of device types that are used. 7.
